1. 1865: The End of the Civil War

1The end came in early spring 1865. General Robert E. Lee knew his tired Confederate army could do no more. He would rather die a thousand deaths than surrender, but he saw no choice. On April 9, he met General Ulysses S. Grant at a home in Appomattox Court House, Virginia. Grant wore an old muddy uniform, and the two generals ended the war. Lincoln had offered Lee command of the Union armies, but Lee would not fight his state of Virginia. The government took Lee's estate, Arlington, across the Potomac from Washington, D.C. Those grounds became Arlington National Cemetery.

2The North and South were already divided before the Civil War, and slavery was one important difference. By 1804, all Northern states had outlawed slavery, while the South's cotton economy used enslaved labor. By the mid-1800s, nearly four million Black people were enslaved in the South, mostly on cotton plantations. Enslaved families could be separated by their enslavers at any time. Northern abolitionists tried to end slavery, but the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 required free states to return people who escaped. The nation expanded west into land forcibly taken from Native peoples, and those territories became states. Congress had to decide whether those states would allow slavery. The South wanted a balance of slave states and free states so it would not be outnumbered in Congress.

3The country reached a breaking point in the election of November 1860. Abraham Lincoln, of the antislavery Republican Party, became president. The South feared his government would end slavery and destroy its economy. Seven Southern states seceded and formed the Confederate States of America in February 1861. War began on April 12, 1861, at a Union fort in Charleston, South Carolina, and four more states joined the Confederacy. Lincoln's generals failed him at first, but a Union victory in 1862 let him issue the Emancipation Proclamation. Lincoln's first goal was to save the Union, but he now planned to end slavery for good. Frederick Douglass said the proclamation liberated everybody, yet freedom and equality were still a long road.

4The Emancipation Proclamation freed enslaved people only in Confederate areas not yet under Union control. It redefined the war as a crusade against slavery, and nearly 200,000 Black Americans fought for the North. Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment in January 1865, ending slavery except as punishment for crime. Lincoln won reelection in 1864 and continued the war to save the Union and end slavery. Grant and Sherman sought to end the war quickly, and Sherman burned much of Atlanta. His men marched across Georgia, tore up rail lines, destroyed bridges, and set fire to homes. Susan Baker King Taylor was born enslaved in Georgia in 1848. She taught school at fourteen. She nursed soldiers.

5Harriet Tubman was born enslaved in Maryland and escaped North at age twenty-seven. She helped family members and dozens of others reach freedom, and she served the Union as cook, nurse, scout, and spy. She led an armed raid in South Carolina that liberated more than seven hundred enslaved people. Grant proved himself in the western campaigns, took command in March 1864, and later became the eighteenth president. At Cold Harbor in mid-1864, about seven thousand Union soldiers became casualties in twenty minutes. Lee fled Petersburg before dawn on April 3, 1865, after Grant had trapped him in trenches. Grant let Confederate soldiers go home with horses and mules and sent food because they were nearly starving. Jefferson Davis was captured on May 10 and spent two years in prison, and other Southern forces soon surrendered.

6On April 14, 1865, John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln in the head at Ford's Theatre in Washington, D.C. Lincoln died the next morning, and Booth, who opposed abolition, was later shot at a farm in Virginia. The plot also targeted Vice President Andrew Johnson and Secretary William Seward, who received serious knife wounds. Four men were found guilty and hanged, and Lincoln's funeral train carried his body home to Illinois. By December 6, 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment was ratified, and two more amendments soon gave civil rights and voting rights. In 1870, Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black American elected to the U.S. Senate. After Reconstruction ended in 1877, Black codes and Jim Crow laws enforced segregation until the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

7The Civil War established that the United States is an indivisible nation. States do not have the right to secede from the Union. The nation has seen other times of great strain, and Americans remain divided in many ways. Yet we remain one nation, the United States of America. Lincoln was elected on November 6, 1860, and South Carolina, first of eleven states, seceded on December 20, 1860. War began on April 12, 1861, and Tennessee seceded on June 8, 1861. The Emancipation Proclamation came on January 1, 1863. Lee surrendered on April 9, 1865.

2. A Fish That Strikes with Electricity

1A legendary shocker opens this book, from old reports to newer science. The animal is shown to be a fish. Its electricity is explained. A stunning attack is described. A warning says where not to swim. A last question asks if the animal could supply energy in the future. Special words close the pages. The year 1800 found the German naturalist Alexander Humboldt hunting electric eels. The search was in the land now called Venezuela. He believed the eels, and the shocks they make, could help his work. Catching some alive had to come first. Electricity as a force was poorly understood then. Mysteries about that force might be solved with living eels. Bare hands were too dangerous, and Humboldt knew it. Severe pain through a whole body can follow a shock. Local fishermen were asked for help. Five years of his life, from 1799 to 1804, were spent exploring South America. The eel hunt was one piece of that journey. Living animals were what he needed. Pain from a shock was already known. The cause of the force was still unclear. Fishermen who knew the water could bring him close enough to learn. The five-year journey covered a wide part of South America. Eels were not the only thing he studied, but their shocks were a special prize. A living eel could be tested. A dead story could not. Pain was the warning that kept his own hands off the animals. Help from local people was the safe path he chose.

2Humboldt watched the fishermen guide about thirty horses into a pond. The pond was murky and shallow. His description says what followed. Eels as thick as snakes rose out of the water. Hundreds of shocks hit the horses. Five eels could be caught only after that. Study of the eels taught Humboldt a great deal. A picture drawn from his writing shows the horse method. Horses stand in the pond while eels rise, and the power of the animals is clear. Modern gear that would have made the catch safer was not his to use. Scientists came to know his horse-fishing account widely. Doubt lasted a long time. Some thought the tale was stretched, the way fish stories often are. A scientist confirmed a key point only in recent years. Eels do rise from the water to protect themselves, matching what Humboldt saw. The body is long and shaped like a tube. Color is gray-brown. Yellow or orange often shows under the head and on the throat. Catfish are closer relatives than other eels are. The shape still looks more like an eel. Knifefish is the common name of their scientific order. Every knifefish can use electricity to some degree. Length can reach 2.1 to 2.75 meters, or 7 to 9 feet. Weight can reach 20 to 22 kilograms, or 44 to 48.5 pounds. Thickness can match an average adult human thigh. Color is much the same for males and females. Size is much the same too. Telling the sexes apart can be hard for scientists. Electrophorus electricus is the scientific name. The animal type is fish. Fish, crustaceans, and amphibians are the diet.

3Air is breathed through the mouth, which sets electric eels apart from most other fish. Gills are present, as in other fish. Breathing out is mostly what those gills do. The mouth opens at the surface. Special organs in the mouth take oxygen from the air into the body. Used air leaves through the mouth and the gills. A breath of air is needed every few minutes. Trapping an eel underwater can drown it. Fins are present, as in most other fish. Small fins sit on either side of the head. One long fin runs along the belly. That belly fin stretches the length of the body. A backbone also runs the full length and helps the eel move. Swimming uses an S-shape wave of the belly fin. Slow movement is the usual pace. An attack is when the pace quickens. A cut-off tail can grow back. Worms can regrow parts as well. Sea stars can. Certain lizards can. The mouth breath is not optional. A few minutes is the longest usual wait between breaths of air. Gills do not do the main job of taking air in. They help send used air out. Surface visits are therefore constant. Fins on the head are small. The belly fin is the long one, and the S-shaped wave is the swimming stroke. Speed stays low until an attack starts. A lost tail is not a permanent loss, because that part can return. Worms, sea stars, and some lizards share a similar power to replace a missing part.

4Electricity is what sets an electric eel apart from other fish. No fish on Earth is more electric. Protection is one known use of the power. Finding the way, or navigating, is another. Hunting is another. Prey can be stunned or killed. Bioelectricity is the tool. Electric currents acting inside a body are what bioelectricity means. Weaker electrical skills show up in other fish. Other knifefish have them. Some skates, rays, and catfish have them. Navigation, communication, or self-protection can be the use. None of those fish matches the attack shock of an electric eel. Headaches once brought a risky treatment from ancient Greeks and Romans. A live electric ray was held to a person's forehead. Numbness in humans can follow a ray's shock, so the treatment might have helped. This is not something to try at home. The electric ray, the clearnose skate, and the electric catfish are other electric fish. Three electric organs fill most of the inside of an electric eel. Their names are the main organ, Hunter's organ, and Sachs' organ. Shocking power comes from these organs. They begin just behind the head. They continue down the back. They run along both sides into the tail. Two-thirds of the body is electric organ. Shocks leave the body from these organs. A battery with a positive end and a negative end is a fair comparison. The head is the positive end. The tail is the negative end. Curling the body around prey can make the shock stronger. Head and tail have to touch for that boost.

5Prey can be hit with as many as 650 volts from the electric organs. Small animals can be killed by that. Large animals can be stunned. Water within 8.5 meters, or 28 feet, carries a shock that can be felt. A typical wall socket in the United States is already dangerous to people. Five times the volts of that socket is what an eel can produce. Their own shocks do not harm them. The reason is not settled. Size of the eel compared with size of the prey might matter. Speed of the shock moving away from the body might matter. Inner structures that are not fully understood might matter too. Electrocytes are known. They are special cells inside the electric organs, and they help create the shock. Long rows are how the electrocytes line up. Each one gives a tiny shock when bioelectricity is used. The tiny shocks come at nearly the same moment. Stacking the cells and timing the shocks together makes the tiny shocks larger. One big stunning zap is the result. Prey must be found before that zap. Murky water is home. Eyesight is poor. Night is when they are most active. Eyes are not the hunting tool. Bioelectricity is. Bats and owls locate prey from sound that bounces off objects. Electricity gives eels a similar skill. About fifty low-volt pulses go out every second. A pulse is a beat of electricity that repeats. Plants, animals, and nearby objects break into those pulses. The breaks reveal what is around the eel. A short burst follows when prey seems close. Two or three high-volt pulses make that burst. Muscles clench because of the shocks. Muscles twitch even though the animal does not choose to move. Exact location of the prey shows up in that movement. A high-volt shock comes next. Twitching stops. Sometimes the prey dies. The eel moves fast. Prey is sucked through the mouth straight into the stomach. Recovery and escape do not have time to happen. Small fish, crustaceans, and amphibians are the usual food of adults. Worms, insect larvae, and small fish are the usual food of the young.

6Top predators is the rank of electric eels. They are common where they live. Muddy or sandy rivers that move slowly are the usual places. The Amazon River holds them. The Orinoco River holds them. Tributaries of both rivers in northern South America hold them. The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean border that continent. Swamps, creeks, and ponds can hold them too. Lake edges in tropical plains or forests can hold them. Low-oxygen water is survivable because they breathe air. Hours out of water are possible if the skin stays wet. Mating mostly happens in small ponds. Males make nests from bubbles of their saliva. Hundreds of eggs are laid in the bubbles by females. Males guard the nests. They guard the babies after hatching until the young are about 10 centimeters long, or 3.9 inches. Self-defense must start then. Shocks from the young are weaker than adult shocks. Animals that will risk a bite threaten the young. Crocodiles are one threat before the eels grow. Black caimans are crocodile relatives. Few predators will risk eating an electric eel, and black caimans are among those few. Slow rivers with mud or sand bottoms are the common home. Northern South America is the region, along the Amazon, the Orinoco, and the streams that feed them. Air breathing lets an eel stay in water that holds little oxygen. Wet skin is enough for hours on land. Bubble nests in small ponds are where most mating happens. Males both build the bubbles and guard what hatches. At about 10 centimeters, the young must shock for themselves, though the shock is weaker than an adult's.

7More is known about electric eels now than Humboldt knew. Learning is not finished. Electrocytes are being studied at Yale University as a model. The hope is cells that could stand in for batteries inside medical devices. A pacemaker is one device. It keeps a human heart beating. Chemicals inside a pacemaker battery could poison a patient if the device broke. A safer battery is the goal, one that will not harm the inside of a body. A battery that does not run out of power is the other goal. A line Humboldt set down over two centuries ago still fits. He wrote that people remained a long way from knowing every secret of how fishes act through electricity. The next secret these eels will open is still unknown. Words from this account are gathered here. To amplify is to increase amount, strength, or importance. Electric means charged, powered, or producing energy from moving particles that carry charge. Electric currents are electric charge moving through matter. Immune means shielded from something, or able to resist it. Internal means inside, or happening on the inside. To navigate is to find a way across a long distance, or to steer toward a place. Organs are body parts with set jobs, such as kidneys or lungs. Shocks are sharp jolts felt when electric current touches a body or passes through it. To stun is to knock a creature out, or into a daze. Top predators stand at the top of a food chain, where no other animal eats them. Tributaries are rivers or streams that join a larger river. Volts measure the force that starts an electric current moving.

3. A Living Sea of Grass

1Sections of this book follow. A Sea Made of Grass. Three Prairie Kinds in North America. Why Fire Matters. How the Prairie Works Together. Keeping Prairies Alive. Plants You Can Find. Animals You Can Find. Words and Topics. A question opens the topic. Picture a ship with open sea in every direction. Or picture a boat with a large lake stretching all around. Every direction shows water. Now picture a different sea. This one is grass. Waves of green surround you. Gold is there. Brown is there. Reddish grass is there. Flowers of many colors run as far as sight can go. Hundreds of species of plants live in this grassy sea. Hundreds of animal species live there too. Birds of different kinds fly overhead. Some swoop. Some dive. Their prey spends most of life hidden in the grasses. The land is flat, or it rolls gently. Names change by continent. South American grasslands are called pampas. Asian grasslands are called steppes. South African grasslands are called veld.

2A large natural grassland is not the turf in a yard. Yard turf is mostly one color. It stands about 2 inches tall. Little hides there beyond insects. Grasslands are not all the same. They grow in North America and in South America. They grow in Europe and in Asia. They grow in Africa and in Australia. Every continent has them except Antarctica. Rainfall sets the pattern. Grasslands usually grow where rain is too much for a desert. The same places have too little rain for a forest. Grasses, of course, are the main plants. Not every grass is the same grass. Hundreds of species fill the world's grasslands. Most share one trait. They are tough. They are hardy. Fire can be survived. Heat can be survived. Freezing can be survived. Drought can be survived. Grazing can be survived. What else could live through all of that? Roots grow deep underground. Water is found there. Nutrients are taken in there. Stems and leaves above ground may die. Fire can burn them. Animals can eat them. New plants can still rise from those roots. A note on size: More than 140 million acres of North America once lay under tallgrass prairie. That area is 56.7 million hectares. About 10 percent of it remains. A map shows the old area of each prairie type. Three Prairie Kinds in North America. Prairies is the name used for grasslands of North America. Rainfall amount makes each prairie different. Soil type makes each one different too. Three main types exist. Tallgrass is one. Mixed-grass is one. Shortgrass is one. The main difference is easy to guess. Height of the grasses is the answer.

3Travel starts in the east of North America's prairie region. The direction is west, the way many European settlers went in the 1800s. Tallgrass prairie comes first. Much of Illinois is included. Iowa is included. Minnesota is included. North Dakota and South Dakota are included. Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas are included. Yearly rain is 30 to 40 inches. That is 76 to 102 centimeters. Some grasses there grow taller than an average human. Big bluestem is one. Indian grass is one. Height reaches 8 feet or more. That is 2.4 meters. Roots can go even deeper, to 9 feet. That is 2.7 meters. Soil in a tallgrass prairie is deeper than soil in other prairie kinds. It is darker. It is richer in nutrients. Walking through on foot would make it easy to get lost. A photo shows Pembina Trail Preserve in Minnesota. Westward travel reaches mixed-grass prairie. Parts of North Dakota and South Dakota hold it. Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas hold parts of it too. Yearly rain is between 15 and 25 inches. That is 38 to 64 centimeters. Little bluestem grows here. Sideoats grama grows here. Height falls between 2 and 3 feet. That is 61 to 91 centimeters. Soil is usually dark brown. A photo shows mixed-grass native prairie in South Dakota. East of the Rocky Mountains is where shortgrass prairie sits. Yearly rain is only about 10 inches. That is 25 centimeters. The prairie spreads onward from there. A photo shows shortgrass prairie in Montana.

4States in this shortgrass region include Montana. Wyoming is included. Colorado is included. New Mexico is included. Texas is included. Little rain falls because the mountains make a rain shadow. Warm, dry winds blow down from the mountains and dry the land. Most grasses here grow between 8 and 18 inches tall. That is 20 to 46 centimeters. Buffalo grass is one example. Bunch grass is another. Roots reach about 3 feet deep. That is 91 centimeters. The soil is light brown. A chart title mentions prairie plants and uses feet as the measure. People who manage prairies start fires on purpose. The fires are called controlled burns. Trees and shrubs are kept from growing. Why Fire Matters. Most things cannot live through fire. A prairie can. A prairie grows stronger because of fire. Deep roots are the reason. New stems grow from those roots with ease. Flames in a fire may pass 400 degrees Fahrenheit. That is 204 degrees Celsius. Underground, the temperature rises only a few degrees. Once the fire stops, roots quickly send up new stems. Young trees on the prairie face a different fate. Shrubs do too. Flames will probably kill them. Without fires, those trees and shrubs would keep growing. The prairie would become a forest.

5Until the 1800s, Lightning hit the ground and started prairie fires. Fires were also set by Native American people. The Sioux did. The Pawnee did. The Cheyenne did. A ring of fire was sometimes set around bison. Buffalo is another name for those animals. The herd was forced to run past one chosen spot. Hunters killed the bison there. Food came from the animals. Clothing came from them. Shelter came from them. Burning had another purpose. Burnt plant material decomposed and added nutrients to the soil. Americans whose ancestors came from Europe entered the prairie region during the 1800s. Putting fires out was their usual choice. Danger was what they saw. Because of that choice, many prairie places became forests. A note on herds: millions of bison once lived in huge groups on the prairies. New settlers did not want the animals where farms and towns would rise. The killing was huge. Bison did not make a hard target. Flight was not their response. Circles formed around the young so the young stayed protected. About 500 bison were all that were left when 1890 arrived. Some people then began breeding the survivors. Zoos held some. Ranches held some. Today about 200,000 bison live in protected areas. Yellowstone National Park is one of those places. How the Prairie Works Together. Plants, animals, and nonliving things all interact. Fire is included. Together they make the prairie ecosystem. Six main parts form it. The Sun is part one. Producers are part two. Primary consumers are part three. Secondary consumers are part four. Decomposers are part five. Nonliving substances are part six. Light and heat from the Sun supply energy for everything else. That energy flows through the whole system. Producers are the grasses and the other plants. They build their own food. Sun energy is used. Water is used. The air supplies carbon dioxide gas, and that is used too. Nutrients from the soil are used. Primary consumers eat the plants. Jackrabbits are an example. They eat grasses and clover. Herbivores is another name for these animals. Nutrients and energy come straight from plants. Secondary consumers eat meat. Carnivores is their other name. They eat the animals that eat plants. A fox that eats jackrabbits is an example. A jackrabbit is pictured.

6Prairie potholes are a special case. Some prairie areas hold water for part of the year, or for all of it. Those areas are prairie wetlands. If the water lasts only part of the year, the name is prairie pothole. Ducks rest there. Other birds rest there. They also breed there. These birds migrate, which means they travel long distances in spring and in fall. Rainwater is taken in by prairie potholes, the way a sponge takes water in. Flooding is reduced. Decomposers are organisms in the ecosystem. Dead plants and dead animals are broken down. Chemical substances left in the soil are the result. Bacteria are included. Fungi are included. Mushrooms are a kind of fungus. Nutrients form from those chemical substances. Plants use the nutrients to grow. These chemical substances and water are the parts of the ecosystem that are not alive. Keeping Prairies Alive. North America has little natural prairie left. Most were changed into farms long ago. Cities replaced others. Some places still let you sense what early settlers saw. They saw a sea of grass. Prairie preserves are those places. Scientists work there. Volunteers work there. People like you can join. The aim is to restore prairies to a natural condition. A state department of natural resources can tell you whether a prairie is near you. Ask if any task needs a volunteer. Seed collecting is one task. Bird counting is another. Few lessons about North America's great grasslands are better than these tasks. A photo shows cord grass seeds gathered so the prairie could be restored. A note on deep time: where prairies stand today, a warm, shallow ocean once lay. The span runs from about 440 million years ago back no farther than about 410 million years ago. Fossils tell scientists this. The region also holds further traces of sea animals from that ancient time.

7Plants You Can Find. A few examples follow. Grasses come first. On the tallgrass prairie, few grasses stand taller than big bluestem. Height reaches 8 feet or more. That is 2.4 meters. Early summer is when new shoots appear, and only then is the color blue. Red shades come afterward. Brown shades come too. Long clusters hold the flowers. Those hairy clusters are called spikelettes. A bird's foot has three toes in front. The clusters copy that shape. Extra names follow from that shape. Turkeyfoot is one. Beardgrass is one. Drier ground suits little bluestem better than it suits big bluestem, the larger relative. Height can reach about 4 feet. That is 1.2 meters. Short hairy clusters, called spikelettes, hold the flowers. The stem tops arrange those clusters in a zigzag. Seed heads look fluffy. Thin stalks carry the flowers of sideoats grama, all hanging toward one side. Usual height is 32 inches. That is 81 centimeters. Mixed-grass prairies hold it. Shortgrass prairies hold it too. This grama grass, and other types, were important forage. Large bison herds of earlier times grazed on them. A reddish tint on the prairie comes from sideoats grama flowers. Bison also relied on buffalo grass as forage. Height is about 6 inches. That is 15 centimeters. In the 1800s, settlers cut slabs of sod formed by this grass. They used the slabs like bricks to build houses. A lawn in central Texas would suit buffalo grass well.

8Other plants come next. Composites: The composite family includes a large share of prairie plants. Sunflower is another name for that family. Each large flower is really many tiny flowers. Tiny flowers in the center are called disk flowers. A ring of other flowers surrounds them. Those are called ray flowers. Blazing stars are composites. Bright pink flowers appear. Red flowers appear. Purple flowers appear. Colorful shooting stars are what they resemble. Large leaves mark the compass plant, and it too is a composite. Edges of those leaves always point north and south. Goldenrods carry bright yellow clusters of flowers. Late summer brings them. Fall brings them too. Legumes: The legume family includes a large share of prairie plants. Pea is another name for that family. Flowers on these plants have complicated shapes. Say the family name leh-GYOOMZ. Wild indigo is one picture subject. Clovers of several kinds are prairie legumes. Flower colors include white, yellow, red, and purple. Wild indigos are included too. Their flowers can be white or cream-colored. Stems of wild indigos hold a blue dye. Early settlers used that dye to color clothing. Animals You Can Find. A wide variety lives on prairies. A few examples follow. Grouse are brown birds that look like chickens. They live on the prairie ground. Seeds are on the menu. Leaves are eaten. Grains are eaten. Berries, buds, and flowers are eaten too. A male who wants a female dances. He makes cooing sounds. His neck carries a purple sac. It swells until it looks like a balloon. Flocks of grouse are called coveys. A sharp-tailed grouse is shown proving he fits his name. Snakes include a large prairie reptile, the bullsnake. It is brownish. Length can reach 8 feet. That is 2.4 meters. It slithers through the grass. Rodents are food. Birds are food. Eggs are food. A loud hiss is part of its warning. The prairie kingsnake lives here too. So does the massasauga. Timber rattlesnake is another name for it. The fox snake is included. A bullsnake hisses loudly. The hiss warns others to stay away.

9Western prairies are home to prairie dogs. Dogs they are not. Barking is the doglike habit of these rodents. Towns are their groups. Hundreds of animals share one town. Large systems of underground burrows are dug. Hawks send them running to hide. Coyotes do too. Other enemies do too. Burrows can be 16 feet deep. That is 5 meters. Dirt mounds ring the entrance holes. Daytime hunters overhead include several kinds of hawks. They search for rodents, for songbirds, and for other prey. At night, owls take over that hunting role. The northern harrier is also called the marsh hawk. It stands about 2 feet tall. That is 61 centimeters. Hunting flight glides low over the ground. The call is kee kee kee. Speed can reach 40 miles an hour. That is 64 kilometers an hour. Chicks share a prairie nest with an adult hawk. Coyotes are sometimes called prairie wolves. Size is about that of a medium-sized dog. Usual weight is between 20 and 50 pounds. That is 9 to 23 kilograms. Rodents are eaten. Rabbits are eaten. Dead animals are eaten. Fruit is eaten. Howls sound spooky. Night is when they can be heard. A coyote mother is shown with a squirrel she has caught. Coyotes outweigh foxes. Usual weight is between 8 and 15 pounds. That is 4 to 7 kilograms. Like coyotes, foxes may turn almost any catch into a meal. Gray foxes live on prairies. Red foxes live there too. North America has few foxes smaller than the swift fox.

10No animal in North America outruns the pronghorn antelope. It is a long-legged mammal. It eats plants. Home is the shortgrass prairie. Running speed can reach 60 miles an hour. That is 96 kilometers an hour. Most highways set a lower speed limit. Shoulder height is about 40 inches. That is 102 centimeters. Males have two black horns. Hooklike prongs mark those horns. A photo shows a female pronghorn on the left and a male on the right. Other animals pictured include a gray fox, a fox snake, a massasauga, and a northern harrier. Preserves of tallgrass prairie include these places. Flint Hills National Wildlife Refuge stands with Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve in Kansas. The preserve named Goose Lake Prairie stands in Illinois. It is a state natural area. Living Prairie Museum is in Manitoba, Canada. Tewaukon National Wildlife Refuge is in North Dakota. Waubay National Wildlife Refuge is in South Dakota. Preserves of shortgrass and mixed-grass prairie include these places. Caddo National Grassland and Lyndon B. Johnson National Grassland are in Texas. Comanche National Grassland is in Colorado. National Bison Range is in Montana. Prince Albert National Park is in Saskatchewan, Canada. Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge is in Oklahoma.

11Words to Know. Bacteria are organisms of one cell. Some of them cause infections and disease. Fungi are small organisms. They grow on material that once was living, and they make spores. Burrows are holes or tunnels. An animal digs them in the ground and uses them as shelter. Grazing means animals feed on field grass. Animals that eat only plants are herbivores. Plants are their only food. Carnivores are animals. Meat is their only food. Interactions are the relationships that link living things with things that are not alive. A drought is a long stretch of time. Very little rain falls. An ecosystem is a biological community. Organisms live there together with their habitat. A mammal is warm-blooded. Hair or fur covers it. It nurses its young. Its babies are born live. Forage is food for animals that eat plants. Hay can be forage. Grain can be forage. Grass can be forage. Nutrients are substances in food or in soil. Organisms need them to live, to stay healthy, and to grow. Rodents are small mammals. Large gnawing teeth keep growing for the animal's whole life. A species is a group of animals. Members are similar. They can breed with one another. Topics include indigos, bacteria, legumes, and bamboo. Little bluestem and big bluestem are listed. The massasauga is listed. Bison and the northern harrier are listed. Blazing stars and prairie dogs are listed. Buffalo grass and the prairie kingsnake are listed. Carbon dioxide and preserves are listed. Clover is listed. Prairie types listed are mixed-grass, shortgrass, and tallgrass. The compass plant and the pronghorn antelope are listed. Composites and coyotes are listed. The Rocky Mountains are listed. The ecosystem and sideoats grama are listed. Fire, the fox snake, the fox, and soil are listed. Fungi and grouse are listed.

4. A Run Called Hope

1Reporters listen as Terry talks, and his parents stand beside him. The moment is the end of his run. A hard road starts. School, then college. A crash, then cancer. Still an athlete. The plan. Across Canada. Support grows. The worst news. The race continues. Words to know. A hard road starts. Spring of 1980 is when Terry Fox set off to run the length of Canada. The effort would be historic. The goal was bold. He wanted money that could help people find ways to treat cancer. He also wanted ways to cure it. Doctors had amputated his right leg when he was eighteen. A prosthetic leg let him run. It attached above the knee, on the residual limb. Day two of the journey covered 32 kilometers, or 20 miles. A blizzard was blowing. The wind was fierce and full of ice. His plan was the whole width of Canada. This single day was already brutal. More than 8,000 kilometers still lay ahead. That distance is 5,000 miles.

2A family photo shows them resting together. From the left, beside Terry, are his father Rolly, his brother Darrell, his mother Betty, and his sister Judith. Childhood was spent in big cities. Winnipeg was one. Vancouver was the other. He loved inventing sports. He loved games so complicated they could run for days. Projects, once started, got finished. He was persistent that way. A run the length of a nation could therefore look possible. It would still be a very long project. As a boy he loved baseball. He loved soccer. He loved riding a bike. His little brother Darrell often played along. So did his best friend, Doug Alward. Love of sport showed when he tried out for basketball in eighth grade. Practice lasted hours. Many sessions started early in the morning. Commitment and effort won him a place on the team. High school and after. By high school he was in games on a regular basis. In time the coach put him in the starting group. During the last year of high school, the school picked a top athlete. He and his buddy Doug shared that honor. Classrooms went well too. He graduated with grades of A and of B. College came next. The future job was unclear. Maybe he would teach gym. Basketball, he knew, had to continue. Simon Fraser University took him in during 1976. That school had the strongest team in British Columbia, the province where it sits. Focus and determination were his tools. He meant to make the roster and play basketball in college.

3When things broke. He did make the Simon Fraser team. Then life shifted. Freshman year brought a car crash. The month was November. Serious injury passed him by. Afterward his knee felt sore. He told no one. Basketball practice, he thought, explained the pain. Late winter changed that picture. He was limping badly. His mother took him to a doctor. The diagnosis was not the sore knee people expected. A rare cancer was the source of the leg pain. Its name is osteogenic sarcoma. Nobody knows the cause. It spreads fast. It can threaten life. What cancer is. The word covers related diseases. Body cells start growing with no control. Almost any site can be the start. Bone can. Soft tissue can. Blood can. Cancer cells may travel through the body. Lumps called tumors often form. Normal tissue is destroyed. Only one cause of death ranks higher than cancer worldwide. A diagram shows a tumor, a cancer cell, a healthy cell, and the way cancer cells double. His first feeling was anger. He was only eighteen. None of this matched his plans. Treatment started as he worked through those feelings. A hospital ward became his room. Surgeons amputated the right leg above the knee. Doctors hoped the cut would stop the cancer from moving through his body. Nothing guaranteed it would stay gone. After surgery he learned to walk on a prosthetic leg. Chemotherapy followed for months. His body weakened. His hair fell out. The drugs were treating the cancer even so. Other patients filled the hospital. Cancer treatment was their reason for being there as well. He saw that his days looked like theirs. He met a boy of ten named Greg Scott. Cancer had taken one of Greg's legs as well.

4Life as an athlete, still. Sports remained open to him. Play continued, with some changes in method. Summer 1977 made him a basketball player in a wheelchair. He trained hard, building strength the way he always had for sports he loved. Running came next. An artificial leg felt awkward at the start. He adjusted. His first race was a mini-marathon of 27 kilometers, or 17 miles. He finished last. Contentment stayed with him, because he had completed the distance. The plan takes shape. Like many people who survive cancer, he lived with a chance the disease would return. He designed a way to help the search for cures that would last. Different cancers would be included. He would run the full span of Canada. People would learn more about the disease. Money would be raised for research. At each stop he would ask for donations. A journey of 8,000 kilometers, or 5,000 miles, would feel daunting. That difficulty was part of the point. More attention meant more money. The route was planned with care. Marathon of Hope would be the name. Doug, his friend, would come along and drive a van. Terry's stride was a hop. Springs in the artificial leg could reset after every step.

5Running the country. Training covered more than 4,800 kilometers, or 3,000 miles. Then he was ready. April 12, 1980, opened the Marathon of Hope. The start was St. John's. That city is in Newfoundland, the province farthest east in Canada. From the first day the work was incredibly hard. Days ran long. Spring in the maritime provinces can still be freezing. At breaks, Terry and Doug crowded into the van. They cut oranges. They cut other snacks. Highways in the countryside were dangerous. Trucks at high speed nearly forced him off the pavement. Legs ached every day. Wind burned his skin quickly. Sun burned it too. Some towns found him exhausted, with nobody waiting and nobody giving. Other towns met him with warmth. Whole communities lined up to cheer. A picture shows him studying a map during a van break. Support widens. Four maritime provinces of Canada were behind him before Quebec began. Each day he covered about a marathon's distance. Every week left him exhausted. Spirits rose when Darrell, the younger brother, joined the trip. As the country passed slowly under his feet, the crowd of followers grew. Late June brought him into Ontario. Dozens of television stations were covering the run. Newspapers were covering it. Soon it was obvious that attention had widened. The whole nation seemed to be following, and Canada's prime minister was among them. In Toronto, thousands stood along the streets while he ran. Money for cancer research poured in. Toronto City Hall gave him a roaring welcome on July 11, 1980.

6A map traces the Marathon of Hope across Canada, with North America around it. The start is marked at St. John's on April 12, 1980. Newfoundland is on the route. So is Prince Edward Island, with Charlottetown. Nova Scotia is on it. Quebec is on it, including Montreal and Quebec City. Ontario is on it, including Ottawa, Toronto, and Thunder Bay. The finish mark reads September 1, 1980. The United States and Mexico appear beside Canada on the wider map. The worst news. On September 1 the run stopped without warning. By then he had covered 5,300 kilometers, or 3,300 miles. He had been feeling sick. He had been coughing. Chest pains had started. Doctors in Thunder Bay, Ontario, were his next stop. They found that the cancer had come back. He asked to take treatment and keep running. Doctors said no. The run he called the Marathon of Hope had to stop. He flew home for care. His death would shock people. It would sadden people across Canada and far beyond. A large crowd later filled his funeral in Vancouver. The race goes on. Eight further months of treatment followed. The cancer kept advancing. He died on June 28, 1981. A few days later the funeral was held in Vancouver. Hundreds of letters of condolence reached the family. Poems reached them. Gifts reached them. Hearts around the world had been touched. He never completed the cross-country run. Even so, the Marathon of Hope met his aims. Millions of people learned why more research must be funded. Treatments were the goal. Cures were the goal. His wish to end cancer did not stop when he died. Family members founded the Terry Fox Foundation in 1988. It still raises money for cancer research.

7Each year, people join Terry Fox runs. A run lasts one day. Participants collect money to fight cancer. Cities all over Canada host them. Countries as distant as New Zealand have hosted them. Zimbabwe has hosted them. To date, the sum raised has passed 800 million dollars. It has not stopped growing. No complete cure for every cancer has been found yet. Progress has still been huge. New treatments have lifted survival rates for different kinds of cancer. Donations from groups like his have mattered a great deal. The run taught people something large. One person can change the world. Runners in Stanley Park, in Vancouver, appear in a picture. They honor his memory. They raise money for research. Words to know. Amputated means cut off. Limping means walking unevenly, often because a leg or a foot is hurt. An athlete is a person trained for sports, games, or other tests of speed, strength, and skill. A marathon is a long running race of 26 miles, about 42 km. Chemotherapy uses chemicals as medicine. The usual aim is to destroy cells that are cancer. Maritime describes the sea, sailing, or jobs done on the water. A condolence offers comfort after a death among family or friends. Prosthetic describes an artificial stand-in for a body part that is gone. Research studies a subject in detail so that new facts can be learned. A diagnosis is the naming of an illness or an injury. A disease is an illness. A residual limb is the part of a limb still there after amputation.

5. A Voice for the Living World

1In 1945, Rachel Carson spent months reading research that came across her desk. She worked as a scientist and editor in chief for the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. It was her job to edit the department reports. Other biologists worried about DDT, a pesticide that killed mosquitoes and other pests. Wherever it was sprayed, birds and other wildlife were also dying. Tests raised concerns about long-term effects on humans, but officials ignored the reports. That July she asked Reader's Digest to print an article on DDT, but the magazine was not interested. Twelve years later DDT was used more than ever, and the famous author planned to protect nature by telling the truth.

2Exploring nature was among Rachel Louise Carson's earliest and happiest memories. Born in 1907, she grew up on a large homestead in western Pennsylvania as the youngest of three children. She and her mother, Maria, wandered their land and watched wildlife. Rachel loved to read, wrote picture books about animals, and published stories in a children's magazine. By age ten she knew she wanted to be a writer. Money was short, her father Robert struggled to keep a job, and Maria taught piano, did odd jobs, and sold china. In 1925 she enrolled at a nearby college for English, but a biology course changed her life and the professor became a lifelong friend. She switched to zoology, graduated with high honors in June 1929, and that summer first visited the ocean at Woods Hole in Massachusetts.

3There she studied marine creatures up close in their habitats during a summer of bliss among aquatic scientists. She later credited that time as inspiration for her work. She had already been accepted at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, for more study in zoology. Money problems continued, her parents moved in with her, and lab work made her the family's main support. In 1932 she completed her master's degree, but she had to quit her doctorate two years later for lack of money. Women ecologists often struggled for respect, yet they made great contributions to the environmental movement. Marjory Stoneman Douglas helped save Florida's Everglades, and Margaret Murie helped establish the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. Wangari Maathai won the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize, Jane Goodall studied wild chimpanzees in Tanzania, and Greta Thunberg inspired students to demand climate action.

4In 1936 Carson began part-time work in Washington, DC, at the future Fish and Wildlife Service, writing radio scripts about marine life. A year later she became an assistant aquatic biologist, and she later rose to editor in chief of all publications. She explained complex science so average readers could understand and enjoy it. She also wrote articles for extra cash, since her father had died in 1935 and she still supported her mother and other family. In 1941 she published Under the Sea Wind, a poetic and accurate book about life in the sea and along the shore. Critics praised it, but it sold poorly during World War II, from 1939 to 1945. The job sharpened her writing as she studied new research, and vacations with her mother took her to birds, tidal pools, and mud flats. In 1951 The Sea Around Us stayed on the New York Times best-seller list for eighty-six weeks and won the National Book Award.

5Her earnings let her leave the service in 1952 and write full-time. She built a cottage on the rugged coast of Maine, with the ocean right outside her door. She had many other subjects, and one would become her most important work. In 1966 the Rachel Carson National Wildlife Refuge was established near that summer cottage. It stretches 50 miles, or 80 kilometers, near Kennebunkport and protects wetlands for migratory birds and other wildlife. About three hundred thousand bird-watchers and nature lovers visit each year. After the war, atomic bombs, nuclear energy, and antibiotics made science seem bright, but DDT was the main weapon against insects. Trucks sprayed it over houses and gardens, aircraft dropped it on forests and fields, and officials said there was nothing to worry about.

6Salmon, butterflies, bees, and birds were among the many victims of DDT. By 1957 her doubts returned as biologists and naturalists reported dead birds, poisoned fish, and dying helpful insects. She collected evidence that pesticides and herbicides might cause serious illness in people, including cancer. She knew the proof had to be rock solid, because friends warned that huge chemical companies might destroy her reputation. She sent every chapter to experts to check the facts. In 1957 a niece died and Carson cared for a young great-nephew, her mother died the next year, and in 1960 Carson learned she had cancer. Surgery, treatments, and intense pain slowed the book. In September 1962 Silent Spring came out, stayed a best-seller for more than a year, and was translated into more than thirty languages.

7Carson did not call for a total ban on these chemicals. She urged the government to test them more carefully and regulate them more closely. She also asked readers to consider the long-term danger of poisoning the environment. Again she explained complex science in ways nonscientists could grasp. Chemical makers attacked her research and qualifications, some simply because she was a woman. They called her against business and a nature fanatic who would rather see people starve than use chemicals for food. She stayed calm in speeches and interviews, other scientists defended her, and she testified before a Senate subcommittee in June 1963. President John F Kennedy and other leaders pointed to Silent Spring, and that summer she made a last visit to her favorite cottage in Maine.

8Long before Silent Spring, a new insect killer appeared. In 1939 Swiss scientist Paul Müller developed DDT. It killed insects and seemed to spare other animals. It helped stop malaria and typhus. He won the Nobel Prize for that work. The chemical was used widely in the 1940s and 1950s. Biologists later found its poison built up in animal tissues. That process is called biomagnification. Bird eggs grew brittle. Some populations fell by more than 80 percent, including bald eagles. In one food chain, DDT passes from plankton to small fish, then to big fish, and then to an eagle. On land the buildup starts with plants. Silent Spring brought more study of these harms. In 1963 Carson said conservation has no end. She died the next year, but her vision lived on. The United States banned DDT in 1972. Bird populations rebounded after the ban. Her writing helped lead to clean air, wilderness, clean water, and endangered species laws. Eagle pairs rose from 417 to nearly 10,000.

9Carson's environmentalism grew out of her love of nature. She was fascinated by the beauty and science of ecosystems. Her life's work was sharing that joy, because she believed people would protect what they loved. She thought of humans as belonging to the natural world, not as its enemies. In 1961 she kept company with a cat at her home in Maine. Today wilderness areas and wildlife populations continue to shrink. Threats are greater than ever, including the global danger of climate change. At the same time, awareness and activism have grown, and Carson's determination, courage, and passion still make her a role model.

6. A Voice Named Ella Fitzgerald

1The parts of this book come in this order. One Night on Stage. The First Lady's Early Years. The Lady's Big Break. The Lady on Tour. The Lady Makes Her Mark. The Curtains Close. Glossary. Fitzgerald's career as a performer began at the Apollo Theater. One Night on Stage. Tellings of that evening mostly match. Called up to perform, Ella could not move. The light held her in place. Along one cheek, sweat began to run. Her gaze dropped. She wore boots made for work. Those boots felt heavy. Scuff marks covered them. Seats creaked as listeners grew impatient. A performance was what they had come to see. Nothing about this scared teen promised that any performance would start.

2Ralph Cooper was running the contest. Off to the side, he hissed a warning. His order was simple. His order was that she act. Frustration made his head shake. The show that night was called Amateur Night. Its stage was the Apollo. Harlem was the neighborhood around that theater. The city was New York. Cooper felt the whole evening sliding downward, and he blamed this girl. Ella then bent toward Benny Carter. A well-known band of his was playing behind every contestant. Cold air filled the room that night in 1934. Her request was the song Judy. Carter said yes. He called her kid. Dancing to a piece like that one seemed unlikely to him. He told her to choose it anyway. She moved once more to center stage. As the band began, she cleared her throat. Nerves had not left her. The opening note broke in her throat. Together the crowd moaned. Booing started. Shouts told her to get off. Her heartbeat raced. She feared it might burst. In one picture, Benny Carter holds his trumpet. Panic showed on her face, and he noticed. The players halted and waited. Thanks showed in the look she gave Benny. A long breath came next. Then she nodded. Music began a second time. Her eyes shut. Boos no longer reached her. Only one song stayed in her ears. It was the favorite of her mother. Memory carried her home to the kitchen. In that memory, her mother lived. Young Ella danced there while her mom's voice filled the room. The final note drifted away. Ella's eyes opened. Nobody in the seats was moving. She believed the song had failed them. Panic climbed through her throat. She spun, ready to run off. Clapping began with a single person. A second person joined. A third followed. All at once the Apollo roared with applause. Ella turned toward Benny. His news was happy. The crowd was hers. They were calling for another song. He wanted to know what she would offer next.

3No time remained for an answer. Carter turned from her. The band jumped into a new piece called The Object of My Affection. Ella stayed right with the beat. Her grin was wide enough to split her face. She sang once more. Years later, the reason stands out. During her lifetime, Grammy Awards came to Ella Fitzgerald 13 times. A title stuck to her. People call her the First Lady of Song. One photo catches her just a few years past that Apollo evening. The First Lady's Early Years. April 25, 1917, was her birth date. Ella Jane Fitzgerald was her full name. Newport News, Virginia, was the town of her birth. William was her father. Temperance was her mother. Friends shortened Temperance to Tempie. Not long after the birth, the parents went separate ways. Yonkers, New York, became the next home for Ella and her mother. Tempie later had a boyfriend named Joe Da Silva. The household included him. Part of Joe's work was driving people. Tempie's job was at a laundromat. Extra money came from food she prepared for events. A child arrived in 1923. They named her Frances. Across their whole lives, Ella and Frances stayed close. One photo shows Ella while she was still a girl. Third grade was when she chose a future. Professional dancing was the dream. Street corners became her stage, and passersby got a show. Singing mattered to her just as much. Classmates turned into friends when she copied famous singers in a lifelike way. One singer she loved to copy was Louis Armstrong. Another was Connee Boswell.

4Dancers knew the Savoy Ballroom as the place to be. Its doors stayed open for that kind of night until 1958. Then the ballroom closed. A bit later, Ella and a friend named Charles often slipped away. Harlem's Savoy was where they went. Newest dance steps got practiced there until the pair could do them cold. Age fifteen found Ella and Charles taking those routines into clubs. The clubs were spread through Yonkers. Money came to Ella for the dancing. She was a paid dancer. Tragedy arrived next. Life shifted hard in 1932. A heart attack killed Tempie, Ella's mother. Only a few months passed. Then a heart attack killed Joe as well. An aunt in Harlem took in Ella and Frances. Grades sank during those months. Day after day, she was missing from class. Officers who track students away from school caught her. Their work was to see that children showed up. Those authorities placed her at a reform school. Its name was the Riverdale Children's Association. Rigid rules there met her rebellion. Suspicion remains that teachers beat her. Abuse is part of that same suspicion. Autumn of 1934 was when she ran. Housing was something the teen did not have. Tips from songs and dances were how she tried to live. The stretch of Harlem where she worked had a nickname. People called it Black Broadway. Come the 1930s, Black residents were most of Harlem. Stages such as the Apollo hosted entertainers who were already known. Out on the sidewalk, lesser-known acts played for anyone walking by. A picture shows Harlem during the 1930s.

5Nightclubs in Harlem were filling with talent tryouts in those days. Ella sent her name to more than one contest. Organizers chose her for a special night at the Apollo. That night was for amateurs. Dollars in the prize purse totaled twenty-five. About five hundred dollars is what the same prize would be now. November 21, 1934, was the date. Seventeen was Ella's age. Fitzgerald learned her real calling on that night. Dancing was not it. Singing was. Love went both ways between her and the listeners. She left a saying behind her. The road ahead, she said, counts more than the road behind. Winning that amateur contest did not convince everyone. Some doubted she could last as a singer. Appearance was the likely cause. Plain clothes meant for work were what she wore. Boots were on her feet. Glamour of the kind people expect from a star was missing. Months had passed with no home, while she cared for herself. Different clothes were beyond her means. A poster promotes a show she did with Chick Webb and his orchestra. The Lady's Big Break. Chick Webb led a band and was still rising. At their first meeting he refused to hire Fitzgerald. A player from Webb's own band had brought her over. That player said he would leave the group if Webb would not listen to her. Webb backed down. A two-week job at the Savoy was the offer. She could sing with them there. Dislike from the crowd would end it. Pay would not follow her out.

6One detail is easy to miss. Age 21 brought Ella her earliest major hit. Chick Webb's orchestra was behind that record. Playfulness filled the tune. Wording came out of a nursery rhyme from the 1800s. A-Tisket, A-Tasket is the name of that rhyme. A photo catches Fitzgerald mid-song, with Chick Webb beside her. Crowds took to her at once. Affection grew inside the band as well, Webb included. Sis became their name for her. The Braddock Hotel is where they rented her a room. Clothes fit for a stage act came with help from some bandmates. Touring found her among the singers whose outfits drew the most notice. Inventing a look of her own became a joy. Records followed, made by Fitzgerald with the Webb orchestra. Decca was the company on the label. Several of those songs climbed all the way up the charts. Travel took the group around the country. Death came for Chick Webb in 1939. Leadership of the band passed to Fitzgerald. A split ended the band after three more years. World travel did not stop for her. The Lady on Tour. Moving from city to city was harsh for Black musicians, Fitzgerald among them. Racism met them often. One flight crew made her surrender a seat. White passengers took that seat. A booked show in Sydney, Australia, then fell through. Three days passed before any flight could carry her to Australia. Earlier years held a similar wound. She was aboard a train. Hours went by on her feet. Black riders were limited to one section, and that car was jammed. A free seat finally appeared. It sat in the section saved for white riders. She took it. Right away the conductor scolded her. He commanded her to leave. Outside a station in 1956, a photo shows a white officer of the police. He sets out a sign. Words on it reserve the waiting room for white people alone. Black passengers were not to share that room.

7An extraordinary voice let Fitzgerald do astonishing things. The Lady Makes Her Mark. Popularity still found her, even with the racism in her path. Jazz singing had few bigger names in the world. She also helped polish a fresh branch of that singing. Scat is the name for it. Orchestra instruments got copied by her voice alone. Made-up speech sounds joined that copying. Bo-dube-be is one of those sounds. Rebop is another. Many scat singers slip off pitch. She did not. Scales could rise or fall, and her tuning stayed exact. Musicians call this gift relative pitch. Hear any note, and she could judge how every other note sits beside it. The sung result stayed in tune each time. Perfect pitch is a narrower gift. It lets a person name one note after hearing it, then sing that note. Relative pitch serves a singer far more. Respect arrived from other headliners because of the art she gave to scat. Frank Sinatra was one of them. Bing Crosby was another. Nat King Cole stood with them. Louis Armstrong did too. Mel Torme was on that list as well. A private title came from Torme. He named her High Priestess of Song. Celebrity fans were part of her public. Marilyn Monroe, the actress, was among the keenest. Peggy Lee, the singer, was another. A photo places Fitzgerald with Monroe at a jazz gathering. Hollywood's Tiffany Club was the room. A second photo shows a duet with Frank Sinatra.

8Louis Armstrong and Fitzgerald share a studio picture. They are recording a song. Her album count passed 200 during her career. Phoebe Jacobs was on Fitzgerald's staff. Fame, Jacobs said, never pulled Fitzgerald away from ordinary life. She stayed grounded. One tale got told often. A television interview had brought both women to New York City. Hunger made Jacobs want a stop for food. She urged Fitzgerald to continue without her. Hunger had Fitzgerald too. A street seller's hot dog was all Jacobs planned to grab. Fitzgerald chose to come along. Mid-meal, a man approached. His comment was that the woman facing him matched Ella Fitzgerald. Eye to eye, she met his look. Her reply was calm. People said that to her constantly, she told him. Off she walked, the hot dog still held in one hand. Confidence and a grounded air show in a picture from 1961.

9Care for others ran deep in her. Time and money both went to children who had less at school and less at home. Day programs for children opened with her help. Fundraisers for children drew her again and again. Ray Brown was her second husband. Together they adopted a boy. Ray Brown Jr. was his name. Later life found her devoted to a granddaughter. Alice was that child's name. A picture seats Fitzgerald next to her son. Taking Requests. Guests at one private party got a question from her. Did anyone want a particular song? Rap was the request from a young man. Laughter rolled through the room. Her reply came right back. Word-play like that, she told him, had been hers since before his birth. Scatting started on the spot. Delight took the listeners. A photo shows the song she gave a cheerful crowd.

10Recognition followed the talent in her voice. The Curtains Close. Death came in 1996. Her age was 79. Sales of her records had passed 40 million. Carnegie Hall had presented her 26 times. Movies had included her. Guest spots on television shows had been numerous. Headline status at the Copacabana belonged to her before any other Black artist. That New York club was famous worldwide. America's president placed the National Medal of Arts in her hands. France offered a matching honor. People know it as Commander of Arts and Letters. Music doctorates of the honorary kind came from noted universities. Yale was one. Princeton was one. Dartmouth was one. Yonkers was the town that raised her, and she lost her mother while still young. Racism stood in the way. Sexism stood in the way. Classism stood in the way. She continued. Few artists have reached what she reached. Legend is the word that fits. Every age claimed her as a fan. Every race did too. Every background did too. Those fans remain. A 1988 photo catches her in performance.

11Glossary. Auditions are tryout performances. Actors give them. Musicians give them. Dancers give them. A compassionate person notices suffering. That person wants to help. Engagements are entertainment jobs. Each one lasts only a short time. Frustration is a heavy disappointment. It grows strongest when nothing you do can fix the problem. A gig is stage work. It does not stay for long. Impersonations copy another person. The copy may be a voice, a look, or a set of actions. The aim is to entertain. Improvised work is invented while it happens. Jazz keeps a strong rhythm. On top of that rhythm, players invent as they go. Petrified means deeply scared. Racism judges people by race. It treats some races as lesser. A reform school houses young people. Its aim is to change behavior that breaks the rules. Scat belongs to jazz singing. Nonsense syllables stand in for words. The voice copies an instrument.

7. A Water Road Across New York

1In the 1600s and 1700s, most European colonists stayed near the Atlantic coast. They lived no more than about 400 miles, or 640 kilometers, inland. The Appalachian Mountains rose as a huge barrier. They ran north to south for more than 1,500 miles, or 2,400 kilometers.

2In the early 1800s, Americans lived in states and territories. Many wanted the fertile, resource-rich land west of the mountains, though it belonged to Indigenous people. Settlers still wanted to colonize that land and ship goods across the mountains. They looked to Europe, where artificial canals were popular and efficient. The New York State Canal Commission planned a canal from Lake Erie, a Great Lake, to Albany, the state capital. From Albany, boats could take the Hudson River south to New York City and the Atlantic Ocean. The canal would link Buffalo, Syracuse, and New York City, and towns such as Rome, Lockport, and Little Falls would prosper. An early 1850s painting shows Daniel Boone leading settlers through a pass in the Appalachian Mountains.

3The canal would bring success to many New Yorkers but great suffering to the five Haudenosaunee Nations. They were also known as the Iroquois and were forced to move to reservations to clear the canal's path. The canal crossed land that first belonged to them, and their communities relied on it. DeWitt Clinton was elected governor in 1817 and promised jobs, money, and new settlers. Thomas Jefferson turned down federal funds, so Clinton used New York State tax money. Work began in 1817 on a canal 4 feet deep and 40 feet wide, with a 10-foot towpath for horses and mules. With no engineering schools in the United States, most engineers were self-taught. They started in the flattest middle, then dug down or added soil to keep a constant flow of water.

4Workers also built eighteen aqueducts to carry the canal over rivers and ravines. At eighty-three points they built locks, using new technology to raise or lower boats in hard places. A boat enters a lock through a gate, the water is raised or lowered, and the other gate opens when the levels match. Opponents called it Clinton's Folly and Clinton's Big Ditch, and it cost 7 million dollars, about 130 million in 2019. Clinton refused to run in 1822, people said the work would never end, but it finished in 1825 and he was re-elected governor. In October 1825 he led a festive first trip from Lake Erie to Albany, then along the Hudson to New York City. On November 4 he dumped a barrel of Lake Erie water into the Atlantic, a symbolic joining of the two waters. A tour boat can enter a lock to reach a lower part of the canal.

5Artwork from 1829 shows the Erie Canal passing through farmland. Travel from Albany to Buffalo once took two weeks, but the canal reduced it to five days. More settlers became farmers in present-day Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, and Illinois. It was easy and cheap to ship lumber, gravel, and crops east from the Midwest. The Midwest became known as America's breadbasket. Wheat exports grew from fourteen thousand bushels in 1826 to eight million in 1840. Settlers could also get stoves, nails, cloth, and other supplies made on the East Coast. Seven tons of wheat cost 700 dollars to ship before the canal and 70 dollars after, a difference of 630 dollars.

6Tourists traveled the canal for pleasure in packet boats where they could lounge, dine, and sleep. Horses and mules pulled the boats along the towpath at about 4 miles, or 6 kilometers, per hour. Passengers could get off for a stroll and catch up with their boat later. Travel cost four cents a mile, including tolls, meals, and a bed, and tolls helped repay building costs. In 1862 the canal was widened to 70 feet, or 21 meters, and deepened to 7 feet, or 2 meters. In the early 1900s a new, larger canal used parts of the original route for giant barges. By the 1950s, trains and trucks were faster and cheaper, so leisure boaters used the canal instead. Museums and learning sites entertain visitors today, and a 2009 tugboat pushed two barges on the widened canal.

7A view of the South Street docks in New York City comes from the 1870s. Between 1820 and 1850, the population of New York City grew to four times its size. The Erie Canal was a central reason for this growth. Before the canal, New York City was a smaller port than Baltimore, Philadelphia, and New Orleans. Today it is the largest city in the United States. The canal opened Indigenous land in the West to American settlers and changed the nation's landscape. Merchants could ship goods across the country cheaply and easily. It remains an exceptional feat of engineering and one of the most impactful large-scale projects of the nineteenth century.

8. Adaptive Sport and the Paralympic Games

1He Junquan is a swimmer from China. Say the name HU, then jin-CHEN. His Paralympic medals include nine gold, six silver, and six bronze. He has set several world records. All of this was done without arms. Beijing, China, in 2008 looked ready to yield him one more gold medal. He led the 50-meter backstroke final as he neared the last wall. The crowd was screaming. A reporter who was there put the excitement this way. Anyone present who had feet was up and using them. A short side note belongs here. A child who fell into a river was once saved by He Junquan. The child was in danger of drowning. His legs were what kept the boy from sinking. He used them to push the boy to safety. A photograph shows him competing at the 2008 Paralympic Games.

2The names Special Olympics and Paralympics can be confused. They are very different. Only athletes with intellectual disabilities may enter the Special Olympics. Age six is old enough to take part. Elite athletic competition is the focus of the Paralympics. The Special Olympics uses sport another way. The aim is to help every participant fulfill their potential, whatever their skill level. Washington State in 2016 is the setting of a photograph of Special Olympics participants. A swim race ends when a swimmer touches the final wall. He Junquan had to slow down. The only body part he could use to hit the wall was his head. That slowdown let Daniel Dias of Brazil tap the wall first. Dias reached it with an outstretched arm. He Junquan finished second. Silence fell on a stunned crowd. Dias had won the race. Junquan had won their hearts. At the medal presentation, a silver medal went around his neck. He accepted the medal with his teeth. He accepted the flowers with his teeth. A bow showed his respect. He had proved himself an amazing athlete. He had also proved himself a good sport. The Paralympic Games are about that spirit. Adaptive athletes are competitors who have one or more disabilities. The disabilities may be physical. They may be intellectual. Arms or legs are missing for some adaptive athletes. Others use a wheelchair. Others have limited vision. Many disabilities are not obvious, yet they affect life in important ways. A disability may have been present from birth. An injury or an illness may have changed that athlete's life instead. These competitors enjoy the contest. What their bodies can do is amazing. Desire plus hard training has let them compete at the highest level. From 1960 onward, adaptive athletes have entered the Paralympic Games. Ancient Greece is where the Olympic Games first took shape. Athletic contests there were held every four years. Those ancient contests stopped in the fifth century of the common era. The modern Olympic Games started again in 1896. About fifty years after that restart, the first Paralympics got underway. British war veterans with injuries to the spine were the first group in the program. The idea belonged to a British doctor, Sir Ludwig Guttmann. His name is said LOOD-wig GOOT-muhn.

3Doctor Guttmann wanted his competition to grow as famous as the Olympic Games. Worldwide, nations joined the Paralympic movement, and his hope came true. The first official Paralympic Games took place in 1960. The city was Rome, Italy. About four hundred athletes came. They represented twenty-three nations. Eight events were on the program. Archery was one. Fencing was one. Swimming was one. Basketball was one. The first Winter Paralympic Games came in 1976. The host was Sweden. Nordic skiing was among the winter events. Amputees could compete. Visually impaired athletes could compete. Both the summer Games and the winter Games have followed a four-year rhythm ever since. A change arrived in 2001. The city that hosts a Summer or Winter Olympic Games must also host the matching Paralympics. A side note tells more about Doctor Guttmann. He was Jewish, and Germany was his original home. Sixty other Jewish people were saved from certain death while he still lived in that country. German officers were told the patients could not leave, because he described them as too sick. Just before World War II started, he and his family left Germany. Nazi persecution was the reason. A portrait shows Ludwig Guttmann. Today's Paralympic Games welcome athletes in ten categories. The categories cover physical disabilities. They cover visual disabilities. They cover intellectual disabilities. Relative ability in the sport is what sorts athletes inside each category. Organizers group athletes whose disabilities affect performance to a similar degree. A swimmer with a spinal cord injury may share a race with swimmers who have cerebral palsy. Athletes with missing limbs can share that race. Team sports use a points system. Wheelchair basketball is one example. Disability determines the points assigned to each player. A team may put on the field only a group whose points stay at or under a maximum. Perfection is not what the classification system achieves. Mistakes are sometimes made. Fairness is the goal that keeps the International Paralympic Committee at work. A 2016 photograph shows Great Britain and Spain in a wheelchair basketball match.

4Many Paralympic events match events in the Olympic Games. Cycling is one shared event. Rowing is one. Swimming is one. Alpine skiing is one. Snowboarding is one. Other sports belong only to the Paralympic Games. Football 5-a-side is one of those. Goalball is one. Sitting volleyball is one. Para ice hockey is one. The unique events are worth a closer look. In sitting volleyball, a player must stay seated whenever the ball is hit. The net stands 1.15 meters high for men, which is 45 inches. For women it stands 1.05 meters high, which is 41 inches. Several groups of athletes may compete. They include athletes with spinal cord injuries. They include athletes with amputations. They include athletes with cerebral palsy. They include athletes with brain injuries. They include athletes who have had a stroke. A full list of Paralympic events splits by season. Summer events include judo and wheelchair fencing. They include powerlifting, archery, and wheelchair rugby. They include rowing, athletics, and wheelchair tennis. They include shooting and badminton. They include sitting volleyball and boccia. They include swimming and canoe. They include table tennis and cycling. They include taekwondo and equestrian. They include triathlon and football 5-a-side. They include wheelchair basketball and goalball. Winter events include Alpine skiing and biathlon. They include cross-country skiing and Para ice hockey. They include snowboard and wheelchair curling. Para ice hockey is played by athletes with physical disabilities in the lower body. Sticks drive a rubber puck into the other team's goal. Players do not wear ice skates. Each player sits on a sledge. One blade or two blades run beneath the sledge. Two sticks serve each player. The sticks handle the puck. They also push the player around the rink. The five-player form of football, also called soccer, is full of excitement. Every player except the goalies has a visual impairment. Outfield players wear blackout masks so the match stays fair. A noisemaking device inside the ball lets players find it by sound. The playing field has walls. Tackles occur. Fouls occur. Penalty kicks occur, as in other football. Sighted guides stand on the sidelines for each team. They shout instructions. Goalball was created specifically for Paralympians with visual disabilities. Events for those athletes show how many ways a contest can be adapted. Three players make up a goalball side. The aim is to send a big rubber ball into the other team's goal. Jingling bells inside the ball tell players where it is. Every competitor must wear a blackout mask. Vision is completely obscured.

5A football match from the 2012 Paralympic Games shows the play. Blind athletes on the track, and partly sighted ones, also get guidance from sound. Spoken information gives cues. Clapping gives cues. Electronic signals give cues. The cues serve competitors who cannot see. While such sounds are in use, spectators must stay absolutely silent. A guide runner uses the lane beside the athlete. A tether, fastened loosely around both wrists, usually links the pair. During a race the guide may give verbal cues. A 2008 photograph shows Australia in a cycling event at the Paralympic Games. Visually impaired cyclists ride a bicycle with two seats. A pilot sits in front. The athlete pedals. The pilot steers. Swimming uses helpers called tappers. A tapper stands at each end of the pool. Each one holds a long pole. The pole taps a swimmer who is nearing the wall. Every swimmer must wear blackened goggles. The rule stops a partly sighted swimmer from gaining an advantage.

6One challenge for the Paralympics is wider participation. A wider set of countries still needs a route onto the athlete list. High-income economies send more than their share of athletes to the Games. Equipment is easier for those countries to provide. They are often better able to supply training. Success for Paralympic athletes depends on both. The problem is not limited to the Paralympics. The Olympic Games show the same imbalance. It is true of many other international sporting competitions. In many countries, prejudice still blocks athletes who have disabilities. Support for adaptive athletes is steadily growing. Support for Paralympic competition is growing too. Five athletes from around the world show the range. A 2016 photograph shows shot put medalists celebrating. Iran is one of the countries. Great Britain is another. South Africa is the third. Chantal Petitclerc is from Canada. Her name is said SHAWN-tel PE-tee-klair. A photograph shows her winning gold in 2008. At thirteen, she lost the use of both legs. She was struck by a barn door of great weight. She was visiting a friend's farm. After the accident she could not attend gym class. A different plan came from the physical education teacher at her high school. She swam during the school's lunch hour. At eighteen she entered her first wheelchair race. She finished last. She did not stop. Barcelona, Spain, hosted the 1992 Paralympic Games, where wheelchair racing brought her two bronze medals. Further Paralympics followed. Her career ended with fourteen gold medals.
