She had twenty-one medals in all. She set five world records. After she retired from sport, she became a senator. The seat represents the Canadian province of Quebec.

7Ntando Mahlangu is a runner from South Africa. Say the first part n-TAHN-doh. Say the second part mah-LAHN-goo. His nickname is Blades. From birth, a condition stopped development of the legs under the knees. Childhood was spent in a wheelchair. He could not walk. At age ten he chose amputation at the knee. The surgery let him wear prosthetics. He could walk. He could even run. Running blades reached him for the first time before that year ended. Jumping Kids, a charity in South Africa, was the source. Catching him has been difficult from then on. His first Summer Paralympics was in 2016. The city was Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Silver was his medal in the men's race over 200 meters. In the Paralympic running community he is seen as an up-and-coming star. He was only fourteen at that first Paralympic Games. Terezinha Guilhermina is from Brazil. She and her guide appear in a photograph after gold at the Paralympic Games of 2012. Say te-re-ZEE-nyah for the first name. Say geel-air-MEE-nah for the last. Several of her siblings shared a rare genetic disease. She was born with it too. The disease left her completely blind. Running began at age twenty-two. She had borrowed running shoes from her sister. Starting in 2004, she entered four Summer Paralympic Games. Her medals include four gold. They include four silver. They include three bronze. Colorful blindfolds in her races are a known part of her style.

8Momoka Muraoka is a skier from Japan. Say MOH-moh-kah for the first name. Say moo-rah-OH-kah for the last. At age four she was diagnosed with a condition. The condition causes swelling in the spinal cord. A wheelchair became necessary for mobility. Sit-skiing began at age nine. Paralympic training began at fourteen. Her first Winter Paralympics was in 2014, in Sochi, Russia. She entered three events. She fell in one. She did not medal in the others. The 2018 Paralympics were held in Pyeongchang, South Korea. There she won one gold medal. She won two silvers. She won two bronzes. The 2014 Paralympic Winter Games include a photograph of her sitting super-G run. Devendra Jhajharia was born in India. Say de-VEN-drah for the first name. Say JAH-jah-ree-ah for the last. At eight years old he was climbing a tree. He grabbed a branch that touched a live electric cable. The shock nearly killed him. Doctors could not save his left hand. Former playmates shunned him after the accident. They taunted him. They ridiculed him. He locked himself in the house rather than face the other children. Sport entered his life because his mother insisted. He made a javelin at home. He practiced with it on his own. At fourteen he won a district championship. He had no formal training. His first Paralympic gold came in 2004. The Games were in Athens, Greece. A second gold came in 2016. Those Games were in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. India had never had a Paralympian with two gold medals before him. Both gold-medal performances set world records.

9Mike Schultz, a snowboarder from the USA, competed at the 2018 Games. He won a gold medal. He won a silver medal. The leg he used was a prosthetic he had designed himself. The Paralympics began in a humble way in 1948. They have grown into a huge sporting event. They have grown into an important one. They, like the Olympic Games, show the human spirit when it is at its best. Top athletes are on display. They achieve excellence in the sports they have chosen. They are strong examples of competitors who worked hard to reach greatness. Years ahead will still see that spirit on display at the Paralympic Games.

9. Africa's Tallest Free-Standing Mountain

1A line of climbers goes up the slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro. They are heading for the peak covered in snow. The mountain stands in Tanzania, in Africa. Africa's highest peak has earned a nickname. People call it the roof of Africa. Its altitude is 5,895 meters (19,341 ft.). It rises 4,877 meters (16,000 ft.) above the land around it. No freestanding mountain on Earth rises higher. A freestanding mountain does not belong to a mountain range. Tanzania is the country that holds Mount Kilimanjaro. The name is said tan-zuh-NEE-uh. It sits close to Tanzania's border with Kenya. Kilimanjaro National Park is a World Heritage Site. Officials established the park in 1973. The goal was to protect the mountain above the tree line. In 2005 the park grew larger. The added land protects forest lower on the slopes. Park status shields the habitats on the mountain. Its life forms stay under protection too. The government of Tanzania provides that protection.

2Mount Kilimanjaro began as a volcano. The buildup began roughly 750,000 years ago. The cause was eruptions along East Africa's Great Rift Valley. The Great Rift Valley is an enormous crack in Earth's crust. It lies in East Africa. Those eruptions built Shira. Shira is Kilimanjaro's oldest volcano. Eruptions at Shira ended about 500,000 years ago. After it collapsed, a huge caldera remained. During the next forty thousand years, two more volcanoes formed. Their names are Mawenzi and Kibo. Eruptions kept happening across a long span of time. Kibo's summit grew taller than the other two peaks. The eruptions also shaped many features on all three peaks. The latest strong eruption took place about two hundred years ago. Outside South America, Kilimanjaro is the tallest volcano. Shira is extinct. Mawenzi is extinct as well. An extinct volcano is not expected to erupt again. Kibo is dormant. A dormant volcano might erupt again someday. Black rock set against white glaciers is part of the mountain's beauty. Glaciers have helped shape Mount Kilimanjaro too. Their great weight cut into the rock below. Moving downhill, the ice carved ridges. It carved valleys as well. Glaciers on Kilimanjaro may seem surprising. The peak is only about 322 kilometers (200 mi.) from the equator. Lower slopes have warm weather through the whole year. Sunlight that hits the pale ice is mostly bounced away. That bounce of light lets the ice stay cool. People believe the name Kilimanjaro comes from two words. In Swahili, kilima means mountain. Kichagga uses njaro for the pale color of those snowy summits.

3The ice on the mountain is still shrinking, little by little. Global warming is one reason. Cutting down nearby forests is another reason. Cut trees leave the air beside the peak with less moisture. Fewer clouds form. Less rain falls nearby. More moisture then leaves the glaciers by evaporation. The glaciers were first measured in 1912. More than four-fifths of that ice mass has disappeared. Some researchers predict they may be gone completely by 2060. Glacier ice stores important information from the past. The record concerns Earth's atmosphere and its climate. For the whole of Africa, Kilimanjaro's ice is the only record of this kind. If the ice melts, that record will be gone forever. A large share of the mountain's beauty will be gone too. An ice core is a cylinder of ice. Scientists drill it from an ice sheet or from a glacier. Bubbles inside the ice hold bits of Earth's old atmosphere. Some bits are thousands of years old. Others are hundreds of thousands of years old. Scientists study these pockets of air. They measure how the mix of gases has shifted across long periods. Old temperatures leave clues inside ice cores too. They hold clues about other parts of the environment. Around Kilimanjaro's foot live the Chagga people. Small villages keep traditional Chagga culture alive. For centuries, human communities have stayed on these slopes or close by. Large groups entered northern Tanzania early in the eleventh century. They came from places across Africa. Many belonged to various Bantu tribes. They made homes on the southern slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro. They made homes on the eastern slopes too. They also settled Mount Meru. They settled the nearby town of Moshi. Together they became a new community, the Chagga people. Several other tribes already lived there when the Chagga arrived. As time passed, only the Chagga remained. The Chagga are Tanzania's third-largest ethnic group. They have remained speakers of a Bantu language. That language has several dialects. A dialect can sound like a fully separate language.

4German colonists arrived in the late 1800s. Missionaries arrived then too. Before that arrival, Chagga chiefdoms often fought one another. German colonial rule then forced order on the region. Afterward, the Chagga banded together. They built advanced methods for farming the slopes. They prospered. Tanzania became independent in 1961. After independence, the Chagga kept improving how they farmed. Today they are the wealthiest communities in Tanzania. They are also the most highly organized. Bananas are their main crop. In the rich volcanic soil they also raise yams. They raise beans. They raise maize. A coffee grown by the Chagga is famous far beyond Tanzania. That coffee now matters to Tanzania's national economy. As years passed, older Chagga ways of daily life shifted. Pride in their cultural identity is still strong. Moshi Town in Tanzania looks out on a beautiful view of Kilimanjaro. On the rim of Kibo's crater, the top spot is Uhuru Peak. Climbers from many nations try this mountain each year. The number is at least twenty-five thousand. It is the tallest mountain in Africa. It is one of the Seven Summits. One peak from each of Earth's seven continents belongs to that group. Many mountaineers set a goal of climbing all seven. Among them, Kilimanjaro is one of the easier climbs. Most paths to Kibo's peak do not call for special training. On Mount Kilimanjaro, the top of Kibo is the highest spot. Climbers do not need ropes. They do not need mountaineering gear. Good hiking boots are enough, along with camping equipment. Even so, the climb is not easy. Air grows thinner on the way up. Climbers must get used to it slowly. That care helps them avoid altitude sickness. A climb up and back usually takes from five to nine days. Success comes to roughly two in every three people who try.

5Reaching Kibo's summit is not the only reason to visit. Many nature walks suit guests with smaller plans. Day trips go to Lake Chala, a beautiful lake in a crater. Day trips also go to Shira Plateau. That plateau formed when the first volcano on Kilimanjaro collapsed. Trout fishing is popular in the mountain's rivers. The whole district is excellent for taking photos. Visitors add over $20 million a year to the economy nearby. Climbing and other activities create work. Guides find jobs. Porters find jobs. Hotel staff, food growers, and travel agents find jobs. Construction workers and still more people find jobs too. The whole region's economy gets a lift. Lake Chala can look blue. It can look turquoise. It can look green. The shade depends on the time of year. A striking part of a Kilimanjaro climb is the changing view. Climbers move through several ecosystems on the way up. Sea level sits far below the cultivated zone, which runs from 800 meters to 1,800 meters (2,625 to 5,906 ft.). This zone receives the most rain. Melted ice from glaciers forms many rivers there. Water is plentiful, so the zone holds farmland. Small villages stand there too. This zone circles the base of the mountain. The montane forest begins at 1,800 meters and reaches 2,800 meters (5,906 to 9,186 ft.) over the sea. Climbers start in this forest. Plants grow thicker on the south side. They grow thicker on the east side too. Those sides get the most rain. Monkeys live in the forest, along with elephants, leopards, giraffes, and rhinos. Other animals live there as well. The animals are hard to see. Cool forest slopes higher up are home to elephant's trunk flower. The flower is a semiofficial symbol of Mount Kilimanjaro.

6Above the trees lies the heather and moorland zone. Heights here run from 2,800 meters up to 4,000 meters (9,186 to 13,123 ft.) past sea level. Some lists split this belt into two zones. The zone is drier than the forest under it. It is windier too. Daytime heat can reach 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees F). At night the temperature can fall below freezing. Climbers often see clouds level with their eyes. Wild grasses are a main plant here. Giant heathers are the other main plant. The animal seen most often is the four-striped grass mouse. Bigger animals sometimes wander uphill. They do not remain for long. Giant groundsels grow in the moorland zone. They belong to the sunflower family. They can live where the air is thin and the land is high. From 4,000 meters to 5,000 meters (13,123 to 16,404 ft.) over the sea lies the alpine desert. Yearly rain there is less than 20 centimeters (8 in.). Few plants can live at this height. Survivors must handle strong sunlight. They must also handle cold below zero. Animals include birds that hunt. A spider that lives at high altitude is here too. The summit belt of Kibo reaches from 5,000 meters to 5,895 meters (16,404 to 19,341 ft.) over the sea. Almost no life stays here. Water is missing. Lichens are the main living things. The country that holds Mount Kilimanjaro once had another name. People called it Tanganyika (tang-guh-NYEE-kuh). It became free of British rule in 1961. Two years before that, Julius Nyerere (nih-RAIR-ee) spoke about the future. He later became the country's president. He said the people of Tanganyika wished to light a candle. He wanted the candle set on the top of Mount Kilimanjaro. He imagined its light reaching past the borders. The light would stand for love in a place that had known hate. It would stand for hope and respect in a place that had known neither. Nyerere's words turned Kilimanjaro into a sign of independence for all of Africa. The summit of Kibo is called Uhuru Peak. Uhuru is Swahili for freedom. Julius Nyerere was president of Tanzania from 1964 to 1985.

7The writer Ernest Hemingway pictured Mount Kilimanjaro in a famous description. He said the mountain seemed as wide as the entire world. He called it great. He called it high. He said the sun made it look astonishingly white. Nature on this peak is rich. Many kinds of plants live there. Many kinds of animals live there too. Some of those living things exist nowhere else on Earth. The mountain is a dramatic sign of what volcanoes can create. It is a fascinating piece of Earth's geologic past. Travelers arrive from every corner of the world. For them, Kilimanjaro is a peak to climb. It is a personal goal to meet. For people who live nearby, it brings prosperity. It brings pride. It is a strong sign of freedom. It is a strong sign of self-government. People of many different lives sometimes get to see it. For them, the mountain is a place of stunning beauty. These words help with the topic. Geologic describes land, rocks, soil layers, or minerals. Altitude sickness is how the body reacts when oxygen is short at a great height. A headache can be one sign. Vomiting can be another. Glaciers are big masses of ice piled with hard-packed snow. They last through every season. They creep downhill. A caldera is a wide basin with a bowl shape. The ground there fell into a magma chamber that had emptied. Montane describes cool country in the mountains. Evergreen trees and other plants grow in that country. An ecosystem is a community of living things plus the places they live. A plateau is high, flat land spread across a wide area. The equator is a made-up line circling Earth. It lies midway between the North Pole and the South Pole. A porter carries goods, gear, or bags for someone else. Evaporation happens when water turns from liquid into gas. Heat brings on that change. A summit is a mountain's topmost point. A tribe shares both customs and a homeland.

10. Albert Einstein

1When Albert Einstein was five, his father showed him a magnetic compass. Watching its floating movement filled him with curiosity and wonder. Why did the needle stay still while his father turned the casing around and around? He was too young to understand the answer, but he never forgot the mystery. Later he wrote that something deeply hidden had to be behind things. He also believed that knowing facts does not by itself tell us what we ought to do. That curious boy became a scientist who spent his life trying to understand what was hidden. By pursuing hard problems, he forever changed how people think about the universe.

2Albert Einstein was born on March 14, 1879, in Ulm, Germany, and the next year the family moved to Munich. His sister Maja was born there and became his closest childhood friend. His mother Pauline played the piano and encouraged him to learn the violin when he was six. He disliked the structured lessons, but he loved playing, and the violin stayed with him all his life. He thought a table, a chair, fruit, and a violin were enough to make a man happy. His father and two uncles, all electrical engineers, taught him math, science, and algebra through games. A friend brought science books, and Einstein pored over them for hours, especially one about geometry. He could concentrate on hard problems until every solution was considered. As a child he often repeated words quietly to himself, and this speech habit worried his parents.

3Einstein's talent for math and science showed at once. A U.S. stamp later honored his creative thinking. He questioned strict German schools, where teachers seemed like sergeants drilling students to memorize lifeless facts. At seventeen he entered a leading European science university and often skipped lectures to test ideas in the laboratory. Professors agreed he might have a bright future if only he would do as he was told. After finishing school in 1900, his independence and curiosity made him unpopular with teachers who could have helped him find work. He felt the lack of a teaching job was a setback, but he did not give up. In 1902 he began work at a patent office in Bern, Switzerland, checking that new devices worked as claimed. On his first day his boss told him to assume that anything an inventor said was wrong.

4Einstein held patents for a compass that large amounts of iron did not affect and for a quieter, safer refrigerator pump. That compass became standard equipment on metal ships and submarines. Regular pay and hours let him meet the Olympia Academy, friends who shared his curiosity about science. The group often talked and socialized late in cafes or in Einstein's apartment. Those years of work and friendship helped him form ideas that would change science forever. By 1905 he sent five papers to a leading German journal, and the first appeared in March. The papers explained light, proved molecules and atoms and how they moved, and rethought space, time, and motion. It is now common knowledge that water molecules contain two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

5In six months Einstein challenged ideas of the universe held for over two hundred years, and scientists were astounded. They were amazed that a curious twenty-six-year-old patent clerk, not a professor, had written the papers. His career took off through speaking invitations, congratulations from the 1905 Nobel physics winner, and Max Planck's teaching. In time, 1905 came to be known as Einstein's miracle year. He worked at the patent office until 1909, then moved from university to university while refining his ideas. The new ideas were so hard that he often thought he was on the wrong track or even losing his mind. In 1915 he finally united his earlier ideas into one system called the general theory of relativity. In 1919 British scientists used a solar eclipse to test a star's place, and the shift matched what he had said.

6Time magazine named Albert Einstein Person of the Century. Newspapers around the world announced the findings and declared a revolution in science and a new theory of the universe. A German newspaper called him a new celebrity and said his ideas completely changed concepts of nature. Overnight Einstein became one of the most famous people in the world. The Sun's gravity bends light from a star, so the star seems to be in one place while it is really in another. Some scientists had built careers on ideas he proved wrong and did not want to believe him. Others did not want theories that were hard to test in a laboratory, or disliked him as a Jewish man amid growing prejudice. Einstein took the criticism in stride, knew his theories were not perfect, and won more recognition with each new paper.

7Fame brought demands for interviews, photographs, speeches, and writings, and he felt this attention stole time from research. He still hoped to be a man of value, and he used fame to open minds and spread his ideas. He believed war should be avoided, and in 1914 only three scientists, including him, signed against Germany entering World War I. More than one hundred scientists signed a different letter supporting Germany's entry into the war. Reporters greeted him and his wife Elsa in New York in 1921, and he kept speaking out for fair treatment for everyone. In the 1930s his articles The World as I See It discussed war, liberty, progress, and education for general readers. He worked for peace, and although some views changed, his belief that violence and war are never the answer stayed firm. He did not join the bomb project, though others used his discoveries, and he warned President Franklin Roosevelt of its destructive power.

8Einstein believed pleasure in work, in its result, and in its value to the community was the most important motive for school and life. Despite many efforts for peace, Germany moved closer to war in the 1930s. Until then the German government had tolerated Einstein and his criticism of its plans. He knew this tolerance would not last, because the Nazi Party was on the rise. His open criticism of Nazi politics and his Jewish heritage put him at risk. In 1933 he left Germany and took a job at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey. In 1949 he met India's prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, at his Princeton home, and he often sailed on Princeton's Lake Carnegie. Townspeople asked uninvited visitors if they were expected, which kept strangers from bothering him at home.

9For the next twenty-nine years he worked to expand his ideas, even when some people said he was losing touch. He ignored that criticism and hoped for a theory that would unify his original ideas with newer ones. Hard work did not bring discoveries like those of the miracle year or the general theory of relativity. He remained in demand for speeches, articles, and regular meetings with other scientists. Secretary Helen Dukas worked with him from 1928 until his death in 1955 and helped him go over matters. Ideas about light led to television cameras, remote controls for home electronics, and flatscreen computers. He was the first person to think of laser light, now used in CDs, DVDs, and store checkout equipment. His proof of atoms and molecules led to or improved shaving cream, toothpaste, computers, and portable phones.

10Einstein's theories give scientists a framework for studying space objects such as the Helix Nebula. Current ideas about the origins of the universe, the nature of space, and black holes all come from his work. He said the most beautiful experience we can have is the mysterious. He believed it was enough to try to understand a little of this mystery every day. Until his death on April 18, 1955, his curiosity led him to work on nature's greatest mysteries. In doing so, he changed the way people think about time, space, energy, and matter. Those are the foundations of the universe.

11Algebra is a branch of math that uses letters for unknown numbers. A patent gives an inventor the right to make money from an invention. Physics is the study of matter and energy. Astounded means greatly amazed. To pore over a book is to read it with great attention. Atoms are tiny pieces of matter, and molecules are the smallest parts still identifiable as a substance. A compass is a direction tool whose needle points north. A revolution can mean a sharp change in old ideas. Theories are possible explanations. The universe is all things that exist in space. Mysterious means not easy to understand.

11. American Athletes Who Changed the Game

1Pages ahead: Jim Thorpe, 1887 to 1953, ranked above every other athlete of that century. His move into paid sport. Mildred Didrikson Zaharias, 1911 to 1956, sometimes called the other Babe. Play that seemed to have no limit. Jackie Robinson, 1919 to 1972, bold on a baseball field. Althea Gibson, 1927 to 2003, who went first. Jesse Owens, 1913 to 1980, quicker than the field. A Games story that does not fade. What these lives mean. Words to know. Jim Thorpe stands above the century People still argue over the finest athlete of the century just ended. Football's Jim Brown is a fair name to offer. Basketball's Michael Jordan is a fair name. Tennis has Billie Jean King. Baseball has Babe Ruth. Each of those stars reset what a sport could be. Records fell around them. Any of them could claim the highest chair. The name that was placed above the rest was Jim Thorpe. His people were the Sac and Fox Nation, and he was Native. Oklahoma is where life began for him, in 1887. Paid baseball was on his list. Football of that era had no larger star. Track and field still tells of feats that sound legendary. One hard fact sits next to the fame. Being born inside the United States did not make him a citizen on paper. Most other Native people of that time were in the same position. A law in 1924 changed it. That law is the Indian Citizenship Act.

2Fans of college football already knew him before he reached the Summer Olympics of 1912. His school was in Pennsylvania. Crowds loved this All-American halfback. His speed looked blinding. His strength matched it. A tackler might be run through. A tackler might be left behind. He punted for the team. He kicked placements too. The school's baseball team starred him. So did the basketball team. Golf suited him. Tennis suited him. Swimming suited him. Give him a sport and he usually excelled. One picture catches the shot put leaving his hand. Those 1912 Games put him in a United States uniform for the two roughest tests in track and field. Five events make a pentathlon. Ten events make a decathlon. Across only a few days he did what had seemed past imagining. The pentathlon gave him four wins out of five. The decathlon gave him a world record. Gold medals came for both tests. Nobody in the history of the Olympics had managed that. Nobody has managed it after him. Sweden's King Gustav V called him up to the stand where medals are given. What the king told him was plain. No athlete alive, the king said, stood higher than Thorpe. Another picture freezes his long jump at those same 1912 Games. Skill of many kinds is required. The mix is how judges see an athlete's full ability. Five events, kept in this order. A long jump opens the pentathlon. A javelin throw follows. A discus throw follows that. A run of 200 meters comes next. A run of 1,500 meters closes it. Ten events, kept in this order. The decathlon opens with a run of 100 meters. A long jump is second. A high jump is third. A shot put is fourth. A run of 400 meters is fifth. Hurdles of 110 meters are sixth. A discus throw is seventh. A javelin throw is eighth. A pole vault is ninth. A run of 1,500 meters finishes the ten.

3Medals and records did not stay with him. The International Olympic Committee, known as the IOC, removed the medals. It wiped the records. Officials said he had broken amateur rules in a technical way. Minor-league baseball had been his summer work in 1909. The same work continued in 1910. Other athletes had taken that same summer path. Their amateur standing survived because they hid behind false names. Thorpe had not. He apologized to the Olympic Committee. He explained that the rule was news to him. Nothing he said moved them. Families received replacement gold medals only in 1983. The official record still does not hold his scores. Paid sport came next After the Games, the whole world knew his name. Congratulations arrived in a letter from the White House. Pro teams offered contracts that would make him rich. He said no. College football at the old school got one last season. Touchdowns that season numbered twenty-five. Points totaled 198. Marriage came too, to Iva Miller, the girlfriend from his college years. The year was astonishing. Baseball paid him starting in 1913, on the New York Giants. Swinging a bat, he was great. Covering the outfield, strength and speed made him great as well. Skill in baseball was real. Preference still bent toward football. That pro game was young in 1915, and Ohio is where he joined the Canton Bulldogs. Championships arrived three times: 1916, then 1917, then 1919. Baseball filled the summers in between. Leadership followed in 1920. The American Football Association made him its first president. Years later that group was the National Football League. He wanted the game loved by more people. Halftime was his stage. From the 50-yard line he drop-kicked a ball through the goalposts. Facing the opposite end, he did it once more. A statue of him greets people at the Football Hall of Fame. The figure honors pro football's founding father and the game's earliest true star. Across the twentieth century, no athlete ranks above him. A 1925 picture shows a Giants game, with Thorpe fielding.

4Another Babe belongs in the argument. Mildred Didrikson Zaharias lived from 1911 to 1956. Thorpe's century-wide rank is famous. Fans of sport might still put her name beside his. Mildred, called Babe, ruled women's basketball. She ruled track and field. She ruled golf. The decades were the 1930s, the 1940s, and the 1950s. Competition from her was serious and rough-and-tumble. Women of that time were expected to stay modest and polite. Texas is where 1911 brought her into a family of seven children. She was number six. High school showed her off in volleyball. Baseball did too. Swimming did too. Tennis did too. Basketball did most of all, and it was then the women's sport with the biggest following. Loss never touched her high-school team. Thirty points from her alone was a normal night. Twenty points from an entire team was what people called respectable. A picture shows free throws leaving Babe's hands. Track and field pulled her interest next. Lifting weights was a belief she held firmly. Few women trained that way. Work that serious, plus ability she was born with, showed up at a national meet during July of the year 1932. Eight events received her name. She won five. She also won the whole meet with no teammates. Squads of twenty stood on the other side. The Summer Olympics came weeks afterward. Gold and world records arrived in three tests: hurdles of 80 meters, the javelin, and the high jump. Golf is where wider fame waited, and no game stayed out of her reach. She did not pick up a club until she was twenty-one. Focus and determination then drove the swing. A thousand balls a day raised blisters. Tape went over the blisters. Hitting continued. Her first championship arrived a year on, in 1935. George Zaharias, a pro wrestler, became her husband in 1938. Golf is where they had met. Twenty years after the wedding produced eighty-two tournament victories. Seventeen arrived back to back in 1946 and again through 1947. The LPGA, short for Ladies Professional Golf Association, was founded with her help in 1949.

5The year 1953 found her at the peak of her play, and the diagnosis was cancer. Surgery followed. Doctors believed she would not play again. Four months was all it took for a return to the pro tour. Cancer took her life the year after that. She was forty-five. Family grieved. Millions of fans grieved. Achievements across a life in sport put her into a Hall of Fame for golf. A second hall, for track and field, took her too. Six times voters named her Woman Athlete of the Year. Nobody else has been honored on that scale. A picture puts Babe Didrikson at the far right of the frame. Hurdles of 80 meters took her 11.7 seconds, and that sprint broke yet another world record. Rights for female athletes had a fierce advocate in her. The push for equal treatment stopped short of every peer. Remarks she made about people of color were sometimes racist. One infamous moment went past words. Water from a pitcher was dumped on two teammates as they slept. Those two women were the earliest Black women on the Olympic track team of the United States. Athletic greatness here is beyond doubt. Character did not rise to the same prowess. Jackie Robinson lived from 1919 to 1972, and baseball had never seen a bolder player. Try to picture today's Major League Baseball with no Frank Thomas. Take away Derek Jeter. Take away Alex Rodriguez. Try the Hall of Fame with no Hank Aaron. Take away Willie Mays. Take away Roberto Clemente. Take away the many other brilliant players who are Black or Latino. The blank spaces are hard to picture. They might have stayed blank. Courage from Jackie Robinson blocked that. Determination from him blocked it too. Major League Baseball had its first Black player in 1947, and that player was Robinson. A picture shows Jackie Robinson.

6Discrimination pressed on people of color in many parts of life then. Sport was one part. Big-league clubs fielded white players only. Black players who loved the game built leagues apart from those clubs. Stars of real talent came out of those leagues. Large crowds came too. The Brooklyn Dodgers had a general manager named Branch Rickey. Keeping talent out struck him as wrong. Players were harmed. Baseball was harmed. Integrated clubs were his aim. He knew the person who faced racism and crossed the color line would need to be unusual. Jackie Robinson was the person he found. A picture remembers the U.S. Army in World War II, when Black officers were few. Robinson was one of them. Any hitter would respect his bat. Any runner would respect his legs. Any fielder would respect his glove. Base running of a daring kind excited crowds. Players on the other side felt unsteady. He competed with a fierce edge. A soft bunt could beat you. A hard blast could beat you. Character could beat you, and that mattered most. Minor-league ball filled a year. That year he owned the top batting record. His club won a championship. Age twenty-eight is when the Brooklyn Dodgers added him. Rookie life was hard. Opponents shouted insults. Pitchers aimed the ball at his body. Boos came from the stands. Teammates, some of them, treated him badly. April 15, 1947, was the first official day he spent in the Major Leagues. A picture shows him that day with other Dodgers.

7Dignity stayed quiet, and it stayed with him. So did determination. Temper did not win. Fists did not answer. The diamond did the talking, through his skill. Hitting in that rookie year was solid. Stolen bases led the league. Rookie of the Year was the prize. A batting title in the National League arrived in 1949. The Most Valuable Player award, the highest honor, arrived the same year. Pay in 1950 made him the Brooklyn Dodger with the largest salary. Leadership of the club was his as well. The lesson was about ability. Perform at that pro level and the major leagues were where you belonged. Black players soon found jobs on other clubs. Latino players did too. Players in this country's national pastime now come from every race. They come from every nationality. So does management. Integration of modern baseball is complete. Talent of every player is celebrated. A scholarship had come from UCLA. The letters name a university in Los Angeles, a city in California. Four sports produced varsity letters: baseball first, then basketball, then football, then track and field. Pressure later, as the first Black player in this league, was easier to carry because of that leadership. Althea Gibson lived from 1927 to 2003 and led others through a closed door. Baseball's color line may have broken under Robinson. Tennis needed a Black woman before the door would open. Sharecropper parents in South Carolina had her in 1927. At age three the family shifted to Harlem. That neighborhood sits inside New York City. She grew tall. She grew athletic. Street games around home were hers to rule. City paddle tennis, across the whole city, was a title she took at twelve. School lost hours because she wanted more play. By seventh grade she had left school. A picture shows the hard work she put into skills on a court.

8Tennis skill drew two young Black doctors. One was Dr. Robert Johnson. The other was Dr. Hubert Eaton. They were hunting young Black talent in tennis. Her game improved with their help. High school was finished with their help too. She climbed to the top rank of the ATA. That group, the American Tennis Association, was entirely Black. Competition at the National Indoor Championships came in 1949, and no Black woman had entered before her. Race barred her, that same year, from the U.S. National Championships. Today's name for that event is the U.S. Open. Twelve months later, an invitation to that Open arrived. Round two was close, and she lost. Respect remained. A year later, Wimbledon in the United Kingdom invited her, a first for a Black player. Few tennis championships in the world are bigger. One picture from the year 1956 shows her rushing the net at the National Championships held in the U.S. Study did not stop away from the court. An athletic scholarship came from Florida A&M. That campus stands in Tallahassee. She played tennis there. She played basketball. She played golf. Physical education was the degree, finished in 1953. The year 1956 was the breakthrough. A Grand Slam means the world's four leading tennis tournaments, all inside one year. No Black player had won one until she did. Wimbledon doubles, on the women's side, was also hers that year. Wimbledon singles followed in 1957. The trophy came from the hands of Queen Elizabeth II, ruler of the United Kingdom. New York welcomed her home with a parade of ticker tape. The U.S. Nationals fell to her before that year ended. Both of those titles were hers again the next year. Sports Illustrated put her on its cover. Time magazine did too. Female Player of the Year was the Associated Press choice, two years straight. The 1957 Wimbledon trophy passes from Queen Elizabeth II to Althea Gibson in one picture.

9A legacy as a top athlete was already safe because of tennis. More was coming. Membership in the LPGA, the Ladies Professional Golf Association, opened to her in 1964. No Black golfer had been a member before. Clubs across the country often refused Black golfers both membership and the chance to play. Where Gibson was allowed on the course, the clubhouse was often closed. Bathrooms were often closed. Threats said she might be killed. Insults from crowds were racist. She did not bend. Certain tour courses turned events that had been open into invitation-only events, hoping to keep her out. Players in the LPGA voted. They would boycott any tournament that did not welcome every player. Clubs gave way. Two sports lost a color line because of her talent and her determination. Black tennis stars who came later walked a road she had cleared. Arthur Ashe walked it. Venus Williams walked it. Serena Williams walked it. Golf events on her schedule from 1963 through 1977 numbered 171. Jesse Owens lived from 1913 to 1980, and people called him the fastest man. Junior high in Cleveland, Ohio, is where this sprinting legend first burst into view. His age group lost a world record in the high jump. It lost one in the long jump. A high-school coach wanted him on the track team. Work after school helped his family, so afternoon practice could not happen. Morning training with the coach began at 5:00 a.m. Stories about him grew. A national meet for high-school track saw the teenager tie a world record in the dash of 100 yards. The long jump gave him a world record that was new. One picture shows him leading at the Olympic Games of 1936.

10College athletes met in 1935, and more world records fell. The dash of 220 yards was one. The long jump was one. Low hurdles of 220 yards were one. The dash of 100 yards, at 9.4 seconds, was a world record he tied. Track and field had never seen one athlete do so much. An hour, more or less, held all of it. His back was hurt the entire time. Triumphs greater than the records were still waiting. His parents had named him James Cleveland Owens. Jesse was what people called him. An Olympic name that stays Berlin, Germany, held the Summer Olympic Games in 1936. The Second World War had not started. Owens made the trip, and the hosts did not want him. Germany's ruler was Adolf Hitler, leader of the Nazis. Their belief set non-Jewish white people above everyone else, a so-called master race. Black people, in their words, were primitive. Attitude from Hitler did not make Owens feel small. Threats did not either. Berlin's track was the proof. Gold medals numbered four. Olympic history had not seen that before. Home from Germany meant a parade of ticker tape and cheers full of admiration. Playgrounds in Cleveland later had him as director. Speeches made his name familiar. Young people, in this country and abroad, heard him tell them to give their best. America's Ambassador of Sports was a title the government gave him. The Presidential Medal of Freedom arrived in later years. Home in 1953 is where one picture finds Jesse Owens.

11Names that stay An amazing stretch of time, the twentieth century, built the pro sports world familiar now. It also produced athletes who rose out of a field already full of huge talent. Ability of a rare kind left the world astonished. Their sports were changed forever, and changed for the better. Their societies were changed the same way. Competing at the very top became possible for everyone. Memory will keep each of them as a legend of American sport. Words to know Accomplished: managed to do a thing, or to reach a goal. Dominated: stood ahead of others in success, influence, or power inside a sport or a contest. Achievements: results that effort made real. Integrate: to join separate ideas, or separate groups of people. Astonishing: able to surprise you. Intimidated: pushed into fear, or into a sense of being overwhelmed. Determination: resolve, the commitment that keeps you on a hard goal. Legend: someone famous for one special talent, or for one special deed. Dignity: a state in which respect and honor are deserved. Omissions: people or things that were not included. Revolutionized: changed something on an enormous scale. Discriminated: acted unfairly toward someone over race, over age, over sex, over religion, or over some other difference.

12. Animals Found in Hidden Places

1New animals can be plotted on a map of the world. Europe appears among the labeled lands. Asia appears there too. North America is labeled. So is the Atlantic Ocean. So is the Pacific Ocean. Africa is labeled. The Indian Ocean is labeled. South America is labeled. Australia is labeled. Congo’s Democratic Republic is the home of the lesula monkey. Colombia is the home of the Caquetá titi monkey. Borneo is the home of the Matang narrowmouthed frog. New Guinea is the home of the long-nosed tree frog. The blossom bat comes from New Guinea as well. Madagascar is the home of Goodman’s mouse lemur. Brazil is the home of Sazima’s tarantula. Brazil’s Amazon Rainforest is the home of the troll-haired planthopper. The Atlantic Ocean is the home of the Gorgon’s head starfish. Indonesia is the home of the walking bamboo shark. Ecuador and Colombia are the home of the olinguito. Cambodia is the home of the Cambodian tailorbird. Readers meet an introduction first. Monkeys come in the next part. Frogs follow. Furry animals follow the frogs. Invertebrates have their own part. Life under the water has a part too. One part is about animals that stayed hidden in open view. A closing part asks what may lie ahead. Important words are explained at the end. Tamoya ohboya is the scientific name of the Bonaire banded box jellyfish. The name came from a contest. The winner expected a common reaction. Most viewers, the winner said, would blurt Oh boy! Imagine that you hope to find an animal species no one has named. Which place would you choose? Choose a place that no one has searched. Trips to far corners of Earth produce many of the new species. A microscope can reveal still more. DNA can separate two animals that look alike. They can still be different species. Busy places hold some new life forms as well. People walk past those spots every day. A single year can bring more than 15,000 new animal species. Set beside species already known, that yearly haul is about 1 percent. Known species already number past 1.5 million. Species are also vanishing. The pace is a record one, and it reaches around the globe. A newly named species gives scientists a thrill. It also matters a great deal.

2The year 2007 brought a newly identified monkey. Its forests are remote. Democratic Republic of the Congo is the country that holds them. Large eyes give the lesula a look full of feeling. Observers call it shy. They call it quiet too. The first animal scientists saw was not wild at that moment. A girl was keeping it as a pet. Twenty-eight years had passed with no new monkey species. The lesula broke that gap. The year 2010 brought yet another new monkey. Scientists found it through its calls. The calls were complex. Colombia’s Amazon jungle is home to the Caquetá titi monkey. About twenty other titi species share that jungle. A bushy beard of red fur sets this monkey apart. Its forehead has no white bar. Babies of this species make a soft sound. The sound is a purr, like the purr of a cat. Thousands of these monkeys would mean a healthy population. The number thought to be alive today is smaller. It is fewer than 250. The titi that was just discovered is already listed as endangered. A pea is about as big as the Matang narrowmouthed frog. Few frogs anywhere are known to be smaller. The discovery year was 2010. The place was the island of Borneo. Borneo lies in Southeast Asia. Museums already held examples. Those collections were a century old. Staff had treated the tiny frogs as young of a different species. Calls heard at dusk changed that idea. The sounds came from inside pitcher plants. Calls are made only by adult frogs. Full-grown animals, then, could be this small. The frog depends on pitcher plants. A female places eggs along the pitcher’s sides. Young tadpoles live in liquid that collects inside.

3Spike-nosed tree frog is a second name for the long-nosed tree frog. A herpetologist found the species during a 2010 expedition. The route led into New Guinea’s Foja Mountains. Few people had explored that country. Its distance from other places earned a nickname. People call it the Lost World. Size is not what makes this tree frog stand out. A long nose does. No other frog has a nose quite like it. A calling male lifts the nose. The nose then looks like a spike. The call ends, and the nose drops. The reason is unknown. The long nose also earned the nickname Pinocchio frog. Discovery happened at a campsite. The frog sat on a bag of rice. The same 2010 Foja Mountains trip produced the blossom bat. A bat is a mammal. Even so, people compare this one with a hummingbird. The nickname is hummingbird of the bat world. Nectar is its drink. A long tongue reaches the nectar. Rainforest trees supply the flowers. Feeding does a second job. The bat pollinates the flower. Seeds can form after that. New plants can grow from the seeds. Madagascar was the site of an expedition in 2005. That trip revealed Goodman’s mouse lemurs. A mouse is close to their size. Night is when these tiny lemurs move. They jump from tree to tree. Daytime rest sometimes happens in a nest. The nest is a vacant one that birds once used. Madagascar is the only place where lemurs live.

4Brazil’s tabletop mountains are the only home of Sazima’s tarantulas. Climate on those heights is not the climate of the land below. Animals with backbones are called vertebrates. Scientists think vertebrates are a small slice of life. Their share of all species is only 3 percent. The familiar animals sit in this group. The ones most similar to people sit here too. Amphibians belong in the group. Reptiles belong in it. Birds belong in it. Fish belong in it. Mammals belong in it. Animals without backbones are called invertebrates. They make up the other 97 percent of animal species that science knows. Some invertebrates frighten people more than others. Tarantulas can be in that group. Their bodies are big. Hair covers them. About nine hundred species exist. They hunt other animals. Small mammals can be killed by the largest species. Lizards can be killed by them. Birds can be killed by them. Sazima’s tarantula looks different from a typical fright. Beauty is its special trait. Dark blue covers the body. The color almost seems to glow. The habitat of this arachnid is extremely small. High mountains in Brazil are the only place it lives. Insects usually pass through several stages as they grow. Planthoppers do the same. Wings on a young planthopper are only starting to form. South America’s rainforest hid the troll-haired planthopper until 2013. Good looks may not be its strength. Its hair, at least, is striking. The strands are not true hair. Wax leaves the insect’s belly as secretions. Those secretions become the wild coat. One idea explains the coat. A predator grabs, and the coat breaks away. The planthopper then leaps clear. That idea is still only a theory. Scientists have not confirmed it.

5Greek stories tell of the Gorgons. Hundreds of snakes covered each Gorgon’s head. Hair was absent, and snakes stood in its place. Those beings gave this starfish the Gorgon’s head name. The year 2010 is when scientists found this starfish. It lives far below the waves. The depth is about half a mile. In meters, that depth is 800. The ocean there is the North Atlantic. This animal is a basket star. Five appendages leave the body. They curl, and they branch, and they look like arms. Tips on those five appendages can number five thousand. Plankton is part of the diet. Shrimp drifting in the water is part of it too. The tips gather that food. Walking is another use for the appendages. The animal moves along the seabed on them. Danger brings a third use. The appendages wrap the body. A tight ball is the result. The ball is a shield. Much of Earth’s ocean is still unknown. The seas are simply huge. The walking bamboo shark was not unknown for that reason. People did not name it until 2013. Spots and bands on its body do not match other bamboo sharks. Humans have little to fear from it. That is true of most sharks. Indonesia’s coast is where it lives. Color is what revealed the new species. Scientists saw that its coloration was not the same. Experts expect a length of about 30 inches. That is about 80 centimeters. Fins push the body over the ocean floor. The shark is hunting while it moves. A wiggle makes the motion look like walking. Rarity is a problem for these sharks. Indonesia’s government has begun steps that protect them.

6An olinguito can be confused with an olingo. The olinguito face is smaller. It is also rounder. The tail is shorter. Say the name as oh-lin-GEE-toh. For a long time, nobody noticed the olinguito as its own animal. People kept treating it as something else. Researchers caught the error in 2013. The wrong name had stuck past a hundred years. A teddy bear is a fair comparison for this mammal. Night is when it travels. It leaps among the trees. Raccoons have a family of relatives. This animal is the smallest member of that family. Ecuador is one place it lives. Colombia is the other. Thirty-five years had passed since the Americas gained a new species of this type. The olinguito was that next species. A species can stay unnamed even while people see it. They may file it under a species they already know. Similar looks are the usual reason. The match is on the outside, at least. Science calls these cryptic species. Genetic code is what finally separates them. DNA tools are spreading. Distinct species are being reported more often because of those tools. Dense brush hides the Cambodian tailorbird. New birds are nearly as seldom found as new mammals. A find inside a major city is rarer than that. The year 2009 brought this bird to researchers. They found it in Phnom Penh and in the area around the city. One bird turned up amid a road construction site. Tests, taken as a full set, showed a species of its own. Genes were part of the study. Feathers were part of it. A pretty song was part of it too. Warbling is something every tailorbird does. The songs are never quite the same from one species to another. This bird’s song marks it off from every other tailorbird.

7From 2000 to 2009, finds can be sorted by type. Insects lead, at 88,598. Plants come next, at 23,604. Arachnids total 12,751. Fungi total 11,984. Crustaceans total 7,070. Mollusks total 5,949. Bacteria total 4,417. Fish total 3,587. Everything else totals 18,351. International Institute for Species Exploration gathered the figures. A review is where the count was published. The title reads Retro SOS 2000–2009: A Decade of Species Recovery in Review. New species still surprise people. How many animal species share the planet? The estimates do not agree. They spread across a wide range. Experts do share one view. Discovery has not yet reached most species. Known animals also show hard problems. Populations of many species are tiny. People change the land. Habitats become small because of that activity. They become smaller still as time passes. Hope sits beside those problems. A new find can restart work to protect a habitat. It can also restart work to bring a habitat back. Rare animals in that place can be saved. Surprising animals can be saved too. Some of them are already known. Some are not known yet. DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. It is the code that holds genetic information in a living thing. An endangered living thing is in danger of vanishing completely. Extinction means a full group of animals or plants is gone. A gene is a basic piece of heredity. Traits move from parents to offspring through genes. Habitat means the natural home of a plant or an animal. A herpetologist studies reptiles and amphibians. A juvenile is a young person or a young animal. Maturity has not arrived yet. Population means every member of one species inside a set area. Something rare does not happen often. Another word for it is uncommon. A remote place is distant or cut off. A secretion is a substance, often a liquid. A plant or an animal makes it and lets it out.

13. Animals on Long Seasonal Journeys

1Caribou cross a river inside Alaska's Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. African elephants move through Kenya on migration. A severe dry season can push their travel past 100 kilometers (62 mi.). A trip of a thousand miles, people say, starts with one step. It might also start with a swish. It might start with a flutter. Many animals travel by land. Many travel by sea. Many travel by air. Each year they go hundreds of miles in order to eat and to raise young. Some go thousands of miles. This move, made each season or each year, is called migration. The distance makes the trips impressive. The exact paths make them impressive too. The many hardships along the way make them amazing.

2In much of the world, seasons are marked by which wild animals are present. A summer forest full of birdsong grows quiet in winter. Early spring feels still. Then tiny frogs begin to chirp as the air warms. Some animals that seem to vanish are only dormant. They rest when food is scarce and life is harsh. Frogs, for example, dig underground for the winter. They dig down during a severe dry spell too. Plenty of other animals do not become dormant. They do not shrink their need for food. They do not shrink their need for water. The journey leads to habitats with enough food and water for adults and for young. In Australia, burrowing frogs leave the ground after the first rains of winter. Winter sends many animals southward on the northern half of Earth. In the Southern Hemisphere they do the reverse. They go north. Seasons on the lower half of the globe run the other way. A closed road helps red crabs of Christmas Island cross in safety. The crossing is part of their yearly migration. Some migrating animals cover a fairly short distance. Those red crabs walk 8 kilometers (5 mi.) each year. They leave the island's forests for beaches nearby. They breed there when the rainy season begins. Set that walk beside the flight of monarch butterflies in North America. These bright insects fly as far as 4,800 kilometers (3,000 mi.) in autumn. They fly that far again in spring. Monarchs pollinate many kinds of wild flowers. Milkweed is what they need in order to reproduce and lay eggs.

3Every animal migration returns at set times of the year. Exactly how an animal knows the moment to leave is still a bit of a mystery. Leaving before the food is gone is essential. What, then, sets a migrator in motion? For some birds, the length of the day is the cue. These birds are called obligates. Their bodies are set to depart at a fixed time, whatever else happens. The semipalmated sandpiper is one example. Arctic coasts are where these birds nest and raise young in summer. They feast there on life from the sea along the shore. They store fat. Extra weight matters on a flight this long. When days start to grow shorter, the sandpipers leave. The flight covers an astonishing 4,000 kilometers (2,500 mi.) with no stop. They head south to winter homes in South America. Most of the path lies over open water. No place offers a rest or a bite of food. Sandhill cranes on migration, about half a million of them, often appear when spring is just starting. They gather along the Platte River in Nebraska. Other birds seem to time spring and autumn trips by temperature and by weather. The sandhill crane is one of them. Their long route runs between the Arctic Circle and Mexico. The start may slip by days. It may slip by weeks. It may also come early by that much. The cranes ride tailwinds. They ride thermals, which are rising columns of warm air. On a good day those aids can carry them 650 kilometers (400 mi.). Waiting for the best weather lowers the effort. The journey crosses North America.

4Gray whales mate in warm water off Mexico's Baja Peninsula. They give birth there too. A mother waits until her calf is strong enough. Then the pair swims the long way back toward cold Arctic seas. Food is abundant there. No other mammal on Earth makes a longer trip every year. Good conditions can also start a migration in other species. Gray whales spend summer in cold water between Siberia and Alaska. They may eat for as many as twenty hours a day. In fall, ice spreads over the sea, and the whales turn south. They look for warmer water. A pregnant female can give birth safely there. On the journey they eat very little. The route covers 16,000 to 23,000 kilometers (10,000 to 14,300 mi.). Summer blubber, rich in fat, keeps them alive. People find their way with memory, with maps, and with technology. Animals on long migrations use several navigation tools as well. Birds and insects in the air carry a sense of direction inside them. Celestial bearings are the base of that sense. In daylight they judge where they are by where the Sun sits. Birds that migrate at night use the stars. Warblers do this. Blackcaps do this. One scientist cast pictures of a night sky onto a ceiling shaped like a dome. He wanted to learn how some night fliers pick a direction. Caged indigo buntings sat under the star display. They fluttered and faced the way they would normally fly. When he turned the star picture, the birds turned too. The test showed that star positions guide these birds.

5Cloudy skies hide the stars. What do birds use then? Birds can steer by Earth's magnetic field. Some other animals can too. Earth behaves a bit like a huge magnet. A magnetic field wraps around it. Certain animals feel the pull of that field at their own spot. The pull helps them choose a path. Researchers still do not fully know how this sensing works. One idea says sockeye salmon carry a compass inside the body. The compass aims them at their goal. At birth, a salmon can somehow tell its exact place in the magnetic field. That place is imprinted in memory. The Gulf of Alaska may hold sockeye salmon for up to four years. After that they go back to the fresh water where they were born. The swim covers thousands of kilometers. They release eggs, which is called spawning, at that exact point. They can sense the spot while coming in from the sea. In British Columbia, sockeye salmon return to the birthplace to spawn. Monarch butterflies raise a harder question, because the trip spans more than one lifetime. A full loop from Hudson Bay to Mexico lasts longer than one monarch lives. Butterflies born in Mexico must find a region they have never seen. Some animals are born ready to leave on certain days. In a similar way, monarchs are born ready to follow routes used by earlier generations. A magnetic map kept inside their genes may explain the instinct. Genes are the basic units of heredity. A trait moves from parents to offspring by means of a gene. In monarchs, genes somehow write the destination into memory. Thousands of monarchs can blanket one tree. The tree stands in an oyamel fir forest in central Mexico. They crowd together so they stay warm. They wait through the winter. In spring they fly north.

6Late November brings wildebeest onto Serengeti plains where the grass is short. Calves are born in February. In April the herd begins the great move back toward the north. September is when the herd fords the Mara River. By October they are turning south again. Many mammals on the move trust landmarks. A keen sense of smell guides them too. Two mammal migrations among the biggest ever recorded happen in Africa. Each year 1.5 million wildebeest take part in the great Serengeti migration. They travel between feeding lands in Tanzania and in Kenya. The route covers 2,900 kilometers (1,800 mi.). Grassy plains lie on the way. So does the rushing Mara River. The herds follow rain and greener grass toward the north. Zebras often join them. Gazelles join them too. Bats arriving at Kasanka National Park each autumn come hungry. By late December, when they leave, they have eaten more than a billion fruits. The bat gathering at Kasanka is just as astonishing. It is the largest mammal migration on Earth. Ten million straw-colored fruit bats come from nearly every part of Africa south of the Sahara. Northern Zambia's swamp forest is the patch where they gather. For several weeks they feast. The fruit appears after rains begin. By day they cover the tree trunks. At dusk they fly out to feed. Sooty shearwaters are dark birds that live by the ocean. They migrate vast distances over open ocean. Their route covers 14,000 kilometers (8,700 mi.). New Zealand lies at one end of the route. The North Pacific Ocean lies at the other. If the bird needs 29 days, a typical day covers 483 kilometers (300 mi.).

7Choosing the right time is only one problem for animals that migrate. Choosing the right direction is another. A still larger problem is getting past hazards. Some hazards come from nature. People build others. A jackal is one hunter these travelers may meet. Many migrators are animals that other animals eat. They must watch for predators the whole way. Lions rely on Serengeti wildebeest as a chief food. Jackals eat them too. Crocodiles wait in lagoons and in rivers. Hawks hunt the fruit bats of Africa. People hunt those bats as well. Dates and figs make the bats plump. Hawks also hunt songbirds along their migration paths. Those paths are the flyways of North America. Bad weather adds more trouble. A sudden storm can wreck a bird's flight plan. A big flock may be forced down in an odd place. People call that event a fallout. One fallout of songbirds struck south Texas in April 2013. Thousands of tired, hungry birds landed on South Padre Island. The island sits off the Texas coast. People who lived there set out fruit. They set out worms. The food gave the birds strength to fly north again. Changing weather has also broken migrations on land. It has broken migrations in the water. A warm spell can melt snow early. Floods then make travel harder for animals such as elk. A flooded river can spill over its banks. Salmon on the move can be pushed off their route. When the water drops, they can be left on dry ground. A drought can leave little food. It can also start wildfires that threaten herds on the move. Barriers made by people threaten long trips too. A dam blocks a waterway that fish once followed. A highway across a migration path puts animals and drivers on a crash course. A fence stops range animals that are migrating. They cannot follow old trails to feeding grounds that matter. In Wyoming, migrating pronghorn meet a wire fence. The lower wire, seen up close, has no barbs. A pronghorn can slip under it and not get cut.

8Structures that people value can still harm animals on the move. Giant turbines turn wind into clean electric power. Their huge blades kill migrating birds. They kill migrating bats. Big solar farms kill birds as well. The Ivanpah plant in the Mojave Desert of California is one example. Thousands of birds fly into tightly focused beams of sunlight. The beams burn them to death at once. Researchers answer these problems with tracking devices. They follow migratory animals. The records go into studies. The studies show how building projects change the environment. The facts can help planners keep new buildings off migration routes. Knowing the routes has moved people to help rather than harm. Knowing how the animals behave has done the same. In Florida, a scientist tags a young loggerhead sea turtle. After the tag is on, the young turtle begins a 7,250-kilometer (4,500 mi.) swim. More amazing still, the turtles finish in only seventy days. If one species earned the title of grand champion of migration, the arctic tern would earn it. Tiny trackers let scientists follow this bird. It flies between the North Pole and the South Pole. The finding stunned the researchers. The trip was twice as long as people had thought. The distance was an incredible 70,800 kilometers (44,000 mi.). Many Arctic terns do not fly a straight line from north to south. The route bends back and forth between Greenland and Antarctica. Swirling winds are the reason. The winds carry them along. The added miles spare the birds a huge effort. They avoid flying straight into the wind.

9Some areas now build wildlife bridges over roads. They build tunnels under roads. The crossings sit where a road meets a land migration route. Bridges and tunnels keep animals and drivers apart. Both stay safer. Engineers are improving energy machines that hurt migrators without meaning to. Vertical wind turbines are being developed. Someday they may take the place of the huge horizontal blades on wind farms. Fish ladders, built for this purpose, now stand beside certain dams. Those dams lie on routes salmon use. The ladders let the fish reach spawning grounds without harm. Pollution weighs on animals already tired from a long trip. Facts about that harm could lead to rules that protect them. In Alaska, a salmon leaps up a fish ladder. What stands out most is that the journeys continue. Year after year, the animals set out, even with every obstacle. Trips across land, through the air, and under the sea keep these species alive. Seeing why the trips matter can move us to act. We can help the journeys go on for many years. These words help with the topic. Celestial bearings are a sense of place in space and in time. The Sun, the Moon, the stars, and other sky bodies are the guides. Dormant means not active now, but able to become active later. A hazard is a possible danger or risk. Imprinted means planted in memory so it stays. A magnetic field is the space around a magnet, an electric current, or a moving electric charge. Magnetic force fills that space. To monitor is to watch how something proceeds over time. A multigenerational event covers several generations. It can cover more than one life cycle. Navigational describes the work of steering toward a destination. An obligate animal must repeat a set behavior in order to survive. It may also need a set kind of living place. Optimal means best, or most fitting. Relocation means moving from one place to another. To trigger is to make something start.

14. Anne Frank’s Hidden Years

1Today Prinsengracht 263 is a museum. It is the Anne Frank House. The rooms have been restored. The rooms match their look from the time the family was hiding. More than a million people visit the site each year. July 5, 1942, in the afternoon, was when the bell at the door sounded. Anne Frank was thirteen years old. She expected the caller to be a friend. The postman instead carried a letter meant for Margot, the older sister. The letter told Margot to report for transport. The letter called the destination a work camp. Edith Frank, mother of both girls, was badly shaken by that news. Almost three years of World War II were already behind the family. Much of Europe was already under German control. Jewish families such as the Franks were being gathered in growing numbers. They were sent to concentration camps. Otto Frank arrived home. He reassured his daughters. He promised the family would not be split apart. Secret plans were already in place, made by Otto and by Edith. Both girls were told to fill their school bags. A diary was the first object Anne placed inside her bag. The diary had a red-and-green checkered cover. She had already begun to fill it with her private thoughts. The next morning, the Franks left their home. Heavy rain was falling. A small warehouse was where they went. That building was part of a company Otto had owned before German troops invaded. An apartment hidden upstairs swallowed them from public view. They would hide there for more than two years. During that time, Anne poured her thoughts onto paper. She poured her feelings onto paper too.

2Family pictures show Edith Frank. They show baby Anne with Edith. They show Otto Frank. They show Margot Frank. One picture shows Margot, Otto, and Anne together. Otto Frank was an officer for Germany during World War I. World War I ran from 1914 to 1918. Frankfurt, in Germany, was where he made his home once the fighting stopped. Everyone who described him called him kind. He was smart. He was hardworking. Edith's family was Jewish, and it was wealthy. Before she met Otto, she worked for her family's business. She married Otto in 1925. They soon had two daughters. Margot was born in 1926. Annelies Marie Frank was born on June 12, 1929. People called her Anne. Germany's loss in World War I left the country in deep trouble. The country was left broke. Many Germans felt angry. Many felt desperate. Rival political groups fought one another for power over the government. Germany felt the Great Depression with special force starting in 1929. Adolf Hitler used that public desperation for his own gain. Hitler had also served during World War I, just as Otto had. Hitler was antisemitic. In his telling, Jewish people inside Germany had caused the nation's loss. A picture shows Adolf Hitler at the center of a group in 1933. The party under Hitler's lead was called the Nazis. More Germans looked to that party, and its power grew. Those Germans wanted the Nazis to solve their problems. Full command of Germany's government passed to Hitler and his party in 1933. Otto and Edith Frank saw the danger at once. Law followed law under Nazi rule. The laws took away the property of Jewish citizens. The laws took away their rights. Both parents knew their children must leave Germany. They needed to leave before the situation grew worse. The Netherlands became their new country during 1933 and 1934. Many thousands of other Jewish people from Germany departed as well.

3The move to Amsterdam came before Anne's fifth birthday. No Dutch city is larger than Amsterdam. Anne was outgoing. She was curious about people. She was curious about the world around her. She liked school. Friends filled her days. She went to Ping-Pong parties. She ate ice cream. She had the love of her family. A picture shows Anne in 1939. Poland was attacked by Nazi Germany on the first day of September 1939. That attack started World War II. German forces entered the Netherlands in May 1940. By the end of that year, Germany's powerful army held most of Europe. Its air force did too. The Frank family had already fled Nazi Germany. Many other Jewish families had fled it too. Many of those refuge countries were now in Nazi hands. Otto searched for a path that would carry his family to safety across the ocean. Each try was stopped or turned down. Under those German occupiers, freedom for Jewish residents of Amsterdam kept shrinking. A series of anti-Jewish decrees did that work. Radios owned by Jewish people had been taken by 1939. Jewish people had to obey a curfew. Phones were taken from them during 1940 as well. A badge became required in 1941 for every Jewish person older than six. The badge was a yellow Star of David. The word Jew was written on it. Bicycles had to be handed over. They were forbidden to use trams. They were forbidden to ride in cars. The ban included their own cars. Keeping a pet was not allowed. They were forbidden to leave the country. Jewish children lost every school in 1942. Many Dutch people protested. Protecting Jewish friends meant real danger, and many Dutch people accepted it. They were often arrested for trying to help. They were often imprisoned. The situation grew worse. The four Franks began their hiding in July 1942. Hermann van Pels soon joined the family. He was Otto Frank's business partner. His wife, Auguste, joined them. Their son, Peter, joined them too. Peter was sixteen. That November, dentist Fritz Pfeffer moved in. He became the eighth person in the hideaway. A picture shows Peter van Pels.

4Visitors can still see that bookcase at the Anne Frank House. It once hid the way into the rooms Anne named the Secret Annex. In her diary, Anne called their hiding place the Secret Annex. The annex was livable. It was cramped. It included a kitchen. It included a bathroom. It had cold running water. Each room served as a living area. Each room also served as a bedroom. There was a single entrance. A bookcase hid that entrance. They covered the windows in every room. Covered windows kept lamplight from leaking out after dark. The people in hiding got great help from their helpers. Anne's word helper meant the friends, not Jewish themselves, who had promised support. Those friends would supply food. They would supply other things the family needed. The helpers included Miep Gies. They included her husband, Jan. They included other friends. People who used to work for Otto Frank were among the helpers. So were people who used to work for Hermann van Pels. The helpers risked imprisonment. They risked execution. They were helping to hide Jewish people. A 1935 picture shows Otto Frank seated at the center of his office workers. Miep Gies appears in that office photo with Otto. Johannes Kleiman is in it too. Victor Kugler and Bep Voskuijl are also there. A few years later, those workers labored to keep Otto and his family alive. Anne wrote that the helpers never complained. Each day they came upstairs with a smile. They brought newspapers. Best of all, perhaps, they brought conversation. On weekdays, employees worked on the floor below the secret apartment. Perfect quiet was required of Anne and of every person with her. Tiptoe was the only safe way to walk. They had to whisper. No one could run water. No one could flush the toilet. They feared someone would hear them. A reward was offered for reporting any Jewish person. Finding the family would have meant instant arrest.

5Anne used those silent hours for writing in the diary. She told about her family. She told about her housemates. She glued in old family photos. She wrote about how it felt to be growing into a young woman. The circumstances were grim. Many times she expressed despair. She expressed a great fear that they would be caught. The first diary ran out of space quickly. She moved on to notebooks. She moved on to sheets of loose paper. Writing made the fear easier for Anne to bear. It helped her cope with boredom. It let her shake off her cares. It let her shake off her sorrows. One hope she wrote down was work as a journalist. She also dreamed of becoming an actress. Pictures of film stars went up on a wall in the small room she used. Downstairs opened to them only after every worker had left. They could never go outside. The radio was a spot where they often sat together. They listened to broadcasts. June 1944 brought news they were glad to hear. A very large Allied army had come ashore in France. To the east, Soviet troops were pushing German forces backward. Otto started following how the fighting moved. He marked it on a wall map. People in the annex began to hope the Nazis would lose before long. Freedom might then return for the Franks and for the friends beside them. One photograph shows Germany's secret police. Their name was the Gestapo. The scene is 1940, with Jewish men marched out of Warsaw, a city in Poland. Hidden rooms were stormed by that secret police on August 4, 1944. How those rooms were found is still not certain. No action was open to the Franks or to the others with them. They raised their hands at gunpoint. Police looked through every part of the Secret Annex. One officer of the Nazis dumped out the briefcase Otto carried. Anne's writing was inside it. The officer wanted the briefcase so he could carry the Franks' valuables. Pages from the diary lay spread on the floor. Helper Miep Gies picked the pages up afterward. A drawer in a desk was where she stored them. She wanted Anne to have the pages again once peace returned.

6Early in September 1944, the family was sent to the camp called Auschwitz. Auschwitz was a concentration camp in Poland. Once inside, the family was separated. Otto was placed in the men's camp. The camp for women received Edith, Anne, and Margot. The winter cold took a terrible toll. Tiny amounts of food took a toll too. Backbreaking work took a toll as well. Edith tried with all her strength to aid the two girls. She even gave them all of her food. November 1 was the day the girls were taken away from Edith. The two sisters were moved to another concentration camp. That camp was in Germany. A picture shows women prisoners packed into barracks at Auschwitz. People labeled inferior were the ones Hitler and his party wanted gone from Europe. Those people included Jewish people. They included Romany people. They included gay people. They included people with disabilities. Pushing Jewish citizens out of Germany was their first effort. They made life so miserable that people fled the country. Mass killing had become the plan by 1942. Across Europe, Jewish people were seized and taken away. They were sent to concentration camps. Most of those camps were in Poland and Germany.
