When the war stopped, Nazi murder had taken six million Jewish lives. Five million people from further groups were killed as well. Germany surrendered in May 1945. That surrender ended World War II in Europe. What the freeing soldiers saw inside the camps filled them with horror. They found stacks of bodies. People still alive looked like skeletons that could move. Trainloads of children had been killed there. Trainloads of women had been killed there. Trainloads of men had been killed there. Otto Frank survived. He returned to Amsterdam. He already knew starvation inside Auschwitz had killed Edith. He still hoped that Margot and Anne were alive. Soon a friend brought horrible news. That friend had met both girls inside the camps. Illness had struck Anne. It had struck Margot too. They died in February 1945. Her age was only fifteen. A picture shows Otto Frank in 1976. Miep Gies gave Otto Frank five notebooks. Loose pages of Anne's writing, more than two hundred of them, came with those notebooks. He was struck at once by Anne's talent. He later said he had not known how deep her thoughts went. He had not known how deep her feelings went.

7Seventy years of readers have opened this diary. Translators have put the text into more than sixty languages. Buyers around the world have taken more than thirty million copies. Anne's work has been adapted into a play that won awards. It has been adapted into a film. It has been adapted into two television miniseries. In the United States, schools have read the book for decades. Teachers have taught it for decades too. Anne's writing offers keen insights. Readers meet the inner life of a teenager trapped in a terrible time. Her story warns every age about hatred. It is a warning against extremism. Printers in the Netherlands produced the book first. Its title is Anne Frank: The Diary of a Young Girl. That was two years after the war. In time the book sold widely, as a best seller, in many countries. Through Anne, a great many readers see a single person inside the Holocaust's terror. She was a young writer. She was a talented writer. The years she should have lived were taken away. The world also lost how far her talent might have gone. Her potential was stolen from the world too. A picture shows Anne at age twelve.

15. Beasts in the Myths of Old Greece

1A map of ancient Greece around 750 bce marks Macedonia and Troy. It marks Asia Minor, Greece, and the Aegean Sea. It marks Delphi, Athens, and Mycenae. It marks Europe, the Mediterranean Sea, and Sparta. It marks Africa and Crete. Coming pages open with an introduction. Centaurs come next. Sirens come after them. Medusa follows. The Minotaur follows her. Typhon follows him. A conclusion comes last. Useful words close the book. A greeting appears on one vase made in the fifth century bce. Heracles, said HAIR-uh-kleez, is the Greek hero. Cerberus is the dog he meets. That dog guards the underworld. It has two heads, or sometimes three. Myths appear in many cultures. A myth is a story that explains a big idea in a way people can grasp. Good and evil are ideas of that kind. A myth can take more than one shape. It can be a lesson. It can explain a historical event. It can explain a natural phenomenon. It can be a warning. In ancient Greece, religion and myth were tightly joined. The stories were not told for entertainment. Gods and goddesses carried deep meanings. Greek people used those meanings as guidelines for living. Heroes and villains share the spotlight with the gods. Fantastic creatures often stand at the center too. Another vase shows the goddess Athena. She helps Heracles attack the Hydra. That monster is made of many snakes.

2A Centaur had a human head and a human chest. The rest of the body was a horse. These creatures were violent. The animal part ruled the human part. Their weapons came from nature. Giant stones were one weapon. Wooden sticks were another. Greeks met them with metal shields, with spears, and with swords. Greeks saw the untamed Centaurs as their culture's opposite. Centaurs seemed animal-like. Emotion drove them. Greeks saw themselves as civilized. Reason drove them. Ixion, a king from Greece, is where the Centaur story starts. Zeus allowed him a life beside the gods and the goddesses. That home was Mount Olympus. What reached Zeus next was a rumor. Love for Hera, his own wife, had supposedly seized Ixion. Zeus tested Ixion. He made a cloud. The cloud looked exactly like Hera. Ixion did fall in love with that cloud. He believed he had found Hera. Birth came from the cloud. The child was the first Centaur. Anger drove Zeus to a punishment. Ixion had to spin forever. The spin was on a wheel of blazing fire. A sculpture from the Parthenon shows Centaurs winning a fight with Greeks. The Parthenon is a temple in Athens from the fifth century bce. Pictures of these battles were common all over ancient Greece. Drinking cups carried them. Stone temples carried them. Current events rarely appeared in Greek art. Myth pictures were how Greeks showed their feelings about the world around them. One great enemy was the Persians. Greeks tied the Persians to how wild the Centaurs were. Battle scenes of Greeks against Centaurs displayed Greek superiority over the Persians. Guest and host had a bond that ancient Greek culture treated as important. That bond is the lesson inside Ixion's tale and the birth of the first Centaur. Ixion showed disrespect to Zeus. Zeus was his host. The punishment taught what follows when that accepted custom is broken.

3Sirens, like Centaurs, were hybrid creatures. A Siren was a woman. She also had the wings of a bird, the legs of a bird, and the body of a bird. The story stands for self-control. Home for the Sirens was an island. Sea lay on every side of that island. Beautiful songs went out to sailors. The sailors lost control of their ships. The ships crashed on the island's rocky shores. Myth says a human life came before the Sirens' winged one. They served the goddess Persephone as maids. Say her name pur-SE-fuh-nee. Hades ruled the underworld. He carried Persephone away. He wanted her as his wife. Wings let the Sirens search for her. The search failed. They settled on the island. Many sailors died there, caught by surprise. A few sailors went past and lived. Orpheus, said OR-fee-uhss, was a famous Greek musician. He played so loudly that the Sirens' song could not be heard. Odysseus was a Greek king. He was sailing home from the Trojan War. He told his sailors to tie him tightly to the boat's mast. The sailors blocked their own ears. They would not be tempted to stop rowing. Greeks were proud of their restraint. Getting past the Sirens' song stood for a strength of will. Ancient Greeks valued that strength. Odysseus appears lashed to the mast on a Greek vase made in the fifth century bce. He could hear the song. He could also stay alive. The mythological Sirens connect to an everyday word. A siren, the device, blasts a warning that is loud. The same stories gave us siren song as an idea. That is something so appealing that you want it. The want remains even when the thing is dangerous.

4Beauty was what the Sirens were known for. Medusa was famous for a look that frightened people. Greek artists usually drew the Gorgons a certain way. The Gorgons were Medusa and her two sisters. The heads were large and round. The eyes were huge and staring. Hair was absent. Snakes grew from the skulls instead. Pointed tusks finished the face. Flared nostrils finished it. Tongues stuck out of the mouths. Medusa's sisters were immortal. Medusa herself was mortal. Humans could therefore harm her. She still had a defense. A direct look into her eyes turned a person to stone. The myth begins with an evil king. The woman he loved was mother to a boy, and the boy was Perseus. He wanted Perseus out of the way. He tricked the boy into a promise. Whatever the king named, Perseus had to fetch it. The wish was Medusa's death, and her head as proof. The king believed the deed could not be done. Gods and goddesses helped Perseus. He cut off Medusa's head. Two creatures sprang from her body. One was Chrysaor, said kriss-AH-or. He was a giant. His name means golden blade. The blade may refer to grain. The other was Pegasus, a horse with wings. Springs of water are what the name points toward. Some people read the killing as the end of a drought. Chrysaor and Pegasus then stand for the good that followed. Thriving crops are one part of that good. Flowing water is the other. Ancient Greeks trusted a frightening Gorgon face. They believed it would protect them. They believed it would ward off evil. Gorgon pictures went everywhere. Shields carried them.

5Another creature of mixed parts was the Minotaur. A bull's head sat on a man's body. The name joins two sources. Minos was the king of Crete, and the monster lived there. In the Greek language, taurus means a bull. Destruction followed the monster, so it was locked away. A maze held him, twisted in its paths, and people called it the Labyrinth. The maze lay beneath the king's palace. Athenian boys killed the king's son. Minos wanted revenge. He attacked the city of Athens. Athens wanted the attacks to end, so it made a deal. Every year it would send seven boys. It would also send seven girls. The Minotaur would receive them. Theseus was a brave boy from Athens. He volunteered to be one of the victims. In Crete, he was put in a cage. The other victims were in that cage too. Ariadne, said ah-ree-AHD-nee, was the princess of Crete. Love for Theseus struck her as soon as she saw him. She did not want the Minotaur to kill him. She asked the man who had built the Labyrinth. She wanted to know how Theseus could get out. The answer was a ball of yarn. Theseus should unwind it as he walked the maze. She also gave him a sword. The sword was for killing the Minotaur. After the kill, Theseus followed the yarn trail. The trail led him out of the maze. Once Greece ruled Crete, this myth became popular. Centaurs often stood for the Persians. In a similar way, bulls could stand for Crete. An important goddess in Crete held bulls as sacred. Theseus beating the Minotaur could stand for something larger. It could stand for the Greek conquest of Crete.

6The fierce Minotaur was tiny next to Typhon, said TY-fon. Typhon was a giant. Wings grew on him. One hundred heads grew on him. He stood for the destructive forces of weather. One head was human. Ninety-nine heads belonged to other creatures. Lions were among them. Bulls were among them. Boars were among them. Snakes were among them. Dragons were among them. From the knees downward, giant snakes took the place of legs. Fingers were missing. Fifty serpent heads coiled out of each hand instead. Fire flashed in his eyes. Flames whipped from his mouth. Only Zeus could match Typhon in battle. Zeus was the king of the gods. Rule of the whole world was what Typhon threatened to seize. Zeus answered with thunder and lightning. Typhon fought with fire and wind. The whole world shook from their battle. Zeus set fire to every one of the hundred heads. He then locked the monster under Earth. Ancient Greeks blamed Typhon for fierce winds. In great storms, those winds ran across land and across sea. Lava was blamed on him too. The lava poured from volcanoes. Comfort came from one idea. Zeus was able to beat the wrecking forces of nature for which Typhon stood.

7Ancient Greeks did not keep these creatures only to be entertained. They did not keep them only to be terrified. The creatures and their myths carried deep meanings. The meanings helped people understand the world of their own time. Challenges they faced were easier to cope with because of those meanings. A large place in ancient Greek culture belonged to these mythical creatures. They are still popular now. Children stay fascinated by the amazing stories. Adults stay fascinated too. Famous business marks borrowed pictures from these old creatures. A fashion label uses the head of Medusa. A fuel company uses Pegasus. A coffee company uses a Siren. To cope is to handle a difficulty with success. It can mean to overcome that problem. Hybrid means made from a mix of different things. Immortal means living forever. Death does not apply. A creature, in this book, is an animal. The word fits best when the animal is strange or unusual. Myths are traditional stories. They explain historical events, natural happenings, or social customs. Supernatural elements often appear. A culture is a particular society. It has its own ideas and customs. Defeating means winning a victory over someone else. A phenomenon is an event or occurrence that stands out. Dominated means controlled. It can mean overpowered. Restraint is control over one's actions. It is also control over one's emotions. A drought is a long dry spell. Little rain falls, or none. A water shortage can follow. Symbolized means an object, a picture, or a sign stood for an idea.

16. Bonfire Night and Guy Fawkes

1Pictures of the day often show masks of Guy Fawkes. An old nursery rhyme in the United Kingdom tells people to keep the fifth of November in mind. The rhyme names gunpowder, treason, and a secret plot. It says there is no reason this gunpowder treason should ever be forgotten. Adults and children across the United Kingdom meet each November 5. They come for fireworks. They come for bonfires. Friends and families shout with joy when flames take the figure on the fire. People call the dummy a Guy. People call this old festival Guy Fawkes Day. People also call it Bonfire Night. The day celebrates an event in 1605. King James I, together with his ministers, halted a secret plan that day. The plot would have blown up Parliament. Lewes, England, holds the largest Bonfire Night gathering anywhere. The account ahead asks who Guy Fawkes was. It tells the story of the Gunpowder Plot. It tells how the plotters were caught. It asks whether another conspiracy was involved. It follows the legacy of the plot. It then closes the story.

2York, England, in the year 1570, was his birthplace. Queen Elizabeth I was reigning then. Catholic lands and Protestant lands in Europe were fighting one another then. Struggles over power between the two faiths fed those wars. Under Elizabeth, practicing the Catholic faith was against English law. A fine was a common punishment for Catholics found at worship. They were often killed. Guy's grandparents were Catholic. His parents were Protestant. After his father's death, his mother took a Catholic husband. When Guy was a teenager, he decided to convert to Catholicism. Violence aimed at England's Catholics filled him with anger. He was angry about the cruelty too. England was behind him once he reached his early twenties. He traveled to the Netherlands. He joined the Catholic Spanish army. That army was fighting the Dutch Protestants. Twelve years of his life went to soldiering in Spain's army. He became an expert with explosives. A picture of the Gunpowder Plotters shows their leader, Robert Catesby, second from the right. In 1603 Elizabeth I, who was queen, died. King James I took the throne after her. He said Catholics would find him more welcoming. What followed instead were laws that pressed Catholics even harder. Many English Catholics had stayed loyal to the king. That same year Fawkes traveled to Spain, a later journey, not his first leave from England. He described the hard situation of England's Catholics to Spain's king. No help would come from that king. Fights between the armies of Spain and England already stretched back many years. A recent agreement had stopped that fighting. During his service he met other Englishmen in Spain's army. Violence against England's Catholics angered those soldiers just as deeply.

3At the same time, Robert Catesby was shaping a revolt in England aimed at King James I. Thomas Wintour, his cousin, was brought into the plan. Fawkes received their invitation in April 1604. They needed his skill with gunpowder. They needed that skill to make explosives. Fawkes did not hesitate. May 1604 found him back in London, meeting fellow conspirators inside a nearby inn. Secrecy was the promise they swore. Many women were part of the wider movement. Anne Vaux was one of them. Men alone took part in the plan itself. Their aim was an explosion at Parliament on the day it opened. All the ministers would be there. The king would be there too. The plotters would then place King James's daughter on the throne. Her name was Princess Elizabeth. Nine was Elizabeth's age then. The plotters believed they could shape her reign if they raised her Catholic. The sworn group numbered thirteen people altogether. Lambeth was where Robert Catesby kept a house. The Thames flowed between that Lambeth house and the Parliament buildings. Extra gunpowder was on hand because Spain and England were at peace. The plotters bought thirty-six barrels of gunpowder. They stored the barrels in Catesby's house. A royal bodyguard post went to the plotter Thomas Percy. His new house stood close to Parliament. By chance, he heard that a cellar under the Parliament buildings was available to rent. By night, the conspirators moved the gunpowder. They used a rowboat. The boat crossed the Thames, leaving Catesby's house for the cellar. Guy Fawkes took a false identity. He called himself John Johnson. Thomas Percy's servant was the part he played. That disguise let him walk inside Parliament's buildings without alarm. He did not raise suspicion. Watching those thirty-six barrels, kept under the building, was the task given to him. November 5, 1605, was the date chosen for Parliament to open. The plotters were ready. Some historians believe the powder he had was no longer fresh. They think it would not have exploded.

4A few days before Parliament opened, Lord Monteagle received an anonymous letter. He was a Catholic nobleman. He was loyal to the king. Stay away from Parliament on November 5, the letter told him. A dreadful event was coming, the letter said. The king's leading helper was the person who next saw that letter, from Lord Monteagle's hand. After the king learned of the plot, he ordered a full search of Parliament. Stacked wood filled much of the cellar when the first searchers looked. A second search was ordered. This time the searchers found Fawkes in the basement. He had fuses with him. He had matches that he was hiding. The searchers looked through the cellar more carefully. At last they found the thirty-six barrels of gunpowder. The guards caught Guy Fawkes in the act. He struggled against the men who had seized him. They tied him up. Questions waited in the king's own rooms, and that is where they led him. Fawkes told the king's guards what he had meant to do. Destroying the king had been his goal. Destroying Parliament had been his goal as well. He claimed that nobody else had taken part. He told the king he was sorry only because the plot had failed. The Tower of London became his prison. Exactly what he suffered inside that prison has never been proved. His last confession carried his signature by November 9. By that date he had given out the rebellion's full details. He had named his fellow plotters.

5News of the arrest reached the other plotters on November 5 in the morning. Giving up was not the choice of Robert Catesby or of several partners. A rising against the government was still their aim. Horses were taken at Warwick Castle by Catesby's small rebel band. The authorities chased them. The king's soldiers closed around the rebels on November 8. They fatally wounded Robert Catesby. They fatally wounded three others. The men still alive were locked inside the Tower of London. English courts heard treason cases against all eight plotters who were still alive. The courts sentenced them to death. January 1606 brought Guy Fawkes and three partners out to the yard. The place was the yard outside Parliament. They were executed there. The harshness of the punishment was a warning. Anyone else thinking of treason was meant to take that harsh end as a warning. Later, King James I spoke well of how loyal Fawkes had been to his cause. An inside scheme is what some experts think this powder plot may have been. In that view, the king's own ministers planned it. They hoped he would accept rules against Catholics that were harsher still. In that telling, the note of warning to Lord Monteagle may have been drafted by the king's top minister. Their work happened very near the king's own guards, which is hard to explain any other way. Some readers ask if the plotters served only as scapegoats. Did leaders want more support for a king who was unpopular? Clear proof for this idea has not been found. Once the plot came to light, the public felt relief. Knowing the king had survived eased people's fear. His survival, the king declared, counted as a miracle. He treated that survival as proof that divine right put him on the throne. A new law came from Parliament that same year. The law made November 5 an official day of celebration every year. The law turned an unpopular king into someone people would celebrate.

6Gunpowder Treason Day was the first name of the holiday. Church bells were rung, according to writings from those years. They lit bonfires. England already liked to burn models of disliked people on outdoor fires. Evil spirits, people thought, would leave if those figures burned. From November 5 onward, the figure on the bonfire was made to look like Guy Fawkes. Newer pictures sometimes put fireworks in his hands and set Parliament behind him. Local customs for this night survive in parts of Britain. Bonfire societies exist in Lewes, a town of southern England. Those societies date back to 1679. The participants wear elaborate costumes. They carry torches through the streets. Some towns now burn images of well-known people the public dislikes. They burn those figures instead of the traditional Guy Fawkes. Late in the nineteenth century, grand shows of fireworks grew very popular in towns and in cities. Torch-lit processions had become popular too. The processions led to the place where the bonfire was held. They led to the firework displays. Today, local charities usually organize the bonfires. Municipal organizations organize them too.

7What this day marks is that the powder plot failed. Their goal had been the death of England's king. That attempt was more than four hundred years ago. Millions across the United Kingdom still gather around bonfires each November 5. They still enjoy fireworks that night. Some people see Guy Fawkes in another way. To them, he is someone who defended his own beliefs. They see a person who fought against oppression. Parliament's buildings get a traditional search by guards once each year. That search happens ahead of Parliament's State Opening. They make sure no would-be plotters are hiding in the cellars. A calculation was worked out by scientists at the Institute of Physics. The conspirators hid 2,500 kilograms of gunpowder. That weight equals 5,512 pounds. They figured harm could have reached about 490 meters out from the blast's middle. That distance equals 536 yards. Guards prepare for their yearly search of Parliament. Guy Fawkes has an island named after him. The island is in the Galapagos Islands, in Ecuador. People call it Isla Guy Fawkes. Anonymous describes a thing with no known name, no known identity, and no known origin. Large outdoor fires made for a celebration are called bonfires. People who join a secret plan are conspirators. Convert means a person leaves one faith, belief, or outlook and takes up another. A dummy is a figure that looks like someone or models that person. Loyal means faithful to a person, a government, an institution, or a cause. A plight is an unfortunate or terrible situation. A plot is a plan or scheme. Processions are lines of people or vehicles moving in a formal parade. Rising against authority, or against power, is a rebellion. It is an uprising. An uprising aimed at a government, or at some other power, is a revolt. Betrayal of one's own government, or of one's ruler, is the crime called treason.

17. Breathing Gear for Swims Underwater

1In California, in the United States, a group of boys built diving helmets in 1933. The boys made those helmets from sections of hot water heaters, from boilers, and from other objects they had found. The found pieces supplied the parts, and the boys joined those parts into helmets a person could wear in the water. A world map is worth a close look. Notice how much of it is blue. Water covers more than 70 percent of the surface of planet Earth. That blue is not a thin rim around the land. It is most of the surface the map can show. Experts reckon that less than 5 percent of Earth's oceans has been explored. Most of what hides under the surface is still a mystery. People can name the oceans and trace their shores, yet the greater share of that water has not been visited in any close way. An invention from the 1940s helped open the world under the sea. Two men from France created the Aqua-Lung. One man was Jacques-Yves Cousteau. Say his name ZHAHK EEV koo-STOH. The other was Émile Gagnan. Say his name ay-MEEL GAN-yahn. Today that gear is known as scuba. The long name behind scuba is self-contained underwater breathing apparatus. Each part of that long name has a job. The apparatus is for breathing. It is meant for use underwater. It is self-contained, so the breathing supply travels with the diver. The new gear weighed less than earlier equipment. It was easier to handle. A diver could swim under the water. A diver could breathe there too. Jacques Cousteau was a famous researcher from France. He photographed the oceans and explored them. The lighter gear let a swimmer stay down, look closely, and keep a steady supply of air.

2Cousteau also used a vehicle built for research under the water. In later years he filmed wonders of the sea around the world. Scuba gear and a camera sealed against water made the films possible. He could move with the gear and still record what he saw. His shows on television captured the thrill of scuba. They captured its grace. They captured its freedom. Adventurous people felt moved to try scuba themselves. Millions of trained scuba divers now live around the world. Their skills and knowledge let them explore under the waves. They can meet amazing animals there face to face. People have long wanted to swim underwater and still breathe. The first modern diving bell was built in 1535 by Guglielmo de Lorena, an Italian. Say Guglielmo as goo-lee-EL-moh. It was shaped like a cup turned upside down. Oak wood formed the shell. A small window was set in it. The bell covered a diver from the top of the body down to the elbows. The hands stayed free so the diver could work. A valve at the top let used air out. A small cask was linked to the bell by a tube. Fresh air came from that cask. Air pressure inside the bell held the water back, so the diver's head and chest stayed in a pocket of air. About a hundred years later, someone invented the air pump. Helpers on the surface could then push air down to divers. Suits covering the whole body came into use for divers early in the 1800s. They wore helmets of copper. They wore boots made heavy on purpose. The outfit let them move more easily under the water. It let them work more easily too. Some worked as salvagers. They raised valuables from ships that had sunk. Air still had to be pumped down from the surface. One picture shows a diver from the late 1800s. That picture records the older way of going down, with weight on the feet and air sent from above.

3In 1825 the Englishman William James built the first sort of scuba unit. Tanks of compressed air connected to a diving helmet. Divers could carry their own air. They controlled the flow by hand. A valve had to be turned on and off. The air was no longer only a stream sent down from helpers above, yet the diver still had to manage the valve with care. Cousteau and Gagnan brought out the Aqua-Lung in the 1940s. Scuba diving changed completely. Other inventors were chasing similar ideas. The French pair built a breathing system that was small. It was simple to use. The price was fairly low. The great step forward was a regulator designed with care. The diver held it in the mouth. Fixed to the tank, it fed high-pressure air to the diver. The air arrived at a pressure the body could use. Breathing felt natural. For the first time, a diver could swim easily while carrying the air supply. The gear opened paths into the undersea world. People who were not professional divers could enter too. A photo from California in 1950 shows Cousteau on the right. He wears a dive suit of fabric and rubber. He is trying an early Aqua-Lung. For a person who likes snorkeling or other fun in the water, scuba adds a real extra depth. Study is part of learning to dive. Training is needed to dive safely and well. Most people begin with Open Water Certification. A scuba shop can provide it. A training center can provide it too. Classes meet in a classroom. Students also train in a pool with an instructor. A written test must be passed. Four practice dives must be done in a lake or in some other open water. New divers must show the instructor a set of skills. They must put scuba gear together and use it the right way. They must go down safely and come up safely. They must deal with gear that fails. Most Open Water courses last two weeks or longer. At the end, the diver gets a certification card. One of several approved training groups issues the card. With the card, a certified diver can rent gear. The diver can dive in places around the world. An instructor shows junior divers what to do if a mask comes off underwater.

4Junior Open Water Certification is open to children aged ten through fourteen. A junior diver must stay with an adult who is already certified. For safety, training for ages ten and eleven stops at 12 meters (40 ft.). Groups that train divers usually tell adult beginners to stay above 18 meters (60 ft.). A shallower dive makes the surface easier to reach if trouble starts. Training gets divers ready for conditions that are unlike anything on land. It gets them ready for surprises. The gravest hazards come from breathing air that has been compressed. Pressure grows as a diver goes deeper. Every dive needs a careful plan for depth. It needs a careful plan for time. Nitrogen narcosis is one risk. Deeper dives raise that risk. Air holds nitrogen, which is a gas. Under the water, nitrogen from the compressed air leaves body tissues more slowly than it does at the surface. Bubbles can form. The bubbles affect the nervous system. Narcosis can weaken vision. It can make a diver feel light-headed. It can cause confusion. Signs of nitrogen narcosis are not the same for everyone. Depth matters. The dive site matters too.

5Decompression sickness is another grave danger. People also call it the bends. It can strike if a diver stays down too long. It can strike if the trip upward is too fast. Dives past 30.5 meters (100 ft.) raise the risk in particular. Gas bubbles form and then swell inside muscles and other tissues. The pain can be severe. The sickness can kill. Divers learn to rise slowly so they can avoid it. They may pause at set depths on the way up. The pauses are decompression stops. During each pause, risky gases can exit the body. A diver who gets the sickness can be treated. A decompression chamber is used when one is nearby. Divers are not the only people who have suffered this sickness. Work on New York's Brooklyn Bridge started in the 1870s. Laborers went down into huge underwater boxes called caissons (KAY-sahnz). Pumps kept air pressure high inside the boxes. The pressure held the water out. The laborers dug into the bed of the East River. They were making the base of the giant bridge. Back on the surface, many of them reported headaches. They reported pain in their joints. At least five of them died. Each death was later tied to decompression sickness. A barracuda may swim near a diver. Someone new to diving may fear sharks. Stingrays may seem just as frightening. In truth, these animals rarely threaten a diver. Attacks by sharks or by other sea animals are extremely rare. Divers are taught to treat every wild animal with great respect. They keep a safe distance. The gap protects ocean life. It protects the diver. Scuba training can also open jobs. Extra certificates often prepare a diver for harder work. A salvage diver is a specialist. This diver finds cargo lost at sea. This diver brings that cargo up. An offshore diver or a water welder works in construction. The job is building and fixing oil rigs and other platforms at sea. A police diver is an officer. The work includes search and rescue. It includes investigations under the water. An underwater photographer runs a camera. The specialty is pictures and films made below the surface. A scientific diver is a scientist. Geology is one field studied this way. Archaeology is another. Marine biology is another. Further fields use scuba too.

6Once training and a certificate are in hand, a diver can go exploring. Wonderful dive sites exist all over the globe. Four places show different kinds of diving done for enjoyment. Reef diving is one kind. The Great Barrier Reef is a famous site for that kind. Coral reefs are the finest places to see bright fish and other sea life. This reef system is the largest on Earth. It stretches some 2,300 kilometers (1,400 mi.) beside the coast of Australia. Visitors can swim beside whitetip reef sharks. They can swim beside potato cod. They can swim among many forms of coral. Wreck diving is another kind. Biscayne National Park in Florida is a site for it. The marine park holds more than one hundred places of archaeological interest. Forty-three of them are shipwrecks. One ship was the Guerrero. It went down in 1827. It was carrying Africans who had been enslaved against the law. Young divers get training in a program called Diving with a Purpose. They study the Guerrero site and other sites. They hope to find ships wrecked during the Atlantic slave trade. They hope to record those ships. Freshwater diving is a third kind. Riviera Maya in Mexico is a site for it. Eastern Mexico holds many caverns underground. Pools of fresh water in them are called cenotes (sih-NOH-teez). Clarity is usual in this water. It is cool. Dos Ojos ranks among the most impressive cenotes for diving. It is a large underground web of caverns and caves. Cold-water diving and drift diving form a fourth kind. The Channel Islands of California are a site for both. Ocean water off California is cold. Warmth comes from a thick wet suit or from a dry suit. A dry suit lets in no water at all. Many divers choose dry suits for cold water. They choose them for diving under ice. Channel Islands dives also call for drift-diving skill. Ocean currents carry the divers from place to place. A chase boat follows behind. The boat picks them up when the dive ends. Divers can see forests of kelp under the sea. Around the Channel Islands, those forests shelter many kinds of marine animals. Lobsters live there. Bat rays live there. Sea lions live there. Otters live there.

7A dive into a lake or an ocean feels like a drop into a different world. Life under the surface does not match life on land. Scuba lets a diver see that strange, beautiful place up close. Divers often say that gliding underwater is an awesome feeling. It is like hovering. It is like flying. In Mexico's Sea of Cortes, a diver takes a photo of a sea lion. Scuba is an enjoyable skill to learn. Training plus good judgment makes it very safe. It is thrilling as well. It is a bold way to visit places that few people ever see. Advanced divers who dive for fun may go no deeper than 30.5 meters (100 ft.). To avoid the bends, training says a diver should rise no faster than 9 meters (30 ft.) each minute. A diver at 30.5 meters (100 ft.) needs a set time to reach the surface at that rate. The time is 3 minutes and 20 seconds. These words help with the topic. Air pressure is the push of air in the atmosphere. Nitrogen narcosis is a confused state of mind. It happens when nitrogen enters the blood while pressure is high, as in a deep dive. An ascent is a move upward. A certification is an official paper. It proves that a goal was met. Recreational describes rest or an activity done for enjoyment. Compressed describes something squeezed tightly. A regulator may be a device. It may be a person. Either one controls how much of something flows, or how fast. Decompression sickness is a dangerous illness. Staying down too long can cause it. Rising too fast can cause it. A salvager recovers pieces of a ship after it has wrecked. A valve opens and closes. It manages the flow of a liquid, a gas, or some other material. A descent is a move downward. A hazard is a possible danger or risk.

18. Cathy Freeman

1Cathy Freeman lit the Olympic torch at the opening ceremonies of the 2000 Games. Those ceremonies were in Sydney, Australia, and included the Sydney Opera House. The whole world watched her win gold in the 400-meter race. More than one hundred thousand Australians cheered when she crossed the finish line. On her victory lap, the Australian flag and the Aboriginal flag wrapped around her shoulders. It was the first time the Aboriginal flag was carried at the Olympic Games, and it became an important moment in Australia’s history. She was the first Aboriginal Australian to win an individual Olympic gold medal. She became an inspiration for Aboriginal Australians and a role model for people all over the world.

2Catherine Freeman was born in Mackay, Queensland, Australia, on February 16, 1973. She was one of five children. Both of her parents were Aboriginal people. Her mother, Cecelia, was of the Kuku Yalanji people. Her father, Norman, was of the Birri Gubba people. Norman left the family when Freeman was five. Cecelia later married Bruce Barber. Barber became her stepfather and her first coach. Aboriginal peoples were the first people on the mainland of Australia. Torres Strait Islanders live on islands north of Australia. About five hundred groups have their own languages and traditions. Indigenous people are about 3 percent of the population.

3At age sixteen, Cathy won gold with the 4 × 100-meter relay at the 1990 Commonwealth Games. More than seventy teams from nations and territories compete, and she was the first Aboriginal gold medalist there. She was voted Young Australian of the Year by the National Australia Day Council. In college she studied history and politics and learned about the British takeover of Australia that began in 1788. She also learned about the genocide of Aboriginal peoples, and her grandmother was part of the Stolen Generations. From 1910 to 1970, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were forcibly taken from their families. They were sent to boarding schools, pushed to adopt white culture, and barred from their languages and traditions. The government sought to erase Indigenous life, many children never saw their families again, and survivors later heard a prime minister’s apology.

4Freeman said she was often made to feel ashamed of her Aboriginal heritage as a child. She did not want other Aboriginal children to feel the same way. As she learned her people’s history, she grew determined to represent them and be a role model. At the 1994 Commonwealth Games she won gold in the 200- and 400-meter races and carried both flags. Some non-Indigenous people called it a protest, but she showed pride, ancestral injustice, and ongoing racism. In 1996 she won Olympic silver in the 400 meters, but rules barred the Aboriginal flag, so she wore a tiny one on her shoe. She then took two months off to visit schools and meet Aboriginal children around Australia. She believed her success brought dignity and pride, and in 1998 she was named Australian of the Year.

5The Aboriginal flag became an official Australian flag in 1995, after Freeman first carried it on a victory lap. Artist Harold Thomas designed it with a black top, a red lower half, and a yellow circle. Black means the Aboriginal people, red means the earth and their bond with the land, and yellow means the Sun. The flag was first flown on National Aboriginal Day in 1971. In Sydney in 2000, Freeman won the 400-meter gold and again wrapped both flags around her shoulders. That broke a rule against any flag but the national flag, and she was warned she might be disqualified. She was not disqualified, the crowd cheered, and many people saw the flags as a sign of unity. She became a symbol of reconciliation after one of Australia’s largest marches, when 250,000 people walked four months earlier.

6Reconciliation means better relationships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous people in Australia. Supporters want respect for Indigenous cultures, equal rights, honesty about past harm, and real unity. On National Sorry Day, Australians march to recognize Aboriginal grief and loss. In 2001 Freeman received the Medal of the Order of Australia for outstanding achievements. She retired from running in 2003 and gave time to charity and Aboriginal issues. Since the takeover, racism has limited Aboriginal jobs and education, and about 30 percent live in poverty. In 2007 the Cathy Freeman Foundation began working with elders to improve education for remote Indigenous children. It seeks the same chances for those children, and Freeman runs with them to promote athletics in remote communities.

7Freeman wanted to show Australia and the world that Aboriginal people deserve respect and dignity. She wanted Indigenous people, especially children, to know what they are capable of. She wanted them to feel pride in their heritage. During her career she brought attention to the mistreatment of Indigenous people in Australia. She still supports their fight for equality today. Long after her Olympic gold, she is a role model for Aboriginal people and for all people. In 2001 she posed with her World Sportswoman of the Year award.

19. Children Who Marched for Rights

1On May 5, 1963, a group of Black girls sits inside a fairgrounds building. The city is Birmingham, Alabama. Arrests during civil rights demonstrations had brought them there. May 2, 1963, arrived in Birmingham, Alabama. School was skipped by over 1,000 Black children. The plan was to gather at 16th Street Baptist Church. They did. At one in the afternoon the march started. Groups held about fifty children each. Pairs stepped out of the church doors. Hands clapped. Voices laughed. Songs rose. Lessons of nonviolent direct action were already in them. Their target was racial segregation. That system forced Black people apart from white people. Some people ranked this city as the most divided by race in the United States. Police in the city were all white. They waited with batons. Dogs waited with them. Fire hoses waited too. The days that followed became one of the movement's most dramatic confrontations. Through the Children's Crusade, the nation watched anti-Black racism show its ugliness. The world watched too. Fresh energy entered a long struggle. Black people were demanding equal rights in the country that was theirs. Young marchers appear in a picture from the Crusade.

2The long fight. Separation by race still happens in many American cities. In the early 1960s the separation was law. The name for those policies was Jim Crow. Under them, Black people were treated as second-class citizens in the towns where they lived. Whites Only signs turned Black people away from restaurants. Other public places did the same. Terror kept many Black citizens from casting votes. To stand up was to risk being killed. Violent supporters of segregation were the danger. The White Citizens' Council was one group. The Ku Klux Klan was another. Local officers often pretended not to see. Sometimes they aided the white groups. Racial violence took thousands of lives. Men died. Women died. Children died. A growing share of Black Americans was ready to resist. About that hate group. Members who join the Ku Klux Klan share a racist belief. It claims white people are superior to every other race. Founding came after the Civil War, fought from 1861 to 1865. Violence and terror were the tools. The goal was to seize white control again in Southern states. Lynchings, which are hangings, numbered in the thousands. Black Americans have been the chief targets. Hatred is also aimed at Jewish people. It is aimed at Catholics. It is aimed at members of the LGBTQ+ community. It is aimed at immigrants. Across generations, Black people had built a large part of American life. Work was hard. Taxes were paid. Military service was given. Equal rights were still refused. Justice was still refused. In 1954 the highest court in the land ruled on schools. It said separating students by race broke the Constitution. The year 1955 brought another shock. Two white men killed a teenager who was Black. His name was Emmett Till. A jury of white men only found them not guilty. Equal rights suddenly felt more urgent. Justice did too. The civil rights movement gained supporters. Momentum grew. Reporters paid attention. The best-known leader to emerge was Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. He served as a Baptist minister. He headed the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. People shorten that name to SCLC. He and others built a plan called nonviolent direct action. Big demonstrations would test laws that were unfair. Segregated towns would be disrupted. Police would face more arrests than they could handle. Training taught marchers to keep the peace no matter the blow. Even an attack was not a reason to strike back. The belief was this. Once more Americans who were not Black saw the cruelty, more would back the cause. Seeing the injustice would move them. A portrait shows Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.

3By 1963 some of that momentum had slipped away. Fewer bodies showed up to demonstrate. Papers sent thinner crews. TV networks sent fewer cameras. White officials were also learning. Softer attacks meant kinder headlines. SCLC leaders wanted a win too large to ignore. A new protest campaign was the answer. They aimed at Birmingham, Alabama. Tellings of this history often stay on the South. Discrimination was widespread in the North as well. It was widespread in the West. Black people met it. So did other minority groups. Unofficial rules called sundown laws set a curfew. People who were not white had to be out of the city limits. Homes there were forbidden. After dark, being caught could turn dangerous. Such sundown towns existed by the thousand. The map ran from Darien in Connecticut, to La Crosse in Wisconsin, to Glendale in California. Segregation signs used wording that readers today call offensive. Young people step forward. Early in 1963 Fred Shuttlesworth invited guests to his city. He preached as a Baptist minister in Birmingham. He was a cofounder of the SCLC. The guests were Dr. King and other organizers from that group. Their name for the effort was Project C. The letter C meant confrontation. Birmingham already had a grim name among Black people. Bombs had destroyed Black houses. Bombs had destroyed Black churches. Some called the city Bombingham. Attempts on Shuttlesworth's life had failed more than once. He was still alive. Not everyone welcomed Dr. King. Some Black residents did not. Most white residents did not. Atlanta, Georgia, was his base, so they labeled him an outsider. Trouble in their streets was not wanted. Nationally, though, he pulled attention the way lightning pulls the eye. The press arrived wherever he arrived. Project C opened in a slow, heavy way. Church rooms filled when he spoke. Asked to march, people paused. Most Black households in the city were working class. Pay was low. A lot of Black providers worked for white bosses. Jail might mean a lost job. Something worse was easy to imagine.

4Children had been watching the whole time. They had been listening. Workshops had also trained them in civil rights. Nonviolent direct action was part of that training. Youth organizers inside the SCLC suggested a dangerous shift. The idea drew on leaders from SNCC. The long name is Student Non-Violent Coordinating Committee. Let students stand at the front of the protests. Excitement ran through the young people. Jobs they might lose were rare. Putting children in jail would stain the city badly. The protests needed exactly that stain. Groups from churches supplied a key part of the stand against segregation. A picture shows them gathered. Argument followed. The plan was controversial. Dr. King refused at first. So did other leaders. Harm to children and to teens was not acceptable to them. Most parents refused too. Safety worried them. The youth still pushed to join. Discrimination was the air they had grown up in. They had seen parents humiliated. They had seen grandparents humiliated. Pools open to the public, but marked Whites Only, barred them from swimming. A lunch counter would not serve them a hamburger. A chance had come to speak. Inhumane treatment could be protested out loud. Word spread among Black students about a day called D-Day. One reading was Demonstration Day. Another was Ditch Day. On the local station aimed at Black listeners, DJs slipped hints between songs. The clock time was eleven in the morning. The calendar day was May 2, 1963. Grade-school children were included. Teens were included. College students were included. Pack a toothbrush, they were told. The meaning was clear enough. Night might not find them in their own beds. The hour struck. At one Birmingham high school, youth held a sign outdoors. It read It's Time. Minutes later, hundreds aimed for the doors. Classroom windows became exits for some. The jail letter. Police in Birmingham seized Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. on April 12, 1963. They said he had been parading without a permit. Eight days in jail followed. From that cell he answered white clergy of the city. Their plea had been patience. Their plea had been less disruption. He wrote that patience across centuries had gained Black people nothing. He told white religious leaders to quit offering excuses for discrimination. He told them to stand with civil rights for Black Americans. Readers know the piece as the Letter from Birmingham Jail. Few arguments for racial justice have ever hit harder. The young people met at 16th Street Baptist Church. From there, they marched straight into history.

5The man in charge of safety. Voters chose Eugene Bull Connor as commissioner of public safety. They did it seven times. His racism was vicious. It was aggressive. Public safety, in his hands, served white residents. Black people, children included, were abused to keep that order. Officers and firefighters held the front. Their job was to block young Black marchers. Downtown lay several blocks off. That was the marchers' goal. A photo shows Connor in those days. By three in the afternoon on May 2, more than 600 young people were behind bars. Prayer kept them going. Songs kept them going. The march was working as planned. National eyes were on the scene. Friday was May 3. Students skipped class again and tried for downtown. Connor prepared force. News writers were in place. Camera crews were in place. He ordered arrests to start. Batons shoved bodies. Batons struck them. Next he ordered hoses onto clusters of marchers. Streams hit with high power. Heads took the blast. Chests took it. Legs took it. The pain was sharp. Some people were thrown off their feet and sent rolling down the pavement. Trees became shelter. Buildings became shelter. Police dogs were brought in to attack and to scare. One picture freezes a firefighter aiming a firehose. High-pressure water slams into protestors. Before night, about two thousand more young people had been taken in. Local jails could hold no one else. Buses carried children and teens to the fairgrounds. Lockup waited there. Some cells were animal pens, and they stank. Plenty of marchers were not finished. Released prisoners turned around and got arrested once more. Courage like that pulled adults in. Ranks swelled. The city started to stop.

6How pressure worked. Saturday made Birmingham the lead story nationwide. TV pictures caught firefighters blasting water at young bodies. Newspaper fronts showed dogs. The dogs ripped clothing on marchers who had not fought back. Kennedy, the president, was in the capital. Reports said the pictures made him ill. He called SCLC leaders. He called Birmingham officials. A truce was his request to all of them. People he sent tried to help both sides negotiate. A settlement of some kind was the hope. His televised talk on civil rights came later, on June 11, 1963. A picture marks that speech. Protests, meanwhile, picked up again. Terror in Connor's style was biting less. Fear dropped among Birmingham's Black citizens, young and old alike. White owners of businesses had enforced segregation by choice. Now they counted what the trouble cost in money. Civic leaders counted the damage to the city's name. May 8, 1963, brought a pause. King and fellow leaders chose a pause. Marching would wait while talks went on. Tension filled the talks. May 10 produced a cautious deal. Public restrooms would lose their color line within ninety days. Drinking fountains would too. Downtown shops promised open lunch counters. They promised open rooms for trying on clothes. Young people still jailed would be let out. Arrangements covered that release. Bias in hiring was postponed to future meetings. So were other disputes. The drive had begun to desegregate a city long ranked among the most separated in the land. Young activists of a new generation had inspired the win. Another bombing. September 15, 1963, fell on a Sunday. Services were being held at 16th Street Baptist Church. A bomb went off. Robert Chambliss was named. Thomas Blanton was named. Bobby Cherry was named. The dead were four girls. One was Denise McNair, age eleven. Cynthia Wesley was fourteen. Addie Mae Collins was fourteen. Carole Robertson was fourteen. New support grew for the civil rights law that Congress would pass in 1964.

7What the march of children achieved. Energy from that march carried the wider movement forward. In hindsight, Birmingham was a turning point of real weight. One month later, Kennedy addressed the country by television. Birmingham was in the speech. He dared the nation to finish segregation completely. Federal laws on civil rights were promised. Black Americans would be protected. Tears came to many Black listeners. At last the president was backing their cause. Later years turned many movement aims into statutes. Congress acted the next year. The Civil Rights Act carried the date 1964. Segregation was outlawed. So was discrimination tied to race. Color was covered. Religion was covered. Gender was covered. National origin was covered. The Voting Rights Act came in 1965. State policies that had stopped Black Americans from voting were struck down. New laws did not erase racial prejudice. They did not erase discrimination. Fair treatment and equal treatment, though, opened doors that had been shut. Black Americans gained chances they had been denied. The United States entered a different chapter. Words to know. An activist works to change social life or political life. To negotiate is to seek a formal deal by talking it through. A confrontation is a clash, in words or in blows, between opposing sides. Nonviolent direct action stays peaceful on purpose. A strike can be the tool. A boycott can be the tool. A group, a company, or a government is pushed to change. Controversial means a matter that splits people into strong disagreement. Racism ranks one race above another and treats people unequally for that reason. A demonstration lets a crowd show that it supports something, or that it opposes something. Discrimination treats a person or a group unfairly over gender, race, age, faith, or some other difference. Segregation is a rule for keeping groups apart, and race is a common reason. To disrupt is to block the usual way a thing happens, or to slow it. Urgency is the sense that a problem must be handled at once. Momentum is the force that keeps a movement going, or growing, over time.

20. Code Talkers

1Cecil Trosip, a Navajo code talker, worked a radio in July 1944 on Saipan. Saipan is an island in the Pacific Ocean between Japan and Hawaii. On February 19, 1945, U.S. troops unloaded supplies at Iwo Jima, an island in the Pacific near Japan. A platoon of Marines jumped from a landing craft and struggled through the surf. Japanese gunfire met them on the beach. The unsure platoon leader radioed his commander for instructions. But they felt confident with Navajo radiomen who sent a code no one else could read. The Navajo call themselves Dine, which means The People.

2In 1942 World War II raged and good communication kept troops supplied and safe. The enemy intercepted messages and Japanese code breakers caused many American casualties. Philip Johnston learned of the problem from newspaper stories. He moved to the Navajo reservation with his family in 1896 and learned the language as a child. Few outsiders understood Navajo, which was only spoken and had no written symbols. He contacted military authorities in California about a Navajo code. Leaders were skeptical at first but agreed to test if it was fast and secure. The Navajo Nation is the largest U.S. reservation at 27,000 square miles, about the size of West Virginia, and it surrounds the Hopi reservation.

3People have sent hidden messages since ancient times. Invisible ink hid words until heat or chemicals made them appear. Ancient Greeks shaved a messenger's head, tattooed words on it, and let hair grow to cover the message. The receiver then shaved the head to read the words. Modern codes hide meaning rather than the message itself, so the code must be known. Julius Caesar shifted letters to make his cipher. A rail fence cipher writes letters on alternating lines and then joins them. Early in World War II, Japanese students who knew American English cracked U.S. codes almost as fast as they were sent.

4Using Native languages for codes was not new. In World War I Cherokee soldiers helped the 30th Infantry Division at the Second Battle of the Somme. Choctaw men of the 36th Infantry Division helped win battles in France, and Comanche codes helped too. Adolf Hitler, Germany's ruler from 1933 to 1945, sent students to learn Native languages after the Choctaw success. Japan sent students to study the languages as well. Other groups were too small to supply enough speakers, but Navajo men were more numerous and willing. Recruits once turned down for not speaking English became an asset because Navajo was hard to learn. Navajo belongs to the little-known Na-Dene family, so the Marines trusted that no one outside the United States would understand the code.

5Despite long mistreatment of Native peoples, Johnston recruited twenty-nine Navajo men for a marine platoon. They worked with the Field Signal School to build a code from their language. One part used Navajo words for letters, so shush, the word for bear, stood for B. A second part assigned new military meanings to 211 Navajo words based on looks or use. Owl meant observation plane, shark meant destroyer, and iron fish meant submarine. Whale stood for battleship and eggs stood for bombs. Oral tradition and strong memories helped the men learn the new words. Two cousins from the same reservation relayed orders over a field radio in the code.

6After brief training, time trials showed Navajo soldiers could send messages in seconds while others needed half an hour. The military adopted the code and more than four hundred code talkers served in the Pacific. At Iwo Jima six code talkers sent and received more than eight hundred messages with no errors. Keith Little said his weapon was his language and it probably saved countless lives. He spoke in 2009 and died in 2012 at age 87. Japan could not understand the code, which stayed secret after the surrender on September 2, 1945. The men stayed silent for years, then found jobs scarce and faced discrimination. Citizenship began in 1924, but the vote was not guaranteed until forty years later, and New Mexico saw first registrations in 1948.

7The secrecy ended in 1968 and the world learned of the code talkers' work. In December 2000 President Clinton signed a law awarding the Congressional Gold Medal to the twenty-nine original code talkers. In 2001 at the U.S. Capitol President Bush gave medals to four of the five survivors and shook hands with John Brown Jr. One code talker said that just maybe he had become an American citizen. The 2008 Code Talkers Recognition Act honored men who used their language to change history when native culture was discouraged. Their language and honorable actions helped the code succeed and helped the United States win the war. It is still the only spoken military code that has never been broken.

21. Come Explore Mexico

1A copper sculpture shows a mariachi player. This guide sets out its parts in order. First comes a travel brochure. Next comes the land. Then comes the best time to visit. The story of the country follows. Mexico City comes after that. The center and the south come next. Then come the Gulf Coast and the Yucatán Peninsula. Northern Mexico follows. Quick facts about Mexico come near the end. A word list closes the guide. A mariachi band plays together. This travel brochure is by Juan Rodriguez. It comes from Ms. Brown's Fifth-Grade Class. Welcome to Mexico. I love this beautiful country. I am glad we can explore it together. The history here is rich. The culture here is rich too. People who live here are very kind. Their hospitality feels out of this world. There is a great deal to see. There is a great deal to do. The real question is whether you will have enough time. You might rest on the shore of a beach. Mexico has many beaches for that. You might visit wonderful museums. You might see historic sites. You might walk through ancient ruins. A horseback ride in the mountains is possible. A boat ride through the wetlands is possible too. You could listen to mariachi music played nearby. Whatever you hope to do, Mexico has something for you.

2The Land. Let us start the tour with the geography of Mexico. Mexico lies in the southern part of North America. The neighbor to the north is the United States. Guatemala is a neighbor to the south. Belize is a southern neighbor too. Mexico is divided into a north and a south. The Americas are divided in that same way. In southern Mexico, most states have wide rural areas. A large farming population lives in those areas. Northern states are wealthier than southern states. The northern states are mostly urban. They are mostly industrialized as well. The central part holds more than half of the people. That central area is called the Valley of Mexico. The capital is Mexico City. Mexico City sits in the valley. Lists of world cities place it among the twenty largest. The Mexico City area is home to about 22 million people. The whole country of Mexico has about 130 million people. A map names the states and the federal district. The names include Baja California Norte, Sonora, Zacatecas, and Chihuahua. They include Coahuila, Nuevo León, Sinaloa, and Tamaulipas. They include Durango, San Luis Potosí, Baja California Sur, and Querétaro. They include Nayarit, Campeche, Hidalgo, and Yucatán. They include Jalisco, Distrito Federal, Aguascalientes, and Tabasco. They include Veracruz, Colima, Guanajuato, and Quintana Roo. They include Oaxaca, Chiapas, Michoacán, and México. They include Morelos, Tlaxcala, Guerrero, and Puebla. The Gulf of Mexico is marked along the east. A picture shows the Mexican flag. A seal is shown with it. Mexico's land covers 756,066 square miles, which is 1,972,550 sq km. How large is that area? The United States has room for about five Mexicos inside its borders. Mexico is divided into states. There are 31 states, plus a federal district. Every one of these areas has cool places to visit. The blue water is as varied as the people. The landforms are as varied as the culture.

3Mexico has many landform regions. Very few of those names sound like one another. One region is the Mexican plateau. Another is the central plateau. The Gulf Coastal Plain is a region. The Pacific Coastal Lowlands are a region. The southern highlands form a region. The Chiapas Highlands form a region. The Tabasco Plain is a region. The Yucatán Peninsula is a region. Say Yucatán as yoo-kah-TAHN. The Sierra Madre Occidental is a mountain region. The Sierra Madre Oriental is a mountain region too. The Sonoran Desert is a region. A map adds more names to the picture. The Gulf of California lies to the west. The Pacific Ocean borders the western side. The Gulf of Mexico borders the eastern side. Mesa Central sits in the middle. Volcán Pico de Orizaba is marked on the map. Sierra Madre de Chiapas rises in the south. Rivers on the map include the Yaqui and the Conchos. The Fuerte and the Lerma-Santiago are rivers too. The Montezuma, the Balsas, and the Suchiate are rivers as well. The Chihuahuan Desert covers dry ground. Baja California stretches as a long peninsula. Mexico City is marked on the map. A wider view shows North America and South America. Asia appears on the Ring of Fire map. Australia appears on that map too. Do You Know? Volcán Pico de Orizaba last erupted in 1687. Nobody reached the top until 1848. Only two peaks in North America stand higher. Do you know those two highest points? Mexico is a diverse land. For varied plant and animal species, it ranks third in the world. Mexico also lies in the Ring of Fire. That name means a Pacific zone where volcanoes are very active. I hope you will visit Volcán Pico de Orizaba. This dormant volcano is fascinating to see. No point in the country stands higher. The top reaches 18,406 feet, or 5,610 m. Mexico has cities. Mexico has rural areas. Mexico has deserts. Mexico has rainforests. Mexico has wetlands. Mexico has canyons. Every kind of environment you might want is here. Let us look further into my country.

4When to Visit. Keep the coastal climate in mind. Along the coast, the weather is hot. The coastal weather is humid too. If hot, humid days do not suit you, travel from October through May. Inland temperatures are almost always milder. Mountain temperatures are milder as well. Travelers who love dry weather should try Baja California. Say Baja as BAH-hah. The Sonoran Desert stays dry all year. The Chihuahuan Desert stays dry all year too. A picture shows desert cacti growing in Baja California's Sonoran Desert. My Country's History. The Spanish conquered the Aztecs in 1521. Before that year, Mexico was part of Mesoamerica. The Olmecs lived in Mesoamerica. The Maya lived there. People of Teotihuacán lived there. Say Teotihuacán as tay-oh-tee-wah-KAHN. The Toltec people lived in Mesoamerica. The Aztec peoples lived there too. All of these groups were here long before the Spanish arrived. Buildings they left can still be visited. Those buildings include temples. They include pyramids. They include ball courts. Among Mesoamerican civilizations, the Aztecs held the most power. The Spanish invasion changed the people. The invasion changed the land as well. Some people from Spain came here to live. Spanish colonizers forced many Indigenous peoples to leave their own religions. Those peoples were made to become Catholic. Learning Spanish was also forced on many Indigenous peoples. Many Indigenous languages are no longer spoken. Náhuatl is still spoken by about 1.5 million people. That language belonged to the Aztec Empire. The official language in Mexico today is Spanish. Until 1810, Spain held Mexico as a colony. A revolt by many Mexicans rose against Spain. Official independence came to Mexico in 1821. The country is a republic today.

5A picture shows the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlán. Tenochtitlán was the capital of the Aztec Empire. Mexico City. Now the tour turns to great cities. We start in the heart of Mexico. That heart is Mexico City. Under Aztec rule, this city was called Tenochtitlán. Say Tenochtitlán as tay-nohch-teet-LAHN. Aztec builders made many ancient ruins in the city. They made ruins around the city as well. Templo Mayor means Great Temple. That temple marked the site of the Aztec capital. Workers built it during the 1300s and the 1400s. The Spanish tried to bury the temple. In 1978, the amazing ruins were uncovered. The site is a museum now. Many cathedrals stand in Mexico City. Other Spanish architecture stands here too. Catedral Metropolitana is the largest cathedral in all of Latin America. Would you believe the building took nearly 300 years? Famous Mexican artists left painted art across the city. They left sculpted art as well. One of the best known is the muralist Diego Rivera. His murals of Mexican history date from 1929 to 1935. The murals are in the courtyard of the Palacio Nacional. Say Palacio as pah-LAH-see-oh. Say Nacional as nah-see-oh-NAHL. Many rulers have lived on the palace site. Moctezuma was an Aztec emperor. Before the Spanish conquest, Moctezuma lived on this same site. After the conquest, the site became home to Hernán Cortés. Cortés was a Spanish conquistador. Say his name as air-NAHN kor-TESS. Today the president's offices are inside the palace. Plaza de la Constitución is the square in front of the palace. People often call that square the Zócalo. It is one of the largest public squares in the world. Another major stop is the city's largest park. You can spend part of a vacation at Bosque de Chapultepec. Say Bosque de Chapultepec as BOHSS-keh DEH chah-pool-teh-PEK. A zoo is inside the park. A botanical garden is inside the park. You can buy a balloon there. You can buy a snack there. Museums are inside the park. Art galleries are inside the park. You can do all of this and never leave the park.

6More art museums and centers fill the city. One is the Palacio de Bellas Artes. Another is the Museo Dolores Olmedo Patiño. The Museo Mural Diego Rivera is here. The Museo Frida Kahlo is here. Many further museums wait as well. Frida Kahlo taught herself to paint. She is known for bold self-portraits. The painting of hers that I like best has a monkey in it. A picture shows Frida Kahlo's painting Self-portrait with Monkey. Shoppers in Mexico City will not leave disappointed. Visit the Bazar del Sábado in the Plaza San Jacinto. Bazar del Sábado means Saturday Market. The market sits in the San Ángel neighborhood. Mexican fruits are for sale at the Mercado de la Merced. Vegetables are for sale there. Candy is for sale there too. A picture shows candy sold at that Saturday market. The Center and the South. Northwest of Mexico City, buildings from the Spanish colonial years still stand. People sometimes call this area the Colonial Heartland. Rich farming has its center in this same area. The Spanish built many cities and towns in this area. They built them to use the silver deposits. Taxco lies southwest of Mexico City. Taxco has many beautiful silver shops. Farther west, the coast has many beaches. Acapulco is known for those beaches. Say Acapulco as ah-kah-POOL-koh. Decades ago, Puerto Vallarta grew into a popular beach resort. Hollywood stars came there to stay. A picture shows Spanish colonial architecture. Travelers who tire of the beach can visit Colima. Colima has been rebuilt again and again. Earthquakes hit often and keep damaging the city.

7After Mexico City, Guadalajara is the country's second largest city. Say Guadalajara as gwahdah-lah-HAH-rah. Many great places wait in Guadalajara. The famous Cathedral took more than two centuries to build. A short walk from the Cathedral passes a lot of Spanish colonial architecture. A picture shows the Cathedral at Guadalajara. Like much of Mexico, this region is a pleasure outdoors. Lago de Chapala is the country's largest lake. Boating there is a fine plan. Fishermen on Mexico's Lago de Chapala appear in a picture. Huasteca Potosina offers waterfalls, tropics, and mountains. Say Huasteca Potosina as wahss-TEH-kah poh-toh-SEE-nah. It lies in the state of San Luis Potosí. I also suggest a boat ride to Tamul waterfall. The water drops 344 feet. It falls into a canyon. Central and southern Mexico hold many ancient ruins. The ruins come from Mesoamerican civilizations. Teotihuacán may be one of the greatest Mesoamerican cities of all. Two great ancient temples stand there. They are the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon. Visitors come here more than to any other Mesoamerican site. A picture shows Teotihuacán's Pyramid of the Sun. So what was Teotihuacán? In about ce 400, about 125,000 people lived there. The name Teotihuacán stands for the place where gods were created. Residents were called Teotihuacanos. Many different Indigenous peoples lived in Teotihuacán. At that time it ranked among the largest cities in the world. Monte Albán was a city of the Zapotec people. Say Monte Albán as MOHN-teh ahl-BAHN. It is in the state of Oaxaca. Say Oaxaca as wah-HAH-kah. Their ceremonial site can be visited on a mountaintop. For a time, the Olmec used this place as a cultural center. The Teotihuacanos used it as a cultural center too. A picture shows Teotihuacán's Pyramid of the Moon.

8A picture shows El Tajin in Veracruz. Coast of the Gulf and the Yucatán Peninsula. The tour now reaches the tropical plains of the Gulf Coast. Jungle covers much of this land. Several Mesoamerican cultures once lived here. The Maya were one of them. The Olmec were one of them. The Totonac were one of them. Olmec artifacts turn up all over the region. A rich share of them is in the Parque-Museo de La Venta. A picture shows Mayan hieroglyphics. Ancient pyramids can be visited at El Tajin. For the Totonac, El Tajin was a major center of religion. Totonac people lived here between ce 900 and 1150. Quiahuiztlán is another place to see. Say Quiahuiztlán as kee-uh-weet-ZLAN. It was a city on a hilltop. Some 15,000 Totonac people once lived there. A picture shows an ancient Mayan ball court. Chichén Itzá holds the best preserved ruins the Maya left behind. Temples stand at Chichén Itzá. Mexico's largest ancient ball court is there. An observatory is there too. The Maya loved to study the stars. I love looking at the stars too. The Maya had a writing system of their own. Uxmal is another Mayan site worth a visit. Most Spanish cities in the Yucatán were built on top of Mayan ruins. Most Spanish towns there were built the same way. What else can a visitor do on the Gulf Coast? Almost anything. Museums are plentiful. Cathedrals are plentiful. Churches are plentiful. Do not skip the city of Veracruz. The waterfront promenade is a lot of fun. The arcades are a lot of fun too. Like the Colonial Heartland, this region grows a great deal of food. Sugarcane is grown here. Cacao is grown here. Cacao tastes wonderful. Coffee is grown here. A picture shows coffee beans.

9White sand beaches make the Yucatán Peninsula famous. The peninsula has plenty of those beaches. Water wraps three sides of it. Baja California is wrapped by water in that same way. A barrier reef near two islands is the world's second longest. Australia's reef is the longest one. The islands are Cozumel and Isla Mujeres. Say Isla Mujeres as EES-lah moo-HEH-ress. People like to snorkel at the reef. People like to scuba dive there too. Cancún is probably the favorite place for a suntan. This region is known for natural wells called cenotes. The wells are breathtaking. The Cenote de Dzitnup is probably the one people visit most. Say Cenote de Dzitnup as si-NOH-tee day ZEET-nup. It lies near Valladolid. Say Valladolid as bah-yah-doh-LEED. Can you believe the well was found only a half century ago? A picture shows scuba lessons. A picture shows that long reef beside the islands of Cozumel and Isla Mujeres. People call the reef the Great Mesoamerican Reef. A picture shows the deep northern canyon known as Copper Canyon. Northern Mexico. Many Mexican deserts lie in the north. Many mountains lie here. Many canyons lie here too. You may know the Grand Canyon in the United States. Copper Canyon is even bigger. The canyon is more than one mile deep. It belongs to the Sierra Madre Occidental range. A train can take you close to the view. From the train you see the deep canyon. You see waterfalls. You see lakes. The Rarámuri people live in this canyon country. Say Rarámuri as rah-RAH-moo-ree. They are famous for drums they make. They are famous for violins they make. For beaches and resorts such as Cabo San Lucas, choose Baja California. Baja California is a peninsula. Water lies along three sides. In winter, whales swim along the shore. The whales are migrating south. A picture shows Cabo San Lucas along the Baja California shore.

10Baja has no Aztec ruins. The reason is that the Aztecs never lived here. Ancient cave paintings can be found instead. Many people believe ancestors of the Cochimi made the paintings. The pictures show people. The pictures show animals. The colors used are black and red. Baja California's cave paintings appear in a picture. The most amazing ancient ruins here may be the adobe buildings at Paquimé. Say Paquimé as pah-kee-MEH. Adobe is brick made from mud and grass. Builders often stacked many of these bricks. The finished buildings look like apartment buildings of today. More than 3,000 people made those adobe buildings their home from the 900s through the 1300s. The buildings stood near the Casas Grandes river. The fate of the people who lived there is still unknown. A picture shows ancient ruins at Paquimé. A picture shows a whale diving in the Sea of Cortés. The tail is above the water. Visitors who skip ruins and beaches may still like whales. A boat is one way to watch them. At Guerrero Negro, blue whales are often seen. They swim along the Sea of Cortés. People who get seasick can watch from land. Many other sea mammals can be seen on land too. The nearby places are Laguna San Ignacio and Bahia de Magdalena. Mexico has a vibrant culture. The land is breathtaking. The waters are beautiful. The history is abundant. The food is delicious. You will have to agree that Mexico offers a great deal. So come for a visit. A picture shows the cultural center of San Miguel de Allende.

11Quick Facts About Mexico. Among ethnic groups, Mestizo people are both Indigenous and Spanish. Mestizo people make up 62 percent. Indigenous people make up 28 percent. Other groups, mostly European, make up 10 percent. Roman Catholic followers make up 78 percent. Protestant followers make up 11.2 percent. Other religions make up 0.2 percent. People listed as unaffiliated make up 10.6 percent. Languages include Spanish, Mayan, and Náhuatl. Other languages are spoken as well. In government, the executive branch has a president and cabinet members. The legislative branch has a Senate with 128 seats. The Chamber of Deputies has 500 seats. The judicial branch is the Supreme Court of Justice. That court has 11 judges. The currency is the peso. Natural resources include petroleum, silver, antimony, copper, and gold. They also include lead, zinc, natural gas, and timber. In the workforce, agriculture accounts for 13.4 percent. Industry accounts for 24.1 percent. Services account for 61.9 percent.
