Industries include food and beverages, tobacco, chemicals, and iron and steel. They include petroleum, mining, textiles, and clothing. They include motor vehicles, consumer durables, and tourism. Exports include cars, vehicle parts, computers, and delivery trucks. Exports also include crude petroleum and insulated wiring. Cathedrals are large churches. Geography means the natural features on the surface of Earth. A century is a span made of one hundred years. Indigenous describes people who are native to the place. Civilizations are societies that are organized and developed. A landform is a physical feature on Earth's surface, such as a mountain. A colony is a land ruled by a different country. Mariachi is traditional music of Mexico. That music goes back to the 1800s. Conquered means one group attacked another and took control of the land. Murals are pictures painted on walls. A republic is a country with a president and with representatives the people elect. A conquistador was a conqueror who came from Spain. Dormant means not active. Ruins are what remains after a place is destroyed or damaged. An empire is land controlled by one ruler. That ruler is an emperor.

22. Condors, Birds of Enormous Wings

1A rare California condor holds its enormous wings open to the sun. This book begins by meeting the condor. Life on wind and rock comes next. A closer look at the body follows. A nest with one egg has a part. Trouble for condors has a part. A closing part calls the condor a truly giant bird. A glossary explains key words. South America’s Andes Mountains rise in majesty. High above them, a huge bird takes off. Weight is over 30 pounds, or 13.5 kilograms. Powerful wings measure an amazing 10.5 feet across, or 3.2 meters. The climb reaches a dizzying 15,000 feet, or 4,600 meters. No flying bird on Earth is larger. This is the giant Andean condor. Gliding along, it searches for food far below. A huge wingspan helps. Extra-keen eyesight helps too. A size chart compares three bodies. An Andean condor can stand up to 4 feet, or 1.2 meters. Wingspan can reach 10.5 feet, or 3.2 meters. Weight can reach 33 pounds, or 15 kilograms. A California condor can stand up to 4.6 feet, or 1.4 meters. Wingspan can reach 9.7 feet, or 3 meters. Weight can reach 25 pounds, or 11 kilograms. A person in the chart is 6 feet tall, or 1.8 meters, and weighs 175 pounds, or 79.4 kilograms. The opening bird is the Andean condor, already past 30 pounds with a 10.5-foot wingspan. The chart’s top weight for that species is 33 pounds. California birds are a little taller in the chart and a little lighter. Eyes and wings work together while the bird glides and hunts the ground far below.

2A map of condor homes shows South America and the Andes Mountains. It shows the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean. One shaded area is the California condor range. Another is the Andean condor range. Western South America is home to Andean condors. The American Southwest is home to California condors. Every condor needs a wide-open habitat. When food appears, there must be room to drop down on huge wings and land. Wind currents must be strong enough too. Those currents let the birds climb high. They also let the birds cover long distances. A single day of travel can reach 150 miles, or 240 kilometers. Speed can reach 50 miles per hour, or 80 kilometers per hour. The sea is home for some of these birds. High cliffs are their perches. The shoreline is easy to see from there. Most condors, though, live where the land is dry. They soar over rocky canyons. They soar over deserts and mountains. Nests are preferred on elevated landforms. A lofty nest helps keep eggs safe from predators that walk on the ground. Twigs and feathers are not gathered into a cozy nest. The birds settle on rocky cave floors instead. Jagged outer ledges are used too. Large holes are nests for some California condors. Those holes sit high in California redwoods. Those trees tower over every other kind. The year 2006 revealed nests in redwoods near Big Sur. The Andes Mountains gave Andean condors their name, and that range is their home. Open ground matters because the wings are too broad for a tight landing. Wind does the heavy work of the climb. A day can cover 150 miles. Cliffs, dry canyons, deserts, and mountains are all part of the picture. Eggs stay safer when the nest is high, whether the floor is a cave, a ledge, or a redwood hole.

3Andean condors eat many kinds of animals. Llamas are among them. Alpacas are among them. One day of feeding can reach 4 pounds, or 1.8 kilograms. After that, days may pass with no meal. The diet is carrion only. Carrion means animals that are dead and decaying. You would not find it tasty. Rabbits can be a meal for California condors. Gophers can too. Both are small mammals. Larger mammals are preferred. Deer are preferred. Cattle are preferred. Near the ocean, condors clean beaches of seafood. Small fish are included. A stranded whale of great size can be included. A dead animal can be full of harmful bacteria. Those bacteria can cause disease. Condors are not in danger from them. Special digestive systems are the reason. Nature gets an important service. Rotting flesh is swallowed. Ecosystems stay a little more free of germs. Smell is not a strong sense for condors. Eyesight is excellent, and it is the tool used to find food. Even a great height does not hide a meal from those eyes. Other birds that eat carrion may circle nearby. That circle is a sure sign of a meal. The condor swoops in and eats what those birds have found. A beak that is sharp and curved tears the flesh. Food is shared. One picture shows a California condor about to eat what remains of a whale. Llamas and alpacas show how wide the Andean menu is, yet every meal is carrion. Four pounds can be enough for one day, and then the bird may fast. Bacteria in rotting flesh do not sicken a condor. Other scavengers circling overhead often reveal the next meal, and the condor simply drops in to share it.

4Strength and a sharp edge mark the bill. Width across the wings can hit 10.5 feet, or 3.2 meters. Feathers cover the body. The head does not have them. Legs are strong. Talons are wide. Every bird has a backbone. Every bird has feathers. Every bird has wings. Every bird has a bill. Every bird lays eggs. Every bird is warm-blooded. Adult California condors, male and female, share clear likenesses. Both have black feathers. A fluffy black ruff circles the neck like a collar. Andean birds, whether male or female, wear black body feathers. Necks on those birds are white. Males of that species also grow large fleshy lumps on the head. Those lumps are called combs. California condors do not have combs. A comb, if you see one, means the bird is a male Andean condor. Excitement or anger changes the head color. The head turns deep pink or deep orange. Storks are among the closest relatives of condors. The two birds do not look alike at all. Condors stay very clean. After a meal, the head is rubbed clean on rocks. Tree branches are used the same way. A bath in water follows. Hours can then go to smoothing feathers. Black feathers and a black neck ruff mark both sexes of the California bird. White necks mark Andean birds, and only the Andean male adds a comb. A head that flushes deep pink or deep orange is showing excitement or anger. The bill, the wings, the feathers, the legs, the talons, and the eggs all fit what makes a bird a bird.

5A bald head is shared by all condors. The bare skin is a useful adaptation. No feathers from the neck upward makes grooming simpler. That matters after the head goes into a decaying animal. Messy bits have almost no feathers to cling to. Two years pass between eggs, and only one egg is laid. Protecting that egg is crucial. The female sits on it. The male sits on it too. About fifty-six days pass before hatching. Growing up changes the feathers step by step. Gray yields to black. Flight begins around six months of age. Luck in the wild usually means a life of about sixty years. Zoos and refuges can stretch life past seventy-five years. Most animals live longer in captivity, and condors do too. Protected places pamper them. The wild holds many hazards. People have done some of the greatest harm. An Andean condor chick waits in one picture. Parents are on the way with food. A bare head keeps the mess of a carcass from sticking. Two years is a long wait for a single egg, so both adults take turns sitting. Fifty-six days is the usual wait until hatching. Gray feathers darken toward black, and flight comes near six months. Sixty years is a lucky wild life. Past seventy-five years is possible in a zoo or a refuge, where the birds are protected and even pampered. People remain a major hazard outside those safe places.

6Andean condors are endangered. California condors are endangered. Two centuries ago, far more of these birds were alive. Trouble started when people moved into condor country. Many people in North America disliked the big birds. Many people in South America disliked them too. They shot the birds. Coyotes were disliked as well. Wolves were disliked. Poison was left out to kill them. Condors ate those dead animals and died from the poison too. Lead poisoning killed many more. People had shot an animal. A condor feasted and sometimes swallowed lead bullets by accident. Electrical power brought a newer danger. Eyesight is sharp, yet power lines are not always seen. A strike on the wires kills the bird. Extinction was frighteningly near for California condors in 1987. Wild survivors numbered only about ten. Scientists caught those wild birds. Refuges became their new home. There the birds could be protected. Scientists could also help them raise young. Five hard years of dedication passed. Releases back to the wild then began. May 2013 found over 230 California condors free in the sky once more. Andean birds have had a rescue of their own since 1973. Groups in South America have reserved land for them. Numbers are rising. A few thousand are estimated to live in the wild. Rescued birds in one picture were later released. Numbered tags let researchers keep track of them. Shooting, poison set for coyotes and wolves, lead from bullets, and unseen power lines all cut the numbers down. About ten wild California birds remained in 1987. Capture, refuge care, and a five-year effort made release possible. By May 2013 the free count was over 230. Andean numbers, helped since 1973 by land set aside, are climbing toward a few thousand.

7Utah is the setting of one picture. A canyon there holds a California condor in flight. Picture a bird that gigantic passing overhead. The sight is amazing. An eagle’s wings would have to double to match this span. A falcon’s wings would have to be multiplied by five. Protected reserves now shelter many California condors. Little other land still gives these huge birds a sky. Serious dangers have not gone away. Continued protection of the birds can keep them with us. Protection of their environments matters just as much. If that care continues, wonder at these giant high fliers can last for centuries. An adaptation is a shift in a living thing or in its species. Survival in that home becomes easier. Captivity is a life shut in, without freedom. Carrion is meat left after an animal dies and begins to rot. A current is moving air or moving water that keeps one direction. Decomposing means rotting, or falling apart into tiny pieces. An ecosystem binds living things to the habitats around them. To propel is to drive a person or an object ahead. A refuge is a place that offers safety, ease, or protection. Wingspan is the measure from one wingtip across to the other. A canyon flight in Utah shows the scale. Set against an eagle, the wings are twice as wide. Set against a falcon, they are five times as wide. Reserves are among the last skies these California birds still use. Dangers remain, yet steady care for the birds and their homes can keep that awe alive for centuries.

23. COVID-19 and a Worldwide Health Crisis

1An employee at an elementary school in Orlando, Florida, takes a student's temperature. The check comes before the student may enter the school. An artist's rendering shows particles of COVID-19. Spikes cover the particles. The spikes help the particles bind with host cells and invade them. December 2019 brought alarm to doctors in Wuhan, China. A new illness had appeared. Shortness of breath was one symptom. Fever was another. Fatigue was another. Some patients struggled so hard to breathe that a hospital stay was required. Good medical care let many patients recover. Not every patient survived. A new coronavirus caused the illness. The illness was named COVID-19. Spread came quickly. The World Health Organization, known as the WHO, issued a declaration in March 2020. The status of COVID-19 was now a pandemic. A pandemic is a disease that has raced across the whole world. Daily life is shaken hard by a pandemic such as COVID-19. All of us have to put in effort if a pandemic is to be beaten. Scientists have a part. Students have a part. Each of us has a role when a pandemic crisis must be solved.

2A chart of history's deadliest pandemics lists several outbreaks and their dates. The Plague of Justinian is marked 541 to 542. The Black Death is marked 1347 to 1351. Smallpox is marked 1520. The Spanish Flu is marked 1918 to 1919. Pandemics reach back to ancient times. One example is the Plague of Justinian. Around 541 of the common era, it moved across Europe, Asia, and Africa. Thirty to fifty million people died. That toll was about half the world's population then. After about eight hundred years, the Black Death left Asia and entered Europe. Fifty million people died. Bacteria were behind the Plague of Justinian. Bacteria were behind the Black Death too. Drugs called antibiotics now kill many bacteria that cause disease. Bacteria therefore start fewer pandemics. Viruses are the more common cause of modern pandemics. Viruses have driven deadly pandemics many times. Smallpox, a viral infection, moved around the world for centuries. It caused blindness. It caused death. Scientists in 1981 identified AIDS, a viral disease new to them. The death toll from AIDS around the world is thirty-two million. Viral influenza in 1918 reached five hundred million people across the world. Influenza pandemics returned in 1957. They returned again in 1968. A 2009 flu called H1N1, also known as swine flu, reached 1.4 billion people. Masks were on people's faces during the Spanish Flu pandemic of 1918. What turns a disease into a pandemic? A new disease such as COVID-19 tends to spread easily. Bodies have no defenses against it yet. Contagion is far stronger in some diseases than in others. Danger is far greater in some diseases than in others. A pandemic usually requires both traits at once. The disease must be very contagious. It must also be very dangerous. A dangerous disease does not always become a pandemic. A contagious one does not always become one either. Ebola is deadly, yet fairly rare. Africa has seen several terrible Ebola outbreaks. A worldwide spread has not happened for this disease. The common cold is very contagious. It usually is not deadly. Colds do not cause pandemics either.

3Medical help today is far stronger than it was in earlier pandemics. Disease can also travel faster now than ever before. On every continent, city life packs people close together. Those cities are larger than cities of the past. Where people live and work in tight quarters, sickness passes easily. More of the planet is now home to humans. Contact with wildlife has grown closer. Viruses that live in animals can infect humans more readily because of that contact. Travel spreads disease as well. Hours are enough for a flight to reach any region on Earth. Sickness can ride along. A timeline tracks how fast COVID-19 moved in early 2020. On January 20, 2020, five countries had cases. On February 3, 2020, the count was twenty-eight countries. On February 29, 2020, it was sixty-four countries. On March 20, 2020, it was 184 countries. Five countries had the disease, and nearly every world region had it only two months later. One photograph shows a COVID-19 patient leaving a hospital in Wuhan, China. The patient had received a lung transplant. Early signs of a new disease, even one that might turn into a pandemic, are often easy to miss. Understanding how it behaves takes time. Doctors and nurses need training so they watch for new diseases. A doctor in Wuhan, China, named Li Wenliang sounded a warning late in 2019. His warning described a new illness aimed at the lungs. The illness he warned about was COVID-19. A few months later, Doctor Li died of it himself.

4Quick cooperation among countries is required once a new disease is spreading. Detection and a halt to the spread both depend on that speed. The World Health Organization helps countries talk to one another. Scientists around the world can then share what they learn. A test worked out in one country can be used in others. During the COVID-19 pandemic, scientists in China identified the new virus very quickly. What they learned about the virus went to the WHO. The WHO shared it so that COVID-19 tests could be developed everywhere. Some countries could test huge numbers of people at once. Others struggled. Preparation was strong in South Korea, to take one example. After COVID-19 arrived, that government managed daily tests in the tens of thousands. The United States struggled to produce enough tests for a large population. Personnel there made a first batch of tests. A flaw made those tests useless. Testing delays let the virus spread unseen for several months. The United States then had many more cases than South Korea. Early testing helps a government control a disease. When large numbers of people can be tested, medical workers can act quickly. Sick people can be treated. They can be kept from passing the illness on. Rapid spread in the United States was fed by several local issues. First, the country chose to build its own test. A German lab had the earliest test on offer, and the country did not use it. Faults spoiled the earliest tests that the United States government supplied. Rapid testing became impossible. COVID-19 moved through the population without being detected. Many people already carried the disease when working tests finally arrived. Making enough tests for everyone grew very hard. Mask-wearing was not a social custom in the United States at the pandemic's start. In many Asian countries, a sick person customarily wears a mask in any public place. Most people in Japan covered their faces once COVID-19 showed up. China did too. South Korea did too. That habit helped slow the virus early. Few masks were worn in the United States, and that gap helped the virus move. No single national plan covered closing schools or businesses. Some states temporarily shut businesses and public spaces. That procedure is known as a lockdown. Other states did not lock down. The virus spread more easily where lockdown rules were less strict. A COVID-19 test kit is part of this picture.

5Everyone has to contribute if a pandemic is to be contained. People in every part of society must work together. The goal is safety for themselves and for others. One government task is to stop people from passing the infection along. Officials might temporarily forbid travel. They might temporarily close businesses. They might tell people to stay home. A sick person might need to quarantine, which means staying away from others for a time. Officials might also require quarantine before a person enters a country. The aim is to keep illness from spreading. Hospitals and officials track where the disease is moving. Governments and hospitals share the latest information so people can protect themselves. Care for sick people depends on hard work by doctors and by nurses. The work can be very dangerous. Some medical professionals picked up COVID-19 from the patients they treated. Some of them died. Doctor Li in China was one of those deaths. Other workers keep going during a pandemic. Farmers do. Postal workers do. Grocery store clerks do. Firefighters do. Police officers do. Schoolteachers do. These people, and many others in important jobs, are called essential workers. Society keeps functioning for everyone because of the work they do. Citizens must also protect one another. Public health orders can be obeyed. Masks can be worn. Hands can be washed often. Large gatherings can be avoided. Trips away from home that are not needed can be skipped. Schools may close. Offices may close. School may shift online. Jobs may shift online. Time with friends may shift online. New ways to connect have to be found. During COVID-19, people in Italy began a daily routine. Each afternoon, singing rose from the windows of their homes. Alertness from governments and from scientists has to continue even when a pandemic seems over. They must keep sharing information. A very contagious disease can return with ease. Control often happens in cycles. Final defeat usually comes only after the disease has been fought again and again.

6Control means slowing the spread, then stopping it. Countries around the world take up that work. Hospitals keep treating sick people at the same time. Scientists race to discover a vaccine. Immunity to a virus is what this substance, a vaccine, is meant to create. Once vaccinated, the body can repel the disease and stay well. Finding an effective vaccine, testing it, and making it available worldwide usually takes years. Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine in 1796. People gained protection from the deadly smallpox virus. Some viruses still have no known vaccine. The virus that causes AIDS is one of them. For a disease like that, communities must contain the virus together. The aim is to keep it from spreading through the whole population. A picture shows a volunteer receiving a shot. The injection, part of a medical trial, is one possible vaccine against COVID-19. Countries share the work of seeking a vaccine able to stop COVID-19. In 2020, scientists tested dozens of possible vaccines. The work went on in the United States. It went on in China. It went on in the United Kingdom. It went on in Germany. Other countries took part as well. A vaccine for this disease will require the sharpest thinking scientists can offer, in every country. Two rankings use figures dated November 5, 2020. One ranking orders countries by how many COVID-19 cases they had. The United States leads that case list. India comes next. Then Brazil. Then Russia. Then France. Then Spain. Then Argentina. Then Colombia. Then the United Kingdom. Mexico is last. A second ranking orders countries by COVID-19 deaths. The United States leads that death list. Brazil comes next. Then India. Then Mexico. Then the United Kingdom. Then Italy. Then France. Then Spain. Then Iran. Peru is last.

7Cheers greeted healthcare workers outside hospitals in New York City in 2020. They were met with thanks. The scene belongs to the COVID-19 pandemic. A pandemic can strike at any time. It can spread with lightning speed. Travel, work, and shared living all help it move. During a pandemic, every person has a role in stopping the spread. A child may stay home from school. A store clerk may put on a mask before work. A nurse may help a sick patient breathe. A scientist may study vaccines in a lab. Each of these acts is a way to keep one another safe and healthy.

24. Desert Animals That Bite and Sting

1Sections follow this order. A Child in the Emergency Room. Bites and Stings That Can Kill. Bites and Stings That Do Not Kill. Final Advice. Words and Topics. A map marks California, Arizona, and New Mexico. Tucson and Mexico are marked too. Jude McNally holds a tarantula in a photo. He uses the spider to teach people how spiders behave. A girl of two years arrives at the emergency room. A red mark shows on her leg. She is too young to tell anyone what happened. Her parents believe an animal bit her or stung her. How can a doctor in that room name the animal that caused the injury? Jude McNally is managing director of a center in Tucson. The state is Arizona. His workplace is the Poison and Drug Information Center. He studies things that poison the body or harm it. A talk with Jude will explain desert bites and desert stings.

2Bites and Stings That Can Kill. Question: A young girl like this one reaches the emergency room. What is the first step? Jude: Doctors search for signs of bites and stings that can threaten life. Four possible animals are in mind. Black widow spiders are one. Scorpions are one. Insects that fly and sting are one. Rattlesnakes are one. Question: If the animal is a black widow, what do doctors watch for? Jude: Venom is made by every spider. Most spiders cannot push that venom into a person. The black widow can. The female black widow is the one to watch most closely. A bite from her injects venom. Muscle cramps follow a black widow bite. Burning, stinging pain starts where the bite landed. Swelling stays small. Major puncture wounds cannot be seen. Muscle cramping begins, usually near the sting. Small children suffer that cramping worst of all. A child may cramp in muscles all over the body. Sometimes the belly turns stiff, like a board. Sometimes breathing grows difficult. Puffy eyes can appear in children too. No muscle cramping means the case is not a black widow bite. Doctors set that animal aside. A note: many insecticides fail against black widow spiders. Those chemicals are made to kill insects. Remember a key difference. Spiders are arachnids. They are not insects.

3A bark scorpion is pictured. Tail included, it is about two inches long. Question: A scorpion sting would show which signs? Jude: Arizona holds over thirty kinds of scorpions. Only the bark scorpion can threaten a life. A two-year-old stung by one will be restless. Sitting still will be impossible. Muscle twitching is common. The mouth area shows it most. Another clear sign is roving eye syndrome. The eyes cannot focus. Movement disorders appear too. The child may look caught in a strange dance. Stings from other scorpions bring swelling in one local spot. The bark scorpion brings almost no reaction where it stung. With a two-year-old, a tap test is used. Fingers run up and down the body. A scream marks the sting site, because the pain is so sharp. Careful looking sometimes finds a single puncture wound. Three signs have to show up. Restlessness is one. Twitching is one. Roving eye syndrome is one. If they are absent, scorpions are ruled out. Homes sometimes get visits from scorpions. Dark places are where they hide.

4Question: Flying insects that sting leave which clues? Jude: Bees raise a worry about allergic reactions. Wasps do too. Ants do too. Most people see some redness where they were stung. Itching appears. Swelling appears. Those signs fade in a couple of days. A reaction somewhere other than the sting, inside the first hour, is different. It is called a type 1 allergic reaction. Life can be threatened. The window is described as an hour. Usually you know within 20 to 30 minutes if allergy is the problem. Unless allergy is present, discomfort from a wasp sting or a bee sting usually fades in a few days. Breathing trouble is a major warning. Another warning is an itch in the hands after a sting on the back. Trouble swallowing after a sting on the leg is a warning too. Each of these means the whole body is reacting. Emergency medical care is required for this type 1 reaction. The patient can die. A note for readers: a bite or sting problem should lead to a call. Phone a center that handles poison. The center for your region knows which animals in your area deserve concern. A doctor in a photo checks a girl's blood pressure. Deaths from insect stings outnumber deaths from a combined group. That group is black widows, scorpions, and rattlesnakes. Ruling out allergy to flying, stinging insects is that important. Breathing ability is checked to rule allergy out. Blood pressure is tested too. An allergic reaction drives blood pressure down in an extreme way.

5Question: A rattlesnake bite shows which signs? Jude: Ruling a rattlesnake bite out right away is harder. The illness moves in stages. It starts with a puncture wound. Some bleeding is possible. Swelling then shows at the bite. Discoloration shows there too. Hours later, the skin may blister. Tissue destruction can follow. Skin around the site dies. Muscle tissue dies too. A photo shows a western diamondback rattlesnake. When bruising travels across the body is a definite sign of a snakebite. Blood is drawn. Parts of the blood that handle clotting are measured. Snake venom destroys those parts. The patient starts bleeding on the inside. Tissue dies because of that bleeding. The whole process covers 24 to 36 hours. Antivenom is given the entire time. The goal is to halt how the body reacts once venom is inside. A math note gives costs. Each vial of rattlesnake antivenom bills a patient about 3,000 dollars. One patient stayed in the hospital 10 days. He received more than 50 vials. Other hospital costs sat on the same bill. The total was 326,000 dollars. How much of that bill was the antivenom? How much was everything else?

6Small, sharp teeth fill the mouth of a Gila monster. The name is said HEE-luh. Bites and Stings That Do Not Kill. Question: Some animals do not cause signs that threaten life. A bite from a Gila monster would look like what? Jude: Teeth marks usually form a little row. Sometimes they form a circle. A single puncture is not the pattern. Teeth remain in the wound in about one case out of three. Pain is severe. The lizard hangs on a long time after biting. Half a minute is common. Longer is possible. Most people bitten by a Gila monster, Jude says, brought the bite on themselves. The animal is very docile. Harassment is what most victims were doing. A note: this venomous lizard lives mostly in Arizona. Northern Mexico is the other main home. Question: What about scorpions that are not bark scorpions? Jude: Swelling often starts at the site when the scorpion is some other kind. The start comes minutes after the sting. Pain is felt there. Tingling may occur. Numbness may occur. Hours are usually enough for it to fade. Swelling is the clue that bark scorpion is the wrong answer. A bark scorpion causes no swelling. Fine hairs cover the body of the desert hairy scorpion. Question: Spider bites other than the black widow show which signs? Jude: Venom from most other spiders causes local inflammation. Full-body signs usually do not follow. Brown recluse spiders are the other bites watched closely. Often the bite itself is not felt. Hours pass, and a blister rises where the bite landed. The blister later breaks open. A scab forms. Tissue dies. A large area can be involved. Weeks can pass. Months can pass.

7A brown recluse is pictured. A bite from this spider may need months before it fully heals. Emergency-room diagnosis rarely includes brown recluse bites at the start. The signs need time to develop. Set aside the black widow. Set aside the brown recluse. Other spider bites cause no serious problem unless infection sets in. Harm to humans is absent in most spiders. Some spiders eat common pests. Houseflies are one example. Mosquitos are another. A common garden spider is shown. A garter snake is shown. A note on deaths: snakebite death is rare in the United States. Worldwide, it is common. India is one example. An estimate says 40,000 people die there from snakebites each year. Deadlier kinds of snakes are one reason. Less access to health care is the other. Question: What about snakes besides the dangerous ones already named? Jude: Nonvenomous snakes far outnumber venomous ones. Plenty of snakes called nonvenomous do carry venom. A bite from them is still not a serious health risk. Soreness can follow. Once in a while, blisters develop at the site. Swelling can develop too. Nothing serious follows. Estimates for the United States pass 35,000 snakebites each year. Of that total, 6,000 to 8,000 carry venom. A bullsnake is pictured.

8Final Advice. Question: What guidance do you have for readers? Jude: Rattlesnakes are the exception. Almost every other bite and sting we treat happens in homes or near them. Night is when spiders are active. Night is when scorpions are active. By day they look for a dark crack or a crevice. Meeting them is more likely at night, while they are active. Lights switched on at night lower the risk. Nighttime lighting is a useful safety step. The picture makes that point. See something dangerous, and one step backward usually does the job. You leave the reach of the danger. Leaving the animal alone lowers risk further. More than half the rattlesnake patients we treat had already seen the snake. They knew the danger. They still put themselves at greater risk. Smart choices make safety much more likely. Pictures show a raccoon, a bat, a fox, and a skunk. Rabies cannot be carried by cold-blooded animals. Many smaller mammals cannot carry it either. Skunks can carry rabies. Bats can. Raccoons can. Foxes can. Coyotes can. A county health official should hear about bats inside your house. Time around any of these animals is a reason too. Any risk means you need a series of vaccines. Full-blown rabies has been survived by only one known person.

9Words to Know. Antivenom is a medicine. It stops the damage a venom would do. Discoloration is a shift in color. Disorders are ways a body works that are not normal. Assessing means evaluating. It can also mean measuring. Docile means peaceful. Aggression is absent. Blood pressure tells how strongly the heart pushes blood. Embedded means stuck firmly in place. Harassing means bothering someone. Tormenting is another word for it. Clotting means parts stick together so bleeding stops. Inflammation is redness that hurts. Swelling comes with it. A culprit is whoever caused an injury or a crime. The cause can be a person or another animal. Local means limited to one particular body part. A diagnosis names an illness or an injury. A puncture is a tiny opening through the skin. A site is a location. Symptoms are signs. They point to an illness or an injury. A syndrome is a group of symptoms. They show up together. Venom is a poisonous liquid from an animal. A snake can make it. A spider can make it. An insect can make it. Topics include antivenom, insects, a lizard, mammals, and rabies. Reactions listed cover blood, breathing, movement, sight, and skin. Scorpions, snakes, and spiders are listed too.

25. Earth's Highest Mountain

1What this book covers: a beginning. The mountain itself. Getting ready to climb. The route up. The Sherpa people. The first to arrive on top. Later climbers. Dangers. A closing word. Places to learn more. Words to know. A beginning Each year, when the weather allows it, hundreds of people begin a brutal climb. They bring a powerful hunger for adventure. They hope the climb will place them at the highest spot on Earth. That spot is the summit of Mount Everest. It is the tallest mountain in the world. Strength plays a part in a successful summit. Careful planning plays a part. Good weather plays a part. The right equipment plays a part. A share of luck plays a part too.

2The mountain itself Mount Everest stands in Asia. Nepal lies on one side of its border. On the other side is the Tibet Autonomous Region. That region is part of China. The peak is sixty million years old. Among a chain of peaks that rise extremely high, this one stands tallest. People call that chain the Himalayas. A map shows where this peak and the Himalayas are found. Both the range and the peak sit near a fault. Two plates meet there. A plate is a moving piece of Earth's crust. One plate slides beneath the other. The upper plate is pushed up. Mountains rise from that push. The peak is still growing. Each year it adds about 6 centimeters. That gain is 2.4 inches. The summit stands 8,850 meters over the level of the sea. In feet, the height is 29,035. A passenger jet flies at nearly that height. K2 is the second-tallest mountain on Earth. This peak rises almost 305 meters above K2. Those 305 meters equal 1,000 feet. A chart lines up several famous mountains for comparison. Many people call the highest point on Earth the ultimate challenge. The way up is filled with danger. Steep cliffs of rock stand in the way. So do cliffs of ice. Deep crevasses stand in the way. So do slabs of ice and snow that shift. Air near the top holds much less oxygen than air lower down. Breathing is very hard. Climbers tire easily. High winds may blow. Temperatures may fall below zero. With all of that, the highest place on Earth can seem almost impossible to reach.

3How the peak got its names In English, the peak is called Everest. The name honors Sir George Everest. He was Surveyor General of India during colonial rule. The Nepali have a much older name for it. They say Sagarmatha. That word is Sanskrit. It means peak of heaven. People in Tibet say Chomolungma. That name means Mother Goddess of the World. Blocks of ice keep moving in the Khumbu icefall. On the path up from the south, this icefall ranks with the worst hazards. Getting ready A person who wants to climb this mountain must be in excellent shape. The work is very strenuous. The body faces huge demands. Most climbers train for years. They build skill on other hard mountains. They also stay extra days at high elevation. That time lets the body acclimate to thinner air. The trip costs a great deal. A trip run by seasoned leaders may be priced as high as 65,000 U.S. dollars. Personal gear is extra. Air fares are extra. Insurance is extra. The lowest price people estimate is around 30,000 dollars. Oxygen costs 300 dollars for one bottle. A climber may need up to twenty bottles. That oxygen bill is 6,000 dollars. Nepal's government charges 10,000 dollars just for a permit. Gear and preparation can save a life. A climber here must stay warm. The climber must stay dry. The climber must rest. The climber must drink enough water.

4Staying alive here calls for piles of special clothes. It also takes climbing gear, camping gear, and food made for high altitude. Some of those supplies are listed below. Clothing: pants and a jacket that keep water out. A lightweight coat filled with down. Warm covering for the head. A heavyweight suit filled with down. Several pairs of socks that hold heat. Dark glasses for bright sun, and goggles as well. Gloves that keep water out. Heavy mittens filled with down. A fleece top and fleece pants. Climbing gear: a harness. Heavy boots for climbing, chosen two sizes too large so more socks will fit. Crampons, the metal spikes worn on shoes. An ice ax. A face mask. Maps. A compass. Oxygen in 20 canisters. A rope 15 meters long. Camping gear: bottled gas. A large tent for Base Camp. A stove for cooking. Smaller tents of high quality for the higher camps. A tool that purifies water. Down sleeping bags, two or three of them. Pads to sleep on. The route up The safest seasons are spring and fall. May draws the most climbers. A climb can last two months. The dates must be planned so that dangerous weather is avoided. In winter, the temperature can drop to −50 degrees Celsius. That reading is −58 degrees Fahrenheit. In summer, enormous storms lay meters of snow on the slopes. Climbers often visit old temple sites before the trek starts. The sites are in Kathmandu. That city is Nepal's capital.

5Advance Base Camp stands on the northern slope. It sits at 6,400 meters. That height is 21,000 feet. Up to fifteen routes reach the top. Base Camp is the start for most of those routes. The camp's height is almost 5,500 meters above the sea. That is 18,000 feet. The summit is still 3,219 meters higher. That remaining gap is 11,000 feet. Reaching Base Camp on foot may use up ten full days. Once there, climbers rest for about a week. Their bodies adjust to air that is thin. For the next few weeks they walk toward camps that sit higher. They also walk back down. They go to each camp and return several times before they move on to the next camp. Those trips let them practice hard work in thin air. After the highest camp becomes home for a while, weather news is what they study. They look at the sky. Several tries over several days may be needed. Conditions must be favorable. Wind should be no stronger than 32 kilometers an hour. That limit is 20 miles an hour. Snow should not fill the sky. Weather that turns harsh and inhospitable can hold them inside the tents. Several days may pass that way. They may even return to Base Camp. Climbers need about twelve hours to leave the top camp and touch the summit. They usually set off near the middle of the night. Climbers can then come back before dark the following day. The last 100 meters are the hardest. Those meters equal 300 feet. This stretch includes the Hillary Step. The step is a cliff made of ice and of rock. Sir Edmund Hillary gave it his name. A map shows the path followed by Edmund Hillary together with Tenzing Norgay.

6Once climbers are on top, they may stay about an hour. They take in the view. They take in the feeling of sitting at Earth's highest point. Then they try to head down before the sun sets. The return down to that top camp lasts about four hours in most cases. Some climbers do not take a slow path to the top. In 2003, two sherpas each made the trip on a different day. Each one left Base Camp and stood on the summit in less than thirteen hours. One of them returned in 2004. That climb took eight hours and ten minutes. It was a record. Few visitors can match a Sherpa's speed on the climb. Their bodies are already adjusted to thin air at high altitude. A picture shows sunset from the highest point. Climbers have little time to look at the view. The Sherpa people The earliest Sherpas entered Nepal some five centuries back. They crossed over from a region called Tibet. In the beginning they herded animals and traded goods. After they settled beneath this mountain, they became famous for leading climbers upward. Their bodies have adapted to the small amount of oxygen in the Himalayas. They easily outperform visitors from lower regions. Most climbers could not reach the top without sherpas. Sherpas serve as guides. They also serve as porters, and they carry most of the gear. A load can weigh more than the carrier's own body. Loads past 150 pounds are common. The capital letter matters. Sherpa names an ethnic group of people. Written with a small s, sherpas are the guides for trips on this mountain and for other climbs. Some members of the Sherpa people become those guides. A guide is not always a member of that people. A picture shows two Sherpa girls. They are at a festival in Nepal.

7Guides from Nepal, and the people who plan the routes, are necessary on every climb here. Sherpas are strong. They know a great deal. They adjust to what the mountain demands. For many listeners, their work and the climb are one and the same. What they understand, and what they can do, is a vital service. They lead the way. They give advice. They haul gear. They cook. Their pride in a mountaineering heritage is easy to understand. The legend around that heritage is part of the pride. Names in this community follow a pattern. A boy's name frequently matches the weekday of his birth. A name may also honor a particular virtue. That custom explains why so many share one first name. Most people here use a single name only. Names you will often hear are Tenzing, Ngawang, Tashi, and Dorje. Who stood there first Climbers from Great Britain were the first to attempt the top. They started toward the summit in 1921. The attempt failed. George Mallory had been on that 1921 trip. In 1924 he tried again, with Andrew Irvine. Someone saw them for the last time above Camp VI. That camp is also called Camp 6. Many years passed with their fate unknown. In 1999, a group came upon Mallory's body. It lay 305 meters short of the summit. That gap is 1,000 feet. No one can say for certain that he had made the top and was heading down when he fell and died. Success on his part is doubtful. Another team tried in 1953. On May 29 of that year, Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay moved slowly up the icy face. They were the first to stand on the summit. Seven weeks had gone by since they reached Everest Base Camp. Back home in New Zealand, Hillary kept bees. The climb brought him a knighthood. From then on, people said Sir Edmund Hillary. Norgay was a Sherpa. The whole world celebrated what the two had done.

8A photograph places Sir Edmund Hillary on the left. Tenzing Norgay stands with him on the summit. The photo marks their historic climb in 1953. Fame was not what either man was seeking. Fortune was not the goal either. They still used their fame to help people in Nepal. Sir Edmund Hillary started a foundation. Hospitals have been built through it. Medical clinics have been built. Schools have been built. Bridges have been built. The same foundation has planted trees across the Himalayas, numbering in the hundreds of thousands. Tenzing Norgay started a school for climbing. Dozens of the students there have reached this summit. Like Hillary, Norgay used what he had achieved to open more schooling for Sherpa children. The climbers who followed Once those two had been to the top, plenty of people expected that nobody else would bother. What happened was the reverse. From the 1920s onward, thousands have attempted the summit. By 2010, the number who had succeeded was over 3,300. Every age group is represented. Attempts arrive from every region of Earth. Climbers who have summited include people from Austria. Bosnia is on the list. China is on the list. Germany is on the list. Great Britain is on the list. Canada is on the list. Italy is on the list. Japan is on the list. Mexico is on the list. Russia is on the list. The United States is on the list. Many further countries are on it too. A picture shows Takao Arayama, a mountaineer from Japan. He was seventy at the time. In May 2006 he was nearing the summit by the Tibetan route.

9The years have brought many firsts. In 1975, Junko Tabei came from Japan and was the first woman on this mountain. A 1978 summit was done with no oxygen carried in bottles. During 2000, one person skied the full descent from the peak. The next year, a different climber came down from the summit on a snowboard. Blindness did not stop Eric Weihenmayer in 2001. He was the first person without sight to stand there. Future firsts are still unknown. Peter Hillary is Sir Edmund Hillary's son. He took up the same climb his father had made. Peter has been to the top twice. One climb was in 1990. The other was in 2002. Apa Sherpa, who is a Sherpa, holds the record for visits to the summit. He has been there twenty times. The twentieth visit came in May 2010. That same month, Jordan Romero was thirteen. He became the youngest to make the climb. The record he broke belonged to a Sherpa who was fifteen. That earlier climb was in 2001. Over the same weekend in May 2010, the summit saw more than two hundred climbers. As of May 2008, the oldest summit climber was a Nepali man of seventy-six. A timeline of major feats 1921: the first attempt, by a British team. 1924: George Mallory vanishes. 1953: Hillary, called Sir Edmund, stands on top with Tenzing Norgay. 1975: a woman reaches the summit for the first time. 1978: a climber gets there with no bottled oxygen. 1980: the first climb made alone, by Reinhold Messner. 1996: a storm takes 15 lives, the largest one-year toll known then. 1999: the body of George Mallory is discovered. 2001: a person who is blind reaches the top for the first time. 2004: the quickest climb on record, 8 hours and 10 minutes. 2008: the oldest summit, at age 76. 2010: Apa Sherpa sets a new personal record of 20 summits. 2010: the youngest summit, at age 13. 2015: a quake strikes Nepal. At South Base Camp, 18 people or more are killed. 2020: the government of Nepal stops issuing climbing permits for a time. The pause came from concern about the COVID-19 pandemic. A picture shows Apa Sherpa, a Nepali guide who works at high altitude. May 2010 was his twentieth time on the summit, a record.

10Dangers Death comes to nearly one climber in every ten who try. In 1996 the mountain was especially deadly for climbers. Fifteen people died in that one storm. Between 1922 and 2009, deaths on the climb passed 220. Avalanches kill more people here than any other cause. Many routes follow glaciers. Those glaciers are rivers of ice, and the ice moves. While the ice creeps downhill, enormous pieces can break away and collapse. The ice also opens huge cracks. Those cracks are crevasses. Snow may cover them. A single misstep can drop a climber to death. Climbers have to handle air that lacks oxygen. Trouble can start above just 3,000 meters. That line is 10,000 feet. The body may feel nausea. Headaches may come. Confusion may come. Muscle coordination may be lost. Hallucinations may appear. Still higher, edema can strike. The condition can kill. Fluid gathers in the brain. It can gather in the lungs instead. Breathing grows harder as a person climbs. At 5,500 meters, only half the normal oxygen is available. That camp height is 18,000 feet. Near the summit, breathing capacity is down to 30 percent of what is normal. The heart pounds. Each breath is a struggle. Even pulling on boots forces a stop for rest. Thin air at these heights screens out fewer harmful rays from the Sun. Skin left bare can be burned severely. Eyes without proper cover can be burned within minutes. White snow throws the light back. That glare can leave a person unable to see for a while. Covering the eyes matters even under cloud. Winds here can reach hurricane force. They can exceed 161 kilometers each hour. That speed is 100 miles each hour. The cold wind can freeze bare skin in under a minute. Frostbite is a grave danger. Some climbers have had fingers removed. Toes have been removed. Noses have been removed. Doctors amputated those parts. Crowds are a problem even in this harsh place. A picture shows lines of people gathered to go up.

11Climbers also face serious dehydration. Drinking plenty of water is important. Because the temperature is so low, water freezes. It must be melted again before anyone can drink. Crowding has turned dangerous. As many as 354 people have aimed for the summit on one day. Some died in the line because their spare oxygen was used up while they waited. Trash has collected. Bodies are sometimes met on the way up. They are met on the way down as well. Inexperience brings huge risk. Nothing requires a climber to prove past experience. Novices who attempt the trek are unprepared. Injury is more likely for them. Death is more likely for them. A picture shows a porter bearing a basket woven from straw. An injured climber rides in that basket. The pair will travel hard for two days. Only then can a helicopter fly the injured man to a hospital. A closing word This mountain is no place for a faint heart. Look at the dangers and you may ask why anyone comes. Cold that freezes is a threat. Wind at high speed is a threat. Snow that blinds is a threat. A shortage of oxygen is a threat. Avalanches are a threat. Crevasses are a threat. Slopes of ice are a threat. People come anyway. Adventure thrills them. Finishing the climb fills them with pride. Standing at the top of Earth fills them too. Those feelings draw thousands here. A picture shows Jordan Romero at age thirteen. May 2010 was when he set the mark as the youngest climber to finish this ascent.

12If you want to know more Libraries keep many books about this mountain. Some tell the lives of famous climbers. Some tell true stories of climbing trips. Some explain how a person can start climbing mountains. Other useful subjects are mountain climbing, exploration in the arctic, and the Himalayas. Films, movies, and television programs about the peak can be found at a library or a video store. Some reports even follow climbers while they are still going up. Words to know Acclimate: to adjust when the climate is new, or when a situation is new. Amputated: cut off. Crevasses: deep cracks in the ice of a glacier. Dehydration: a dangerous shortage of water in the body. Edema: a condition in which fluid gathers in organs or in body tissues. Fault: a crack in Earth's crust. The crust moves along that crack. Hallucinations: sights or sounds a person experiences that are not really there. Inhospitable: harsh and unwelcoming, and hard to live in. Nausea: the feeling of being sick in the stomach. Porters: workers who haul supplies and gear. Strenuous: needing a lot of hard work and energy. Summit: the highest point on a mountain.

26. Egypt's King for Sixty-Six Years

1A carving on an Egyptian temple shows Ramses II. The British Museum holds a huge statue of him. The statue weighs 6.58 metric tons, or 7.25 tons. Ramesses II is another spelling of his name. He reigned in the New Kingdom. That period lasted five hundred years. People call it the golden age of ancient Egypt. He was the third king of the Nineteenth Dynasty. His reign ran from 1279 to 1213 BCE. He ruled for sixty-six years. Most people in that era died before age forty-five, so a reign this long was unusual. Across those years Egypt gained one of its most powerful pharaohs. He earned the title Ramses the Great. In ancient times he was almost certainly the most famous pharaoh. This book follows the beginning of that fame. A royal surprise, childhood training, and a warrior's rise to king are part of the story. His battles and the name Ramses the Great are part of it too. Special words close the account.

2Birth came around 1303 BCE. Seti I, a military commander, was his father. Mut-Tuy was his mother. Say her name MOOT TOO-ee. At least one older sister, named Tia, is what experts think he had. Another sister, Henutmire, may have existed. Say that name he-nuht-MEE-ray. Pharaoh was probably not the future his parents expected. The royal family did not even include them. Tutankhamun died with no heir. A short reign as pharaoh went to one of his officers. Horemheb replaced that officer a few years later. Army command under Tutankhamun had been Horemheb's post. An army general named Paramessu was Ramses II's grandfather. Service beside Horemheb was part of Paramessu's past. Heir was the role Horemheb gave Paramessu after becoming pharaoh. Several years later, Paramessu himself became pharaoh. Ramses I was the name he took. A new royal line was what he made of his family. Seti I, father of Ramses, became pharaoh only a few years after that. The throne's line then included Ramses. Tutankhamun's funeral mask is a famous object from the earlier king. A map of Egypt in the reign of 1279 to 1213 BCE names many places. The Orontes River and Kadesh are named. The Mediterranean Sea, Pi-Ramesse, and the Nile River Delta are named. The Nile River, Abydos, Thebes, the Ramesseum, and Karnak are named. The Red Sea, the Egyptian Empire, Abu Simbel, the Hittite Empire, and Nubia are named. Artwork and carvings found in buildings he raised are the source for his early life. Successor to Seti I was a title given at a young age. Watching his father do a pharaoh's work supplied much of the education. Wild birds are offered to Amun, a god, in one scene of father and son sharing a religious duty.

3Two carved scenes show Ramses with Seti I. A bull is roped in one scene. An offering to the god Amun is made in the other. Egypt's army would one day be led into battle by the crown prince. Strength and endurance had to be built. Training probably started while he was still a small child. Fighting's demands were the point of the physical tests. Bulls to be roped were one test. Wild horses to be ridden were another. Captain in the army was a title given early. The rank may have been a name only. A title and authority in the boy's hands helped Seti prepare the nation for the coming rule. Adulthood, in that time, arrived with the teenage years. Military campaigns were shared with his father. Diplomacy and war were learned on those trips. Pharaoh's work would need that practice. A household of his own was already his. Nefertari became his first wife when he was about fifteen. Many wives were common for rulers then. Ramses followed that custom. Eight or more royal wives is the number historians think he married. Several minor wives were married as well. Favorite status belonged to Nefertari. He wrote that his love for her was unique. He wrote that nobody could rival her. The most beautiful woman alive is what he called her. Chief wife is the place she kept until she died. An elaborate temple at Abu Simbel was dedicated to her after her death. Colossal statues decorate it. Nefertari, Ramses, and their children are the figures. A pharaoh's image is usually larger than the rest. Her statue matched his in size. Solid sandstone is the rock her temple was carved from.

4Battle is the subject of a scene at the Nubian temple of Beit el-Wali. Ramses and his two sons appear in the fight. A large role filled much of his father's reign. Military campaigns were his to direct. Courage as a warrior became his reputation. The artwork puts him in a charge, and his two oldest sons ride with him. A rebellion in Nubia is where historians place this fight. South of Egypt is where the country of Nubia lay. Gold and riches came from Nubia. Control of it was fought over by Egyptians and Nubians. Thirteen years was the length of Seti I's rule. About twenty-five was Ramses's age when Seti died. Pharaoh was the result of that death. Several building projects of his father were restarted early in the new reign. An immense hall at Karnak had been ordered by Seti I. Stoneworkers and artisans were to build it. Tall columns numbered 134. Raised relief, also called bas-relief, decorated the walls. Background of a scene is cut away in that process. The images stay raised. Honor for Ramses II was the aim of the Ramesseum. Memory of him was meant to last for eternity. Five thousand square meters, or 53,820 square feet, is the area of the Great Hypostyle Hall of Karnak. A different cut was ordered before long. Images were carved straight into the stone. Speed improved, and detail fell. Sunk relief is the name of those less detailed images. Temple building moved at double the earlier rate. More temples were built by him than by any other pharaoh. Many new projects were commissioned. A second temple at Abu Simbel, larger than the first, was one. His mortuary temple, the Ramesseum, in Thebes, was another. A new capital city was another. Pi-Ramesse was the name he chose. Ramsesopolis is a loose translation of that name. Closer reach to old enemies was the gain. The Hittites were those enemies. East of Egypt, in a region now called Syria, was their home.

5Hittite armies were beaten by Ramses with success. Many small provinces they had taken were reclaimed. Some of those provinces were ones his father had failed to win back. Kadesh was attacked and captured by the Hittites soon after Ramses II became pharaoh. Trade made Kadesh important. About twenty thousand soldiers were led by Ramses to retake it. The fifth year of his reign was the time. Fame of this battle is among the highest of his reign. A record belongs to it once Hittite chariots are counted. About 4,500 chariots make it the largest chariot battle the world has known. The first military ambush on record was part of the battle. Temple walls across Egypt and Nubia carry the story in pictures, which is another reason for the fame. Ramses is drawn larger than every other figure. Total defeat of the enemy is how he appears. A large Ramses II beating the Hittites is repeated in many similar images. The victory people were meant to believe was not quite real. Death nearly took Ramses. A draw is a fairer word than a clear Egyptian win. Egyptian records have been read by scholars. Hittite records have been read too. Separation of the army as it neared Kadesh is their conclusion. Scouting ahead was the job of Ramses's division. A day behind came another division. A third group swung wide to strike from the far side. Two local people told Ramses where the Hittite army was. Many miles to the north was their report. The truth arrived quickly. The Hittite army was much closer. An attack was already being prepared. One carving places Ramses II inside a chariot during the fight at Kadesh. Around 2,500 chariots belonged to the Hittite army. Three men rode in each one.

6Word was sent by Ramses to his other divisions. Reinforcements that were coming still met a Hittite ambush. Chariots in that ambush numbered 2,500. The small force that had gone ahead with Ramses was attacked next. His own account says he held the enemy off alone. Flight of the rest of the army is what he claimed. A different rescue appears in other records. The Ne'arin, an elite division, arrived just in time. The pharaoh was saved by that division. Heavy losses hit both sides. A truce was then declared by the two leaders. Forces were pulled back to Egypt. Poems were commissioned over the next year. Wall carvings were commissioned too. Every one of them told the battle. Every one of them cast him as a hero. History's first propaganda campaign, some experts say, had begun. Fifteen years later, war again seemed close. Distance from his base made fighting hard. Peace was chosen instead of battle. Ramses II and the Hittite king joined to write a peace treaty. Pieces of that treaty still appear in peace treaties of modern times. One piece was a promise not to attack each other's lands. Allies for years to come was another result. A copy of the treaty hangs on a wall today. The United Nations General Assembly building is where that wall stands. Giant sculptures of Ramses II stand at Abu Simbel. They flank the entrance of the larger of two sandstone temples. Rule lasted until 1213 BCE. Natural causes ended his life that year. Ninety-one was his age. His oldest son, the first heir, died before him. The next eleven sons in the line died before him too. The thirteenth son became pharaoh next. Decline of the dynasty started soon. One hundred fifty years after the death, the New Kingdom ended. Fame in ancient Egypt was so great that later kings borrowed the name. At least nine later pharaohs were named for him. Ramses the Great is the name used today. Monuments built by him outnumber those of any other pharaoh in history. Temples built by him do the same. Art, architecture, and historical records are the legacy. People and culture of his time can be understood more clearly because of them.

7A timeline can mark the life of Ramses II. The scale notes 1310 BCE and 1210 BCE. Ramses I became pharaoh in 1298 BCE. Seti I became pharaoh in 1291 BCE. Ramses married his first two wives in 1289 BCE. He put down a revolt in Nubia in 1281 BCE, and his two oldest sons went into battle with him. The throne was his in 1279 BCE, and work on the Ramesseum began around then. The battle at Kadesh was fought in 1274 BCE. Work at Abu Simbel began around 1264 BCE. The Ramesseum was finished in 1259 BCE. Peace with the Hittites was signed in 1258 BCE. Nefertari died in 1252 BCE. Isetnofret, the second wife, died in 1244 BCE. He married his first Hittite princess that same year. Abu Simbel's construction was finished around then as well. He married a second Hittite princess in 1231 BCE. Death at age ninety-one came in 1213 BCE. Words from the reign are gathered here. An ambush is a surprise attack launched from a place of hiding. Campaigns are series of planned actions aimed at chosen goals. Diplomacy is the skill, or the practice, of bargaining between people who speak for different countries. A dynasty is a run of rulers from one family inside a country. A legacy is a thing passed from earlier times into the present. Mortuary describes what belongs to burial, or what relates to it. Pharaohs were the rulers of ancient Egypt. Propaganda is news, art, or other media that often uses false or stretched information to sway people. A rebellion is a fight against authority or power, also called an uprising. Reigned means held rule over an area as its leading person. A successor is the person who comes next in a job or in a post won by election. A truce is a promise to stop fighting.

27. Eiffel Tower

1Visitors often call the Eiffel Tower breathtaking. Over 125 years ago, four men had a wild idea. They wanted the tallest structure in the world. It would stand 300 meters, or 984 feet, high. They planned more than 18,000 metal pieces held by 2.5 million metal pins. They said it would look good and stand firm in high winds. Many people thought the dream was impossible or ridiculous. Today that dream is the Eiffel Tower, one of the world's best-known and most-loved landmarks.

2The tower stands 300 meters high, and its antenna adds 24 meters. The total height is 324 meters, or 1,063 feet. Platforms sit at 57, 115, and 276 meters in a tower of 108 stories. It weighs 10,100 metric tons, and the iron weighs 7,300 metric tons. Over 250 million people have visited this most-visited paid monument. Its base is 100 meters on each side, and it was finished in 1889 for the World's Fair. Four huge beams of wrought iron, strong yet easy to shape, curve together at the top. It stayed tallest until New York's Chrysler Building passed it in 1930, and a few buildings have passed it since.

3Paris, the capital of France, lies between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. The Eiffel Tower stands on the south bank of the Seine, by Avenue Gustave Eiffel and the Champ de Mars. People come from around the world to enjoy the landmark and many nearby sights. Museums, gardens, palaces, monuments, hotels, and shops show old and new side by side. The tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair, one hundred years after the French Revolution. Gustave Eiffel, who lived from 1832 to 1923, worked on the Statue of Liberty, a railway station, an observatory, and bridges. Chief engineers Maurice Koechlin and Emile Nouguier entered four curved crossed-strip beams, joined by flat beams, in a contest. His company knew tall bridges, and architect Stephen Sauvestre helped make the 300-meter tower attractive and solid.

4Chosen over 106 other projects, work ran from January 26, 1887, to March 31, 1889. The tower uses 18,038 wrought-iron pieces weighing 7,300 metric tons to prove light metal can match stone. Over one hundred workers bolted sections about 5 meters long at Eiffel's factory. By July 1888 the second level was in place, and by late November the tower was nearly done. Teams of four set 2.5 million heated pins that shrank tight, and up to three hundred men worked on site. The stone and cement base sits on gravel at a careful angle against strong winds. Workers kept each level flat with wooden scaffolds and small steam cranes. In sunlight the tower can lean 18 centimeters, and one elevator's 103,000 kilometers a year equal two and a half trips around the equator.

5The World's Fair ran from May 6 to October 31, 1889, as a celebration of French achievements. Over eighty structures on the Champ de Mars held exhibits from Europe and North and South America. A math professor and others said strong winds could collapse even a shorter tower. Three hundred artists, writers, and architects said it would look ridiculous, like a black smokestack on the skyline. Fair leaders ignored them, and the tower was finished just over a month before the fair. Visitors were amazed and delighted, but the tower was supposed to be torn down after twenty years. The day after it opened, Eiffel installed a weather lab, invited scientists, and ran his own tests. Radio began in 1909, television tests began in 1925, and the tower now has 120 antennas.

6Each floor of the tower has its own attractions. The first floor, 57 meters up, has a glass floor that feels like walking on air. It has displays, city views on three walls, shops, restaurants, part of the original spiral stair, and a winter ice rink since 2004. The second floor, 115 meters high, has shops, restaurants, and story windows about the build. A glass window looks straight down, and a glass elevator shows the tower from many angles. At 276 meters, covered and open decks let people enjoy Paris day or night in any weather. Eiffel's restored office has maps and wax figures, with Eiffel on the right talking with Edison on the left. All three floors offer chances for outstanding photos.

7The countdown to the year 2000 at the tower was televised around the world. If Eiffel and his team were alive, they would be glad their wonder brings joy around the world. Almost seven million people visit the tower each year. It plays a part in dozens of novels and movies. It has inspired more than thirty copies. Dazzling lights and fireworks include a great show for the year 2000. Travelers can see this famous landmark from nearly every part of Paris. It still soars over the city, just as Eiffel intended.

28. Elephants, Huge Mammals of Land

1Big and brainy elephants open this book. A closer look at the body comes next. African elephants and Asian elephants are compared. Places they gather come after that. Their plant diet has a part. Family life has a part. A closing part calls them giant friends. A glossary explains key words. Size can be set beside a person. An African elephant’s shoulder stands 13 feet high, or 4 meters. Weight can reach 14,000 pounds, or 6,350 kilograms. A human example is 6 feet tall, or 1.8 meters, and 175 pounds, or 79.4 kilograms. An Asian elephant’s shoulder stands 10 feet high, or 3 meters. Weight can reach 11,000 pounds, or 5,000 kilograms. No land animal alive today is more gigantic than an elephant. A walking creature of still greater size would have to be sought in dinosaur times. Huge is not the whole story. Intelligence is high. Messages pass between elephants in many ways. They are clever enough to join forces and finish a task. The size chart is there so a reader can compare. Shoulder height is the measure for both elephant species. Weight is listed beside it. A person is drawn into the same comparison so the giant scale is clear. Land life today has no bigger walker. Brains and teamwork sit beside that size. A touch can carry a message. A sound can carry one. A shared job can too. The same animal that far outweighs a person can also plan with the herd.

2A stately elephant has no real match. The body is giant. Skin is thick and gray, or thick and brown. Legs are round and sturdy. The strangest part is the trunk. It is long and shaped like a snake. Nose and upper lip are joined in that one appendage. Feeling at the tip is very sharp. Breathing is one job of the trunk. Lifting food is one. Lifting water is one. A blast of air makes a trumpet call loud enough to hurt ears. Touch is a language too. Two elephants often wind their trunks together. Affection is the message. A mother may stroke her calf gently with the trunk. The stroke can calm the calf. It can also scold a calf that misbehaves. Ears on an African elephant are twice the size of ears on an Asian elephant. Elephants are mammals. Every mammal has a backbone. Every mammal has hair at some point in life. Every mammal is warm-blooded. Every mammal makes milk for its babies.

3African and Asian are the two main elephant species. The continent under your feet is a simple clue. Other clues exist too. African elephants are the larger relatives. Females are shorter and lighter than the males. Height is around 9 feet, or 2.7 meters. Weight goes up to 10,000 pounds, or 4,540 kilograms. An Asian male is shorter than an African male by around 3 feet, or 0.9144 meters. He is lighter by about 3,000 pounds, or 1,360 kilograms. Asian females are smaller still. Tusks are often missing on them, which is not the usual case for African females. The African back sinks in the middle. An Asian back does not. Two finger-like flaps sit on an African trunk tip. Food and small objects can be grabbed by those flaps. Tusks dig. They also fight. They also shift objects around. African elephants use them to dig for water as well. Large round bumps sit on top of an Asian elephant’s huge head. Often they are the tallest point on the animal. The Asian back is flat, or it arches. The trunk tip has a single finger-like flap, not two.

4Many habitats can hold elephants. Food must be enough. Water must be enough. Africa gives them hot, dry grasslands. It gives them rainforests. It even gives them deserts. Sea level is possible. High mountains are possible. Asian elephants use wet rainforests and swamps. They also use drier forests that face long seasons without rain. Lions are fierce. Tigers are fierce. Even they seldom threaten an elephant, because the elephant is so massive. Humans are the greater danger. Ivory tusks are taken in illegal hunts. Elephants that harm crops are shot. More people mean less wild land. Roads keep being built. Crops keep being planted. Trees keep being cut. Animals that need huge amounts of food and space lose ground fastest. Elephants once walked across almost all of Africa and almost all of South Asia. Today those habitats are much smaller.

5Plants are the only food elephants eat. That makes them herbivores. Inside that limit they are not choosy. Grass is eaten. Leaves are eaten. Branches are eaten. Bark from trees is eaten. Seeds are eaten. Fruits are eaten. Quantity matters most. An adult can put away more than 300 pounds of food in a day. That is 136 kilograms. Water intake is about 20 to 60 gallons. That is 75.7 to 227.1 liters. The trunk works like a giant straw. Water then sprays from the trunk’s end into the mouth. Digestion uses only about 44 percent of what was eaten. A pregnancy lasts eighteen to twenty-two months. No other animal carries young longer. One close living relative is the hyrax. It is small, cute, and furry. A family link is easy to miss. Woolly mammoths are close relatives too. More than ten thousand years have passed since those mammoths died out. An Asian mother may spray water with her trunk. A sunny day may send her rolling in sand or dirt. The roll helps her avoid a sunburn.

6Social life is strong in elephants, and strongest among females. Adult females share family groups. The oldest female usually leads. A herd may include a grandmother. It may include her grown daughters. It may include the calves of those daughters. Care is shared. Meals are shared. Baths and play are shared. A newborn weighs 250 pounds, or 110 kilograms. From the first moment, every member of the herd gives the mother help. Predators are driven off by adults working as a team. A hungry calf may even be nursed by another adult. Childhood lasts a long time. Nursing can go on until three years have passed. Across that time, and across several later years, vital skills are learned. The young elephant learns where food is. It learns where water is. It learns how the trunk works. Full maturity waits until age ten to fifteen. Males leave the herd. They live alone, or they live with other males. Females remain. In time they raise calves of their own. A life without serious trouble can last sixty to seventy years. Only six sets of teeth grow in a lifetime. After the last set is gone, chewing becomes poor. Marshes are a common home for older elephants. Softer plants grow there.

7A bond with these king-sized elephants is hard to avoid. They are brainy. They are caring. Fun matters to them. Size is awesome. Personalities are distinct. Ignoring them is nearly impossible. Protection from all of us can keep these giants roaming Earth for a long time still. Kenya, in Africa, holds the Samburu National Reserve. African elephants in one picture stand on that reserve. Affection is a caring or loving feeling. An appendage is an outside body part that juts away from the body. An arm is one example. A leg is another. A habitat is the natural home of a plant or an animal. Herbivores are animals whose food is plants alone. Immense means very large. Ivory is the white material in the tusks of elephants and of other animals that have tusks. Mature means developed in body or in mind. To nurse is to give milk made by a mother. A baby may drink it. A young animal may drink it. Tusks are large teeth that stick out past the closed mouth of some mammals, including elephants and wild boars.

29. Elizabeth Tudor Rules England

1A map of the 1500s shows three kingdoms: Scotland, Ireland, and England. Wales is marked on the same island. London is shown with a star. The Atlantic Ocean and the North Sea border the land. France lies across the water, and the wider map also shows Asia, Europe, and Africa. This book follows Elizabeth from her world and her youth to her last years. It tells about Mary and Elizabeth, her early challenges, and a threat from Spain. It tells about the Elizabethan Age, and a word list closes the book. Elizabeth Tudor may have been England's greatest monarch. To understand her, a reader first needs her family story. Her father was Henry VIII, king of England. Before Elizabeth was born, Henry married Catherine of Aragon. They had a daughter named Mary. Henry wanted a son. While he was still Catherine's husband, he came to love Anne Boleyn. He wanted Anne to be his wife. He asked the pope, leader of the Catholic Church, to annul the marriage to Catherine. The pope refused to grant that wish. Henry then formed a separate church. He made himself its supreme ruler on Earth. The Church of England was the name of the church he had formed. Next he declared that his first marriage had no legal force. Free from the pope, Henry married Anne in secret. Anne became queen of England.

2Greenwich, England, was the place of Elizabeth Tudor's birth on September 7, 1533. Henry felt affection for Elizabeth and favored her over Mary. He still wanted a son who could inherit the throne. Henry started to lose interest in Anne Boleyn. It seemed she, too, would not give him a son. In time he accused Anne of treason and had her executed. He declared that their marriage had no legal standing. He declared Elizabeth illegitimate, a child of parents who were not married. That ruling meant she could not inherit his throne. In 1537 Jane Seymour, Henry's third wife, gave birth to the son he wanted. The boy was named Prince Edward. Jane was already weak and exhausted. She caught a high fever and died soon after the birth. By then Elizabeth had begun her schooling in a serious way. Private tutors taught her math, history, geography, architecture, and needlework. She learned to speak and write fluent French, Italian, Greek, and Latin. She was an excellent student, and her tutors regarded her highly. Elizabeth was intelligent, and she relished her schoolwork. Her manner was witty and captivating. She charmed every person she met. In her free time she enjoyed riding horses, dancing, and playing the lute. She rarely saw her father. She often spent time with her older sister and her younger brother. Henry married three more times, but none of those marriages produced another child. His sixth and final marriage, in 1543, was to Catherine Parr. Catherine Parr pushed him hard to set a line of succession. A Tudor family portrait lines up five figures from left to right. They are Lady Mary, Prince Edward, Henry VIII, Jane Seymour, and Lady Elizabeth.

3At Catherine's urging, Henry restored Mary and Elizabeth as heirs. Their brother Edward still stood first in line. Henry VIII died in 1547, and Prince Edward became king at the age of nine.
