Under Edward, the Church of England leaned toward Protestantism, a newer kind of Christianity. His reign was short. Edward died in 1553, and Mary, Elizabeth's older half sister, became queen. Mary was the daughter of Henry and his first wife, Catherine. Mary was Catholic and held that faith strongly. A growing number of people were turning toward Protestantism. Mary's goal as monarch was to stop every Protestant practice. She believed that people who rejected Catholic teachings were heretics. During her reign she ordered the execution of about three hundred people. Those people had been found guilty of standing against the Catholic Church. The killings earned her the nickname Bloody Mary. Elizabeth had been raised as a Protestant, and she valued that faith. She did not trust Mary. She believed she had to look Catholic if she wanted to stay alive. She attended mass in public and studied the Catholic religion. Artwork of the sixteenth century shows the Tower of London. People were sent to that tower to be locked up. Many of them were tortured or killed. Mary still believed that Elizabeth followed Protestant ways in secret. When people tried to overthrow Mary, Mary thought Elizabeth was behind the plot. Mary had Elizabeth arrested and sent to the Tower of London. Elizabeth said she was innocent. She was kept in the tower for two months. She was then released and kept under house arrest for a year. Mary married Prince Philip of Spain and hoped for an heir. She wanted England to remain Catholic. She wanted to block Elizabeth from the throne. Mary had no children. She had to accept that Elizabeth, next in line, would lawfully follow her. Mary died of an illness in 1558. The crowning of Elizabeth as queen took place on January 15, 1559.

4At that moment her age was twenty-five. She quickly showed that she would rule as a Protestant, yet she tolerated Catholics. From the start of her reign, some advisors tried to find her a suitable husband. A marriage could create new alliances between England and other countries. A child would also give England a sure heir. Elizabeth saw the danger in a foreign king. England might then fall under another country's rule. An English husband would rank beneath her royal status. She might also lose power as queen. Many proposals came to her, and she rejected all of them. Elizabeth had fair skin and fair hair. People in Tudor England considered her beautiful. Once she was queen, she dressed in a very elaborate way. She favored bright oranges and bright reds, with jewels as accents. She exuded power and authority. One famous image shows her in coronation robes. More urgent problems pressed on her. Early in the reign, Catholic and Protestant faiths split Europe. Elizabeth worked to stop Catholic Spain and Catholic France from invading England. An invasion might aim to defeat Protestantism. She also watched Scotland, the neighbor to the north, so it would not join her enemy. Mary, Queen of Scots, was Elizabeth's cousin and the Catholic queen of Scotland. Mary posed a grave threat. Many English Catholics tried to depose Elizabeth. They wanted Mary to ascend the English throne and restore Catholicism. Some of those threats were linked to Mary. When Mary came to England, Elizabeth imprisoned her for nineteen years. In 1586 Elizabeth's patience came to an end. She learned that Mary had joined yet another plot to assassinate her. Elizabeth had Mary tried for treason. The judges ruled that Mary had plotted against Elizabeth. Mary was executed on February 8, 1587. She had spent nineteen years as Elizabeth's prisoner. She was forty-four years old.

5King Philip II of Spain was Catholic. He had already been planning an invasion of England before Mary, Queen of Scots, was executed. Once Mary was dead, Philip judged that Elizabeth had to be removed from the throne. He wanted the Catholic faith restored in England. Up to that point, the explorer Sir Francis Drake had been making Philip angry. Elizabeth supported Drake. Drake plundered Spanish ships that were sailing home from new lands in the Americas. He ordered his seamen to raid those ships. They seized large amounts of gold and silver bound for Spain. In 1587 Drake sailed into Cadiz Harbor in Spain. He destroyed many Spanish ships sitting at anchor. After that setback, Philip prepared to attack England and overthrow Elizabeth. In 1588 he sent the Spanish Armada to sea. The fleet's purpose was to invade England. About seventeen thousand soldiers on foot also served Philip from the Netherlands. Those troops were under Spanish rule, and they backed his Armada. Those soldiers were unready, so the invasion could not begin. English sailors were the better seamen, and their ships were more maneuverable. They scattered the Spanish ships and drove them into the North Sea. As the Spanish sailed north, the winds did not favor them. The weather slowly beat them. Elizabeth's troops had triumphed, and her crown had survived another challenge. A map traces the Spanish Armada in 1588. The fleet sailed north toward England. It then went around the coasts of Scotland and Ireland on the way back to Spain.

6Elizabeth built a strong government and a powerful navy. She wanted her beloved country to grow and to gain wealth. She encouraged exploration of new places and trade with foreign lands. Trade in silk, food, and spices gave large help to England's economy. She believed strongly in support for the arts. During her reign she encouraged music, art, and literature. Musicians, poets, writers, and other artists were always welcome at her court. England's arts had reached a flourishing state by 1590. Many people rank William Shakespeare as the finest writer of plays. He grew very popular while Elizabeth ruled. He often brought his troupe of actors to perform at her court. England was on the path to a global empire. Her years later took the name Golden Age in English history. Among countries of the world, England rose until it stood near the top in importance. A picture shows Queen Elizabeth I making Sir Francis Drake a knight. She honored the English explorer for what his voyages achieved. In her later rule, Elizabeth eased the religious fights that had torn the country apart. Protestantism was quietly set in place as England's official religion. Education and the arts, both firmly backed by her, made great strides. More people than ever before learned to read and to write. Elizabeth died in 1603 after a reign of forty-four years. She named James VI, son of Mary, Queen of Scots, as the next ruler. That choice brought England and Scotland together. She was highly educated and a keen observer of human nature. Her reign showed allies and enemies the same truth. A woman could rule as an effective monarch and as a successful leader. The English loved her and respected her. They would remember their queen for all the years to come. The Tudor family had no monarch after Elizabeth I. The Tudors had ruled England since 1485.

7These dates show the life of Queen Elizabeth the First. In 1533, Elizabeth was born. Her father was Henry the Eighth. Her mother was Anne Boleyn. In 1536, Anne Boleyn was put to death. In 1544, a law set who would rule next. In 1547, Henry died. Then Edward became king. On July 6, 1553, King Edward died. On October 1, 1553, Mary was made queen. In 1554, Mary put Elizabeth in prison. In 1558, Mary died. Then Elizabeth became queen. In 1587, Mary, Queen of Scots, was put to death. In 1588, Elizabeth beat the Spanish Armada. In 1590, the arts grew strong. Elizabeth helped the arts grow. On March 24, 1603, Elizabeth died. James the First became king of England and of Scotland. The two lands were joined as one. An alliance is a close link between lands that work as one. Heretics are people who reject the set beliefs.

30. Energy Sources: Good Points and Bad Points

1The parts of this book come in this order. First comes the nonstop need for energy. Fossil fuels come next. Power from water follows. Energy from the Sun comes after that. Power from atoms follows. A look toward later years comes next. A word list and an index close the book. The Nonstop Need for Energy. The United States counts as a modern society. Every modern society uses a great deal of energy. To scientists, energy means the ability to do work. Work can take many forms. Moving an automobile along a road counts as work. Sending an airplane into flight counts as work. Making electricity counts as work. Keeping factory machines running counts as work. Energy for the United States comes from many places. Other modern societies draw on many places too. A large share comes from burning fuel. Coal is one such fuel. Gasoline is another. Flowing water supplies some energy. Sunlight supplies some. Wind supplies some. Splitting atoms supplies some. A picture shows machines inside a car factory. Those machines need energy before they can build cars.

2Every energy source has good points. Every energy source has bad points. People call the good points and the bad points pros and cons. Modern societies face many choices about energy. They must pick a sound way to produce it. Society's needs have to be weighed against care for the environment. The choices are not always simple. A chart tracks energy use in the United States from 1949 to 2005. The unit on the chart is the quadrillion BTU. The four measures are consumption, production, imports, and exports. The figures come from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The report is the Annual Energy Review 2005. More energy is used in the United States than the country produces. What might that gap mean for energy in the United States in the years ahead? In 1949, consumption was 31.98, production was 31.72, imports were 1.45, and exports were 1.59. In 1950, consumption was 34.62, production was 35.54, imports were 1.91, and exports were 1.47. In 1955, consumption was 40.21, production was 40.15, imports were 2.79, and exports were 2.29. In 1960, consumption was 45.09, production was 42.8, imports were 4.19, and exports were 1.48. In 1965, consumption was 54.02, production was 50.68, imports were 5.89, and exports were 1.83. In 1970, consumption was 67.84, production was 63.5, imports were 8.34, and exports were 2.63. In 1971, consumption was 69.29, production was 62.72, imports were 9.53, and exports were 2.15. In 1972, consumption was 72.7, production was 63.92, imports were 11.39, and exports were 2.12. In 1973, consumption was 75.71, production was 63.58, imports were 14.61, and exports were 2.03. In 1974, consumption was 73.99, production was 62.37, imports were 14.3, and exports were 2.2. In 1975, consumption was 72, production was 61.36, imports were 14.03, and exports were 2.32. In 1976, consumption was 76.01, production was 61.6, imports were 16.76, and exports were 2.17. In 1977, consumption was 78, production was 62.05, imports were 19.95, and exports were 2.05. In 1978, consumption was 79.99, production was 63.14, imports were 19.11, and exports were 1.92. In 1979, consumption was 80.9, production was 65.95, imports were 19.46, and exports were 2.86. In 1980, consumption was 78.28, production was 67.23, imports were 15.8, and exports were 3.69. In 1981, consumption was 76.34, production was 67.01, imports were 13.72, and exports were 4.31. In 1982, consumption was 73.29, production was 66.61, imports were 11.86, and exports were 4.61. In 1983, consumption was 73.15, production was 64.15, imports were 11.75, and exports were 3.69. In 1984, consumption was 76.79, production was 68.89, imports were 12.47, and exports were 3.79. In 1985, consumption was 76.58, production was 67.76, imports were 11.78, and exports were 4.2. In 1986, consumption was 76.83, production was 67.13, imports were 14.15, and exports were 4.02. In 1987, consumption was 79.22, production was 67.61, imports were 15.4, and exports were 3.81. In 1988, consumption was 82.87, production was 68.98, imports were 17.3, and exports were 4.37. In 1989, consumption was 85, production was 69.41, imports were 18.77, and exports were 4.66. In 1990, consumption was 84.73, production was 70.79, imports were 18.82, and exports were 4.75. In 1991, consumption was 84.67, production was 70.43, imports were 18.33, and exports were 5.14. In 1992, consumption was 86.01, production was 70, imports were 19.37, and exports were 4.94. In 1993, consumption was 87.65, production was 68.33, imports were 21.27, and exports were 4.26. In 1994, consumption was 89.29, production was 70.72, imports were 22.39, and exports were 4.06. In 1995, consumption was 91.2, production was 71.13, imports were 22.26, and exports were 4.51. In 1996, consumption was 94.23, production was 72.47, imports were 23.7, and exports were 4.63. In 1997, consumption was 94.8, production was 72.46, imports were 25.22, and exports were 4.51. In 1998, consumption was 95.2, production was 72.84, imports were 26.58, and exports were 4.3. In 1999, consumption was 96.84, production was 71.71, imports were 27.25, and exports were 3.71. In 2000, consumption was 98.98, production was 71.29, imports were 28.97, and exports were 4.01. In 2001, consumption was 96.5, production was 71.91, imports were 30.16, and exports were 3.77. In 2002, consumption was 97.97, production was 70.86, imports were 29.41, and exports were 3.67. In 2003, consumption was 98.27, production was 70.14, imports were 31.06, and exports were 4.05. In 2004, consumption was 100.41, production was 70.39, imports were 33.54, and exports were 4.43. In 2005, consumption was 99.89, production was 69.17, imports were 34.26, and exports were 4.64. Fuels from Ancient Life. Coal, oil, and natural gas are fossil fuels. Around the world, fossil fuels are a leading energy source. The name comes from the way they formed. They formed from remains of plants and of animals. Those living things died many millions of years ago. Underground, great heat worked on the remains. Great pressure worked on them too. The remains turned into materials we burn as fuel. Fossil fuels supply about 85 percent of the energy the United States uses each year. Many power plants burn coal in order to make electricity. Oil is turned into gasoline. Oil is turned into diesel fuel. Oil is turned into jet fuel. Those fuels move cars. They move trucks. They move airplanes. In most homes, stoves run on natural gas. Water heaters in most homes run on natural gas too. A picture shows gasoline, a familiar fossil fuel.

3How Oil Forms. Marine plants die. Marine animals die. The dead plants and animals fall down to the ocean floor. Dirt mixes with them. Sand mixes with them too. The mix becomes a layer of sediment. Time goes by. Further layers are added. Pressure grows. Buried plant and animal material changes into kerogen. While that happens, the sediment hardens into sedimentary rock. Still more time passes. Still more layers are added. Still more pressure builds. The added pressure turns the kerogen into oil. The new oil starts to rise. It moves through tiny holes in the sedimentary rock. The oil rises until it meets rock it cannot cross. Oil rigs drill through that blocking rock. Pumps then draw out the oil that has collected. A picture shows a close view of coal. A picture shows a pump jack. The pump jack pulls petroleum from an oil well. A main advantage of fossil fuels is abundance. Abundant means they occur in many places. It also means they occur in large amounts. Fossil fuels hold a lot of energy that people can use. Coal is found in especially large amounts. Enough coal remains in the United States for another 200 to 300 years. Natural gas has one special advantage. It burns in a very clean way. Burning natural gas gives off mostly carbon dioxide. It also gives off water vapor. Oil's main advantage is efficient burning. Efficient means little is wasted as oil becomes energy. The refining that makes gasoline also makes diesel fuel. That same refining makes other petroleum products. Some of those products go into crayons. Some go into bubble gum. Some go into eyeglasses. Some even go into artificial heart valves.

4Fossil fuels are, in essence, nonrenewable sources of energy. Nature cannot make new supplies fast enough to match demand. Many experts expect the world's oil wells to run dry within a few decades. Even sooner, the oil on hand will be too small. It will fail to meet demand around the globe. Fossil fuels give off pollutants. Natural gas is the exception to that. Cars send harmful chemicals into the air. Factories send harmful chemicals into the air. Many power plants do the same. Because these fuels are burned, dirty air will remain a problem. A further problem is known as the greenhouse effect. Gases from burned fossil fuels hold extra heat in Earth's atmosphere. The heat held is greater than the heat nature would hold alone. That warming of the atmosphere is called global warming. Carbon dioxide, scientists think, does the most to worsen the greenhouse effect. Natural gas adds to the problem as well. A picture shows pollutants climbing into the atmosphere. Power from Moving Water. In many places, people use water to make electricity. You may ask how water can do that job. The answer is a dam. Picture a dam as a huge wall that is also very wide. Concrete is the usual material. The wall is built across a river. It stops the river from flowing on. Water then gathers in a wide area behind the dam. The gathered water becomes a lake, or a reservoir. Lake water is let out through the bottom of the dam. That water travels very fast. It passes through large machines called turbines. Inside each turbine are blades shaped like fans. Rushing water makes those blades spin. Turbines link to other machines called generators. The generators spin as well. Inside a generator, giant magnets surround a shaft. A huge coil of wire surrounds the shaft and the magnets. Spinning shafts and magnets shift electrons inside the wire coil. Moving electrons make an electric current. Power made this way at a dam is known as hydroelectric power. The word hydro is a prefix. A prefix is the first part of a word. Hydro means water.

5A picture shows generators inside a dam. Parts of a Working Dam. The labeled parts are the reservoir and the power lines. They include the dam and the generator. They include the penstock and the turbine. Water leaves the reservoir and enters the penstock. The water races downward. On the way, it turns the turbine blades. After that, the water empties into the river. Dams turn out a large share of the electricity people need. More than 2,000 hydroelectric dams stand in the United States. Those dams make about 10 percent of the nation's electricity. Around the world, hydroelectric dams make about 20 percent of the electricity. Dams serve other purposes too. One purpose is flood control. A dam can store water that comes from heavy rain. It can store water that comes from melting snow. The stored water is released slowly at a later time. Hoover Dam crosses the Colorado River. The dam forms Lake Mead. Lake Mead is among the largest lakes made by people. A picture shows boat docks on Lake Mead. The lakes open many chances for recreation. People boat on them. People fish on them. Homes draw water from the lakes. Industries draw water from the lakes. Farmers draw water from the lakes. They use it to irrigate crops in the drier months.

6Holding back floods helps people. The same choice is harder on the environment. A river is meant to flood. Floodwater lays down sediment. Sediment mixes gravel, sand, and topsoil. Sediment left by floods keeps riverside farmland rich. Once a river is dammed, it cannot refresh the soil around it. A picture shows salmon swimming toward the river's source. Dams also cut the path of fish. Some of those fish travel up a river. Some travel down a river. In the Pacific Northwest of the United States, dams have hurt salmon badly. Every three to five years, salmon leave the ocean. They swim up rivers to the places where they were born. They make the trip in order to lay eggs. A dam makes the upstream swim difficult. A dam makes the downstream swim difficult too. Salmon numbers have fallen sharply because of this. The fall has taken place over the past 100 years. Energy from the Sun. Sunlight carries enormous amounts of energy. On a summer day you can feel that energy. The sunlight warms your skin. Scientists made solar cells to catch energy from the Sun. The cells are called photovoltaic cells. Say photovoltaic as FOE-toe-vole-TAY-ik. A solar cell changes sunlight into electricity. When light strikes the cell, some of the light energy is absorbed. Particles inside the cell begin to move faster. That faster movement produces electricity. In some places, big panels of solar cells collect sunshine. The panels supply electricity to homes. They supply electricity to businesses. Solar cells have been fitted to cars. They have been fitted to appliances. A picture shows a solar panel powering a phone booth.

7A picture shows a solar water heater. Towns use many heaters like this one to warm their water. Collectors of solar heat use the Sun to warm water. Collectors of this kind often sit on roofs. Water moves through pipes inside the panels. Radiant energy from the Sun heats that water. Pumps send the hot water into a building. Further pipes carry it. Heat passes out of the water. That heat warms the rooms. Cooled water travels back to the roof. On the roof it is heated once more. A picture shows solar panels on the roof of a house. The panels give the house its energy. Some regions have many days of sun. The southwestern United States is one such region. There, solar cells can make a lot of electricity. Solar panels there can make a lot of heat. The Sun sends free energy toward Earth in abundance. The stream of energy continues through all 24 hours of a day. People far from the sunniest lands still mount solar cells on roofs. They mount solar panels on roofs too. Some roofs belong to houses. Some roofs belong to businesses. The aim is a lower energy bill. Experts say vast sets of solar panels in sunny regions could make enough electricity for a whole country. Catching this energy can help us deal with a diminishing supply. Fresh methods for catching the energy keep being developed. The aim of the new methods is to maximize efficiency.

8Solar cells bring two main problems. The first problem is the price. Making the cells costs a great deal. That price leaves other plants as a cheaper energy source. A hydroelectric plant costs less. A fossil-fuel power plant costs less. Until the cells can be manufactured at a low price, this free energy stays costly. The cost is in catching the energy. The cost is also in turning it into electricity. The second problem is uneven sunlight. Not every part of the world receives abundant sun. Backup sources would be required beside the solar cells. Backups raise the total cost of energy. Some neighbors of solar houses dislike the look. They see rooftop cells and panels as ugly. They believe that look will lower the value of their own homes. A picture shows power plants that could back up solar farms. Power from Atoms. A nuclear power plant releases the energy stored in atoms. The plant uses that energy to make electricity. Every split of an atom lets energy out. An atomic bomb explodes by a chain reaction that is very fast. A nuclear plant uses the element uranium. Uranium is radioactive. The plant runs a chain reaction that is slow. The reaction is kept under control. Energy from broken uranium atoms heats water. The heated water becomes steam. Steam then drives the making of electricity. A coal plant makes electricity in much the same manner. A picture shows cooling towers. The towers hold the plant's core at a safe temperature.

9A picture shows nuclear waste being handled with great care. The energy from uranium is incredible in amount. One kilogram of uranium can yield more energy than 3 million kilograms of coal. One kilogram equals 2.2 lbs. Three million kilograms equal 6.6 million lbs. Nuclear plants hold another advantage over coal plants. They do not send out gases that dirty the sky. They do not add those gases to global warming. Many people reject nuclear power because of danger. One danger is an accident. A nuclear plant cannot blow up the way an atomic bomb does. It can suffer a steam explosion if the core grows too hot. The core is the part that holds the uranium. Such an explosion would throw out a lot of dangerous radiation. Waste is a second danger. The plants produce this waste material. Uranium can reach a point where it no longer makes electricity. Even then, it stays highly radioactive. The danger lasts for thousands of years. A picture shows wind turbines that could add energy in later years. The Years Ahead. In coming years, substitutes for oil will have to be found. Hydroelectric power may be set aside as well. Many people are troubled by what dams do to the environment. They want a large number of dams taken down. Solar energy will probably see wider use. Energy experts say more nuclear plants will need to be built. Growing demand for energy is the reason.

10A chart compares energy made and energy used by world region in 2004. The unit is the quadrillion BTU. One column records production. Another column records consumption. North, Central, and South America produced 126 and consumed 143, so that region used more than it made. Europe produced 51 and consumed 86. Eurasia produced 67 and consumed 45, so it made more than it used. The Middle East produced 62 and consumed 21. Africa produced 32 and consumed 14. Asia and Oceania produced 105 and consumed 138. In three world regions, people use more energy than those regions create. Why might that be so? Where do those regions get the extra energy? A second chart shows energy use by type, past and estimated. The years on it run from 1980 to 2030. Oil is one type on the chart. Coal is one type. Natural gas is one type. Renewables are on the chart, including wind and solar. Nuclear energy is on the chart. Part of the chart is history. Part of the chart is projections. With today's rates as a guide, the chart shows world energy use growing through the year 2030. What does the chart say about how people will use energy later? These figures come from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The report is the International Energy Outlook 2006. Scientists are studying still more ways to make energy. Wind turbines are one way under study. Geothermal energy is another. A wind turbine makes electricity when wind turns its blades. No fuel is required. The turbines create no pollution. The machines are huge. Birds that live nearby can be killed by them. Geothermal energy begins deep under the ground. At that depth the Earth is very hot. Pipes can carry water down to that heat. The water takes the heat in. Hot water from below can warm homes. It can warm other buildings. In many places the underground heat is difficult to reach. Reaching it can also be expensive. A picture shows a geothermal plant.

11A chart lists the countries that created the most energy in 2004. The unit is the quadrillion BTU. The United States created 70.4. China created 56.0. Russia created 51.7. Saudi Arabia created 24.2. Canada created 18.6. Iran created 12.1. India created 11.1. Norway created 10.8. Australia created 10.6. Mexico created 10.3. Two things are sure. People need energy. Fossil fuels provide most of our energy. Those fuels will not last forever. Renewable substitutes are the key. They matter to the energy future of the whole world. Scientists will go on with their research. Every new source will have pros. Every new source will have cons. Governments will keep arguing over which sources are best. Businesses will keep arguing too. Environmentalists will keep arguing too. While they argue, the need for energy will keep growing. Energy means the forms of power that people and machines need when they do work. Environmentalists are people who want Earth's ecosystems to stay healthy. Fossil fuels are sources of energy taken out of the earth. Coal, oil, and natural gas are fossil fuels. Global warming is the rise of temperatures across the world. The rise happens when air pollution traps heat. Hydroelectric describes electricity that is produced from water. Pollutants are chemicals that harm the environment. Sediment is earth in small bits that floodwater carries. A turbine is a wheel spun by the force of water, air, or steam. Index. The index names carbon dioxide and coal. It names dams and floods. It names fossil fuels and gasoline. It names geothermal energy and global warming. It names hydroelectric power and kerogen. It names natural gas. It names nuclear power, also called atomic power. It names oil and pollution. It names solar energy and steam. It names the Sun and uranium. It names water and wind.

31. Europe’s Big Night of Song

1England's group Bucks Fizz took the top prize in 1981. The show was the Eurovision Song Contest. Their song was Making Your Mind Up. Years earlier, another win had already stayed with me. Dana's winning song in 1970 was All Kinds of Everything. Charts across Europe put that sweet ballad in the top spot. I first saw this contest on a television screen in 1970. I watched with my family. My family is Irish. I could not follow the languages the songs used. After every contestant had sung, jurors from other countries voted. They chose their favorite songs. The presenters spoke politely to the jurors in each juror's own language. Television carried the point totals out to Europe's other countries. We waited with excitement. Ireland's entry was the one we hoped would finish with the top score. That first memory of the yearly show has never left me. That night I realized something for the first time. My home belonged with the other countries of Europe. Ireland's victory is why the memory stays sharp.

2At the 2010 contest held in Norway, fans stand together for photos. No song competition in Europe is larger than the Eurovision Song Contest. It is also Europe's most spectacular song competition. A strong national showing fills people with pride. Countries promote themselves to their neighbors. Audiences across the continent join the fun. They judge the songs for themselves. Friends and relatives enjoy teasing the cheesy-looking acts. They argue about the votes. Singers from 1963 stand for a photo before the board of entered songs. Before 2013, the performance order was chosen at random. Today, producers choose the order. The contest started in 1956. Its aim was to help bring European countries together. The Second World War had torn those countries apart. Switzerland hosted the earliest contest. Just seven countries from Europe entered. The show lasted more than an hour and a half. Each of the seven countries sent two entries. Famous singers from each country performed the songs. A live orchestra backed them. Early rules said each song must use the official language of its country. Some songs got around that rule so they could appeal to international judges. They used nonsense words that listeners could recognize. Lulu won for England in 1969 with Boom, Bang-a-Bang. Massiel won for Spain in 1968 with La, La, La. The 1974 winner was ABBA, a pop act from Sweden. They sang Waterloo in English. By then, the rule about national languages had been relaxed.

3No other contest works quite like this one. Countries vote on one another's songwriting. They also judge one another's performance skills. Each country begins by picking its own song at home. A country may hold a competition on television. A committee may pick the entry instead. Every song must be sung live. Every song must last three minutes or less. The group Twin Twin is one act fans remember. Winning titles have included A-Ba-Ni-Bi, from Israel in 1978. They have included Diggi-Loo Diggi-Ley, from Sweden in 1984. France could have taken a 2014 prize for the strangest song name. The same prize could have gone to the oddest song. France's song was Moustache, by Twin Twin. Its subject was a man hoping to grow a moustache. Identical twins called Jedward, known for style, finished eighth during 2011. Their song was Lipstick. They wore jackets that paid tribute to Michael Jackson. During contest week, the acts go to whichever land is the host. They rehearse. Then they compete to reach the semifinals. The semifinals take place over two days. The twenty-six highest scorers move on to the Grand Final. Prime time is the usual hour for airing the final. Half the points come from viewers, and half come from the jury. Five experts from the music industry also vote. They use a point system. A phone call is one way people at home can send a vote. They can vote by text message. They can vote through the official app. To keep the contest fair, people cannot vote for their own country.

4Finalists sing once more when the last round begins. Juries in every country still taking part vote a second time. The viewers vote again too. After the votes are in, hosts ask one speaker from each land to announce results. On the live broadcast, that speaker reads out the jury score from home. Next, workers add up the total points for each country. The totals are revealed from the lowest score to the highest. In that tense last moment, fans wait to hear the winning name. The winning song is performed once more. The winner receives a glass microphone trophy that fans know at once. Finally, the winning country receives the honor of hosting the next year's contest. Ireland has won seven times. No country has a stronger record across the contest's history. Putting the 1996 show on stage cost 3.5 million dollars. Estimates still said Ireland's economy gained more than 9 million dollars. Norway has lost the most. Norway has also won three times. Four lands in 1969 ended on one shared point total. All four had to be declared winners. Tie-breaker rules were introduced so that would not happen again. The contest's 60th anniversary was marked in 2015. It is the longest-running yearly television music competition in history. Fans call the excitement Eurofever. The show is theatrical. It is flashy. Many viewers love the event. People watching can enter special prize drawings. Fans can download scorecards. They can join the fun at home. The early contests felt serious rather than playful. Women wore ball gowns. Every act in those years was stiff and formal. Lys Assia, singing for Switzerland, was the earliest champion. She won in 1956. She was also the first singer to repeat her entry as the night ended. Emotion overcame her. She forgot her lyrics. She made up the rest of the song as she went. Her winning song was Refrain.

5In later decades the show became a stage for talent from each nation. Color and style shifted like a bright kaleidoscope. Now, performers wear costumes covered in sequins. Jewels cover the costumes too. The set designs can be very imaginative. The performances can be surprising. Mariya Yaremchuk of Ukraine amazed audiences in 2014. Her song was Tick-Tock. A man ran behind her inside a giant wheel. Playful words helped the Grannies from Buranovo draw notice during 2012. On popular television talent shows, contestants with unusual styles may not reach the final round. Eurovision welcomes everyone. Most Eurovision winners do not go on to successful pop careers. There are exceptions. ABBA won the 1974 contest. Switzerland's 1988 singer was Celine Dion. The song that wins is often not the entry people find most interesting. The Russian entry in 2012 was the Grannies from Buranovo. They were the runner-up. Their song was Party for Everybody. Listeners smiled at the Grannies' playful lines. Joy and happiness, those lines claimed, fill each person. Dogs share that feeling. Cats share it too.

6Honoring diversity is the aim this contest sets for itself. It also acts as a showcase for the wide range of cultures across Europe. Eurovision has now grown to more than forty countries. Its audience is more than two hundred million people worldwide. Europeans can use a vote to back the pop alliances they prefer. A 2006 study by two colleges in London found a pattern. Neighbors often hand points to one another, voting as a bloc. Scandinavian voters can be trusted to back their own neighbors. Eastern European acts getting points from Eastern Europe surprise nobody. Points moving between Ireland and the United Kingdom are always watched. Being part of a bloc does not always mean a win. That northern bloc of countries includes Norway. Contest history still treats Norway as the land with the worst luck. Last place has been Norway's finish a record eleven times. It has earned nul points four times. Nul points means no points. Some voting patterns might cause bad feelings between countries. Azerbaijan, next door, placed Armenia at the bottom in 2014. Voters in Armenia answered with their lowest marks for Azerbaijan. The Armenian jury did the same. People thought the reason was resentment. A military conflict between the two countries had ended in 1994. In 2015, both countries again ranked each other last. A list of Eurovision winners from 1956 to 2017 names twenty-seven countries. A repeated win belongs to several of those lands. The countries are Austria, Azerbaijan, and Belgium. They include Denmark, Estonia, Finland, and France. They include Germany, Greece, Ireland, and Israel. They include Italy, Latvia, Luxembourg, and Monaco. They include the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, and Russia. They include Serbia, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland. They include Turkey, Ukraine, and the United Kingdom. They include the former Yugoslavia. Public broadcasting companies, joined in one big body, operate the show. The group is the European Broadcasting Union, or EBU. A land inside the EBU is allowed to send a song. Israel is a member even though it is not in Europe. Armenia is a member too, though it is not in Europe. After the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991, Eurovision welcomed the new countries of Eastern Europe. Some countries that are not in the EBU have also been invited. Morocco is one of them. Australia is another.

7Salvador Sobral, singing for Portugal, took the prize in 2017. Sweet and old-fashioned describes the tune that won. Any time period could have produced that melody. A rap performance from Romania lost to this plain melody. It also beat a dancing gorilla from Italy. Could this contest encourage Europe to grow more united? Can it offer hope for a Europe that is more inclusive? The contest is about joyful celebration. Different values and different customs meet with acceptance here. Every year its popularity grows. Friends and families come together to watch the big show. They cheer for their favorites. Nothing now in view suggests this lively custom will stop. Francesco Gabbani of Italy shared the 2017 stage with a gorilla that danced. An audience is a gathering that has come to watch or to listen. Sending radio programs, or television programs, out to listeners is broadcasting. People, teams, or businesses chasing the same prize are in a competition. Contestants are people who take part in a competition. Shared ideas and shared customs of a group make up its culture. A culture can also mean one society that keeps customs and ideas of its own. Bringing in many cultures, or many kinds of people, is what diversity means. Experts are people who know a great deal about a subject. Inclusive means available or open to anyone. Matters that involve two nations, or more, are international. Lyrics are the words of a song. To mock is to make fun of someone, often by imitating that person. A trophy is a prize object handed to the winner of a contest.

32. Expedition 60: The Subarctic

1Girls try out new winter boots at a factory near St. Petersburg, Russia. At 60 degrees north, the summers are short and the winters are cold. Welcome aboard for a flight around the world at 60 degrees north. We will travel over the subarctic, south of the Arctic Circle. The subarctic is known for long, cold winters and short, cool summers. This trip will not visit that same latitude in the Southern Hemisphere. At 60 degrees south there is no land, so there are no airports.

2Some subarctic mountains hold glaciers built up over hundreds or thousands of years. The subarctic holds bears, wolves, caribou, moose, and huge taiga forests. Taiga trees can stand cold as low as −65 degrees Fahrenheit in winter. Mendenhall Glacier in southeast Alaska is popular with tourists. Our June trip starts in Anchorage, the northernmost major city in the United States. Anchorage lies at 61 degrees north, in time for the Summer Solstice Festival. On June 21, the longest day, it gets about nineteen to twenty-two hours of daylight. The Arctic Circle at about 67 degrees north marks where the Sun does not set that day.

3At Anchorage's Summer Solstice festival, people play water balloon volleyball at the Annual Heroes Games. Anchorage lies on Cook Inlet, a narrow channel on the Gulf of Alaska. This area is the homeland of the Dena'ina Athabascan people. Large bodies of water keep places warmer in winter and cooler in summer. Summer highs average 65 degrees Fahrenheit, and winter highs average 20. Many Alaskans celebrate outdoors into the night under the midnight sun. We fly east and land in Oslo, Norway, on an inlet of the North Sea. The North Atlantic Drift keeps summer near 70 degrees Fahrenheit and winter in the mid-20s.

4Oslo's Viking Ship Museum holds a ship found in a large burial mound. Vikings were seafarers who lived here about 1,000 years ago. They reached coastal Europe, Iceland, Greenland, and North America. Children in Oslo celebrate Constitution Day in traditional clothing with flags. You arrive in Helsinki at 60 degrees north just in time for Nightless Night. The Sun will not set until almost 11:00 pm. Sweden built Suomenlinna in the 1700s to guard the Baltic Sea, and Russia later conquered it. The fortress spans six islands, is part of Finland again, and still has old cannons.

5St. Petersburg is called the Venice of the North because of its many canals. Peter the Great, a Russian czar, founded the city in the 1700s. He built canals and filled swampy land by the Neva River and the Gulf of Finland. In June, people take all-night White Nights walks along canals and drawbridges. Indigenous Peoples developed dogsledding thousands of years ago for icy landscapes. Teams of two to twelve dogs carried game, mail, and medicine over vast distances. Inuit scouts used sleds in World War II, and the Iditarod races 1,000 miles from Anchorage to Nome. The same cities feel very different on December 21, the winter solstice.

6The winter solstice is the shortest day, with about five hours of daylight. Coastal highs are in the 20s Fahrenheit, near −4 degrees Celsius. Near large water, the four cities stay warmer than inland towns. Inland highs average about 5 degrees Fahrenheit, or −15 degrees Celsius. Long cold winters can leave permafrost, ground that never fully thaws. Permafrost makes roads and buildings very difficult to build. This telephone pole tilts because the permafrost beneath it is melting. Powerful electrical discharges high up cause the northern lights and the southern aurora australis.

7Iñupiat people and visitors enjoy a blanket toss in Kotzebue, Alaska. This traditional hunting technique is now used for celebrations and competitions. I hope you enjoyed our summer trip to 60 degrees north latitude. The temperatures were warm, and the days were long. That is because the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun in summer. This tilt extends the time between sunrise and sunset. The four countries you visited have very different cultures. In each place, people celebrate the summer solstice, the day with the most sunlight.

33. First Footprints on the Moon

1On July 20, 1969, half a billion people around the globe were glued to their television screens. At the same time, millions listened to radio broadcasts. An event marking a milestone in human history was unfolding. For the first time, astronauts were walking on the Moon. Only sixty years earlier, powered flights rose barely off the soil. Imagination drove that leap in skill. Determination drove it. So did the courage of countless people who chased a dream. In 1903 two American brothers flew a powered aircraft. Their names were Orville Wright and Wilbur Wright. The flight kept going. The pilots stayed in control. No powered flight before theirs had done both. By 1918, airplanes were important to armies in World War I. Forces used them in operations around the globe. From the earliest ages, people have longed to slip free of Earth's gravity and take to the air. Stories and myths spoke of beings who swept across the sky. Greek tales told of Icarus. He was mortal. He aimed for the Sun. Feathers formed his wings, and wax held them. Mercury was a god of Rome. Winged feet carried him fast through the heavens. In Greek belief, Apollo was god of the Sun. He was also god of light. A chariot carried him over the clouds.

2World War II ran from 1939 to 1945. It brought planes that were faster. It also brought planes that were larger. Some could pass 800 miles in an hour, or 1,287 kmph. Some could fly higher than 40,000 feet, or 12,192 m. Scientists wanted to push flight farther. Engineers did too. Outer space was the new boundary. Late in the 1940s, the United States tested rocket planes. They could fly at speeds that were supersonic. President Dwight Eisenhower, in the year 1958, put his name on a law from Congress. The bill formed an agency that stood on its own. Space flight was its work. National Aeronautics and Space Administration is the agency's long name. The short name is NASA. A race in space. Catching up was one of NASA's first aims. The rival was the Soviet Union. That country is now called Russia. Its space program was ahead. The Soviets had launched Sputnik, a satellite made by humans. That launch is what drove the United States to form NASA. The nation poured itself into the contest. People began to call it the space race. The Soviets were the other side. A drawing by an artist shows Sputnik 1. Steps ahead, and steps back. America's earliest program of flights into space was called Project Mercury. By 1961 it had put satellites into space. It had also placed humans in orbit around Earth. Those results moved President John F. Kennedy. Speaking in public, he set a deadline of nine years. In that time the country would place a man on the Moon. It would return him safely to Earth. Researchers at NASA knew the promise demanded new technologies. The tools had to be invented. They had to be tried out. Suddenly the team was in another kind of race. The clock was the opponent. John Glenn is shown in a picture. Among American astronauts, he was first to orbit Earth. Mercury showed that NASA could send a single person into space and bring that person back without harm. Leaders then asked about two people, or a larger crew. What if the stay lasted many days? Project Gemini was created to find out. Its chief purpose was practice in space, getting ready for travel to the Moon.

3The Gemini craft was larger than Mercury's capsule. It was also far more capable. A Mercury capsule, while in orbit, could only change which way it faced. A Gemini capsule could change the orbit itself. Gemini 4 flew in June 1965. On that flight, Ed White stepped outside the craft. That spacewalk was NASA's first. The formal name is extravehicular activity. The short name is EVA. Later in 1965, the Gemini 7 crew stayed in orbit for fourteen days. One year on, Gemini 10 proved a docking. One craft joined another. One engine then shifted both. With every success, NASA's leaders felt surer. They thought the astronauts could start the Moon missions. Those missions would be called Apollo. A picture shows the Apollo 1 crew. Fate would be cruel to them. By 1967 NASA planned to launch its first Apollo flight. Even after all the preparation, tragedy struck. On a launch test dated January 27, 1967, fire started inside the Apollo 1 capsule. Gus Grissom could not escape. Ed White could not escape. Roger Chaffee was trapped as well. Flames raced through the cabin. All three died. The nation was stunned. For a time, every launch stopped. NASA studied the accident with care. Pure oxygen in the cabin helped the fire race ahead. Material that could burn was also inside. The cabin air was changed. A mix of gases, closer to the air of Earth, replaced pure oxygen. Nylon had covered seats and other parts. It catches fire easily. Fiberglass that would not burn took its place. The biggest fix was the hatch. Designers rebuilt it. A hand lever could open it. The lever sat inside the craft. Another sat outside. The hatch could swing out in a few seconds. A special device and a seal kept it from popping open by accident. Two photos show the Apollo 1 command module. The left view is before the fire. The right view is after. The blaze started during that launch test.

4Apollo flies again. Ten months later, a stronger craft left the pad. The craft belonged to Apollo 4. It joined a command section to a service section. Crews shorten that pair to CSM. No pilot was aboard. The flight entered orbit around Earth. It ran without a problem. NASA trusted its work again. More Apollo missions followed. In December 1968 the Apollo 8 crew was sent on a trip around the Moon. Half a year later, three people launched on Apollo 10. This was the final rehearsal before a true lunar landing. Crews call the lander the LM. It pulled free of the CSM. Then it flew downward. Two of the crew were inside. The LM came to 47,000 feet from the surface, or 14,326 m. One short scare followed. The LM began to spin wildly. The crew solved it fast. The LM climbed again and docked with the CSM still circling above. Those two crew members went back into the CSM for the ride home. A photograph taken from Apollo 8 shows Earth. Apollo 10 had succeeded. A real landing was the next try. Leaving the ground. The year was 1969, and little time remained to meet President Kennedy's promise. Apollo 11's crew had trained. They stood ready to enter history. Neil Armstrong commanded the flight. Michael Collins piloted the Command and Service Module. Buzz Aldrin piloted the Lunar Module. Launch morning was July 16, 1969. Local clocks read 9:32. The three men entered Columbia, the CSM. With a huge roar, the Saturn V rocket sent them off. The journey was planned for eight days. The route covered 953,054 miles. In kilometers that is 1,533,792. Three minutes after launch, the craft was already 37 miles up, or 60 km. Speed was 6,340 miles each hour, or 10,203 kmph. Near midday the engine of the third stage fired. That burn took Apollo 11 off the path around Earth. The new path pointed at the Moon. Earth slipped behind them. The crew started unpacking. Their moon lander, Eagle, sat inside a storage bay. Explosive bolts released Eagle. They also blasted the compartment walls aside. Columbia shifted about 100 feet ahead of Eagle, a gap of 30.5 m, then turned and docked with it end to end. After that, the rest of the outer shell blew away. Still joined, Columbia and Eagle continued toward the Moon.

5By the third day, Apollo 11 lay 175,000 miles from Earth, or 281,635 km. The Moon was 48,000 miles away, or 77,248.5 km. Armstrong and Aldrin passed through a tunnel that linked Columbia with Eagle. They made sure the equipment worked. On the fourth day Columbia slowed so lunar gravity could draw it into orbit. Next morning Aldrin entered Eagle and started its engines. Armstrong came aboard sixty minutes afterward. They unfolded the legs used for landing. They closed the hatch. Eagle pulled away. Collins flew the CSM off from the LM and kept orbiting. Armstrong fired the engine used for descent. He guided Eagle toward the smooth site already chosen, a place called the Sea of Tranquility. The path was taking them at a crater littered with rocks. Alarms rang. Armstrong seized control and aimed for safer ground. Strain ran high in Eagle. It also ran high among Mission Control, the NASA team on Earth. When the LM at last touched down, thirty seconds of fuel remained. Armstrong told them Eagle had set down. Cheers broke out at Mission Control. A timeline uses Eastern Standard Time. On July 16, 1969, at 8:32 a.m., the Apollo Saturn V rocket launches. The Saturn V then separates from the booster engine. At 11:16 a.m. that same day, the third-stage engine sends the LM and the CSM toward the Moon. At 11:56 a.m., the CSM is freed from that stage, turns, and docks with the LM. On July 19 at 12:21 p.m., the CSM and the LM orbit the Moon. On July 20 at 1:11 p.m., the LM separates, heads for the surface, and leaves the CSM in lunar orbit. At 3:17 p.m. the LM lands. At 9:56 p.m. Armstrong steps onto the lunar surface, and Aldrin follows. On July 21 at 12:54 p.m. the LM lifts off. At 4:34 p.m. the LM docks, and Armstrong and Aldrin enter the CSM. The LM is cast off to crash on the Moon. At 11:54 p.m. the CSM turns and starts home. The Service Module is cast off from the Command Module, and the astronauts descend in the Command Module. On July 24 at 11:50 a.m. the Command Module enters the atmosphere, opens parachutes, and splashes down in the Pacific.

6Armstrong and Aldrin clipped on portable gear for life support and for talking during the EVA. At 10:39 p.m. Armstrong opened the hatch. He moved slowly downward until he reached the last rung. During that climb, he switched on a television camera fixed to the ladder. The world could watch. Nearly twenty minutes after leaving Eagle, he set his left foot in the gray dust of the surface. He said that was one small step for a man and one giant leap for mankind. Twenty more minutes passed before Aldrin came out and stood with him. They planted a flag of the United States. President Nixon offered congratulations. Armstrong then set the camera to record their work. The pair carried out several experiments. They collected lunar soil. They collected samples of rock. Their time outside lasted two hours and then forty-seven minutes more. Afterward they climbed inside Eagle again. On July 21 the ascent engines fired, and Eagle climbed at 80 feet each second, or 24.3 meters each second. Four hours later it met Columbia again. Armstrong and Aldrin climbed back in with Mike Collins. July 24 arrived. Columbia's service module was cut loose. Moments later the Command Module began its plunge into air. Moving faster than sound, the craft plunged toward the planet. Rubbing against the air charged the gas around the craft into fiery, glowing plasma. Plasma covered the craft, cut off every radio signal, and caused a blackout of four minutes. A protective shield against heat was all that stopped the capsule from being destroyed by fire. Parachutes were let out to slow the drop. The capsule hit the water at 11:49 in the morning by Central Daylight Time. The spot lay about 800 miles southwest of Hawaii. That gap is 1,287.5 km. Crew of the USS Hornet lifted the astronauts out of the craft. Several women were central to the mission's success. Katherine Johnson did the mathematics. Her post was a NASA lab kept apart under segregation, known as the colored computers. Her figures mattered for Mercury. They mattered for Apollo 11 as well. Rita Rapp, a nutritionist, saw that the crew ate well and that leftover food could be disposed of properly in space. Poppy Northcutt, a NASA engineer, calculated the path of the return to Earth. Seamstresses shaped the spacesuits with exact stitches so the wearers stayed warm and safe in the Moon's extreme conditions.

7Homecoming. A helicopter brought the crew to the Hornet, where a trailer held them in quarantine. The ship sailed to Hawaii. The trailer was placed on a plane bound for Houston, Texas. There the crew remained quarantined for twenty-one days. Huge parades followed in Houston, in Chicago, and in New York City. With the epic flight complete, the astronauts and the NASA team had done a heroic thing. They also widened the talk about what space travel could become. The Apollo missions. On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 landed the first people on the Moon. On November 14, Apollo 12 was the second piloted landing. On April 11, 1970, an explosion on Apollo 13 destroyed the Command Module. The crew quit the Moon plan and rode the Lunar Module back to Earth. On January 31, 1971, Apollo 14 made the third lunar landing. On July 26, Apollo 15 made the fourth. On April 16, 1972, Apollo 16 made the fifth. On December 7, Apollo 17 flew the final Moon mission. From July 1966 through April 1968, Apollos 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 were tests with no pilots. On January 27, 1967, all three Apollo 1 astronauts died in a cabin fire while a launch was being tested. On October 11, 1968, Apollo 7 was the first Apollo flight with pilots, and the first trial of the CSM. On December 21, 1968, Apollo 8 was the first piloted flight to orbit the Moon. On March 3, 1969, Apollo 9 gave the Lunar Module its first piloted trial, in orbit around Earth. On May 18, 1969, Apollo 10 rehearsed a Moon landing but did not land, as preparation for Apollo 11. Words to know. A capsule is the spacecraft section that can detach. People and instruments ride inside it. A compartment is a divided space inside a craft. Ships have them. Trains have them too. To dock is to link two craft while both are in space. A hatch is the door of a ship, a plane, or a spacecraft. Jettisoned means a crew dropped something off a ship, an aircraft, or a spacecraft, often because of danger. Lunar describes whatever belongs to the Moon. A module is a spacecraft piece that can leave the main body and keep working. Plasma is a gas of charged bits that can carry electric current. Quarantined means kept alone so illness cannot spread. Satellites are natural bodies, or bodies people build, that travel in orbit around Earth or another world. Supersonic means quicker than sound. Technologies are tools and machines that scientific knowledge makes possible.

34. Five Wonders Shaped by Nature

1Several continents hold the wonders in this book, and a map marks them. The Grand Canyon sits in North America. South America is named on that same map. Mount Everest is marked near Europe and Asia. Victoria Falls is the mark for Africa. The Great Barrier Reef is the mark for Australia. Paricutin, in Mexico, belongs with this set of places. A crater in Arizona, the Barringer Meteorite Crater, shows another kind of shape in the land. Rocks from space can strike Earth and leave amazing landforms. How can a place earn the name natural wonder? The answer is a natural structure so amazing and so beautiful that people pause and wonder how it formed. Nature, not humans, makes these landforms. A few years is enough for some wonders to appear. Millions of years are needed for others. Many such wonders share our planet. Five of them fill this book. A river carved one of them, a canyon of layers. A young volcano took over a village. A waterfall is breathtaking. A coral reef is immense. A mountain towers. The Grand Canyon opens the tour. Paricutin follows. Victoria Falls comes next. Mount Everest follows the falls. The Great Barrier Reef follows the mountain. A last chapter finds wonders in still more places. Special words and a finding list close the pages.

2Five to six million years ago, a large plateau lay in the path of the Colorado River. Raised ground is what a plateau is. Say it pla-TOE. Small pieces of that plateau were picked up by the river as time passed. The pieces rode the current all the way to the sea. Water erosion is the name of this process. Say it e-RO-zhun. How much soil and rock leaves depends on two factors. Speed of the water is one. Volume of the water is the other. The kind of rock matters too. Soft rock breaks with ease. Limestone is soft in this way. Shale is soft too. Hard rock does not break so easily. Granite is hard. Slate is hard. Softer rock was carried downstream by the Colorado River inside the Grand Canyon. Harder rock stayed. Deep canyons were cut into the rock by this work across millions of years. Arizona, in the United States, is where the canyon lies. What visitors see today is the wondrous shape left by that slow cutting. Rock layers in the walls hold a long record. Across two billion years, geologists can read what happened here. The wall itself is made of these layered rocks. Youngest rock is at the top, where most visitors take a first look. Oldest rock is the bottom layer, close to the river. Some loose rocks on the canyon floor are as old as two billion years. Rocks and the history of Earth are easy to study here. The layers can be seen, and they can be reached. Visits by geologists are common. Among the earliest was John Newberry. His trip to the canyon was in 1858. No scientist before him wrote down the canyon's layers. Many geologic layers were identified by him. Other people had seen the layers first.

3Reptiles of more than forty-seven kinds live in the Grand Canyon. Harmless is the word for most of them. Snakes still deserve a watchful eye from visitors. Bites on humans are rare. Venom is carried by the Grand Canyon rattlesnake. Venom is carried by the diamondback rattlesnake too. Winter is when rattlesnakes hibernate inside dens. A single den may hold hundreds of them. Living together is rare for rattlers, and the den is one of the few times they do it. Warm spring weather brings the snakes out. Each one then goes a separate way. Live babies are born to females in late summer. The birth area holds the babies for only a short stay. Seven to ten days is about how long. A first baby skin is shed after that. A first rattle is added. Food is what they leave to find. Growing rattlesnakes shed at least once each year. Every shed adds a fresh rattle on the tail. A grown diamondback may reach 2 meters, about 6.5 feet. Weight may reach 6.8 kilograms, or 15 pounds. Twenty-five years is a possible lifespan for rattlers. European explorers arrived only after Native Americans had spent over four thousand years in the Grand Canyon and on the land around it. Local animals were hunted by those early groups. Edible plants were gathered. By 1150, most of the first tribes had left. The Havasupai people were the ones who stayed. Some Havasupai still live in the Canyon and work there. Millions of travelers come each year to Grand Canyon National Park. Hiking, rafting, and looking at this majestic wonder are their reasons. Havasu Falls lies on the Havasupai Reservation. Water is still cutting the western Grand Canyon, and the falls show that work.

4Millions of years of age belong to many of nature's creations. Their start came long before any human lived on Earth. Modern times have produced other creations. Mexico's Paricutin volcano is one of those younger forms. Say the name pah-ree-koo-TEEN. Formation began in a field in 1943. A farmer found a fissure in his cornfield that year. An opening in the ground is what a fissure is. Say it FISH-ur. About 1.8 meters, or 6 feet, was the length of the crack. More openings showed up soon after. Black smoke rose from the holes. Ash stacked on the ground until a cone took shape. Twelve hours or so lifted the cone to 10 meters, or 33 feet. One day lifted it to 50 meters, or 164 feet. Growth did not stop. A week brought the height to 100 meters, or 328 feet. News organizations around the world paid attention to this brand-new volcano. Mexico holds Paricutin, between the Gulf of Mexico and the Pacific Ocean. The eruption year was 1943. Safety for the village was what the people of Paricutin hoped for. A few months later the cone was huge. Lava moved slowly, but it began to reach the town. Leaving became necessary. Homes and farms were left behind. Nine years of lava and ash buried the whole village of Paricutin. San Juan, the town nearby, was mostly buried as well. Almost nothing of the village could be seen at the end. Black rock surrounded a church steeple that still rose above it. Nature's power had a reminder in that steeple.

5Cinder cones are the name for volcanoes like Paricutin. Among volcanoes, they are the simplest kind. A sudden appearance is how they start. An eruption follows. Dormant years then last for decades or for centuries. Pressure inside Earth drives the lava. A central vent in the ground is where the lava shoots out. Cooling happens as the lava blows into the air. Small pieces are what it breaks into. Rocks and ash, called cinders, are the hard bits that fall. They pile around the central vent until a cone stands there. A crater shaped like a bowl sits at the top of most cinder cones. Rock fragments cover the cone. Youth is why scientists have watched Paricutin since the day it appeared. Height today is about 424 meters, or 1,391 feet. Area covered is 26 square kilometers, or 10 square miles. Powerful forces that shape Earth are better understood because of this growth.

6The Zambezi River is where Victoria Falls stands. Zambia and Zimbabwe, in Africa, share the border that the river follows. Millions of years ago the falls began to form. A shallow crack crossed the river's path in the rock. Shifting parts of the earth, about 150 million years ago, caused that crack. Year after year the river ran across the rock. Softer rock wore away. A cliff was left. The river drops over the cliff now. Hard rock remains next to the softer rock. Plunge pool is the name of the pool at the bottom. David Livingstone, an explorer from Scotland, came to the falls in 1855. People from outside Africa had probably never seen these formations before him. Queen Victoria of England is the person he named the falls for. A more accurate name, many people think, is Mosi-oa-Tunya. Two national parks now include the falls. Zambia holds one park. Zimbabwe holds the other. Almost two million visitors come to the parks each year. Six separate waterfalls make up Victoria Falls. Devil's Cataract is one name. Armchair Falls is another. Horseshoe Falls is a third. The remaining names are Main Falls, then Rainbow Falls, then the Eastern Cataract. Bungee jumping draws people to a bridge at the falls. A full moon keeps the park open late. A rainbow can be enjoyed then. Moonlight passing through the vapor makes the rainbow. Rafts run on the water below the falls. Kayaks run there too. Surfing is even possible on the rapids below.

7Sir George Everest gave his name to Mount Everest. Surveying and geology were his work, and he was Welsh. No mountain on Earth is taller. Few sites are more amazing. Forehead in the Sky is the Nepali name. The Himalaya range is where this magnificent landform stands. Height is 8,850 meters, or 29,035 feet. Nepal and Tibetan China share the border under the peak. Far past that border region lies the Pacific Ocean. Old is how the snowcapped Himalayas can look. For mountains, they are actually quite young. Millions of years ago they formed. Two pieces of Earth's crust slammed together. Rubbing under pressure went on for a long time. The ground crumbled, then rose above the sea. Youth is why the peaks of Mount Everest are still jagged and steep. Endless wind, ice, and snow have not smoothed them yet. Looking at the mountain is beautiful. Living on it is very harsh. An average temperature is about minus 36 degrees Celsius, which is minus 33 degrees Fahrenheit. January can fall to minus 60 degrees Celsius, or minus 76 degrees Fahrenheit. July is the warmest month. Even then, the air only reaches minus 19 degrees Celsius, or minus 2 degrees Fahrenheit. Freezing is a line the temperature never crosses. Ice and snow at the top therefore never melt. Elevation lets storms arrive without warning. Temperatures can fall fast when they do. Every year, storms leave still more snow on Mount Everest.

8Survival is hard in the extreme conditions on Mount Everest. Animals have trouble. Plants have trouble too. Few animals manage to live on the mountain, and the wild yak is one of them. Weight can pass 454 kilograms, or 1,000 pounds. Height can reach 1.8 meters, or 6 feet. Blood is one reason the yak survives. More oxygen can enter that blood than enters the blood of other animals. Little oxygen is in the air on Mount Everest, so this adaptation saves lives. A dense undercoat of soft hair covers the yak. A shaggy outer coat helps it stay warm. Grazing is how wild yaks feed on the high land. Early settlers in the Himalayas held a belief about the peaks. Gods, they believed, made homes there. Climbs of Mount Everest were not attempted for a long time because of that belief. The early 1900s brought British explorers and other explorers from Europe. Climbs started only then. Harsh conditions met the first climbers quickly. Freezing air, powerful winds, shifting weather, and rough terrain were what they found. Stories told about Mount Everest and about the Himalayas describe the yeti, also called the Abominable Snowman. Say yeti YEH-tee. Say abominable a-BOM-in-a-bal. Large footprints are part of stories Sherpas tell. Gnawed bones of yaks are part of those stories too. A scalp and some skins, said to be from a yeti, were carried by Hillary's team. Europe and the United States were where they took them. Scientists decided the scalp came from a goat. They decided the skins came from a bear. Proof that a yeti exists has never been found. Climbers with experience kept coming, hoping to be first on top. Climbers without experience came too. Success waited until 1953. Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first men to reach the top. Hillary kept bees in New Zealand. Norgay was a Sherpa from Nepal. Awards for the climb were accepted by the two men later. Climbers from around the world have risked their lives since then. Their aim is the summit that people call Forehead in the Sky.

9Australia's coast holds the Great Barrier Reef. Coral formations there can be explored by a diver. Many reefs together make the Great Barrier Reef. Length is more than 2,300 kilometers, or 1,429 miles. The northeast coast of Australia is where it lies. Enchanting sea creatures fill it. Sea turtles, sea slugs, and urchins are among them. Dolphins, whales, and sharks are among them too. Birds and reptiles of more than two hundred species inhabit the reef system. A chain, or range, of rock is what a reef is. The rock sits at the water's surface or near it. No coral-reef system in the world is larger. Coral polyps, by living and dying, build reefs like this one. Every tropical ocean has coral reefs. Size like the Great Barrier Reef is found nowhere else. Five thousand to ten thousand years is the age of most established coral reefs. Experts largely agree about the newest growth here. It began six thousand to eight thousand years ago. A first look can make the reef seem like rock. Rock is not what it is. The building material is the hard outer body left by millions of tiny animals known as polyps. Say polyps POL-ips. Anemones and jellyfish are relatives of polyps. Dead polyps become a base, and new polyps grow on the old skeletons. Limestone at the base of a coral reef is those many layers of skeleton. Other living things help build the reef. Algae help. Sponges help. Shellfish help. Most of the structure of this wonder comes from the tiny polyp.

10Animals are what reefs are made from. Food and shelter for other animals come from reefs. Ocean temperature changes can hurt them. Thousands of species live on this reef. Fish of 1,625 kinds are included. Marine mammals of more than 30 kinds are included. Seaweed of 50 kinds is included. Marine turtles of 6 kinds are included. Breeding is another reason the reef matters. Birds breed there. Sea turtles breed there. Several endangered species breed there too. The humpback whale is one. The sea cow is another. Interest and beauty both make the Great Barrier Reef stand out on Earth. Scientists, scuba divers, and tourists all like to go there. A World Heritage Site listing came in 1981 from UNESCO. UNESCO is a department of the United Nations. Protection today is the work of environmentalists together with those groups. Future generations should be able to learn from the reef and enjoy how beautiful it is. Life fills reefs, and the creatures are delicate. Important rules belong to responsible snorkelers and scuba divers. Float above the reef while snorkeling. Standing on it is never the right choice. Pictures are the thing to take. Coral should not be taken home as a souvenir. Fish for a saltwater aquarium should be ones raised in captivity. Fish taken off a coral reef should not fill those tanks. Plastics and other trash should always be packed out. Arizona and the Australian coast are far apart, yet natural wonders are in both places and everywhere between. Millions of years is the age of some. A single lifetime is the age of others. Each one is unique. Size, height, and beauty put these landforms among the greatest places on Earth. Study and recreation will keep drawing travelers, scientists, and people seeking adventure. Generations still to come will visit. Five wonders in this book are only a start. The Northern Lights are another well-known wonder. They are a light show in the skies of the Northern Hemisphere. A massive hole in the Arizona desert is the Barringer Meteorite Crater. Almost a mile is its width, and 174 meters, or 570 feet, is its depth. The world's largest solid rock is Ayers Rock. It rises 862.5 meters above sea level, or 2,830 feet, in Australia. Ha Long Bay is in the Gulf of Tonkin in Vietnam. More than 1,600 limestone islands fill that large bay.

11Words from the five wonders are gathered here. Cinder cones are hills in the shape of cones, built when lava and ash blow into the air and settle around volcanic vents. Dormant means quiet for now, but able to turn active again. Edible means safe for eating. Erosion is rock or soil taken away by nature, whether by water, by wind, or by ice. A fissure is a crack that is long and narrow. Geologists study where Earth came from, what it is made of, how it is built, and what its history holds. To inhabit a place is to live there or to occupy it. Landforms are natural shapes on Earth's surface, including valleys, plateaus, mountains, plains, and hills. A plateau is flat land raised over a large area. A plunge pool is the deep water at the foot of a waterfall. Polyps are small sea animals without backbones, coral among them, with bodies like tubes and mouths circled by tentacles. A Sherpa belongs to a cultural group that lives in the Himalayas. Guiding mountain climbers is common work for Sherpas. A species is a group of living things that look alike in body and can reproduce. A surveyor measures land and names its physical features. Terrain means the natural features of a piece of ground. A finding list points back to names already met. Paricutin, the plateau, the plunge pool, and polyps are on it. Rattlesnakes, reefs, Sherpas, Victoria Falls, and volcanoes are on it. The yak, the yeti, Zambia, Zimbabwe, and the Zambezi River are on it. Australia, cinder cones, coral, and erosion are on it. The Grand Canyon, the Great Barrier Reef, Havasu Falls, and the Havasupai are on it. Sir Edmund Hillary, the Himalayas, David Livingstone, and Mexico are on it. Mount Everest, national parks, Native Americans, John Newberry, and Tenzing Norgay are on it.

35. Flying Machines With No Pilot

1In Ukraine, a brown bear at a shelter for saved bears comes upon a flying drone. A camera on an aerial drone can map land and survey it. Look up at the sky. Something buzzes past. That object is not a bird. It is not a plane. It is not a superhero. It is an unmanned aerial vehicle. People also call this machine a drone. Drones were once a rare sight. Now their popularity is growing. Their uses are growing too. Making maps is one task these flying robots handle. They can save lives. They can bring packages very fast. Those jobs are only a few of the things drones can do.

2Drones may look like a fairly new invention. They have been around much longer than some people think. The U.S. military built the earliest form of a drone during World War I. That craft was the Kettering Bug. It was planned as an aerial torpedo. Layers of paper and cardboard went into its body. Building the Kettering Bug cost $400. Charles Kettering developed it with Orville Wright. About twenty years later, more advanced drones appeared. They received the name unmanned aerial vehicles. No pilot rode inside them. A person on the ground flew them by remote control. A person in a nearby mother airplane could fly them too. The first UAVs looked like small airplanes. They were fairly large. A few stretched past 6 meters (20 ft.) from nose to tail. Their wings reached nearly 9 meters (30 ft.) across. During World War II, British forces built UAVs mainly so gunners could practice on targets. The British navy called its prototype UAV the Queen Bee. Radio signals controlled the Queen Bee. The Queen Bee could climb as high as 5,182 meters (17,000 ft.). The Queen Bee could travel as far as 483 kilometers (300 mi.). The Queen Bee passed 161 kilometers (100 mi.) per hour. A United States admiral watched a Queen Bee demonstration. He wanted a similar craft for the U.S. Navy. America's UAVs came from the plans of Commander Delmer Fahrney. He gave them the nickname drones. The nickname honored Britain's Queen Bee, the model for the new craft. The name stayed in use. After that, every U.S. Navy UAV was called a target drone. The word drone fit those target craft in more than one way. Among bees, a male bee is known as a drone. Used as a verb, drone means a long humming sound. A UAV in flight makes a hum like that.

3Across the next eighty years, drones changed into smaller flying machines. Newer ones looked more like small helicopters. Wings were gone. Spinning blades called rotors lifted them instead. Some drones rose on six or more whirling rotors. Rotors made the machines much quicker in the air. These quick craft could swerve. They could switch direction fast. Pilots could aim them at precise places once out of reach. They could also fly nearer the ground. They could hang still in one place. Their size and quick moves fit jobs that planes found hard. Some of those jobs were impossible for planes. Drones then came into wide use outside the military. Nikola Tesla is known as the Father of Unmanned Technology. In 1898 he invented a boat steered by radio. He showed the boat in New York City. His method was an early form of the technology people use to run drones from far away. Users found drones ideal for pictures taken from high above, like a bird looking down. In earlier years, photos from the air usually came from airplanes. Planes had to stay well above the ground so they would miss obstacles. A close picture of the ground was hard to get. Drones could fly much more slowly. They could also fly much lower. They could pass under clouds that blocked clear photos from planes. They could move through tight spaces. Canyons were open to them. Ravines were open to them too. Larger aircraft could not reach those places. People who make films realized their jobs would get much easier with drones. A camera fastened to a drone could record the flight. Special effects were no longer needed to show flying. The footage could show what real flight feels like. Several drones at once also gave views from overhead. Those shots did not get in the actors' way. Crew members were not put in danger. Mapmakers now send drones into far-off land that is hard to cross. The pictures show sharply what that land is really like. Drones can supply fresh photos of glaciers as the ice changes. They can show other landforms that keep changing too.
