4Drones can move near rough land. That skill makes them strong helpers for rescuers. They can help find people who may be lost. They can help find people who may be hurt. A drone can slip beneath the forest canopy. From there it gets a clear look at the ground below. Search and rescue drones do not store video for later viewing. They send a live stream of pictures while they travel. At night they use thermal imaging. That tool senses warmth given off by a person's body. Water, food, or blankets can be released by drone when the need is urgent. The drop lands with better aim than many older methods. The cost stays low. Drones matter especially after a disaster. Earthquakes often make roads impossible to use. Airports can become impossible to use too. Floods cause the same problem. Victims then cannot get the help they need. Drones can also watch disasters that are still underway. A wildfire is one example. A volcanic eruption is another. People can gather the data without standing in danger. A 2015 photo from an aerial drone shows flooding in Bulgaria. A bull elephant meets a drone inside an African reserve. Animals gain from drones, not only people. Watching a huge area, such as a large ranch, takes a great deal of time. It also takes many workers. Drones track roaming animals much faster. They do the job more cheaply too. Drones can locate cattle that have strayed. People have even used them to herd animals back where they belong. Wildlife preserves use drones to watch for danger. They also use drones to follow what animals do. If an animal is in trouble, rangers can reach the exact spot. Drone technology makes that fast arrival possible. Researchers use drones to study how animals live in their home habitats. The animals need not be disturbed.

5Businesses have lately started to test delivery shaped for each buyer. Online sellers want to skip travel on the ground. Local shops want the same thing. They hope to fly small packages from warehouses straight to buyers. In the near future, a pizza you order might not arrive by car. A drone might bring it. In distant parts of the world, drones already carry vital medical goods. Clinics in rural Rwanda, a nation in Africa, depend on these flights. Medical outposts there depend on them too. The drones bring blood for emergency surgery. They also bring medicines that cannot wait. Each drone follows a route set before takeoff. Staff watch that route on computer tablets. Satellite navigation systems guide the flight. At the stop, the drone lets go of its precious load. A paper parachute carries the cargo down to the clinic. This service cut delivery time from hours down to minutes. Countless lives have been saved. Drones serve serious aims. They have playful uses too. One of the newest playful uses is a race between drones. The Drone Racing League holds races for drones built for the contest. Nicholas Horbaczewski started that league. The league offers a real flying experience through races that feel like video games. An obstacle course is set inside a large indoor building. An empty shopping mall can be that building. A sports stadium can be that building too. Small drones fitted with lights fly the course. Their speed is nearly 129 kilometers (80 mi.) per hour. Pilots on the ground steer with joysticks. Tiny cameras on the drones send exciting video into headsets. The pilots wear those headsets. The picture makes each pilot feel like a rider on the speeding drone.

6The league wants every race to feel as thrilling as possible. For that reason, pilots are not asked to bring drones of their own. Race organizers supply the drones for each contest. They also bring a pit crew for the machines. The crew handles repairs. The crew keeps the drones flying. A pilot then does not fear a crash that wrecks a prized machine. Many people expect this new sport to grow more popular. People who like automobile contests may become fans. The sport may attract fans of video games as well. Some sports channels on television have even broadcast drone race contests. The races are held all around the globe. This sport of the future really seems to be lifting off. The 2016 contest drew over one hundred pilots. New York City held the meet. Its title was the National Drone Racing Championships. Safety is not the only worry about drones. Privacy is another worry. A robot overhead that records a private house is unwelcome to most people. Some towns have banned certain drones over neighborhoods where people live. The ban covers drones fitted with smartphones. It also covers drones fitted with cameras. Growing drone use brings fresh problems. Regulators fear that drones may endanger ordinary airplanes with fixed wings. They fear danger to helicopters of a normal size too. Commercial aircraft must file a plan before they fly. No rule forces a drone to file a flight plan. Flight radar does not display these small craft. They are so small that a pilot may not see them until it is too late. Drones flown separately cannot signal one another. They may crash into each other. The Federal Aviation Administration is preparing pilot rules because of those dangers. People often call that agency the FAA. As of 2017, anyone who operates a drone must hold a license. The operator must warn an airport about a flight inside 8 kilometers (5 mi.) of that airport. Drones also must not fly near national monuments. They must not fly over big sports events where crowds gather. A disabled drone could put people nearby in danger. A drone out of control could do the same.

7Even with those risks, drones seem likely to remain. Years ago, people looking ahead made a prediction. They said humans would lean on robots for many tasks. Some tasks were ones people could not do. Other tasks were ones people did not want to do. That old prediction seems to be coming true. Flying robots are taking a larger role in daily life. Drones work together with other advances in technology. The mix offers chances to make lives better. It also lets us view the world from a fresh angle. Sydney, Australia, has seen drones glowing at a festival of the arts. One day, drones may stand in for fireworks. Swarms of tiny drones can carry bright lights in many colors. A program can set them to fly in a formation. The formation can create a dazzling display. These words help with the topic. Agility is the power to move fast and with ease. To navigate is to find a route across a long distance. It can also mean steering toward a chosen end point. To collide is to hit another object in a hard, violent crash. A remote control is a tool held in the hand. It runs a machine from far away, such as a television or a toy. Customized describes something changed so it feels more personal. The change can also fit a special need. A drone can be an aircraft with nobody aboard. It can also be a ship run from far away. Rotors are blades that spin. They lift a flying machine and keep it up. The Federal Aviation Administration is a national agency in the United States. It directs every part of civil flying there. A satellite may be a natural body. It may be an object people built. It travels in orbit around Earth or around another body in space. Terrain means the natural features on a piece of land. The word can also mean the ground itself. To monitor is to watch how something moves forward over time. Unmanned means a craft carries no person. It can also mean no person on board is steering it.

36. Freedoms Written Into the Highest Law

1A family photo catches a reaction to court news from 1969. Mary Beth Tinker stands in that photo. Lorena, her mother, stands with her. Paul, her younger brother, stands there too. Mary Beth's junior high had suspended her. A black armband at school was the cause. The book opens on that story. The country's highest law comes next. A later part tells how a list of rights was joined to that law. Protection under those rights is explained after that. Changes made in later years follow. People who still struggle for rights come after those changes. A brief close ends the story. Meanings of hard words come last. Punishment arrived in 1965. Five students in an Iowa district received it. They had worn black armbands at school. The Vietnam War was what the armbands protested. That war ran from 1955 until 1975. Officials ordered the armbands removed. The students left them on. Suspension was the result. Three of those students sued. Their parents joined the suit. The district was the target of the lawsuit. The case climbed through the courts. In 1969 the nation's highest court agreed to hear it.

2Those judges said the armbands could stay. Their reason was an amendment to the Constitution. An amendment means a change. It can also mean a correction. Wearing the black armband counted as speech, the Court said. The First Amendment guards that kind of speech. That amendment sits inside the Bill of Rights. The Bill of Rights lists the earliest ten amendments. Citizen freedoms are what those amendments guard. A grand court building stands in Washington, D.C. It houses the nation's highest court. The Bill of Rights belongs to the Constitution. That document is the country's first law. It is also the highest law. It was created as the United States took shape. Other laws must follow its principles. Earlier, the land was thirteen colonies, not yet one country. Great Britain had planted those colonies on ground seized by force. Native peoples had held that ground. Colonists believed King George III brushed their rights aside. A revolution began in 1775. Eight years of war with Great Britain followed. Independence was the goal. The original Constitution, Bill of Rights included, sits behind glass. Washington, D.C., is where visitors can see that display. The National Archives Building holds it.

3Founders is the name for colonists who helped form the United States. Wealth described most of them. A strong education described most of them too. Law or politics was the background of many. During the fight with Great Britain, they built a confederation of states. Power at the center of that confederation was weak. King-like power was what they refused to give leaders. States received most of the power instead. A painting shows soldiers of the new country marching toward the British. After the war, the Founders saw failure in their system. They chose to remake it. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was the meeting place in 1787. There they wrote exact rules for a different government. More strength for the central government was the aim. Federal government is the name for that center. They still refused it enough strength to strip citizens of rights. Democracy was the form they wanted. In a democracy, elections let citizens pick leaders. Ideas also came from the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Native nations made up that confederacy. Together they ran a government of many states. Each nation kept a government of its own. September 1787 saw the new constitution finished. By the middle of 1788, only two states had not approved it. The Constitution then stood as the law of the land. George Washington became the first elected president. Independence Hall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was where the Founders argued over the document. We the People are the opening words. All people were not covered by the original text. People held in slavery were left out. Native peoples were left out. Most women were left out. Later amendments, and later laws, widened the circle.

4Women had no seat at the writing of the Constitution. Many of them still helped the new nation grow. Essays by women took up politics. Gender equality was another subject. Abolition was another. Political talks were hosted by women. Sessions of Congress drew women as listeners. Political rallies were organized by women. Abigail Adams ranks among the most important of them. She was wife to the Founder John Adams. She was also a close advisor to him. A letter from her said to remember the ladies. He was then helping to draft the new constitution. North Carolina voted no on the Constitution. Rhode Island voted no as well. They would withhold approval, they said, until rights were listed in a bill. Neither would join the government without that addition. Some Founders called a list of rights dangerous. People might treat any unlisted right as unprotected, they argued. James Madison, a leading Founder, shared that fear. Thomas Jefferson took the other side. A bill of rights was necessary, he said. Both men were Virginians. Virginia's own constitution already held a Declaration of Rights. Bills of rights appeared in several other state constitutions too. Jefferson wanted citizen rights written into the U.S. Constitution. Madison came around. He began drafting a bill of rights. The Virginia Declaration of Rights was one model. His draft proposed twenty amendments. Congress reduced the set to twelve. States received that set in 1789. After receiving them, those two holdout states trusted that rights would be safe. By late 1791, three-fourths of the states had accepted ten amendments out of the twelve. Those ten became the Bill of Rights. Those two Virginians had started out in disagreement. They later joined efforts and helped the Bill of Rights come into being.

5Five important personal rights sit in the First Amendment. Freedom of speech is one. Citizens may ask government to change laws they reject. Peaceful protest gatherings are allowed. Freedom of the press is another First Amendment right. News may be shared by reporters. Opinions may be shared by them too. In the 1700s, public news came only from newspapers and other print. Radio now falls under freedom of the press. Television does too. So does the Internet. A 2017 protest in North Dakota stayed peaceful. Members of the Lakota nation took part. An oil pipeline through sacred land was what they opposed. Limiting a government by listing rights on paper did not start in the United States. England's version passed in 1689. A full century, and more, went by before this country wrote a version of its own. Written protections for civil and political rights now exist in most democracies. Freedom of religion is a further First Amendment right. One official religion is the pattern in many countries. The United States has no official religion. Any religion may be practiced. No religion may be practiced as well. Owning weapons is a right in the Second Amendment. Using weapons is part of that right too. Some readers think the amendment was meant only for militia groups. The National Guard is an example of such a group. Other readers think every citizen may own and use weapons. Housing soldiers by force is blocked by the Third Amendment. British soldiers were allowed to seize private homes in the years leading to the Revolutionary War. A search needs a solid reason under the Fourth Amendment. An arrest needs that kind of reason too. The reason must be a belief that a crime was committed. A judge must grant permission before police search someone's property.

6People accused of crimes are covered by four amendments. Those are the Fifth, the Sixth, the Seventh, and the Eighth. A criminal offense means a crime against the public. It can also mean a crime against a state. The Fifth Amendment blocks a forced trial unless there is solid reason to think the person may be guilty. Court must prove the charge before any punishment. Speed is required by the Sixth Amendment. The trial must happen as soon as it can. The trial must be public. A jury must be present. A civil crime means a wrong against a person. It can also mean a wrong against a company. The Seventh Amendment gives a jury trial for that kind of case too. Cruel and unusual punishments are banned by the Eighth Amendment. Red-hot branding irons were once used on some criminals. Wooden stocks in public places held others. Crowds threw objects at the people in the stocks. Those punishments are banned now. Rights not already written down are covered by the last two amendments. Listing some rights does not erase other rights, the Ninth Amendment says. Only powers named in the Constitution belong to the government, the Tenth Amendment says. Any unnamed power stays with the states. It may also stay with the citizens. A timeline of major steps runs like this. The American Revolutionary War started in 1775. The Declaration of Independence won approval from the Continental Congress in 1776. The war ended in 1781. The Constitution was written in 1787. It was approved in 1788. The Bill of Rights joined it in 1791. Slavery was abolished by the 13th Amendment in 1865. The 14th Amendment, in 1868, gave citizenship rights to everyone born in the United States. Naturalized people received those rights too. The 15th Amendment, in 1870, gave the vote to every male citizen. Color did not matter. Race did not matter. Women gained the vote through the 19th Amendment in 1920. The voting age dropped under the 26th Amendment in 1971.

7The Bill of Rights dates from 1791. Further amendments arrived in the years after that. A new amendment is hard to pass. Congress may propose one. A Constitutional Convention may propose one too. Two-thirds of the state governments must call for such a convention. After a proposal, three-fourths of the state governments must vote yes. That yes vote ratifies the amendment. Ratify means it becomes law. Twenty-seven amendments stand in the Constitution today. The Thirteenth and the Fourteenth rank among the most important after the Bill of Rights. Both followed the Civil War. That war lasted from 1861 to 1865. Slavery in the United States was outlawed by the Thirteenth Amendment. An illustration shows people once enslaved, celebrating that change. Citizenship for all formerly enslaved people came from the Fourteenth Amendment. Equal protection of the laws was promised to every citizen. Race was not allowed to block that promise. Voting is among the most important citizen rights. Before the Constitution, land ownership was required for a vote. White men made up most of those owners. By 1856, every white man could vote. Most Black men still could not, until the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870. Women gained the vote through the Nineteenth Amendment. Their organized fight lasted more than seventy years. The amendment passed in 1920. Racial segregation of public schools ended largely because of the Fourteenth Amendment. Oliver Brown lived in Topeka, Kansas, in the 1940s. He was a Black man. He wanted his daughter enrolled at a school close to home. That school served white students. The school said no. The only place offered served Black students. It lay farther from home. Brown went to court. The case reached the Supreme Court in 1954. The full bench agreed. Nine judges sat on it. Racial segregation in public schools broke the Fourteenth Amendment, they ruled. The schools serving white children did not match the schools serving Black children. The ruling is counted among the Court's most important.

8All Americans are supposed to be covered by the Bill of Rights and by later amendments. Fights for those rights still happen often. California in 2000 was home to Alondra Jones. Her grades made her an honor student. Her high school sat in a low-income area. Black students and Latino students made up most of the school. Textbooks were too few. Computers were absent. Filth covered the buildings. Rats moved through the hallways. Another high school, which Alondra visited one day, looked different. Books were there. Computers were there. The buildings were clean and safe. Funding at her own school was far lower than at other schools in the state, she realized. Almost one hundred other students joined her lawsuit. California was the state they sued. The court found a failure of equal protection. The Fourteenth Amendment requires that protection. A good education is a right of every student, the court said. Socioeconomic status must not decide that right. Samantha Elauf was seventeen in 2008. A clothing store in Oklahoma was where she asked for a job. A hijab was the reason the store refused to hire her. Many Muslim women wear that head covering. The store called the hijab a break in its dress code. Samantha sued. The case climbed to the Supreme Court. The year of the ruling was 2015. The Court sided with Samantha. Religion was the reason for the store's discrimination, the Court said. Her First Amendment right was violated. Samantha Elauf and her mother stand before the Supreme Court building.

9Rights fights by different groups have continued across history. In the United States, the story of each person's rights begins in the Constitution. The story has not ended. Most people in the country stood outside the Constitution's protection when it was written. Alondra and Samantha are among those who later fought to guard the rights promised to citizens. Dozens of amendments have widened that protection. Dozens of laws have done the same. Equality under the law is still the aim of advocates. Protection under the law is still their aim too. A few word meanings help. Founders names the men who helped set up the United States and its government. An amendment is a change added to a document. It can also be a change added to a law. The Bill of Rights means those earliest ten amendments. Certain rights are guaranteed there. Freedom of speech means people may share opinions in public. A confederation joins states, provinces, or groups. Its central authority stays limited. Freedoms are political rights. They are also powers to act as one wishes and to think as one wishes. Principles are basic values. They are ideals that steer actions and decisions. The Constitution is the written rule set under United States law. It is also the set of principles under that law. Force is how a revolution drives a government out of power. A different government then takes the place of the old one. Equality means the same rights for everyone. A right is a freedom a person may justly claim. It can also be a power claimed that way. Excluded means shut out from taking part.

37. From a Bronx Party to a Global Culture

1Three performers pose together. At the center is the rap artist Cheryl James. On the right is Sandra Denton. Together they are known as Salt-N-Pepa. On the left is their DJ, Dierda Roper, known as DJ Spinderella. Life in New York City during the 1970s was tough. Jobs were scarce. Poverty followed. Homelessness followed. Crime rose. The city did not give people the resources needed to face these problems. Decades of racism had built extra challenges for people of color. Black people carried those challenges in particular. Most could not afford to leave the city. Many white people did leave. Underserved neighborhoods grew worse. More businesses shut down. Jobs vanished. Entertainment vanished with them. Clubs closed. Movie theaters closed. Boys stand before graffiti in a 1970s New York City scene. Youth in these communities had to invent fresh ways to have fun. They had to invent new ways to express themselves. Their creativity did more than start a new style of music. It started an entire movement.

2Summer of 1973 brought a request from Cindy Campbell. Her older brother Clive was the person she asked to DJ a party in the neighborhood. DJ means disc jockey. Their neighborhood was the South Bronx, in New York City. Black people and Puerto Rican people made up most of it. Jamaica was the country the Campbell family left for the United States. The move had come five years earlier. Clive's nickname was Hercules. On stage he used the name DJ Kool Herc. Fancy equipment was not his. He chose records from his own collection. He connected two turntables to a device that makes sound louder. Records play on a turntable, which is a platform that spins. Success for the party was huge. Neighborhood fame reached Clive within a day. Music that started in the South Bronx on that day later reached listeners worldwide. The people there did not know they were making history. No one had told DJ Kool Herc that a later title would be Father of Hip-Hop. A later photograph shows him performing in England in 2000. His inspiration included a Jamaican tradition called toasting. In toasting, a person talks or chants while a rhythm plays. It grew popular in the 1950s. An older West African oral tradition shaped Jamaican toasting. That tradition belongs to griots, a word said GREE-ohz. A griot is a storyteller. A griot is a poet. A griot is a singer. A griot is a historian. Many hip-hop fans treat rappers as griots of the present day. Like griots, rappers tell their community's story. Struggles go into the telling. Successes go into it. The result entertains. It also informs. Community history and culture take shape partly through what rappers do. They help preserve both. A photograph shows a griot from West Africa performing in New York City. Hip-hop is more than music. It is a whole culture. At the start, the community had no clubs. It had no stages. It had no art galleries. Artists carried their creativity into the streets. Four key elements make up the culture. One element is the DJ. Another is breaking. Another is graffiti art. Another is the MC. A DJ's job is to keep music flowing. As one song ends on the first turntable, the second turntable fades a new song in. The music never stops.

3Few hip-hop sounds are as distinctive as scratching. A DJ makes the scratchy sound by sliding the record back and forth. The record is playing on the turntable while it moves. Early DJs noticed a crowd favorite called the break beat. Drums are all that remain in that stretch of a song. Both turntables, for early hip-hop DJs, carried copies of one record. They did it so the break beat could repeat again and again. With these methods, DJs built new music out of old music. Music makers for years afterward drew inspiration from that idea. A photograph from 2002 shows Grandmaster Flash among DJs at an event. Street dancers sometimes hear their art called break dancing. The first of them used another name. They called the dancing breaking. The names they chose included b-boys. They included b-girls. They included breakers. A 1984 photograph shows b-boys in a competition. Dance battles were common. Two breakers took turns, or two crews did. Each side showed its best moves. The crowd gathered around them judged creativity. The crowd judged skill. Writing or drawings on public property are what graffiti means. By the early 1970s, hip-hop culture had taken graffiti on as an important part. Artists painted buildings. They painted subway cars. They painted trains. They painted bridges. Part of the thrill was simple. Thousands of people would see the art every day. Lady Pink is shown working on a painting. The painting honors women in hip-hop.

4Painting on public property breaks the law. Some people saw the painting as destructive. Inside hip-hop culture, graffiti counted as art. Art galleries around the world soon invited graffiti artists to display what they had made. Museums have preserved graffiti art. Art books have preserved it too. Early hip-hop used the name MC for a rapper. The letters stand for master of ceremonies. While the DJ played, the MC talked to the crowd. Soon the talking turned into rhyme that rode along with the music. Rappers are judged on content. They are judged on flow. They are judged on delivery. Good flow means the spoken lyrics stay on the beat. Good delivery means the words come out clearly. Breathing must not break the flow. Many fans add a fifth pillar. That pillar is knowledge. The other four elements are tied together by knowledge. Greatness requires knowing one's own history. It requires knowing one's own identity. It requires knowing the community's history. It also requires knowing hip-hop's history, values, and ideas. That knowledge helps artists grow. Fresh forms of expression grow out of it. Art can then push for change in society. Women have helped shape the culture since the beginning. Sharon Green was one of the first. People treat her as the earliest woman to rap. Her career started as a b-girl. She was fourteen. Skill as an MC came quickly. A record deal in 1979 made her the first woman in rap to sign one. National television in 1981 showed her rap group before any other. Few music producers in any era rank as high as Sylvia Robinson. In 1979 she founded Sugar Hill Records. It was hip-hop's first record company. Some of the most familiar early hip-hop records had her help in production. Among them was hip-hop's first hit across the whole nation. Its title is Rapper's Delight. Outside New York, the wider country met hip-hop because of that record. At the time, hip-hop was mostly unknown outside New York City. A portrait shows Sylvia Robinson.

5Control of hip-hop music has always sat with men. Unfair treatment has met women artists from the earliest days. MC Lyte used hip-hop to empower herself and other women. Queen Latifah did too. Salt-N-Pepa did too. Lady B did too. Lauryn Hill did too. Rap became their platform for talking about sexism. They spoke about sexism inside hip-hop. They spoke about sexism in popular culture. A portrait shows Lauryn Hill. Lolita Shante Gooden was fourteen and already one of the strongest rappers then living. She was known as Roxanne Shante. Her 1984 release carried the title Roxanne's Revenge. Women's experience of sexism was the song's subject. It was a huge success. The next year she reached the finals of a freestyle MC competition. In the final rap battle she was the obvious winner. One judge still marked her down, aiming to make her lose. Years later, the judge told her why. He thought a young girl's win would harm hip-hop's reputation as a serious art form. She lost that battle. Two rap albums still came out under her name. Young women in hip-hop later found a mentor in her. The music began as party music. Even early artists still took up serious issues in their songs. Grandmaster Flash was one of the first. Poverty in New York City is the subject of his song The Message. Public Enemy used music to show Black pride. The group also discussed racism. MC Lyte spoke about racism. She spoke about sexism. She spoke about drug use in her community. In the 1990s, few hip-hop groups were more popular than Public Enemy. Gangsta rap, a style of the 1990s, came to dominate hip-hop music. The music industry promoted that style above all others. A record deal was often refused to Black artists whose music sat outside that style. Some listeners found the lyrics offensive. As gangsta rap grew more popular, people outside the culture began to treat all rap as offensive. Many others have seen rap as a form of poetry. Rap and traditional poetry share many elements. Rhythm is one. Rhyming is one. Storytelling is one. Few poets of any era are respected more than Maya Angelou. She worked with some of history's best-known rap artists. She inspired them as well.

6Rap had a path cleared by spoken-word poetry during the 1960s. Performers recited poetry over a beat. One of those groups was the Last Poets, based in New York City. A bongo drum might carry the beat. Jazz music might carry it. Their poems held important social messages. They held important political messages. Black pride was a subject. Racism was a subject. Poverty was a subject. Justice was a subject. Modern hip-hop often looks back to these poets and to what they wrote. A photograph shows the Last Poets. Hip-hop music spread across the country in the mid-1980s and the early 1990s. The culture changed with that spread. Newer artists brought new musical influences. They brought more innovation in style. Local radio stations wanted fresh hip-hop. Club DJs wanted it too. Demand grew. Popularity skyrocketed. Large sums started going from record companies into new hip-hop albums. Cities across the country developed styles of their own. Each style was distinctive. Other kinds of music were folded into hip-hop by newer artists. Sampling was one feature of this era. Sampling means a rapper lifts a piece of an existing song, called a sample, into a new one. Samples came from jazz. They came from blues. They came from rock. Movie sound clips became samples for some artists. Nearly 9,000 miles separate the Bronx from New Zealand. The distance is also 14,484 kilometers. Early in the 1980s, hip-hop music crossed that distance anyway. An eager audience was waiting among the Māori. New Zealand's native Polynesian people are the Māori. Black communities in the South Bronx of the early 1970s had faced a similar bind. Large numbers of Māori lived in communities with limited opportunities. Financial struggle was greater. Crime was higher. Access to health care was poor. Access to education was poor. They felt absent from mainstream culture in New Zealand. The music struck them with unusual force. Māori bands took it up as their own musical culture. Upper Hutt Posse was one of those bands. A photograph shows the group.

7Pictures from around the world catch the culture in motion. Hungary hosts a contest where a b-girl from Japan is dancing. A building in Brazil carries graffiti across its walls. One performer from a duo of Muslim rappers is shown in England. As rap grew more popular worldwide, the wider culture was embraced too. Brazil has break dancing now. Morocco has it. China has it. Graffiti art can be seen across that same span. The starting point was a young girl's street party. The place was the South Bronx. The year was 1973. What began there became a global movement. Scarce resources gave rise to musical inventions that rank among the most creative of the twentieth century. They led to forms of artistic expression just as creative. Hip-hop still influences popular culture worldwide. The mark it leaves is a lasting one.

38. From Samhain Night to Candy Night

1An 1890s picture shows a group of children on Halloween. They hold jack-o-lanterns and use them to frighten an adult away. This book traces a fun and scary holiday from its oldest roots to today. It tells how the Celts kept Samhain and how Halloween got its start. It tells about costumes, trick-or-treating, and jack-o-lanterns. It tells about older customs, the holiday now, crowds, and a blend of old and new. A word list closes the book. Halloween is a colorful holiday, and it is a delicious one. People mark it most in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Ireland. Ireland is the place where it first began. On October 31, people dress in all kinds of costumes. Creepy music oozes from Halloween parties and from haunted houses. Trick-or-treaters pour into the streets in search of candy. Monsters, ghosts, superheroes, and princesses celebrate side by side. People of every age join the night. A 1929 photo from Cincinnati, Ohio, shows three girls in Halloween costumes. A boy in Montebello, California, shops for a costume of his own. Today the holiday is most popular in the United States. There it plays an enormous part in culture and an enormous part in business. Hollywood movies feature Halloween, and popular songs feature it too. American stores do big Halloween business. Each year, millions of people buy Halloween candy, costumes, and merchandise. The holiday celebrated now is part of an ancient tradition. It began with the Celtic peoples, a name said KEL-tik. About two thousand years ago they lived in Great Britain, Ireland, and northern France. At Stonehenge, in the south of England, druids of today offer a blessing.

2Each fall the Celts held a harvest festival called Samhain, a name said SOW-in. Samhain shared some features with our New Year celebrations. It also shared features with Halloween as people keep it now. On the Celtic calendar, October 31 was the final day of the year. The Samhain gathering on that date said farewell to the old year. It closed the harvest season. It helped people prepare for winter. The festival had a supernatural side as well. Celtic tradition said that on Samhain eve the doorways stood open. Those doorways lay between the world of the living and the world of the dead. Spirits of people who had died in the past year could cross into the underworld. The Celts believed the dead could appear during this time. They believed the dead could speak with the living. To help the dead on the journey, the Celts lit bonfires. They also sacrificed crops and animals. People believed that priests could see the future during the festival. The predictions made at Samhain were important. They helped families plan for the new year.

3Later, Christianity spread across Europe. The Catholic Church tried to replace the old Samhain festival with traditions of its own. For example, the Church set All Saints Day on November 1. People also knew that day as All Hallows Day. October 31 is the day before All Hallows. It came to be called All Hallows Eve. In time the name was shortened to Halloween. Hundreds of years later, many older Celtic traditions still lived inside the new holiday. The strongest surviving belief was this one. Supernatural activity was expected on the night of October 31. The Halloween customs known today draw on the Celts. They also draw on the Catholic Church and on legends from medieval Europe. A photo shows Catholic churchgoers walking through a town in Poland on All Saints Day. The custom of costumes has changed many times over the centuries. Halloween dress probably began with the Celts, who dressed as animals at the Samhain bonfires. In medieval England the costumes took a new turn. People dressed as supernatural beings in the hope of scaring those beings off. Many walked through towns in fairy costumes, witch costumes, and ghost costumes. This practice was called mumming. Townspeople often gave the mummers food and drink. The gift echoed an older Celtic practice of making sacrifices at Samhain. People believed the offerings satisfied the spirits. The spirits would then leave without causing trouble. Today that custom is known as trick-or-treating. Adults give candy to children. A child who receives a treat will, people hope, move on. The child will not play any malicious tricks. In England, a modern druid wears an animal costume during Samhain.

4Many people carve jack-o-lanterns every Halloween. A carver cuts a face or a design into a pumpkin. A candle, or some other light, is set inside so the carving glows. Jack-o-lanterns are a newer Halloween custom. They are one of the few customs that did not start with Celtic Samhain. They come from an Irish legend about a man named Stingy Jack. Jack was stingy, and he was cruel as well. He liked to trick his friends. When Jack died, his spirit was forced to wander in the dark. The wandering was a punishment for his unpleasant character. To light the way, he cut an opening in a turnip and put a candle inside. For that reason the Irish called him Jack-of-the-lantern. Later they called him a jack-o-lantern. The tale of Stingy Jack began one major Halloween custom. Some people still carve turnips at Halloween. In Ireland and in England, people once placed candles and coals in turnips, beets, and potatoes. They cut frightening faces into those vegetables. The faces copied the terrifying look of Stingy Jack, or they were meant to scare him off. During the 1800s, huge numbers of Irish people moved to North America. They carried the jack-o-lantern custom with them. The use of pumpkins, though, began in the United States. In 1846 an American newspaper story described the practice. A poem published separately in that same year described it too. Both told of people cutting faces into pumpkins and setting a candle within. From there the custom spread. Pumpkins make excellent jack-o-lanterns. They are large enough for elaborate designs of many kinds. They are also plentiful in the fall. For many families today, making a jack-o-lantern and setting it out is a beloved Halloween custom.

5Several Halloween customs that were once popular are less familiar now. A number of them link back to fortune-telling at Samhain, a Celtic custom. That custom lasted for centuries in changing forms. For example, people sometimes played games on Halloween night to guess whom they might marry. Holding a candle, a girl might gaze into a mirror. She hoped to see the face of the husband she would one day have. Even bobbing for apples, a classic party game, began as a way to tell fortunes. Players try to lift an apple from a tub of water. They may use only their mouths. The first person to get an apple out was expected to be the first to marry afterward. Fortune-telling has now dropped out of many Halloween games. A guest might still meet a fortune-teller at a Halloween party or inside a haunted house. A photo from the early 1900s shows children in the United States bobbing for apples at a party. The Halloween people keep today is a fairly recent invention. It is often mixed with ancient customs, especially the Samhain bonfire. That mix is clearest in North America, where the holiday was not widely kept until the 1800s. Many of the first European settlers in the New World frowned on Halloween. The Puritans are one example. At best, they saw the night as a silly waste of time, and they urged people not to celebrate it. The holiday grew far more popular when huge numbers of Irish immigrants reached the United States in the 1800s. They brought their traditions along. Jack-o-lanterns arrived with them, and so did mumming. Bit by bit, more Americans began to keep Halloween. As the night grew more popular, pranks and vandalism became common. By the 1930s those pranks were a major problem. Some city governments tried to answer the problem. They tried to reshape Halloween into a holiday for families. They organized trick-or-treating and encouraged children to join. In the 1930s and 1940s, the first trick-or-treaters received cookies and fruit. They also received toys and even small change for a pocket.

6In the 1950s, candy became a popular treat as trick-or-treating spread. The tiny, separately wrapped candy bars common now did not appear until the 1970s. The treats have changed across the years. The excitement of children has not. In the United States alone, more than 41 million children went trick-or-treating in 2014. Those children were between five and fourteen years old. A chart shows where costume ideas come from. Other sources account for 10.1 percent. Pop culture accounts for 13.6 percent. Online sources account for 31.4 percent. Friends or family account for 18.1 percent. Ideas found in a store account for 26.8 percent. More Halloween numbers fill out the picture. In 2013, each person in the United States consumed 4.2 pounds of fresh pumpkin. Among dedicated Halloween fans, 5 percent start shopping before September. In 2015, Halloween spending in the United States totaled 6.89 billion dollars. A photo shows children collecting treats at an organized event. The popularity of Halloween is still rising. Each year, more people celebrate, especially in the United States and Canada. Some cities set up community trick-or-treating at malls, churches, and community centers. Children can gather a large amount of candy in a short time. The events also protect them from traffic in the streets. The crowds are not made of children only. Adults are celebrating in greater numbers too. In 2015, buyers planned to spend more on adult costumes than on costumes for children. Many adults, especially young adults, host Halloween parties or go to them. They dress in costume as well. The night is fun for kids, and adults do not want to miss it.

7Halloween now looks very different from the celebrations of the 1950s. It looks different from the celebrations of the 1800s. It looks different from the Samhain festival of the ancient Celts. The customs keep changing, and they mix what is old with what is new. Bonfires stand beside chocolate bars in the story of the night. Turnips once packed with coal stand beside pumpkins lit by candles. Halloween is a holiday that changes as the times change. It offers fun and entertainment for one spooky night each year. Today it is rich with customs from several cultures. People of every age can enjoy those customs. A photo from 1898 shows two girls in the United States dressed for Halloween. A whole industry now surrounds Halloween candy, costumes, and supplies for parties. A survey taken in 2015 produced a startling figure. Shoppers getting ready for the holiday were asked about candy. Of that group, 93.7 percent said they intended to purchase sweets for the night. Those shoppers planned to spend 2.1 billion dollars on candy by itself. They also planned about 28 dollars per household for costumes. Many even planned costumes for their pets. Among people keeping the holiday, 44.8 percent planned to decorate their yards. Another share, 31.5 percent of consumers, planned to host a party or to attend one. The average amount spent by people celebrating was 74.34 dollars. The National Retail Federation reported these plans for 2015. Celtic describes the peoples of ancient Ireland, Scotland, Wales, and western Europe, or things linked to them. Pranks are tricks, or jokes played in a practical way. Predictions are guesses about events that might come later. Consumers are people who buy or rent goods or services and then use them. Puritans belonged to a British Protestant group that opposed the Church of England. They came to North America because they sought freedom for their religion. Immigrants are people who move into a new country in order to settle. Supernatural means outside what the laws of nature can explain, and the word often touches religion. Malicious means full of hate and ready to do harm. Medieval describes the Middle Ages, the stretch of European history from the year 500 to the year 1500. A tradition is a belief or a custom handed down year by year and generation by generation. Merchandise means goods that people buy or sell. In some myths, the underworld is the place where the souls of the dead go.

39. From Trading Goods to Spending Money

1Inside: a beginning. Trading goods directly. Currency. Coins. Money printed on paper. What gives money its worth. How money stays genuine. Money you cannot see: checks and credit cards. A closing word. Words to know. A picture makes a point. A bill is worth far more than the sheet it is printed on. A beginning Plain paper has little worth. Paper that is money may equal thousands of dollars. One check may stand for millions of dollars. Every printed bill is worth far more than its paper. The reason is not obvious. People ask where money came from. They ask what makes it so valuable. Money has value because the people who create it and the people who use it agree on that value. The government that issues it agrees. The mint that strikes coins or prints bills agrees. The banks that hold it agree. Shoppers and sellers agree as well. All of them treat money as worth something. The story of money is a fascinating one. People once traded objects that were valuable in themselves. Later they traded objects that stood for those valuables. Technology added another step. It made invisible money. With that money, people can trade goods and materials all over the world.

2Trading without coins Thousands of years ago, people bartered. They swapped goods in a direct trade. Families near the ocean had fish. They also had salt. Families near the mountains had fruits. They had wood. They had furs. The two groups traded. Barter still happens. Swap the apple in your lunch for another person's candy bar, and you are bartering. Barter has problems. You may want someone's goods. That person may not want yours. Many goods are heavy. Many are hard to carry. Many do not last. A picture explains two ideas. Barter let people obtain products they could not make or gather alone. Currency let people trade value without hauling the goods themselves. Currency People invented currency to escape the troubles of barter. Currency means objects that stand for set values. A community might agree that one cow equaled twenty shells. A large fish might equal two shells. Goods could be swapped for currency. Currency could be swapped for goods. Each culture picked its own object to stand for what its goods were worth. The chosen objects were nearly always light enough to carry. They were also rare. People could not simply gather them from the ground. Greater rarity raised the value. So did the extra work of finding the object.

3Ancient currency took many forms. People used stones that were bright or full of color. They used shells, leaves, and feathers. They used lumps of silver and of gold. They used salt, spices, and gems. Pay for soldiers in ancient Rome came as sacks of salt. Traders from Africa all the way to Asia used rare shells with speckles. Only a handful of islands produced those speckled shells. Those speckled shells come from the Indian Ocean. Among Native Americans, some groups used wampum. Wampum is beads made from clam shells. They used it in trade and in treaties. Other Native Americans used feathers from eagles. People in China used bundles of tea leaves. Colonists from Europe, living in North America, used leaves of tobacco. This kind of currency was hard to price. A shell much larger than another shell might seem to deserve a higher value. You might also meet someone who thought your shells had no value at all. One fact stands out. The Yap Islanders use the largest currency anywhere. They live on an island near the equator, close to Indonesia. Their coins are giant stones. A stone can weigh as much as a full-grown Asian elephant. Each stone has a hole. People push a stick through the hole and roll the coin along. Older coins of another kind were stamped with a picture of the king. Coins Ordinary objects made poor currency. One answer was coins struck from metals that are precious. Those metals are rare. Cultures widely treat them as valuable. They are easy to shape and easy to weigh. The first coins were minted, which means produced, 2,600 years ago. The place was Lydia. Today that land sits inside Turkey. Coins then spread quickly from Lydia into nearby Greece. They also spread into Persia, the land now called Iran. The oldest coins were hammered from electrum. Electrum is a natural mix of gold and silver. Those coins were rough and crude. The sides had no patterns. Sizes were not standard. Weights were not standard. Later coins used pure gold, or they used pure silver. Weights became standard. A seal of the king was stamped on one side. The seal confirmed the coin's quality.

4On many early European coins, one face showed the head of a god. The other side carried a seal from the maker. Later coins showed the heads of kings and of rulers. The reverse side carried elaborate symbols. Those pictures helped people tell when a coin was made. They showed where it was made. They showed who made it. Look at modern coins and you can still see faces. Presidents appear. Kings appear. Queens appear. Greek coins carried words. They showed an owl. Athena, a goddess, appeared in a portrait on them. Workers in China melted copper. They poured it into molds. It hardened into coins. A hole went through the center. Thousands of coins could ride on a ribbon. They could ride on a stick. These coins were called cash. They did not use pictures. Words stated the worth, which is the denomination. Only the government was allowed to produce the coins. A string or a stick made Chinese cash easy to carry. How coins are made Coins are harder to produce than they look. After a government decides on new coins, many steps follow. A designer draws both faces of the coin on a large sheet of paper. Sculptors build a large model with depth, not a flat drawing. An engraving machine reads that model and cuts a die. The die is the stamp for the coin. Dies go to mints. A mint is a factory that produces coins. At the mint, blank coins called blanks are cut from a rolled sheet of the proper metal. Laid out, the metal sheet could match five football fields placed end to end. The blanks are heated. They are cooled. They are washed. They are dried. The raised rim is formed by a machine known as an upsetting mill. A coin press pushes the die's pattern into the coin. Inspectors look for mistakes. Coins made wrong are melted. The metal is recycled. Armored trucks carry the finished coins out to banks.

5Money on paper A man in China named Ts'ai Lun invented paper. That was 1,900 years ago. Paper was not money yet. Seven hundred years passed. Then the government in China ran out of copper for coins. Officials turned to printing money on paper. The earliest bills were printed by hand. Wooden blocks covered with ink were pressed onto paper rectangles of one set size. Coins were still around. The lighter paper money quickly became more popular. A picture shows early paper money from China. In Europe, a different invention changed money's form. Johannes Gutenberg invented the printing press that used movable type. The time was the middle of the 1400s. His press let people print paper money with a machine. Hand printing was no longer the only way. What a bill is worth A coin of gold or of silver has value as metal. Paper money, by itself, is worth very little. Printing one bill costs only four cents in U.S. money. That price covers the paper. It covers the ink. It covers the pay of the person who runs the printer. So why can one sheet be worth a hundred dollars? Why can another be worth only one dollar? The government says so. A century ago, the rule was different. For every dollar moving in circulation, the government stored matching gold in a bank. People called this the gold standard. Each dollar stood for its face value in gold. Face value is the number printed on the bill. In those days you could take dollars to the bank and receive the same amount in gold. Banks once stored bars of gold. Those bars stood for the total of everyone's money.

6Crossing from one country to another has become easy. Changing one nation's money into another's, every time you travel, can be a bother. Most nations of Europe came together as the European Union. A large share of them made their money match, so the euro has the same worth in each of those nations. Each country mints its own euros. The tail side carries a picture. That picture stands for the country that made the coin. Most countries have given up the gold standard. Too many bills are in circulation. The bills stand for more wealth, more goods, and more valuables than all the gold on Earth. Britain left the gold standard in 1931. The United States left it forty years after that. Today a government counts the goods and resources inside the country. It sends out enough money to stand for those goods and resources. A country's money can rise in value next to other currencies. It can also fall. How much the country produces in goods matters to that change. The stock of resources matters too. It depends on how well its businesses do. People call this arrangement a floating system for currency. How money stays real Many people agree that only a government should make currency. The government is the one that tracks the real goods and resources behind it. What if private people try to make money themselves? Fake money is called counterfeit. It is worth nothing. No goods or resources stand behind it. Banks will not take it. Stores will not take it. Restaurants will not take it. Companies will not take it. Worse, counterfeit money in circulation damages the value of real money. If fakes are around, you cannot be sure your own money is genuine. Feel can give the secret away. Set a dollar bill beside plain writing paper. Add construction paper. Add cloth. Add tissue paper. Cut each one to the bill's size and shape. Shut your eyes and the real bill feels different. Cashiers who handle piles of money can tell a genuine bill from a fake by touch alone. Bank tellers can do the same.

7Countries fight counterfeiters with tricks that are hard to copy. Bills use paper made from a secret formula. Cloth in a U.S. dollar is mostly cotton, about three quarters of the sheet. Linen makes up about one quarter. Red fibers and blue fibers are scattered through it. The government keeps the exact recipe secret. A famous maker of soda guards a drink recipe in the same way. A special thread sits below the portrait. It glows under ultraviolet light. Another name for that light is black light. A special pen is used at banks. Some stores use it too. On real money the ink shifts from black to yellow. On fake money the ink stays black. The pictures and the printing are planned so that copying is difficult. The portrait is large. It is full of detail. It sits a little off center. Very thin dashed lines build the face. Designs printed on the bill stay tiny. They are also complicated. A serial number on each bill shows when it was printed. The number also shows where. Many bills add colored inks. They add magnetic inks. They add inks that change color when you tilt the bill. Some bills carry holograms. Some carry watermarks. The hidden picture appears if light shines through the bill. Money you cannot hold as cash Most adults have a checking account. The bank records how much that person has saved. The person writes checks. A check is an official note that stands for a set amount. One sheet of paper can stand for a large sum. Many of these accounts also come with a debit card. The card can pull cash from the account at an ATM. It can pay at shops. It can pay at restaurants. A credit card works like a debit card in the hand. It also works like a checking account at the shop. The difference is borrowing. The person is not spending saved money. The bank lends the money. People use credit cards for purchases that cost more than the bank balance. Later they must repay the sum. They also pay a fee called interest. Wait a long time to repay, and the interest grows. An automatic teller machine, or ATM, lets people take cash from an account at any hour.

8A picture shows debit cards and credit cards. Both kinds of card are made of durable plastic. One side is stamped with the person's name. An individual number is stamped there too. So is the name of the bank that holds the account. A magnetic strip along the top stores encoded information about that account. Swipe the card through a reading machine. The machine calls the bank by electronic signal. It asks whether the account holds enough money. When the balance is large enough, the price leaves that person's account. It moves to the account of the store, the restaurant, or the company. One piece of plastic is easier to carry than a stack of bills. The card also bears your name and your information. Stealing that money is harder than stealing bills. Credit cards still hold a danger. People forget that borrowed money must be paid back. Some users act in an irresponsible way. They owe the banks so much that the banks take back the things that were bought. That taking back is called repossession. A plastic card is less visible than cash. It still buys the same goods. Invisible money lets us exchange goods with partners in far countries. Catalogs help. So does the Internet. A credit card can buy goods from a person in another country. It can buy from a company there. Your money is changed, on its own, into a currency that the seller can use. A purchase on the Internet, paid by credit card, can move money over an ocean at once.

9A closing word Go back three thousand years and a person swapped one good directly for a different good. Today they trade with bills. They trade with coins. They trade with invisible money. What kind of money might exist after another three thousand years is still an open question. A picture shows a stock market. People there buy stock. They also sell it. A stock is a piece of a company. The price rises or falls with the company's value. Until that stock is sold, the money inside it is not real money yet. Words to know Barter: to swap goods or services and not use money. Durable: sturdy, and able to last a long time. Encoded: written in a special code. Cash: a common name for paper money. In Chinese, the word also named ancient coins. Floating currency: money whose value comes from the free market. It is not tied to the gold standard. Circulation: the state of being in use, passing from person to person. Counterfeit: a fake, above all of money, built so people mistake it for genuine money. Holograms: special images that look as if they have depth. Mint: a place where coins are made. Currency: money people accept, in whatever form, standing in for goods and for resources. Watermarks: special pictures in paper, including money paper, that show when the sheet is held up to light. Denomination: the face value of one kind of currency.

40. Goliath Beetles: Giant Insects

1A wild Goliath beetle is about to eat part of a banana. It is striped like a zebra and as agile as an acrobat. Goliath beetles grow as big as sparrows and weigh nearly twice as much. Their larvae are even bigger. They are giants of the insect world. A human hand is 7.44 inches long and 3.3 inches wide. A Goliath beetle is 4.33 inches long and weighs 1.7 ounces. A larva is 5 inches long and weighs 3.5 ounces.

2Pictures show a rhinoceros beetle, a Hercules beetle, and a Goliath beetle. Beetles come in many shapes and sizes, but Goliath beetles outweigh them all. Fossils from three hundred million years ago show dragonflies with hawk-sized wings. Scientists think Goliaths have reached the size limit for modern insects. The air has less oxygen now, so bigger monster insects are gone. Rhinoceros horns nearly double body length, yet Goliaths are the heavyweight champs. No two have the same black stripes, so they were called zebra beetles. Experts once named over two dozen types, but now the six include cacicus, goliatus, regius, albosignatus, atlas, and orientalis.

3You may see ladybugs and other beetles near home. They share features with big Goliath beetles. All beetles have softer hind wings for flying and hard front wings like armor. A butterfly sips nectar, a mosquito pierces skin, and beetles chew. Beetles also sip tree sap, and many eat pollen or flower petals. Scientists think Goliaths are too heavy to feed on flowers. Males have Y-shaped horns, antennae that unfold to sense, and sharp claws for climbing. Insects have wings, mostly six jointed legs, a head, thorax, abdomen, and an outside skeleton.

4There are more than one hundred families of beetles. A family is a group with similar features. Goliath beetles belong to the scarab family, along with rhinoceros and dung beetles. Scarab plates open like a fan, become larger, and may sense more. Goliaths use them to find rotting fruit, and males use them to find mates. London museum X-rays showed a shotgun pellet in a Goliath shot flying upside down. Goliaths fly so well that early collectors shot them out of the sky. Doctor Ratcliffe says they are hard to observe, so fans raise them as pets to study.

5They live in warm African rainforests and dry grasslands with a dry season of several months. In the wet season they chew fruit and use claws to reach sweet tree sap. They may gather at food, but Doctor Ratcliffe says they are not social. Males push rivals off the best sites with Y-shaped horns, which may attract females. Females dig deep and may lay up to one hundred eggs that hatch in about two weeks. The eyeless, wingless larvae eat rotting plants, smaller larvae, and adult insects. They reach full size in about four months. The larger ones can be 5 inches long and 3.5 ounces, like a dollar bill or five mice.

6After an egg hatches, a Goliath goes through four more stages to become an adult. When the wet season ends, the larvae burrow down to sandy soil. There they build thin-walled cells like butterfly cocoons. Over several months, legs and wings grow and the outside hardens into a shell. The adult stays in hibernation in the earthen cell until the dry season ends. Wet-season moisture seeps down, wakes the beetle, and the cycle starts again. Captive adults live about eight months, but wild life is shorter because of food and enemies. They hide so well in treetops that no one knows if monkeys or large birds eat them.

7A male Goliath climbs on a human hand in Cameroon, Africa. Most of us have never seen an insect larger than a grasshopper. In 1766 a navy doctor fished the first known Goliath from an African river. Since then, these giant beetles have interested insect fans everywhere. Their enormous size and flashy stripes make them a sight to behold. Goliaths are speedy fliers, heavyweight champs, and awesome insects. A rare photo shows one in flight in the Ituri Rainforest Reserve.

41. Hidden Tombs of Egypt's Golden Age

1A map of Egypt marks the Mediterranean Sea, Cairo, Memphis, and the Nile River. It also marks Luxor, once called Thebes, and the Red Sea. Coming pages open on treasure past imagining. They enter a valley of kings. They explain the afterlife. They explain how tombs were built. They move into modern times. They look toward treasure still ahead. Useful words close the book. A photo shows Howard Carter on the left. In November 1922, this British archaeologist found a tomb. The king inside was Tutankhamen, said toot-an-KAH-muhn. The find sat in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Explorers had believed that valley was played out. Better still, the royal seal was still intact. No earlier royal tomb had been found that way. Objects inside numbered more than five thousand. Solid gold made many of them. The golden funeral mask of Tutankhamen became one of Egypt's most famous treasures. Pharaohs buried here outranked him in importance. His tomb was also among the smallest ones. Only four small chambers made it up. The objects were still so many that listing continues. Experts are nearly a century past Carter's discovery, and the list is unfinished. The photo shows that small tomb, four rooms packed with objects beyond price.

2A tomb map uses KV numbers. KV 62 is Tutankhamen. KV 9 is Ramses IV. Several tombs stay off this map. Some lie farther west. KV 57 is Horemheb. KV 17 is Seti I. KV can stand for the valley itself. Almost every pharaoh of Egypt's golden age has a tomb in this valley. That age is the New Kingdom. Three dynasties ruled then. They were the Eighteenth, the Nineteenth, and the Twentieth. The years run from 1550 to 1080 bc. Thebes, the city now called Luxor, was the capital. It was also the religious center. Temples there honored the empire's pharaohs. Egyptians believed those rulers joined the gods after death. A royal tomb still needed a hidden place. Across the Nile, steep-sided valleys linked together. That network was the right place. Limestone there could be carved into tombs. Steep cliffs helped guards. A single way in helped them too. Robbers were harder to keep out anywhere else. A photo shows Carter at the coffins. He is lifting a covering from the third coffin, the one farthest inside. For ancient Egyptians, a pharaoh's tomb mattered for a clear reason. It gave safe passage into the afterlife. The physical body needed protection. People then believed that body could live again after burial. After death, mummification lasted seventy days. The goal was to stop the body from breaking down. Priests took out the inner organs. They mummified those organs. A stone box received them. Nested coffins then held the mummified body. A stone sarcophagus held the coffins. Solid stone formed the sarcophagus. Its weight could reach 9 metric tons (10 T). The tomb had another duty. It guarded the pharaoh's spirit on a trip through the underworld. Priests set protective amulets inside the wrappings. They believed those amulets held powers.

3Walls and ceilings of a tomb carried spells and prayers. The sarcophagus often carried them too. Long columns held the hieroglyphs and the images. Some writings aimed to bring the body back to life. Others aimed to scare demons away. A soul on its way to the afterlife might need facts. Hieroglyphs supplied those facts. Ancient Egyptians believed the king's soul had a companion. The companion was Ra, the Sun god, and the road was the underworld. Wall writings told how the Sun god moved through that dark world. They warned of dangers the soul would meet. Demon-guarded gates were one challenge. Another test was the questioning inside the Hall of Judgment. The writings told how to get past both. A photo shows tomb entrances. Ra's many names appear there, with prayers, images, and hieroglyphs. A royal tomb also stocked whatever a king might need after death. Storerooms held wooden models of gear. Boats were among the models. Chariots were among them. Personal things were stored too. Makeup was one. Clothing was one. Board games were one. Everyday things were stored. Furniture was one. Lamps were one. Treasure was there to enjoy. Expensive gems were part of it. Golden jewelry was part of it. Artwork was part of it. Food was packed. Drink was packed. Carved figures called shabtis filled the tombs by the hundreds. Say shabtis as SHAB-teez. Answerers is the other name. A spell was carved on each shabti. The spell would wake it to serve its master. Tutankhamen went into the grave with 413 of these figures. The little statues are wood or stone. They tell us a great deal about what ancient Egyptians believed.

4A diagram compares tomb layouts. Early tombs bent left once, or more than once. Later tombs ran without a turn. Experts think the change had a purpose. Workers would be less likely to cut into an older tomb by accident. Chambers that many tombs share have names. A is the entrance. B is the passage of Ra. C is the hall of hindering, and a deep well sits in it. D is the chariot hall. Sets of pillars stand there. Chariots themselves have never turned up in that hall. E is the burial chamber. The diagram also contrasts an early design with a later one. Most layouts in this royal valley match one another. An entryway leads to a hall. Egyptians called that hall the passage of Ra. Images there show forms of the Sun god. A deep well is cut through the floor of one room in many tombs. Some experts see the pit as a delay for robbers. Some see it as protection if a flood came. Every tomb ended in the burial room. Storerooms often opened off that room, filled with supplies. Similar as they are, no two tombs here are the same. Each one followed the taste of the ruler then in power. That freedom had a limit. Builders started while the king was still alive. Years were needed to finish. Death changed the clock. Only seventy days remained. Mummification would be done then, and burial had to happen. An unfinished tomb forced shortcuts. Paintings might be left half done. Rooms might be left half done. At times the king was buried somewhere else. The tomb he had been building was not the one that held him.

5Time changed how the valley tombs looked. It changed their layouts too. Early tombs of the New Kingdom were usually the smaller ones. Later tombs were larger. Early tombs usually bent. One turn of ninety degrees was common. Two such turns were common too. Later tombs were straighter. Experts suspect a reason. The valley was growing crowded. A straight dig was less likely to strike a neighbor's tomb. Where tombs sat also changed. Older ones usually lay at the bottoms of cliffs. Rain would wash water and earth down over the entrance. Later rulers usually set entrances on slopes that lay lower. A note on Ramses IX tells a rushed story. Experts think death found Ramses IX with only two corridors complete. Workers finished the others afterward. The workmanship looks hurried. Tomb work, experts think, began almost as soon as a new king started to rule. Picking the spot was the important first step. High officials of the court did that picking. Senior workmen did it with them. A bad choice meant they had to stop. A new spot had to be chosen. More than once, cutting had already started when the first spot was abandoned. Limestone bedrock had to receive the tomb directly. Crews began by digging rough passages. Their tools were chisels of copper or bronze. They used wooden mallets. They used hand axes whose blades were stone. A painted line went on the ceiling. That line was the reference for measuring. Walls, ceiling, and floor were built to it. Much of our knowledge comes from writings left behind. The writings are from Dier al-Medina. That village stood near the valley. The workers lived there.

6A photo of Horemheb's unfinished tomb shows early marks and fixes. Red ink is the scribe's outline. A relief is part of the wall. Black ink is the supervisor's correction. Decoration started once the cutting had gone far enough. Plasterers spread white plaster over the surfaces. Scribes drew hieroglyphs. They drew figures. A supervisor came behind them and corrected the sketches. Artists then made the art final. They painted blocks of color. They filled in details. At times, workers cut away parts of a scene. Certain shapes would stand out. Cutting away the background produced raised relief. Details were carved into those raised figures. Paint went on after the carving. Modern care of the valley has its own story. In 1979, the United Nations listed the Valley of the Kings. It was among the first World Heritage sites. Yearly visits to the tombs pass one million. Eighteen tombs open to the public. The set of open tombs rotates. One entry ticket lets a visitor choose three tombs from those that are open. Tutankhamen's tomb is the exception. Seeing it takes an extra ticket. Objects first found in his tomb now stay in the Cairo museum. Crowds that never stop have hurt the tombs. Temperature inside shifts quickly. Humidity shifts quickly. Mold now grows on some walls. A hand that touches a wall by accident can harm old paint. It can harm old carvings. The rotating list lets tombs rest from visitors now and then. Repair teams use that quiet time. Visitors are urged to plan before they come. They should choose their tombs ahead of the walk.

7Tutankhamen's golden funeral mask has traveled to museums around the world. It now stays with every treasure from his tomb. The Cairo museum holds them. Known tombs in the valley today number sixty-three. More than one tomb from the New Kingdom is still missing. Ramses VIII has not been found. Thutmose II has not been found. Several queens of the Eighteenth Dynasty have not been found. Several princes of that dynasty have not been found. This valley is the likely place where those rulers were buried. Archaeological sites rarely rank richer than the Valley of the Kings. Experts believe more treasure is still hidden. Afterlife means the life that follows death, once the physical body is gone. Humidity measures moisture held in the air. An archaeologist is a scientist. The subject is remains of ancient cultures. Limestone is a sedimentary rock. It formed from remains of marine organisms. A chamber is a room or another closed space. It may be natural. It may be made by people. Mummification is a way of preserving a dead body. Ancient Egypt practiced it. Chariots were carriages pulled by horses. They had two wheels. Ancient people used them, usually to race or to fight. Pharaohs were the kings of ancient Egypt. A sarcophagus is a coffin or tomb of stone from ancient times. Writing often covers it. Rich ornament often covers it. Dynasties are lines of rulers in one country. The rulers come from the same family. Scribes copy texts by hand. They also record information in writing. They are writers. Hieroglyphs are pictures and symbols that serve as writing. Ancient Egypt is where that system is best known.

42. Hispanic Americans Who Shaped a Nation

1An introduction opens the book. Dolores Huerta comes next, then Lin-Manuel Miranda. Selena Quintanilla-Pérez follows, then Roberto Clemente. Sammy Davis Jr. has a part. Antonia Coello Novello has a part. Ellen Ochoa and Oscar de la Renta follow. Frank Romero and Sonia Sotomayor follow them. A conclusion and a glossary close the book. Immigrants have always helped make the United States special. People were arriving in the early 1600s, before the land was a country. Freedom was what they sought. Opportunity was what they sought. Native peoples lost both freedom and opportunity in that arrival. England sent some of the early colonists. Spain sent some. Other European countries sent some. Today, Hispanic Americans are among the fastest-growing immigrant groups in the United States. The U.S. Census Bureau is the source of that fact. Home countries include Mexico. They include Central America and South America. The Caribbean is included. Spain is included. Population in the United States is about 331 million. The Hispanic share is above 18 percent. The largest Hispanic American group is Mexican American. Second place belongs to Puerto Ricans. Generations have already passed for some Hispanic families. Others have only just arrived. Government is one field they have shaped. Sports is another. The arts, science, and entertainment are others. Those fields are only a sample. One picture shows a man born in the Dominican Republic. He is saying the Pledge of Allegiance. When the ceremony ends, he will be a citizen of the United States.

2Dolores Huerta was born on April 10, 1930. Her birthplace was Dawson, New Mexico. Her profession is activist. Her life's work has been better conditions on the job. Equal rights for farmworkers have been part of that work. Other laborers have been part of it too. The year 1962 is when she and other activists founded a union. The name was the National Farm Workers Association, or NFWA. Three years later the name changed. It was then the United Farm Workers' Union, shortened to UFW. Her years as vice president ran through 1999. Grape workers struck with her help from 1965 to 1970. Fairer wages came from that strike. Fairer working conditions came from it too. Labor laws carry her help as a writer. She has also worked to ban pesticides. Those chemicals harm workers. They harm the environment. The year 2012 brought her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. She still works hard for people who lack a voice. The word Hispanic mainly means Spanish-speaking ancestry, among people who live in the United States. Latino is a term for a male. Latina is a term for a female. Latinx does not point to one specific gender. Those three words refer to people in the United States whose origins are Latin American countries. Mexico is included. Countries of Central America and South America are included. Race is not what the words name. Color is not what they name. Language is not what they name. Lin-Manuel Miranda was born on January 16, 1980. His birthplace was New York, New York. He works as an actor, a singer, a playwright, and a director. Puerto Rican parents raised him. New York City was his home. Each summer he visited grandparents in Puerto Rico. High school is where theater became his passion. College is where he wrote a first musical. The title was In the Heights. Spoken-word raps were in it. Salsa dancing was in it. Broadway later gave the show awards. A movie followed. Hamilton, another musical, changed musical theater. Miranda wrote it. He also starred in it. It became one of the most popular Broadway musicals of all time. Hip-hop tells the story. Spoken word tells it too. Alexander Hamilton is the person in the story. He helped found the United States. Awards have piled up. The MacArthur Genius Grant is one. A Pulitzer Prize honored his writing. An Emmy honored his acting on television. Three Tonys honored his Broadway plays. Three Grammys honored his music. Puerto Rican roots matter deeply to him. Support for that island is work he continues.
