A traveler leaving New York might expect the shortest route to Madrid to run due east over the Atlantic Ocean. A glance from the window might instead show ice on the Arctic Ocean. The aircraft is on a path called a great circle route. Over a spherical surface, that path is the shorter one. Time is saved. Fuel is saved. Money is saved. On a flat map, the shortest link between two points is a straight line. A string laid on a globe shows something else. A journey from North America to Europe may pass over the Arctic for that reason. Long-distance navigation of every kind rests on life on a sphere. Sailors have steered by this idea for thousands of years. For decades, pilots of airliners have steered by that same idea. Astronauts have done it too. Livelihoods have depended on a round Earth. Lives have depended on it as well.

7Treat Earth as a sphere, and the world grows easier to understand. Time zones fit that picture. So does travel over long distances. Scientific proof, once recognized and used, opens the way to newer and deeper answers. Working through a question on our own builds scientific skill. That skill lets curiosity choose the next path. It also helps us judge whether another person's ideas are sound. Practice makes thinking sharper. Bass guitar practice makes a stronger musician. Basketball practice makes a stronger athlete. A route to proving Earth's spherical shape sits inside the scientific method. Good questions can be formed with it. Exploration can proceed with it. Observations can be explained with it. Questions and observations can be tested to see whether analysis still supports them. A mismatch with the hypothesis is not the end. The test can be run again. New questions can be asked. Different tests can be tried. Practices that have already been proved can be trusted to yield trustworthy answers. Those answers can send a curious mind still farther.

49. Hybrid Animals

1Animal hybrids do exist, even if old imagined creatures do not. The Greeks imagined centaurs, minotaurs, griffons, and manticores. A hybrid animal has parents of two different species. Hybrids mix traits from those species and are more common than many people think. Horses and donkeys are different species, but they can mate. A horse mother has a mule, and a donkey mother has a hinny. Parents that are too different may have no live young, or weak, unhealthy young. Closer parent species are more likely to have healthy hybrid young.

2The traits of a hybrid often depend on which species was the mother. Mules are usually larger and hardier than hinnies. Most hybrid animals cannot reproduce. A mule gets half its DNA from a horse and half from a donkey. Shared DNA lets the mule live, but mismatched DNA blocks healthy eggs and sperm. People have bred mules since ancient times because they are hardy and sure-footed. Mules also handle heat well and are hurt less often than horses. Zebroids get a gentle nature from a tame parent and disease resistance from a zebra.

3A zebra-donkey hybrid shows traits of both parents. Beefalo combine hardy bison with cattle and are easier to handle than bison. Their meat is lower in fat and bad cholesterol and higher in protein than beef. A liger, from a male lion and a female tiger, grows about twice as large. One healthy male weighs nearly 1,200 pounds, and ligers do not occur in the wild. Accredited zoos avoid big-cat mixes, but some breeders raise them as curiosities. Camels and llamas rarely mate, but a test tube made a cama possible. Scientists hope the cama will join camel strength and hardiness with a sweeter llama nature.

4Related species can form hybrids when they live in the same environment. Identifying hybrids is hard because species lines are not always clear. A species can interbreed in nature and produce healthy young that can reproduce. A Great Dane and a Chihuahua look different, but they are the same species. Two fruit flies may look like twins and still be different species. Ring species make the line between hybrids and separate species hard to draw. Seven salamanders changed as they moved south around the San Joaquin Valley. They breed with neighbors, except two southern California species, so the ring is broken.

5Changes around a ring species are like a message changed in a circle game. Neighbors can interbreed, but the first and last species cannot. These animals change slowly as they adapt to local conditions. Where ranges overlap, hybrids arise, but parent populations change little. Sudden meetings can let hybrids compete for food, territory, and mates. Warming and melting ice in the Arctic are shifting animal ranges north. A 2006 grolar bear had white fur, brown legs and paws, and a wide grizzly head. More grolar bears since then suggest that wild interbreeding is regular.

6This bear is not confirmed, but its shape, short neck, and odd face suggest a hybrid. Polar bears may disappear if grizzly genes dilute genes made for the Arctic. Polar bears risk extinction, so every polar bear birth matters. German zoo grolar bears seem to hunt seals but lack strong swimming ability. No one knows if wild grolar bears survive as well as non-hybrids. Spider silk is stronger than steel, but fourteen thousand spiders make one ounce. Spiders eat their neighbors, so scientists put silk genes into goat DNA instead. The goats make silk proteins in milk, yet they are transgenic, not hybrids.

7Scientists once thought hybrids were an evolutionary dead end. Most were sterile, and fertile ones often fit neither parent environment. In most cases, hybrids are poorly adapted and fail to survive and reproduce. Drastic change may come too fast for a species to adapt in time. Hybrids let two species exchange genetic information. A hybrid might live where one or both parents could not. Are hybrids a threat to at-risk animals like polar bears, or a way to cope? They may be a bit of both, and only time will tell!

50. Isaac Newton and the Rules of Force

1A popular legend ties Newton's grasp of gravity to an apple that struck his head. What really happened is quieter. What he saw was an apple dropping ahead of where he stood. That fall led him to understand gravity. Falling fruit seldom catches our interest. Eyes usually go to grander sights, such as a rainbow or a sunset. Isaac Newton cared about natural events on both scales. Careful attention to ordinary events made him ponder the mechanics beneath them. Study and experiment then produced groundbreaking scientific theories. The theories cover light. They cover force. They cover motion. Modern-day physics is built on that foundation.

2Christmas Day of 1642 was the day Isaac Newton was born. The place was Woolsthorpe, an English village. It sits about 100 miles north of London, a distance of 161 kilometers. His father was a middle-class British farmer. Isaac was that farmer's only child. The father had died two months before the birth. The boy never met him. His mother remarried when Isaac was two. He was sent to live with his grandmother. Her home was in Grantham, a village nearby. Nine years later she lost her second husband. Only then did Isaac live with her again. She sent for him because she wanted help managing her property. The work did not fit him well. Outdoor time pleased him. Still, thinking suited him better than doing. Reading beneath an apple tree appealed more than tending herds of cattle. Before long he was back at school in Grantham. Neighbors were impressed by a skill he showed while young. He built working models of machines. Clocks were among the models. Windmills were among them. Study continued. He prepared hard for college. Trinity College had been founded in 1592. Queen Elizabeth I was the founder. Newton enrolled there in 1661. His tie to Cambridge University would last a long time. Students took a traditional course of study. It opened with Aristotle, the ancient Greek philosopher. In Aristotle's picture, Earth sat at the center of the universe. Nature, for him, was built from basic elements. Earth, air, fire, and water could combine in that account. Beyond Cambridge's walls, a different style of thought had taken hold. The Scientific Revolution, begun in the Renaissance, was moving across Europe. A group of modern philosophers wanted explanations that were more scientific. They also wanted explanations that were mathematical. René Descartes was one such thinker. He pictured the physical world as tiny particles. The particles never stopped moving. Any event in nature, he said, came from particles acting on each other.

3The newer perspective reached Newton, and he became intrigued. Maybe those physical interactions could be named. Maybe they could be measured. For a long time he had asked why falling objects always head downward. He had also asked why light sometimes breaks into different colors. The new way of thinking looked like a path toward the answers he sought. A side account of the Scientific Revolution belongs with this story. Until the sixteenth century, European science leaned heavily on ancient Greek philosophy. Then mathematical and scientific ideas arrived from the Islamic world. The way European scientists investigated nature started to change. Many people trace the revolution's start to Copernicus. He was a Polish astronomer. Math let him propose a new center for the solar system. That center was the Sun, rather than Earth. Ideas passing between cultures did a great deal to feed the Scientific Revolution. One drawing in Newton's notebooks shows calculus being used to solve problems. Course homework lost his attention. Notebooks filled instead with notes he wrote himself. The title he gave them was Certain Philosophical Questions. He learned eagerly. Soon he had mastered the writings of the new thinkers. From that base he built theories of his own. He built calculations of his own. A form of calculus was his own invention. The math is used to analyze curves. It is also used to analyze the areas under those curves. Graduation from Cambridge came in 1665. He was ready to summarize his findings. Mathematical scholars in England were the audience he had in mind. Scholars in other parts of Europe were part of that audience too. Fate set a different plan. In August of that year, bubonic plague broke out. The illness was deadly. Officials at Cambridge shut the university for two years. Newton stayed quarantined at home. Experiments and writing were nearly all he had to do.

4Important theories about light took shape in that same stretch of time. Descartes had called light a type of motion. In his view, the motion traveled through natural substances. Air was one such substance. Water was another. Newton granted that this told how light travels. It did not tell what light is. Experiments with a prism followed in 1666. White light, passed through the prism, separated into bands of color. His notes describe pure white light as colored rays combined. Tilt the path through glass or through water, and one ray shows on its own. The name of that process is refraction. Rainbows, he had discovered, are made this way. A picture of a prism shows the colors being pulled apart. He believed a glass lens would always refract white light to some degree. Anything viewed through the lens would look slightly changed. In 1668 that knowledge became a new instrument. He developed the first reflecting telescope. Mirrors focused the light, and lenses did not. The images came out more accurate. Cambridge opened its doors again in 1667. By 1669 he headed the university's mathematics department. The role required lectures. He could pick the topic. He chose his recent work on light. The book Opticks held that explanation. Word of the lectures reached the Royal Society of London. The members asked to examine a model of the reflecting telescope. They were impressed enough to invite him in as a member. A delighted Newton, in 1672, handed them a paper on light and color. Robert Hooke did not share the delight. He was one of the society's leaders. Before Newton, Hooke had been treated as the top expert on optics. His review of the new paper was scathing. Later he charged that Newton had taken ideas from Hooke's own earlier work. Rage followed, and a feud between the two men lasted for life. More harsh reviews from other scholars upset Newton further. A nervous breakdown came in 1678. He left public life completely.

5A likeness of Newton dates to about 1680. Stepping away from public life gave him time. He could evaluate the work. He could refine it. Interaction between substances still puzzled him. So did interaction between objects. Why will one chemical react with a second chemical, yet ignore another? Why does water seem to climb through a narrow space? Why do the Moon and Earth stay in orbit? A governing principle, he thought, might cover these mysteries. Force and attraction would sit at its center. Letters from Hooke, the old rival, started a discussion. The subject was the elliptical path of planets. Hooke said the paths fail to be circles because two influences are out of balance. One influence is attraction. The other is the velocity of a moving object. Momentum pulls one way. The attraction toward nearby objects pulls the other way. The contest is a tug-of-war. Hooke had the right idea. Proving the statement was difficult. Newton supplied the proof. His tool was calculus. Both Earth and the Moon follow elliptical orbits. Elliptical means oval-shaped. Velocity and gravity are not quite equal, and that mismatch makes the ovals. With elliptical orbits understood, calculus could do finer work. Planetary motion could be predicted more accurately. Lunar motion could be explained more accurately. Their real movement could be shown. Modern missions to the Moon, among other efforts, were informed by that knowledge. A diagram places the Sun, Earth, and the Moon, and it traces each orbit.

6Halley's Comet is named for an astronomer who solved a puzzle of three sightings. The comets of 1521, of 1607, and of 1682 were a single comet. It comes back near Earth every seventy-five years. The next return is projected for 2061. Edmond Halley learned of the calculations Newton had made. A visit followed in 1684. Halley asked Newton to demonstrate the principles at work. What Newton sent was a short essay titled De Motu. The words mean On Motion. Most of the essay concerns how planets move. Newton still thought the account fell short. Force and attraction, across all of nature, were not yet explained well enough. He went on refining both the ideas and the calculations inside De Motu. Two and a half years after that visit, the year 1687 brought his masterpiece. The book carried the title The Principia. Its full name is Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy. It was a landmark. The scientific world was rocked by it. His stature grew in country after country. Three laws of motion are set out in the book. Law one concerns a body, or an object, that is at rest. It stays at rest unless some force acts on it. Floating objects in outer space illustrate the point. No force is acting on them. A second part of the law covers an object that is already moving. Without a force acting on it, the motion continues unchanged. Picture an astronaut throwing an object. The object travels in a straight line. Direction stays the same. Speed stays the same. Change waits on some interfering force. Gravity from a planet could be that force. A bump from space debris could be that force. Resting or moving, an object has inertia. Inertia is the tendency to continue whatever it is already doing. More than one force usually acts on an object. Whether motion starts, or changes, depends on how those forces balance. Equal forces leave a resting object unmoved. They leave a moving object on its same path. Unequal forces start a resting object into motion. They can also change a moving object's speed. They can change its direction.

7A bowling ball and a soccer ball can both be thrown. The throws are not alike. Mass is far greater in the bowling ball. Raise one behind the head, and the thrower might tip over backward. Law two sets out how mass and motion connect. The matter inside an object is what mass measures. Put a great force on an object with less mass, and you get more motion. That extra motion is acceleration. The same force on a more massive object yields less acceleration. Throw a soccer ball and a bowling ball with equal force. The soccer ball goes faster. It also goes farther. Less mass is the reason. Law three states a pairing. Each action is paired with a reaction of equal size in the opposite direction. Daily life is full of examples. Riding a skateboard is one. A foot pushes, and the wheels carry the board ahead. A harder kick raises the board's speed. Forward motion is the reaction. The foot's backward push is the action matched to it. A picture catches a skateboarder demonstrating that third law.

8A chart asks what a person weighs in different places. On Earth the mass is 32 kilograms, or 71 pounds. On Earth the weight is 32 kilograms, or 71 pounds. On the Moon the mass is still 32 kilograms, or 71 pounds. On the Moon the weight is 7.5 kilograms, or 16.5 pounds. On Jupiter the mass is again 32 kilograms, or 71 pounds. On Jupiter the weight is 107 kilograms, or 236 pounds. Mass is not the same thing as weight. Mass means how much matter an object contains. Any object that has mass pulls on every other mass. The strength of that pull depends on the masses involved. Mass itself does not change. Weight does, because weight depends on gravity. Your weight is how strongly Earth attracts you. The Moon's mass is smaller than Earth's. Standing on the Moon, you would feel less attraction. Your weight would drop. Jupiter's mass is larger. Standing there, the attraction would be stronger. Your weight would rise. The chart invites a look at how weight and gravity relate. Some scientists resisted the ideas Newton offered. Many others came to treat them as a great achievement. Young mathematicians flocked to Cambridge, hoping to learn more. Newton turned into something of a celebrity. A friendship grew with Charles Montagu. Montagu later became a powerful politician. Across the next few years, Newton's focus drifted. Politics drew him, and science drew him less. In 1696, Montagu made him Warden of the Mint. Cambridge was behind him by 1701, when he moved to London. Pay for the post was good. Earlier wardens had been less active. Newton oversaw the making of coins in a direct way. Election as president of the Royal Society came in 1703. Knighthood came in 1705. No scientist had been knighted before him. Later years were spent refining Principia. He revised that greatest work. New papers did not appear. Death came in 1727. Wealth and wide fame were his by then. Queen Anne had performed the knighting. A knighthood remains a high honor now. Jousting is not part of it. Armor is not required.

9Theories were only part of Newton's work. Mathematics let him demonstrate how each theory operated. Notes taken with care, and calculations made with care, carried him far. A bookish boy from a village became one of the greatest scientists ever known. He also became one of the most influential. Our picture of the universe was changed for good. Woolsthorpe Manor was once the family home. An apple tree still grows there. Did that tree inspire the gravity theory? Nobody knows. What is known is that he liked to read in its shade.

51. Japan's Quiet Giant

1Ocean wind hits this mountain and is forced to rise. Unusual cloud shapes form because of that. People call one shape a cap cloud. Religious shrines of great importance stand on the land nearby. Cherry blossoms stand there too. Peaceful Mountain Earth's tallest peaks are famous for fierce wind. Cold is part of their fame. Steep cliffs of rock are part of it. Ice is part of it. Visitors often meet a harsh scene. They often meet a scene that does not welcome them. The highest mountain in Japan does not feel that way. Scientists class it as a volcano that is still active. What it offers instead is peace. It also offers calm. For most of each year, snow lies on top. Many people place it among the loveliest mountains known. Lots of people in Japan see more than stone. They see a symbol of the nation. They see ground set aside for worship. Through the past it has stirred human imagination. It still does.

2A national treasure. The summit rises 3,776 meters over the country around it. In feet, that is 12,388. The site is about 100 kilometers from Tokyo, on the southwest side. The same gap is 60 miles. Honshu is the island beneath it. No island in Japan is larger. The Pacific lies roughly 46 kilometers away, or 29 miles. A national park holds the peak at its heart. The park's name is Fuji-Hakone-Izu. Say the name in three beats. First comes FOO-jee. Next comes HAH-koh-neh. Last comes EE-zoo. The park was established in 1936. Landforms shaped by volcanoes fill the park. Hot springs are there. Coastlines are there. Islands are there. During 2013, UNESCO acted. It belongs to the United Nations. It gave the mountain the standing of a World Heritage Site. Protection is part of the standing. Conservation is part of it. UNESCO chose the peak because of its cultural weight for people in Japan. A map shows the location. How the cone was built. Old Fuji erupted and covered Komitake with lava. New Fuji erupted later and covered both older volcanoes with lava. The outline is a cone. Three enormous plates of crust meet here. The Pacific Plate slides underneath the Philippine Plate. Heat farther down melts stone. Volcanic action comes from that melt. A Buddhist legend tells another origin. An earthquake, it says, raised the mountain in 286 bce. The real growth took far longer. The base may be 65 million years old. What people see today grew mainly as lava stacked higher. Hundreds of thousands of years passed during that stacking.

3Eruptions in a span of 2,200 years add up to more than seventy. The greatest blast written down took place in the year 864. Writers mark that year with ce. The latest large blast took place in 1707. A massive earthquake had come less than two months before it. Volcanic ash fell in huge clouds upon Edo. The modern name of Edo is Tokyo. Villages nearby were wiped out. Farmland nearby was wiped out. Famine followed. It lasted ten years. Since then the volcano has stayed dormant. Scientists still judge it active. They look for another eruption someday. The base stretches roughly 50 kilometers from side to side. That width is 30 miles. One side of the crater sits about 500 meters from the other side. That width is 1,600 feet. Japan was hit by a huge quake in the year 2011. Afterward, scientists feared this peak might erupt. When a large quake hits near a volcano, an eruption often is signaled. Gauges recorded more volcanic action. The blast did not arrive. Tokyo is among the biggest cities anywhere, and the volcano is close. Officials put fresh safety measures to work. More than a million residents might have to leave quickly. A new plan lays out that escape. Watching continues with care. A warning system stands ready. Lava would threaten people if an eruption came. Ash riding the wind would threaten them. Hot rocks mixed with gases can rush downhill. That rush would threaten them too. When the sky is clear, Tokyo can see the mountain.

4Plants and animals. Many sorts of plants grow on these slopes. Climb in elevation and the habitat turns colder. Each higher band is colder than the band under it. Temperature helps decide which plants a vegetation zone can hold. The mountainous zone grows several trees. Beech grows there. Oak grows there. Maple grows there. Cedar grows there. Fir grows there. A thick forest fills part of this zone. The forest is Aokigahara. Say ou-kee-gah, then HAH-rah. Another name for it is Sea of Trees. The Asagiri highland is in this zone too. Say ah-SAH, then gee-ree. Grass covers that highland. Cattle ranches use it. At lower altitudes, hemlock grows. Fir grows there as well. Farther up, birch takes over in places. Larch takes over in places. Past about 2,200 meters, trees do not grow. That height is 7,218 feet. Snow is common in the alpine zone. Readings stay under zero. Moss can live there. Lichen can live there. The mountain is home to thirty-seven mammal types. The Japanese serow is one type. It is a goat-antelope. Say suh, then ROHS. Japanese deer live on the mountain. An Asiatic black bear appears only at times. Japanese squirrels show up more often. Foxes show up more often. They occupy many habitats. The range runs from the base to nearly the upper end of the subalpine band. Serows keep to forest in the mountainous zone. Bird types that breed around the base number more than a hundred. Mixed habitats are the reason. A few kinds remain all year. Other kinds migrate through the area. Some live here in summer. Some live here in winter. Amphibians are few. Reptiles are few. One tree frog is part of that small group. Insects reach their peak numbers in the mountainous zone. Many sorts of butterflies are among them. Japanese paradise flycatchers keep to the slopes down low. A male's tail may grow to three times his body length.

5A picture shows a Shinto shrine. The shrine honors this mountain's spirit. A holy sign. Japan holds the peak as its sacred symbol. People have seen a sacred mountain here for as long as Japan has had residents. Near 800 ce, early people built a shrine close to the base. They wanted the shrine to quiet a god. They believed that god made the volcano erupt. Two faiths lead religious life in Japan. Shinto is one. Buddhism is the other. Each faith holds the mountain sacred. Shinto practice says a goddess makes her home on it. She is Konohana Sakuya Hime. Hear the name in parts. Koh-noh-HAH-nah comes first. SAH-koo-yah comes next. HEE-meh comes last. She is goddess of trees when they flower. Cherry blossoms are the sign linked to her. Shrines raised for her sit in more than one place. Some sit at the base. Some sit on the summit. Some sit on the crater floor. Buddhists give the summit a special word, zenjo. The word points to meditation brought into a perfect state. Both faiths treat the climb as important. Worshippers go up as a religious pilgrimage. Where the name came from. Certainty is missing. A folktale from Japan links the peak to life without end. The tale uses fu-shi. Say foo, then SHEE. The meaning is not death. Another trail of thought leads to Fuchi. She was a goddess of fire. Her people were the Ainu. The Ainu are described as Japan's earliest people. Names used in Japan today include Fuji-san. They include Fujiyama. They include Fuji no Yama. San is a word for mountain. Yama is a word for mountain too. Katsushika Hokusai made art from 1760 until 1849. Say kaht-SOOSH-kah, then HAWK-sie. He took the peak as a mark of life that lasts forever. Between 1826 and 1833 he cut a set of woodblock prints. He described the set as thirty-six views. No Japanese artwork is better known. He added ten prints to the set later on. In 1834 he produced a further set. That set holds one hundred views. One print carries the title The Great Wave off Kanagawa. The mountain appears behind the wave. Around the world, that picture ranks with the most famous art ever made.

6Seen from a distance, many people report, the beauty grows. Close up, much of the face is bare rock left by the volcano. Dust lies on it. Climbing the slopes. Tourist sites in Japan rarely draw a bigger crowd than this peak. It may also be the mountain that the most people climb. In a year, climbers can number four hundred thousand. Japanese visitors make up close to two out of every three. Judged by hard mountain craft, the path is not a hard one. Special gear is not needed. Going up feels more like a long backpack walk. It feels less like a technical climb. The challenge is real even so. Rocks cover the trails. Weather turns often. Wind shows up again and again. Pavement reaches the halfway line. Public rides go as far as the 5th station. The station's height is 2,305 meters, or 7,562 feet. Four main trails leave from that point. Hours to the top depend on the trail chosen. The short end is four hours. The long end is ten hours. Descent takes about half the climbing time. Lakes often build a stunning picture, and one view is a sunset mirrored in the water. Climbing is officially open from the start of July, or from mid-July, until mid-September. Trails stay open in that window. Services stay open. Weather is fairly mild. Snow has usually melted. Crowds come with the season. At some points, people have to queue and wait their turn. Winter brings very hard conditions. The advice is to leave winter climbs to people with the deepest experience. Reaching the top is not the only aim. Lakes beside the route please visitors. Shrines please them too. Shiraito Falls is a favorite stop. It is counted with the most beautiful falls in Japan. Mount Tenjo is close. Photographers use it for a fine look at the higher summit.

7Many gifts in one place. Worldwide, the peak stands as a mark of peace. It stands as a mark of calm. Because the volcano is active, it also marks the power in nature. It marks danger as well. For some, a look at the mountain becomes a spiritual moment. Beauty that will not hold still inspires people who paint. It inspires people who take photographs. It inspires people who write poems. Habitats here suit many plants. They suit many animals. Those same habitats draw hikers. They draw people who love wild nature. So many gifts reach so many kinds of people. Little wonder the peak is loved as few places on Earth are loved. Special sights. On a few days each year, the top aligns with the Sun at sunrise. It can also align at sunset. Light flashes in a star shape, and the moment is dramatic. The name for it is Diamond Fuji. Across a lake, the flash can reflect. The reflected pair is called a Double Diamond Fuji. If the Moon aligns with the top, the sight is called a Pearl Fuji. Words to know. Alpine points to high peaks and to whatever lives higher than trees can grow. Sacred points to a god, a faith, or a spiritual aim, and it can mean holy. Altitude is a measure of height, starting from sea level or from the ground. A shrine is a place set apart as a holy honor for a person or for a god. Conservation is care that keeps historical or cultural things, buildings, and sites from being lost. The summit is the highest spot a mountain has. A tourist visits a place in order to enjoy it or to learn about it. Dormant means resting, with the ability to act again. A famine is food falling terribly short across a wide region. A volcano is a break in the planet's crust. A mountain often holds that break, and a crater may ring it. Gases can spill out. Ash can spill out. Lava can spill out. A habitat is the home setting a plant or an animal uses in nature. A pilgrimage is a trip toward a holy site or another site set apart, and a shrine may be the goal.

52. Jupiter, the Planet That Keeps Changing

1Sections of this book follow. A Night of Surprise. Where Jupiter Sits and What It Is. The Stuff Inside Jupiter. A Weather Report. Moons Around the Giant. Rings Around the Giant. Robot Visitors. Watching It Yourself. What Comes Later. Words to Know. A Night of Surprise. A sketch is dated August 7, 1985. Night-sky watching with a telescope is a pleasure of mine. Most objects, I have learned, look the same on every visit. Surprise broke that pattern one night in August 1985. Jupiter was in the eyepiece. A pencil sketch of the planet was underway. Then I noticed the stripes. They are swirly and full of color. They were moving. They were changing while I watched. Excitement from that discovery is still with me. Finishing the sketch grew harder because of it.

2July 1994 brought another change, and again I watched it happen. A comet had broken into big chunks. Its name was Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9. That night was the last night those chunks collided with the planet. Several dark bruises marked the impact spots. I drew those as well. Seeing them through a telescope felt wonderful. Jupiter holds the title of largest planet in our solar system. Night-sky brightness puts it near the top as well. Skip the telescope, and it could pass for a star. Surprises keep turning up. I think no planet is more exciting. A sketch is dated July 16, 1994. Where Jupiter Sits and What It Is. Distance from the Sun is about 484 million miles. That is 779 million kilometers. Earth is five times closer to the Sun than Jupiter is. Counting outward, Jupiter is planet number five. Earth is planet number three. A single trip around the Sun takes Jupiter 12 Earth-years. The distance is that great. Giant of our solar system is a fair title. Diameter across the middle, the equator, is about 89,000 miles. That is 143,000 kilometers. Picture Earth as a small grape. Jupiter would then be a large grapefruit.

3A diagram of our solar system shows Mars, Earth, Venus, and Mercury. The Sun is marked. Jupiter and Saturn are marked. An asteroid belt is marked. Uranus and Neptune are marked. Jupiter's path around the Sun runs between Mars and Saturn. Where does Earth sit compared with Jupiter? One turn on its axis takes Jupiter 9 hours and 55 minutes. No other planet spins faster. A day there lasts only that long. Earth's own spin raises a question. How long is one full turn on its axis? A hint asks how long one day lasts. A note on origins follows. Jupiter formed inside a vast cloud made of gas and of dust. The Sun formed in that cloud too. Every other planet in our solar system did as well. The time was 4.6 billion years ago. A picture shows a younger solar system than ours. Dusty disks orbit the central star. Planets are thought most likely to form in those disks.

4A size comparison lines up Venus, Mercury, Earth, and Mars with the Sun and Jupiter. Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune appear as well. The drawing sets each planet beside the others so sizes can be compared. A question asks how many Earths, set side by side, could stretch across Jupiter. Middle widths and usual gaps from the Sun are listed next. Mercury's middle is 3,032 miles, or 4,879 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 35,980,000 miles, or 57,910,000 kilometers. Venus has a middle of 7,521 miles, or 12,104 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 67,240,000 miles, or 108,210,000 kilometers. Earth has a middle of 7,926 miles, or 12,756 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 92,960,000 miles, or 149,600,000 kilometers. Mars has a middle of 4,222 miles, or 6,794 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 141,620,000 miles, or 227,920,000 kilometers. Jupiter has a middle of 88,846 miles, or 142,984 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 483,780,000 miles, or 778,570,000 kilometers. Saturn has a middle of 74,898 miles, or 120,536 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 890,750,000 miles, or 1,433,530,000 kilometers. Uranus has a middle of 31,763 miles, or 51,118 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 1,784,860,000 miles, or 2,872,460,000 kilometers. Neptune has a middle of 30,775 miles, or 49,528 kilometers. Usual gap from the Sun is 2,793,100,000 miles, or 4,495,060,000 kilometers. The Stuff Inside Jupiter. Earth has a solid surface you can walk on. Not every planet is like that. Jupiter is mostly a huge ball of gases and of liquids. Hydrogen is the main material, as in the Sun. Helium is the other main material. Those two are the lightest chemical elements. Water is present too. Ammonia is present. Methane is present. Clouds of gas make the stripes I saw through my telescope. The stripes are swirly. Colors include reddish, whitish, and yellowish. Zones are the stripes that look bright and wide. They are clouds of gas. Belts are the stripes that look dark and thin. They are clouds of gas too. Belts and zones both travel around the planet. Their winds do not agree. Zones blow from west to east. Belts blow from east to west. A note on elements: they are the simplest materials known. Natural elements number 92. Every other material is a mix of those elements. A note on molecules: nothing smaller still counts as that material or that substance. Atoms are the smaller particles. A molecule needs at least two of them. Water is written H2O. Each water molecule holds two atoms of hydrogen and one atom of oxygen. A drawing labels H, H, and O.

5The Stuff Inside Jupiter. Layers of Jupiter are shown in a diagram. Hydrogen is in the gas atmosphere. Helium is there too. So are methane, ammonia, and water. A ball of rock and of ice sits at the center. Liquid metallic hydrogen is a layer. Liquid hydrogen is a layer. Scientists think these layers stack inside the planet. Under the thin, cloudy atmosphere, gases become liquids. Clouds overhead press down with great weight. Gas molecules are forced very near one another. Molecules sit nearer one another in liquids than they do in gases. Farther down, liquid hydrogen starts to act as a liquid metal. That metallic hydrogen moves through the planet's interior. At the very center, the deepest part, rock and ice may form a core. That core may be bigger than Earth. Scientists are still unsure what the core is really like. A Weather Report. Have you heard today's weather from Jupiter? I heard an average temperature near minus 236 degrees Fahrenheit. That is minus 149 degrees Celsius. The cold is serious. Highest cloud tops can be a different story. Heat might reach 1,500 degrees Fahrenheit on the cloud tops that face the Sun most directly. That is 800 degrees Celsius. Winds today blow out of the north. Speed is about 400 miles an hour. That is 650 kilometers an hour. Hundreds of swirling storms cover the planet. They resemble gigantic hurricanes. Do not get caught in one. Largest of the storms is the Great Red Spot. Its width could hold three Earths side by side. A telescope on Earth can see this storm. More than 300 years of raging have not stopped it.

6Seeing the planet from space is a subject of its own. Many sharp photographs of Jupiter have come from the Hubble Space Telescope. Other planets have been photographed too. Galaxies and other deep-space objects have been photographed. Fine detail is possible because the telescope orbits high above Earth's atmosphere. Photos from the ground can blur because of that atmosphere. A high orbit avoids the blur. The year 1990 is when astronauts set the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit. They rode the space shuttle Discovery. Later shuttle missions added new equipment. Equipment updates left it working as late as 2025. A picture shows that orbiting telescope above Earth. Huge lightning flashes have been reported. They light the storm clouds. Would you pack a picnic for a day like that? Moons Around the Giant. At least 95 moons of many sizes orbit Jupiter. Sixteen of them are more than 6 miles wide. That width is 10 kilometers. Four moons are the largest. Their names are Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. An Italian astronomer found them in 1610. His name was Galileo Galilei. Say it GAL-uh-LAY-oh. These huge moons are known as the Galilean satellites. A pair of binoculars is enough to see them. Ganymede is said GAN-uh-meed. It is Jupiter's largest moon. It is also the largest moon in the whole solar system. Mountains cover the surface. Valleys cover it. Craters cover it. Ice mixed with rock is there too. Callisto is said kuh-LIHS-toh. Many craters cover it. Comets made them when they crashed into the moon. Asteroids made them too. An ocean of salty water may lie under the surface.

7Europa is said yu-ROH-puh. Ice covers the surface. Deep cracks run through that ice. Large chunks are split apart. They resemble icebergs on Earth. These icebergs are the size of cities on Earth. Under the cold, cracked ice, a deep ocean of warm water may wait in the dark. Scientists think alien creatures might live in that ocean, if the ocean is real. Io is said EYE-oh. More than 300 volcanoes mark the surface. Sulfur dioxide gas leaves in hot plumes. Bubbling flows of melted rock shoot out too. That rock is lava. Chemicals in the lava flows paint the surface in different colors. Yellow appears. Red appears. Orange appears. Green appears. A note on those volcanoes follows. Rock and other material pour out of the deep interior in such quantity that Io has turned inside out many times. Loki is one of those volcanoes. Its heat output beats the combined output of all volcanoes on Earth. Sizes and usual gaps from Jupiter come next. Io's diameter is 2,264 miles, or 3,643 kilometers. Usual gap from Jupiter is 262,000 miles, or 421,600 kilometers. Europa's diameter is 1,940 miles, or 3,122 kilometers. Usual gap from Jupiter is 416,900 miles, or 670,900 kilometers. Ganymede's diameter is 3,270 miles, or 5,262 kilometers. Usual gap from Jupiter is 664,900 miles, or 1,070,000 kilometers. Callisto's diameter is 2,996 miles, or 4,821 kilometers. Usual gap from Jupiter is 1,170,000 miles, or 1,883,000 kilometers. A discovery that changed ideas follows. Galileo lived from 1564 to 1642. Many people then believed the planets revolved around Earth. They thought the Sun did too. Those moons were the first evidence against that belief. Not everything moves around Earth. Other scientists grew more willing to accept a different path. The Sun is what Earth circles. The other planets circle it too.

8Rings Around the Giant. Saturn once seemed to be the only planet with rings. From Earth, a telescope can see rings around that planet and no other. Surprise came in 1979. The Voyager spacecraft flew near Jupiter. Rings around the planet showed up in the camera pictures. Four rings showed in those Voyager pictures. They are much thinner than Saturn's rings. Saturn's rings are made partly of large ice chunks. Dust in tiny bits is what Jupiter's rings are made of. The idea is that meteoroids struck the moons. Dust was thrown into space. That dust collected into rings. A craft passing close to this giant planet can see the main ring. Tiny particles that make the ring create a fuzz around it. Robot Visitors. Many spacecraft have been launched toward Jupiter by NASA. NASA means National Aeronautics and Space Administration. The agency belongs to the United States. These robot explorers send pictures back to Earth. Other information rides along. Radio waves carry the reports. Signals that reach a radio ride on that same kind of energy. They carry signals to televisions too. Two craft led the way. One was Pioneer 10. The other was Pioneer 11. Jupiter had never been photographed from so close before those pictures. The years were 1973 and 1974. Those photos showed clouds more colorful than people had believed. The clouds were also more complex. Much of our knowledge arrived from several NASA craft. Pioneer was one. Voyager was one. Ulysses was one. Galileo was one.

9Robot Visitors. Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 made finds in 1979. Lightning was one find. Auroras were another. Auroras are colorful shows of light. On Earth, aurora borealis is the northern lights. Aurora australis is the southern lights. Energy particles leave the Sun and hit gas in the atmosphere. That meeting creates Jupiter's auroras. Big features on the moons were another Voyager find. Volcanoes are among them. Ice is among them. Craters are among them. The year 1992 brought Ulysses near Jupiter. It passed close again from 2003 to 2004. How strong Jupiter's surrounding magnetic field is was one measurement. Charged particles trapped by that field were studied. No spacecraft before Galileo had orbited Jupiter. Circling lasted from 1995 to 2003. The mysterious planet was studied. Its moons were studied. A small probe was released. The probe parachuted into the atmosphere. Instruments measured wind speed. They measured how much of different chemicals the atmosphere held. Watching It Yourself. To the eye, Jupiter could be mistaken for a bright star. Look toward the south in the sky if you want to find it. Only certain times of the year work. Exact place and time can be found in a local newspaper. Check the weather section or the astronomy section. An astronomy magazine can help. A website can help. Binoculars reveal the four largest moons. Night by night, you can watch them change position around the planet. A telescope of medium power shows the belts and the zones. The Great Red Spot shows too. Night follows night, and each of these looks different. Sketching what you see is fun. A certain kind of telescope lets you use a camera instead, and take photos. A chart for March 24, 1997, says rise time is 3:35 a.m. PST. Set time is 2:03 p.m. PST. The horizon is marked E, SE, S, SW, and W.

10A refracting telescope is labeled with its lens and its eyepiece. A reflecting telescope is labeled with its mirrors. Two telescope designs matter most. One is the refracting telescope. The other is the reflecting telescope. A large lens in the refracting kind focuses light rays from an object. The focus is a point inside the telescope. Mirrors do that focusing job in the reflecting kind. Either kind is viewed through an eyepiece. The eyepiece shows you where those light rays meet. What you see is the object, made larger. What Comes Later. A big ball of surprises is a good description of Jupiter. That is why the planet stays exciting. New knowledge about this huge world keeps arriving. The next discovery cannot be predicted. Many new plans aim at Jupiter and at its moons. One plan would send a spacecraft from the United States and from Europe. The landing target is the moon Europa. The craft would melt through the icy surface. Study would turn to the ocean scientists believe may lie inside Europa. Ocean life on this moon might be discovered. Plenty remains to look forward to. Something new about this giant of surprises might someday be yours to find.

11Words to Know. Asteroids are small rocky objects. They revolve around the Sun. An astronomer is a scientist. The subject covers planets. It covers stars. It covers galaxies. It covers other objects in the universe. Learning about whatever is out in space is the field called astronomy. An atmosphere is a layer of gases. It can surround a planet, a star, or a moon. An axis is an imaginary line. A planet, or another object, turns around that line. A comet is an object in space made of ice and dust. Near the Sun, it grows a long, bright tail. Craters are holes in the ground. Objects from space strike and leave them. To find a diameter, draw a straight line. Pass the line through the middle of a circle. Or pass it through the middle of a sphere. Stop where the outside edge is. Around a planet's middle, an equator is a circle that is only imagined. Helium is often a gas. Among chemical elements, only one is lighter. Hydrogen, often a gas, is that lighter element. Around a magnet, or around a planet, a magnetic field is the region where the force reaches. Magnetic force can be felt there. Meteoroids are particles of metal or of stone. They travel through space. An orbit is the path one celestial body follows around a larger one. A planet or a moon can follow that path. The Sun can be the larger body. Electric force and magnetic force make patterns. Those patterns are radio waves. They carry information in radio broadcasts and in television broadcasts. Take the Sun. Add every celestial body that travels around it. That is the solar system. Topics include Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9. Spacecraft listed are Discovery, Galileo, Pioneer, Ulysses, and Voyager. Galileo Galilei is listed. The Great Red Spot is listed. Jove is listed. Jupiter topics cover atmosphere, distance from the Sun, the interior, moons, rings, and size. Telescopes listed are Hubble, the reflecting kind, and the refracting kind.

53. Languages That May Die Out

1A world map marks languages talked about in this book. Mandan belongs to North Dakota and South Dakota, in the United States. Hawaiian belongs to Hawaii, in the United States. Taíno belongs to the Caribbean Islands. Languages of Aboriginal peoples and of Torres Strait Islander peoples belong to Australia. Swahili belongs to the coast of East Africa. Languages of Inuit peoples and of Aleut peoples belong to the United States, Canada, and Greenland. Maori belongs to New Zealand. Languages resemble living things. They grow when people use them to share ideas. They spread. They change. Sometimes a language fades. It can die out completely. The Linguistic Society of America says more and more languages are becoming endangered. An endangered language may die out soon. Anthropologists are scientists who study cultures. They sometimes set endangered languages beside endangered species. Without care and protection, the languages may go extinct. Often only a few elders still speak one. Young people no longer learn it. A chart groups languages of the world by how endangered they are. Fifty-seven percent are safe, or the data are missing. Those languages are not about to go extinct. Ten percent are vulnerable. Adults speak these languages. Children speak them too. Most of that speech happens in one place, such as home. Eleven percent are definitely endangered. At home, the language is not the first one children learn. Nine percent are severely endangered. Grandparents and elders speak it. Parents may understand it. Parents do not use it with one another. They do not teach it to their children. Ten percent are critically endangered. Only a portion of the language remains with some grandparents and elders. Four percent went extinct between the 1950s and 2003, the year the study ended. No speakers remain.

2More than 7,000 languages exist in the world. Linguists are experts on language. They predict that 3,500 languages will die out by 2100. That share is half of every language on Earth. Every two weeks, about one language dies out. Linguists work hard so languages will not vanish. Speakers of endangered languages work hard too. Edwin Benson belonged to the Mandan people. The Mandan are one of three tribes on the Fort Berthold Reservation. North Dakota, inside the United States, is where that reservation lies. Mandan people now live in many communities around the world. Long ago they lived on wider tribal land along the Missouri River. That land is where North Dakota and South Dakota stand today. Benson died in 2016. Part of his people's culture died with him. He had been the last person who spoke Mandan with full ease. The language had been spoken for centuries. Before he died, he helped build Mandan dictionaries. He helped make recordings too. Fluent speakers now teach intense language classes to young students. Linguists hurry to record last speakers such as Benson. They write down what those speakers know. The shared aim is to keep these vital pieces of culture from being lost for good. Languages have faded across human history. They have disappeared too. Sometimes an outside culture conquers a people. Then the losers' language can be wiped out very fast. The Taíno (tah-EE-noh) of the Caribbean Islands are one case. They met the men of Christopher Columbus in the 1490s. Those men had just reached the Americas. Columbus and his men forced many Taíno into slavery. They crushed Taíno traditions. They crushed Taíno culture. They also carried diseases the Taíno could not fight. Millions of Taíno and other native peoples died quickly from those illnesses. Within fifty years, nearly every Taíno person was dead. Almost the whole culture died. Almost the whole language died. People with Taíno heritage still lived on. Some Taíno words entered other cultures. English took in canoe, barbecue, hammock, and hurricane. A rock carving made by the Taíno is called a petroglyph.

3In more recent times, Aboriginal peoples of Australia lost much of their old way of life. Torres Strait Islander peoples suffered the same loss. The first arrival on that continent may date back sixty-five thousand years, researchers think. They formed hundreds of nations. Each nation had its own culture. Each had its own language. In 1788, colonists sailed in from England. Foreign disease soon hit indigenous people in Australia, as it had hit the Taíno. Soldiers killed many of them. Settlers killed many too. Researchers think the indigenous population fell from 300,000 to 75,000. The fall took place within 150 years after the British colonists landed. Outside pressure made languages fade. Old parts of many cultures faded. Some went extinct. Linguists think about 250 indigenous languages were spoken in Australia before Europeans arrived. Today people in Australia use only 60 of them in regular life. From the 1870s through the 1960s, governments in the United States and Canada ran boarding schools. Many Native American children were sent to those schools. Many First Nations children were sent too. The children had to speak English. Speaking a native language brought punishment. At times one culture is assimilated into another. Assimilated means taken in, or absorbed. Outside force can cause the shift. Benefits offered by the other culture can cause it too. The first culture often drops its own language. Money and trade can drive the change. People may gain by using the language of partners they trade with. They may use the language of people they do business with. After a while, that outside language can become everyday speech. Swahili people form a small ethnic community. They live along East Africa's coast. Across the wider region, Arab traders took up Swahili for business. They used it for politics. Other African peoples did the same. As Swahili spread, it picked up many words from Arabic. Kenya has made Swahili its official language. It is the official language of Tanzania. More speakers meant less room for older local languages. The language of the Dahalo in Kenya was pushed aside. The language of the Zaramo in Tanzania was pushed aside. Other languages were pushed aside too. In Kenya, a child reads a book called Brother Rabbit. The book is in Swahili.

4Assimilation from another culture has also changed Hawaiian. Hawaiian is listed as severely endangered. Hawaii is the only state in the United States with two official languages. The two are English and Hawaiian. Late in the 1800s, these islands in the Pacific came under United States control. Bit by bit, younger native Hawaiians shifted to English. English became the daily language of school. It became the daily language of business. A report from the U.S. government looked at 2011. That year, only about 6 percent of Hawaii's people spoke Hawaiian at home. Hawaii then had more than 1.3 million people. Popular culture helped push these language shifts. Modern technology helped too. Young speakers may be hit again and again by music, films, and news. The flood arrives in some other culture's language. The extra pressure wears the endangered language down further. The Internet can also help keep endangered languages from disappearing. Other media can help too. They can share a language with many more people. Today some public schools teach through Hawaiian the whole day. Students in those schools do not start English until fifth grade. Why care if a language disappears? One reason is that words help form who we are. The ideas inside the words do the same work. Language is a deep part of culture. It is a deep part of identity. It ties people to their communities. Speech gives people a way to make sense of the world. When a language vanishes, descendants of its speakers usually suffer. Important pieces of history are often lost. Religion can be lost. Values can be lost. Daily ways of living can be lost. Some ideas cannot be said in any language except their own. Each language belongs to the time and the place that shaped it. Hebrew stopped being a language of daily life almost two thousand years ago. People still used it in Jewish religious practice. They still used it in some writing. During the nineteenth century and the twentieth century, Jewish leaders restored Hebrew as speech. No other dead language has made so successful a return. In some cities, street signs use Hebrew and English together. Shop names do the same.

5Linguists go all over the world to record languages in danger. They write down what they find. They want a record before a last speaker says a last word. Speakers of one language may hold wide knowledge that no other group has. The knowledge can be scientific. It may cover plants of the home region. It may cover animals. It may cover patterns in the weather. Far northern lands have been home to Inuit peoples for many generations. Say Inuit as IN-yoo-it. Aleut peoples have shared that cold region. Say Aleut as A-lee-oot. For most of the year, dark and cold surround them. Their languages hold dozens of words for kinds of snow. They hold dozens of words for kinds of ice. Inuktitut (i-NOOK-tuh-toot) is one of those languages. Central Siberian Yupik (YOO-pik) is another. In Juneau, Alaska, a teacher holds alphabet cards for the Tlingit (TLING-kuht) language. The cards are a tool for teaching this language, which is critically endangered, to new speakers. A boy in Nunavut, Canada, studies letters at a school for Inuit children. Through stories told aloud, Inuit elders passed knowledge onward. Each generation taught the next in a traditional language. That expert knowledge has helped scientists who study climate. They understand better how the Arctic has changed across time. Inuit people can describe ice and snow that used to be common. Those kinds no longer form. They can also tell how shifts in the environment affect animals. Some of these northern languages are endangered now. Researchers want this knowledge kept.

6Most endangered languages today share a few traits. First, they usually belong to a small ethnic group. Second, most are oral languages. People have spoken them, yet writing them down was never a strong tradition. Third, other cultures press on them. Those cultures are often stronger in money and trade. Together, these traits can put a language at risk. Field linguists travel widely to list the languages closest to disappearing. They make recordings of them. Some linguists work on the Enduring Voices Project. Partners include National Geographic Society and Living Tongues Institute of Endangered Languages. Recording a fluent speaker helps protect the range of human knowledge. Researchers want to save vocabulary. They want to save pronunciation. They want to save grammar. A library of materials is how they do it. Linguists record people using the language during ordinary tasks. Someone may sing a song. Someone may cook a meal. Someone may put up a house. From those recordings they build living dictionaries. The pages show how the speakers talk about the world around them. In New Zealand, two children point at a sign written in Maori. That sign shows a place name longer than any other on Earth. Children in many countries take immersion classes, as students in Hawaii do. Communities use the classes to bring an endangered language back. Every lesson is taught only in the language people hope to keep. A Polynesian people native to these islands speaks Maori, and the language is endangered. About 125,000 people speak it. New Zealand has 4.7 million people. Many children now take Maori immersion classes. The goal is daily use of Maori by very young children. If the young learn the language, its chance of surviving is much higher. The film Moana tells of a Polynesian girl. She sets off on a quest over the ocean. In 2017 the film was dubbed into Maori. Local movie theaters showed that version.

7Linguists sit with one of the last people who speak Kanakanavu (kah-nah-kah-NAH-voo). The language is critically endangered. A mountain village in Taiwan's south uses this tribal language. Saving a language means guarding knowledge so it does not vanish. Human experience should not vanish either. Chinese keeps spreading across the world. Spanish keeps spreading. English keeps spreading. That spread makes it harder to stop other languages from disappearing. Linguists know that saving Maori takes more than learning words by heart. Saving Mandan takes more than that. Saving any endangered language takes more than correct sounds. The real work saves a culture. It saves a way of living. That way of living can teach us more about being human. These words help with the topic. Assimilated means drawn into something else and made part of it. Extinct means gone from existence. It means wiped out entirely. Fluent means able to use a language with ease, smoothness, and accuracy. Bombarded means hit by a huge, repeating flood of things, such as questions or complaints. Heritage is a way of life, a custom, or a trait handed down across generations. A culture is a particular society with its own ideas and customs. Immersion is a way to teach a language that is new to the learner. Only that language is used. Documenting means saving notes or photos about what happened. Indigenous means native to one particular place. Endangered means at risk of dying out fully. To preserve is to care for something and keep it for later. Erosion is the wearing away of something. It can also be a slow destruction.

54. Lighter Than Air

1Smoke rises from a fire. A balloon can float away if you let go of the string. You may have seen a blimp over a stadium. Have you wondered why these things float? They float because they are lighter than air. Smoke, balloons, and blimps are all lighter than air.

2More than two centuries ago, Joseph Montgolfier watched a fire. He thought the fire made a gas, and he called it Montgolfier Gas. He held a silk bag over the fire, and the bag rose. Later he and his brother made a cloth and paper bag nearly 12 meters around. It rose over 1,800 meters and traveled more than 1.6 kilometers. Then they sent a duck, a rooster, and a sheep up in a basket. These were the first aircraft passengers. In 1783 two other Frenchmen flew for 25 minutes and landed more than eight kilometers away, but frightened farmers tore the balloon apart with pitchforks.

3The first silk balloons were hot-air balloons. Today the sport is popular, and balloons are safer than the ones the Montgolfiers knew. Pilots use propane burners and change the flame to go up or down. Small balloons of helium or hydrogen carry instruments to study and predict the weather. Larger balloons can reach 37 kilometers or more, almost to the edge of space. They carry equipment to study the atmosphere and to watch objects in space. One research balloon is 176.6 meters across, holds 2.0 million cubic meters, and starts only partly full of helium before it expands. A Boeing 747 is 70.4 meters long, the Goodyear Airship America is 58.5 meters long with 5,740 cubic meters, and the Eiffel Tower is 300 meters high.

4One great challenge was to fly a balloon around the world. Bad weather, fuel shortages, and technical problems ended many flights early. Distance and time records were set, but nobody had circled Earth. In 1999 Bertrand Piccard of Switzerland and Brian Jones of Britain did it in the Breitling Orbiter. Balloons cannot be steered, so they go where the wind takes them. Pilots can change height to find winds that blow in other directions. Soon after balloons were invented, people tried to steer them, and a steerable one is a dirigible. An international balloon contest was held at Aero Park in Chicago on July 4, 1908.

5In 1852 Henri Giffard made the first powered flight and flew 27.4 kilometers. He landed safely in a dirigible driven by his own steam engine. The engine made three horsepower, about as much as a lawnmower. It was too weak to fly against the wind. Almost 40 years later, the gasoline engine gave dirigibles useful power. Count Ferdinand Graf von Zeppelin wanted to navigate the sky the way ships navigate water. A rigid frame covered with fabric would hold the engines, fuel, people, cargo, and gas cells. He chose hydrogen because it is lightest, used it carefully because it can explode, and called his huge rigid airship a zeppelin.

6Count von Zeppelin wanted military zeppelins to serve as scouts and bombers. The military was not interested, so he used private gifts and his own fortune. In 1900 he flew the LZ 1, but it made only three flights. He ran out of money and had to take it apart. Five years passed before he could build again, yet the LZ 1 had proved the idea. Early zeppelins, like the LZ 3, had hangars that floated on a lake. In 1909 he formed DELAG to carry passengers between German cities in comfort with fine food and champagne. By 1914 DELAG had carried more than 34,000 people about 160,000 kilometers with no problems, and the LZ 10 Schwaben made almost 100 flights in 1911.

7In September 1928 an enormous airship was pulled from her hangar. She was named Graf Zeppelin to honor the count, a national hero in Germany. She was 236 meters long, longer than three 747 jetliners and almost as long as the Titanic. In 1927 an airplane had struggled to fly across the Atlantic. A year later she took 20 passengers across the ocean in luxury matched only by the finest liners. In the 1920s many people had never seen an airship or an airplane. They were awestruck by a silver ship the size of a skyscraper and gathered by the thousands. The Graf made regular passenger flights to and from Germany, flew around the world in twelve days in 1929, and helped explore the Arctic.

8She also made the first passenger flights between Europe and South America. The Graf flew until 1937 and was then made into a museum. When World War II began, the Nazi government melted her down to make fighter planes. She landed at Lakehurst, New Jersey, after her flight around the world in 1929. A number of countries issued stamps that showed the Graf Zeppelin. In the 1930s the U.S. Navy had two flying aircraft carriers, the Akron and the Macon. They carried small airplanes that could be launched and recovered in mid-air. A hook on the wing met a trapeze that lowered the airplane through an opening.

9The opening was in the bottom of the airship. The plane started, unhooked, and flew off, and the return reversed those steps. Some planes had their wheels removed because the pilots landed so well. Bad weather and human error lost the Akron and the Macon, and the Navy kept smaller blimps. The Graf inspired the luxurious Hindenburg, 245 meters long and still the largest flying machine ever. She began service in 1936, designed for helium but filled with hydrogen. Helium was scarce, and the United States, the only country with enough, refused to sell it to Nazi Germany. Despite a careful crew, she burst into flames while landing in a storm at Lakehurst in 1937. People blamed hydrogen, but new evidence suggests the flammable fabric, and passenger zeppelins ended.

10After World War II, most people lost interest in big airships. Ocean liners were less expensive, and airplanes were getting bigger and faster. The fiery Hindenburg crash made people afraid to fly zeppelins even with helium. But people never lost interest in lighter-than-air flight. Goodyear blimps, like Spirit of Goodyear, are probably the most famous airships. In the 1930s Goodyear teamed with the Zeppelin Company for navy ships and ads, and it has not stopped. Millions see them each year, and Fuji Film and Metropolitan Life use blimps too. The Zeppelin NT is for patrol, exploration, ads, and travel, and after almost 70 years you can buy a sightseeing ticket over Germany.

11The Zeppelin NT can take off for these flights. Other companies have started to build airships as well. Lockheed Martin has the Hybrid Airship for very heavy and bulky cargo. It can pick up a load at the factory and drop it where it is needed. This helps places that do not have decent roads. The P-791 Hybrid Airship can lift more than 450 metric tons. First came hot-air balloons, then steerable dirigibles that grew bigger, better, and safer. Dirigibles still fascinate and excite people 150 years after they were invented.

12There is no such thing as Montgolfier Gas. The brothers did not know about density. When fire heats air, the molecules spread apart and the air becomes less dense. It is lighter than the air around it, so it rises. Wood floats in water because it is less dense than the water. A hot-air balloon floats because the hot air is less dense and lifts the passengers too. Hydrogen and helium are also less dense than air, so people used them in balloons. Hydrogen can lift more than helium, but it is very flammable.

55. Lives Spent Making Peace

1What you will meet in these pages starts with an opening. Wangarĩ Muta Maathai comes next. Nelson Mandela follows her. Martin Luther King, Jr. has a part after that. Óscar Romero is included as well. Mairead Corrigan and Betty Williams share the part that comes later. A peacemaker's work that can be yours is set out after those lives. Further paths appear near the end. Words to know finish the book. Opening. Someone who makes peace tries to bring wars to an end. Conflicts are part of that work. So are disagreements that split people, groups, or countries. Respect for this work is wide. Argument about it can be wide too. A peacemaker may refuse to choose either side. That refusal stirs debate and can make the person controversial. Violence can reach these people. They can be victims of attack. Belief itself has cost some of them their lives. Awards for this work are many. None is better known than the Nobel Peace Prize. The pages ahead follow several people who labored for peace. A Nobel Prize reached many of those lives. Each year the world gives this international prize. The giving started in 1901. The money that comes with it is 1.3 million dollars. Winners divide that sum into equal shares. The prize also includes a medal made of gold. A diploma comes with it too. Money, medal, and diploma together honor a life spent working to end conflict.

2One picture catches Wangarĩ Muta Maathai as she sets a tree into the soil. Wangarĩ Muta Maathai was born on April 1, 1940, in Ihithe, a village in Kenya. Teachers saw a gifted student. A Catholic boarding school invited her to study. She quickly rose to the top of her class. After graduating, she went to the United States and earned two biology degrees. When she returned to Kenya, she earned a Ph.D. from the University of Nairobi. She was the first East African woman to earn a Ph.D. She was deeply interested in the health of the environment. Her education helped her see problems and find creative solutions. Deforestation means humans removing too many trees. She knew it was harming the environment. Streams dried up. Crops died off. Desert spread into areas that had once been healthy forest. Her husband won a seat in Kenya's Parliament. He had promised jobs for more Kenyans. She formed a plan that would answer both problems at once. The new work would heal the land and give people jobs. A 2005 picture shows her planting in Kenya. U.S. Senator Barack Obama stands with the group. Tree planting was the work she created. Seeds went into the ground all over the country. Women made up most of the hired planters. People called the effort the Green Belt Movement. The goal was a green belt, a strip of trees, along a line 8,000 kilometers long. That distance is about 5,000 miles. The tree line was meant to push back a desert on the move.

3Planting was not the last task of the Green Belt Movement. Maathai felt that passing laws to protect the environment was important. The movement helped with voter registration. It demanded changes in government. Members protested actions that would harm the land. Police arrested and beat Maathai many times. Supporters were arrested and beaten too. They were trying to stop people from selling public land or building on it. The protesters knew that building on forested land meant removing more trees. That clear reason kept them going. Protest continued. In 2004 she became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. She was also the first environmentalist to win it. Cancer ended her life in 2011. A picture shows her beside others as they take up worries about Kenya's environment. Nelson Mandela was born on July 18, 1918, in Mvezo, South Africa. At birth he was named Rolihlahla Mandela. He took the name Nelson when he was in school. Law was his study. Politics became his active work. Late in the 1940s, South Africa put a system in place and called it apartheid. The sound is ah-PAR-tide. Races were kept apart. Contact between people who were not white and people who were white had to stay limited. Political power did not belong to the first group. Native Black people formed 75 percent of the population. Their schools were poor, or they had none. Their houses were poor. Servant work or laborer work was all that most of them could get. A picture shows Nelson Mandela.

4A Black political group had Mandela's labor for many years. Apartheid was the enemy. Peaceful protest was answered with violence. A ban from the government stopped the group's protests. Mandela decided that violence must be met with violence. He helped form a new military wing. He helped obtain weapons for it. Arrest came in 1962. Prison followed. A life sentence arrived in 1964. Other countries pressed South Africa to give up apartheid. Inside the nation, Black people and white people led protests against the system. F. W. de Klerk was president, and he was a white man. He started a path toward ending apartheid. More than twenty-five years had passed in prison. Freedom then came from de Klerk. One picture returns Mandela to his former cell on Robben Island. The year of that visit is 1994, four years after release. Another picture, from 1990, shows de Klerk at the left, walking beside Mandela. The two men worked together to change the government of South Africa. Elections arrived in 1994 because of them. Every citizen could take part, a first for the country. Race was no longer a block. Both men received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993. The honor was for opening elections that were free and fair to every South African. April 1994 made Nelson Mandela president. He was the first Black person in that office. He understood the office as a chance to lead the country toward full equality of races. A new constitution was written under his lead. Law took it up in December 1996. Advisors around him came from every race, and he was known for that. Plenty of white South Africans had fought the idea of political power for others. Many of those people changed their view because of him. Death came for Nelson Mandela in 2013, at the age of 95.

5Martin Luther King, Jr. was born on January 15, 1929, in Atlanta, Georgia. School trained him as a minister. One reason was a belief he held. Leaders in Black churches, he thought, ought to direct the movement against discrimination. Southern cities of the United States were segregated in that era. Separation kept Black Americans away from white people. Treatment marked them as inferior. White people forced Black people to use separate bathrooms. Separate water fountains were forced on them too. Voting was not allowed. A try at the polls brought intimidation. A picture shows him addressing his Montgomery congregation. From that congregation in Montgomery, Alabama, he asked people to fight discrimination. Joining a civil rights group was part of the ask. The group is the NAACP. Those letters stand for National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. Voting was the other ask. Police, in 1955, arrested Rosa Parks, a Black woman. Her seat on a bus in Montgomery was one she would not surrender to a white man. King backed what she had done. He led a boycott of the city bus system. A boycott means you will not use something, and the refusal is how you make your point. A lawsuit grew out of the boycott, and the NAACP filed it. Alabama's segregation laws were declared illegal by the U.S. Supreme Court because of that case. After the boycott, a picture shows Rosa Parks on a bus that is integrated. People then counted King as a central civil rights leader in the United States. Speeches of his moved listeners so far that some treated him as leader of the Black population of the nation. More Black citizens got onto voting rolls with his help. Restaurants were integrated with his help. Active life as U.S. citizens, for all Black people, was the goal. Violence was sometimes aimed at him. Arrest happened. Prison happened. Threats against his life happened. Quitting was not his choice. Violence was not his answer. July 1964 is when President Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act. From then on, segregation was a federal crime.

6A picture shows him delivering the speech people tie to a dream. The Nobel Peace Prize of 1964 was his. It honored resistance to segregation that stayed nonviolent. Memphis, Tennessee, was the place on April 4, 1968. A white man fired the shot that killed him. Tribute came in 1983 from the U.S. Congress. The third Monday of January became Martin Luther King, Jr. Day. Listeners still hold words from August 28, 1963. He spoke of holding a dream on that day. In the dream, sons of people once held as slaves could sit with sons of people who had owned slaves. One table would hold them as brothers. Óscar Romero was born on August 15, 1917, in El Salvador. A Catholic family raised him. Age 13 is when he entered a special high school aimed at the priesthood. Studies continued in San Salvador once high school ended. Graduation made him a priest. A picture shows the clergy collar he wore. Rutilio Grande, priest and friend, died at the government's hands in 1977. Speech about human rights had made leaders dislike Grande. They feared that people seeking rights would put the government's power at risk. The death shook Romero. Poverty became something he spoke against. Social injustice became something he spoke against. Other human rights violations, killings by the government among them, became something he spoke against. His urging was that people keep teaching love and not grow weary of it. Love, he said, is the force able to overcome the world. The Violence of Love is the book that carries those words.

7Several military dictatorships seized power across the following years. Control of the government sat with the military. People of El Salvador struck back at military control. Out of that fight came the Salvadoran Civil War. Opponents of the dictatorship were hunted by the military. They were killed. Only government-approved words could appear in the newspapers. Radio carried Romero's speeches instead. He spoke the names of the missing. He spoke the names of the harmed. He spoke the names of the killed. A target was what that honesty made him. Reliable news of the war still reached Salvadorans. Print was closed to that news. A picture places Archbishop Óscar Romero in a gathering at the Church of Divine Providence. San Salvador is the city. 1979 is the year. March 1980 brought a speech about whose orders to follow. God's orders, he said, mattered more than orders from government or from military leaders. Soldiers were asked to lay weapons down. They were asked to refuse orders that broke human rights. A shot killed him once the speech was finished. Sainthood came from the Catholic Church in 2018. Another picture shows him sending a mass out over the air in March 1980. Death followed not long after.

8Mairead Corrigan was born on January 27, 1944, in Belfast, Northern Ireland. Betty Williams was born on May 22, 1943, in that same city. Their childhood fell in years when the Catholic Irish Republican Army, the IRA, killed people and spread terror. Driving the British from Northern Ireland was the aim.
