Protestant groups replied with the same kind of violence. Both sides lost hundreds of dead. Thousands more were injured. August 1976 is when Betty Williams met Mairead Corrigan, after a crash. An IRA member's car swung out of control. Protestant troops backed by the British had shot him. Loss of control sent the car into a family. Corrigan's sister was the mother, and she was hurt. A niece of Corrigan was killed. Two nephews, both young, were killed. Betty Williams witnessed the crash. She vowed to do whatever she could so peace would return. A petition was her start, calling for the fight to stop. Television, the day after the crash, carried Corrigan's criticism of IRA violence. Two nights after that, television showed Williams talking about her petition, and Corrigan saw it. A phone call invited Williams to the funeral. About 10,000 women followed the two of them in a protest demonstration. The graves of the victims were the destination. Friendship followed. Feelings about violence in their country bound them. An organization, they decided, could help build peace in Northern Ireland. Ciaran McKeown, a popular journalist, joined them. Peace People is the group they founded. A booklet was written and handed out under the title The Price of Peace. Marches were organized under the name of peace. The marchers numbered in the thousands. A picture shows Betty Williams. Travel took Corrigan and Williams through countries across the world. Peace for Northern Ireland was their message. Their lives drew threats. The goal still held them steadfast. Summer 1977 was ending when violence tied to the conflict in Ireland had fallen past the halfway mark.

9The Nobel Peace Prize of 1976 went to Williams and to Corrigan. Work with Peace People did not stop. Survivors of attacks got help. Victims of violence got help. Rallies raised money. So did other fundraising. Communities in areas struck by poverty could rebuild buildings that bombs had broken. Millions of dollars went into the programs. One of those programs brought terrorists to hand over weapons. Further awards for making peace reached both women. March 17, 2020, is the day Betty Williams died. A picture shows the two women on a peace march. A peacemaker's work for you. The world grows better where peacemakers work. Your effort can do that too. Arguments among friends are a place to start. School is a place to start. Your community is a place to start. That is how a person becomes a peacemaker and changes something. Student conflicts can grow into violent feelings. Violent actions sometimes follow. Peer mediation programs exist in some schools. Students with training guide the others toward working out differences. Talk, plus respect, can settle a conflict, and people learn that. Solving stays in the students' own hands. Friends who practice talking through trouble practice keeping peace.

10A picture shows students in peer mediation finding a peaceful compromise. Starting such a group begins with a teacher willing to help. Training in mediation usually comes first for the teachers. Volunteers then supply a small set of student mediators, either chosen or nominated. Training for most middle school mediators runs 12 to 15 hours. Conflict gets a definition in that training. Communication is practiced. Listening is practiced. The role of an effective go-between is practiced. An argument gives teachers a choice to offer. One path is a peer mediator. The other path is the principal. Students always decide. Those who pick mediation sit with a trained student guide. Compromise is what the discussion teaches each person. A meeting can run like this. First the mediator asks if the students in the argument want the problem solved. A yes sends all of them to a spot reserved for solving problems. A no from one student, or from both, means mediation cannot go on. Agreement is required. No name-calling is allowed while the problem is solved. Interrupting is also off limits. Truth-telling is required. Each person tells what took place. Each person tells how it felt. Both are asked for fixes. A fix that both can like is the search. Congratulations from the mediator close the meeting. Time and energy go, for many people, into standing against war. Injustice draws that same effort. Others may be inspired by you to act as peacemakers. Every effort, whether large or small, leaves the world more peaceful. Results that show up. Do the programs work well? Some schools say far fewer students are suspended because of fights. One survey found success in the eyes of more than 8 middle schools out of every 10.

11Paths for more reading. The Nobel Peace Prize is one subject worth following further. Peer mediation programs are another. Terms inside this book, and the words defined below, can guide a search. Students sit together in one picture, using peer mediation. Problems get discussed. Compromises get found. Words to know. Apartheid is the South African policy that was unfair to anyone outside the white population. Discrimination is unfair treatment of people. Mediation is a way of settling differences between people or between groups. A boycott is refusing to join in something so that a point gets made. Protested means gave voice to strong disagreement or disapproval. A congregation is people gathered as a church group. Segregated means split along lines of race. Controversial means the cause of much disagreement. Threatened means in danger of being harmed. Violations are times when laws are broken or rules are not followed. Demanded means asked for in the tone of a command. Dictatorships are governments seized by a leader the people never approved.

56. Macedonia's King of Many Lands

1A map shows Alexander's empire at its largest in 323 BCE. Macedonia and the Caspian Sea are named. The Black Sea, Taxila, and Asia Minor are named. The Hydaspes River, Persia, and Babylon are named. The Mediterranean Sea, Alexandria, and the Persian Gulf are named. The Euphrates River, India, and Egypt are named. The Nile, the Red Sea, and the Arabian Sea are named. Both the empire and a route of exploration appear. More than 2,300 years ago, Macedonia, a Greek state, was the birthplace of a prince. Power came later, when that prince was king. People came to call him Alexander the Great and the greatest leader yet seen. Nations and kingdoms fell to him, some near Greece and some far away. Violent oppression was one of his methods. Forcing his culture onto defeated people was another. Education had been deep. A hunger for knowledge had grown in him. Empire and power were goals. Curiosity, some historians think, also pushed him. No Macedonian before him had gone so far, and he wanted to pass that mark. Parts of Europe, Africa, and Asia would lie inside his kingdom. A birth in Macedonia opens this book. Training for leadership follows. Kingship follows that. A journey, the conquest of Asia, and a legacy close the account.

2King Philip II, Alexander's father, is where the story starts. A son usually receives a king's title from his father. Philip did not wait for that path. He took the throne from a young nephew. Macedonia's king was the result. A strong will, plus a fierce army, put Macedonia under his control. Greek states around it came under his control as well. Olympias, Alexander's mother, held a firm plan. Her son, she decided, would be king someday. Her own place would be safe if he were. The year 359 BCE is when Philip II became Macedonia's king. Affection from Olympias was lavish. She told Alexander the crown would be his. Eighteen years was how long the horse Bucephalus stayed with Alexander. Drive for power came to Alexander from both parents, and much of his later greatness grew from that inheritance. Intelligence showed early. At age twelve, a beautiful but nervous horse was refused by his father. Alexander saw the cause. The horse feared its own shadow. Turning the head away from the shadow calmed the animal. Control came easily after that. Riding came easily too. Bucephalus was the horse's name. Say it byoo-SEF-uh-luhs. For the rest of Alexander's life, this horse mattered deeply.

3Philip was often gone while Alexander grew up. Tutors and teachers were hired to ready the boy for kingship. Horse riding and hunting were part of training for young noblemen of Greece. Swords, javelins, and bows were part of it too. Hard battles lay ahead for Alexander and his boyhood friends. Readiness was required. Manhood tests of Macedonia were passed as he grew. A wild boar was killed by him. A man was killed by him in combat. A philosopher named Aristotle became one of his teachers. Knowledge brought Aristotle respect. Culture became something Alexander could understand and value, with Aristotle's help. Art became something he valued too. Science, philosophy, history, politics, and ethics were all taught. Love of reading was sparked. Love of learning itself was sparked. Stagira, Greece, is Aristotle's birthplace, and a statue of him is displayed there. Much of Asia was held by the Persian Empire. Greece counted Persia as an enemy. Greek cities in Asia Minor had been destroyed by Persia years before. Control of the area had been taken. Philip wanted a war with the Persians. Regaining control and conquering Asia were his aims. Leadership duties started while Alexander was still young. A small revolution was stopped by him at sixteen, during a time Philip was away. While still a teenager, he led soldiers during battles his father was fighting. Kingship was the future he was raised for. Then Philip took another wife. Pure Macedonian blood was not Olympias's. A baby with the new wife could change the line. She was Macedonian. Alexander might lose the place of chosen heir. A daughter was born to the new queen in 336 BCE. Philip was killed not long after that birth. Soon afterward, Alexander's mother had the baby killed. The baby's mother was killed as well. The crown was then Alexander's. His father's army was rallied at once. Conquest of Asia was his wish, as it had been Philip's. A strong army was not enough. Support from the people was needed too.

4Macedonia had the backing of most Greek city-states. Philip had never won the approval of some of them. His son in charge did not calm that wariness. Fighting back could block Alexander's plans. Rule over Greece could be denied. Conquest of Persia could be denied. Support from many Greek states was still gained. Persuasion was the tool. Force often traveled with the persuasion. Opposition remained in some Greek states and in territories around Macedonia. Rebellion was their wish. The army crushed them. Mercy was not Alexander's way as a leader. Rebels were made into an example. Some were killed. Others were sold into slavery. Submission of every Greek city-state was locked in by that extreme punishment. A year after he became king, he was ready to push farther. Macedonian control beyond Greece was the aim. A map of the region names the Black Sea and Macedonia. Pella is named, and so is Asia Minor, then part of the Persian Empire. The Aegean Sea, Thebes, Delphi, Corinth, and Athens are named. The Mediterranean Sea is named. Some of the strongest capitals of the Greek city-states appear on that map. Equipment was added to strengthen the troops. Body armor, shields, and helmets were included. Daggers and enormous spears were included. Cavalry numbers were increased. Foot soldiers were sent in a tight formation called a phalanx. Cavalry would go first. Enemy soldiers still standing would be crushed by the phalanx. Vision could be shared, and troops could be rallied, because Alexander led with strength. Example was his method. Battle always found him in front of his men. Rough moments found him beside them. Instincts were sharp. How to attack, when to attack, and where to attack were clear to him. Spring of 334 BCE was when he left for Asia Minor. Turkey is the modern name of that land. A spear thrown into the ground was his bold claim on the land. Tight groups in the phalanx held thousands of his soldiers. About sixteen rows of men made each phalanx. Spears were often 6 meters long, or 20 feet.

5The first fight with the Persian army came soon, at the Granicus River. Darius III, the Persian king, was absent from the lead. Training was strong on both sides. Foot soldiers and cavalry served both armies. Preparation favored the Macedonians. The Persians fell. An hour of bloody fighting nearly cost Alexander his life. The army then moved along the Aegean Sea. Greek city-states were taken back. Resistance was met with brutal fighting. A larger Persian army met him in 333 BCE at the Battle of Issus. Darius was present this time. The hard fight still ended in a Persian loss. Darius got away. Failure to capture him left Alexander frustrated. South was the next direction. Cities along the Mediterranean Sea were the way he hoped to take the Persian fleet. Syria and Lebanon are those lands today. Surrender came from some cities. Tyre refused in 332 BCE. Seven months of resistance followed. Brutal defeat came at the end. The Mediterranean coast was the path after Tyre fell. Later that same year, 332 BCE, he reached Egypt. Power was given up by the Persian who had ruled Egypt. Egyptian religion was treated with respect. Egyptian governors were appointed. Welcome was what Egypt gave him. Plans for a city called Alexandria were started. Other parts of the Persian Empire in Asia lay to the east, and he moved that way. The year 331 BCE took him east of Asia Minor. Iraq is that region today. The Battle of Gaugamela was where he met Darius. A larger army had been rebuilt by Darius. Alexander's army overpowered it. Defeat sent Darius running. Much of his army ran too. Deeper movement into the Persian Empire followed. Cities were conquered. Persian ways were explored. Darius was still the man he hoped to catch. A different man killed Darius in 330 BCE, before Alexander arrived. That killer was later executed by Alexander. King of Persia was the title people then gave Alexander. A mosaic from ancient times shows Darius fighting Alexander at the Battle of Issus. Far from Macedonia, daily life began to change. Persian customs were taken up. Two local princesses became his wives. Low bows, the Persian form of honor, were what he began to expect from Macedonians. Many Macedonians disliked the new behavior. Other soldiers copied him. Persian women became their wives.

6One writer is the final source of most of what is known about Alexander. Callisthenes was that writer, a Greek who worked for Alexander. Absolute fact is not what his stories can be treated as. Another telling deserves a thought. Enemies who fought Alexander might have described the same events differently. War's consequences are passed over lightly by Callisthenes. Results of the conquests are passed over lightly too. A fully positive view of Alexander was not his constant stance. Disagreement with Alexander led to the writer's untimely death. Exhaustion had taken the army. Farther east was still the direction Alexander persuaded them to take. India was the name he knew for the lands ahead. Pakistan and Afghanistan are those lands today. Porus, a leader who resisted, was fought in 326 BCE. The Hydaspes River was the meeting place. Say it hy-DAS-peez. Elephants were used in battle by soldiers of this area. Some harm to the Greeks was done by Porus's elephants. Panic took the elephants when the fighting grew too intense. They pulled back. Surrender was Porus's choice. No later battle of Alexander's was as large. Unrest among the soldiers was great. Farther travel could not be won from them. Turning back was the agreement. Babylon was reached. A fever struck him in the spring of 323 BCE. June of that year was when he died there. Power and exceptional leadership both belonged to him. Europe, Asia, and Africa all held parts of his empire. Savagery belonged to him as well. Close to 750,000 people were killed under his rule. Control of people and land was not the whole of the conquests. History of each place was explored. Customs were explored. Around 100 BCE is when the Alexander mosaic was made. A painting from about his own lifetime is what people believe it copies. Later leaders took him as a model, generation after generation. Knowledge of the places he reached was opened. New religions were learned. New governments were learned. Greek ways were forced on conquered people. Later conquerors followed that pattern. They seized lands and pressed their cultures onto Indigenous peoples. Alexander the Great is the name he carries. People he defeated did not see greatness in him. Fifteen years of conquest passed without a lost battle. No military genius the world had seen could match his abilities.

7Years of Alexander's life and wars can be set on a timeline. The scale marks 360 BCE and 320 BCE. Birth in Macedonia came in 356 BCE. Bucephalus became his horse in 344 BCE. Aristotle became his teacher in 343 BCE. A revolt on Macedonia's eastern border was stopped by him in 340 BCE. Philip was killed in 336 BCE, and Alexander became king of Macedonia. Persia was entered in 334 BCE, and the Battle of Granicus was won. Persians led by Darius were defeated at the Battle of Issus in 333 BCE. Tyre was captured in 332 BCE, and Egypt was invaded and welcomed him. Darius and the Persians were defeated at the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BCE. Darius was killed in 330 BCE. Central Asia was still being conquered in 327 BCE, and India was entered. Porus was defeated at the Battle of Hydaspes in 326 BCE. Death in Babylon came in 323 BCE. Words from his story are gathered here. Cavalry means soldiers who fight from horseback. It can also mean soldiers who fight from armored vehicles. City-states are cities, or urban areas, that behave as countries of their own. Destined means set ahead of time, or sure to happen. Ethics are moral rules that steer how a person acts. Executed means killed, above all as punishment for a crime. Inherited means traits or characteristics, including genetic ones, received from parents or earlier ancestors. Javelins are long spears thrown in sport, in hunting, or in war. Persuasion is convincing someone else to believe a thing or to do a thing. A philosopher looks for knowledge and truth about life, or studies that search. Rallied means gathered for a purpose. To rebel is to fight, in an active way, against a government or an authority already in place. Submission is giving in to another person's power, or the state of having given in.

57. Machines You Steer from Afar

1A father and his son share a car that is steered from a distance. The picture shows them enjoying that car together. The book starts with a new record. Next comes the start of radio control. Basic parts of the hobby follow. Cars on four wheels have a section. Racing has a section. Flying has a section. A later section looks at where the technology may go. A word list ends the book. Jet engines power some aircraft that are flown by radio. The picture shows one of those aircraft. Niels Herbrich runs through a preflight checklist. His airplane is a red jet. The wings sweep back. This jet is not an ordinary one. A car trunk is big enough to hold it. An airliner is only a little faster. Herbrich is not an ordinary pilot either. His feet stay on the ground the whole time. The engine begins with a hum. Moments later the sound becomes a whine that hurts the ears. Flame bursts out. The jet skids over the grass. Then it races upward. Whoosh! A handheld radio remote control is how the pilot steers. The jet rolls. It also turns. Top speed reaches 440 miles per hour. That is 708 kilometers per hour. A world speed record now belongs to Herbrich. Helicopters, trucks, cars, boats, and planes have all been radio-controlled toys. Children have played with them for decades. Adults have too. Herbrich’s jet is faster than most of those machines. The fun, though, is just as real.

2In 1898, Nikola Tesla showed a boat that radio could steer. It was the first machine of that kind in the world. Tesla deserves the credit for that first radio-controlled machine. A lightning storm was under way when he was born. The year was 1856. He grew up to be an inventor. Work he did with electricity gave later people ideas. Radios grew from those ideas. Radar did too. Robots did too. As a young man, Tesla pictured a boat under the control of radio waves. Those waves are ripples you cannot see. They travel in the air. They are a form of electromagnetic radiation. The experiments led him to a famous hall. The hall was Madison Square Garden in New York City. The year of the show was 1898. Curious people in the crowd were shocked. They were also delighted. Radio itself was still unknown to most people. Tesla’s show came years earlier. A transmitter he had built at home sent the commands. The commands were a series of radio signals. The craft floated in a big tank. The tank had been built for the show. Silent orders from Tesla made the small boat travel. It moved around the tank in a graceful way. Audience members asked math questions. Blinking lights carried the answers. Shock held the crowd. Some people said Tesla was steering with his mind. Some said the show was magic. Some guessed a trained monkey was hidden in the hull. The show became front-page news. A toy was not Tesla’s goal. He wanted the U.S. Navy to buy the device. He hoped it could guide torpedoes through the water. The Navy never made that purchase. The technology did get some use later. One period was World War I, from 1914 to 1918. Another was World War II, from 1939 to 1945. In those years, radio control fit large machines best. Electric motors needed bulky equipment. The batteries were huge too. The year 1947 changed that picture. The transistor was invented then. A transistor is tiny. Even so, it makes an electric current stronger. Engineers used transistors to make electric motors smaller. Some builders even placed transistors inside radio-controlled toys. A new hobby had begun.

3Robots, boats, and many other vehicles now run by radio. People have created hundreds of types. The mechanics are not all the same. The basic technology is shared. A transmitter sends the radio signals. People also call that device a remote control. The signals travel on one chosen frequency. A receiver sits inside the vehicle. It watches all the time for the transmitter. The signals get decoded. Electric current then goes to the motors. Those motors move the vehicle and steer it. Batteries power the transmitter. Batteries power the receiver too. Radio is a kind of electromagnetic energy. Visible light is that same family of energy. Radio energy moves as waves you cannot see. The waves pass through the air. They also pass through most walls. Wave size changes the form of this energy. Frequency changes it too. Frequency means how many waves pass in one second. Some radio waves are longer than a football field. Some are about as long as a person. Their frequency runs from 1 million waves each second to 100 million. Light is electromagnetic energy as well. Microwaves are too. X-rays are too. Those forms have much shorter wavelengths. Their frequencies are much higher than radio. An early radio-controlled model car was a Ferrari P4. The model was built at one-tenth scale. It was among the first cars of this kind ever made. An Italian company called El-Gi created it. The year was 1969. Toy makers started selling radio-controlled cars in the mid-1960s. Cars sold today are smaller. They are also more powerful. Gasoline can power them. Electricity can power them. A fuel called glow fuel can power them too. Drivers nickname that mix nitro. It is a high-performance fuel mixture. Basic cars in many toy stores cost little. They are easy to maintain. Serious drivers buy hobby-grade cars instead. A price in the hundreds of dollars is common. Kits let many people build those cars. Every part arrives boxed together. Drivers can swap parts. They can paint the body. They can add accessories. Bigger engines go into some kit cars. Bigger motors go into others. Ready-to-run cars are a different choice. Those cars are also called RTR cars. They arrive already assembled.

4Three cars powered by nitro race around a track in one picture. The cars are at the top. Off-road buggies appear below them. The buggies catch big air on jumps. The event was a national contest for radio-controlled cars. It took place in Kingsville Township, Ohio. The date was August 10, 2013. Kit cars and ready-built cars come in many shapes. They come in many sizes too. Touring cars are one group. Ford Mustangs are among the models. Chevy Camaros are among them. Porsche 911s are among them. Off-road vehicles are popular. Large tires come with them. Heavy-duty shock absorbers come with them too. Almost any ground will do. Uncut lawns are fine. Vacant lots are fine. Dirt fields are fine. Some of these vehicles look like classic monster trucks. Some look like sporty pickup trucks. Some look like buggies. Racing is the favorite part for some owners. Friends may race in a vacant lot. They may race in a park. Other drivers enter organized contests. The tracks can look like real speedways. Organized classes sort the cars in several ways. Size is one way. Class is another. A kit-built car is marked apart from other cars. Power source is marked too. An electric motor is one source. A gasoline-powered engine is another. Touring cars form one racing class. Sports cars form another. Off-road vehicles form another. Some of those are two-wheel drive. Some are four-wheel drive. Some contests are straight-line races. A drag strip is a usual site. An airfield is another. Oval tracks with a closed course are used as well. Truck-pulling and tractor-pulling events are among the most exciting off-road meets. The trucks drag sleds. A light sled is 35 pounds. A heavy sled is 100 pounds. That is 16 to 45 kilograms. The load is like an average-sized bulldog. It is also like a German shepherd. The letters RC can also be written R/C. Either form can mean remote-controlled. Either form can mean radio-controlled. A wire may link some remote-controlled vehicles to a controller. Most modern ones do not need a wire. They send messages on radio frequencies.

5Radio-controlled planes did stunts at a contest in 2009. Bob Motta lives in Danbury, Connecticut. He remembers the moment the flying hobby took hold. The time was the 1960s. His first radio-controlled plane was an F4 Corsair. It was a replica of a Navy plane from World War II. Motta is 66 now. World War I models are what he mostly pilots. The progress of these planes amazes him. Electronics got much smaller, he says. After that, the hobby really took off. Sky time is the joy for many hobbyists. The aircraft might be a plane. It might be a blimp. It might be a helicopter. Most new pilots start on training planes. People call those planes trainers. A trainer is meant to be simple. It is meant to make flight easy. Foam is a common building material. Foam keeps the plane light. A crash is less likely to wreck it. Computer networks now link some radio-controlled cars. A driver can use a wireless connection. A smartphone can be the controller. A tablet can be the controller. Wireless computer networks already speak in radio waves. That is why these systems work. Some vehicles use the link to a computer for extra jobs. One example is the Rover Revolution. It looks like a robot. It rolls on four wheels. Two cameras are on board. A microphone is on board. A speaker is on board. The driver can watch video. The driver can talk. The driver can listen. All of that happens while the rover moves.

6A pilot who can handle a trainer often moves on. The next step is often a sport plane. Complicated aerobatic maneuvers are possible in those planes. A special wing design is common. Flying upside down is easier with that wing. Motta has heard from pilots of real 747s. They told him model airplanes are harder to fly than real planes. The model pilot must stay on the ground. Every sense has to be used. Whatever goes up has to come down. Replicas of war planes are a favorite for many pilots. The real planes flew in World War I or World War II. Hobbyists call the models warbirds. Some come as kits. Some come as RTF models. Germany’s three-wing war plane is one popular warbird. The real aircraft flew during World War I. Pilots can also build a plane of their own. Motta recalls spending hundreds of hours on one plane. A crash does not end the parts. He saves every piece that is not damaged. Those pieces become spares for other planes. Almost-Ready-to-Fly planes are sold today. People shorten that name to ARTF. Motta compares the build times. An older project could take two hundred hours. An ARTF plane can be ready in about twenty. The finished plane, he says, can look respectable. It can look good too. A boy in China flew a mini helicopter in 2013. He steered it through an obstacle course. The flight was part of a contest. A plane already takes skill. A helicopter asks still more of the pilot. Mini helicopters make the first lessons easier. Indoor practice is especially helpful. The small craft still teach many skills. Those skills are needed for bigger helicopters. Quadrocopters have another name. People also say quadcopters. Four blades spin on them. They can fly in every direction. An autogyro looks partly like a plane and partly like a helicopter. A propeller pulls or pushes the craft forward. The propeller may sit at the front. It may sit at the back. Blades on top are not powered. Forward motion makes them spin. The spin keeps the autogyro in the air.

7A delivery drone in the form of a quadcopter appears in a test. It carries a package. Radio control is not only a children’s game. Pilots can sit miles away and fly drones. The basic technology is the same. The jobs are many. A remote-controlled drone may already have crossed your neighborhood. Some farmers hang cameras on drones. They look for insects that eat crops. Hospitals have used drones to carry human organs. The flight takes an organ to a team that will transplant it. Package delivery is another new use. Some companies have started that work. Television crews use drones at big events. Athletic events are covered that way. Entertainment events are covered that way too. A hundred years ago, this power seemed like magic. It is quickly becoming part of ordinary life. Playing with it is still a blast. Aerobatic describes hard or thrilling moves an aircraft makes in flight. A remote control is a handheld device. It can run something from far away, such as a television or a toy. Drones are aircraft or ships with no crew on board. A person operates them from somewhere else. A replica is a copy of something. Electromagnetic radiation is energy that travels as electromagnetic waves. Shock absorbers are parts tied to a vehicle’s wheels. They make a rough surface feel smoother. To maneuver is to move something around or guide its motion. A transistor is a small electronic part. It controls how electricity flows in a device. Mechanics are the details of how a thing works. Miniaturization means designing or building something at a smaller size. A transmitter sends out electromagnetic signals. Radio signals and television signals are examples. A receiver detects those signals. It turns them into sound, pictures, or some other form.

58. Manhattan's Record-High Tower

1Visitors like the long look from the high deck of the Empire State Building. Later pages follow a landmark that reaches into the sky. They follow two partners who made a winning team. They follow a hotel cleared away until a hole remained. They follow workers who became the city's favorite sight. They follow a rush toward the top. They follow the claim that Al Smith had been right. Useful words are explained at the end. Manhattan Island holds the tower near its center. New York City is the city around that island. Five states can be seen in a span of five minutes. The way to do it is to go to the top of this tower. The observatory offers an awesome view. New Yorkers take delight in it. Travelers who come from every part of the world take delight in it too. Construction years were 1930 and 1931. After that, the tower was a landmark known in many countries. Forty-one years passed while no building on Earth stood taller. No other skyscraper kept that height title for so long. Manhattan's skyline still shows the tower standing high.

2Strange science comes with height this great. Views that take the breath away come with it too. During one summer, a scientist made a film of lightning hits. The count of those hits was forty-eight. The film and the count showed the tower working as a giant lightning rod. Sunrise reaches the roof about a half hour sooner than the street. LED lights at the crown are driven by computers. Sixteen million colors are available to those lights. Night light shows can be seen for many miles. People at that distance can enjoy the shows. The building's height is the reason. On a clear day, walking the observation deck reveals parts of five states. Looking out to the horizon is how a person sees them. First comes New York. Then comes New Jersey. Then comes Connecticut. Then comes Massachusetts. Pennsylvania is the fifth. A map of this lookout includes the Atlantic Ocean. About 80 miles (129 km) is as far as the view can reach. Measured to the tip, the tower is 1,454 feet (443.1 m). The observation deck on floor 102 sits at 1,250 feet (381 m). The observation deck on floor 86 sits at 1,050 feet (320 m). Offices fill 2.7 million square feet (250,838 sq m). The whole structure weighs 365,000 tons (331,122 mt). One nickname calls it the world's most famous office building. Another nickname calls it America's favorite building. The Seven Wonders of the Modern World include it. The base measures 79,288 square feet (7,366 sq m).

3One photo places Alfred E. Smith on the left. John J. Raskob stands on the right. Low-income families were the start for both men. Later life still held great achievements for each of them. The world's tallest building was what these two friends chose to construct. Each boy had grown up in a New York family with little money. That likeness gave the pair much in common. While they were young, both left school. Finding work was the reason they left. Their families needed support. By 1929, wealth had come to Raskob. Open chances in those years helped him. Hard work helped him as well. Rich friends stood around him. Those friends would put money into the skyscraper as an investment. Smith grew famous because he ran to be president of the United States. The contest ended in a loss. He talked very well. The press received exciting stories about the building from him. Side by side, the two men made a winning team. They had already picked the ground they wanted. A problem came with that ground. The Waldorf-Astoria Hotel already occupied the spot. The team purchased the hotel. Opening year for the Waldorf-Astoria was 1893. No hotel in New York was bigger at that time. None was more luxurious either. Pulling the grand hotel down was hard. Its size was one cause. Another cause was a plan that the hotel should endure across a long span of time. Demolition was the job of some six hundred people. They kept working through the day. They kept working through the night. An enormous hole was dug next. Solid bedrock was the depth they had to reach. The massive skyscraper would rest on that rock. Digging and blasting carried the crews downward. The bottom lay 40 feet (12.2 m) under the street. Dump trucks, a whole fleet of them, carried off the diggings. Those loads numbered 28,529. Earth filled the loads. Stone filled them too. So did what remained of a hotel that had once been proud. Barges waiting on the East River took the loads. Tugboats moved the barges toward the ocean. Out there, the loads were dumped. When five months had passed, a gaping hole was all that was left.

4Huge cranes shifted giant beams into position. April 7, 1930, was the first day of construction. A skyscraper presses hardest at its base. Vertical columns were set in that low part. The columns numbered 210. Each one weighed 44 tons (39 mt). Beams that ran across came after the columns. Crews joined those beams to the columns. A strong grid of steel was the result. People on the ground stopped as the grid climbed. Sidewalks filled with the crowd. Their eyes stayed on the steelworkers. Those workers kept their balance on beams that were narrow. Newspaper reporters named this the city's best show. The papers gave the men a nickname, sky boys. Danger was so great that sickness changed the day. A crew of four went home together if even one man was ill. Men on a crew had to know one another fully. They had to trust one another fully. A stranger stepping in could make the work unsafe. Rivets were the fasteners that locked the steel beams. The heater made each rivet red hot. Coals that burned in his bucket did the heating. He then threw the rivet through the air. The catcher dropped it into the hole waiting in the beam. The bucker-up pressed one end of that hot rivet. A metal bar was the tool he used. The riveter struck the opposite end. An air hammer delivered the blow. The enormous beams were then bonded tight. Crews from the Mohawk Nation did this job best. These Native people were from New York State. They could place one rivet every minute. Water boys also walked those high beams. Some of them were only sixteen years old. Buckets of cool water for drinking went with them to the crews. A few thought beam work would be fun. They learned a strict habit very quickly. Eyes had to stay on the beam end under their feet. A look downward was not allowed. Mohawk ironworkers had a name for pride. They had a name for bravery too. These Native people lived in New York or nearby. Downtown Kahnawake was home for more than 800 Mohawk. Say that name as gahnah-WAH-geh. A restaurant sign there honored the workers. The words were The Greatest Ironworkers in the World Pass Through These Doors. One picture shows a Mohawk ironworker setting a girder on a New York building site.

5Smith and Raskob wanted the skyscraper finished in a great hurry. Investors could earn nothing until tenants were paying rent. Speed guided every plan. Speed even guided the design. William F. Lamb was the architect. Art deco was the style he selected. That modern look was popular then. Machine-made parts suited it. Parts that arrived ready for use suited it too. Holes for rivets were already drilled in the steel beams when they arrived. Floors therefore rose at an incredible pace. Four-and-a-half floors were added every week. By summer the grid of steel had climbed to floor forty. The outer wall was gaining on it. The outer wall's design was made for building in a rush. Columns of windows went up. Columns of metal plates went up beside them. Columns of stone went up as well. Each of those pieces came ready to set in place. Higher on the tower, crews closed in the outside at one floor a day. Inside jobs continued while the outside climbed. Plumbers were among the inside workers. Electricians were among them. Carpenters were among them. August swelled the workforce. More than 3,500 people could be on the site during one day. More than sixty kinds of jobs were filled. Pipe was required by the plumbers. Bricks were required by the bricklayers. Supplies were required by every worker. In that era, wheelbarrows moved the supplies. A building so large made wheelbarrows too slow. Tracks were laid as the answer. The tracks circled each floor. They even ran inside the elevators. Supplies, once delivered, went straight into big carts. Workers shoved the carts along the tracks. Elevators carried the carts upward. Crossing a floor was then quick. Injuries came often with so many people working. The builders put a hospital of their own inside the building. Autumn found the crews on the tower's smaller upper floors. The work then moved faster.

6Hours of labor for the whole job came to 7 million. Steel that crews set and riveted weighed 57,000 tons (51,709 mt). The windows numbered 6,400. Limestone set in place measured 200,000 cubic feet. That volume is 5,663 cubic meters. Bricks set in the walls numbered 10 million. Plaster put on the surfaces weighed 10,000 tons (9,072 mt). Radiators put in numbered 6,700. Sinks and toilets put in numbered 2,500. Pipe put in stretched 51 miles (82 km). Elevators put in numbered 67. Their shafts stretched 7 miles (11 km). The finished building weighed 365,000 tons (331,122 mt). Some smaller floors near the top rose at a pace of one floor a day. Lunch turned into a problem because the crew was huge. Too many people wanted food at the same time. Workers began returning late. The builders would not allow lateness. Late returns slowed the job. Cafeterias on the site were the answer. The first sat on floor 3. Another sat on floor 9. Another sat on floor 24. Two more opened as the tower grew. Floor 47 received one. Floor 64 received the other. The contractors, who were the builders, had a schedule they were meant to keep. They kept it. They planned each part of the work. They also recorded each part. They counted the bricks that went in. They measured the plaster that went on. Plans this careful can make a smooth job seem certain. The job was not fully smooth. One idea failed in a huge way. Al Smith wanted airships to stop at the spire. That spire rises above floor 86. Dirigibles is another name for those airships. At the time, they were seen as the modern way to travel. His plan for passengers was simple. They would leave a dirigible by walking down a plank. They would step onto floor 102. An elevator would take them down. Fifth Avenue would be only minutes away. The plan sounded wonderful. The first airship drew near the mast. Wind at the mast was too strong. Wind around this skyscraper is always that strong. The airship idea was abandoned. Thousands of watchers stood in the street for one failed try. Columbia was the dirigible they saw. Taking mail off the roof was beyond what it could do. The year of that try was 1931.

7Special holidays bring shows of light to the building. A new system of LED lights makes the shows. Sixteen million colors belong to that system. May 1, 1931, was the day the doors opened. The first steel columns had gone in a little over a year earlier. How fast the world's tallest building went up set a record. That record still stands. Landmark status arrived just after the fiftieth birthday. The law says the appearance must stay as it has always been. On the skyline of New York City, people still notice this most famous office building. Smith said the tower had been made for generations still to come. He was absolutely right. An architect is someone who designs buildings. Demolish means to destroy a thing completely. The thing is usually a building or another large object. Art deco is a bold style. It belongs to decorative art, to design, and to architecture. Its time is the 1920s and the 1930s. Strong lines mark the style. Geometric shapes mark it too. To invest is to place money in a business chance. A later profit is the hope that chance offers. Rivets are small pieces of metal. They clamp things together. Barges are boats whose bottoms are flat. They carry freight. A canal or a river is where they usually go. A skyscraper is a building of great height. Bedrock is the solid rock layer under the ground's surface. A spire is a pointed crown. A tower or another building can have one. Steel is a strong metal. Iron and carbon are what it is made from. Cafeterias are rooms where meals are served. The serving happens at a counter. To construct is to make a thing. It can also mean to build that thing.

59. Maria Tallchief, Star of American Ballet

1On September 29, 1999, an awards ceremony took place in Washington, D.C. The honor was the National Medal of Arts. A president of the United States gives this medal. It is the highest honor that president gives to one artist for outstanding achievement. The artists who receive it come from many fields. Those fields include music and visual art. They include singing, writing, and filmmaking. Maria Tallchief was one honoree that year. She was a tall, elegant dancer. Half a century before the medal, she had shaken the world of ballet. She became the first Native professional ballerina. She was also American ballet's first prima ballerina. The tale starts on Oklahoma land set aside for Native peoples. When she won the medal, she joined a very small group of artists. The parts of her story move from her early years to New York, where a star was born. They then turn to her years in Chicago as a master teacher. They close with the legacy she left.

2Quiet and shy describes Betty Marie as a girl. Her birthday was January 24, 1925. Elizabeth Marie Tall Chief was her full name. People nicknamed her Betty Marie. She belonged to the Osage nation. Speakers say that name as OH-sayj. Fairfax, Oklahoma, on the Osage Reservation, was her birthplace. In the Osage language, the family was called Ki He Kah Stah Tsa. Her father was Alexander Tall Chief. He was full-blooded Osage. Osage land yielded oil while Alexander was still young. Those profits brought wealth to many members of the tribe. Grown up, Alexander held a large amount of property in Fairfax. Ruth Porter was the name of Betty Marie's mother. Ruth's family were low-income settlers. They had come from Scotland and Ireland. Ruth saw a musical gift in Betty Marie. She saw the same gift in Betty Marie's sister, Marjorie. Ruth encouraged both girls to develop that gift. She arranged piano lessons for them from an early age. She arranged dance lessons too. In 1933, Betty Marie was eight. Her mother decided the girls needed more chances to learn. Their father agreed that chances in Fairfax were limited. Los Angeles became the family's new home. Lessons in dance were arranged for the girls before any house was bought. Ballet was one subject the sisters learned at that school. They studied tap dancing. They studied tumbling. They studied acrobatics. They studied Spanish dancing. A picture from 1930 shows Betty Marie on the left and Marjorie on the right. Their mother stands with them. Before long, the sisters were performing at rodeos. They also performed at county fairs. Their shows included a staged Native dance. They wore feathered headbands. They wore buckskin costumes. They wore bells. They wore moccasins. The dance made both girls uneasy. It was not authentic. It stressed stereotypes many people held about Native peoples. In ceremonial Osage dances, only men are active dancers. Women make a ring around the dancing men. Those women step a short way sideways, then return. They move in time with the drumbeat. Ceremonial Native dances were against United States law while the sisters were growing up. Grandma Tall Chief regularly led the girls to Osage ceremonies. Those dances went on in secret. The yearly Osage In-Lon-Schka dance still continues. It is no longer secret. Photography is not permitted.

3Vaslav Nijinsky's sister was Madame Bronislava Nijinska. He was one of the greatest male dancers of the twentieth century. Speakers say her name brah-nuh-SLAH-vuh nuh-JIN-skuh. Betty Marie was twelve when her father gave her a short order. She should follow one star. He insisted that she pursue piano or dance. He did not want her to pursue both. Choosing dance was something she wrote about later. She wrote that dance was the true start of her life. Madame Nijinska accepted Betty Marie as a pupil not long after that choice. Nijinska was her first important ballet teacher. Betty Marie studied with her from 1937 until 1942. Power in movement was one lesson of those years. She learned grace. She learned feeling. When high school ended in 1942, she felt sure this art was her path. She later explained her choice in her own book about her life as America's prima ballerina. She loved music. She felt that music grew inside her. Her hands on an instrument could not show it in the same way. The music ran through her body. During her teen years, ballet was still a young art inside the United States. Russian dancers were the only famous ones in ballet then. A Russian troupe, Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo, performed this art. Speakers say that name ROOSS DU MOHN-tee KAR-loh. The company toured the world. People all over the United States met ballet through this company's tours. The company was based in New York. Los Angeles saw the company arrive in 1938. Betty Marie attended all of their performances. She was amazed. In her final high school year, the company's leader watched her dance. He recognized her talent. New York was her destination once she had graduated. Several dance companies rejected her. Hiring came at once from Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo. Her professional career began without an audition. She then took the name Maria Tallchief.

4Two years after Tallchief joined the Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo, George Balanchine began creating dances for that company. He had studied ballet in Russia. Many people count him among the most important choreographers of the twentieth century. Classical ballet was graceful and flowing. Balanchine built on that base. American ballet gained a fresh style from his work. The new style asked dancers to be very strong. It asked them to be quick. It asked them to be streamlined. It asked them to be athletic. Balanchine's choreography came alive through Tallchief's dancing. She became his muse. A muse is a person's greatest source of inspiration. Each of the two artists respected the other's gift. They married in 1946. The marriage itself went on for only five years. They kept working together for decades. They practiced ballet for as long as fourteen hours a day. In 1948, Balanchine worked as a visiting choreographer for the Paris Opera Ballet. France was where she traveled with him. She became that company's first American dancer. The next year, Balanchine helped found the New York City Ballet. Plenty of people in New York felt no need for a ballet company based in America. They changed their minds when they saw Tallchief dance. The ballet was Balanchine's Firebird, in 1949. That role made Tallchief famous. New York City Ballet's first prima ballerina was Tallchief. Thirteen years was how long she kept that title. She held it until 1965. Tallchief later wrote about dancing in Firebird. She compared the roar inside City Center to a stadium just after a score.

5In 2006 she spoke at a diversity celebration held by the Producers Guild of America. She said a wish to move and to dance seems born into American Indian people. She said this is the way they are. She said they show happiness in dance. She said they show sorrow in dance too. Some of Balanchine's loveliest roles were made with Tallchief in mind. Those roles included parts in Swan Lake. They included parts in Scotch Symphony. One part was a sugar-plum fairy in the ballet called The Nutcracker. Her Sugar Plum Fairy helped ballet win more fans across the United States. During her years there, she traveled on tour with New York City Ballet. The tours reached nineteen different countries. She also danced on television. The film Million Dollar Mermaid gave her a brief part as a ballerina. That film came out in 1952. American Ballet Theatre also invited her to dance as a guest. Erik Bruhn partnered with her in Swan Lake. He partnered with her in many other ballets. Wherever she performed, audiences covered her with praise. Those audiences kept asking to see another performance. The reviews from critics were full of strong praise. They praised her strength. They praised her musicality. They praised her technical precision. Tallchief had a fiery presence on stage. Her steps were light. She danced in a regal way. She also danced in a free way. That combination made her unlike the other dancers. She never failed to speak her mind. People respected her intelligence. They respected her honesty. In Balanchine's Swan Lake, her part was the Swan Princess. She publicly rejected unfair images of Native people. She supported the nonprofit group America for Indian Opportunity. A 1965 talk with the Des Moines Register let her explain her art. She said a ballerina receives steps and then makes them her own. One shared role still changes, because every dancer adds something of her own. As an American, she believed in great individualism. She said that was the way she was brought up.

6In 1965, Tallchief was forty-one. She grew tired of performing. All the trips her work demanded wore her out as well. Her marriage to Henry Paschen had taken place nine years before that move. He was from Chicago, Illinois. They had a daughter together. Tallchief retired from dancing. She moved to Chicago so she could give time to her family. Chicago Lyric Opera Ballet made her its creative director in 1975. The year 1980 was when she started the Chicago City Ballet. She believed a major ballet company belonged in Chicago. She led that company, in the creative role, through 1987. A number of students she taught later built strong careers in ballet. Her only child, Elise Paschen, danced beside her in Chicago. After she stopped performing, she also worked to keep Balanchine's dances as he had made them. He died in 1983. She felt strongly that dancers should perform his ballets as he first intended. Tallchief and several other dancers from his companies filmed parts of those ballets. Future students could learn from those recordings. In 1996 she was added to a national hall that honors women. People know it as National Women's Hall of Fame. That hall honors extraordinary achievements by women. The same year, she received a Kennedy Center award. This prize honors artists who have given outstanding things to the culture of the United States. Chicago was the city. The date was April 11, 2013. She was eighty-eight. People around the world honored the life she had lived. They also honored the work she had done. A timeline of her life marks 1925 as the year of her birth on January 24. It marks 1933 as the move to Los Angeles with her family. It marks 1937 as the start of dance lessons with Madame Nijinska. It marks 1942 as her high school graduation. In that same year she left for New York City and entered Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo. It marks 1944 as the year George Balanchine joined that company. It marks 1948 as the year she joined the New York City Ballet and became its first prima ballerina. It marks 1949 as her performance in Firebird. It marks 1956 as her marriage to Henry Paschen. It marks 1959 as the birth of her daughter, Elise. It marks 1965 as her retirement from performing at age forty-one and her move to Chicago. It marks 1980 as the founding of the Chicago City Ballet. It marks 2013 as the year she died in April.

7In the United States, Maria Tallchief broke a new path. The United States had never had a prima ballerina before her. A fresh style of ballet drew inspiration from what she did. Professional ballet had not had a Native star before her. She opened its doors to ethnic groups that had been underrepresented. Grace was one gift she used to push ballet ahead. Her talent helped too. Her achievements helped as well. A fellow dancer, Jacques d'Amboise, once spoke about her. Speakers say his name ZHAHK dahm-BWAHZ. He said one word fit her. The word was grand. He said she was absolutely grand. In 1964, she and Jacques d'Amboise performed at the White House. The event was a state dinner. In 1999, President Clinton gave her a National Medal of Arts. He said she had taken an art form from Europe and made it belong to America. In his view, it was right that a Native American woman was the one who did it. An achievement is an accomplishment reached through effort. Inspiration is a good influence. It can spark a creative idea or a creative act. An audition is a tryout performance by an actor, a dancer, or a musician. The performer hopes to win a new role or position. Being exact, or accurate, is what precision means. A reservation is land where the United States once compelled Native peoples to live. Authentic work follows an original or traditional form. Such work is not a false copy. A stereotype is a too-simple picture of a group, and that picture is often unfair. Those images are often unfair or untrue. Ballet is a form of dance. This dance joins exact formal steps with set movements. A choreographer chooses the style of a dance. That person also arranges the steps and moves. A streamlined form can slip easily through water or through air. A trailblazer is the first person to do something new. That person inspires others to follow. To be inducted is to be chosen as a member of a group.

60. Microbes: Friend or Foe?

1Air from a sneeze may go as fast as 120 kph (75 mph). A sudden sneeze is often the first sign you are getting sick. You may cough, feel tired, and have a sore throat from a tiny germ. Long ago, every sickness was a mystery, and people often died from mild infections. Doctors and medical schools did not exist, and some people feared a witch's curse. Doctors often used leeches to treat illnesses. No one knew what caused illness or how to prevent or treat it. Now we know many microbes can make us sick.

2Microbes are tiny living things that you can see only with a strong microscope. They ride in the air, cling to surfaces, sit on skin and shoes, and hide in our bodies. They multiply fast in our cells, the small living units that help us grow and stay healthy. We have blood, bone, stomach, skin, and muscle cells, and some microbes can cause disease. Flu virus, strep bacteria, protozoa, and yeast fungus are different kinds of microbes. Louis Pasteur proved that contact with harmful microbes causes disease. Heating sealed food kills many organisms, and this process is called pasteurization. Milk is heated to 145 degrees Fahrenheit for 30 minutes, or to 163 degrees Fahrenheit for 15 seconds.

3The immune system protects us from harmful microbes. It is made of cells, glands, and tissues that work together. Some microbes can double every 20 minutes. The immune system remembers which microbes cause trouble and how to fight them. If you had mumps or measles, you are unlikely to get that sickness again. One drop of blood holds 7,000 to 25,000 white blood cells. Some make antibodies, and others surround a microbe and destroy it. Skin shields us, so clean and bandage cuts, and white blood cells hunt germs in the blood.

4Bacteria live everywhere, even in barren ice and extreme heat. Some are good, and some are not, and they outnumber other living things. Some eat milk sugar and make lactic acid, which turns milk into yogurt or sour cream. Good bacteria in the intestines help digest food, and we could not live without them. Strep bacteria can cause a sore throat, fever, swollen neck glands, and white spots of pus. Scientists grow these bacteria in a gel dish so they can study them. Harmful bacteria on raw food, hands, or food surfaces can cause food poisoning. Cooking to the right heat kills many of them, and salmonella causes many cases.

5A virus can invade cells and spread fast from cell to cell. Some viruses can cause death, and a virus can change so the immune system misses it. The flu, chicken pox, HIV, and the common cold are caused by viruses. An influenza virus may be shown at 295,000 times its real size. Scientists study using viruses to slow cells that grow out of control, as in cancer. A cold usually has no headache and little or no fever. The flu often brings a headache, chills, and a fever of 102 to 104 degrees Fahrenheit. Both can cause coughing, but muscle aches and tiredness are more sure with the flu.

6Some fungi look like plants, but tiny fungi can cause ringworm and athlete's foot. Ringworm makes an itchy red ring on the skin. Athlete's foot makes the skin on feet and between toes itch, crack, and peel. Protozoa often live in dirty water and can cause nausea, vomiting, and mouth infections. Malaria is a protozoa disease from a mosquito bite, and it kills hundreds of thousands each year. Most infections spread by contact with a sick person, or through saliva, blood, and mucus. Rabies can come from dogs, raccoons, or skunks, and salmonella may be on chickens, birds, fish, or reptiles. Mosquitoes can pass West Nile virus, sick birds can pass avian flu, and ticks can pass Lyme disease.

7One sick person can infect dozens, and those people can infect hundreds more. People can infect others before they feel sick, and a healthy carrier can be hard to find. An outbreak is a small group in one place with the same disease. An epidemic spreads fast to many people, and a pandemic spreads around the world. Buses and airplanes carry germs, so a local outbreak may not stay in one place. A vaccine helps the body recognize and fight a disease-causing microbe. Smallpox carried to the Americas killed nine out of ten people in the largest Native cities. About two hundred years ago, Dr. Jenner saw that cowpox patients did not get smallpox.

8Dr. Jenner thought cowpox and smallpox were related, like cousins in one family. He believed a weak case of cowpox could protect people from deadly smallpox. Healthy people volunteered, got mildly sick, and then got well. While they were sick, their immune systems learned how to fight the pox microbe. Those people did not later catch deadly smallpox, and his idea saved thousands of lives. He is credited with stopping smallpox around the world. Vaccines can be given by mouth, as nasal sprays, or as shots. About seventy-five years later, Louis Pasteur made weak microbes into vaccines such as the flu shot.

9Some microbes kill other microbes without harming healthy cells or helpful microbes. They make antibiotics, strong medicines that attack only the targeted infection. The strongest microbes may survive by changing, or by resisting an overused antibiotic. Scientists keep trying to make new antibiotics for deadlier microbes. In 1928, Dr. Alexander Fleming found that a bread mold could kill bacteria. That discovery led to penicillin, still the most widely used antibiotic. When you are sick, stay home, rest, and do not share cups, plates, or food. Cover a sneeze with a tissue or your arm, throw tissues away, and wash your hands.

10Eat fruits and vegetables, drink water, breathe fresh air, exercise, and get enough sleep. Wash knives and boards after raw meat, and do not let raw meat touch cooked food. Skip dented or swollen cans, and do not eat food that has fallen on the floor. Eighty percent of diseases spread by touch, so wash with soap for twenty seconds. Brush and floss, see a doctor each year, and get all of your shots. Do not touch wild animals, use insect repellent, and drink only purified, chlorinated water. Vaccines and antibiotics come from more than two hundred years of medical research. We cannot erase every harmful microbe, but we can learn how to stay healthier.

11Antibiotics are medicines made from microbes to fight infection in the body. Contaminated means something was made unsafe or unusable. An epidemic is the rapid spread of a disease in a community. Eradicate means to destroy something completely. To mutate is to change in a lasting way. Organisms are living things, such as people, animals, and plants. A microscope is a device used to view tiny objects. Invading means entering in a forceful way to weaken or injure.

61. Napoleon and the French Empire

1By 1812 the French Empire stood at the height of its power. A map of that year marks the French Empire. It marks French allies and French enemies. It also marks countries under French control. Napoleon orders French troops across the Neman River. The order sends them to invade Russia in 1812. Napoleon Bonaparte ruled France. He felt sure of himself. He stands among the most notable military leaders in history. By 1810 he had taken control of much of Europe. Many armies had marched against him. He had beaten most of those armies. He had built an empire in Europe. The empire was not going to last. In 1812 he chose to invade Russia. Trade linked Russia with Great Britain. Great Britain was the main enemy of France. Russia was about to join the British against the French. Napoleon wanted to guard his empire. Blocking that alliance meant marching his huge army into Russia. He saw little reason to doubt a victory over Russia. The choice would become the greatest error of his career.

2Corsica was his birthplace in 1769. The island is French and lies in the Mediterranean Sea. His family belonged to the Italian nobility. France had taken the island from Genoa, an Italian republic, one year before his birth. The family remained on Corsica after the takeover. He attended grade school on Corsica. Two army schools in France gave him later training. In 1785 he finished school as an army lieutenant. France's people rebelled against the king in 1789. The French Revolution brought the monarchy to an end. Kings had ruled France for centuries before that break. The Revolution stood on several ideals. One ideal was brotherhood among all male citizens. Another was freedom from unfair treatment by the government. Many people believed the Revolution would improve France. Early in 1793, revolutionaries killed King Louis XVI. His death opened a bloody stretch called the Reign of Terror. In that stretch, Queen Marie Antoinette was executed. Many other powerful nobles were executed too. So many officials died that France lacked strong leaders. The gap let an ambitious man picture himself in charge. Napoleon believed he was that man. Toulon was where he went in 1793 to battle British troops. Toulon is a city in the south of France. Great Britain and other nations in Europe wanted the Revolution stopped. They wanted the French monarchy restored. They feared revolutionary ideas would spread. Those ideas might threaten their own kingdoms. Napoleon forced the British out of Toulon. The victory made him a general. He was twenty-four. A picture shows his campaign with troops in northern Italy's Piedmont region. Some people inside France also wanted the kings brought back. These royalists started an uprising in Paris in 1795. The Directory called on Napoleon to stop it. From 1795 to 1799, France was led by a small circle of men called the Directory. After he succeeded, the Directory put him at the head of France's army. In 1796 he married Joséphine de Beauharnais. Say the last name BOH-ar-nay. She was a widow. She had two children. Her first husband had been a general. He was killed during the Reign of Terror. France already knew Napoleon's skill in command. His ambitions grew larger. He set out to control the whole nation.

3Napoleon went on winning battle after battle. The Directory's 1796 order sent French troops under him into Italy. The task was to push Austrian armies out of the country. Italian armies were to be pushed out too. He won a run of battles. He took Italy for France. He came home to France as a hero. Two years later, in 1798, he led a small army into Egypt. He hoped to cut Britain's commerce with the Middle East. He won several fights in Egypt. Then ships of the British navy beat a French fleet at the Battle of the Nile. The loss blocked his plan to move the army over the channel into England. In 1799 he overthrew the Directory. He made himself first consul of the republic. He took the powers of a dictator. In 1804 he placed the crown on his own head and became emperor. France had only recently thrown off its kings. An emperor now ruled the country. A picture shows him in an emperor's crown and robes. The scene is the coronation ceremony in Paris in 1804. In running the government he was as full of energy as he was in battle. He was just as focused. He changed how the government worked. He set up a national bank. He tried to repair trouble in the economy. He worked on the courts. He worked on higher education. The Napoleonic Code may have been his most important change inside France. The code put France's laws into an organized system. It took rights away from women. Husbands gained more power. Fathers gained more power. Male citizens received equal rights under the code. They received freedom of religion. The code said a job should go to a person because of merit. The code also brought enslavement back. France had abolished enslavement earlier. He shut down the old way of collecting taxes. Elected collectors had done that work. He picked new collectors. Each one received a salary. He watched spending by the government very closely. He wanted tax money used in the way he chose. The changes supplied enough money for his wars, which never seemed to stop. In 1815, inside the Tuileries Palace, a picture shows him at work on a letter.

4Admiral Horatio Nelson was Britain's great commander at sea, a kind of Napoleon on the water. His first name is said huh-RAY-shee-oh. On the mainland of Europe, Napoleon kept winning. At sea, Nelson blocked his hopes. Nelson led the British fleet at the Battle of the Nile. He led it again at an even larger sea fight in 1805. In October of that year, brilliant tactics let him crush a fleet of French and Spanish ships. Spain was on France's side at the time. The battle is called Trafalgar. Spain's southwest coast was the site of the battle. After that victory, Napoleon no longer had a real hope of invading England. He wanted to build a European empire and rule it. The nations of Europe rejected French control. They fought him with everything they had. For twelve years the Napoleonic Wars tore across Europe. The years were 1803 to 1815. He signed up enormous numbers of soldiers. Many of them came from lands he had conquered. He poured France's resources into the fighting. His force was called the Great Army. In time it numbered about 680,000 men. France's enemies built alliance after alliance. Each alliance tried to end his ambitions. On land he beat them. The empire kept growing. He set friends in place as rulers of conquered countries. He set relatives in those roles too. He hoped the new rulers would make those countries into allies. Money kept crossing the sea to British merchants. He tried to stop that flow. He banned the countries of mainland Europe from trading with Britain. French ships closed off ports all over Europe. The closures made the ban hold. In December 1805 he won a victory that ranks among his greatest. People call that fight Austerlitz. Say it AW-stur-lits. The ground is now inside the Czech (CHEK) Republic. He commanded 68,000 soldiers. He defeated 90,000 Russians and Austrians. In 1810 the French empire stood at its largest. Holland had been added. Parts of today's Germany had been added too. He worried because he had no heir. He divorced Joséphine. In 1810 he married Archduchess Marie Louise of Austria. In 1811 she had a son. The boy was named Napoleon too. The marriage did not make Austria an ally of France. A painting shows Marie Louise beside her husband and their son. Both father and son carried the name Napoleon.

5A seated Napoleon directs French troops at the Battle of Borodino. The enemy is the Russian army. The date is September 7, 1812. Invading Russia in 1812 was the worst military blunder of his career. Russia had broken his trade ban with Great Britain again and again. Czar (ZAR) Alexander I of Russia was about to side with Britain. Napoleon chose to move first. June 1812 saw him enter Russia at the head of over six hundred thousand soldiers. He hoped the win would come quickly. Russian forces would not stand for one huge battle. They pulled back ahead of the French. They burned crops as they left. French troops then found no food on the land. They found no supplies either. The Russian army finally stood and fought on September 7. Borodino was the nearby town. Say it bor-uh-DEE-noh. Losses were terrible. About 45,000 Russian soldiers died. About 30,000 French soldiers died. One picture shows Napoleon leading French troops who are cold and hungry. They are falling back from Moscow. He chased the Russian army farther into the country. His own army shrank. A lack of supplies made it weaker. He entered Moscow in the middle of September. The city was almost empty. Czar Alexander I would not meet him in battle. The czar had cleared supplies out of Moscow. He ordered his army to burn much of the city. The fires started after the French arrived. By the middle of October, food was nearly gone. Winter was coming. Napoleon turned the army toward home. Russian forces kept attacking the French during the withdrawal. About ten thousand soldiers were all who got back to France. The ruin in Russia was the start of Napoleon's end. In 1814, armies from a group of nations closed in around Paris. They made him give up the throne. He was sent away to Elba, an island of Italy. Early in 1815 he got away. He gathered a new army.

6Allied armies from across Europe close in on Napoleon's men at the Battle of Waterloo. His last defeat came there. The battle was fought in Belgium on June 18. He faced a mixed army of Austrians, British, Prussians, and Russians. That loss brought the Napoleonic Wars to a close. For a time, France's monarchy was put back in place. Later, a government with wider representation replaced it. He was sent away to St. Helena, a remote island held by Britain. The island lies in the South Atlantic Ocean. He spent the rest of his life there. Death came in 1821. France later received his body. The burial was in Paris. His ideas still shape modern politics in a major way. Many countries borrowed pieces of his civil code. The countries lie in Europe, in Latin America, and in the Middle East. They used those ideas as a base for their own laws. His legacy also includes a new way of making war. In that way, every part of a nation is turned toward the war. Support from the public is not required. Military schools worldwide have studied how he fought battles. They have studied how he planned campaigns. Later wars have used those lessons. He was ready to spend lives to reach his ambition. He was ready to spend resources too. Estimates put the dead across Europe at three million to six million because of his actions. His actions left France in ruins. The Duke of Wellington of Britain commanded the allied army at Waterloo. Asked to name the greatest general of every era, he picked Napoleon for the present, for earlier times, and for any time at all. The tomb of Napoleon stands in Paris, France.

7A list of dates traces Napoleon's life. In 1769 he was born on Corsica. In 1785 he left military school as a second lieutenant. In 1793 he put down a revolt inside France. He was raised to brigadier general. In 1796 he married Joséphine de Beauharnais. The year 1804 is when he placed the crown on himself as emperor of France. Russian forces and Austrian forces fell to him in 1805 at Austerlitz. In 1810 he divorced Joséphine. He married Archduchess Marie Louise of Austria. In 1812 he invaded Russia and met a terrible defeat. In 1814 he gave up the throne. He was exiled to the island of Elba. In 1815 he escaped Elba and raised an army. He lost at the Battle of Waterloo. That same year he was exiled to the far-off island of St. Helena. In 1821 he died on St. Helena. His body was brought back to France afterward. These words help with the topic. An alliance joins two or more groups or countries. They agree to work as partners and to fight on one side. An empire gathers nations or peoples under one ruler or one government. Exiled means a person was forced out of the home country. Punishment is a common reason. Politics is another. An ambition is something a person badly wants to reach. It may be a goal or a dream. An ideal is a guiding principle. It is a standard of what seems perfect. Blockaded means a route through a place was shut. Merit is a strong quality that earns praise or a reward. A casualty is a person hurt, killed, or missing. War, an accident, or a disaster can cause it. A monarchy is rule by one person who was not elected. A king is one example. A queen is another. A czar was a man who ruled Russia before the Russian Revolution of 1917. A revolution pulls a government from power by force. A different government takes its place. An emperor is a man at the head of an empire.

62. Nikola Tesla and the Electric Age

1Crowds at the 1893 World’s Fair in Chicago stared at electric displays. Tesla and Westinghouse had built those displays. The sight amazed people. This book calls its first part The Magician. Then Tesla meets Mr. Edison. Ditch digging comes next. A battle over currents follows. Radio days come after that. A great tower has its own part. A lasting influence closes the story. A glossary explains key words. In one laboratory picture, Tesla sits and reads. Artificial lightning fills the room. He looks calm. One day a dark-haired man with a mustache opened his laboratory. The room was in New York City. He asked a group to watch an experiment full of electricity. Nikola Tesla was that man. Guests took their seats. Tesla walked to a wooden platform without rushing. He sat in a chair. A generator sat under the platform. It could make millions of volts. Tesla flipped a switch. Wild streaks of light jumped across the room. The scene looked like a lightning storm indoors. Some streaks even hit Tesla. The show ended. Tesla left the stage without a wound. Clapping filled the room. The crowd had watched a man sit inside a storm of light and walk away fine. That calm figure, and that wild light, are the picture of the magician at work.

2New technology often became a spectacle in Tesla’s shows. He was a scientist, not a magician. The show had a point. A newly found kind of electric current could be safe. That current is alternating current, or AC. The discovery changed the world. In time it would run modern industry. It would also light whole nations. Tesla was a visionary as well as a scientist. Established scientists of his day met a challenge in him. His inventions were astonishing. His ideas were astonishing too. Many experts give him a large share of the credit for later devices. Smartphones are on that list. Wireless communication is on it. Television is on it. Robots are on it. Radar is on it. Other amazing devices are on it too. Genius in science did not make him a strong businessman. He died without money. Other people made millions of dollars from his work. A lightning storm was raging when Tesla was born. The year was 1856. The place is the country of Croatia today. It lies in Eastern Europe. As a boy he studied hard. His father served as an Eastern Orthodox priest. A large library filled the home. Tesla read those books eagerly. His mother gave him a love of inventing. In spare hours she built small appliances for the house. Electricity caught his interest while he was still a boy. He wanted to be an electrical engineer. Years of study and work followed. He found a better way to make electricity. Alternating current made that way more efficient. It also made it safer. In 1884 he sailed for the United States. He was twenty-eight. His second day in America took him to an office in New York. The office belonged to Thomas Edison. Tesla carried a letter. A European friend of Edison had written it. The writer greeted Edison warmly. The writer claimed to know two great men. Edison was one of them. The young man in front of him was the other. Edison was an inventor. Business skill sat beside that inventing skill.

3In those years, people treated Edison as the parent of the electrical age. A lighting system was among his creations. Incandescent lamps were part of it.
