He was about to sail to Europe to join America's British and French allies. His pet was a young bull terrier. The hard problem was how to get the dog onto the ship. For a small dog, Stubby was very strong.

2Conroy was in the 102nd Infantry of the Yankee Division from New England. He found the dog at Yale's football stadium in New Haven, Connecticut, and named him Stubby for his stump tail. Stubby learned bugle calls, marching, and a salute with his right paw. A sailor hid him in the coal bin of the ship Minnesota, and they sailed in September. The voyage lasted nearly a month, and Stubby ate soup bone after soup bone. In early October Conroy hid him under an overcoat and walked down the gangplank. Friends made him dog tags, and he became the regiment's unofficial mascot. When officers found him, Stubby saluted and won many fans.

3In early 1918 Colonel John H. Parker ordered that Stubby remain with Conroy. Soldiers joked that only Stubby could talk back to Parker and get away with it. He was one of about twenty thousand dogs who served the Allies. Dogs pulled machine-gun carriages, carried messages, stood guard, killed rats, and searched for wounded men. Stubby was happiest beside Conroy, but he would stand out. The trenches were filthy and dangerous. By late 1917 Germany and the Allies, including Britain and France, were stuck in a stalemate. The Yankee Division trained in the Lorraine region with French troops for a spring attack.

4On March 21, 1918, the Germans began a poison-gas attack. Both sides used gas that hurt eyes, throats, and lungs, so soldiers wore masks. A French officer made a mask for Stubby. His nose found gas, and he barked and nipped men so they would mask up. He woke a sleeping soldier in a low bunker at the start of an attack. His sharp ears warned of shells and of Germans leaving their trenches. He led walking wounded back and stayed barking beside men who could not stand. In April a shell wounded his chest and left foreleg, but he lived and returned in June with a Purple Heart on a new jacket.

5In September 1918 Stubby caught a German who may have been mapping the American trenches. The man cried Kamerad, then ran, but Stubby bit his leg until soldiers took him prisoner. For that capture Stubby became an unofficial sergeant, above Corporal Conroy. The man's Iron Cross was pinned to Stubby's coat. Stubby posed in his jacket beside Conroy. President Wilson shook his hand and was the first of three presidents to honor him. Germany surrendered in November 1918. They had fought in four offensives and seventeen battles, and the Yankee Division spent 210 days in combat, more than any other American division.

6As a war hero, Stubby held a place of honor in many parades after coming home. He and Conroy arrived in the United States in April 1919, and he loved the fame. The American Legion made him a star at parades and conventions. The YMCA promised three bones a day and a place to sleep for life. In 1920 he attended the convention that nominated Warren G. Harding. Harding and the next president, Calvin Coolidge, welcomed him at the White House. The Hotel Majestic in New York let him stay despite its no-pet rule. On July 6, 1921, Pershing honored his heroism with a gold medal, and Stubby wagged his tail.

7In 1922 he marched in an American Legion parade in New Orleans. Conroy and Stubby were never apart. In 1921 Stubby went with Conroy to Georgetown law school. He became the football mascot and butted the ball with his nose. By the mid-1920s the old dog was slowing down. He died in his sleep in 1926, cradled in Conroy's arms. The Smithsonian recognized him as a war hero. His preserved body stands alert beside a mannequin of a soldier who stands for men saved by this brave dog.

70. Seven Wonders You Can Visit

1The three Great Pyramids of Giza were built beside the Nile over eighty years. The largest one used 2.3 million blocks of stone. Ancient Greek writers loved to make lists of great wonders. A final list of seven sites became the Seven Great Wonders of the World. They were built from about 2500 bc to 290 bc. The list named pyramids, gardens, a temple, statues, a tomb, and a lighthouse. Only the Great Pyramids of Giza still stand today. Archaeologists still dig at Babylon and may one day find the Hanging Gardens.

2A map places the seven ancient wonders near the Mediterranean Sea, the Black Sea, and the Red Sea. The pyramids and the lighthouse are in northern Egypt. The Hanging Gardens are in Iraq, next to Turkey. The temple and the mausoleum are in Turkey, the statue of Zeus is in Greece, and the Colossus is on Rhodes near Turkey. This book looks at seven newer wonders that people can still visit today. More than one hundred million people voted, and these seven sites got the most votes. The Itza founded Chichen Itza in Mexico about ad 600, and its name means mouth of the well of the Itza. A jaguar head repeats in Mayan art, and the sacred ball court is 545 feet long.

3The observatory at Chichen Itza helped the Maya track the Sun. The Spanish named the famous pyramid El Castillo, which means the castle. It is about 24 meters high and 58 meters wide at its base. It was built on an older temple that held Chac Mool and a red jaguar decorated with jade. Archaeologists say it is a calendar, with 365 steps, one for each day. Christ the Redeemer stands on 710-meter Corcovado Mountain above Rio de Janeiro. Finished in 1931, it is the newest new wonder and the largest art deco statue. With its base, it rises 38 meters, and a four-million-dollar repair in 2010 fixed wind and rain damage.

4For six months, scaffolding covered the statue while workers repaired its soft stone. Citizens of Rio watched the repair closely. The open arms and gentle face are a symbol of peace and welcome. At night the statue is lit and glows above the city. A small electric train, built to carry supplies, takes visitors up Corcovado Mountain. From the top there is a full view of Rio, the forests, the beaches, and the bay. The Taj Mahal in Agra is white marble that shifts from pale gold to white to pink. Shah Jahan built this monument to love from 1631 to 1648 for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

5Cut marble, mosaic tiles, and graceful arches complete the Taj Mahal design. Its white marble glows pale pink at sunset. The design mixes Persian, Central Asian, and Islamic styles, with colorful cut stones. A large dome and four slim towers called minarets rise above a vast garden. A long narrow pool leads to the entrance, and the whole site fits in perfect harmony. Pollution, weathering, disasters, and people have harmed the Colosseum, and it has been restored many times. Almost two thousand years ago it held at least fifty thousand people for races and bloody contests. Gladiators fought each other and wild animals such as tigers, bears, and elephants.

6Canvas awnings shaded hot crowds, and statues filled the outer arches. Below the wooden floor, gladiators waited while cages kept animals apart. Hand-turned elevators and ramps moved gladiators and animals to or from the arena. After Rome lost power in the late ad 400s, the building slowly fell apart. A strong earthquake hurt the outer walls, and people took many stones. A 2011 project began to save the walls, and almost four million people visit each year. The Great Wall crosses mountains, valleys, forests, and farms for 8,851 kilometers, over twice the width of the United States. Early walls rose from the 700s to the 300s bc, and Qin Shi Huangdi later joined many into one.

7Ming emperors turned the old earth-and-rock wall into a strong stone barrier. Guard towers let soldiers see far, and the new wall stretched about 8,850 kilometers. Walking the wall is a goal for travelers, and over two million people visit each year. A longer wall did not save the Ming, who fell to the Manchu in 1644. Farmers later took stones for homes, but some sections have been rebuilt for visitors. Machu Picchu stands 2,500 meters up in the clouds, high above the Urubamba River Canyon. The Incas built the greatest empire in the Americas, but the Spanish never found this city. In 1911 farmers showed Hiram Bingham the site, and he mapped it and wrote about it.

8Temples, storage buildings, an observatory, and houses at Machu Picchu were built without mortar. About 1,000 people lived there, and terraces on the steep hills were used for farming. The city may have been for worship or a winter palace, but archaeologists are not sure. It is among the hundred most endangered sites in the world, so only 2,500 visitors may come each day. Its stones fit so tightly that a thin knife blade will not go between them. Petra in Jordan was cut from pink and gray rock about two thousand years ago, and petra means rock. It stood where two trade routes met, so camel caravans stopped for food and water. Johann Burckhardt rediscovered it in 1812, and much of Petra was restored in the 1960s.

9Visitors enter Petra on foot, on a horse, or in a cart through a narrow canyon called the Siq. The Treasury stands at the end of the Siq and is the most famous building in Petra. It is only the first of many sights in this city carved from stone. Between twenty and thirty thousand people once lived there. Their buildings included apartments, hotels, restaurants, stores, banks, and mausoleums. The Seven New Wonders are amazing, but today’s world is much bigger than ancient Greece. It is hard to limit a wonder list to seven, so which places would you vote to add? Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, Turkey, was the world’s largest cathedral for over one thousand years.

10The huge Leshan Buddha is carved from a river canyon wall outside Leshan City in Sichuan Province, China. It is over 71 meters high and 28 meters wide. Visitors love to sit on its feet. The Golden Gate Bridge is in San Francisco, California. The Three Gorges Dam in China is the world’s largest dam. The temples of Angkor Wat are in Cambodia. The Eiffel Tower is in Paris, France.

11The Millau Bridge crosses the River Tarn in France. Mount Rushmore is in South Dakota, in the USA. The Statue of Liberty stands in New York Harbor, in the USA.

71. Spacecraft from Private Companies

1The Dream Chaser is a spaceplane. Its design goal was resupply runs to the International Space Station. Coming pages mark the end of one era. They mark the dawn of another. They describe a second race into space. They describe a ticket for the ride. They describe deliveries in space. They describe ships that move people. They describe stations owned by private firms. A conclusion follows. Useful words come last. A photo shows the shuttle Atlantis ready to dock. The partner in that photo is the International Space Station. The date is July 10, 2011. The flight was the shuttle program's last mission. Early on July 21, 2011, Atlantis came back to the ground. Twelve days in space were behind it. A shuttle had gone to space 135 times. This landing was the last of those flights. A shuttle belonging to the National Aeronautics and Space Administration would not leave Earth again. NASA is the short name. The shuttle was the first spacecraft the world could use again and again. People rode it into orbit around Earth. Scientific experiments rode with them. Satellites were launched from it. Satellites were recovered by it. Satellites were repaired by it. The International Space Station was built with its help. Once Atlantis was down, museum halls were the only place left to see these craft.

2A photo from May 7, 1992, shows three NASA astronauts. They are outside the shuttle Endeavour on a spacewalk. They are grabbing a satellite that has stopped working right. Age was one reason NASA quit the shuttles by 2011. Cost was another. Each launch was expensive. Keeping the ships fit to fly was difficult. Some jobs were still amazing. No other craft could snatch a satellite out of orbit and bring it home safely. Those jobs had simply grown too costly for NASA to keep doing. Sadness was common when the program stopped. NASA stepped away from the routine hauling of people. It stepped away from the routine hauling of cargo between Earth and space. Space science became the focus. Exploration became the focus. New missions were planned. Robotic rovers would go to exciting places. People would go too. Mars was one of those destinations. For the first time, NASA handed the more ordinary missions to commercial companies. A photo set recalls earlier flights. At the lower right is Yuri Gagarin. No human had gone into space before him. A Vostok rocket, at the left, carried him around Earth. The date was April 12, 1961. A Gemini-Titan rocket, at the upper right, helped the United States get ready. The goal of that preparation was astronauts on the Moon. Commercial firms had plenty to learn. Their vehicles had to stay safe while burning dangerous fuels. They had to stay safe at high speed. They had to stay safe in extreme heat and in extreme cold. Systems were also needed to hold a spaceship on its course. The Space Age opened in the late 1950s. Only two powers then had the money, the resources, and the technology. One was the United States. The other was the Soviet Union. Later, more nations joined the space business. Some commercial companies joined too. In the 1960s, private firms built communications satellites of their own. Government rockets still lifted those satellites. By the 1980s, private firms were building rockets of their own. Those rockets put satellites into orbit.

3A drawing shows a rover being lowered onto Mars. A Sky Crane helps with that lowering. By the middle of the 1990s, smaller companies were new to space work. Experience was what they lacked. Effort was what they supplied instead. Better technology brought space within reach of many owners of businesses. Firms competed with one another for a share of that business. Plans today cover several kinds of missions. Tourists would ride out to where space begins, then return. Crews and supplies would be delivered to orbit. New stations would be put up. The year 1996 brought an announcement. The contest was the Ansari X-Prize. Its aim was to hurry the building of private spaceships. Ten million dollars was the prize. The winner had to be a private company. It had to build a spaceship and pilot it into space. At least one person had to be aboard. Room for two more people was required. Height on the winning flight had to be at least 62.1 miles (100 km). The ship had to return to Earth. The whole trip then had to be flown again. Two weeks was the limit for that second flight. Eight years passed before anyone claimed the ten million dollars. The year of the win was 2004. The American firm Scaled Composites won. Its vehicle was SpaceShipOne. The ship did not roll down a runway like an airplane. It did not blast off on top of a rocket. A plane named WhiteKnight carried it. The release height was 50,000 feet (15.2 km). SpaceShipOne hung beneath the carrier's belly until the drop. Seconds later, its rocket engines roared. Speed passed 3,000 miles per hour, or 4,828 kmph. That speed is almost four times as fast as sound travels. Past that burst of speed, the little spaceplane rose higher than 62.1 miles (100 km). Space begins just short of that height.

4Virgin Galactic joined with the makers of SpaceShipOne. The shared aim was space tourism for people all over the world. Tickets went on sale. The starting price was $200,000 for each passenger. Some people have paid more than one hundred times as much for a trip into space. Virgin Galactic will fly its tourists on a spaceplane named SpaceShipTwo. Paying tourists are the passengers it is meant to carry. WhiteKnightTwo is its mothership. The design resembles SpaceShipOne. SpaceShipTwo is larger. Like the earlier ship, it is meant to reach the edge of space and return. About six minutes of weightlessness is what passengers will feel before the trip home. A drawing shows SpaceShipOne just after it leaves WhiteKnight. Return begins when the pilot tilts the wings. The tilt slows the vehicle. SpaceShipTwo then drops back toward Earth much more slowly. A slower fall keeps the ship from growing too hot. Re-entry is the name of that return into the air. Less heating means a heavy heat shield is not required. The kind many other spaceships use can be skipped. Leaving from WhiteKnightTwo also cuts the fuel needed to reach space. Lower fuel use helps hold costs down. Wings go back to their normal position at one set height. That height is 13.2 miles (21.24 km). The spaceplane can then glide. The landing strip is a wide runway, and it is in New Mexico. The whole flight is expected to last about two hours. October 2014 brought a death. A test flight in California ended in a crash of SpaceShipTwo. One pilot lost his life. The risks of the new technology were suddenly clear to everyone. The company still plans to keep working. Safe commercial spaceflight is the goal. A model holds the wings of SpaceShipTwo at a tilt.

5People who live and work in space for long stretches need supplies on a regular schedule. They need equipment on that schedule too. The Ansari X-Prize contest ended in 2004. Soon afterward, NASA offered prizes of its own. Private firms were invited to find creative ways to move cargo. Cheaper ways were the point. The cargo would go from Earth to the ISS. The offer brought still more private firms into vehicle design. One hard worker on a regular ISS trip was SpaceX. A high price tag was what it hoped to avoid. Dragon is the reusable spacecraft SpaceX built. It can fly with no crew aboard. A Falcon 9 rocket carries the Dragon capsule up. SpaceX builds that rocket too. Near the ISS, the capsule waits. A bump into the station is what the wait avoids. The station's crew then uses a robotic arm. The arm grabs the spacecraft. Supply and equipment deliveries by SpaceX began in 2012. Cargo also comes back to Earth. Dragon leaves the ISS and splashes down. Splashdown happens near California, in the Pacific Ocean. Afterward, SpaceX picks up the capsule. It also collects two parts of the rocket. Those pieces fly again. Space stations are a different kind of spacecraft. Earth is circled for a long stay. Builders often assemble a modern station out of many pieces. Once a station is finished, crews can come aboard. They work there. They live there. Scientists use stations to study people on long missions. They also run experiments where gravity is low. Earth's labs cannot host many of the ISS experiments. No station built before the ISS was as large. Many nations helped create it. The cost was billions of dollars. On a clear night, the naked eye can see it from Earth. The first crew entered on November 2, 2000. The station has never been empty since. Visitors number more than two hundred. They have come from fifteen nations. Moving people safely to a station and back is an important job. A drawing shows Atlantis in 1995. Russia's station is the craft it has docked to.

6Seven people can ride in the Dream Chaser. Each trip links the ground with the ISS in either direction. The year 2010 was when NASA asked commercial firms for a design. The spacecraft would move people to space stations and home again. Seven astronauts had to fit on a trip to the ISS. The ship then had to stay docked. The docked time could last up to 210 days. After that, it had to fly home and land safely. NASA judged the early designs. Money went to four companies. One company was Sierra Nevada. Its proposal was the Dream Chaser, a glider meant for space. A rocket would carry it up. The return would be a glide down to Earth. A different Dragon capsule came from SpaceX. This version would move people to stations and back. Two further firms designed capsules as well. They were Boeing and Blue Origin. Their capsules would ride a rocket up. Mission's end would put them in the ocean with a splash. A longer visit to space raises a new question. What if the stay lasted more than a few minutes? Bigelow Aerospace is at least one company working on an answer. A space hotel is the reality it wants to build. The design is a balloon habitat. Folded, the habitat fits in a rocket's cargo area. In orbit, it expands. The unit now in progress would house six people. Inside space would match the ISS for size. Models built at full size show the habitats that inflate. Strong fabrics form the skin. Mylar is one of those fabrics. Kevlar is another. A station made of fabric can seem strange. Bigelow engineers say the fabric will actually do better than metal. The blow-up habitats are not ready yet. Two empty test models went into space. The years were 2006 and 2007. If the plan holds, more pieces will be launched. They will be joined. The result would be the world's first private space station.

7The shuttle's final flight closed one period of space travel. It also opened an exciting new age. Commercial spaceflight is that age. Around the world, private firms are putting in hard work. They want spacecraft to leave the drawing board. They want those craft in the real world. New choices will appear for sending cargo into space. New choices will appear for sending people. Staying in orbit for a long stretch will be a choice too. The commercial space age asks a simple question. Are you ready? Space tourism began in 2001. Dennis Tito, an American, paid $20 million for a ride. A Russian rocket carried him to the International Space Station. His time aboard the ISS lasted eight days. Then he returned to Earth. After his flight, other private citizens made similar trips. Each of them paid millions of dollars. Richard Garriott was among them. He is a famous designer of computer games. Anousheh Ansari was among them. She is an Iranian-American businesswoman. In 2006, a photo caught Anousheh Ansari during her time on the ISS. Aeronautics is the science or the practice of flight. A mission is a set purpose for doing something. It can be a special task. Altitude is height above a surface. An orbit is the path one space object takes while circling a larger one. A capsule is the part of a spacecraft that can come away. People and their instruments ride in it. Re-entry is the return into Earth's atmosphere from space. Commercial describes buying and selling. Robotic describes a device programmed to do tasks. A destination is a place someone or something is going. A satellite is an object that orbits Earth or another body in space. It may be natural. It may be made by people. Docked means temporarily joined in space. Docking ports make that join. A spacecraft is a vehicle for travel in space.

72. Sports at the Outer Edge

1American skateboarder Dashawn Jordan practices in 2017 at the X Games held in Minneapolis. The first 900. How these games began. A meet that keeps changing. A workshop for action sports. The trick had failed for him on ten earlier attempts. Each attempt ended in a fall. On the eleventh try he dropped in. The halfpipe ramp forms the letter C. Speed built. On the second pass he left the surface. He curled his body into a ball. Sideways, he turned two times and then a half turn more. He came down. He wobbled briefly. Then he stayed upright. In a contest, nobody had landed the 900 before him. A 900 is two full spins plus half of another. Each full spin covers 360 degrees. A photo shows him at the fifth X Games. The year is 1999. Each one drives past ordinary limits until the feat seems unbelievable.

2How the games began. ESPN is a cable channel built around sports. The company is based in America. Viewers in more than sixty countries can watch it. Early in the 1990s it was turning into a giant of media. To grow the business further, executives studied young American fans of sports. What they found was a surprise. A shrinking share of young people still followed football. Basketball drew a shrinking share too. So did baseball. Those games are the traditional ones. Meanwhile a rising number of young people felt passionate about extreme sports. Such sports test the skill of one person. They also test courage. ESPN wanted those fans. It created a new sort of sports gathering. In the summer of 1995 the first Extreme Games opened. Rhode Island was one host state. Vermont was the other. Both sit in the country's northeast. Nearly 200,000 people showed up. Thousands more saw the action on television. Athletes arrived from around the world. They jumped. They skated. They biked. They did still more. Medals of gold, silver, and bronze were the prizes. Money prizes were offered as well. Planners placed twenty-seven events into nine categories. The nine groups included Bungee Jumping and also Eco-Challenge. In-line Skating was a group. Skateboarding was a group. Skysurfing was a group. Sport Climbing was a group. So were Street Luge, Biking, and the events held on water. Photos mark sky surfing in 1997, ice climbing in 1999, and street luge in 1999. Reporters who had covered sports for a long time scoffed. One writer joked that this was an Olympics performed with no hands. Even so, no one could dismiss the athletic fire. No one could dismiss the creativity the athletes showed. Young fans devoted to extreme sports loved the meet. Organizers set the date again for the following year. They cut the word Extreme down to the letter X. The year after that was 1997. A winter version opened at Big Bear Lake, California. Skiing filled most of the card. Snowboarding did too.

3Winter and summer versions each last four days. Both have continued strongly from then until now. For a long stretch they moved among different places in the United States. Some of those contracts pay millions of dollars. Tony Hawk is among them. Most athletes make much less. Some make nothing, especially at the start of a career. Kelly Slater is shown surfing. The meet is the ninth X Games. The year is 2003. Companies that sell surf gear have paid him millions in sponsorships. Two more scenes show the wider map. In 2000, athletes in Thailand try to qualify for the Asia events. In 2018, a skier launches a big jump at the Norway meet. The home base of the games is the United States. 4Most of the action happens inside America. A worldwide field still shows up. Athletes from many countries enter qualifying rounds. Their hope is a spot in the X Games. Racing on super-modified shovels was one. In the barefoot jump, a speedboat pulls a skier who has no skis. The skier performs tricks. Then the skier leaves a ramp and hopes to come down upright. 5A small word list from the athletes. These athletes enjoy wordplay. Some of their inventiveness sits in the names of stunts. A digger is a bad fall while a trick is being tried. It seemed closer to play than to sport. Competitors jumped off a platform. Long cords that stretch were wrapped around their ankles. They dropped, sprang upward, and added twists and flips. Judges scored the moves. Surfing was removed. Wakeboarding was removed. Both demand locations that are hard to find. A small set of main sports now carries most of the events. Skateboarding sits at the center of that set. Summer 2018 included six events for skateboards. Vert is short for vertical. Riders shoot up and down ramps and throw tricks. Street sends skaters through a park. Steps, rails, ramps, and slopes stand in the way. Judges grade technique. They also grade style. Leticia Bufoni of Brazil is shown in the street contest. The city is Sydney. The year is 2018. The country is Australia.

6The winter meet has fewer choices. In 2018 it offered only four sports. They were skiing, snowboarding, snowmobiling, and biking on snow. Slopestyle takes skiers and snowboarders down a hill. Tricks happen on ramps, on rails, and on other built features. Snowmobile sessions include races. They also include trick events. Snow BikeCross sends athletes racing and doing stunts. Their bikes started as motorcycles. Builders changed them so they run on snow. While these games evolved, the Olympic Games tried to borrow some of the appeal. Younger fans were the target. Events that grew popular here were added there. Halfpipe contests for skateboarders are one example. Halfpipe contests for snowboarders are another. Plenty of athletes enter both gatherings. An Olympic athlete is part of a national team. An athlete here is not. Each one competes alone. Sponsors provide the pay. A more surprising addition is the set of events for major-league gamers. Since 2017, eGamers have joined. They are competitors with high skill at video games. Letting them in has been controversial. Many people ask how a gamer can seek the same medals as an extreme athlete. Names that rose here. Through this meet, a whole generation of extreme athletes became legends. Newer names are still climbing. A few stand at the top and have shaped the history of these sports. Brighton Zeuner rides a skateboard. She won the women's park event at age thirteen. The meet was Minneapolis. The year was 2017. Chloe Kim rides a snowboard. At seventeen she took gold in the women's halfpipe at the Winter Olympics of 2018. She already owned six medals from these games. Nyjah Huston rides a skateboard. From 2009 to 2016 he dominated the summer street contest. His prize money is greater than that of any other skateboarder. Travis Pastrana rides Moto X and also races rally cars. Across fifteen years in the motorsport events he collected seventeen medals. Eleven were gold.

7A workshop for action sports. To someone new to extreme sports, these athletes can look a little wild. They launch to astonishing heights. A board or a bike of some kind stays with them. Then they land in a graceful way. Or the crash is spectacular. Trying tricks brings road rash. It brings bruises that are black and blue. It brings broken bones. A crowd can feel awe when a huge stunt seems to land with no effort. Fans rarely notice how many years of practice fill each day. Athletes experiment again and again until a goal is reached. Tony Hawk says the 900 took him thirteen years of practice before a clean landing. These daredevils are bold in the extreme. Reckless is the wrong word for them. Mastering fear, and then succeeding, leaves a strong feeling of empowerment. Snow BikeCross shows that same drive. These games helped move extreme sports into ordinary public view. Audiences love watching an attempt that looks impossible. Both the misses and the landings prove a point. The human mind can be astonishing. The body can be astonishing. The spirit can be astonishing. Words to know. An athlete trains to race, play, or perform, and needs strength plus speed plus skill. Passionate describes intense feeling or belief about a person or a thing. Promote means to put an idea forward and hope others accept it. A competition is an event in which people or teams oppose one another to win. Propel means to drive somebody or something ahead. A consumer pays to own or borrow a product or a service, and then uses it. A ramp curves up on both sides and dips in the center so athletes can do tricks. Controversial describes a subject that stirs strong disagreement. Scoffed describes a mean or mocking show of dislike. Extreme sports carry more risk, more thrill, and harder tests than ordinary sports. Stunts are daring physical feats, often staged as entertainment. An obstacle is anything that blocks progress or movement.

73. Steam, Mills, and a New Way of Life

1Late in the 1800s, linen was made on a roving frame. A woman in an English factory did that work. About 1764, the Scottish inventor James Watt took on a repair job. The machine in need of repair was a Newcomen steam engine. Mines that filled with water already depended on engines like it. Miners used them to pump the water clear. Those engines were not new. Decades had passed since they were invented. Watt redesigned the engine. Fuel went further in his version. Running it also cost less. Later years brought still more changes to the steam engine. Watt stayed part of that work. Other inventors joined in. Steam could then drive machines of many sorts. Looms that wove cloth could run on it. Locomotives could run on it too. The redesigned engine was a single advance among many. That group of advances is what sparked the Industrial Revolution. The older Newcomen design had prepared the ground. From the middle of the 1700s through the middle of the 1800s, new technology remade Great Britain. The wider world changed after that. Nearly every part of daily life felt the shift. Work was done in new ways. People lived in different places. Travel could cover greater distances. Clothing was not what it had been. The foods people ate changed as well.

2New machines were a leading cause of the Industrial Revolution. They were not the only cause. The East India Company was another. Traders formed that company in England in the year 1600. Over time it held military power. It held political power as well. A large private army belonged to it. Cotton products from India were among the goods it brought in. Those goods stayed cheap. Indian laborers received little pay for their work. In Britain, cotton goods won extreme popularity. Around the middle of the 1700s, Indian territories came under the company's control. Raw cotton in India was then within Britain's direct reach. Britain imported that cheap cotton. The aim was to finish goods at home for still less money. A scene from 1799 shows a battle in India's Kingdom of Mysore. Soldiers serving the British East India Company face local troops. An 1815 map of the British Empire marks many overseas places. Canada is on that map. Newfoundland is on it. Bermuda, the Bahamas, Jamaica, British Honduras, and Trinidad are on it. Gibraltar and Malta are on it. Sierra Leone, Ascension Island, Saint Helena, and Cape Colony are on it. Mauritius, India, Ceylon, New South Wales, and Tasmania are on it too. Late in the 1700s, colonies in the West Indies sat under British control. Colonies in North America and South America did too. Canada was part of that reach. Wool came from those lands. Silk came from them. Lumber came from them. Coal lay in large supply inside Britain. Iron did too. Resources of that kind mattered for industrialization. Farmers had found new ways to grow more food. The population rose because of that extra food. During those same years, lords who held wealth bought up wide tracts of common land. Small farmers had once worked that land. Many people could no longer raise their own food. They had to seek jobs in cities.

3In the 1700s, cloth and clothes formed the largest industry. People call that work textile production. New inventions transformed it before they transformed other trades. Until the Industrial Revolution, most clothing was sewn at home. Village workshops were the other common place for that work. Cloth-making often stayed inside one family. The family split the jobs. Yarn might be spun from cotton. It might be spun from flax. It might be spun from wool. Cloth was then woven on a hand loom. The work moved slowly. Even a skilled worker found it tedious. Late in the 1700s, a run of new inventions raised the efficiency of spinning. Weaving grew more efficient as well. Richard Arkwright worked as both an industrialist and an inventor. In his design, a waterwheel turned a machine that spun thread. Strong cotton thread came off that machine. No ordinary workshop could hold an invention of that size. He put up a large mill at Cromford, in Derbyshire. Hundreds of workers soon had jobs at Cromford Mill. More factories followed from Arkwright's hand. Other makers of textiles copied the pattern. Many people treat Cromford Mill as the earliest modern factory. An 1840 engraving records how Bridgewater Factory looked. Factories altered the way goods were produced. They also altered what a working life felt like. Water power ran the earliest factories. A river had to flow nearby. A factory that ran on steam had no such limit. It could stand in almost any spot. A cluster of them grew up near Manchester. That city lies in the north of England. Cheap coal could reach Manchester along the Bridgewater Canal. Sitting near the coast made overseas trade easier. Raw materials could come in. Finished products could go out. A population boom followed the new mills and factories. About 25,000 people lived in Manchester in 1773. Fifty-two mills stood there by 1802. Inhabitants numbered about 95,000. By 1851 the city had sprawled past 300,000 people. A new nickname stuck to it: Cottonopolis.

4Factory rooms were usually loud. Space inside was tight. Light was poor. A workday ran from twelve hours to sixteen. The week ran six days. Paid vacations did not exist. Sick days did not exist. Safety regulations did not exist. Owners kept strict rules. Some beat the people who worked for them. Some used a whip. Children met that treatment most often. A fine could follow a whistle. Opening a window could bring a fine too. The manufacturing process was split by a method called division of labor. One person handled only one part of the work. Production moved faster under that system. Owners could offer low wages. Little skill was required. Factories grew more complex as the Industrial Revolution went on. The huge machines were dangerous to run. Some of the full-time hands were only four years old. Their families worked beside them. Early in the 1800s, some British factories had a striking mix of ages. More than half the workers were younger than fourteen. A child's pay could fall as low as one-tenth of an adult wage. Some children earned no wages. Room and board were their only return. Adults were too big for certain jobs. A child could crawl under a textile machine and gather thread that had dropped. Adults were often hurt. Children were often hurt. Coal mines employed children as well. Gas could explode at any time. A shaft could fall in. Trappers in the mines could be as young as five. Their job was to open and close doors. Fresh air entered when the doors moved. Older children shoved and hauled heavy tubs of coal. Women did that hauling too. The tubs traveled dark, narrow tunnels. Public outrage pushed the British Parliament to act. A series of laws followed. The laws cut how many hours a child could work. They lifted the youngest age allowed for work. Enforcing the laws was hard. For many children, a factory was the only place to earn money for food and a place to live. A mine was the other place.

5School in Britain cost money before the 1800s. Rich children learned at home. Governesses and tutors did the teaching. Churches ran Sunday schools that poor children could attend. A poor family could also pay for a small private school. Those informal classes met inside a teacher's house. The Factory Act of 1833 added a rule. A child working in a factory was to get two hours of schooling each day. Charities opened free schools in working-class neighborhoods. People knew them as ragged schools. Fresh printing methods put more books within reach. Fresh papermaking methods did the same for newspapers. Prices for both fell. Literacy rose. Charles Dickens was born in 1812 and died in 1870. In his day he was Britain's most popular writer. At age twelve, he saw his father sent to prison. Debt was the cause. Dickens was the oldest son. He had to take a job in a blacking factory. Blacking means shoe polish. Three years passed before he could go back to school. Readers still love his novels and stories. Oliver Twist is one title. Hard Times is another. A Christmas Carol is a third. His pages showed how hard the Industrial Revolution could be. Children stood at the center of that picture. He also argued that society needed reform right away. A gain in one field pulled other fields forward. Cheap coal, for instance, sped up the making of cast iron. Once iron cost less, stronger tools were built from it. Stronger machines were built from it too. Firms needed better ways to move goods. Canals were dug. Roads were improved. Heavy raw materials had to travel. Finished goods had to come in and go out. Engineers built steam locomotives so coal could be hauled. A railway opened in 1825 between Stockton and Darlington. British engineer George Stephenson led the building. His son Robert worked with him. The track stretched 25 miles, or 40 kilometers. No earlier railway had carried a passenger car. Riding a locomotive was among the most exciting changes of the Industrial Revolution. Some people found it frightening. A few critics thought a human body might melt if the speed grew too high. Opening day in 1825 put members of the public on a train. The line was the Stockton and Darlington Railway.

6Chemical production moved forward, and many industries gained from it. Scientists learned how to mass-produce sulfuric acid. They learned how to mass-produce sodium carbonate, also called soda ash. Textile makers used sulfuric acid when they bleached cloth. They used it when they dyed cloth. The same acid could lift rust off iron. It went into fertilizer as well. Glass needed soda ash. Soap needed it. Paper needed it. The year 1824 brought Portland cement. Building gained an important advancement. Construction gained one. Transportation gained one. The Thames Tunnel was built with Portland cement. No underwater tunnel in the world had come before it. The tunnel opened in 1843. A chart follows coal output in the United Kingdom from 1800 to 1900. The figures are in millions of tons. Through the 1800s, coal production climbed quickly. The Industrial Revolution needed that fuel. Change did not stay inside Great Britain. Mainland Europe felt it first. North America felt it next. Britain was reluctant to hand over its inventions. It was reluctant to share its wealth and its power. Sending machines abroad was forbidden. Sending techniques abroad was forbidden. Profit was too large to ignore. Secrecy around the new technologies did not last. William Cockerill had been born in England. He was an expert at making iron. He carried the new technology into Belgium. An ironworks there was opened by his son. France then picked up the methods. Germany did too. The rest of Europe followed. Samuel Slater had studied how textile machines were designed. That study came before he left Britain for the United States. He rebuilt the machines from memory. People nicknamed him Slater the Traitor. A spinning mill rose in Rhode Island in 1793 under his direction. That mill helped start the American Industrial Revolution. Much of the money behind early factories came from rich people who traded in enslaved people. Technological improvements drew money from the same trade. Shipping enslaved people made many British port cities powerful. Those cities also handled raw materials from plantations in the Americas. Cotton was one material. Sugar was another. Tea was a third. A law in 1807 abolished that trade in Britain.

7A broad judgment is shared by many historians. During the Industrial Revolution, the overall standard of living rose for most people. Average income went up. Affordable goods could be chosen from a selection, and that choice was new. Mass-produced clothing sat in the selection. Household items sat there too. So did other goods. Harm came with the gains. Air was polluted by fossil fuels used in manufacturing. Water was polluted by them. Chemicals used in manufacturing polluted both. Life was harsh for poorer people. Work was harsh for them. Children carried the heaviest burden. Big cities grew overcrowded. They grew filthy. Some of those problems eased as the Industrial Revolution moved forward. Sanitation in cities got better. Sewage systems got better. Laws were passed so working lives would improve. Workers formed unions by joining together. The push for fair treatment later reached further groups. Women were one of those groups. Modern society rests on groundwork laid by the Industrial Revolution. Conveniences we rely on today rest on it too. A phone is one such convenience. A car is another. A photograph from 1909 was made in Macon, Georgia. The setting is a mill that made textiles. Young boys climb on the machinery to do their jobs.

74. Stock Cars Built for Speed

1Sections in this book follow this order. Roaring Start. Parts on the Way to Victory. Out in Front of the Others. Beneath the Hood. Tires That Truly Burn. A Flag of Checks. Words to Know and Topics. One picture shows racing of stock cars during 1953. Another shows racing at Bristol Motor Speedway. Roaring Start. The cars streak past. Speed climbs past 200 miles in an hour. This kind of racing began in the 1940s under the name NASCAR. Those letters mean the National Association. That group governs Stock Car Auto Racing. Drivers in that era used everyday cars from the road. Another name for them is stock cars. Dirt was the surface of the tracks. The sport did not stay there. It grew into a major contest. The machines now are custom-built. They are superior cars.

2A present-day NASCAR car still has four wheels. Windows are there. An engine is there. A seat for the driver is there. Likeness to a normal road car mostly ends at that list. Each piece is engineered on purpose. The goal is fast travel. Another goal is surviving the pounding of a race. A third goal is the driver's safety. Pictures show a modern race car of this type, and they show its interior. Martinsville Speedway is in Martinsville, Virginia. Race meets take place all around the United States. Shapes of the tracks are not all alike. Length can be under one mile. Length can reach three miles. Distance for a single race may run from 250 miles up to 600 miles. The cars keep looping. Their speed goes beyond 200 mph. Inches are all that separate a car from its rivals. Success then depends on strength. It depends on durability. It depends on speed. Equipment for the drivers and for the cars makes each race safer. Fine tuning touches every part, so the vehicle can perform at its peak. A careful balance is required. Driver safety sits on one side. Speed sits on the other. Strength serves safety. Inventors keep creating lighter materials. Those materials make the cars better.

3Safety is the first concern. Heat inside one of these cars can reach 150 degrees Fahrenheit. That reading is 65 degrees Celsius. Space travel led NASA to invent many materials. Those materials now shield drivers from fierce heat. Vents are built into the driving suits. Cool, dry air flows in through them. Hot, humid air next to the skin is pushed out. Temperature inside the suit falls by 24 degrees. Heat-blocking blankets guard the cockpit. Heat comes from the engine. It comes from the exhaust. It comes from the transmission. The blankets lower temperature inside the car by 40 degrees. A picture shows the racing helmet and the Hans device. In a crash, that device protects the neck. Kevlar insulates and also bounces heat away. Nomex does the same work. Clothing that resists fire is made from these materials. Gloves are part of that clothing. Socks are part of it. Underwear is part of it. NASA is the source of these details. Gary Nelson speaks to the media in a 2006 photo. NASCAR had given him the vice president role. His department covered research. It also covered development. Parts on the Way to Victory. Each year brings fresh methods. Racing teams introduce them. So do the companies that build cars. They are pushing the edge of performance. Millions of dollars go into the search. Wind-tunnel tests are one expense. Engine design is another. Development of the car is another. Small gains from that spending can open a path to the championship.

4Here is a surprise. For every race, each team builds a car that is brand new. The work can take weeks. Completion starts with the frame. The engine follows. The body follows that. Electronics are installed next. Steering is installed. The driver's seat is installed. At that point the car is close to ready. Testing comes after. The crew takes the car apart and inspects it. They put it back together in time for race day. A crew labors on the car their driver will use. The garage sits at Daytona International Speedway. Highly skilled engineers design these cars. Mechanics build them. They work in teams. Four main pieces make up each car. The frame is one. The engine is one. The body is one. The tires are one. Chassis is another name for the frame. The word sounds like CHAH-see. Protection of the driver is one duty of the frame. Forming the car's main structure is the other duty. Rolled steel tubing, thick and strong, makes the roll cage. That cage is the frame's guard around the driver. The remaining frame uses rolled steel tubing that is thin. A crash makes it crumple. A hit against a wall does the same. Engine, body, and wheel axle all fasten onto this frame. Keeping those pieces joined is the purpose. A diagram labels the engine, the frame, the axle, and the tires.

5Further labels mark the seat, the body, and the paint. Kevin Harvick drives a NASCAR car along the inside lane. Talladega Superspeedway is the track. It is in Talladega, Alabama. Fabricators, two of them, assemble the body. Welding joins sheet metal that has been rolled thin. Primer covers the shaped body. Primer gets the surface ready for color. Sanding follows. Colors of the sponsor go on next. A logo from that sponsor covers the car. The car's number is added. The team's name is added. Decals from several advertisers are added too.

6Out in Front of the Others. The outer form is meant to resemble regular cars from the road. Designers also shape it for conditions that change. Track conditions are one factor. Car speed is another. Shifting aerodynamics is a third. Aerodynamics names how air moves as it passes the vehicle. NASCAR's rules on shape are strict. A template, which is a model, goes to every design team. The model keeps them inside limits. Those limits cover height. They cover width. They cover shape. They cover airflow. One image is the 2006 Dodge Charger sold as a production car. Another is a Dodge Charger redrawn for this kind of racing. Raise the downforce, and grip increases. Extra grip helps the car work through corners. Drag increases at the same time. Speed is what drag takes away. Downward pressure comes from the rear spoiler. Stability gets help from that pressure. During a spin, the side skirt stops air from slipping underneath. How air travels around the car matters deeply in this sport. That airflow can add downforce. It can also reduce downforce. Downforce is energy in the air that presses the car onto the racing surface. The air dam has a matching job. It stops air that tries to pass beneath the vehicle.

7Rules about how these cars perform exist for clear reasons. The contest should excite the fans. It should keep drivers safe. It should stay competitive for the teams. Large objects that fly loose are a danger. The Earnhardt bar helps shield the driver against them. A rollover can throw a driver out. The window net holds the driver in the car. Harnesses cross a seat that fits the body closely. Together they secure the driver. A fire extinguisher rides in the car. Downforce is not left to chance. NASCAR decides how much a car must have. The decision depends on the track type. It also depends on the race series. If a car spins, roof flaps pop up. Their job is to prevent a flip. A typical engine of this sport is shown sitting in the chassis. Power from that engine is extreme. The design is a V8. Eight cylinders form a V. Measured size is 5.87 liters. In cubic inches, that is 358. Output can climb to 800 brake horsepower. The short name is bhp. A typical car on the road produces 150 bhp. Placement is under a hood, at the front. Most road cars put the engine in that same spot. The stock-car theme stays intact because of it.

8Designs of the body are regulated. Engine output is regulated as well. Some races use restrictor plates inside the engine. Those plates reduce how much horsepower can be produced. A turbo system is banned. A fuel-injection system is banned too. George Metrick, an official with NASCAR, studies a restrictor plate. The look happens during inspection before a race. The site is Talladega Superspeedway. At that track, NASCAR demands the plates. One picture presents a modern engine from this sport. A block of cast iron sits at the engine's core. Blocks of that kind have served engines for decades. Even so, technology and modifications have raised what the modern version can do. The gain is dramatic.

9Testing of this engine is intense. Tuning is precise. Running at 200 mph for longer than three hours is within its ability. Output has to stay at the maximum. The engine must run in an efficient way. It must run in a reliable way. Radical new elements show up in these power plants. A few short years may be all it takes before road cars include those developments. Mechanics are shown swapping in a fresh engine. Tires That Truly Burn. Layers of rubber build each tire. Fabric is layered in. Steel belts add strength. The build must stand extreme speed. It must stand extreme temperature. Blowouts are the risk being prevented. Incredible strength is required. California Speedway is where one photo shows a tire just mounted. Daytona International Speedway is where another photo shows a tire torn to shreds. Air is what fills a tire on a road car. Nitrogen is what fills these race tires. Extreme heat makes air expand. Pressure then shifts, and the tire grows unstable. Nitrogen bears the harsh conditions of a race more successfully. Tire pressure stays steady. So does performance. One view shows the tire mounted on its wheel. A cutaway view shows the interior.

10Grip on the track is built into these tires. Very high speed through a corner becomes possible. Stress on a tire during a race is extreme. Track shape creates some of it. Downforce creates more. Sheer speed creates more. About 150 miles is the life of each tire. Because speed decides the sport, a pit stop must replace all four tires. Crews can do that job in under 15 seconds. Jeff Gordon appears in a photo during a pit stop. Talladega Superspeedway is the track. Crossing the finish line as the winner is what the checkered flag announces. A Flag of Checks. Designers never stop seeking airflow changes. Some changes aid cornering. Some changes lift speed. Asphalt tracks today carry these cars at incredible speeds. A future version of the sport may use cars that hover over the surface. Fascination with speed is certain to last. So is fascination with vehicles that can arrive the fastest.

11Words to Know. Aerodynamics studies the movement of air as it passes an object's shape. An axle is a steel bar. It runs between the wheel on the left and the wheel on the right. Bhp means brake horsepower. It measures all the power an engine can give for high performance. The chassis is the frame. It binds the car and shields the driver. A component is one part. It combines with other parts and works beside them. Cylinders are tubes inside the engine. Fuel is compressed there and then ignited. Downforce is air pressing a car down. That press helps the car stay on the track. Drag is the push of air against a moving car, slowing it. Fuel injection delivers fuel. The fuel arrives at the cylinders by a more direct path. A logo is a small design. It stands for a company, a product, or both. NASCAR names both an organization and the events it runs. The full name is the National Association. It governs Stock Car Auto Racing. Nitrogen is a gas. It makes up 78 percent of the atmosphere of Earth. A sponsor is a company. It gives money to a racing team. In return it gets advertising space on the stock cars. Stock cars are ordinary automobiles. They are the sort used on city streets. A turbo is a turbine inside a housing. The turbine is a fan. It increases horsepower. Topics in this book include Jeff Gordon, Kevin Harvick, and Gary Nelson. Race-car subjects include airflow, the body, the chassis, the components, the engine, high performance, maneuverability, safety, speed, temperature, and tires. Tracks are listed too. So are rules, sponsorship, and testing.

75. Stone Dragon on China's Northern Edge

1In every season, millions of visitors come to the Great Wall. The wall is a landmark known in many countries. Pages ahead look at this remarkable landmark. They look at a wall that seems to flow. They look at its separate sections. They look at why a wall was wanted. They look at the building work. They look at what a visit is like. They look at how the wall inspires people. A list of useful words ends the book. In 1987, a world body made a choice about this wall. The United Nations named the Great Wall of China a World Heritage Site. Among human-made features on Earth, few are more famous. It also belongs to the New Seven Wonders of the World. The engineering is a remarkable feat. The design is a remarkable feat as well. Construction projects rarely get more challenging than this one. Taken together, the many sections are China's largest draw for tourists. Their combined length beats the distance from the North Pole to the South Pole. A long record of China sits in the wall. That record is a rich one. Work on it began more than two thousand years in the past. The story it tells includes shifts in power. It includes shifts in technology. It includes shifts in how people lived. The span runs from ancient days to now.

2An old Chinese mix of art and science is called feng shui. Say it FUNG SHWAY. That system governed the wall's design. Its principles offer advice on arrangement. Things should sit in a way that follows flowing energy. A curve was chosen, rather than a straight line. Harmony with the shape of the land was the aim. Builders set the wall on China's northern border. In China, many people see the wall as a dragon asleep. The west holds the tail. That western place is Gansu Province. Say it GAHN-soo. The east holds the head. That eastern place is Liaoning Province. Say Liaoning as lee-OW-ning. The Yellow Sea lies near that head. From tail to head, deserts ring the dragon's body. Steppes ring it too. Mountains ring it. Lakes ring it. Rivers ring it. Fertile lowlands ring it. Beaches ring it as well. Part of the wall lies near Beijing. Say Beijing as bay-ZHING. Beijing is the capital of China. A map marks Hushan Great Wall as the eastern end. It marks Jiayu Mountain Pass as the western end. Mongolia appears on the map. Inner Mongolia appears too. So do Beijing, the Yellow Sea, and China. A key points out important sections. The border of Inner Mongolia is marked. A scale on the map reads 150 km (93 mi.). Badaling is one section that remains well preserved. It sits about 70 kilometers (43 mi.) northwest of the capital, Beijing. The Great Wall is not a single wall. Separate sections, many of them, make it up. Some of those walls run parallel to one another. Four of the main sections lie inside a range of 121 kilometers (75 mi.) from Beijing. In 2007, a vote placed the Great Wall on the list known as the New Seven Wonders of the World. The section people know best is Badaling, said BAH-dah-ling. It is also the section kept in the best shape. Steep mountains northwest of Beijing are where it winds. The winding stretch is about 12 kilometers (7.5 mi.). Watchtowers there number forty-three. East of that, Mutianyu is a scenic portion. Say Mutianyu as MOO-tyen-yoo. High mountains are what it spans. The length is 2.25 kilometers (1.4 mi.). Watchtowers there number twenty-two.

3Translated from Chinese, that name is Long Wall of Ten Thousand Li. A li is a unit used in China. One li is about half a kilometer. One li is also about a third of a mile. Ten thousand li therefore comes to about 5,000 kilometers (3,100 mi.). For a long time, people believed the wall was not much longer than that figure. A new measure took place from 2007 to 2012. Scientists did the measuring. Advanced technology was their tool. They learned the real length is over four times the old figure. Add every section, and the total is about 21,196 kilometers (13,171 mi.). Jinshanling lies northeast of Beijing. Say it JIN-shahnling. This section is well preserved. It runs about 10 kilometers (6 mi.). Watchtowers there number sixty-seven. In earlier times, soldiers slept inside some towers. Other towers held hay. Other towers held weapons. Windows appear on some watchtowers. Archers used those windows to shoot at enemies. Simatai sits just east of Jinshanling. Say Simatai as SU-mah-tie. This part runs about 5 kilometers (3 mi.). Workers have done a great deal of restoration here. The ground is extremely steep. Watchtowers number thirty-four. Mandarin Duck Lake has the towers split about evenly, half along each shore. Inner Mongolia's southern edge is roughly the line the wall follows. Today that region governs itself as part of China. During the building years, peoples who were not Chinese held most of the control. Long ago, the Mongol people stood as enemies of China. Keeping them outside was why the wall was constructed. Chinese culture was also shielded from influences beyond the wall. Invaders still got through at times. Getting through was made hard, though. Ancient days held small groups of nomadic people. They lived in lands that are now China, and near those lands. Wild animals gave them food. Wild plants gave them food. Clothing came from those same wild sources. Other needs came from them too. A change started around 4000 bc. People on richer soil began to grow crops. They began to tame animals. They settled in one place. Village walls went up around them. Northern nomads might raid, and the walls were meant to stop that. Andrew Howat, a British artist, painted a scene called Great Wall of China. In it, Chinese soldiers take aim at invaders.

4One picture marks the time after Qin held every part of China. Zheng was then emperor, the earliest one the new country had. By 500 bc, China held many states. Each state was independent. Those states fought one another. States in the north also fought enemies farther north. More walls went up during that period. By 221 bc, one powerful state held all of China. That state was Qin. Say Qin as CHIN. Zheng was the new emperor. Say Zheng as ZHUNG. He wanted enemies kept away from China. His order put workers onto border walls. The length he called for was almost 4,828 kilometers (3,000 mi.). Some experts treat this project as the beginning of the Great Wall. Zheng died in 210 bc. Neglect followed his death for about one hundred years. Parts of it fell apart. A later emperor then called for a new stretch. That stretch measured 483 kilometers (300 mi.) along the borders. From ad 386 until 1279, emperor followed emperor with fresh orders. Some orders said to repair old parts. Some orders said to raise new parts. During the middle years of the 1200s, enemies were not held out. Mongols invaded from the north. Genghis Khan led them. Their hold on China lasted over one hundred years. Maintenance of the wall was not something they did. In 1368, the Mongols were driven out. The emperor who followed wanted them kept outside. He had the wall built again. So much had already crumbled that the task was huge. For roughly the next 275 years, emperors rebuilt the Great Wall. They also expanded it. A large part of the wall people see today was raised in that span. A large part was repaired in that span. Since that span ended, the work has mostly been repair. Genghis Khan also conquered Mongol tribes one by one. He formed the Mongol Empire. Many countries sat inside his empire. Together they covered a huge area of Asia.

5A picture of hang-tu building shows three steps in order. First, a frame made of wood was built, and earth was packed into it. Second, they made the wall taller. Third, the frame came off. The Great Wall grew in stages. Those stages covered thousands of years. Soldiers labored on the wall. Convicts labored on it. Prisoners taken in war labored on it. Peasants labored on it. Other people labored on it too. Often they worked because they were forced. Every wall was made by the hang-tu method. Rammed earth is the other name for it. Packed earth was pounded down inside a frame. The frame might be wood. The frame might be bamboo. Deserts had no earth to use. Packed sand was used instead. Shrubs were used instead. The earliest walls were mainly earth. One earth wall stands in the far western part of the Great Wall. A later time in China's history is the Ming dynasty. Its dates are 1368 to 1644. During those years, many sections took on the face they show today. People still built with hang-tu methods. After that, brick went over the earth. Stone went over it in other places. The cover made the walls look uniform. Workers shaped large bricks in wooden molds. Then kilns baked the bricks. After each brick was set, mortar went into the spaces between. Harsh conditions fell on so many builders that a myth started. People said the mortar held bones of dead workers, ground into powder. Historians in recent times found the true extra ingredient. Sticky rice was that ingredient. A cutaway of a Ming wall labels the parts. At the top are a crenellation and a parapet. A paved surface runs along the top. The outer face is brick or stone. Earth and stones fill the inside. A stone base sits underneath.

6A caption gives Simatai a measure of its own. The length is 5 kilometers. Beacon towers there number thirty-four. Every year, over ten million people travel to China so they can see the Great Wall. Watchtowers along the sections reach an amazing 25,000. Outposts reach 15,000. Put every section together, and the length is about 21,196 kilometers (13,170 mi.). No chain of structures built anywhere has run longer. The widest section measures about 9 meters (30 ft.). The tallest part of the wall measures about 8 meters (26 ft.). Sea level is where the wall sits at its lowest. The highest point stands more than 500 meters (1,600 ft.) above that. A visitor fortunate enough to tour the wall has a choice to make. Badaling is the section people visit most. Closeness to Beijing is one reason. It is also the safest section for walking. The Great Wall Museum stands there. Nine exhibition halls fill the museum. Their topics are history, construction, art, and culture. Badaling can be crowded. Souvenir shops crowd it as well. Most other sections draw fewer tourists. Those sections are much steeper too. A challenging climb is what to expect. Visitors can walk. They can climb. They can take pictures. A guided tour can explain the wall's history. It can explain the construction. Cable car rides exist at some sections. Mutianyu offers a toboggan ride. People who hike the mountainous sections should be in good physical condition.

7A picture from the 2008 Olympic Games shows a woman lifting China's flag. North of Beijing, bicycle racers go past the wall during a race for cyclists. The Great Wall of China remains a remarkable landmark. People around the world still find it inspiring. They still find it fascinating. Beijing was host to the 2008 Summer Olympic Games. The Games always give honor to the host country's history. They always give honor to that country's culture. A representation of the wall stood out in the Opening Ceremony. One course for cyclists made loops between two passes. Those passes were Badaling and Juyong. Say Juyong as JOO-yoong. Fabian Cancellara is a cyclist from Switzerland. He won a gold medal. He also won a silver medal. Afterward he talked about the wall. The labor of building it supplied him with inspiration. It supplied him with strength. An enormous stretch of human history has passed in front of the wall. Early farmers belong to that stretch. Warring states belong to it. Powerful empires belong to it. So does modern-day China. Many people are working so the wall will be preserved. They want it to keep telling part of Earth's story. They want coming generations to hear that story. A convict is someone a court found guilty of a crime. That person serves a sentence in prison. Prisoner is another name. Culture is the set of ideas held by one group of people. Customs of that group belong to culture too. A feat is an amazing action. It can also be an amazing accomplishment. Harmonious means the parts relate, combine, or work as one. The result is a pleasing effect. Kilns are ovens with a special job. They burn materials, bake them, or dry them. Clay, brick, and glass are materials they handle. Nomadic means shifting from place to place. No lasting home is part of that life. Parallel describes things that lie or move in one shared direction. An equal gap stays between them. Raiding is an attack that comes as a surprise. It may be an invasion aimed at one purpose. Restoration is the work of bringing something back. The goal is the condition it had at first. Steppes are grasslands that are flat and dry. Summer there can be very hot. Winter there can be very cold. To wind, as a verb, is to travel a curving line. The course can bend many times. Uniform means matching. It can also mean nearly the same.

76. Stone Mountains for the Dead

1Workers have found more than 100 pyramids in Egypt. This book explains those monuments and the people who raised them. It describes ancient Egypt, the building of a pyramid, and the care of a body. It names famous pyramids in Egypt and pyramids in other lands. A closing section and a word list finish the book. Egypt lies at the northeastern corner of the continent of Africa. The civilization of ancient Egypt once made its home there. Ancient Egypt stands among the most fascinating cultures that have ever existed. Thousands of years ago, Egyptians studied agriculture and irrigation. They practiced architecture and engineering, and they practiced much besides. They raised great structures, and the pyramids are among those works. Study of the pyramids can teach a great deal about this amazing civilization.

2About seven thousand years ago, Egyptians began to settle on the banks of the Nile River. Village life was how they started. Over time the villages joined into larger groups, and those groups became tribes. By about 3200 BCE, one king had united the tribes. People called that king the pharaoh. Most pharaohs were men, yet powerful women ruled Egypt in later dynasties. Life in ancient Egypt depended on the Nile, a river that gives life. The river supplied fish and birds for food. It supplied water to irrigate the crops. It also served as a waterway, so boats could travel and carry goods. For thousands of years the Nile has stayed a busy waterway. Paintings inside a tomb show scenes of the next life. The ancient Egyptians believed that life continued after death. They believed the next life would resemble the life they already knew. They believed they would need the same sorts of tools and objects. For that reason, many people were buried with a collection of their belongings. No burial in ancient Egypt was more lavish than the burial of a pharaoh. Belief held that the pharaoh was the child of the Sun god, called Re or Ra. During life on Earth, the pharaoh was known as Horus. After death, the pharaoh was joined with Re. The new pharaoh, taking the dead ruler's place, became the new Horus.

3Egyptians believed a pharaoh could live forever and go on blessing the people. For that to happen, the body had to be preserved so the spirit would remain alive. They built pyramids to honor pharaohs who had died. Each pyramid held the ruler's body, together with riches and treasures for the next life. The pyramid also guarded the tomb and those treasures against theft. It stood, too, as a monument to the pharaoh's greatness. A pyramid's shape stands for rays of the Sun falling on the Earth. Ancient Egyptians believed a dead pharaoh climbed to heaven along those rays. A pharaoh planned the building long before death was expected, because the work took many years. A large pyramid might need as many as twenty years. Thousands of people were required. Some were skilled, including architects who designed the whole form on the pharaoh's orders. Special knowledge was needed to cut stone out of a quarry and to shape it. After the pyramid stood, skilled sculptors and painters decorated it. A scribe listed every material the work required. The scribe wrote in hieroglyphics, the writing of ancient Egypt. Hieroglyphics are rows of small pictures, and each picture stands for an idea. Old carvings still show samples of that writing.

4A large crew was needed to haul each heavy stone on a sledge. Beyond the specialists, other workers had to move those stones. Some stones traveled by boat from the quarry to the building site. Other stones were loaded onto sledges, which are large sleds made of wood. Workers then dragged the sledges over the desert sand. Until not long ago, historians thought much of this hard labor was forced on enslaved people. In 1990 a tourist in Egypt came upon the remains of an ancient city. Builders of the pyramids at Giza were once thought to have lived in that city. Evidence there suggests the builders were not enslaved. They were skilled craftspeople, about 15,000 of them. Written records suggest that workers were treated well during the job. Farmers are also thought to have helped, especially in the flood season, when fields could not be worked. Farmers counted on floods to lay down fertile soil for crops. Because the pharaoh was believed to be a god's son, farmers thought the ruler could promise good floods. They were glad to serve, and the fertile soil from the floods was their return. A pyramid's site had to be picked with great care. The ground had to be rocky, strong enough for the immense weight of the finished monument. Stones in the Great Pyramid each weighed as much as two tons, or 2000 kilograms. A car weighs about that much.

5Heavy stones were sailed along the Nile River. A pyramid also had to stand near the river, so some stones could move by water from quarry to site. The site had to lie on the west bank. The Sun sets in the west each night, and the dead were believed to dwell in the west. The exact facing of the pyramid had to be set with equal care. Each side had to point to true north, south, east, or west. An astronomer-priest was called to watch the stars and to find true north. While the pyramid was actually going up, many ceremonies took place. The rites were meant to win the gods' help for the endeavor. Several kinds of stone went into the building. Local limestone formed the core. Finer limestone, carried from far away, formed the outer shell. Granite from still farther away was used for the coffin, called a sarcophagus. That same granite decorated the burial chamber. Once place and position were chosen, workers made the ground level. Only then did the real labor of raising the pyramid begin. A picture shows the tomb of King Tutankhamun, known as King Tut.

6The inside of a pyramid was planned to fool thieves and to keep them from the burial chamber and its treasures. If that chamber sat at ground level, or under it, workers set the chamber first. They then raised the pyramid around it, layer upon horizontal layer. Ramps leaned against the sides. Huge stones were dragged up those ramps and set in place. Passages and rooms included dead ends and empty chambers. The maze was meant to confuse anyone who tried to loot the tomb. Enormous stone slabs blocked the way into the real tomb. A drawing shows the tunnels and passages inside a pyramid. A reader can build a small pyramid at home. Sugar cubes will work, and so will cubes shaped from clay. The model may have steps, or flat sides, or a shape the builder invents.

7Ancient Egyptians used a special method to ready an important body for burial. The method is called mummification, and it kept a body whole for thousands of years. The body went to an embalmer, who took out the inner organs and preserved them in canopic jars. Each jar lid had the shape of a guardian god. The body was then left to dry for forty days. After drying, it was washed, rubbed with oil and spices, and packed with preservatives. Many layers of linen, soaked in resin, were wrapped around it so the form would hold. A decorative mask was set on the head, and the whole body was laid in a sarcophagus. Every sarcophagus was painted in an ornate way. Thieves hunting souvenirs damaged one mummy shown in a picture. Burial of a pharaoh came with an elaborate ceremony. The decorated coffin and the canopic jars were carried to the pyramid. Priests and priestesses led a parade of mourners. Servants came behind them, carrying goods for the next life, including food, clothes, and furniture. Before the burial, a priest opened the mouth of the dead pharaoh. People believed this act let the person breathe, eat, and speak in the life to come. The coffin was then set in the tomb and sealed inside the pyramid, in a chamber built to keep it safe. Pharaohs were buried with servant statues called shabtis. People believed a shabti would come alive in the next world and serve the pharaoh again. A picture shows a group of these shabtis.

8The Sphinx watches the pyramids and the other buildings at Giza. The earliest pyramid was made for King Zoser at Saqqâra. People call it a step pyramid because the sides rise like giant stairs. Later pyramids used smaller steps. In time the form changed to pyramids with straight sides, such as the Great Pyramid at Giza. That pyramid was built about 4,500 years ago for King Khufu. It stands 147 meters tall, or 482 feet, and it holds about 2,300,000 blocks of stone. The Great Pyramid belongs to a larger group of pyramids at Giza. King Khufu, his son Khafre, and his grandson Menkaure built them. Other buildings stand around those pyramids. Queen Meritites and Queen Hetepheres have pyramids there. Stone mastabas, tombs of mud brick, hold the rest of the royal family and members of the court. The Sphinx guards the whole site. It is a limestone figure with a king's face and a lion's body, and it stands for the Sun god. Looters have taken the treasures from every ancient Egyptian pyramid. Very few tombs remain intact. Archaeologists have found only one burial of an Egyptian king still whole. That burial is the tomb of King Tutankhamun. It lies in the Valley of the Kings, and it was dug underground rather than set inside a pyramid. Because the tomb was still whole, it has taught archaeologists a great deal about ancient Egyptian culture. Egyptian archaeologists study objects from the tomb, which was found in 1922.

9People in the Americas built pyramids too. The first rose in Central America and in the northwest of South America. Before long, pyramid building spread into North America as well. Several cultures of the New World that raised pyramids are described here. The Maya, and other peoples of Central America, built stepped pyramids. Stairs decorated with sculptures and with writing climbed to temples at the top. Some of these pyramids held tombs of kings, and some did not. Chichén Itzá is one of the best-known Mayan pyramids. It was rebuilt over an older pyramid, and the pyramid seen today was raised around 1100 CE. A map marks pyramid sites in the New World, and a picture shows Chichén Itzá. The older pyramid, built 100 years earlier, held a stone jaguar. The jaguar was painted red, and its eyes were jade. For the Maya, the jaguar symbolized the fertility of the Earth, and people worshipped it as a god. The Aztecs, another people of Central America, built the Great Pyramid Temple. They most likely raised it in the 1300s. It stood in their capital, Tenochtitlán, on an island in Lake Texcoco in Mexico. Aztec belief said the Sun god needed blood from human hearts in order to stay strong. Without that blood, the Sun would die and the world would end.
