Prisoners captured in war were sacrificed, and those killings were a regular part of Aztec life. The sacrifices happened at the Great Pyramid Temple.

10Peoples of northwestern South America also raised pyramids with flat tops and with steps. The Moche, who flourished from 100 BCE to 800 CE, built the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon. After a gap of 600 to 700 years, pyramids were raised by the Inca. In the Inca empire, the Temple of the Sun was the shrine held most sacred. The temple was a pyramid, and a huge disk of gold inside it stood for the Sun god. The Inca believed their rulers descended directly from the Sun. A picture shows the Pyramid of the Moon at Teotihuacan in Mexico. Another picture shows the pyramids at Meroë in Sudan. Builders in other cultures around the world have used the pyramid form. The pyramids at Meroë show exchange between cultures. That exchange linked ancient Egypt with Nubia, an empire and one of Africa's earliest civilizations. When two cultures exchange in this way, each helps the other change, grow, or take shape. Pyramids in the Nubian style were built from 700 BCE to 300 BCE. They joined Egyptian forms of culture with other influences from Africa. Pyramid designs also appear in parts of Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. Modern buildings in many countries use the pyramid shape, including works in France, England, and the United States. A pyramid of modern times was raised in Egypt to honor President Anwar Sadat, who was assassinated in 1981.

11People are working to preserve the pyramids of ancient Egypt and to protect pyramids elsewhere. Pollution, the spread of cities, tourism, and other troubles threaten the pyramids at Giza. The Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza still stands. It is the single survivor among the seven famous wonders left from ancient times. Every pyramid and every tomb is a wonder that deserves to be preserved. Study of pyramids teaches us about ancient cultures that were complex and fascinating. It teaches what people of those times were able to accomplish. It also teaches how those cultures honored their leaders and how they worshipped their gods. Each year, millions of tourists from around the world visit the pyramids at Giza. An embalmer is a person who treats a dead body with chemicals so it will not rot quickly. Mastabas are tombs of ancient Egypt. They are oblong, built of mud brick, with a flat roof and sides that slope. An endeavor is a serious effort to carry out a hard task. Mummification is the ancient Egyptian way of preserving a dead body. Enslaved describes someone kept in slavery, owned by another person or forced to work for that person. Pharaoh is the title of a ruler in ancient Egypt. Hieroglyphics are pictures or symbols that stand for words, syllables, or sounds. Ancient Egyptians and other peoples used them instead of letters of an alphabet. A quarry is a place where stone, marble, or slate is dug out for building. A sarcophagus is a coffin or a tomb, often of limestone, and often carved and richly decorated. Historians are people with expert knowledge of the past. Lavish means extravagant, or very generous. A scribe was a writer by trade, paid to record information.

77. Stone Ruins of Great Zimbabwe

1A person on a hilltop wall looks out over the striking land around Great Zimbabwe. The ruins of that once-magnificent city spread across a wide area. Rolling hills fill the land. Huge piles of boulders rise in many places. Massive stone walls stand across the landscape. In some spots, the walls reach 11 meters. That height equals 36 feet. The ruins cover 728.4 hectares. That area equals 1,800 acres. About 1,400 American football fields, set side by side, would cover nearly the same ground. The ruins offer a glimpse of life at Great Zimbabwe from the eleventh century to the fifteenth century. The empty city also holds many mysteries that no one has solved. The account ahead starts with the size of the place. It then tells why the nation takes pride in the ruins. It describes a city of stone. It describes an empire that grew rich. It explains how people raised the walls. It asks who built the city. It ends with the work of protecting Great Zimbabwe.

2Zimbabwe's southeastern area is where these mysterious ruins stand. Zimbabwe is a nation in southern Africa. Mozambique lies next to it. South Africa lies next to it as well. Zambia is another neighbor. Botswana is a neighbor too. Lake Mutirikwi is a landmark nearby. The town of Masvingo is nearby too. A map of this part of Africa marks Zambia and the Mozambique Channel. It also marks Harare, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and Masvingo. Botswana and South Africa appear on that map as well. In the late 1800s, the land now called Zimbabwe was a colony under British control. People called the colony Southern Rhodesia. Zimbabwe gained independence from Britain in 1980. Their new country needed a fresh name. For a long time, this ancient city made the nation proud. They chose to name the country after that famous ancient city. At the city's north end is the Hill Complex. Three main sections stretch across the ruins. One section is the Hill Complex. Another is the Great Enclosure. The third is the Valley Ruins. The Hill Complex measures about 100 meters long. That length equals 328 feet. It measures about 45 meters wide. That width equals 148 feet. A steep hillside at the site's northern edge lifts this section high. The rest of the city looks beautiful from that height. They also see the valley around it. Six upright posts stand on the hill. Sculptures of birds top those posts. Experts think the Hill Complex may have been the city's spiritual center. They also think it may have been the home of the kings. A site is the place where something is found or where an event happened. Something spiritual connects to the spirit, to the soul, or to a divine being. To say a place functioned as something means it served that purpose.

3Religion in the city probably centered on the Hill Complex. It was also probably the place where the kings lived. Experts think the people of Great Zimbabwe lived in the Valley Ruins. The city's wealthy residents likely lived in the Great Enclosure. Some stretches of wall rise 11 meters. That height equals 36 feet. A three-story building is about that tall. In some places, the walls are up to 6 meters thick. That thickness equals 20 feet. The walls curve without a break. In some places they are quite smooth. In some places they are decorative. Curves in the Great Enclosure's walls show what the builders preferred. The builders favored rounded shapes. They did not favor angular shapes. Visitors find the Great Enclosure on the site's south side. Workers built it in the 1300s. The city was at its most successful then. South of the Sahara Desert, no ancient African structure is larger. An oval is the shape of the Great Enclosure. Around the outside, it measures 250 meters. That distance equals 820 feet. The builders used about one million stones. Just inside the outer wall, an inner wall forms a narrow passage. The passage leads to a tower shaped like a cone. The tower's purpose is unknown to archaeologists. They also do not know why people built the Great Enclosure. It is possible that the enclosure was a royal palace. The Valley Ruins occupy the ground that separates those two stone areas. Many smaller houses fill that valley area. Those houses are made from a mix of clay and gravel. People call that mix daga.

4In the fourteenth century, a powerful empire had this city at its center. The number of residents may have passed ten thousand. Some researchers estimate a population as high as twenty thousand. Stone buildings may have housed the empire's wealthy people. Those stone buildings are found in the Hill Complex. The Great Enclosure has stone buildings as well. Peasants likely lived in daga structures through the valley. Someone here may have carved a woman from soapstone. The people grew crops. They raised cattle. They also took part in a large trade network. The city lay on a busy trade route. Ports on the Indian Ocean connected, along this route, with other African regions. People of Great Zimbabwe mined gold from the hills around the city. They traded that gold for goods from West Africa. They also traded it for goods from the Middle East. They even traded it for goods from China. A sculpture that may come from Great Zimbabwe mixes two kinds of features. Some features belong to an eagle. Other features belong to a person. The city was once very rich. It was once very powerful. Around the midpoint of the fifteenth century, the city stood empty. Some people think too much farming ruined the land around the city. Others think the people moved so they could follow trade routes that had shifted. Why this great city collapsed is still unknown to scholars. The most famous artworks recovered from Great Zimbabwe are eight soapstone bird statues. Workers found them in the Hill Complex. The sculptures may have stood for royal authority. They may instead have stood for the ancestors of the kings. The bird statues sat on top of columns. They likely served as protectors. Those sculptures gave Zimbabwe the idea for its national symbol. The symbol appears on the country's flag. It also appears on the country's coins.

5The Great Enclosure's walls took an estimated million bricks, or even more. Most walls at Great Zimbabwe are made of stones shaped like bricks. The builders cut those stones from the huge boulders around the city. Fire was used to heat the boulders. Cold water came next, poured over the hot stones. That process made the stones split. The granite boulders they used split along straight lines by nature. Those lines made the rock excellent for shaping into bricks. The builders stacked the brick-shaped stones one on top of another. In most brick walls made today, mortar holds the bricks together. Mortar is a substance like cement. Mortar was not part of the building method at Great Zimbabwe. Each wall is a bit thicker at the bottom than at the top. That shape made the towering walls stable. Huge boulders form part of the Hill Complex walls. They also used cut stones. Some of the more careful walls are as smooth as walls people make today. Another striking feature of the ancient walls is their path. They form curves. They do not form straight lines. A characteristic is a feature that helps identify a thing or a group of things. Researchers are not sure why the people built such massive walls. It seems clear that the walls were not designed to hold up weight. Defense against enemies may have been one reason for the walls. They may have built them to give the ruling class more privacy. The walls may also have displayed the king's power.

6Exploration of these ruins by Europeans started late in the nineteenth century. They did not believe builders from the local African community could have made such a city. Wood found at the site had come from the far north. That wood led some Europeans to think another civilization had built the city. They pointed to people who lived along the Mediterranean Sea. Proving that idea took them decades of effort. Objects at the site pointed to local builders, yet the explorers paid those objects no mind. Their search harmed sections of the site. They destroyed other parts during that search. What they hoped to find were signs of a culture from far away. Shared ideas and customs of one group of people make up that group's culture. Artifacts are objects that humans made or used long ago. Finally, in 1905, an archaeologist studied the artifacts from the site. His study showed that local Africans were the builders. Scientists who study what ancient cultures left behind are called archaeologists. In 1892, artists drew how the Great Enclosure was laid out. They also show artifacts found near the site. Several tribes say the people of this ancient city were their ancestors. A descendant comes later in the family line of a person or a group from earlier times. Today, most people credit the Shona with building that ancient city. For many centuries the Shona have made their home in that area. Some artifacts match items the Shona used in a later time. Tools from the ruins look much like tools Shona people used in the nineteenth century. Many people say a Shona phrase is the source of the word Zimbabwe. That phrase means stone houses. Traditional clothing is still worn by Shona people today.

7At night, starlight falls across these ruins. In 1986, a United Nations organization named the ruins a World Heritage Site. The organization works in education, science, and culture. People know it by the short name UNESCO. Because of that title, nearly every country accepts the importance of the site. They see it as worthy of admiration. They also see it as worthy of protection. Time has still harmed the site. Visitors arrive from many countries. Those visits add to the need for repair. Plants may cover many structures that are still standing. Weather has also worn the site down. More funding is needed to study the ruins. More funding is needed to preserve them. More staff are needed for that work as well. Roughly a thousand years have passed since the oldest walls here were raised. Good care could keep them standing for another thousand years. Heritage is a way of life, a tradition, or a feature passed down from one generation to the next. What is left of old buildings, or of other old structures, is called ruins. An enclosure is an area that something surrounds and seals off. Daga is a building material. Daga can also be described as clay mixed with mud.

78. Storms Made of Dust and Sand

1A sandstorm in China surrounds people who are walking. The year is 2008, and they are marking a festival. In September 2009, residents of eastern Australia watched the color of their world change. Strong winds had lifted dirt that was dry as bone. The storm rolled toward the east. It grew into a moving cloud of dust. The cloud was more than 500 kilometers (311 mi.) wide. It was 1,000 kilometers (621 mi.) long. Dust settled over towns. It settled over cities. Sky and land turned a strange reddish orange. Australians said the 2009 sky looked like a scene from a film about disaster. Meteorologists said that region had not seen so bad a dust storm in nearly seventy years. Drivers could not see well, so they slowed down. They switched on their headlights. Airlines called off flights because the conditions were hazardous. Doctors told people with asthma to remain indoors. They gave the same warning to people with other health problems. When the dust finally settled, a huge mass had fallen into the ocean. The mass was about 2.5 million metric tonnes (2.75 million tn.). Meteorologists label this dramatic Australian storm an SDS event. The letters stand for sandstorm or dust storm. These fierce weather systems seriously threaten human health. They threaten the land itself.

2Thunderstorms often create powerful winds. Other strong weather that stirs the atmosphere does the same. When a hard gust crosses dry ground, it shoves bits of earth ahead. It can also lift those bits into the air. Earth plus wind is the simple recipe for an SDS event. These events happen most often in arid parts of Earth. Deserts are arid. So are other places that get little rain. Such land covers about 40 percent of all the land on Earth. A 2016 map from the United Nations Environment Programme shows regions at risk. A sandstorm is shown blowing across Jordan. Jordan is a country in the Middle East. People sometimes treat every SDS storm as the same kind. Some meteorologists separate the kinds. Other scientists do too. Sandstorms, as the name says, happen where the ground is sand. The Gobi Desert in Asia is one of those places. Another sandy region is the Middle East's Arabian Desert. A strong gust lifts the upper layer of sand. A sandstorm stays near the ground. It seldom climbs higher than 15 meters (49 ft.). Dust is lighter than sand, so a sandstorm usually carries dust as well. A dust storm can start wherever the soil is dry. Land dried out by drought is especially likely. With no moisture, dirt does not cling together. It crumbles into smaller bits of dust. Those bits are smaller than grains of sand. They are lighter. Wind can therefore move dust farther than sand. It can move dust faster. Dust storms often lift dust 10 kilometers (6 mi.) or more into the atmosphere.

3A haboob is one particular kind of SDS event. Violent weather is the cause. A haboob can form anywhere SDS conditions already exist. It begins when a powerful weather front sends down very cold, very fast wind. A thunderstorm can be that front. Downward gusts can scoop up a great load of sand and dust. The wind builds giant walls of that material. A wall may stand 457 to 1,524 meters (1,500 to 5,000 ft.) high. The wall can hide the Sun. Seeing ahead becomes very hard. Day can look like night, so people also call haboobs black blizzards. One storm can cover a huge area. The width can reach 160 kilometers (100 mi.). The storm can travel 320 kilometers (200 mi.). Now and then it goes even farther. Some have crossed the Pacific Ocean. Haboobs arrive with thunderstorms. Cold air drops from high in the sky down to the ground. The drop drives sand and dust up to great heights. In Arabic, habb means wind. It can also mean to blow. Haboob means blowing with fury. Each year, storms carry orange dust out of the Sahara Desert. The dust crosses the Atlantic Ocean and reaches North America and South America. About 2,600 kilometers (1,616 mi.) separate those lands. How often an SDS event happens depends on place and on conditions. How severe it is depends on those things too. Sandstorms and dust storms usually come in the driest season. In much of China, and in other parts of Asia, that season may run from November to April. In the Sahara of North Africa, the events come most often from June to September. Summer brings haboobs often to Arizona and the wider American Southwest. Heavy rain is frequent then. In 2012 a massive haboob crossed Phoenix, Arizona.

4A sandstorm or a dust storm can make ordinary life miserable. Blowing dust pushes people indoors. High wind can cut off electric power. Drivers face serious risk as well. Dust that suddenly blinds them can cause crashes. Officials tell drivers to leave the road and wait until the storm passes. In 2014, drivers in Kuwait faced those dangers during a sandstorm. Kuwait is in the Middle East. The worst harm from an SDS event often shows up after the sky clears. Dirty air is linked to about three million deaths worldwide each year. The World Health Organization, called WHO, estimates that SDS events make some of those people sick. Counting the people harmed directly by sand and dust is difficult. As a safeguard, WHO says to wear a mask outdoors during an SDS event. The advice covers anyone who must walk or work outside. People with asthma are asked to stay inside. People with lung trouble are asked to stay inside. People with heart trouble are asked to stay inside. Bacteria are another major threat. Viruses are a threat. Fungal spores are a threat. Grains of sand and dust can carry all of them. Once the grains are in the air, breathing them in is easier. Research shows that SDS events can carry grave infections across long distances. Thousands of meningococcal meningitis cases in North Africa have been linked to these storms. The first part of the name is said muh-nin-juh-KAH-kuhl. The second part is said meh-nin-JY-tiss. This bacterial illness attacks the brain. It attacks the spinal cord. It can cause death. In the American Southwest and in northern Mexico, some dust storms carry fungal spores. The spores cause valley fever. Chest pain can be a sign. Coughing can be a sign. Rashes and infections of the breathing system can be signs. In some cases valley fever ends in death. In 2010, a woman in Beijing, China, shields herself during a sandstorm. Not every dust storm is bad news. Saharan dust lifted by wind each year weighs about 18 million metric tonnes (20 million tn.). The dust crosses the Atlantic. Much of it comes down in South America. Some comes down near the Amazon River. African dust brings nutrients the Amazon region does not have. The Amazon's thick rainforest depends on that dust.

5Farmland and the food grown on it face a different danger from these storms. The lands most at risk have few plants to stop erosion. Erosion can mean water or ice carrying soil away. It can mean wind blowing soil away. Roots of trees usually pin soil down. Roots of bushes and of grasses do the same. Without those roots, one storm can strip the soil. Dry weather can turn the top layer of soil into dust. Plants need that layer. Nutrients in it let them grow. After wind removes the topsoil, bare ground remains. Crops cannot be grown there. The Dust Bowl in the United States during the 1930s is an extreme case. The case reveals the harm these dusty winds can bring to farmland. Farmers on the Plains suffered a harsh drought through the whole decade. Those states lie in the middle of the country. From 1934 onward, huge dust storms made life even harder. The Dust Bowl was one major cause of the Great Depression. In those years, many Americans went hungry. Many had no home. In the hardest-hit places, animals died because they could not breathe. Dirt buried houses halfway. Some 2.5 million people were gone from Dust Bowl country by 1940. They hoped to begin again somewhere else. The U.S. government answered with programs for rural places. Farmers were taught better ways to guard the soil. The lessons also covered how to slow erosion. Another serious SDS threat is deserts spreading outward. The name for that spread is desertification. Each year, topsoil along a desert's edge dries up and blows off. The desert grows. Storms that come often and hit hard speed the process up. A loss has been reported by China's State Environmental Protection Administration. China loses nearly a million acres of fields every year. Desertification pushes residents out of some lands in Asia, in Africa, and in the Middle East. Farmers must leave. Villagers must leave. Fields and gardens cannot grow food once the soil is no longer healthy. In 2014, a farmer in Yemen herds animals during a drought. Yemen is in the Middle East.

6The World Meteorological Organization, called WMO, watches sandstorms and dust storms worldwide. It warns that these storms are growing more numerous. They are growing stronger. Officials fear the rise is a worrying sign of climate change. Slow climate change, over a long time, is natural. Across that long time, energy coming from the Sun shifts. Right now Earth is warming at a frightening pace. Most scientists say certain human actions are the cause. Destroying forests on a huge scale is one major example. Burning fossil fuels is another. Oil and coal are fossil fuels. If world temperatures keep climbing, the danger stays. Stronger SDS events, and more of them, remain a steady threat. Scientists are also fascinated by dust storms on other planets. Mars is one of those planets. Some Martian storms grow large enough to circle the whole planet. Telescopes on Earth can see them. Dust on Mars can spoil a space mission to the Red Planet. It clings to machines. It covers solar panels that refill electric batteries. An artist pictured the look of blowing dust on Mars. WMO officials urge towns and countries to prepare more carefully. One way to cut future harm is to protect land that is easily damaged. The main step is to reduce erosion. People and governments fight desertification by planting. They plant new forests on land that is at risk. Rows of trees and shrubs, set in the right places, work as windbreaks. A windbreak can stop a strong wind. It also keeps dirt in place. It keeps moisture in place. Farmers in West Africa plant trees and look after them. The trees help hold soil. They help hold crops. They help stop the Sahara from moving onto more farmland. The work has brought back millions of acres of trees that hold the desert off. Sharper forecasts can limit damage too. Closer watching of the storms can do the same. Like other weather reports, a forecast warns people that a storm is coming. People can then take care ahead of time. Watching the storms also gathers useful data. The data show where storms form and how they form. They show how storms behave and what they do. The Great Green Wall includes a tree planted by a woman. That project fights desertification along the Sahara.

7Dust from a Sahara sandstorm turned snow orange. The snow lay in Russia and in eastern Europe. Climate scientists have recorded more sandstorms. They have recorded more dust storms. The increase covers the last fifteen years. They also report that dry regions are growing at a worrying rate. Higher temperatures worldwide are feeding more thunderstorms. The winds are stronger. Those winds bring SDS events more often. More sand lies ahead for the globe's driest regions. They are set for more dust and more storms. Slowing the conditions behind this rise will take large efforts by many nations. Fresh ideas will be required. Plans that last many years will be required too. These words help with the topic. Arid means very dry. Asthma is a condition of the lungs that makes breathing hard. Encroaching means creeping into a place beyond the usual or allowed limit. Erosion is rock or soil taken away by water, by wind, or by ice. A gust is a short, strong burst of wind. A haboob is a large sandstorm or dust storm. Violent weather over dry land creates it. Hazardous means full of risk or danger, above all to life or health. To inhale is to draw breath in. A meteorologist studies the air around Earth, along with climate and weather. Parched means dried out badly by heat or by a lack of water. Respiratory describes breathing, or the body parts used to breathe. Vulnerable means easy to damage or easy to attack.

79. Taj Mahal

1Agra, India, is the home of the Taj Mahal. The Yamuna River runs by Agra, and Burhanpur, the Arabian Sea, and the Bay of Bengal are shown with it. The Taj Mahal is a magnificent creation of the Mughal dynasty. It was built in the 1600s to honor someone who was loved very much. The Mughals are famous for rich works of art and beautiful architecture. Their family name, Mughal, gave rise to the word mogul. A mogul is someone as wealthy and powerful as the richest king. The fifth Mughal ruler, Shah Jahan, built the Taj Mahal.

2People picture the white dome, but the Taj Mahal is a 16-hectare, or 42-acre, complex. It was designed as the paradise home of Shah Jahan's favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal. Buildings, walls, gates, and gardens follow the Islamic idea of a perfect heaven. Flowers and fruit trees once grew here, but grass fills the grounds now. Four water channels meet at a center pool and stand for four rivers in the Koran. The layout includes towers, a riverfront terrace, a mosque, a jawab, gardens, a forecourt, and the Great Gate. Visitors enter the Great Gate of red sandstone and marble, with words from the Koran and inlaid flowers. Two eight-sided towers stand beside the gate, the arch frames the onion dome, and the channels mirror it.

3The framed mausoleum is the first thing visitors see through the Great Gate. It sits on a raised marble platform that dominates the grounds. Four towers surround it, and each is more than 40 meters, or 130 feet, tall. Most buildings are red sandstone, but the mausoleum, platform, and towers are white marble. White is the Islamic color of mourning and shows the faith of the person buried there. Shah Jahan's public tomb lies next to the tomb of his third wife, Mumtaz Mahal. Carved marble screens cover the windows and surround both coffins in an eight-sided room. The eight-sided tomb stands for her paradise mansion, and the marble can change color and glow.

4The upper coffins are fake, and the real graves lie in a private room below. Some experts say this richest tomb stands for Mumtaz's heavenly crown. The word taj comes from the Persian word for crown. Geometric designs cover the floor, while vines, flowers, and butterflies cover the walls. Artisans set jade, jasper, turquoise, lapis lazuli, diamonds, rubies, amethysts, and other gems into the art. Thousands visit daily, but his other two wives lie in unmarked tombs. Shah Jahan met Arjumand Banu at fifteen, when she was fourteen, and they married in 1612. He gave her the title Mumtaz Mahal, Chosen One of the Palace, and she died at thirty-eight in his camp in 1631 giving birth to their fourteenth child.

5A court historian said Shah Jahan's beard turned white and he cried so often he needed glasses. He gave up jewelry, fancy clothes, and music, and banned celebrations every Wednesday, the day she died. Each year on her anniversary, he required his court to wear white. He chose a slow bend on the western bank of the Yamuna in Agra, near royal garden mansions. The river kept the banks from washing away, mirrored light on the marble, and fed the garden channels. Building began in 1632, lasted nearly twenty-two years, and used over twenty thousand workers and a thousand elephants. Stone and gems came from China, Tibet, and Afghanistan, and ox teams hauled marble for ropes and pulleys. The tomb is about 70 meters tall, is estimated to weigh 11,000 metric tons, and cost about 32 million rupees.

6The Taj Mahal is open from sunrise to sunset every day except Friday, the Muslim holy day. Visitors may view it by moonlight on the full moon and the nights just before and after, except in Ramadan. It is not the same place Shah Jahan built, for after his death it was nearly abandoned. Thieves took gems, gold lamps, Persian carpets, and other decorations. In the late nineteenth century the British ruled India and began to restore the Taj Mahal. They repaired damaged marble, replaced missing screens and lamps, and made lawns like the gardens of 1899. Pollution, marble cancer, and crowds harm it, so India made a 2-kilometer traffic-free zone and banned polluting industries. It has survived earthquakes, lightning, wars, and floods, and artisans still restore its old marble art.

7Early and late in the day, visitors get unforgettable views of the changing light. Thousands of visitors from all over the world come every day. The United Nations declared the Taj Mahal a World Heritage Site. An international vote made it one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Shah Jahan wanted a memorial for his beloved wife that the whole world would admire for all time. The Taj Mahal may not last forever. Yet centuries after it was built, it remains one of the most beautiful memorials ever created.

80. The Air Around Earth Is in Danger

1Inside: an opening. The air around Earth. The ozone layer. Finding the ozone hole. Chemicals that open that hole. How the world answered. A warming planet. Gases that hold heat. A debate across nations. What a person can do. A closing word. Words to know. Topics in this book. A satellite picture shows the layers of air around Earth. Opening A protective blanket wraps Earth. That blanket is the atmosphere. Many gases mix together to make it. Three of those gases matter most. Nitrogen is one. Oxygen is one. Carbon dioxide is one. Survival for living things depends on those gases. Harmful rays from the Sun are filtered by this blanket. Heat is kept from racing away into space too fast. Life on Earth stays inside a narrow band of conditions. The amount of gas has to be right. The temperature range has to be right. The balance of sunlight has to be right. Proper conditions for life are kept in place with the atmosphere's help.

2The air around Earth Five layers divide the atmosphere. Move upward and the conditions change. Farther from the surface, the air grows colder. It also grows thinner. The troposphere is the layer nearest the ground. Clouds form there. Precipitation falls there. Next comes the stratosphere. It reaches about 50 kilometers above the ground. That height is 31 miles. Passenger jets on commercial routes cruise near 11 kilometers of altitude. That distance is 6.84 miles. They ride in the calmer, lower part of the stratosphere. Above that sit the mesosphere and the thermosphere. Those layers begin at 50 kilometers. They continue past 90 kilometers above the surface. In miles, the span is 31 to 56. The exosphere is the outermost layer. It is very thin. A shield made of ozone Oxygen gas has a special form, and that form is ozone. Each of the five layers holds a different amount. A great deal sits in the upper stratosphere. People treat that band as its own sublayer. They call it the ozone layer. The Sun's harmful ultraviolet rays are taken in by that sublayer. Protection is the reason it is called good ozone. All matter in the universe is built from tiny particles called atoms. Earth has ninety-four natural substances. Scientists call those substances elements. No two elements share the same kind of atom. Atoms join, and the things on Earth are the result. A combination of atoms is a molecule. The oxygen we breathe has two oxygen atoms in one molecule. The symbol is O2. Ozone is an oxygen molecule with three atoms. The symbol is O3.

3Ordinary oxygen molecules are broken apart by UV rays. Two separate atoms are what remain. Those atoms can join other oxygen molecules. Ozone is the result. Inside this layer, ozone is always being made. Destruction never pauses. In ordinary conditions the total barely shifts. The balance does not tip very far either way. Ultraviolet light, called UV, does both jobs. It creates ozone. It also destroys ozone. Creation starts when UV splits O2, the gas we call oxygen, so that two lone atoms remain. Each of those atoms is written O. One of those atoms may join an oxygen-gas molecule. Ozone, with three atoms, is what forms. UV can also alter ozone that already exists. It pulls away one oxygen atom. That freed atom then reacts with a molecule of ozone, written O3. The ozone splits into two molecules of oxygen. Those two are O2 plus O2. Sunlight is a mix. Some of the light we can see. Some we cannot. Wavelengths differ. The colors we can see run from the red end to the violet end. Long wavelengths carry less power. They make red light. Shorter wavelengths are more powerful. They make blue light. They make violet light. Keep shortening the wavelength and the light turns invisible. Ultraviolet light is powerful, and it cannot be seen. Skin cancer can come from it. Eyes can be damaged. Plants can be hurt. Ocean life can be killed. Some biologists think extra ultraviolet light is bleaching color from corals around the world. Rainbow colors are the range people can see with their eyes. Those waves are the longer ones. The shorter waves, called ultraviolet, stay unseen.

4Creation and destruction of ozone never stop. Because of that, the amount in the ozone layer stays fairly constant. Harmful UV is kept from Earth's surface by the layer that forms. Ozone also forms close to the ground. Plants are harmed by this kind. Animals are harmed by it. People call it bad ozone. Cars release chemicals called pollutants. Factories do the same. On a hot day, sunlight starts a reaction. The pollutants meet oxygen, and harmful ozone forms at ground level. Polluted air can mean limits on time spent outdoors. A warning goes out if ground-level ozone climbs to a dangerous height. People who have trouble breathing are told to remain indoors. Finding the hole Scientists working in Antarctica, back in the 1970s, measured a rise in ultraviolet light reaching Earth. Satellites later confirmed a change. In some places the ozone layer was absorbing less UV than in earlier years. Maps from those satellite readings showed a gap. The gap sat above the South Pole, inside the ozone. The year 1994 found ozone down to half the level measured in the 1970s. Signs showed the hole above Antarctica spreading past the polar region. The spread was heading for the equator. More people live in that direction. People were under threat. So was the environment. A small piece of math belongs here. Lose one percent of the ozone in the stratosphere, and UV-B light at the ground rises by two percent. A chart then asks what the rise would be if the ozone loss were ten percent.

5Destruction of ozone is greatest near the North Pole and the South Pole. Winter is the season, because polar regions have strong winds and low temperatures. Warmer months let the ozone layer rebuild. Winter at Antarctica, the South Pole, falls during summer in the Arctic, the North Pole. An instrument goes up from Antarctica, launched by scientists there. Measuring the ozone layer is its job. Charts from NASA record how much ozone is present each day. The lowest level ever recorded came in 2006. Chemicals that open the hole Scientists looked for reasons the ozone levels were changing. Factories, they learned, were sending out chemicals known as CFCs. The longer name is chlorofluorocarbons. Those chemicals can destroy ozone. Chlorine, an element inside CFCs, was the main problem. Air conditioners used CFCs. Insulating foams used them. Spray paint used them. Large amounts of chlorine were released into the atmosphere on a regular basis. Another chemical, bromine, can destroy ozone too. Bromine sits in substances called ODCs. Those letters mean Ozone Depleting Chemicals. Match the amount of bromine to the amount of chlorine in CFCs, and the bromine destroys forty-five times as much ozone. Fire-control chemicals often contain ODCs. Planes drop chemicals onto forest fires to slow them or to stop them.

6Harmful chemicals that break ozone apart can come from nature. An eruption is one example. CFCs rise into the stratosphere. ODCs rise there too. Sunlight breaks those molecules apart. Chlorine atoms come free. Bromine atoms come free. Those atoms then break ozone molecules apart. One atom of chlorine is enough to wipe out 100,000 molecules of ozone. Drift beyond the air is what ends the process for chlorine and for bromine. Natural sources of chemicals can destroy ozone as well. An eruption sends hydrochloric acid far upward, into the stratosphere. Up there the acid separates, and chlorine gas is the result. That gas breaks ozone apart. Some loss does come from eruptions and from other events in nature. Most of the damage still comes from CFCs and ODCs made by industry. How the world answered The link between ozone loss and these chemicals was known. Many countries kept producing them anyway. The chemicals were so useful that people did not want to give them up. Fixing a problem this large took governments working together. In 1987 those countries signed the Montreal Protocol. The agreement called for cutting production of CFCs and of ODCs. A later ban would finish the job by 1996. This counts as a success. It was the first time many nations took on an environmental issue at a global scale. From 2000 onward, the atmosphere has held less and less CFC. ODC levels have fallen as well. Years may pass before anyone can say whether the ozone layer will recover fully. People who study this, in many nations, pass along the satellite findings. Those satellites watch the atmosphere.

7A warming planet Engineers moved fast. They built other chemicals to replace CFCs and ODCs. The hope was to help the ozone layer recover. Some of those replacements are friendly to ozone. They are also powerful greenhouse gases. Carbon dioxide is one greenhouse gas. Methane is another. Released into the atmosphere, they trap heat near Earth's surface. Glass in a greenhouse traps heat the same way. That trapped heat is known as the greenhouse effect. A rise in these gases, in the view of some scientists, has made the air around Earth warmer little by little. A hotter Earth could melt polar ice that sits on land. That ice could break off into the sea. Ocean water levels would climb. A hundred years of records show a warmer Earth, by one degree. The change can look small. Scientists are still concerned. A warming trend that persists could push the temperature higher and higher as time goes on. A hotter Earth may melt the polar ice caps. It may warm the oceans. Ice that melts on land would make the oceans rise. Land near the coast would flood. Habitats of living things would be destroyed. Weather patterns would change on a warmer Earth. Those changes could destroy more habitat. Some plants could die. Some animals could die. Living things that cannot move would be trapped. Corals in the ocean are one example. They would be doomed. Sea life that needs coral reefs for shelter would die too. Sea life that needs those reefs for food would die as well.

8Gases that hold heat Four greenhouse gases add to global warming when they enter the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide is one. Methane is one. Nitrous oxide is one. Fluorocarbons are one. Most scientists give carbon dioxide the blame for roughly three quarters of the warming increase. That share is 76 percent. Machines with gas-powered motors make carbon dioxide. Power plants make it too. They burn fossil fuels. Coal is one of those fuels. Oil is one. Natural gas is one. Cars release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Planes do. Trucks do. Trains do. More warming may follow that release. The trends seen now, most scientists say, come from these four gases. About 13 percent of the warming traces back to methane. Swamps produce it naturally. Livestock produce it when they pass gas. Rotting garbage produces it too. Third place among the contributors belongs to nitrous oxide. Fertilizers are where most of it is found. Nitrogen in fertilizer is important food for plants. Mix that nitrogen with soil and nitrous oxide is produced. Animal waste also produces it as the waste decomposes. Fluorocarbon gases are the last contributor. They also help destroy ozone. Nature almost never makes them. They are almost entirely made by people, so making them can be stopped. A picture shows rotting garbage at a landfill. Methane, a greenhouse gas, comes off that garbage.

9Sharing car rides would cut the carbon dioxide that gas-powered cars and trucks release. So would public transportation. A debate in the world Not everyone agrees about how serious global warming is. Some people say the rise is no cause for worry. Others think the problem will grow worse. They think people should act now, so later warming can be prevented. Their belief is that greenhouse gases should be reduced before it is too late. Cutting those gases may also slow the loss of the ozone layer. Heat gain down low has a cooling result higher up. That cooling sets up conditions for still more breakdown of the ozone layer. Learn how to make fewer greenhouse gases, and further damage to the ozone layer might be avoided. No final answers exist for global warming. The search for working solutions involves scientists on every continent. They say everyone gains if the understanding goes as far as it can. The subject is how to release fewer greenhouse gases. A bicycle instead of a car helps cut greenhouse gases. A skateboard helps. A scooter helps.

10What a person can do Governments have taken steps to cut chemicals that destroy ozone. Industries have taken steps too. They cooperate in programs that measure the ozone layer. They cooperate in programs that monitor it. Each person can protect the atmosphere as well. Less driving means less ground-level ozone. A mower powered by hand can replace a mower that burns gasoline. Guarding ozone high in the atmosphere means trying not to release CFCs. It means trying not to release ODCs. Chemicals that cool old refrigerators should be recycled. Chemicals that cool old air conditioners should be recycled. Foam packaging should be avoided when that is possible. Industries that still use CFCs can be asked, in a letter, what they are doing. The same letter can ask about ODCs. The question is what alternatives they are seeking. A picture makes one comparison. Buses and trains are better for the ozone layer than driving alone is. A closing word Factories release chemicals. So do certain products people use. Part of the protective blanket around Earth is being destroyed by those chemicals. The same releases may be warming the atmosphere. Governments all over the world have acted, and some chemicals are now banned. More action is still needed if future harm is to be prevented. The ozone trouble has taught many lessons. Certain chemicals have to be controlled. Scientists work toward shared goals. Politicians do too. Concerned citizens do too. Perhaps the largest lesson is about our actions right now. We need to think about them. We need to ask how they will affect our well-being later. We need to ask how they will affect the health of our planet.

11Words to know Atmosphere: the gas that surrounds a body in space, such as Earth. Global warming: a rise in Earth's temperature, large enough to change the climate. Atoms: the smallest particles of elements that can exist on their own. Greenhouse effect: heat trapped inside Earth's atmosphere by gases. Chemicals: substances made by a chemical process, or used in one. Molecules: what you get when two or more atoms lock together. They are the tiniest complete bits of a substance. Constant: steady, and not changing. Pollutants: things that make something no longer pure. Contributor: a donor, or a supplier, of something. Precipitation: water falling to the ground. Hail is one form. Sleet is one. Rain is one. Snow is one. Mist is one. Decomposes: breaks down by decay. Ultraviolet: having to do with unseen light energy. Fossil fuels: organic substances such as coal and oil, found underground and used as sources of energy. Topics you can look up Invisible light. Antarctica. Methane. The atmosphere, including the exosphere, the mesosphere, the stratosphere, the thermosphere, and the troposphere. Molecules. The Montreal Protocol. Nitrogen. The North Pole. Oxygen. Ozone, including atoms, the hole, breathing, and the layer. Bromine. Ozone Depleting Chemicals, the ODCs. Carbon dioxide. Chlorine. Satellites. Skin cancer. The South Pole. Damage. Ultraviolet light, called UV, including UV-B. Visible light. Elements. Fluorocarbons. Fossil fuels. Volcanoes. Global warming. Wavelengths. Greenhouse gases. Further reading can follow global warming. It can follow the ozone hole. It can follow CFCs.

81. The Great Dam in Black Canyon

1On guided tours, visitors go inside Hoover Dam for a behind-the-scenes look at how the dam works. From the western side of the dam, they can look across to Arizona. Kayaking is popular on Lake Mead. The pages ahead begin with water in the desert and ask why a dam was built here. They measure a massive structure, follow the construction, and follow a visit. They also follow how the Southwest changed. A glossary ends the book. Every summer in parts of the southwestern United States, temperatures often exceed 100 degrees Fahrenheit, or 38 degrees Celsius. Much of the region receives less than 10 inches of rain.

2The Colorado River is where Hoover Dam stands. Around it lies the Mojave Desert, said moh-HAH-vee. The state line of Arizona and Nevada runs through this spot. The distance to Las Vegas, Nevada, is about 30 miles (48 km). The dam lies to the southeast of that city. Black Canyon was the government's choice. Tall walls and a narrow gap defined the canyon. Solid bedrock was there. Solid walls were there. Nothing weaker could hold a structure so huge. No earlier dam stood on the Colorado River. Hoover Dam therefore had to be extremely large. The river's control rested on this one dam. Only a very tall canyon would do. A watershed map names Nevada, Utah, and Colorado. It names Lake Mead and California. It names New Mexico, Arizona, and the Colorado River. The Pacific Ocean and the Gulf of California appear as well. One photo shows Black Canyon with no dam yet. Another recalls 1905. Floodwater from the Colorado spread across much of Imperial Valley. The Salton Sea came into being. Control of that water took two years. The river bends its way across the southwestern United States. Life-giving water reaches a land that would otherwise stay dry. For centuries, people have made homes on the Colorado's banks. Crop irrigation used that water. In earlier times the supply fluctuated. Spring snowmelt swelled the river. Farms often went under floodwater. By the later part of the year, only a trickle remained. Crops died. Settlers who came early grew discouraged. The water would not stay steady. A search began for control of the river. The year 1901 brought the Alamo Canal. A private company built it. It lay just north of Mexico's border. The plan was to turn the Colorado westward. Imperial Valley, in California, would receive irrigation. Farms then did very well. The year 1905 brought a severe flood that undid the gain. Control gates on the canal were ruined. Much of Imperial Valley was ruined with them.

3Residents of Imperial Valley asked for a bigger canal. Arthur Powell Davis served as chief engineer. His agency was the government office that handles western water. He believed a river dam would work better. More people could receive more water. He studied the Colorado first. Congress heard his findings in 1918. A decade later, Congress approved the building of Hoover Dam. A canal was approved with it. Imperial Valley would get irrigation from that canal. Spending won approval from President Hoover in 1930. The Great Depression was already underway. Its start came only eight months before the project was approved. Hard times in the economy gripped the United States. Work was gone for millions of people. Southern Nevada drew 21,000 arrivals in total. Construction jobs were the magnet. President Hoover pushed to employ as many people as he could. He told crews to begin before the support was ready. Houses were missing. Water fit to drink was missing. A hospital was missing. Other facilities were missing. Early on, camps held some workers and their families. Electricity did not reach the camps. Running water did not reach them. Tents were the homes. The Colorado River was the bathtub. Hoover Dam counts as an arch-gravity dam. A sketch labels downstream, gravity, arch, and upstream. At the time of building, no dam on Earth was taller. The engineering feat was amazing. Six companies had to join their skills. The design shows a gravity dam. It also shows an arch dam. Weight is what a gravity dam relies on. Stored water pushes, and that weight pushes back. An arch dam bends upstream. Canyon walls then take most of the water's push. Squeezing follows. The dam compresses and gains strength. Inside the power plant, moving water is converted into electricity. Lake Mead, the reservoir, holds the stored water. Lake Mead is a lake that people made. No larger one exists in the United States.

4Measurements of Hoover Dam fill one diagram. Thickness at the top is 45 feet (13.7 m). Intake towers number four. Each one rises 395 feet (120.4 m). They control water headed for the power plant. From foundation rock up to the crest, height is 726.4 feet (221.4 m). Across the top of Black Canyon, width is 1,244 feet (379 m). Weight passes 6,600,000 tons (5,987,419 mt). Thickness at the base is 660 feet (201 m). A second map shows how the river was diverted. Arizona and Nevada are labeled. Diversion tunnels, a rock barrier, and cofferdams are labeled. Dry ground was required at the site. The Colorado had to be sent around it. That huge job started in May 1931. Dynamite opened the rock. Each side of the canyon received two tunnels. River water would use those tunnels to pass the site. Concrete then lined the finished tunnels. Danger in the tunnels was extreme. Rocks fell on the crews. Fumes filled the air. Vehicles that burned gasoline, working underground, made the fumes. Up on the surface, other crews raised barriers. Water could not leak through them. Cofferdam is the name. One cofferdam stood upstream of the site. One stood downstream. The upstream cofferdam would push the river into the tunnels. The downstream cofferdam worked beside a rock barrier. Water would not be allowed to run back up the canyon. The work area would stay dry.

5During those same months, high scalers worked the walls. Loose rock came off. Grooves were cut for the dam to lock into. The men often dangled far above the water. Wooden swings held them. Heat reached 120°F (49°C). Jackhammers were their tools. Dynamite was used as well. Several other builds happened alongside the dam. Boulder City rose so workers could live there. A hospital was part of the town. Other facilities were part of it. Tracks for trains went in near the site. Deliveries of supplies used those tracks. A road linked Boulder City with the dam. A power line went in too. Its length was 222 miles (357 km). San Bernardino, California, was one end. Black Canyon was the other. Construction needed that power. High scalers perhaps faced the roughest work on the whole project. Rocks that fell took dozens of lives. Tools that fell took lives too. Deaths from industrial accidents came to almost one hundred men. Ready tunnels let pumps empty the work area. Solid bedrock had to lie under the dam. A cover of silt and stones sat on that rock. The cover was 135 feet (41 m) deep. June 6, 1933, saw the last of it dug away. Tunnel work had started about two years before that day. Concrete could then go in. Huge buckets carried the wet mix downward. Block-shaped molds received it. Form is the name of each mold. Crews smoothed the surface. They drove out air bubbles. They finished that step before hardening began. Fresh layers followed. Steel pipes, narrow ones, ran through the forms. Cold water inside them chilled the concrete fast. Hardened concrete let workers pull the wooden form apart. The same form was rebuilt above the block just finished. A new block was poured there. The stack continued. Columns grew until they hit their final height. Grout closed the gaps between columns. The picture of the method is simple. Blocks of concrete, piled up, became the columns.

6Spillways came after the main dam. These passages would steer high water around the structure. A Colorado flood would have a path that spared the dam. The power plant was built next. Four intake towers were built with it. Flow toward the power plant would be under their control. February 1, 1935, marked the end of the work. Plugs went into the diversion tunnels. Until then, those tunnels had carried the Colorado past the site. Behind the dam, the water rose. It spilled over the cofferdam. Lake Mead took shape. The workforce, by the end, numbered more than 21,000 men. A typical day saw 3,500 of them. Cost of the project was $165 million. In today's money, that is $3 billion or more. Concrete in the dam, the power plant, and the other structures could pave a road. San Francisco would stand at one end of that road. New York City would stand at the other. Cement used in construction passed 5,000,000 barrels. A single day might use 7,500 barrels. It might use as many as 10,800. On September 30, 1935, President Roosevelt led the dedication. He praised the dam as the greatest anywhere in the world. The public has been invited in since 1937. Each year, millions come. Tours of the dam and the power plant draw close to a million of them. Displays fill the visitor center. Natural history of the region is one subject. History of the dam is another. Construction is another. Visitors often leave impressed. Spectacular is a word they use. Amazing is another. Incredible is another. Lake Mead allows fishing in every season. Boating, picnics, and hikes are available in every season too. Nine wilderness areas lie in the region. Animal types number five hundred. Plant types number nine hundred. Inside the visitor center, the view down on Hoover Dam is a bird's-eye view. Tours with guides add details from behind the scenes.

7Las Vegas in 1930 was a stop on the railroad. Residents numbered only about 5,000. Population swelled once Hoover Dam stood finished. By 2013, the count was over 600,000. Across the southwestern United States, the Colorado supplies more water than any other source. Control of that river began with Hoover Dam. History had not seen the river controlled before. Irrigation that farmers could trust reached Arizona. It reached Nevada. It reached California. Drinking water came from the dam as well. Electricity at a price people could pay came too. Growth followed in Los Angeles. It followed in San Diego. It followed in Las Vegas. It followed in Phoenix. It followed in other southwestern cities. Thousands of men found jobs on the project. In a very hard time, the dam stood as a symbol of hope. More than seventy-five years have passed since the dangerous work. The last construction worker known from the project died in 2014. Stories remain. Every ton of concrete holds them. America's landmarks include this one among the most remarkable. Bedrock names the solid rock lying under the surface. To compress is to squeeze tightly so a thing grows smaller. To convert is to change a thing's nature or its form. To divert is to turn something onto a new path. Facilities are places, often buildings, fitted with gear that eases a task. Fluctuating means a measure will not stay still. It may swing sideways. It may rise, then fall. Level can change. Rate can change. Intensity can change. Impressed means moved in a strong way, often for the good and for a long time. To irrigate is to bring water onto land, most often so crops can grow. Parched means dried out, with moisture gone. A reservoir is a big tank or a lake that gathers water and keeps it. People may drink it. Farms may use it. Silt is fine soil, or similar bits, that flowing water picks up and later drops. Transformed means the form has changed, or the look has changed.

82. The Great Stone Rings of Salisbury Plain

1An English historian, almost nine hundred years ago, told a story about Stonehenge. A mythical wizard in that story told a king to raise the monument. Giants have been offered as builders. Wizards have been offered. Space aliens have been offered. Standing before the giant stones in southern England makes those ideas easier to accept. Human hands seem unequal to slabs of that size and weight. Machinery of the modern kind did not exist when the stones went up. Written history had not started when the monument was made. Mystery grows from that fact. This book treats the place as an ancient sacred site. The stones themselves are described. The land around them is described. A building project that lasted ages is followed. Possible purposes are asked about. A visit today is described. The ancient wonder is named at the end, with special words. Anyone who walks among the stones still feels surprise. The historian's tale is only one old explanation. Giants, wizards, and visitors from space have all been suggested because the slabs look too large for ordinary builders. Weight adds to that feeling. No written record from the building years can settle the question. Southern England is where the circle stands. Sacred is one way this book will treat the site. The stones, the land, the long project, the possible uses, and a modern visit all have a place in the pages ahead.

2Hundreds of years of study have been given to Stonehenge. Scientific theories are what archaeologists offer now. Supernatural explanations are no longer the guide. Clues have been dug from the ground. History, creators, and possible purposes have all been sought. Age is one result of the research. About five thousand years is the figure. Earlier guesses had made it younger. The Neolithic period in Britain is when it was built, around 4000 to 2500 BC. The wheel did not exist yet. Metal tools and weapons were not yet known to people living there. About 3000 BC is when archaeologists believe the work began. More than a thousand years of labor followed, across many generations. New finds still appear as digging and research continue. Amazement at what these ancient people built has not faded. An excavation at Stonehenge in 2008 included an archaeologist at work. Earth and enormous stone slabs make the monument. Megaliths is the name for those slabs. The Eiffel Tower is far taller. Mexico's Pyramid of the Sun is far bigger. Awe still hits the thousands of tourists who come each day. Ancient beginnings supply much of the mystery. The design is circles set inside circles. A ditch is the outer ring, running around an embankment of piled soil. Sandstone slabs called sarsen stones form a circle inside that ring. Stone lintels lie over the upright sarsen stones, from one top to the next. All of those standing stones were once linked by the lintels. Another set of standing sarsen stones sits inside the ring. A horseshoe is their layout. Trilithons is their name. Each one is a square arch. Two upright stones plus a lintel across them make the arch. Height of the trilithons runs from 6.7 meters to 9 meters, or 22 feet to 29.5 feet. Bluestone boulders, smaller than the sarsens, also sit inside the circle. Dolerite is the coarse rock that bluestone is. About 2,994 kilograms, or 6,600 pounds, is the weight of the largest bluestone. Other monuments of this kind existed. Single stones and further monuments have been found nearby by archaeologists.

3About 110 meters, or 360 feet, is the width of the circle made by the outer ring. A football field is about that long. Average weight of the blocks is 22,680 kilograms, or 50,000 pounds. A school bus weighs less than one block. Height is more than 5 meters, or 16.4 feet. About 36,000 kilograms, or 79,366 pounds, is the weight of the largest sarsen. Seventeen upright sarsen stones still trace the curve of the Sarsen Circle. Thirty is the number archaeologists believe once stood there. Stones that stand alone are part of the monument too. They sit outside the Sarsen Circle. A map of this region shows the United Kingdom. The Atlantic Ocean and the North Sea are on it. Scotland, England, Wales, Northern Ireland, and Ireland are named. Glasgow, Edinburgh, Belfast, Dublin, and London are marked. Salisbury Plain is the location of Stonehenge. Hills and grassy flatlands in southern England make up that plain. More than ten thousand years of human living here is what the evidence suggests. Trees covered the area in that early time. Animals moved freely. Hunter-gatherers were the people. Deer and other game were hunted. Roots and nuts were gathered. Sacred is how experts think these Neolithic people may have seen the area. Food in abundance may be why they felt that way.

4A cultural change began around 7500 to 4600 BC. Hunting and gathering slowly gave way to farming. More food could be produced because of agriculture. The supply was more reliable too. Field work could take less time once food was secure. Shared projects such as Stonehenge could take the hours that were freed. Moving the giant stones counts, for experts, as a great feat. Stone Age people, in their view, rarely engineered anything greater. About 32 to 48 kilometers, or 20 to 30 miles, is the distance they give for the source of the giant sarsen stones. Wheels and wagons did not exist yet. How, then, did the enormous slabs move? Different theories have been tested by teams of researchers. Skill and strength of humans, they proved, were enough. May 2016 was when researchers set huge stones on wooden sledges. Wooden rails greased with animal fat were the track, and the sledges were pulled along them. Bluestones stayed a deeper puzzle for a long time. Nowhere near Stonehenge has a source for them been found. A quarry in Wales was the source researchers finally located. More than 241 kilometers, or 150 miles, was the distance. Wood platforms may have been built under the stones while the stones were hauled into place. Raising each standing stone was its own hard problem. A pit under the base may have been the first step. Wedges could lift the top until the bottom dropped into the pit. Ropes may have pulled the stone, with care, until it stood. Lintels may have been the hardest pieces to place. Ramps of dirt and wood are one possible method. Such a ramp would run from the ground up to the top of the standing stones. Ropes could slide a lintel up that ramp. The lintel would then rest in place and complete the arch.

5Master builders made these engineering systems, but their names are unknown. Writing was not used. Art was rarely left behind. Languages they spoke are mostly unknown. Religions they practiced are mostly unknown. Archaeology is the source of everything that is known. Pieces of evidence were fitted together. Chemical tests on human skeletons buried near the site give clues. Some builders seem to have moved to the site from elsewhere. Wales was one homeland. Other lands were homelands too. Teeth from one skeleton told of a longer trip. Mainland Europe was where that man had traveled from. About 1,126 kilometers, or 700 miles, was the distance. Archaeologists were shocked by the find. Fame of Stonehenge may have reached far away in ancient times. The skeleton lay in a burial near the monument. Stone wrist guards lay with it. Archers commonly wore guards of that kind. Purpose has been investigated for hundreds of years. More than a mile separated the monument from any human settlement. Shelter does not seem to have been its use. A marketplace does not seem to have been its use. A kind of religious temple is what archaeologists came to believe. Religious use, they also believe, changed across the long history. Ceremonial use changed too. A burial site is how they think it began. As many as 240 people have been found in remains near the monument. Tools and jewelry were buried with some of them. A ritual site was probably another role. Parades of villagers may have come for special events. Crowning a ruler could be one event. A day to honor dead ancestors could be another. Arrowheads turned up in a burial near Stonehenge.

6On December 21, 2014, sunlight passed through the stones of Stonehenge. That date was the shortest day of the year. Astronomy is the heart of another popular theory. Placement of the giant stones lets the sun pass through some of them at set times of year. Solstices make this easiest to notice. About June 21, the summer solstice, is the first day of summer. About December 22, the winter solstice, is the first day of winter. A giant clock is one way to think of the monument. Seasons are what the clock marks. Ancient farmers needed that information. Planting of crops was planned with it. A further purpose has been considered in recent years. A large community project is one idea. People of the area might have been united by the work. Fifteen hundred years passed with Stonehenge as an important center of activity. About thirty-seven hundred years ago, that role ended. The reason is unknown. More than nine hundred thousand tourists come each year now. Touching the giant stones was once allowed. Climbing them was once allowed. Mostly, the stones are off-limits now. By 1900, many upright stones had fallen. British heritage groups chose to put fallen stones back. Archaeological evidence guided the work. Giant cranes did the lifting. Concrete anchors hold some of the standing stones. A clearer sense of the original look was the restorers' hope for the public. Life in England forty-five hundred years ago can be seen at the visitor center. Huts there were built with authentic materials and methods. Ancient crafts are shown by volunteers. Rope weaving is one skill. Pottery making is another. Stone knapping is another, the chipping of flint into stone tools. Reconstructed Neolithic huts can be entered. Builders of Stonehenge might have lived in huts of that kind.

7Investigation of the Stonehenge site is still going on. Magnetic fields can be detected with special tools. Laser scanners measure possible archaeological sites with care. Radars that see into the ground are used. Artifacts and structures hidden below can be detected. Faster discoveries follow from these advances. Diggers are shown the exact spot to open. UNESCO is the short name. The long name belongs to a United Nations body for education, science, and culture. A World Heritage Site is what UNESCO called Stonehenge. Special recognition and protection are what that name says the place deserves. Amazement at Stonehenge is expected to last for thousands of years still to come. A time machine would be needed to know the exact reason for the building. The exact method would stay unknown without one. Visitors will still be amazed. Minds, strength, and teamwork were all required, and they remain astonishing. Students of archaeology worked at the site in 2008. Words for this monument are gathered here. Neolithic names the latest part of the Stone Age, a time known for polished stone tools and weapons. Archaeologists are scientists who study what ancient cultures left behind. Ceremonial describes a thing tied to a formal event on a special day, or used for that event. A quarry is where stone, marble, or slate is dug out of the ground. An embankment is a dirt wall or mound, often holding up a road or holding back water. Restorers repair old or worn things so those things look as they once did. Engineering is designing and building by means of science and math. Ritual describes an action done as part of a ceremony that follows set steps. Heritage is a way of life, a tradition, or a trait passed from one generation to the next. Solstices are two yearly moments, each one a time of greatest distance between the Sun and the equator. Theories are explanations that might be true. Lintels are lengths of stone or wood set over an open space, a doorway or a window among them.

83. The Land Between Two Rivers

1People cut marks into a clay tablet so they could track rations and goods. A sharp tool cut the images into the clay. A map of this early world marks the years 5000 to 2150 bce. It shows the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. It shows the Fertile Crescent and Akkad. It shows the Tigris River and the Euphrates River. It marks Mari, Babylon, Umma, Lagash, Uruk, and Ur. It also shows the Mediterranean Sea, with Europe and Africa nearby. Mesopotamia is a name for land that lies between a pair of rivers. The name points to land between the Tigris and the Euphrates. The first civilizations started to form about 6,000 years ago. At least some people in a civilization make their homes in cities. Those people do specialized jobs. Civilizations have governments. They often have writing. They often have arts. They often have science. They often have trade. They often have monuments. One of the earliest civilizations was found in ancient Mesopotamia. Today the countries of Turkey, Syria, Iraq, and Kuwait cover that old land. Many historians call this river land the place where civilization was born. The parts of this account move from the first settlers to the city of Uruk. They then follow city-states at war. They follow a time of wealth and new ideas. They close with the fall of an empire.

2Ancient Mesopotamian life centered on ground between the Tigris and the Euphrates. People later gave that land the name Fertile Crescent. The first people in Mesopotamia settled the southernmost part of the crescent. Today that area is Iraq and Kuwait. Modern archaeologists found ancient stone tools near the Euphrates River. They also found bricks. They also found pottery. From these objects, researchers could tell how those ancient people lived. Farming villages were already there as early as the year 5000 bce. These early settlers were given the name Ubaid. The name came from the place where the objects were uncovered. A tiny box covered in mosaic pictures may once have held a musical instrument. Its pictures show life in early Mesopotamia. Sumer is the land these Ubaid people settled before anyone else. Until they built settlements, the Ubaid kept traveling. Other Sumerian tribes did the same. They were nomadic hunters and gatherers. They searched for food. They searched for water. Later, the Ubaid learned how to remain in a single spot. They drained marshes. Rich soil let them raise crops. Irrigation canals carried water into places that were dry. River clay was the material for their pots. Reeds from shallow water were woven into baskets. The river's riches met their personal needs. Those riches also gave them goods to trade with travelers. Busy trade paths from Asia and from Europe ran across Sumeria's rich plains. Traders supplied items the Ubaid could not grow. Traders also supplied items the Ubaid could not make. Copper lion heads were common protective figures on Mesopotamian buildings. People set them there as guardians.

3More Sumerian villages appeared in the Fertile Crescent as time went on. Some grew into true cities. Some of those cities became city-states. Uruk was the city that mattered most. Today that place is Warka, in Iraq. Between the years 4100 and 3000 bce, authority in the area was centered at Uruk. It was also the center of trade. Residents in Uruk once numbered as many as eighty thousand. Its area was greater than 2.6 square kilometers. That area equals 1 square mile. Huge buildings of mud brick stood there. A multilevel ziggurat served as a temple. People used it for worship. They also used it for sacrifice of animals and crops. One picture is a drawing of a Mesopotamian temple tower, called a ziggurat. Uruk's ziggurat still has its stone base in the spot where builders first set it. A clay tablet from about 2350 bce lists grain given out each month. The writer used cuneiform script. Pictographs of Mesopotamia showed up first in the city of Uruk. In writing, a pictograph is a symbol. Trade at Uruk helped this early writing grow. Business dealings at Uruk helped the writing grow as well. People marked simple images on clay tablets. The marks added up workers' rations. The marks also kept a record of goods. Those picture marks later became the writing called cuneiform. In that system, symbols stood for sounds. They did not stand for objects. People could use those sound symbols to write in any language.

4Using sounds instead of pictures brought several benefits. Writers could shuffle one group of symbols and spell many different words. Because of that, fewer symbols were needed. The system also made abstract ideas easier to express. Those ideas would be hard to show as pictures. Wedge-shaped cuneiform on clay tablets shows how Sumerians lived in that age. People in Uruk lived in structured societies. People in other city-states of Sumeria did too. A priest-king stood at the highest level. That person led other officials of different ranks. One official was a leader of the plow. Another was a leader of the law. Other leaders followed the same pattern. Three main classes made up society in Mesopotamia. One class was free people. A second class was semi-free people. A third class was enslaved people. Life among Sumer's lower classes is mostly unknown. Most Sumerian women were wives. Most were mothers. Homes and children were in their daily care. School was closed to most girls. Girls from a wealthy family were the exception. Women in Sumer held more rights than women did in Mesopotamia's later cultures. They could own property. They could run businesses. They could act as judges in court. They could act as witnesses in court. They could become priestesses. They could become scribes. They could become physicians. One of the most famous rulers was King Gilgamesh. In Sumerian, his name was Bilgames. People believe he ruled Uruk around 2700 bce. That was during the Early Dynastic Period, from 2900 to 2350 bce. Song and legend turned him into an epic hero. Poems were written about his reign of 126 years. Stories called him a demigod. He was the son of King Lugalbanda. His mother was the Sumerian mother-goddess Ninsumun. Uruk's huge protective wall is credited to Gilgamesh. That wall still stands today. During 2003, scientists from Germany located a tomb in the riverbed of the Euphrates. They thought the tomb belonged to Gilgamesh. The epic's description of a tomb matches this find quite closely. Ancient poems from Mesopotamia, gathered together, make up the Epic of Gilgamesh. The poems tell of an ancient king's battles. They tell of his struggles. They tell of his achievements. He strives to gain immortality. Many people also think no older work of literature still survives. Stone tablets with single poems date to about 2100 bce. In the story, Gilgamesh wears the skins of lions he killed.

5As the Sumerian city-states grew, they began to fight one another for control of the region. They were thriving while those fights increased. Battles grew steadily more frequent. A battle in the year 2525 bce is the earliest Sumerian war described in detail. The city-states of Lagash and Umma fought that battle. Pictures and words cover a tall stone column known as a stele. Speakers say stele as STEE-lee. The carvings show soldiers carrying swords into battle. The soldiers also carry spears. They also carry shields. Wheeled carts carried the army leaders. Pairs of onagers pulled the carts. An onager is a native species of donkey. Materials for making arms arrived along the trade routes. Smiths learned how to melt copper together with tin. Both metals are soft on their own. Together they make a harder substance. People called this alloy bronze. They used bronze for swords. They used it for spear tips. Tin, however, was rare. Traders from central Asia could supply it. Traders from Europe could supply it too. Cutting off trade routes kept weapons out of an enemy army's hands. One damaged fragment of a stele ranks among the oldest historical records known. The fight of Lagash against Umma is what that fragment records. A map of Sargon's Akkadian Empire marks the Mediterranean Sea, Akkad, Egypt, and Syria. King Sargon, ruler of Akkad, ended those wars by seizing the region. He did so in about 2340 bce. Under him, the separate city-states became one realm, the Akkadian Empire. He held power by giving important posts to allies he trusted. Those allies were people he counted as key supporters. That empire continued until the year 2150 bce. Westward, its farthest reach was the Mediterranean Sea. It reached Arabia in the south. It reached Iran in the east. Northward, its farthest reach was the Anatolian Peninsula. Sumerian was not the language the Akkadians spoke. They did adapt the Sumerian cuneiform script. They wrote their own speech with that script. People used the Sumerian language only in official ceremonies. They also used it only in religious ceremonies. Enheduanna is the first poet in the world's history whose name we still know. She was Sargon's daughter. In the city of Ur, her role was high priestess. Many of her poems praised the goddess Inanna. No deity in Mesopotamia was more widely loved than Inanna.

6Quiet years under the Akkadian Empire changed life in this land. The earliest system for sending messages began in Mesopotamia. Workers inscribed clay tablets with messages in cuneiform. They then wrapped each tablet in a clay envelope. A seal belonging to the sender was pressed on the clay wrapper. It was also marked with the name of the person who should receive it. It showed where that person could be reached. No one but the receiver could read the message. Someone had to crack the clay wrapper open to reach the message inside. A central government enforced laws. It enforced regulations. Trade networks expanded. Commerce boomed. People conducted business with cylinder seals. A cylinder seal was a carved tube.
