The owner pressed it into clay. Pressing a seal into clay was like signing a name today. Place value in numbers was another idea these people worked out. The way people measure time uses this same old system. People use numerical base systems when they count certain objects. When they count dozens of eggs, they use base twelve. Twelve eggs equal one dozen. When people count time, they use base sixty. Ancient Mesopotamians devised that system. Sixty seconds make one minute. Sixty minutes make one hour. The earliest pottery wheels have been found in Sumer. Sumer has also yielded the oldest wheels used for travel. Modern life still depends on wheels. Near 3500 bce, Sumerian potters started shaping clay bowls with a flat round tool. That wheel lay level and turned on a center pin. A spin of the wheel let the potter form a bowl whose rim stayed even. The bowl could also have even surfaces. About three centuries after that, Sumerians found another job for wheels. Wheels made it easier to move objects. Wheels made it easier to transport people. They tested many ideas, and then they tried a fresh setup. A single axle carried one wheel at its left end and another wheel at its right end. Loads became much easier to haul with this new device. Little strength was needed to roll that cart over the ground. The design may have been copied by people in other lands. Soon, people used wheels across the world.

7About 2150 bce, this empire came to an end. A severe drought struck it. An invasion by the Gutians struck it too. Speakers say Gutians as GOO-tee-uhnz. These Gutians were wandering people who came out of northern mountains. Bands of Gutian fighters often struck the kingdom's distant edges. As a result, trade slowed. Fields lay untended. In the end, the city of Akkad fell to these wanderers. The Akkadian Empire collapsed. Running a society this complex was something the Gutians barely knew how to do. The web of canals was allowed to break down. They brought on a terrible famine. Their rule of Sumer lasted 125 years. Later ages gave this hard time the name Dark Age of Mesopotamia. Mesopotamia did not return as a thriving empire until the seventeenth century bce. King Hammurabi reigned then. People called the new empire Babylonia. A statue shows Gudea. He was a Gutian prince. His rule in Lagash ran from 2144 to 2124 bce. Nomadic means moving from place to place with no permanent home. An alloy is a metal made by combining two or more metals. Phonologic describes the study of speech sounds inside one language or across several. A city-state is a city or an urban area that behaves like a country of its own. Pictographs are symbols or pictures that stand for words or ideas. Civilizations are organized societies. They have a stable food supply, a government, a social structure, and a culture. They also have written language and religion. Smelted means melted or fused by extreme heat. Buying goods and selling them is what the word commerce means. A stele is a tall piece of rock set upright, either a slab or a column. Designs or words on it usually honor a person or an event. Another spelling is stela. Cuneiform is a writing system of wedge-shaped characters. Several areas of the ancient Middle East wrote with this script. A ziggurat is a rectangular structure of ancient Mesopotamia. Steps rise up its sides. A temple sits at the top. In myth, a demigod is half human and half divine.

84. The Land Called India

1A map of this country sits in Asia. China lies nearby. So do Afghanistan, Bhutan, Pakistan, and Nepal. New Delhi is marked. Bangladesh and Myanmar, also called Burma, are marked. Mumbai is marked. The Arabian Sea is marked. The Bay of Bengal is marked. The Andaman Islands are marked. The Indian Ocean is marked. Sri Lanka is marked. The Nicobar Islands are marked. India’s place is Asia, and most of the country is a peninsula. The northern border has several neighbors. Pakistan is one. China is one. Nepal, said nuh-PAHL, is one. Bhutan, said boo-TAHN, is one. Bangladesh, said bahng-gluh-DESH, lies east of India. Myanmar, said mee-AHN-mar, lies east as well. Just south of India is an island nation. That nation is Sri Lanka, said SHREE LAHNG-kuh. The Arabian Sea lies to the southwest. The Bay of Bengal lies to the southeast. Islands belong to India too. The Andaman Islands, said AHN-dah-mahn, are one group. The Nicobar Islands, said NEE-koh-bar, are another.

2Say DEL-ee and you have the sound of India’s capital. The capital’s name is New Delhi. It sits inside the older city of Delhi. Delhi reaches far back in time. Construction of New Delhi belongs to the early 1900s. British India needed a capital, and this city was made for that role. India was still inside the British Empire. Delhi feels like a maze. Streets are small. Bazaars are crowded. New Delhi offers a contrast. Avenues have room. Shopping centers are modern. Suburbs joined to Delhi now make a huge metropolitan region. The population there is more than twenty million. New Delhi itself is just a slice of that urban spread. Mumbai, said mum-BY, is the other giant in the race. Each city wants the title of largest in the country. The two population totals sit close. Both totals climb year by year. Bombay was the name British speakers used. They could not pronounce Mumbai. The year 1995 put the original pronunciation back. A huge port earned the city a nickname. People called Mumbai the Gateway of India. A monument uses that nickname. The year 1911 placed the monument at the harbor mouth. British monarchs were making a first visit. India was their colony. Freedom came about forty years afterward. The highest British official in the government left by that same gate. An island holds the city. Mainland India has a west coast. The Arabian Sea lies between that coast and the island. Women in one picture wait at a well. Indoor plumbing is missing from many homes in the countryside. West Bengal is one Indian region where that is true. Head count in India has passed 1.2 billion. China is the only country with more people. Growth continues. Big cities are numerous. Countryside towns and villages still hold most people. Rural houses usually lack plumbing indoors. About half also lack electricity. Classes once split Indian society. The split was called the caste system. A person’s social group brought strict rules. Foods of the group were traditional. Customs of the group were its own. Work of the group followed an old pattern. Lower castes suffered terrible treatment from the castes above them. The system is now against the law. Its grip on society is still strong.

3Half of India’s workers live by agriculture. Cattle are raised. Water buffalo are raised. Other animals are raised too. In many regions, meat from a killed cow is against the law. Cows are sacred in Hinduism. Some other faiths in India agree. Plows are pulled by cattle. Travel can depend on cattle too. Meat comes from sheep. It comes from goats. It comes from chickens. Crops feed people inside the country. Crops also leave the country as exports. The biggest harvests include rice. They include wheat. They include sorghum. Spices sit with those crops. Vegetables sit with them. Shoppers across India buy fresh produce every day. Power supply lags behind need. Population size is the reason. Cities often lose power. Cities often ration power. Rationing limits when power may be used. Pay for an average worker is among the lowest on Earth. Poverty is the condition of many people. Education still runs high for a large number of Indians. Science employs many of them. Technology employs many of them. Shops and crowds jam many city streets. Old Delhi shows one such street. A map of landforms names the Indus River. It names the Himalayan Mountains and Mount Everest. It names New Delhi. It names the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the Thar Desert. It names the Ganges River and the Chota Nagpur Plateau. It names the Sundarban and the Deccan Plateau. It names the Eastern Ghats and the Western Ghats. Say him-uh-LAY-uhz for the Himalayas. Those peaks make the northern border. No mountains anywhere are higher. Asia’s other lands are cut off by them. That separation is why people often call India a subcontinent. Northern India holds a low plain. The name is the Indo-Gangetic Plain, said in-doh-gan-JE-tik. Long ago, rivers flooded over and over. Each flood left sediment. The rich soil is the result.

4Northern India holds the Ganges River. Say GAN-jeez. Hinduism treats the river as sacred. Travelers who follow Hinduism come from every region. They step into the water. The plain’s south side meets raised country. That country is the Deccan Plateau, said DE-kuhn pla-TOH. Over half of India is this high ground. Low hills are included. Coasts are included. Residents are many. Soil is rich. Crops like the climate. Westward, dryness increases until the land is the Thar Desert. Dunes of sand never stay put. Area is about 200,000 square kilometers. The same area is 77,000 square miles. Three seasons cover most of the country. Hot and dry is one. Hot and wet is one. Cool and dry is one. March opens the hot dry season. May or June closes it. Temperatures run high. Winds run strong. Dust storms arrive. Monsoon is the name of the hot wet season. The start is May or June. Hard winds arrive from the south. Rain is very heavy. Afternoon is when it usually falls. Most days get that rain. About three-fourths of yearly precipitation usually comes in this season. Floods reach many regions in some years. Late October stops the rain. Cool, dry weather takes over. October 2 marks a birthday. The person is Mohandas Gandhi, said moh-huhn-DAHS GAHN-dee. His leadership brought independence from British rule. Prayer services are held. Ceremonies are held. Father of the Nation is the title of honor. Autumn brings Diwali, said dee-VAH-lee, a festival built on lights. Five days is the length. Small candles are lit. Firecrackers go off. Sweets are gifts for family. Friends receive them too. Links to Diwali cross many faiths. Spring brings Holi, said HOH-lee. Colors name this festival. A Hindu holiday was the origin. Many religions take part now. The party marks winter’s end. People throw colored water. They throw colored powder. Singing is part of the day. Dancing is part of it. Special foods are part of it. Mess is common. Baths close the day. Clean white clothes follow the baths. Water guns are popular with children. So are balloons full of colored water. August 15 is Independence Day. The celebration remembers freedom from Great Britain. The year was 1947. Kites of many colors go up. Freedom is what the kites mean.

5Civilization here is ancient. Around 321 bce, one ruler held most of the people. Their land is the India of today. The 700s ce brought invasions by several Muslim empires. A kingdom near Delhi was the result of one invasion. Rule by Muslims continued into the 1600s. Shah Jahan, a Muslim ruler, left a landmark still famous today. It is the Taj Mahal, said TAHZH muh-HAHL. Beauty is its fame. After his wife died, the Shah built this mausoleum for her. The same centuries sent Europeans out to explore. A Portuguese sailor reached India in 1498. He was Vasco da Gama, said VAHS-koh DAH GAH-mah. Control of the future India passed to the British Empire by 1858. Resistance gained Mohandas Gandhi around 1920. Violence was not his method. Protest without violence, he showed, could matter. Twenty-seven years passed before independence. A free democracy was born in 1947. Conflict has not disappeared since then. Worry about population has not disappeared. Good changes have still arrived. The first woman to serve as prime minister took office in 1966. She was Indira Gandhi. A woman president came forty-one years afterward. The year was 2007. Rabindranath Tagore won a Nobel prize for poetry. Birth was in Kolkata in 1861. Home was where most of his lessons happened. England came after he turned 17. Writing poured out of him. Poems were included. Plays were included. Short stories were included. Paintings were his too. Some poems received music he composed. A knighthood was given. He gave it back. Colonization by England was what he protested. Wild animals here include many species. Large cats are among them. Wild lions and wild tigers share this one country. Nowhere else do both live wild. Leopards of two kinds live here as well. Rarity marks both kinds. Scarcity is even greater for the snow leopard. Its home is the Himalayas. A famous reptile is the cobra. Poison is its weapon. A threat makes the hood spread wide. Mice and rats are the hunt. Those animals stay near people. Bites therefore happen at times. King cobras are one cobra type found here.

6Strength made the Indian elephant prized in earlier times. Forests were cleared with that strength. Logs were lifted. Crops were hauled. People were carried. Work today still calls on some elephants. Wild herds remain in most regions. Loss of habitat puts them at risk. Crops are still loaded onto some elephants. Other labor still uses them. Along the Bay of Bengal, swamp forest grows thick. The trees are mangroves. The place is the Sundarban, said SHOON-dar-bahn. Few habitats are like it. Sea turtles live in it. Sharks live in it. Crocodiles live in it. Bengal tigers have their greatest stronghold there. Swimming is how those tigers take prey in the swamp. A male can reach 3 meters from end to end. That length is 10 feet. Mass can reach 230 kilograms. That mass is 500 pounds. Scientists keep up hard work to guard this endangered tiger. Crowds like to meet at the India Gate. The gate is in New Delhi. Local people come. Visitors from other countries come. People and many kinds of animals fill this large country. Feeding them all is a challenge. Giving them homes is a challenge. Rare natural beauty must be kept safe at the same time. Among the nations, India still carries great weight.

7A fact list gives a snapshot. Population is 1.4 billion. Land covers 2,973,193 square kilometers. That equals 1,147,956 square miles. New Delhi is the capital city. Hindi is the primary language. Hinduism is the primary religion. The rupee, said ROO-pee, is the currency. Central Intelligence Agency published the figures in February 2022. The World Bank is a second source. Bazaars are markets. Rows of small shops fill them. A peninsula is land that stretches out long. Water wraps nearly all of its edge. The caste system locks social rank in place. Birth sets the rank. Profession sets it too. Snow, rain, sleet, and hail are all precipitation falling from the sky. A mangrove is a tree of the tropics. Swamps suit it. Shallow salt water suits it. Sacred describes a link to religion or to the spiritual. A mausoleum is a tomb built large. Several tombs can share one structure. Sediment is small pieces of dirt and of rock. Water can move those pieces. Wind can move them. Ice can move them. A monsoon is a storm tied to a season. The rain it brings is heavy. A subcontinent is one large portion of a continent. A Muslim follows Islam. The Sundarban is swamp packed with forest. India and Bangladesh both contain it. The Bay of Bengal lies beside it.

85. The Long Road West from Chicago

1This book follows Route 66, a road that carries drivers across the whole American West. It tells how the highway began and how songs, shows, and films used it. It points out roadside sights, including Cadillac Ranch, a ranch of bottle trees, and a blue whale. It describes giants, dinosaurs, and the effort to save the road. A word list ends the book. Picture the year 1957. You have just lowered the top of a convertible painted a bright cherry red. Sunlight flashes across the car's shiny metal fins. Rock and roll pours from the speakers. Nothing but open road waits ahead. Could the drive improve? You doubt it, until an ice cream cone three stories high comes into view. Sprinkles cover the cone, and your mouth waters. Should you stop? Then a cheeseburger as huge as a bus appears. A quick lunch can come first. When night arrives, you park beside a hotel room built in the shape of a teepee. Inside are a bed, a bathroom, and a shower. The day on the road has been spectacular. No one can say what the next day will bring. If this trip sounds like a dream, or like a made-up journey, that guess is wrong. The drive is a real one, down the highway Americans have loved best. That highway is Route 66.

2A road map of the United States looks a great deal like a spiderweb, and the web is intricate. Huge highways zigzag from one coast to the other. They crisscross from Canada down to Mexico. They link nearly every city that lies between. Travel is simple. A person gets into a car and starts driving. A hundred years ago, a trip across the country was much harder. Most roads were only small trails of dirt. Cars were new inventions. They often broke down, sank into mud, or blew a tire on jagged rock. A driver who ran out of gas had no luck left. Only a few gas stations stood in the wild country. A traveler who needed sleep had a single choice. Set up a tent at the roadside. During the 1920s, the government of the United States built a new highway plan. Roads received numbers so cities and states would connect more effectively. The first road paved along its full length ran 2,400 miles, or 3,862 kilometers. It stretched from Chicago to Los Angeles. People named it Route 66. Many came to call it the Main Street of America. A severe trial arrived for that road not long after it opened. The crash of the stock market came in 1929. Large numbers of people lost their money, their jobs, and their homes. The dire time that followed is known as the Great Depression. In those same years, drought followed drought. Giant dust storms wrecked farms on the Great Plains. Kansas, Colorado, Oklahoma, Texas, and New Mexico suffered the worst of it. People named this phenomenon the Dust Bowl. All at once, many families had to leave home and search for a better life. A great number believed that paradise waited in the West, above all in California. Thousands packed what they owned and made the long trip. They traveled a new road called Route 66. Many trusted that road to carry them away from trouble. They hoped it would lead them toward work and toward riches. A famous novel tells that story. John Steinbeck published The Grapes of Wrath in 1939, and the book is now a classic. It follows a family leaving Oklahoma during the Dust Bowl years. The family drives Route 66 in search of work in California. Steinbeck named Route 66 the mother road. He also named it the road of flight.

3During the 1930s, California gained 1.2 million new residents. More than half a million of them left because life was so hard in the Dust Bowl years. On December 7, 1941, Japanese forces bombed naval ships of the United States. The ships lay at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The next day, the United States entered World War II. Soldiers, workers, and supplies had to move quickly. They were mobilized from many parts of the country toward military bases in the West. Their route was Route 66. The journey was long, and wartime travelers needed food, gasoline, and a place to sleep. Restaurants, gas stations, and hotels sprang up along the road to serve them. Life in America was hard, yet business along Route 66 was booming. The war ended in 1945, and Americans celebrated. Soldiers came home, started families, built houses, and bought cars. Many wanted to drive those new cars toward the West. They hoped to see the Grand Canyon and the Pacific Ocean, traveling by way of Route 66. The years after World War II were glory days for the highway. Shiny blue roadsters rolled along it. So did convertibles of cherry red, coupes of bubble-gum pink, and yellow Checker cabs. Route 66 was no longer only a path to some other place. It had become the place people wanted to be. In 1946 a song titled Route 66 rose to the top of the hits. Its best-known line invited listeners to go find fun on that highway. The line helped fix the road's place in popular culture. The Nat King Cole Trio sang the first version of the song in 1946. In 1960 a television show took the same name, Route 66. It followed two friends who crossed the country in a Corvette. They had no single destination. They were hunting for adventure on the road. The show stayed on the air from 1960 to 1964.

4By 1970 a newer highway had bypassed most of the original Route 66. Mentions of the old road still showed up in American popular culture through the century's end. Move ahead to the year 2000. John Lasseter, the director at Pixar Animation Studios, drove Route 66 with his family. He fell in love with the imaginative buildings he passed. He loved the colorful art installations as well. He chose to turn those sights into a film. Disney and Pixar released the movie Cars in 2006. Lasseter sent a team along Route 66 to study the road for the film. Some of the roadside art they found became the seed of characters in Cars. Landmarks from the highway appear in the movie too. The Wigwam Motel in Holbrook, Arizona, for example, turned into the Cozy Cone Motel. Cars succeeded so fully that many families who watched it took vacations of their own on Route 66. That new interest helped the old route grow popular once more. A rusty tow truck in Galena, Kansas, gave artists an idea. The truck became the movie character Tow Mater. A map of stops runs from Chicago to Los Angeles across Illinois, Missouri, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California. Canada lies to the north, Mexico to the south, with the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean at the coasts. The Gemini Giant stands in Wilmington, Illinois. Paul Bunyon stands in Atlanta, Illinois. The Brooks Catsup Bottle Water Tower stands in Collinsville, Illinois. The Red Rocker stands in Fanning, Missouri. The Blue Whale stands in Catoosa, Oklahoma. Slug Bug Ranch stands in Conway, Texas. Cadillac Ranch stands in Amarillo, Texas. The Wigwam Motel stands in Holbrook, Arizona. Elmer's Bottle Tree Ranch stands in Oro Grande, California. The Cabazon Dinosaurs stand in Cabazon, California. Chicken Boy stands in Los Angeles, California. Museums, motels, and shops unlike any others appear in every state the route crosses. Unusual art, old gas stations, and lively theaters line the road as well. Travelers can also watch live shows. At Lookout Point, New Mexico, a visitor can see a real Native American dance ceremony. At Vinita, Oklahoma, the Will Rogers Memorial Rodeo is held. One promise holds. A traveler will not feel bored on Route 66.

5Cows graze in the pasture that surrounds Cadillac Ranch. Ten Cadillacs were set nose-down in a field in 1974 by alternative artists who came from San Francisco. The rear bumpers point up at the sky. Over the years the cars have worn many bright coats of paint. One of the easiest to notice came in 1990, when every car was painted pink. Today the cars show every color of the rainbow, because visitors have covered them with graffiti. Close by, the VW Slug Bug Ranch in Conway, Texas, plants five colorful Volkswagen Beetles in the ground. Elmer Long is a folk artist who looks at garbage and sees a forest. He built Bottle Tree Ranch from bottles that had been used before. He also used car parts and objects of every sort, including jawbones of buffalo. Seeing the forest is only half the visit, because music fills the place too. Wind off the desert blows through the open bottles and makes a medley of tones. As a boy, Elmer Long saved bottles and other things people had thrown out. What gift suits a woman who already has everything? Hugh Davis answered that question with a blue whale for his wife, built for an anniversary. The whale measures 80 feet, a length of 24.4 meters. For many years children loved to slide and dive from the whale into the swimming hole below. Visitors can now climb inside and look out through tiny windows in the head. The Blue Whale of Catoosa, Oklahoma, has a boardwalk that follows its spine.

6Route 66 is truly a land of giants. A California factory named International Fiberglass made thousands of colossal statues from fiberglass. The factory sold the statues to businesses on Route 66 so the businesses could advertise. Workers at the factory built unusual costumes for the giants. The costumes turned them into cowboys, Native Americans, astronauts, and even chickens. Food statues are among the largest figures on the route. Oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers, and ice cream cones of humongous size make a hungry kind of ride. Near Collinsville, Illinois, a rider may glimpse the biggest catsup bottle on Earth. That bottle is the Brooks Catsup Bottle Water Tower. Dinny cost 300,000 dollars to build, and the builders used materials from roadside construction. Dinosaurs have died out almost everywhere else on the planet. They have not died out on Route 66, where tall prehistoric creatures of many shapes greet travelers. Dinny stretches 150 feet, equal to 45.7 meters. He is likely the biggest dinosaur made of concrete in America. He lives in a dinosaur park at Cabazon, California. Claude Bell built the park to draw guests to his restaurant nearby, the Wheel Inn. The park grew famous, and the 1985 film Pee-wee's Big Adventure even showed it. Mr. Rex, a Tyrannosaurus rex as tall as three stories, is a favorite at Cabazon Dinosaurs.

7Fame brought traffic, and the traffic was heavy. Congestion wore the highway down. From 1956 through the 1980s, the government of the United States built new interstates around Route 66. Those fast highways have many lanes. As more travelers picked the interstates, shops and services on Route 66 suffered. Peeling paint, faded signs, and windows boarded shut became ordinary sights. In 1999 the United States Congress passed a law meant to protect Route 66. The government began to offer money. Towns and businesses could use the money to help pay for saving important landmarks. In 2008 the World Monuments Fund called Route 66 endangered. The fund made plans to draw tourists, including a map that uses virtual reality. A photo shows the Red Rocker of Route 66 in Fanning, Missouri. Today the old road is growing popular again. People come back to enjoy its playful art and its creative spirit. The surest way to feel that spirit is to drive the road and live a classic American journey.

86. The Mud Mosque of Djenné

1Each week, an open-air market meets beside the mosque. Djenné is one of the oldest towns in Africa south of the Sahara. People pronounce the town name je-NAY. A religious building in the town is unlike any other. People call it the Great Mosque of Djenné. Muslims worship in buildings called mosques. Muslims follow the religion of Islam. Islam ranks among the largest faiths on Earth. More than one billion people follow Islam. Five ideas form the base of the religion. A statement of faith is one idea. Prayer is a second idea. Fasting is a third idea. Charity is a fourth idea. A journey to Mecca is the fifth idea. Mecca is the city where Islam began. Followers of Islam travel to Djenné's famous mosque when they want to learn about their faith. They also visit so they can worship. This mosque is the largest mud-built structure on Earth. South of the Sahara, few buildings matter more than this one. The account that follows begins with trade routes. It then turns to a place for worship. It tells about the first mosque on this ground. It tells about a later mosque linked with Amadu. It describes the mosque people see today. It explains walls formed from mud. It explains how builders raised the mosque. It shows why the building matters to the town. It closes with the mosque in the present and in the years ahead.

2Mali is the country of this small town. Mali lies in West Africa. The town stands on a floodplain. The Niger River borders that plain. The Bani River borders it as well. People can reach the town only by boat. In the thirteenth century, the location made a strong link to Timbuktu. Timbuktu lies 483 kilometers to the north. That distance equals 300 miles. Timbuktu was a major stop on trade routes across the Sahara. Traders left the coast and traveled north toward Timbuktu. Their path passed through Djenné. The town grew because of that traffic. Islam spread along the same desert routes that carried goods. Islam had reached Mali in the ninth century. Mansa Musa was a Muslim king of Mali. During the 1300s, Islam gained greater influence under his rule. As years passed, students of Islam gathered in Djenné. In 1896, an artist drew the mosque as workers rebuilt it. Followers of Islam in Djenné needed a place to worship. Work on this mosque started in the thirteenth century. The mosque visitors see today is not the first building on this ground. King Koi Konboro ruled Djenné when the first Great Mosque was built. He built it during the thirteenth century. He placed the mosque where his palace had stood. He used materials from the local area. He followed a traditional design. He added towers that rose high. He added large walls around the building. Rain damaged the mosque as years passed. The mud washed away. By the 1800s, wear had left Djenné's great mosque in poor condition.

3In the 1800s, a tribal leader from West Africa took control of Djenné. His name was Seku Amadu. He let the first mosque fall into even worse condition. In 1834, Amadu began a new mosque. The new building was plainer than the old one. Workers raised it on a site nearby. The job lasted two years. They finished the building in 1836. In 1893, soldiers from France took the city. The mosque Amadu had built was already in ruins by then. The French put a school in its place. Workers finished the mosque visitors see now in the year 1907. Workers built it on the ground of the original Great Mosque. That 1907 project was the last time the whole mosque was constructed. Repairs still change the building from year to year. Yearly repairs mean the present building does not match the first mosque. Palm-wood bundles called toron are not only decoration. During the yearly restoration, workers climb by using the toron. The Great Mosque of Djenné looks plain next to mosques in Egypt. It also looks plain next to mosques in India. It looks plain next to mosques in Turkey as well. Its walls are tall. Its walls are brown. Builders made the walls from mud. The Sun baked that mud until it was hard. The hard mud gives the building a smooth surface. The surface looks sculpted, as if a carver had shaped it. At regular spaces, bundles of palm-wood sticks poke out from the walls. People call those sticks toron. These wooden bundles brace the walls. The prayer wall is called the qibla wall. Speakers say qibla as KIB-luh. The qibla wall faces east. It faces toward Mecca. The wall looks over the city's marketplace. The city of Mecca stands in the Middle East. People regard Mecca as the place where Islam began.

4Three towers rise from the mosque. Each tower has a boxlike shape. People call the towers minarets. An ornate ostrich egg crowns each tower. The egg stands for purity. The egg also stands for fertility. A golden ostrich egg, shaped as if carved, sits atop each minaret. Religious leaders go up the stairs five times daily. They call local Muslims to prayer. The mosque chooses a man to stand by the minarets and give that call. Visitors enter by climbing stairs. The mosque has six sets of stairs. As many as three thousand worshippers can fit in the big hall. Ninety wooden pillars span the closed space and carry the roof. The roof covers half of the mosque. Vents let hot air leave the hall. Removable caps made of ceramic sit on those vents. Worshippers use the remaining half as an outdoor hall. An arched passageway surrounds that courtyard. From the passageway, visitors can watch activity inside. The Great Mosque of Djenné covers 5,625 square meters. That area equals 60,547 square feet. No mud-brick building anywhere is larger. Many people count it among Africa's greatest works of architecture. The year 1988 brought this mosque the title of World Heritage Site. The walls measure 41 to 61 centimeters in thickness. That thickness equals 16 to 24 inches. Smooth mud forms the walls. The tallest minaret reaches 16 meters. That height equals 52 feet. The building has three minarets. Eighteen decorative projections stand along the main wall. The mosque rests on a raised platform. The platform is 3 meters high. That height equals 9 feet. The raised base helps the building avoid floods.

5Builders of the Great Mosque of Djenné used traditional materials from the region. Mud was the material they relied on. They formed bricks from mud. They made mortar from mud. They made plaster from mud. Locals baked mud in the sun to produce bricks. They called the bricks ferey. They used mud mortar to bond the bricks while the walls rose. They coated the walls with mud plaster. The coating leaves a smooth surface that looks shaped by hand. Butter and clay are mixed to make this mud. Workers lay the mud as thick as 61 centimeters. That thickness equals 24 inches. Weight from above rests on that thick lower section. The mud walls keep heat from passing through too fast. They take in the heat of the day. They hold that heat. During daylight, the mosque stays cool. After dark, the outdoor temperature falls. The walls then release the heat they stored. People inside stay warm through the night. A man from Djenné spreads fresh mud over an outer wall so the building will last. In West Africa, temperature can change in a sharp way. Moisture in the air can change sharply too. Those shifts can make the walls crack. Builders set bundles of toron into the walls to limit the cracking. The bundles stick out at even distances. They help the walls crack less. During each year's upkeep, workers also use the toron as scaffolding that is already built in. Water could harm the mosque. For that reason, builders set the mosque on a platform 3 meters high. That height equals 9 feet. The platform keeps floodwater from the nearby Bani River off the building. Ceramic gutters run along the roof. The gutters collect rain. They send the rain away from the walls. That path protects the outside from water damage. Repair crews scale the mosque's outer face. They use the toron as scaffolding while they work.

6Once each year, excited crowds race past the front of this mosque. They carry baskets filled with mud plaster. Today the mosque stands at the center of life in Djenné. Citizens take an active part in its care. Each year the whole town takes part in a plastering festival. Its name is Crépissage de la Grande Mosquée. Speakers say that name as kray-pee-SAZH DU LAH GRAHND MOSS-kay. During the festival, people put new plaster on the outside walls. Changing weather has cracked those walls. Citizens gather fine clay soil during the days leading up to the festival. They take soil from the Niger River. They also take soil from the Bani River. They use the soil to make mud plaster. Women of Djenné usually supply the water for the mixture. Young boys mix the plaster. They do that mixing in special pits. A race opens the festival. Runners compete to be the first to bring plaster from the pits onto the walls. After the race, the repair work can start. The men climb ladders. They use the mosque's toron as scaffolding that is already in place. They spread the mixture on the cracking walls. The festival includes music along with the labor. It includes food as well. Musicians play for the workers. The music keeps spirits high. The music also helps the labor move faster. Elders of the town watch from seats set aside to honor them. They watch the work go forward. They offer advice when workers need it. Young children sing during the festival. They run. They play. Only Muslims may enter the Great Mosque of Djenné. People who are not Muslims may view the mosque only from the outside.

7Lights on the outside are one of the only modern additions to the mosque. Many ancient mosques now have electrical wiring. Many also have indoor plumbing. A loudspeaker system is one modern tool now used at this mosque. Local people have opposed any further updates. They want the building preserved. Their culture treats this building as precious. Their faith treats the building as precious too. In 1988, the United Nations made Djenné a World Heritage Site. That decision brought protections. The protections help save the city's history. The Great Mosque stands inside the historical zone. Other buildings stand there too. Modern materials are not allowed on those buildings. Modern technology is not allowed on them either. For the present, the people of Djenné hold on to their cultural heritage. They also keep holding their yearly festival. In the Islamic faith, people worship inside a mosque. Islam is the monotheistic faith of Muslims. The prophet Muhammad's teachings form the base of this faith. Muslims are the people who follow Islam. Mecca is a city in Saudi Arabia. People who practice Islam travel to Mecca as a holy goal. Disrepair means a bad condition that needs repair. Mortar is a liquid mix of materials. It hardens as it dries. Dried mortar locks bricks in place. It also locks stones in place. To insulate is to stop heat from moving through. To jut is to stick out past an edge. Preserving means caring for something and saving it for later years. Scaffolding is a system of temporary platforms. Workers stand on it while they build, repair, or decorate. Minarets are narrow towers near a mosque. Worshippers are called to prayer from those towers. Sculpted means molded or carved, with a clear, sharp outline.

87. The Mystery of the Empty Hives

1A picture shows a honeybee colony in good health. The book opens by asking what would become of strawberries. Busy bees come next. Bees that vanish come after that. Scientists on the case follow. Farms that raise only one crop come next. Bees moved by truck follow. Ways to help come after that. Hard words are explained last. Picture a favorite fruit. Now picture that fruit becoming extremely rare. The same threat could hit other fruit. Nuts, vegetables, and flowers could become rare too. Diets would turn bland and dull without honeybees to pollinate those flowers. Bees are behind one bite in every three that you eat. Yet honeybees started disappearing around the world in 2007. Scientists have been puzzled for a long time. The losses slowed as years passed. The cause is still unknown. Work to save honeybees continues.

2Colonies are where honeybees live. The place is busy and well organized. Every bee has a task. Each bee depends on the rest. A honeybee alone, away from the colony, cannot last beyond twenty-four hours. Bees from one hive may visit over 100,000 flowers during a single day. A bloom is where a bee gathers pollen for food. Nectar is gathered there to make honey. During that work, the bee carries out a critical natural process. The bee does not intend to. The process is pollination. Anthers inside a flower brush the bee. Pollen grains stick to the body. At the next flower, fur sheds some of that pollen onto the pistil. Fertilization can follow. A seed is the eventual result. A diagram marks the anthers. Another marks the pistil and the pollen. A bee is shown pollinating a flower. Plants cannot make new plants without fertilization. Species that need those plants then vanish as well. October 2006 brought an American beekeeper to one of his apiaries in Florida. A beeyard is another name for an apiary. Four hundred hives were there to be picked up. Three weeks earlier, the hives had looked healthy. He found them almost empty. Food remained. Baby bees remained. A few queens remained. Dead bodies were what he searched for. Twenty million bees were simply gone. He was not the only keeper to face this. Similar losses were reported across the United States. Europe reported them. Argentina reported them. China and other countries reported them too. In the winter that spanned 2006 and 2007, about 750,000 colonies disappeared in the United States. The estimated total had been 2.4 million. On average, the loss for keepers in the country came to 38 percent. The biggest known loss came in 2008. It happened among almond groves in California. Two billion bees disappeared there. Farmers wanted science to explain it. Beekeepers wanted the same. Pictures show one colony before the bees vanished, and the same kind of colony after.

3The name scientists gave the problem is colony collapse disorder. CCD is the short form. Symptoms were identified quickly. The collapse can take only weeks. A hive that looked fine falls apart. Dead bees are scarce or absent. Only the youngest bees remain, along with the queen. Those are members that would normally never be left by themselves. Honeybee scientists across the country set out to learn what was killing the bees. Stopping it was the goal. The job proved far harder than anyone expected. Beekeepers were surveyed. Wax was sampled. Pollen was sampled. Live bees were sampled, and dead bees too, when any could be found. Laboratories received the samples. Dissection showed many diseases inside the bees. Immune systems seemed compromised. The open question was why. A picture shows a scientist collecting material from a hive hit by CCD. A chart gives average yearly hive loss by state for 2020 and 2021. Marked levels include 100 percent. They include 70 percent, 60 percent, 50 percent, 40 percent, and 30 percent. The Bee Informed Partnership is the chart's source. Usual suspects that might harm immune systems were checked. Several parasites were among them. One is a mite that drinks bee blood. Viruses are passed by that mite. Its eggs are laid in the same cells where baby bees grow. Fungal bacteria were studied too. Those bacteria make eating difficult. Bees become too weak to forage. A virus that causes paralysis turned up in many CCD hives. Each of these threats is extremely dangerous. Researchers still decided none of them was the cause. Attention turned to how farms are run.

4A truck is shown spraying pesticide across plants. Farms were once small, and they raised many crops. Most farms now are huge. A single crop fills the fields. Wheat is one example. Corn is another. Soybeans are another. Monoculture is the name for that setup. Efficiency is why some farmers prefer it. Bees cannot last long on such a farm. When the single crop finishes blooming, starvation follows. Other troubles come with monocultures. Pests thrive there, so farmers spray chemical pesticides to wipe them out. A large share of food in American agriculture is treated with pesticides. The Environmental Protection Agency tracks the amount used on crops. The yearly total is more than a billion pounds. Finding a spray that kills harmful insects and spares helpful ones, such as bees, is difficult. Many creatures suffer from pesticides. Bees suffer in particular. Farmers try to spray when blooms are finished. Fewer bees are around at those times. Even so, pesticide traces showed up in samples from hives with CCD. One newer class of pesticides worries some scientists more than others. These pesticides are systemic. Seeds are coated with the chemicals. As the plant grows, the chemicals enter every part. One treatment lasts a long time. Many crop pests die, which can seem like a benefit. Bee losses line up in time with the arrival of these newer pesticides.

5Immune systems might be weakened by pesticides. A paralysis virus and similar diseases can then take hold. Systemic pesticides also aim at the nervous system. Learning might be harmed. Memory might be harmed. Navigation might be harmed. Any of those harms would help explain bees that forage and never come back. A bee that cannot find the hive dies. Evidence of systemic pesticides has been found in hives that suffered CCD. The new pesticides also appeared on a timeline that matches CCD. Scientists still cannot say for sure that the pesticides cause the disorder. More factors have to be weighed. Colony collapse is slowing, but a second crisis has arrived. Many native bees now face extinction. Neat, trimmed lawns share the blame for the drop in wild bees. Some bees can live only if certain plants are present. Native plants are fewer. Honeybees are more numerous, because farmers move them in to pollinate crops. Food and shelter are harder for wild bees to find. Ancient Egyptians set hives on rafts and floated them down the Nile. They were following the bloom. Trucks do that moving now, all over the country. For 150 million years, bees have been on the move across the planet. The last 10,000 years changed their tie to humans. People once gathered foods that nature had already pollinated. Later they used bees to serve monoculture farms. Honeybees pollinate very well. Placing them in a field during bloom helps a farmer raise a large crop. Human-built hives made the colonies movable. Trucks in the United States now haul hives across the country. Each year those bees pollinate food worth 15 billion dollars in the United States alone.

6Hauling a million bees along a highway can seem odd. Modern monocultures depend on that haul. One crop may need bees in February. Another crop, far across the country, may need them in April. Take almond trees. They cannot be pollinated unless honeybees do the work. Almond growers in California need 1.4 million colonies. Managed honeybee colonies in the country supply that number. The share is about 60 percent. Near Valentine's Day, trucks carry bees to the California groves. Work begins when the almond trees bloom. For two weeks, 600,000 acres of blooming trees are busy and beautiful. That area is 242,811 hectares. The other fifty weeks, those groves are a terrible place for bees. Nothing is there to eat. The trip itself harms bees. Stress kills millions of them each year. On the road, natural food is unavailable. Some scientists compare the substitute feed to junk food. Moving bees from different regions, or from different countries, also spreads pests fast. A keeper is shown heading out to check more than 100,000 honeybees. They live in a rooftop garden on City Hall in downtown Chicago. CCD is so complex that an exact cause is still missing. A full cure is missing too. Some treatments look promising. CCD rates have fallen over time because of that. The drop is smaller than scientists hoped. More research is required to solve the case of the vanishing honeybees. What is already known can still be used. Places friendly to bees can be made. Plants, bees, and people would all gain.

7Outdoor space is enough for a person to help, if the right plants are kept. Honeybees need many kinds of wildflowers. Sanctuaries full of blooms are appearing to meet that need. Pesticides can be escaped there. Food is plentiful there. Some large cities have also legalized beekeeping. City keepers hold fewer hives. Those hives are not hauled around. Even a monoculture farmer can set aside a small piece of land. Plants grown there could feed bees through the whole year, not merely a couple of weeks. Different pesticides might be chosen. None might be used. Bees are small. Health and well-being for many species, humans included, depend on them. Protecting them helps the bees. It helps people too. A few word meanings help. Colonies are animal groups that live together. The word also names the places where ants live, or where certain other social insects live. Damaged is what compromised means. It can mean impaired. A disorder is a condition of body or mind. It is unhealthy. It is outside what is normal. Dissected means cut open so something can be studied. It can mean separated into parts for that study. Fertilization joins male and female cells so a new animal or plant can form. To forage is to search for food or other supplies. It can mean gathering them. A parasite may be a plant. It may be an animal. It lives on another creature and may take that creature's food. A pesticide may be a chemical. It may be biological. Its job is to kill animals or plants that cause harm. To pollinate is to place pollen in a flower so fertilization can happen. Sanctuaries are places of safety. Surveyed means a group was asked questions so information could be gathered and analyzed. Systemic means tied to a whole system or a whole body, or affecting that whole.

88. The Quiet Pioneer Named Joe Kittinger

1The book is arranged in these parts. Opening. The Man Who Jumped. Another Mark for Joe. Still More Marks. Closing Words. Words to Know and Topics. Pictures name three spacefarers. Alan Shepard is one. Neil Armstrong is one. Yuri Gagarin is one. Opening. Heroes fill the story of exploring space. Asked for names, you might offer Yuri Gagarin. He was first to travel into space. You might offer Neil Armstrong. He was first to walk on the moon. American astronauts who are widely known include Alan Shepard. John Glenn is among them. Sally Ride is among them. Joe Kittinger would probably stay off your list. His heroism went unsung. Even so, many people see him as a real pioneer of exploring space. Further pictures show John Glenn and Sally Ride.

2Joe Kittinger was not an ordinary explorer of space. He was not truly an astronaut. He was not a cosmonaut either. Even so, his deed likely asked for greater bravery than a ride inside a craft that a rocket carries upward. What act was so far beyond the ordinary? The pages ahead will show it. A portrait carries his name. The Man Who Jumped. Rocket capsules were not yet carrying humans into space. Before that era, Joe flew balloons at great height. He went to the very rim of space. A United States Air Force effort called Project Manhigh held this work. The aim was a test. What happens to people who stay a long time in conditions like those of outer space? June 1957 brought the first time he took a balloon up into the stratosphere. Altitude reached 29,565 meters. That is 97,000 feet. He stayed aloft for almost seven hours. Flights like his, and flights by others, gathered information of huge worth. NASA used it while planning the earliest human trips into space. Later, Joe served as engineer for Project Excelsior. That project also belonged to the United States Air Force. Safe escape was the goal. The escapes would be from aircraft at great height, and from spaceships. August 1960 came a year before a Russian cosmonaut was counted as the first person in space. That cosmonaut was Yuri Gagarin. In that same stretch of time, Joe Kittinger managed a feat just as hard to believe. Helium gas filled the balloon that lifted him. Height above Earth was 31,333 meters. That is 102,800 feet. A typical jet with passengers flies near 9,144 meters. That is 30,000 feet. Those passenger jets reached less than a third of Joe's balloon height.

3That height is already hard to believe. Here is the next part. Joe left the balloon by stepping away from it. He left an open gondola. Emptiness waited at 31,333 meters, or 102,800 feet, above Earth. A space walk was not the plan. He jumped. The fall back toward Earth began. A fact box adds more of his record. He piloted 93 kinds of aircraft. Planes were among them. Balloons were among them. Jet-plane flight filled 5,300 hours. Combat missions filled about 1,000 hours. Parachute jumps totaled 101. Three of those jumps left balloons at very great height.

4Before the rest of Joe's fall, consider the conditions at 31,333 meters. That height is 102,800 feet. Air there is very thin. Drawing in enough oxygen with each breath is nearly impossible. Joe carried an oxygen supply. Comfortable breathing was possible because of it. Cold at that height is also fierce. His balloon trip put him deep inside a sky layer called the stratosphere. The layer's low edge is 9.5 kilometers above Earth. Its high edge is 48 kilometers. About 6 to 30 miles is the same span. So he floated well inside it. Temperatures there can sink to minus 68 degrees Celsius. That is minus 90 degrees Fahrenheit. Several layers of clothing kept him warm in those hostile conditions. A special suit with pressure was also required. Without it, his body could explode. His blood could boil. Low pressure in space causes that danger. Very little air is there. Inside the body, pressure far exceeds the atmosphere that pushes from outside. This can begin at 18,900 meters. That is 62,000 feet. The name for that height is Armstrong's Limit. Safety steps were many. Pain still found his right hand. The pressurized glove sprang a leak and lost pressure. A picture shows Joe entering the balloon gondola. The suit he wears is pressurized.

5A math pause uses his jump. He left the high balloon at 31,000 meters. The free fall lasted 4 minutes and 36 seconds before the parachute opened. Height at the opening was 5,500 meters. Find the average speed. Measure it in meters for each second of that free fall. The answer is about 95 meters per second. Follow him farther through this astonishing fall. Gravity was pulling him home toward Earth. His body sped up as he dropped. Speed passed 965 kilometers an hour. That is 600 miles an hour. Some experts say the sound barrier may even have been broken by him. If that is true, he was the only person to do it with no craft aiding him or shielding him. That claim stood for over fifty years. Sixteen seconds into the fall, a small drogue parachute opened. Its diameter was 1.8 meters, or 6 feet. The drogue slowed him. Compared with a regular parachute, a drogue is elongated and thinner. The shape keeps the chute from tearing apart. High-speed falls from great height are what would tear it. He could drift slowly down once the main parachute was open. Joe had shown something important. After an emergency escape, a human can survive near-space conditions outside a spacecraft. The same is true outside an aircraft.

6Was Joe truly in space? In a technical sense, no. Space has no border drawn like a line between countries. You do not step from one nation into the next. Moving away from Earth, the air simply grows thinner and thinner. Many scientists still mark a border. They call it the Kármán Line. It sits 100 kilometers above Earth. That is 62 miles. By that mark, Joe did not reach true outer space. He was high enough, though, for conditions like those in space. Remember also that no spaceship held him. His bold jump set a height record for a parachute jump. The record stood until 2012. Felix Baumgartner, a skydiver from Austria, broke Joe's speed record in 2012. Felix left a gondola at 39,045 meters. That is 128,100 feet above Earth's surface. Free fall lasted 4 minutes and 22 seconds. That was 16 seconds shorter than Joe's 1960 jump. Speed reached 1,342 kilometers an hour. That is 833.9 miles an hour. The pace was about 97 kilometers an hour beyond the speed at which sound travels. Sixty miles an hour is the same gap. Joe and Felix prepared together for years. From the control room, Joe watched. He spoke to Felix on the way back to Earth. Another Mark for Joe. Balloon jumps were not his whole story. He was also a pilot of high skill. Love of flying started early. Birth year was 1928. Birthplace was Tampa, Florida. Early growing-up years were around Orlando, Florida. Obsession with flying is a fair description. Reading on flight took every spare hour. Stories of pilots did too. Model airplanes were something he built in large numbers.

7Teen years were spent at a local airport. He hung around and talked pilots into free rides. Age seventeen brought his first flight alone. College lasted two years. Then he joined the United States Air Force. Soon he was a test pilot. Experimental aircraft were his to fly. Fighter aircraft were his as well. A note about a park belongs here. Orlando, Florida, built one beside the airport that had been Joe's hangout. Other children gained a place to watch planes leave and land. The name of the park is Colonel Joe Kittinger Park. As a teenager he dreamed of flying a Piper Cub. The year 1955 shifted him from airplane piloting to balloon piloting. Several balloon flights at great height came before the record. Several balloon jumps did too. Then 1960 brought the flight and jump that set the record. One earlier jump went wrong. Only 2 seconds passed after he left the gondola. Then the drogue chute opened. The plan had called for 16 seconds. His neck was caught by a cord that belonged to the chute. A downward spiral nearly killed him. Violent spinning knocked him unconscious. Luck held, though. His safety chute opened by itself. The fall slowed. He floated down to Earth in safety. A scare like that might have pushed him toward a new career. It did not. He stayed with the project. Other flights followed. They led to the balloon flight and jump that set his record.

8A photo poses Joe with his jet fighter. After the world record for that high parachute jump, he went to Vietnam. Combat missions were his work. Three combat tours were part of his service in the war. Flight missions reached a record 483. On that 483rd flight, in 1972, luck ended. He was shot down. Combat flying ended for him with that flight. A question sits beside the story. Picture nearly a year as a prisoner, barred from every other prisoner. How would you keep your mind busy in that confinement? He managed to eject from the crashing jet. A parachute brought him safely to Earth. The landing was unlucky. Enemy lines were behind him. The spot was 48 kilometers northwest of Hanoi. That is 30 miles. The country was North Vietnam. Capture was immediate. Eleven months followed as a prisoner of war. The prison was famous for poor conditions. Solitary confinement lasted thirty days. While he was a prisoner, he kept his mind busy. He planned every detail of a balloon trip around the world. No human had yet completed a flight like that.

9Still More Marks. Retirement from the Air Force came in 1978. Work in aeronautics continued. Lighter-than-air balloons added further records. He entered many contests in the United States. A further record fell five years after he left the Air Force. A helium-filled balloon carried him. Franklinville, New York, was where he landed. Las Vegas, Nevada, was where he started. Distance was 3,220 kilometers. That is 2,000 miles. Time in the air was 72 hours. A picture shows the balloon of that flight. The route linked Nevada's Las Vegas with New York's Franklinville. The year 1984 found him at age fifty-six. He decided on yet another record. A solo balloon crossing of the Atlantic Ocean had never been done. That gap was reason enough for Joe to try. September 14, 1984, was the takeoff. He left from the state of Maine. Drift carried him east. Almost 84 hours passed. Distance was 5,633 kilometers. That is 3,500 miles. Italy was where the balloon landed. Another record was his. Joe stands in a photo beside that helium balloon. Its route crossed the Atlantic.

10Closing Words. A dictionary calls a hero someone who does a brave act. Great courage while taking on a task counts as well. By that meaning, Joe is surely a hero. Exploration and fields like it make some heroes famous. Their names show up in the news. Textbooks carry them too. Space exploration does not bring Joe Kittinger's name to mind. In that way he is a hero who went unsung. Early balloon work at great height was not done so he could set records. Benefit to pilots was the purpose. Benefit to astronauts was the purpose. A picture places Colonel Joe Kittinger on the right. President Eisenhower is in the center. The moment follows the Harmon Trophy. The general public knew him relatively little. Recognition for outstanding deeds still came. After the high-altitude jump record, President Dwight D. Eisenhower of the United States awarded the Harmon Trophy. Other awards and honors followed. They marked his military work, his ballooning, and his parachuting. The Silver Star was among them. The Distinguished Flying Cross was among them. The Purple Heart was among them. Courage and bravery of an extraordinary kind mark this man. Important contributions to exploring space are his as well.

11Words to Know. Accelerated means speed went up. Obsessed means a mind is fully taken up with one subject. Aeronautics is the work of flight, or the study of it. Solitary confinement is imprisonment. No contact with other people is allowed. Altitude measures how far something is above Earth. Cosmonaut is the Russian word for a traveler in space. The stratosphere is a sky layer. Its lower bound is 9.5 kilometers above Earth's surface. Its upper bound is 48 kilometers. That span is 6 to 30 miles. Elongated means long when set beside its width. A gondola is an enclosure like a boat. Hostile means unfriendly. Invaluable means so helpful that no price can be set on it. Near-fatal means death was very close. Topics include the Atlantic Ocean and Dwight D. Eisenhower. Yuri Gagarin is listed. So is the Karman Line. Joe Kittinger's records cover distance, flight missions, great height, skydiving, speed, and a crossing of the Atlantic. NASA appears. Orlando, Florida, appears. Project Excelsior appears. Project Manhigh appears. The sound barrier appears. The United States Air Force appears. Vietnam appears.

89. The Rose City Carved in Rock

1You have agreed to take an amazing adventure. You and your host fly to a small city in the southwest of Jordan, in the Middle East. After the plane lands, you board a bus for a ride of one and a half hours. The land around you holds stunning cliffs and canyons of red stone. You reach a visitor center and walk a short way to the mouth of a canyon. This canyon is the Siq, a name said SEEK. It is a narrow passage 1.2 kilometers long, the same as 0.75 miles, and it leads to your goal. Walking through the Siq, you are dazzled by walls of red rock. Those walls rise as high as 80 meters, or 262 feet. Near the end, an enormous building carved from the stone comes into view. Visitors who come through the Siq meet the Treasury first. Your jaw drops, and you stare in wonder. Your host smiles with excitement and welcomes you to Petra.

2Petra is a city of rock that is two thousand years old. It sits in a valley between the Dead Sea and the Gulf of Aqaba, a northern arm of the Red Sea. The city lies about 185 kilometers, or 115 miles, southwest of Amman, the capital of Jordan. Ancient trade routes linking the Middle East, Asia, and Africa pass through Petra. Red sandstone of a dramatic kind surrounds the city, in one of the driest deserts on Earth. The Siq is the main entrance, and in places it is only 3 meters wide, or 9.8 feet. The closest water that lasts all year is about 8 kilometers away, or 5 miles. A dry riverbed just north of the center can flood in a sudden rush from time to time. A map places Petra among Syria, Iraq, Amman, the Dead Sea, Israel, and Jordan. Egypt, Ma'an, Saudi Arabia, and the Gulf of Aqaba appear as well. Europe, Asia, and Africa frame the wider view. Petra takes its name from the Greek word for rock. People sometimes call it the Rose City because the stone is reddish. The whole city covers 264 square kilometers, or 102 square miles. The center measures roughly 6 square kilometers, or 2.3 square miles. Some buildings stand free of the cliffs, but Petra is best known for hundreds of tombs cut from rock. Sacred writings decorate some of those tombs. Other buildings include civic halls, temples, and houses. Many of the structures rise more than 30 meters, or 100 feet. Petra also had a system for managing water, and for its time the system was highly advanced. Dams, channels, aqueducts, cisterns, reservoirs, and a tunnel collected water. They stored it, controlled it, and sent it where people needed it. Because of that system, residents could thrive in the desert. At the city's peak, at least twenty thousand people lived there.

3The Treasury is the most famous monument in Petra, and visitors see it first as they enter. In Arabic its name is al-Khazneh. The Street of Facades leads toward the city center, and tombs cut from rock line the street. Visitors next reach the Theatre, which could seat four thousand people. Then come the Royal Tombs, the burial places of kings. The Colonnaded Street runs through the center and leads to Petra Museum. The museum holds more than six hundred artifacts. From the museum, a hiker with energy can climb about eight hundred steps cut in the rock. Those steps reach the Monastery, called al-Deir in Arabic, one of the largest monuments in Petra. In 1993 the site was protected as an archaeological park. Jordan's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities manages the park. Ancient trade roads around the city are part of the park. The Theatre was cut from solid rock, and centuries have left it with extensive damage. A walking route runs east to west from the Visitor Centre to the Monastery. The stops are the entrance to the Siq, the path inside the Siq, and the Treasury. They continue with the Street of Facades, the Theatre, and the Royal Tombs. They continue with the Colonnaded Street and Petra Museum. At an ordinary pace the walk takes about twenty minutes. Most visitors take much longer, because they pause to study each new place.

4For hundreds of years the Nabataeans, a name said nab-uh-TEE-uns, lived in tents and moved as nomads. Only later did they begin to carve homes from stone. These Arabian herders of camels, goats, and sheep founded Petra. During the first millennium BCE, these people grew more important to the ancient world. Little by little they became successful traders. They took control of routes that tied parts of the Middle East to Asia and to Africa. They offered water and shelter to traders hauling incense, spices, and silks across the desert. They also charged foreigners a fee for passing through the land. In time the traders grew rich, built Petra, and settled. Petra was their capital, and it is thought to have been founded around 300 BCE. The city flourished from the first century BCE onward. It became a center of culture, and a center of people, goods, and money. While Petra thrived, the Roman Empire was pushing east into the Middle East. The empire had its center in ancient Rome, in Italy. Across several centuries it grew until it held all the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. In 106 CE the Romans took Petra without a fight. Daily life went on much as it had before. Even so, Roman rule changed the city in many ways, including building design and new roads edged with columns. The Romans held Petra for three hundred years. They then shifted the heart of their trade to the north and moved much of that trade onto water routes. Petra grew less important as a place of trade. Columns on the Colonnaded Street show the Roman influence in its design. Floods over the centuries have damaged that street.

5In 330 CE the Roman emperor Constantine I, a Christian, moved the capital of the empire. He moved it from Rome to Byzantium, the city now called Istanbul, because he wanted Christianity to spread. Over time the people of Petra became Christians, and the city showed the change. Petra Church was built around the year 450 and was remodeled between 500 and 550. A huge earthquake in 363 CE wrecked much of the water system and nearly half the city. That quake was likely an important reason for Petra's decline. Another large earthquake struck in 551. Early in the 600s, Arab forces gained control of this region. By the end of that century, Petra's last residents had gone. After the decline, only the Bedouins knew the city. Bedouins are Arab nomads who lived in the area. The wider world stayed unaware until the Crusades, which ran from 1095 to 1291. In those years, Christian countries of Europe invaded. They tried to seize Jerusalem and the land around it, and in the end they failed. After the Crusades, Europeans did not know of Petra again until the early nineteenth century. A Swiss explorer, Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, heard of the ancient city of stone and set out to find it. In 1812 he made a short visit, and his reports opened the way for other outsiders to come and study Petra. The buildings fall into two kinds: structures that stand free, and monuments cut from rock. Free-standing buildings were raised from the bottom upward. Rock-cut monuments were carved from the top downward. Unfinished monuments prove the point, because only their tops are carved. Nobody knows for certain how the Nabataeans cut those monuments, which are Petra's most remarkable works. Scholars think the carvers did not use wooden scaffolding, since few trees grow in the desert nearby. One idea is that they cut away large blocks of sandstone, one level at a time. The cuts would leave huge steps, and carvers could stand on the steps while they worked. A second idea is that strong rods fixed in the rock held a wooden board. Carvers stood on the board, and after a level was done they set pins lower on the face and shifted the board. Scientists still hunt for clues that would explain the building methods. Stairs, water channels, and other features were also carved by hand into the natural forms of the cliffs and canyons.

6The unfinished monuments have been important to scientists who study how carving was done at Petra. Nabataean buildings mix many styles. The mix reflects influences from Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, India, and Egypt. Petra is the tourist site people in Jordan visit most. In 2015, more than four hundred thousand visitors made the trip. Tickets are sold to travelers at the Visitor Centre. They enter by way of the Siq, riding a horse cart or walking, or riding a horse, a donkey, or a camel. A person can see Petra in two days, but several days are better. The soft sandstone can be worn down by wind, by water, and by salt. Wind brings that salt inland from the Red Sea. Large crowds of tourists threaten the city as well. Touching the stone wears it away, and so does sitting on it or walking on it. In 1985 the Rose City was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, a status that supports protection and conservation. Hundreds of artifacts are displayed in Petra Museum. Thieves have carried off many other objects across the centuries.

7At sunset on the winter solstice, sunlight falls on the central podium of the Monastery. Little is known about the Nabataeans, yet two facts are certain. First, they worshipped the Sun. The proof is in the light. On the winter solstice, and at certain other times of year, the Sun strikes the main buildings or lines up with them. That alignment happens for 80 percent of those buildings. Second, they were incredibly inventive in the way they brought water into the desert. More pieces of the water system keep being found. Radar lately found a network of water channels under the ground. Scientists also found fountains and gardens that were once lush. Research that continues will surely show more about these ancient people. It will show how they lived, and how they thrived, in their majestic city of rock. Antiquities are objects or buildings that come from ancient times. A decline is a long downward slide in amount, in quality, in value, or in strength. An aqueduct is a channel made by people so that water can move from one spot to another. A facade is the front face of a building. Nomadic describes people who shift from place to place and keep no lasting home. Archaeological describes work that studies what ancient cultures left behind. A reservoir is a large tank or lake where water is gathered and kept. People may use that water for drinking or for growing crops. Architectural describes the design of buildings and the way they are put up. Civic describes matters of a city, of being a citizen, or of community life. Scaffolding is a temporary set of platforms that holds workers while they build, repair, or decorate. Conservation means keeping safe the historical and cultural things, buildings, and places people value. A solstice is one of two days in the year when the Sun stands farthest from the equator.

90. The Writer Who Grew Up on the Prairie

1A map shows where Laura lived. A key marks her homes and the state capitals. Pepin was home from 1867 to 1869 and again from 1871 to 1874. Independence was home from 1869 to 1870. Walnut Grove was home from 1874 to 1876 and again from 1878 to 1879. De Smet was home from 1879 to 1894. Mansfield was home from 1894 to 1957. The map also names Madison, St. Paul, Pierre, Topeka, and Jefferson City. It names Des Moines, Lincoln, and Springfield. Minnesota, Wisconsin, Kansas, Iowa, Nebraska, Illinois, Missouri, South Dakota, and Oklahoma appear. The contents begin with an introduction. The prairie and the big woods come next. Hard times follow. Settling in Dakota Territory comes after that. Young Lady Laura follows. Happiness at Rocky Ridge comes next. The Little House books come after that. Hard words are listed last.

2Inside the little log cabin, Laura stopped short. Ma was in bed. A doctor stood nearby. Ma asked the girls to meet a new baby sister. The voice was tired, and it was proud. This memory is among the earliest and strongest Laura Ingalls Wilder kept. Two forces in it later shaped her famous novels. Family closeness was one. Love of wild, open country was the other. Birth came on February 7, 1867. The place was the northern woods at Pepin, Wisconsin. Laura was child number two. Mary was first. At age two, Laura watched Ma and Pa Ingalls load a covered wagon. Independence, Kansas, was the aim. Many more moves would follow in her childhood. The family were settler-colonists. White families like theirs were some of the first to settle the American West. The Kansas cabin left vivid memories. The stay lasted only about a year. The land was Osage land, and the family had settled there by mistake. They had to go. Wisconsin was the return. For centuries before white settlers came, the Osage had lived in that part of Kansas. Late in the 1800s, the U.S. government used violence to push the Osage off those lands. Indian Territory was where they were sent. That territory is today's Oklahoma. At age four, Laura watched the prairie fall behind the wagon. She felt sad. Baby years in Wisconsin were too early for her to remember. The return revealed another wonderful world. Dark, wild, and mysterious is how the big woods felt. Outdoors was where Laura wanted to be. Snowballs flew between her and her cousins. Firewood had to be gathered. Other chores waited. Long winter nights brought Pa's fiddle. That music belonged to the happiest days of her childhood.

3Hard times came next. Laura later described the packing. Goods from the little house went into the wagon. Beds stayed behind. Tables stayed. Chairs stayed. Pa could build replacements. Restlessness defined Pa Ingalls. Open prairie was what he missed. Minnesota was the move he planned for the young family. Trouble started before departure. Scarlet fever struck Laura. Every blanket the family owned was wrapped around her. She was settled in the back of the wagon. At age seven, she watched a silent, snow-covered home disappear. Minnesota put Laura and Pa back on open prairie, and that made them glad. The first shelter was a sod house. Dense mats of grass roots formed its walls. From far off it looked like a low hill. A creek bank was where that hill rose. Later Pa built a house of wood. Wheat was planted near Walnut Grove. School began for Laura and Mary. Reading pleased Laura. Writing pleased her. Reciting pleased her. Another baby was on the way. Happiness lasted a few months. Then hardship hit. Grasshoppers arrived in swarms the size of thunderclouds. The wheat was eaten. With the crop gone, the family shifted into Walnut Grove. Odd jobs kept them going. Even young Laura cleaned in a hotel and waited on tables. Fever then took the new baby brother, Freddie. Spirits rose a little in 1877, when Grace was born. Hard times continued. Mary became ill. Eye nerves were damaged, either by that illness or by a stroke. The cause was never certain. Blindness lasted the rest of Mary's life. Pa chose to head west and start again. A photo from about 1880 shows the sisters. Laura is on the right. Carrie is on the left. Mary stands with them.

4A train at Walnut Grove carried the family west. Pa had gone ahead to work in Dakota Territory. They were joining him. At age eleven, Laura told what she saw. The train was huge and smoking. The cars were decorated in an ornate style. Wheat fields rushed past as a golden blur. Mary listened to every word. The stop had no town yet. Only a railroad halt was there. The Ingalls family, with a few other white families, became the first citizens of a future town. That town would be De Smet, in South Dakota. Some of the earliest buildings were Pa's work. The first store was one of them. More settlers came. A homestead a few miles out of town was acquired. Pa built a cabin there. He built a stable. He built a garden. Winter sent the family to rooms above the store in town. School would be closer for the girls. The U.S. government urged white settler-colonists westward. Homesteads were offered. They were nearly free places to live. The ground had been taken from Native people. Native people were not counted as citizens then. Laura lived on land that belonged to Native people. Like many white settler-colonists, she held racist views about them. Her books often leave those peoples out. They often show them in a negative light. White settler-colonists are praised. Wintering in town proved lucky. Blizzard followed blizzard. Snow blinded the way to school. Food trains could not get through. Some families nearly starved. Hours were spent grinding raw wheat by hand until it became flour. Almanzo Wilder, a young man, walked through the snow. He went to the only farm already established nearby. He brought back every bit of wheat that farmer could spare. Settlers' lives were saved. Laura would hear of this good man again.

5Laura later wrote that pain ends. Love, she wrote, lasts forever. The long winter finally broke. The family went back to the homestead. The Dakota prairie was in bloom. The farm began to thrive. The new town did too. Mary learned of a college in Iowa for students who were blind. Attending mattered more than anything to her. Laura was old enough to teach. Her pay could help with Mary's college costs. Her teaching job was twelve miles out from De Smet. The place was a small settlement. At sixteen, she said goodbye with courage. A whole semester away from home was what she dreaded. The first school week ended with a surprise. Almanzo Wilder drove up to the schoolhouse. This was Almanzo, already known for helping De Smet survive. A beautiful sleigh, pulled by horses, carried him. Weekend rides home were his offer. Long drives over the prairie turned friendship into love. One night he asked Laura to marry him. Her answer was yes. She called him Manly. His homestead, outside De Smet, became their home. A daughter, Rose, soon arrived. Bad luck then hit in a string. Hail destroyed the wheat. A dangerous infection struck both Laura and Manly. Laura got fully well. Manly's limp lasted the rest of his life. A baby boy was born. He lived only two weeks. Fire then burned the house to the ground. Laura was still a settler. She looked for a place to begin again. She found it before long. A photo from 1885 shows her beside Almanzo Wilder. The picture was made soon after the wedding. Before the twentieth century, vaccines were few. Medicines that worked were very few. Disease was common, and it was serious. Illness touched many people in Laura's family. For that time, this was not unusual.

6Laura later wrote that life's sweet, simple things are the true ones. A visitor once handed her a gleaming red apple. It had come from the Ozark Mountains.
