At twenty-seven, she set out again by covered wagon. East was the new direction. She was heading for the country that grew that apple. Near Mansfield, Missouri, she and Manly bought a plain farm. The Ozark foothills were the setting. The ground was rough. It was wooded. It was rocky. Laura knew at once it was home. Years went into chopping trees. Rocks had to be hauled for years. Plowing took years. Building took years. Planting took years. Rocky Ridge became a beautiful farm, and a prosperous one. After a life of moving, she was content. Rose had inherited Pa's restless spirit. She was intelligent. She was ambitious. San Francisco was where she moved. Journalism there earned her respect. One summer, Laura visited her grown daughter in California. Letters to Manly described towering redwoods. They described a glittering city. They described the Pacific Ocean in thunder. Rose earned her living by writing. Writing was what Laura had always loved. Farm life was comfortable by then. Could Laura do the same work? Back home, memories poured onto paper. Some nights she wrote until morning. Manly had built her a small desk. A whole book grew from her early years under Wisconsin's tall trees. The title has two parts. The first part is Little House. The second part is in the Big Woods. A publisher received the manuscript from Rose. At sixty-four, Laura expected little to come of it. The decade was the 1930s. Cars existed. Electricity existed. Radio existed. Who would care about heavy chores in a dark forest? Readers treated it as a sensation right away. Howling winter wind came alive on the page. A crackling fire came alive. Pa's fiddle, with its joyful skip, seemed to play again. Meeting wild animals felt thrilling again. A simple rag doll's joy, for a settler girl in a rough log cabin, was called up. Letters overflowed the mailbox at Rocky Ridge. Young readers begged for more. Kansas prairie years became another book. Its title is Little House on the Prairie. Walnut Grove years became a book too. Its title puts On the Banks first, and of Plum Creek after. De Smet's terrible winter became a book. The title is The Long Winter. The town's recovery became a book whose title is Little Town on the Prairie.

7Around 1940, a photo shows Laura Ingalls Wilder smiling. She is signing copies of her books. Fan letters were a pleasure to answer. Readings and signings were a pleasure to travel to. Coming home to Manly still made her happiest. Rocky Ridge Farm was that home. Both lived into their nineties. Laura died in 1957. The books continued. A television series followed in 1974. Stories of settler life still hold young readers. Her life is now part of the history of the United States. A few word meanings help. Evoked means a feeling was called up. A memory can be called up that way. A picture in the mind can be called up that way. Receded means something moved back. It pulled away from where it had been. A sensation is great excitement. It can also be a person or a thing that causes that excitement. Hardship is pain. It is loss. It can be the thing that causes either. A homestead was land from the U.S. government. Settlers who farmed it received the property, especially in the 1800s. People who move to a new place and stay are called settler-colonists. They claim ground and treat it as theirs. Income is money from work. It can come from another source too. A stroke is a fast loss of how the brain works. Blood that should reach the brain is interrupted. That interruption is the cause. A prairie is a wide flat plain. Grasses cover it. Vivid means very bright. It means strong. Prosperous means successful. It means well-off. A publisher is a person, or a company, that offers writing to the public. Print is one way. The Internet is another.

91. The Young Pharaoh's Unanswered Death

1A photo shows the British archaeologist Howard Carter at work. He is studying the golden sarcophagus while the digging goes on. He is the man who found King Tut's tomb. Coming pages tell how Tut was found. They describe his homeland. They describe his family. They describe the boy who ruled. They describe a dynasty's end. They describe the tomb. They name suspects. They study the body. They ask whether the mystery is solved. Useful words come last. The year of the find was 1922. Say archaeologist as AR-kee-OLL-oh-jist. The king was Tutankhamun, said toot-an-KAH-muhn. Most people call him King Tut. More than 3,300 years separate his reign from the present. Pharaoh, said FAIR-oh, was his title, and he received it at age nine. The reign lasted almost ten years. Then death came suddenly. Opening the coffin started a long question. How did this young king die? An archaeologist works by looking at evidence. Questions come with that evidence. Where was Tut's home? Who were his family and his friends? Did enemies surround him? Those answers may unlock a harder question. Why did death come to King Tut while he was still so young? A picture imagines his living face. The funeral mask sits behind him.

2For thousands of years, ruling families governed ancient Egypt. Dynasty is the word for one of those families. Historians sort the dynasties into three large periods. The three periods are known as the Old Kingdom, then the Middle Kingdom, then the New Kingdom. Membership in the 18th Dynasty belonged to King Tutankhamun. That dynasty was the first of the New Kingdom. The New Kingdom opened around 1550 bce. Belief in the gods was a major part of life in ancient Egypt. People worshipped many gods. They worshipped many goddesses. Tut's life, and maybe his death, sits inside that religious history. A reader has to know the history to follow him. A map shows ancient Egypt. At the start of the New Kingdom, two gods stood among the most important. One was Ra, said RAH. The other was Amun, said AH-muhn. Ra was god of the Sun. Pictures often gave him a falcon's form. Amun was a god who created. Pictures usually gave him a man's body and a tall crown. Late in the New Kingdom, some Egyptians shifted their worship of the Sun. They named this god Aten, said AH-tuhn. The picture was a golden disk of the Sun. Nobles gave Aten more importance. Other gods received less worship. Religion still filled daily life, and the rules bent. For most people, Aten was simply one more god in a crowd. Their beliefs did not feel threatened. The change came with a young pharaoh. His name was Amenhotep IV, said ah-muhn-HO-tep. He was Tut's father. A caption shows Amenhotep IV.

3Hundreds of gods and goddesses existed. Most people still chose a small group to worship. Help with a career was one reason for the choice. Thoth watched over writing and knowledge. Seshat watched over writing and measurement. Ptah watched over people who made things by craft. Amenhotep IV started his reign in 1352 bce. Egyptian art gives him a long face. It gives him thin calves. It gives him a belly that protrudes. He grew up inside the newer Aten faith. He believed it fully. In his view, Aten was a god for every person in the world. He held that Aten made the world when time began. He held that Aten ruled that world alone. People have called him the world's first monotheist. A monotheist believes in a single god. About five years into the reign, official religion changed all at once. The shift was complete. Egyptians were told they could worship Aten and no other god. The pharaoh took a new name, Akhenaten, said ahk-eh-NAH-tuhn. The name means He Who Serves Aten. Temples of many older gods were shut. He tried to have those temples destroyed. People were upset, and the priests of the older gods were among them. In several regions, locals tried to halt the wrecking of their temples. The pharaoh's army was able to hold those people down. A new capital city was also his project. He shifted the capital away from Thebes. The new city's name was Akhetaten, said ahk-eh-TAH-tuhn. The name means Horizon of Aten. People today call that area Amarna. The wife he favored most was Queen Nefertiti, said neh-fer-TEE-tee. His mother died, and Nefertiti was likely stepmother to the young prince. The prince was Tutankhaten, later called Tutankhamun. Nefertiti's death came in her early thirties.

4Birth came to King Tut in that new capital. The year was about 1345 bce. His name was Tutankhaten. The name means the Living Image of Aten. Not long ago, researchers used genetic tests on mummies. They were looking for his parents and his grandparents. DNA came from bones. One mummy may be Akhenaten, and that mummy may be the father. The result included a chart of the boy king's relatives. His mother was a sister of Akhenaten. Which sister is not clear. Seventeen years was the length of Akhenaten's rule. Two rulers filled the three or four years that followed. After those rulers, Egypt's throne sat empty again. Tutankhaten, age nine, became pharaoh. A temple at Amarna supplied a carving of a family group. Akhenaten is there. Nefertiti is there, and she may be Tut's stepmother. Three of their children are there. Wealth shaped Tut's life. He wore jewelry. He wore clothing of linen. He wore oils that were perfumed. He wore makeup. His tomb held all of those things. A pharaoh was expected to hunt. Members of the royal court hunted with him. A bow was the usual weapon. A chariot was the usual seat. Chariots went into the tomb. Bows went into it. Board games went into it. The afterlife was the reason. He married his half-sister. At least two daughters were born. Neither daughter lived. The court included several servants. One attendant who stayed near him had served the family for a long time. Service began when Tut's grandfather was king. Other servants handled even the smallest tasks. Some of those servants were younger than the king. A cupbearer was one of them. Filling drinking cups was the job. The young king's cup came first. A caption names him King Tutankhaten.

5Youth left the military work to other people. Political work of the court went to other people too. Two men were deeply involved. Ay was the chief advisor. Horemheb, said HOR-ehm-heb, led the army. Both had served Akhenaten. Both strongly disliked the religious reforms Akhenaten had made. They wanted the old ways of worship brought back. Ending Aten's worship was the change they urged on King Tut. Amun, they said, should be chief god again. Tut did restore him. The king also took a new name, Tutankhamun. Living Image of Amun is what that name means. Historians know who pushed the changes during this reign. Ay and Horemheb did the pushing. Youth meant the king followed orders. Back to Thebes went the royal court. Amarna, a city given to Aten, was abandoned. It was left to rot under the Egyptian sun. Death came to King Tut in 1327 bce. His age was about nineteen. No official record says how he died. Workers mummified the young pharaoh. Burial was in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Near Thebes, this valley was a cemetery for royalty, and it was large. No child of Tut was alive. Egypt still needed a king. Ay took the throne. Long experience in the court was the reason. He also married the woman Tut had left as a widow. Ay's own rule lasted just four years. He died in 1323 bce. Horemheb became pharaoh next. Pharaohs carried more than one name. Birth gave them one name. Becoming pharaoh brought further names. Those names often sat inside an oval. The oval is a cartouche, said car-TOOSH.

6A photo shows archaeologists digging in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Horemheb sent men to destroy the temples of Aten. Statues of Akhenaten were smashed. Statues of his family were smashed. Statues of King Tut were smashed too. Later, workers pulled stone blocks out of the city's buildings. Wall art covered those blocks. The blocks were reused in building projects at Hermopolis. The Nile separates Hermopolis from Amarna, with Hermopolis on the far bank. What remained of Akhenaten's capital had been splendid. It was shattered, then covered by drifting sand. People forgot it. Horemheb's rule lasted twenty-seven years. He died in 1295 bce. His death ended the 18th Dynasty. In the 1800s, many archaeologists from Britain and from Europe traveled to Egypt. They came to study Egyptian writing. The writing is called hieroglyphics, said hy-ur-uh-GLIFiks. Walls carried it. Monuments carried it. The writing revealed a great deal about how pharaohs lived and what customs they kept. Archaeologists learned what a pharaoh's tomb was meant to hold. Whatever that person would need after death was supposed to be inside. Profit drew some diggers. They opened many tombs. Disappointment always followed. Robbers had arrived first. The Rosetta Stone has a story of its own. Napoleon's army arrived in 1798 with orders to seize Egypt. One soldier found a flat black rock. Three languages were carved on its face. Two were forms of ancient Egyptian. The third was Greek. Scholars spent the next twenty-five years translating the other languages. The Greek text was one key. Coptic, a later Egyptian language, supplied the other key. A breakthrough came from one scholar. He realized the old writing used symbols for sounds. The symbols did not stand for whole words. Discovery of the Rosetta Stone remains among the most critical finds in archaeology.

7By the early 1900s, archaeologists had settled on a belief. No tomb in Egypt's Valley of the Kings, they thought, was still unknown. Carter's search for Tut went on for more than five years. Luck did not come. In 1922 he asked for one more season of pay. The man funding the search agreed. Later that same year, Carter reached a tomb that was almost intact. Artifacts were plentiful. Thrones were there. Jewelry was there. Weapons were there. Statues were there. A large mask of gold covered the mummy. Three coffins nested around the body. The coffin farthest inside was gold. The gold weighed about 242 pounds (110 kg). The find caused a sensation. History's most famous pharaoh became Tut. Foreign archaeologists worked under Egyptian rules. An intact tomb meant every artifact had to remain in Egypt. Carter disputed the government's view. Intact, he claimed, was the wrong word for this tomb. England was where he hoped to send half the treasure. Not a single object left Egypt. The funeral mask of gold stayed. The jewelry stayed. The statues stayed. Today the Egyptian government partners with researchers from other countries. Artifacts from the tomb are allowed to travel on tour. Egyptians still make the final decision about this treasure. Dying young was common in ancient times. In ancient Egypt, a typical life ran about thirty years. Many people never reached that age. Even so, some historians suspect murder. Ay guided many of Tut's decisions. Horemheb guided many of them too. Both men became pharaohs after Tut died. No natural heir stood ready for the throne. Seizing power had a deadline. It had to happen before a child of Tut survived. It had to happen before Tut himself became an adult. Researchers have named two servants as possible killers. One is the cupbearer. The other is the personal attendant. Few people could enter the king's bedroom. Killing the pharaoh was within either man's reach. Tut's tomb includes a wall painting that shows Ay.

8For years, a blow to the head was the leading idea. People thought that blow killed Tut. X-ray studies of the mummy supported the idea. One study was in 1968. Another was in 1978. The images showed damage in the skull. Experts called the damage strong proof. A heavy object, they said, had hit the back of the head. In 2005, a team in Cairo, Egypt, set out to test that claim. Dr. Zahi Hawass led the group. He is a top archaeologist in Egypt. The tool was an advanced X-ray method. It is called CT scanning, also called CAT scanning. A CT scanner shoots many X-rays. The angles differ. A computer turns that information into pictures. The pictures show much more detail than a regular X-ray machine. A photo shows Dr. Zahi Hawass beside Tut. The mummy has not yet entered the scanner. Hawass reported that the skull was damaged after death. Mummification was the likely moment. The scans also showed several problems in the body. A cleft palate was one. A club foot was another. A further clue concerned the cause of death. Shortly before he died, a leg had broken. The break had not healed properly. Hawass said an infection may have followed the injury. Death may have followed within a few days. Between 2007 and 2010, Hawass and fellow researchers studied the remains once more. Genetic tests were the method. Two important conditions appeared that had not been seen before. One was repeated attacks of severe malaria. Malaria by itself probably would not have killed Tut. Great weakness may have followed. The other was bone deterioration in the left foot. Both parents may have passed the condition down. The parents were siblings. That family link may have made the harm worse. Scientists have also shown the face of King Tut's mummy.

9A question remains. Did the young king die from several troubles stacked together? Physical problems could be part of it. An accident could be part of it. A disease could be part of it. Infection from a broken leg could be part of it. Something else could be the cause instead. Some people on Hawass's team offered another reading of the leg. Embalming, some of them said, might be when the leg broke. Carter's team draws blame from other experts. They say the break came when the mummy was lifted from its inner coffin. That lifting happened years ago. Newer science and DNA evidence make theories easier to prove. Experts can still read the same evidence in different ways. What is your reading? A photo shows Carter's team taking artifacts out of the tomb. An archaeologist is a scientist who studies what ancient cultures left behind. Genetic describes heredity. It also describes variation in living things. Hieroglyphics is a writing system of pictures or symbols. Those marks can stand for words, for syllables, or for sounds. Ancient Egyptians used it. Other peoples used it too. It is not an alphabet of letters. An artifact is any object humans made or used long ago. Depicted means represented. It can mean portrayed. Deterioration is the process of growing worse as time passes. A monotheist believes there is only one god. Dynasties are ruling lines that stay inside one family in a country. Mummified means made into a mummy. A pharaoh is a ruler of ancient Egypt. Embalmed means a dead body was treated so decay would stay away. Protruding means sticking out.

92. Traits Passed from Generation to Generation

1A picture shows members of one family. They look alike because inherited traits are shared among them. The book opens with an introduction. Farming comes next. Breeding animals comes after that. Animals that live in zoos come next. Solving crimes follows. Health follows that. A conclusion closes the main text. Useful words are gathered at the end. Many young people ask what work they will want. Being a doctor is one idea. Being a detective is another. Working among animals is another. Genetics is the one thing these jobs share. Genetics is a science field. It studies the way living things hand traits forward. The handoff runs onward, parent group to child group. A trait is a feature of a living thing. Color of hair is a trait. Length of a finger is a trait. Shape of a nose is a trait. Knowing genetics matters in a lot of work. Farming is one kind of that work. Breeding animals is another kind. Curing diseases is another kind. Stopping illnesses before they start is another kind. Solving crimes is another kind.

2Genetics counts as a new science. Even so, people were already using genetic techniques very early. The early date is 5000 BC. The aim was better crops. The aim was also better animals. Selective breeding is one of those techniques. Scientists pick plants that carry traits they want. Quick growth is one such trait. Fruit that looks attractive is another. Those plants are then bred with other plants that carry the same traits. Selective breeding makes sure the wanted traits move to the next plants. The crops that result grow faster. They also make better fruit. A supermarket can offer many kinds of tomatoes. Selective breeding of tomato plants produced those kinds. Wheat is another common crop raised with genetic techniques. Soybeans are another. Corn is another. Genetics will let farmers raise plants with more protein. It will also let them raise plants with less oil. A picture shows many tomato varieties. All of them were bred out of one wild variety. Scientists use genetic techniques on animals as well. One result is chickens that lay a greater number of eggs. Another result is cows that grow faster. Those cows also give more milk. Farming gains from genetics can sound wonderful. Faster crops that also taste better seem easy to want. More milk from cows seems easy to want too. Some people answer with a warning. They say genetic changes to crops and animals will harm genetic diversity. Breeding for only a chosen set of traits has a cost. Many other useful traits of plants and animals may vanish for good. A thin range of genes can also leave crops and animals open to danger. One virus might then wipe out a whole species. A picture shows piglets from selective breeding. They grow up faster than wild piglets that are their cousins. Supporters of genetics in farming want food production improved. Opponents worry about effects nobody can yet predict. Those effects might touch the environment. They might touch human health.

3People who breed animals use some genetic techniques that plant scientists use. Selective breeding is one shared technique. Hybridization is another. Crossbreeding is another name for hybridization. It means breeding different varieties. It can even mean breeding different species. The goal is to join the best characteristics of both parents. A female horse can be bred with a male donkey. The offspring is a mule. A mule is a hybrid. Horses are one parent type. Donkeys are the other. A mule is tough in the way a donkey is tough. A mule is agile in the way a horse is agile. Mules make very good animals for work. A picture places a donkey at the top. A horse is on the left. A mule is on the right. Plenty of dog breeders raise dogs only so the dogs can be shown. Other breeds are shaped for a set purpose. Hunting is one purpose. Herding is another. Guarding is another. Spaniels were among the earliest dogs used for hunting. Spain is where springer spaniels were bred at the start. Cocker spaniels began there as well. The prey included water birds such as ducks. It also included land birds such as pheasants. A breeder first decides which traits a dog should have. Parents are then chosen so those traits will pass to the offspring. A picture shows border collies. They are excellent at herding. Herding is another trait people choose to breed into certain dogs. Herding dogs guard cattle. They also round the cattle up. They do the same with other livestock. Border collies are popular herding dogs. People also like Australian shepherds for herding work. The breeding has been so successful that herding continues without lessons. Owners of border collies often report a funny habit. The dogs try to herd cars. They try to herd people as well. The border collie breed took shape hundreds of years ago. Its first job was herding cattle and sheep. England and Scotland meet at a border, and that border was the workplace.

4The Australian shepherd came from several herding breeds. The border collie was one of those breeds. English settlers carried border collies with them to Australia. Shepherds of this type are still used widely in Australia. Australia keeps its cattle on fields that are open. Its other livestock live on open fields as well. Some dogs are bred to guard. The Doberman pinscher is one common guard dog. The German shepherd is another. Louis Dobermann, a watchman in Germany, was the first to breed the Doberman. The time was the late 1890s. The breed gained a reputation for danger. Breeders in later years worked hard on a different temperament. They wanted the Doberman calmer. They wanted it friendlier. Many dogs are hybrids. A hybrid here is a cross of two breeds or more. Some people think hybrids make the best pets. Their reason is that each parent can pass a strong quality into the same pup. A picture shows mutts. A mutt can gather strong qualities from a wide mix of breeds. Another picture shows giant pandas. Captive-breeding programs have helped them. Zoos do research on animals. Zoos also teach people. Zoos also entertain people. Genetics is part of the research at some zoos. The research aims at a future in which animal species still survive well. Genetics matters a great deal in protection. Many species that are endangered receive that protection. Many species that are threatened receive it too.

5Zoo scientists have a technique for raising the numbers of endangered species. The technique is called captive breeding. It means breeding animals that live in captivity. A zoo is one kind of captivity. The purpose is to keep genetic diversity inside a species. Some young born in captivity are later set free among wild animals. Those young bring different genes into the wild group. The wild animals then have a better chance to survive. This kind of captive breeding works only under one condition. After release, the animals must live on their own. They must also produce young on their own. Captive breeding is in use for certain species that are endangered. It is in use for certain species that are threatened. The red wolf is one. The gorilla is one. The giant panda is one. The cheetah is one. The rhinoceros is one. A second kind of captive breeding serves species that are nearly extinct. Those species cannot live in the wild. A protected place gives them a chance to produce young. Captive breeding matters. It still cannot take the place of animals that live and breed in the wild. Zoo workers also try to teach the public. They teach why habitats of endangered species must be protected. They teach the same lesson for threatened species. Rhinoceroses need that protection. Tigers need it too. Without it, later generations of people would meet those animals only in books. Crime work has changed as well. A magnifying glass is no longer the only tool. Police now use genetics. Detectives use it. Lawyers use it. DNA is part of that work. Every gene holds DNA. DNA carries a code. The code sets an organism's genetic traits. Fingerprints differ from person to person. DNA differs in that same way. Every organism has DNA of its own. A picture reminds us that detectives now hold more clues than before. Police take fingerprints from criminals. Those prints go into a database. A print found where a crime happened can be compared with prints already stored. DNA is unique, as a fingerprint is unique. Using DNA to solve crimes is therefore called DNA fingerprinting. One advantage is large. A fingerprint does not have to be found. A DNA fingerprint can come from a tiny bit of skin. It can come from one hair. It can come from a drop of fluid. Blood is one such fluid. Saliva is another. A criminal can hardly avoid leaving some trace. The trace may be skin, hair, or fluid. A person leaves microscopic traces of DNA in every place he or she goes.

6Picture an investigation that finds skin cells. The cells are under a victim's fingernails. Investigators can read the DNA in those cells. They can also take a DNA sample from a suspect. A match between the two samples moves the case forward. The case then moves nearer to an answer. A picture shows a lab agent at work on DNA evidence. Agencies that enforce the law are building DNA databases. The collections resemble files of fingerprints. DNA fingerprints of people convicted of crimes sit in those databases. Other evidence from crime scenes is stored there too. DNA has also freed people. Those people had been convicted of crimes they did not commit. Many crimes have been cleared with help from DNA fingerprinting. The first use was in 1985. Some people still worry. Contamination might hurt the accuracy of a DNA test. Misuse of the tests is another worry. Even with those worries, the method is likely to stay. It will stay while it helps name criminals. It will stay while it helps solve crimes. Health workers use genetics too. Medical scientists use it. Health-care scientists use it. Genetics helps them diagnose diseases. It helps them treat diseases. It helps them prevent diseases. It also helps them develop new medicines. Many genes that cause particular diseases are now being found. Finding the gene behind a disease helps scientists build medicines. It helps them build vaccines. The medicines and vaccines may cure the disease. They may prevent it. Genetics counselors use genetics as well. They help parents estimate odds. They help people who may become parents. The odds concern passing genetic disorders to children. That information helps parents choose if they will have children. They also think about care. Caring for a child with a genetic disorder is part of the decision. Some genetic disorders are fairly common as inherited conditions. Cystic fibrosis is one. Huntington's disease is one. Breast cancer is one. In 2000, scientists finished the Human Genome Project. That project is a full map. It shows where every human gene sits. The human gene count is about twenty-four thousand. The genes sit in a set order on our chromosomes. Powerful computers spent ten years on the count. They also spent those years locating every gene. Many diseases come from genes that are missing. Many come from genes that sit in the wrong place.

7A picture shows a scientist at a computer screen. The scientist is comparing DNA fingerprints. Genetics, as a field, offers many chances for jobs. It is an exciting branch of science. It is also a branch that is still relatively new. Fresh developments arrive almost every day. Fresh job chances arrive almost every day too. Plant breeding is tied to genetics. Animal breeding is tied to it. Medicine is tied to it. The study of crime is tied to it. Other fields are tied to it as well. A library can offer more on this science. So can the Internet. Captive breeding means breeding animals that already live in captivity. The young may later be released into the wild. A habitat is the natural environment of a plant or an animal. A hybrid is offspring. The parents are of two different types, breeds, or species. A characteristic is a feature. It helps identify a thing or a group of things. Hybridization is a breeding process. Two different species are bred so characteristics of both can combine. Diversity means a wide variety. Many different things make up that variety. DNA is a code. A living thing's genetic message is what it holds. The long name is deoxyribonucleic acid, and DNA is the short form. Selective breeding means chosen plants or animals are bred together. The purpose is to improve traits their offspring inherit. The purpose can also be to control those traits. Genes are the basic units of heredity. Traits move through them, from parents on to their offspring. A species is a group of living things. Members look physically similar. They can reproduce. Genetics is the science of how traits pass onward. The pass runs from parents to the young that follow. A trait is a feature or a quality. An animal, a plant, a thing, or a group can have one.

93. Two Minutes at a Soldiers' Cemetery

1The fifth version of the Gettysburg Address is the only version President Lincoln signed. The chapters that follow move in a set order. They open with a war inside families. They turn next to President Lincoln and the Civil War. His words come after that. A closer look follows. Life after Gettysburg comes next. Hard words are explained at the end. Fighting between brothers and sisters is so common that people barely notice. Imagine being at war instead. You fight for one side. A brother or a sister fights on the other side as your enemy. The American Civil War was a long fight between two sides of the country. Soldiers sometimes knew their enemy. Men from the same town could stand on opposite sides.

2July 1, 1863, was the battle's first morning. Rudolf Schwarz, a Union soldier, watched Confederate prisoners being led off. One face shocked him. The prisoner was the brother Rudolf grew up with. Those brothers had last seen each other when they left Germany. The United States was their destination then. The two hugged. Seeing each other made them glad. Guards then took the Confederate brother away. The brothers never met again. That same afternoon, Rudolf was killed in action. How did the country reach a point where brothers fought brothers? Why does the fight at Gettysburg stand out? A map for 1860 shows where slavery was legal and where it was banned. Abraham Lincoln ran for president that year. Fifteen Southern states still allowed slavery. People called those the slave states. It was illegal in eighteen Northern states. People called those the free states. Many enslaved people tried to flee north and become free. Lincoln did not want slavery to spread past the South. That stand angered many Southern people. They feared a Lincoln presidency would, in time, end slavery everywhere. Farming paid many Southerners. Plantations, the huge farms, needed enormous labor. Owners believed enslaved workers were the best way to meet that need. Ending slavery, they thought, would wreck their whole way of life.

3The North lived differently. Factories filled the Northern states. Enslaved labor was not how those factories ran. Many Northern people wanted slavery to end. Lincoln won the presidency in 1860. Over the following months, eleven slave states declared secession. They no longer wished to remain in the United States. Their new country took the name Confederate States of America. A map for 1861 shows them. Four slave states stayed out of the Confederacy. Missouri was one. Kentucky was one. Maryland was one. Delaware was one. The eleven that left were Alabama, Arkansas, North Carolina, and South Carolina. Florida and Georgia left too. So did Louisiana, Mississippi, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia. West Virginia took shape while that war was being fought. It is the only state born by breaking away from a Confederate state. That state was Virginia. Lincoln became president in March 1861. War began one month later. Confederate fighters were called rebels. Johnny Reb was another name for them. The South fought hard to be independent. Union was the name for Northern states that backed Lincoln and the United States. Holding the country together mattered more to them than anything else. Yankees was the nickname for their soldiers. Yanks was another nickname. Many in the North wanted slavery ended. They fought hard in a struggle they named the War of Southern Rebellion. Uniforms went on next. Boys sometimes did too. Blue was the Union color. Gray was the Confederate color. Jobs, farms, and families were left behind. Many expected the war to last only weeks, or a few months. By Gettysburg, Lincoln had already been president for two years. General Robert E. Lee, on the Confederate side, had stacked up many victories. He led troops north into Pennsylvania. The route ran through Virginia and Maryland. Union losses had been heavy. Even so, Lincoln had held the nation together.

4More than 93,000 Union soldiers marched into Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. More than 71,000 Confederate soldiers marched in too. Fighting lasted three days. When the guns stopped, the toll was nearly 51,000. Those soldiers were dead, hurt, or missing. Out of every ten who fought, three were hurt or killed. Lee's push toward the north ended there. Devastation still fell on both armies. It fell on the town as well. Wounded men filled public buildings, which had to serve as hospitals. Private homes were used the same way. Every farm became a graveyard. Fighting went on for eighteen more months. No other battle in the Civil War killed more men. The field became the first national cemetery. November 19, 1863, came four months later. The Soldiers' National Cemetery stood ready to be dedicated. Lincoln was asked to offer a few fitting remarks. He was not the main speaker. Edward Everett held that role. Few speakers of that time were better known than he was. His formal speech ran two hours. The crowd already knew Everett well. He had served as a U.S. congressman. He had served as a senator. Speaking to audiences was familiar work for him. Gettysburg gave him still more practice. Two hours is longer than many movies run today. A speech that long might feel overwhelming now. It might feel boring. In the 1860s, such length was ordinary. The crowd applauded. Everett wrote to the president the next day and praised him. He said he would be glad to have reached the heart of the day in two hours as nearly as Lincoln had in two minutes. So much said in so little time impressed him. Lincoln answered that he was glad the speech had not been a total failure.

5Days before the ceremony, Lincoln told a journalist what to expect. He stacked the same word three times. That word was short. He kept that promise. Two minutes was all he spoke. Even so, the solemn day got careful thought. Witnesses say he wrote on the train ride toward Gettysburg. He wrote again on the morning of the ceremony. Writing continued until he had to leave for the cemetery. A photograph shows him in August 1863. That month came one month after the battle. The battle was a turning point. Four months on, few people saw it that way. Confederate leaders treated the loss as a defeat, not a disaster. Some Northerners were tired of the war. They wanted the South released. Lincoln could not promise victory just ahead. He knew victory was not waiting around the corner. He had to keep the Union strong. He had to keep it fighting. A good speech would not be enough that day. He needed a great one.

6Today many people rank the Gettysburg Address with the speeches that most stir Americans. Tape recorders did not yet exist. No one can prove his exact words. Reporters in the cemetery wrote what they heard. Telegraph carried those notes to newspapers. Five copies survive in Lincoln's own hand. Each copy differs a little from the others. The year was 1863, so no sound recording exists. Witnesses and reporters still described his voice. He spoke in a loud, clear way, they said. He also spoke slowly. He spoke with care. The slow pace may have been a choice, to match the serious mood. It may also have come from knowing the remarks were brief. We now know he was falling ill as he spoke. People who saw him mostly call him sad. Mournful is another word they use. His secretary called his color ghastly. Haggard is the word the secretary used for his face. Lincoln spoke of weakness that day. He spoke of dizziness. He had mentioned both the morning before as well. Fever had taken hold by the time his train headed home. A severe headache had set in. Doctors later found he had smallpox.

7The fifth copy is the last one, and it is the favorite. Lincoln signed it. He also gave it a title. That is why printers use it most often. Some value it at nearly half a million dollars. The Lincoln Room inside the White House is where it hangs. Fresh words can carry the meaning of that copy. Eighty-seven years earlier, he said, the founders had started a new nation on this continent. Liberty was its birth. The nation was pledged to one idea. All men are created equal. A great civil war now held the country, he said. The war was a test. Could a nation born that way, and pledged that way, last? The crowd stood on a great battlefield of the war, he said. They had come to set part of the field aside. It would be a burial place. The dead had given their lives so the nation might continue. Doing this was fitting, he said. It was proper. Then he turned. The living could not truly set the ground apart, he said. They could not make it holy. They could not treat it as sacred ground by their own act. Brave men had already done that, both the living and the dead. Their struggle put the ground beyond anything the living could add. It also put the ground beyond anything the living could take away. The world would barely notice the words spoken there, he said. Those words would not be remembered for long. What the soldiers did could never be forgotten. The living, he said, must give themselves to work still unfinished. Fighters there had carried that work forward in a noble way. A great task still waited. From the dead, who were honored, the living should draw a deeper devotion. The dead had given every last bit of devotion they had. The living should decide firmly that these deaths were not wasted. Under God, the nation should see freedom born again. Rule by the public, through the public, and for the public must not die off the earth.

8A line-by-line look makes the address clearer. The opening counts four score and seven years. One score is twenty years. Four scores make eighty. Seven more makes eighty-seven. The speech year was 1863. Count back eighty-seven years and you land in 1776. That year brought the Declaration of Independence. Fathers who brought forth a new nation means the Founding Fathers. Thomas Jefferson was one. They set up the United States of America. Jefferson's pen produced the line Lincoln echoes. The line says all men are created equal. Jefferson called that truth self-evident. Lincoln then leaves the past and speaks of the present. The painful Civil War, he explains, is a test of the country. Strain shows what is strong and what is weak. Gettysburg National Cemetery holds Union dead from the battle. The number is more than 3,500. It is their final resting place. In the 1870s, Confederate dead were sent south. The number moved was 3,200. Southern cemeteries received them. A few Confederate dead remain at Gettysburg. Soldiers from later wars lie there as well.

9Lincoln says the crowd has gathered on a great battlefield of the war. Few battles in that long war were bloodier than Gettysburg. Confederate leaders gave no sign of quitting. Lincoln knew the end was still far off. He says people have come to set aside part of the field. It will be a last resting place. The soldiers gave their lives so the nation might live. Gave their lives says more than died. It stresses sacrifice for the country. Lincoln wanted mourners on both sides joined for the country's sake. He calls the dedication fitting. He calls it proper. Then he shifts. Repetition makes his larger point. He picks words close in meaning to dedicate. Hallow means to honor something as holy. Consecrate means to make something sacred. He is not canceling the cemetery. He means the deaths have already made the ground as sacred as it can be. They have made it as special as it can be. In a way, he says deeds outlast talk. The world will hardly notice what is said. It will not remember those words for long. It can never forget the soldiers' deeds. He then calls the living to unfinished work. The fighters had advanced that work nobly. A great task still remains, and the living must take it up. From the honored dead should come a stronger devotion. The cause received the fullest devotion the dead could give. The living should resolve, with high purpose, that these deaths were not empty. Under God, the nation shall see freedom born anew. Government shaped by the people, run by the people, and aimed at the people shall not vanish from the earth.

10Lincoln stirs respect for the fallen. He calls them noble. He calls them honored. That respect is meant to pull listeners back to their nation. It is meant to pull them back to its freedoms. The great task ahead is named in that pull. Winning the war was part of the task. Ending slavery was part of it. Keeping the country itself alive was part of it. The country was the United States of America. What follows is the speech's most famous part. He speaks of government that belongs to the people. He speaks of government carried out by the people. He speaks of government that exists for the people. That government, he says, must not perish from the earth. Repetition returns, but the trick is different. He does not swap in synonyms. He shifts one idea with small prepositions. Those little words point to what government is about. It is about people. A detail from Elihu Vedder's mural Government, made in 1896, is in the Library of Congress. A tablet there carries Lincoln's famous phrase. Handwritten copies of the address are national treasures today. The words are also carved in stone in Washington, D.C. The place is the Lincoln Memorial. The crowd that day, though, stayed quiet. The memorial was built to look like a Greek temple. The doors opened in 1922. Martin Luther King Jr. stood on those steps forty-one years later. He gave the speech known as I Have a Dream. Lincoln and King show how words can move a country toward change. A statue of Lincoln sits in the central hall. It rises 19 feet. Standing, the figure would reach 28 feet.

11Some accounts say applause came late and in scattered bits. It was barely polite. Others remember a hush, a dignified silence. Historians sometimes read the missing applause as a sign of deep impression. Ten sentences were enough for Lincoln to sum up the war. They were enough to sum up a nation's spirit. No one knows what listeners thought that day. What we know is that Americans have drawn inspiration from the speech ever since. For many people now, the sixteenth president is the most beloved of all. A few word meanings help. An address is a formal speech. Inspiring describes something that encourages a person to act. To commit is to pledge oneself. It can mean dedicating oneself to a person or a cause. To perish is to die, above all in a sudden way, a violent way, or an unexpected way. Conceived means thought up. It can mean imagined. A proposition is an idea set out to be considered, explored, or proved. Dedicated can mean pledged to a purpose. It can mean set apart for a special use. To resolve is to decide. It can mean settling a dispute or finding a way through a problem. To detract is to shrink someone's importance or value. Secession is a formal break from an organization. It can also be a formal break from a government. Devastation means damage on a great scale, or destruction. Devotion means deep love joined with commitment.

94. Two Skeletons and a Fight Over Bones

1A map asks where the dueling dinosaurs once walked. The book tells how the bones were found. It then tells how people fought over them. It asks who the fossils belong to. Hard words are explained last. Clayton Phipps poses beside a fossil he found in Montana. In 2006, he and Mark Eatman hunted fossils on a neighbor's land. The land was in eastern Montana. Dinosaur fossils are common in that area. Eatman soon spotted a huge pelvis. It stuck out of a canyon wall. Phipps then found an enormous thighbone close by. He began to think a full skeleton might be there. Digging started. The bones belonged to a horned dinosaur that ate plants. A couple of weeks later, a surprise appeared. It was a meat eater's claw. Horned dinosaurs do not have claws. The find was clearly important. Two fossil skeletons, almost complete, had been buried as a pair. The animals had died together.

2A plaster cast shows the pose. One animal was a carnivore. The other was an herbivore. They lay side by side. Their tails crossed. The skeletons left the ground still locked in blocks. Rock and soil made those blocks. Matrix is the name for that material. A laboratory received the blocks. Once the matrix was cleared, fifteen teeth from the meat eater were found stuck in the plant eater. An attack on the plant eater was the clear reading. Cracked ribs marked the meat eater. Its skull was crushed. Those injuries suggest a kick from the plant eater. The evidence points to a mutual killing. Each animal also mattered on its own. The plant eater is about as big as an elephant. It seems to be a horned dinosaur unknown before. The meat eater is about as big as a polar bear. In many ways it resembles a small Tyrannosaurus rex. Scientists might use it to decide a question. Is this kind of dinosaur new? Or is it only a young T. rex? Most fossil finds are missing bones. These two skeletons are not. Each skeleton's bones were still joined. They were not scattered apart. Preservation is so fine that patches of skin remain. Skin almost never turns up as a fossil. Museums nationwide might be expected to rush for such rare specimens. They did not. The Montana Dueling Dinosaurs show a debate inside paleontology. A great deal of research has stalled because of it. Two questions stand at the center. Should these bones be the world's? Do they instead belong to whoever held that land? Who should be permitted to collect them? An artist's picture suggests how the pair may have looked. To see why scientists and museums are not scrambling to buy the fossils, begin with the finders.

3Mark Eatman learned fossil hunting from Clayton Phipps. Phipps works as a commercial fossil hunter. Commercial collector is another label. Independent collector is another. Garfield County is home to both men. That county, in Montana, is where the pair was found. About 1,200 people live there. They are spread over roughly 4,800 square miles. That area is 12,432 square kilometers. Ranching or farming is how most of them live. Incomes, on average, are low. Many families struggle to get by. Dinosaur bones are among the few resources the area has in plenty. Fossils fill the eastern portion of Montana. They fill the western Dakotas too. Hunters such as these two ask landowners before they search. Sale money is split with those owners. Each find pays Phipps and Eatman. For a landowner, a discovery like this pair may arrive only once in a life. The hope is money enough to feel secure. Michael Triebold founded a center for dinosaur work in the Rocky Mountains. Its name is the Dinosaur Resource Center. He has said that private land carries a simple rule. The person who owns the ground owns the fossils. That owner may handle them however the owner chooses. Many scientists wanted these specimens open for study. Phipps offered them to three museums. None bought them. The asking price was 15 million dollars. A museum could not pay that sum alone. A second objection was raised. Commercial hunters had done the digging. The diggers were not scientists with academic training who worked for a museum or a university. The museums feared the dig had been done poorly. Care in digging matters. Fossils can be damaged as they leave the ground unless handling is extremely careful. Details have to be written down. Position in the ground matters. The stuff around the bones matters. Nearby fossils matter too. Clues can hide in those details. Paleontologists use the clues to rebuild how an animal lived. They use them to rebuild how it died. A sloppy dig can lose precious data for good. David Trexler, a paleontologist, has put the warning in plain words. A fossil can be collected only one time. A mistake cannot be undone.

4Digging fossils free is slow work. A great deal of time is required. The greatest care is required. Done properly, the work usually leaves bones where they lie at first. Whole blocks of matrix are lifted out. Plaster jackets wrap the blocks so the trip to a lab is safe. Maps are made during the dig. Photographs are taken. Soil samples are collected. As much information as possible is saved. At the lab, preparation is careful. Matrix comes off first. Cleaning follows. Repair follows. Strengthening follows. The fossils are then made ready to store, or to show. A university student is pictured cleaning part of a fossil tree found in Germany. That tree once stood in a forest. The forest is 290 million years old. Another picture shows a paleontologist in a lab. A tool frees a fossil from surrounding rock. The book poses a hard question. Should any person be allowed to collect fossils and prepare them? Should training be limited in some way? If a limit is set, should only academic training count? Who gets to decide? Good digging skills can be learned away from colleges and universities. Some commercial hunters may match university-trained paleontologists. Some may surpass them. Even so, some paleontologists distrust reports of careful commercial digs. They suspect the reports exist mainly to push prices higher. Some scientists and some institutions refuse to buy specimens. Proper collection does not change their refusal. Paying for fossils, they think, invites more people into commercial hunting. David Trexler works at the Two Medicine Dinosaur Center. He repeats the warning. Collection happens once. No second chance follows a mistake. Robert Bakker, also a paleontologist, says this dig met professional standards. He says the opposition is bias. Academic paleontologists, in his view, are biased against commercial hunters.

5How common dinosaur fossils are is another point of debate. Some people call them scarce. In that view, only scientists with formal training should dig them up and study them. Others call them so common that most would erode away. Wind would wear them down. Water would. Other forces of nature would do the same. That erosion would follow if collection were left to only a handful of trained scientists. Burial can last beyond 160 million years. Once weather reaches the fossil, it can disappear quickly. Both sides care where a find like this pair ends up. Some academic paleontologists oppose commercial collecting because of a risk. A wealthy private collector might buy the bones. An institution that would keep them open for ongoing study might lose the chance. Science rests on a principle. Evidence should stay available for other scientists. With dinosaur bones, new finds need to be set beside old specimens. They also need to be set beside finds still to come. Another question is posed. Suppose you found an amazing dinosaur worth thousands of dollars, or even millions. Would you give it to a museum? Would you try to sell it? How much would the final home matter to you? Students are shown searching for fossil remains. The place is Dinosaur Provincial Park. It is in Alberta, which is in Canada. Several endings are possible. Purchase by a museum is one path. Display and research could both follow. A generous buyer might give them to a scientific institution. Someone collecting in private might permit study first and display the fossils later. A private collector might show them only in private and block study. Access refused at first is sometimes granted later. Other family members may inherit the fossil. Decades can pass. Generations can pass. Nothing guarantees that later chance.

6Private land held these two dinosaurs. Current law in Montana gives them to the landowners. The owners may do what they wish. Museums would not buy, so the fossils went to auction. The month was November 2013. The expected price ran from 7 million dollars to 9 million. No bid reached the auction house's minimum. Another question is posed. Which people should have the right of ownership? Should museums and universities be the only owners of the important ones? Should wealthy private citizens buy them for private collections? The choice of who decides is left open. A fossil called Sue is famous worldwide. She is on display in Chicago, Illinois. The Field Museum is the place. She is a Tyrannosaurus rex. She is the largest ever found. She is the best preserved. She is the most complete. In the United States, limits on fossil collecting apply only on public land. Even there, the limits apply only sometimes. Some laws control archaeological remains. Those remains are linked to humans. They are too recent to count as fossils. Rules about fossil collecting are not always clear. They are not always the same from place to place. On private land, the landowner owns what is found. Keeping the fossils is allowed. Getting rid of them is allowed. An auction to the highest bidder is allowed, no matter the buyer's plans. Other countries write different rules. Germany requires a professional paleontologist to inspect each fossil that is collected. A find that matters to science becomes government property. The finder receives a fee. A find that does not matter goes back to the finder. Keeping it is allowed. Selling it is allowed. Some people in this debate want the United States to copy Germany's policy. Others call that a mistake. Strict rules, they say, would cost a lot to enforce. The rules would be inconvenient. They also say a policy like Germany's would break the property rights of citizens in the United States.

7One fossil has helped scientists link feathered dinosaurs with birds living now. Picture a hike, and a fossil at your feet. Should it go home with you? Should the find be reported? Should it be left alone? Children are usually curious about nature. Adults are too. Picking up rocks can be fun. Picking up fossils can be fun. Other objects can be fun to pick up as well. Such objects record the planet's history. Geological cycles are part of that record. Many forms of life are part of it. A great number of those forms are extinct. The Black Hills Institute studies geological research. It reports a striking share. Important fossils have a striking finder. Amateurs account for more than four-fifths of them. This dinosaur pair will not be the last amazing discovery in a reader's lifetime. Many more will surely be made. Academic scientists will make some. Commercial hunters will make some. Ordinary people on nature walks will make some. What will become of those fossils? A few word meanings help. An amateur takes up an activity for enjoyment. A hobby is another way to describe it. Pay is not the reason. Excavating means uncovering something. It means digging it out. A fossil is what remains of a plant or an animal after it has turned to stone. An auction sells goods or property by letting buyers bid. The highest offer wins. Paleontology studies fossils of plants and of animals. Private means not public. It can mean not meant to be shared. Biased means unfair support for one opinion. It can mean unfair support for one group, or for one set of beliefs, over another. To regulate is to control an amount, a rate, a speed, or a behavior. The aim is that something works properly, or follows laws and rules. Commercial describes buying and selling. A debate is a discussion. The people or groups in it hold different opinions. Specimens are examples kept for comparison. Study is another use. Display is another. Dueling means a fight between two.

95. Venus, Both Bright and Dangerous

1Sections come in this order. A Bright Beginning. Heat and Danger. A Surface Full of Wonders. Spacecraft That Went There. Last Thoughts. Words and Topics. A photo shows the planet Venus. Finding this planet is easier than finding any other. Closeness to the Sun keeps Venus close beside the Sun whenever you look up. Search low in the west just after the Sun sets. Or search low in the east just before the Sun rises. Strong binoculars show phases, and so does a telescope. The phases resemble the Moon's. A crescent shape is possible. A half shape is possible. A full shape is possible. A Bright Beginning. Night after night, the brightest point people call a star is Venus. Admiration for that dazzling light goes back thousands of years. Ancient Chinese speakers named it Tai-pe. Say that name tie-PAY. The meaning is beautiful white one. Ancient Romans gave the name we use today. Venus was their goddess. Love and beauty were her domain. No other planet carries the name of a female figure.

2Long ago, people did not know the truth about this world. Venus is a planet. A hard, rocky surface covers it, as on Earth. Towering mountains rise there. Vast plains spread out. Volcanoes of enormous size stand there. Craters cut deep. Many other interesting features appear as well. Telescopes let scientists study Venus. Space probes did the same. Because of that work, we know far more than ancient people knew. Hostility is extreme. Heat there is more than six times the heat of the hottest place on Earth. Beauty is one part of this bizarre world. Beast is the other part. A view shows Venus once the clouds are stripped away. A diagram places the Sun and then Venus. Venus is second in order from the Sun. Seven other planets share our solar system. Among them, Venus sits nearest to Earth. Earth is third from the Sun. Size is another likeness. Venus comes closest to Earth in size. Solid, rocky surfaces like Earth's belong to three planets. Venus is one. Mercury is one. Mars is one. Every remaining planet is a gigantic ball. Gas and liquid make up those balls. Likeness to Earth is only partial. Venus differs sharply from the planet we live on. Average temperature is 870 degrees Fahrenheit. That is 465 degrees Celsius. Clouds as thick as soup wrap the planet and hold heat in. The heat begins at the Sun. Some of that heat reflects upward off the surface. Thick clouds hold the reflected heat in. Glass or plastic on a greenhouse holds heat the same way, so plants stay warm. The name for this heating is the greenhouse effect.

3Clouds belong to the atmosphere of Venus. Atmosphere means the gases that make the air around the planet. That air holds a great deal of carbon dioxide. Trapping heat is something carbon dioxide does very well. Droplets of sulfuric acid ride in many of the clouds. This compound is oily. It ranks among the strongest acids. Skin burns easily from it. Metals dissolve in it. Sometimes sulfuric acid falls from the clouds in drops that act like rain. Layers of air can weigh a great deal. Large amounts of water can weigh a great deal in the same way. Weight creates pressure. The atmosphere of Venus is so heavy that pressure on the surface is tremendous. Standing there, if you could, would end in a crush. A greenhouse effect also comes from Earth's atmosphere. Venus has the stronger effect. Earth's weaker version still keeps the planet warm enough for water. Life can be supported. Scientists believe a change is underway. Burning coal strengthens Earth's greenhouse effect. Burning oil does too. Burning gas fuels does too. Extra carbon dioxide enters the air when those fuels burn. More heat gets trapped near the surface. The planet warms past its natural balance. Under the dense air, Venus holds surface sights as gripping as any planet offers. Massive mountain ranges cross the surface. Maxwell Montes is one range. It is the only feature on Venus named for a man. Venus is the only planet named for a female figure. Near the north pole, the top of this range stands 7 miles up. That is 11.3 kilometers. Mount Everest is the highest place on Earth. Maxwell Montes stands more than 1 mile higher. That extra height is 1.6 kilometers. Thousands of huge volcanoes mark Venus. Some are more than 150 miles wide. That width is 240 kilometers. Many of them sit on high land along the equator. The land is named Aphrodite Terra. Aphrodite is said AF-roh-DIE-tee. In ancient Greece she was the goddess of love and of beauty. A picture shows the volcano Gula Mons. Most volcanoes on Venus erupted many millions of years ago. Hot lava shot out. Scientists still study those volcanoes. They look for signs of eruptions in more recent times.

4Boiling lava left the volcanoes long ago and flowed across the surface. Today much of that surface is flat plains. The lava cooled. It cracked. It hardened. Long, winding channels look like riverbeds. Scientists think flowing lava carved them, millions of years in the past. Streaming water probably did not carve them, as water does on Earth. Heat on Venus is so high that water would turn to vapor and join the air. A cooler Venus in the past might have held water on the surface. That remains a possibility. Deep craters mark the planet. They formed billions of years ago. Meteorites crashed into the surface and made them. Floods of lava covered many craters. That is why Venus has fewer impact craters than the Moon. Heat and dryness lead almost all scientists to the same conclusion. Life would have no way to last there. One massive impact crater measures 43 miles across. That is 69 kilometers. Meteors leave the kind of scar this photo records. The year 2004 let viewers in several regions watch a crossing. Venus crossed the line that joins the Sun to Earth. Safe viewing of such an event must be indirect. Special glasses made for eclipses are another safe choice.

5Spacecraft That Went There. Warm places on Earth once seemed, to many people, like a model for Venus. Some wondered about tropical jungles. They wondered about swamps. Snakes and crocodiles were animals they imagined there. Telescopes on Earth could not settle what the surface was actually like. Opaque clouds hide whatever lies beneath. That surface was almost unknown to scientists until robotic space probes went there. A math question asks how many miles separate Venus and Earth. The hint says to subtract. Use each planet's gap from the Sun, and subtract. Diameter in miles is 7,521 for Venus. Diameter in miles is 7,926 for Earth. Miles from the Sun: Venus stands at 67 million. Miles from the Sun: Earth stands at 93 million. A year is the time a planet needs to orbit the Sun, counted in Earth days. Venus needs 225. Earth needs 365. A day is the time a planet needs to rotate on its axis, counted in Earth time. Venus needs 243 days. Earth needs 24 hours. Fahrenheit temperature on Venus averages 870. On Earth the range is minus 130 to 140. Moons number 0 for Venus. Moons number 1 for Earth. A photo from a Venera lander shows slabs of rock. Part of the lander itself is also in the frame. Several space probes left for Venus from the Soviet Union. That country is now called Russia. Launches came during the 1960s. More came in the 1970s. More came in the 1980s. Some of those craft landed. Every one of them was named Venera. Photographs of a desertlike surface went by radio back to Earth. About an hour or two was all the landers lasted. Intense temperatures destroyed each one. Intense pressures did the same. Space probes to Venus have also come from NASA. NASA means National Aeronautics and Space Administration. The agency belongs to the United States.

6Two Pioneer probes traveled from the United States to Venus in the 1970s. One Pioneer went into orbit. Radar let it make maps of the surface. Radar works by a special instrument. The instrument sends out radio waves. A surface bounces the waves back. Time for the bounce tells scientists about that surface. Another Pioneer flew past Venus. Scientific instruments on it studied the atmosphere. The 1990s brought the deepest learning yet. The U.S. probe Magellan orbited the planet. An advanced kind of radar produced many pictures of the surface. Mountains could be seen in sharp detail for the first time. Volcanoes could be seen that way. Other surface features could too. A shuttle carried the Magellan probe into space. The shuttle's name was Atlantis. The year 2005 brought the Venus Express probe. The European Union launched it. Instruments on Venus Express let scientists study the clouds further. The surface got further study too. In 2010, Japan's launch sent up the Akatsuki orbiter. Lightning was one subject. Volcanoes were the other. An illustration shows the Venus Express probe. The European Union launched it in 2005.

7Last Thoughts. Stargazers noticed Venus thousands of years ago. Everything else in the sky was outshone, apart from the Sun and the Moon. A special place of honor seemed required. The honor came as a name. It came from a goddess of ancient times, linked with love and with beauty. Science is how we honor Venus today. Much light has been shed on this bright point overhead. Science has made the picture clear. Venus is a very special world. It is also a strange one. No planet in the Solar System is hotter. Some of the largest mountains found on any planet are here. Some of the largest volcanoes are here too. Sulfuric acid is what falls as its rain. Earth once seemed a fair match for Venus. That idea is now known to be wrong. Another planet could hardly be less like ours. Hostility is severe. Life of the kind we understand cannot exist there. Venus still holds a beauty that is strange and its alone. Beauty and beast together: that is Venus. Words to Know. Atmosphere is a layer of gases. The layer surrounds a planet. Radar finds objects, or keeps track of them. It sends out radio waves and picks them up after they bounce off an object. The equator is an imaginary line. On Earth it circles halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole. Robotic describes a device programmed to perform tasks. Hostile means very unfriendly. Sulfuric acid is a strong acid with an oily quality. Oxidizing sulfur dioxide produces it. Melted rock is what lava is. It flows as liquid from an opening in a surface. Tropical relates to the region around the equator. Heat and humid air mark that region. Rock pieces from outer space are meteorites. Metal pieces are meteorites too. They have landed on a planet after coming from outer space. Opaque means not see-through. Light is blocked. Topics include Aphrodite Terra and carbon dioxide. The greenhouse effect is listed. Magellan is listed. Maxwell Montes is listed. Pioneer is listed. Sulfuric acid is listed. Venera is listed. Venus Express is listed.

96. Volcanoes

1A plume of smoke can rise from a volcano. In 79 CE, few people in Pompeii paid much attention to the earthquakes. They had felt seismic shaking before and had rebuilt their city. The quakes were usually minor, so people grew used to them. They loved their beautiful city and would not leave when the ground shook. No one linked that shaking to smoke from nearby Mount Vesuvius. People had lived there for centuries without seeing an eruption. Trees, flowers, and grass covered the slopes, and it had been a thousand years since an eruption, so most people thought the volcano was dormant or extinct.

2On August 24, around one o'clock, a huge explosion shook Mount Vesuvius. Dust, ash, and melted rock spewed out, and tephra fell as far as 16 kilometers, or 10 miles. By three o'clock, lava poured from the mouth and destroyed everything in its path. By six o'clock, the cloud stood 32 kilometers, or 20 miles, high, with lightning inside it. Ash about 1 meter, or 3.3 feet, deep made buildings collapse under the debris. People fled with portable treasures, but many died in deep hot ash, under stones, or from choking dust. Near midnight, the cloud fell as a pyroclastic flow at up to 500 kilometers per hour, or 310 miles per hour. The excavated ruins of Pompeii lie in front of Vesuvius, and glowing-hot lava can sit inside a volcano.

3A plaster cast shows a person from Pompeii who died in the eruption. A surge cloud buried the city, ash and mud hardened around the bodies, and scientists later filled the air pockets with plaster. This was Vesuvius's first surge cloud, and it scorched Pompeii and Herculaneum within moments. More surge clouds followed, and the two Roman cities stayed hidden for more than a thousand years. People live near volcanoes for nutrient-rich soil and warm baths in hot springs, yet they respect them. Long ago they could not predict volcanoes, so volcanoes belonged to beliefs, traditions, and lore. Hawaiian stories say the goddess Pele's anger caused eruptions, and volcanic glass is called Pele's hair and Pele's tears. Pele's tears are small drops of lava that cool and become solid while flying through the air.

4Devil's Tower, also called Bear Lodge and Tree Rock, is an extinct volcano in Wyoming. Many Indigenous tribes of the Great Plains hold it sacred as a place of creation and renewal. In ancient Greece and Rome, people believed volcanoes were forges where lightning bolts were made. The word volcano comes from the Roman god Vulcan, and volcanologists say volcanoes smell like a blacksmith's forge. In Japanese Shinto and Buddhist tradition, Mount Fuji is a stairway to another world, the home of Konohana, and a center for pilgrimage and art. Today scientists use tools to learn how volcanoes work and can even predict eruptions. The first volcanoes appeared about 3.5 billion years ago and covered vast areas with hot lava. Earth's crust is made of tectonic plates, and magma about 1,200 degrees Celsius, or 2,192 degrees Fahrenheit, can rise through vents from a magma chamber.

5When an ocean plate crashes into a continental plate, the ocean plate moves down and an active volcanic region forms. A plate-movement view can show a volcanic arc, a trench, continental crust, oceanic crust, and the mantle. More than fifteen hundred volcanoes have erupted in the last ten thousand years. About thirty-five or forty volcanoes erupt somewhere in the world each year. Some show only smoke or steam, some erupt slowly, and others, like Vesuvius, stay quiet for thousands of years. Volcanoes usually form where plates float on magma and crash, pull apart, or grind past one another. At least five hundred active volcanoes exist, and most lie near plate edges, including the Pacific Ring of Fire. Along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, drifting plates let magma build mountains, and Iceland sits on those summits.

6Some volcanoes lie far from the edges of the plates. Hawaii and Kauai sit near the center of the Pacific plate, above a hot spot, as the plate moves. Hot magma close to the crust can build a new island over tens of thousands of years. In Yellowstone National Park, a hot spot under the North American plate heats underground water and shoots geysers into the air. Some volcanoes erupt peacefully and slowly, while others explode with the force of many atomic bombs. Mount Vesuvius, on the west coast of southern Italy, is a composite volcano, also called a stratovolcano. These common volcanoes are large, steep mountains with even peaks. A bowl-shaped crater at the top lets magma, hot gases, and ash come out.

7Pictures show Mount St. Helens before and after the 1980 eruption. On May 18, 1980, sixty-three people died. Hot winds flattened 311 square kilometers, or 193 square miles, of forest. Most composite volcanoes have thick, slow magma that can harden in a vent and plug it. Trapped heat and gas raise the pressure until the volcano explodes. In 1980 the blast obliterated the whole northern side of Mount St. Helens. Clouds of dust, ash, smoke, hot gas, and rock can blacken the sky, cover the ground, and collapse as a surge cloud. Melting ice and snow can send water, mud, and rock downhill at up to 100 kilometers per hour, or 62 miles per hour.

8Crater Lake in Oregon is a caldera formed when a volcano collapsed in on itself. The Klamath people tell of the first coyote, who loved a star, fell back to Earth, and made the hole that became the lake. Some ash clouds travel around the world, block sunlight, and cool the planet. After Tambora erupted in Indonesia in 1815, North America had a cold, snowy summer. If a lake of magma pours out, the surface can fall into the empty chamber and leave a caldera up to 100 kilometers, or 62 miles, across. Calderas often fill with water and become large lakes. Composite volcanoes can destroy forests, bury cities, and kill people because they stay quiet for hundreds of years. Shield volcanoes send runny orange lava that spreads like water and hardens into smooth shield-shaped slopes, as at Mauna Loa in Hawaii.

9Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known volcano in the solar system. It would cover the entire state of Arizona. Shield eruptions are usually gentle, but lava flows can still destroy roads, homes, and forests. Hot gas or steam may spray from the crater and make a bright lava fountain. The flows are stable and predictable, so scientists can often study them up close. Shield volcanoes can stay quietly active for a long time and grow extremely large. Mauna Loa rises 9,170 meters, or 30,080 feet, from the seafloor and is taller than Mount Everest. Short sprays of lava and ash harden into lightweight black cinders that pile into cones, as at Mauna Kea, and most of these cones erupt only once before wind and rain erode them.

10A lava dome may sit on a vent in Alaska, and a scientist may monitor one inside a crater. Thick, pasty lava from a short eruption oozes out, hardens quickly, and may crack as more lava pushes up. These domes often form near other volcanic activity, inside craters or calderas of larger volcanoes. Like composite volcanoes, lava domes often explode violently. Volcanoes are spectacular proof that Earth is a changing planet. Lava makes new rock and new land, and ash makes fertile soil for farming. Geothermal energy can run power plants, and some people even live inside volcanoes, as in the port of Rabaul in Papua New Guinea. People choose to live near beautiful Mount Fuji, Mount Rainier, and Mauna Loa, but volcanoes hold powerful and dangerous forces.

11Magma is melted rock beneath Earth's surface, and vents are openings where magma and gases emerge. A crater is a bowl-shaped hollow where lava, ash, and gases come out. A caldera is a large basin where land has collapsed into an empty magma chamber. Cinders are lightweight black rocks made from small bits of flying lava and ash. A pyroclastic flow is a very hot mix of rocks, water, and gases that moves rapidly. A surge cloud is a fast, superheated cloud of ash, gas, dust, and rock that moves along the ground. Dormant means quiet for many hundreds of years, and extinct means no eruption for thousands of years with no sign of another. Volcanologists study volcanoes, and geothermal describes heat made naturally inside Earth.

97. Watching the Sky with Telescopes

1Puerto Rico once held the Arecibo Observatory. It ranked among the largest centers for astronomy research. Collapse came in 2020. After that, the site was taken offline. Parts of this book follow. An Opening. The First Telescopes That Gathered Light. The Way a Telescope Works. Telescopes of Recent Times. Telescopes Above Earth. Telescopes That Hear Radio Waves. Astronomy Still Ahead. Words and Topics. A comet pictured here is NEAT. Another name for it is C/2001 Q4. An Opening. People full of questions have watched the sky across thousands of years. They wondered about whatever they saw. Only the unaided eye could supply those observations. About four hundred years ago, the telescope was invented. Knowledge of space then leapt forward in a huge way. From that point, telescopes changed. They became powerful tools. Stars can be viewed with them. Planets can be viewed. Other objects in space can be viewed.

2Telescopes come in two major kinds. One kind gathers light from objects that are far away. It also magnifies the images that light forms. People call it an optical telescope. Light-gathering telescope is another name. The second kind collects radio waves that arrive from space. A radio telescope is its name. Those waves cannot be seen. They can be turned into pictures we are able to study. One drawing stands for an optical telescope. Another stands for a radio telescope. Ahead you will meet the history of these tools. You will see how they work. You will see how scientists, and other people, use them on far-off objects in space. A word note explains the name. Telescope comes from Greek. Tele means far off, or distant. Skopos means to watch, or to look at. An early telescope is shown as an example. The First Telescopes That Gathered Light. Glass lenses had to be developed before a telescope could be invented. A lens is glass with a curve. It bends light. It also focuses light.
