Italian makers of glass developed early eyeglass lenses used for reading. Most historians give the first combination of lenses for distant viewing to a Dutch maker. His name was Hans Lippershey. He lined up two lenses. Light from the second lens was magnified by the first. Distant things then looked much nearer. The year 1608 is when Lippershey built his earliest rough telescope. He named it The Looker. Other people were trying lens combinations in that same period. Even so, he was first to seek a patent. Armies found the invention important. Warfare gained a large advantage from it. Dutch forces could watch enemy troops moving, and they could do so from far away.

3One year after that invention, an Italian man worked hard on a telescope of his own. His aim was objects in space. Galileo Galilei improved greatly on Lippershey. He also improved on other Dutch lens makers. Magnification in his telescopes reached five times. Later it reached thirty times. Distant space objects were what he observed. Because of this early labor, people know him as the Father of Astronomy. Important sights he recorded are listed here. Craters mark the Moon's surface. Mountains mark it too. He saw four moons of Jupiter. Phases of Venus showed that Venus orbits the Sun. Sunspots mark the Sun's surface. He found the Milky Way to be a galaxy of stars. Earlier thought had called it a cloud of cosmic dust. He saw Neptune. He did not realize it was a planet. A hard problem faced Galileo. As a professor of astronomy, his job required one taught picture of the solar system. Earth sat in the middle of that picture. The Sun had to be described as circling Earth. Every planet had to be described that way too. What he observed pushed him toward another theory. That theory might fit the sky better. In that theory the Sun sits at the center. Planets revolve around the Sun. Teaching this upset the Roman Catholic Church. Church teaching said God had built the universe with Earth as the hub. Galileo's theory moved humanity out of the center of the universe. Earth became just one planet among others. Those planets turn around one star among many. The Church banned his theory. A life sentence in prison followed. Old age was already his. Serving the sentence at home was permitted. He stayed under house arrest until life ended.

4Other scientists walked the path Galileo had opened. They improved the telescope. Still more about space objects came into view. Famous British scientist Isaac Newton was among the first. He found that a curved mirror, once polished, could gather light from objects. Lenses used by Lippershey and by Galileo did similar gathering. A lens telescope splits light into a rainbow of colors. The mirror telescope Newton built collected light and skipped that color split. A mirror could also be built larger than a lens. Those advantages made Newton's telescope superior. Telescopes that relied only on lenses fell behind. Technicians are shown in 1984 inspecting the mirror of the Hubble Space Telescope. The Way a Telescope Works. Lenses do not all magnify images in one same manner. Every optical telescope gathers light toward a point. A lens in some of them bends light inward until it meets at one center. Those are refracting telescopes. A curved mirror in others bounces light inward until it meets at one center. Those are reflecting telescopes. Three basic parts make a refracting telescope. A tube is one. Two lenses are the others. Correct distance between the lenses is held by the tube. Dust is kept out by the tube. So is stray light that would ruin the picture. Farther from the eye sits the bigger lens. Convex is its shape. That means the middle is thicker than the outer edge. Light enters through this lens and bends to a point. That point is the focal point. An image forms there, of whatever the telescope points toward. The smaller lens is the eyepiece. It magnifies the image before the image enters the eye. A far object then looks larger. It also looks closer. A convex lens appears in a picture of a magnifying glass.

5Labels on a refracting telescope name the focal point. They name the convex objective lens. They name the concave eyepiece lens. Four basic parts make a reflecting telescope. A tube is one. Two mirrors are two more. A lens is the last. Mirrors and lens are held in place by the tube. The primary mirror is large and concave. The curve sinks inward. A bowl's inner surface has that same curve. Light is gathered by this mirror and reflected to a second mirror. The second mirror is flat. It is mounted at an angle. It is much smaller. Because of the angle, more incoming light can pass by without distortion. Up to the eyepiece goes the bright picture bounced off the concave mirror. That lens is mounted on the side. Labels on a reflecting telescope name the eyepiece lens, the focal point, the flat mirror, and the concave mirror. Advantages belong to reflecting telescopes when they are set beside refracting ones. The most important advantage is cost and ease. Making a large concave mirror, and polishing it, is easier. The price is also lower than the price of a big convex lens. A light-gathering lens wider than 10 centimeters is hard to make. Four inches is that same width. Larger mirrors are easier to make. They also gather more light. More light means astronomers can observe a greater number of dim objects. Distant objects in space become visible too. A typical telescope for home use has labels. They name the optical tube, the viewfinder, the eyepiece, the dew shield, the focus knob, and the tripod legs. A math pause gives a result of 8.3 minutes. Light is very fast. One second carries it 300,000 kilometers. That distance is 186,000 miles. The Sun stands 149,000,000 kilometers from Earth. That distance is 93,000,000 miles. How many minutes does light need to leave the Sun and arrive at Earth?

6A telescope image shows Alpha Centauri in white. Distances in space are so huge that astronomers made a unit for them. They call it a light-year. Light travels at 300,000 kilometers each second. That rate is 186,000 miles each second. A light-year is how far that light goes in one year. Nearest stars to Earth include Proxima Centauri. It lies 4.2 light-years off. Alpha Centauri lies 4.3 light-years off. Telescopes of Recent Times. New telescopes keep being built larger. This is true for the refracting type. It is true for the reflecting type. Ireland's scientists, in the 1840s, constructed a big reflecting telescope. Across, the mirror measured 1.8 meters. That is 5.9 feet. At the time, the size seemed incredible. As telescopes grew, people made special buildings to hold them. Those buildings are observatories. They began to appear all around the world. Many stood on mountaintops. City lights and their glare were left behind. Wisconsin gained an observatory in 1897, built by the United States. Inside stood a refracting telescope bigger than any built before or since. Width of its extraordinary light-gathering lens was 40 centimeters. That is 15 inches. Early in the 1900s, new observatories rose for giant reflecting telescopes. Larger size was possible. More power was possible than refracting telescopes could offer. Astronomers wanted to see farther into space, and then farther still. Farther sight needed more light, including light that is dimmer. Two large reflecting telescopes helped southern California emerge. Astronomy gained a major base there. Research did too. One telescope stood at the Mount Wilson Observatory. That site is near Los Angeles. Diameter of its mirror was 2.5 meters. That is 8 feet. Astronomers used this powerful tool to help prove a big idea. Many galaxies exist well past our own Milky Way Galaxy. The Hooker telescope on Mount Wilson measures 2.5 meters, or 8 feet.

7A building houses the telescope at Mount Palomar. When the telescope is in use, the dome opens. Mount Palomar was the second major observatory in California. Opening year was 1948. Mount Wilson's mirror was only half as wide. Distant planets looked much clearer through this powerful telescope. Galaxies looked sharper too. Space objects never seen before were revealed. Reflecting telescopes kept growing. Some mirrors had diameters around 10 meters. That is 33 feet. Set one of those mirrors on edge beside a building, and the top would line up with a fourth-story window. Light-gathering power of these mirrors was tremendous. Still greater distances in space came into view. A modern tool of rare power pairs two large reflecting telescopes. They act as one telescope of extraordinary power. In some ways the setup works like binoculars. That likeness gave it a name. People call it the Large Binocular Telescope. LBT is the short name. Mount Graham in Arizona is the location. Images from the LBT are sharper than images from the Hubble Space Telescope. The gain is more than nine times. Each of the two mirrors measures 8.4 meters across. That is 27.5 feet. Together, their light-gathering power equals one mirror nearly 12 meters across. That is 37 feet. The top picture shows the Large Binocular Telescope and its two mirrors. Distant space objects can be seen more clearly than ever. The bottom picture shows workers looking tiny beside the huge mirror.

8An orbiting Hubble image, on the left, shows a ring of baby stars. They circle galaxy NGC 4314. Distance is about 40 million light-years. On the right, a telescope based on land shows those baby stars as a blur. Telescopes Above Earth. Telescopes that stand on land share one serious limit. Light from far objects has to cross Earth's atmosphere on the way in. Gases wrap the planet in that atmosphere. Height of the blanket is 50 kilometers. That is 30 miles. It surrounds our planet. The gases never stop moving. Light that passes through becomes distorted. Images of stars blur. Other space objects blur too. The blur happens before a telescope is even reached. It resembles looking at an object under the surface of a clear pool. A second problem involves very weak light from some distant objects. That light cannot penetrate Earth's atmosphere. Scattering happens before any telescope is reached. Computers have reduced some of the blur the atmosphere causes. They can predict how much movement will occur. They adjust the curve of a mirror. Sharper images result. Even with those adjustments, astronomers know a hard truth. Severe limits will always remain for land-based telescopes that try to view distant space objects. The Hubble Space Telescope offered a way past the problem. The only real solution was to place telescopes above Earth's atmosphere. Orbiting satellites were developed. Space stations were developed. A chance then existed to put a telescope into orbit, higher than the atmosphere. Scientists designed that orbiting telescope. Launch of the first one came in 1990. Edwin Hubble, famous as an American astronomer, is the person honored in the name. It is the Hubble Space Telescope. Orbit height is 515 kilometers above Earth. That is 320 miles. The planet's atmosphere is far below. From that position in space, distant objects are seen clearly.

9Images are formed with a mirror 2.4 meters across. That is 7.8 feet. Computers ride on the spacecraft. Other equipment rides there too. Light images are changed into radio waves and sent to Earth. Ground stations receive those waves. They change them back into images. Scientists on Earth can view the images. Other people can view them too. Objects never seen before became visible because of the Hubble Space Telescope. Many open questions about the universe gained answers from its evidence. Discoveries from Hubble include these breakthroughs. Black holes gained their first solid proof. Planets beyond our own solar system were shown to be real. A rocky planet like Earth was found for the first time beyond our solar system. Dust disks, the material from which planets form, turned out to be common around other stars. Ancient galaxies were viewed for the first time. Their age is over 10 billion years. Views of stars and of supernovas let astronomers work out how old the universe is with better accuracy. A comet was seen up close hitting a planet for the first time. Jupiter was struck by Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9. Images still come back to Earth from the Hubble Space Telescope. Space now also holds a telescope with far more power. Construction of the James Webb Space Telescope began in 2004. Launch into space came in December 2021. Just past six months after launch, early pictures from this amazing telescope went out to people everywhere. Visible light waves are gathered by the Webb Telescope. Low-energy infrared waves are gathered too. Side to side, the mirror measures 6.5 meters. That is 20 feet. A shield blocks radiation from the Sun. A tennis court would match the shield in size. Compared with the Hubble Telescope, it can gather ten times the light. The start of time can be studied much more closely with Webb. Clues about how the first galaxies formed are the goal. It also watches how galaxies have changed as time passed. Dust clouds can be looked into. New stars forming there can be observed. Planetary systems forming there can be observed. In only its first few years, Webb expanded scientific knowledge about space by a great amount. Space scientists wait eagerly for the next discoveries. The general public waits too.

10Telescopes That Hear Radio Waves. Another telescope type is the radio telescope. It does not collect light from far objects and then magnify that light. It gathers radio waves that cannot be seen. Distant formations in space send those waves out. You might say these telescopes listen to space. Optical telescopes, by contrast, look into space. If optical telescopes are our eyes on space, radio telescopes do the job of ears. Most radio telescopes are large dishes made of metal. The shape is a dish. Radio waves are collected by the metal and reflected to an antenna. The antenna sits at the dish's center. An average-sized dish measures about 25 meters across. That is 82 feet. One dish, though, was immense. Puerto Rico, an island in the Caribbean Ocean, was its site. Diameter was 305 meters. That is 1,000 feet. Scientists have also linked many radio telescopes in one place. A site in New Mexico is an example. A computer receives signals from twenty-seven radio telescopes. One big radio signal is built from them. The Puerto Rico telescope worked for fifty-three years. Collapse came in 2020. Radio astronomy began in 1933. Karl Jansky, an engineer from America, discovered radio waves from space by accident that year. He built a radio antenna 33 meters long. That is 100 feet. A Ford Model-T supplied four tires that held it up and let it rotate. His aim was interference on phone lines. Those lines were laid along the bed of the Atlantic Ocean. Static radio waves from thunderstorms showed up. A hissing sound from far off in space showed up too. At first he thought the hiss was radiation from the Sun. Later he decided the waves came out of the Milky Way Galaxy's center. The find was purely an accident. Other scientists took several years to grow interested enough to build radio telescopes of their own. A radio telescope's collected waves travel to an amplifier. The amplifier magnifies the faint signals. It increases their strength. Amplified signals then go to a computer. The computer turns the signals into an image. Shape in the picture follows the radio waves that left their source. Different colors are assigned to various parts of that image. The colors stand for different strengths of radio waves inside the picture. A picture shows Karl Jansky's radio antenna, the one that rotated.

11Astronomy Still Ahead. Land-based telescopes will keep growing in size. Their technology will grow more specialized. Hawaii holds the Pan STARRS 1 telescope. PS 1 is its short name. A powerful digital camera on it tracks asteroids. It tracks comets that might threaten Earth. One-sixth of the sky can be mapped every month. A newer telescope is the Pan STARRS 4 telescope. PS 4 is its short name. Once the Pan STARRS 4 telescope starts its work, its power will be four times the power of PS 1. Little doubt remains about the best future view of space objects. That view will happen in space, beyond the interference Earth's atmosphere creates. Agreement is wide among scientists on the ultimate telescope. The Moon would be the building site. Plans are underway for an observatory on the Moon's surface. Very little atmosphere covers the Moon. Interference with light from distant space objects would be minimal. Mysteries of space are being revealed slowly. The finds of the newest telescopes are still unknown. These keen eyes aimed at space can show those finds to us directly. A picture shows Earth as it looks from the Moon's surface. Words to Know. An amplifier is equipment. It makes sounds louder. Light rays meet at a focal point. They can also spread from that point. Lenses have focal points. Curved mirrors have them too. Concave describes a shape or a surface that curves inward. Observatories are places for scientific watching of things in nature, including objects studied by astronomy. Convex describes a shape or a surface that curves outward. Distorted means changed so it is no longer accurate. An optical telescope gathers light. Emitted means sent out from a source. A radio telescope collects radio waves that come from space. Topics include Galileo Galilei, Karl Jansky, Hans Lippershey, and Isaac Newton. The Milky Way Galaxy is listed. The Sun is listed. Telescopes listed include the Hooker, the Hubble, the Large Binocular, and the James Webb.

98. What a Trip to Mars Would Take

1Mars One plans to grow a hydroponic garden inside part of a rocket meant for Mars. The book asks whether the trip is close. A bigger rocket is the next problem. Gravity must be brought along. Cosmic radiation is a danger. Dust waits on the surface. Food is missing, though water is not. Living packed together is another test. Cost comes next. Plans that might succeed, or fail, close the story. Hard words come last. A drawing shows a ship that could reach Mars. It comes from Inspiration Mars. That project is a private foundation, and it is nonprofit. Scientists have talked about astronauts on Mars for what feels like forever. So far the United States has sent only rovers, one after another. From 1969 to 1972, astronauts flew to the Moon and back six times. The Moon is the nearest neighbor. Mars then looked like the clear next stop in the solar system. The open question is the date. Something is still holding the trip back.

2Distance to Mars changes with the date you pick. Earth circles the Sun faster than Mars does. Every twenty-six months, Earth swings through the gap that separates the Sun from Mars. Earth may share the Sun's near side with Mars. It may sit on the far side. It may be anywhere else along its orbit. A Mars trip brings problems no astronaut has faced. Mars is vastly farther than the Moon. On average the gap is more than five hundred times as large. Arriving in one piece will be hard. Staying alive there will be hard. Humans will have attempted nothing greater in technology. There is welcome news. Serious planning for a mission is finally underway. Many people want to go. You might be one of them. The obstacles are worth listing. How long would your trip last? Red Planet is the nickname. Reddish minerals full of iron in the soil are the reason. The closest approach is still about 55 million kilometers. That is 34 million miles. The typical gap is about 240 million kilometers. That is 140 million miles. One direction alone would last seven months, or as many as nine. Time on the surface must be added. Ships for a journey that long and that far must be larger than any ship flying now. NASA is the U.S. space agency. Spelled out, NASA is National Aeronautics and Space Administration. A huge NASA rocket is under construction. Its name is the Space Launch System. SLS is the short name. A private firm, SpaceX, is building a giant of its own. Falcon Heavy is that rocket's name. The new SLS is planned to outpower the Saturn V. Saturn V is the rocket that carried crews to the Moon.

3Building the International Space Station took more than thirty flights. ISS is the short name. Pieces had to be delivered and joined. You cannot simply board one of those new rockets and leave for Mars. Neither rocket can serve alone as a Mars vehicle. A Mars ship must be larger still. The crew area must be roomier. Experts say the job is so big that several ships would be needed. Crew would ride in some. Supplies would ride in others. A habitat would ride as well. SLS and Falcon Heavy could lift separate pieces into orbit around Earth. Assembly would happen there. Fuel would be saved. The ISS was built that way, so the method is known. Readiness is what is missing. Gravity is another problem. The lack of it is the real trouble. Gravity lets people walk. It lets someone pour milk. It lets someone shoot a basket. Everyday acts depend on it. Health and fitness depend on it too, because bodies must push against it. A ship in space would have no gravity. Muscles then shrink. Bones grow weak. Nine months of that would leave a person wrecked. Artificial gravity is the proposed fix. A round section of the ship would spin. Centrifugal force would imitate gravity. A diagram shows that section turning without a stop. People standing on the inner surface would keep circling the center. Walking there would feel like a downward pull. To those people, the outward push would feel like gravity.

4Space is full of electrically charged particles. They race about in huge numbers. The Sun sends some. Space between the stars sends others. On Earth a magnetic field pushes those particles away, so the danger stays off us. A Mars ship would be struck the whole way. Engineers are looking for shields for long journeys. One idea wraps crew space in a tank of water. Incoming particles would be soaked up. Water weighs a lot. The ship's mass would jump. More mass means more fuel burned. A magnetic shield of the ship's own might work better. The ship would act like a tiny Earth. Researchers in many countries are trying to design that system. The work now sits with engineers. One NASA drawing sets fuel tanks and shields in a ring around the outside. Crew inside would be guarded from radiation. Arrival will not feel like a picnic. No magnetic field guards Mars. Radiation therefore remains a problem there. Underground is the only escape. A surface habitat would need shielding as heavy as the ship's. Dust, dirt, and rock cover this barren world. Huge dust storms, violent ones, often roar across it. You and your machines would both be threatened. No larger dust storms exist in the solar system.

5Farmland is a poor description of Mars. What would travelers eat? A short stay, followed by a return, allows food to be packed. That is the plan NASA has for the first missions. A person who means to stay and call Mars home would need another plan. Crop plants grown in a hydroponic solution are the best bet. Lots of water would be required. Mars seems able to help. Water appears plentiful. Some sits at the poles as ice. Some lies deep under the ground. Drinking water could come from it. Indoor farming could use it. Other jobs could use it. Some might even be sprinkled on the dust. Shoppers may have seen produce marked as grown without soil. Hydroponic farming uses big tanks of water. Nutrients are mixed in. Lettuce is a common crop grown this way on Earth. Tomatoes are common. Peppers are common. Cucumbers are common. A colony on Mars would surely add many other crops. Biosphere 2 studied how living things behave in a closed space. Long confinement can create a serious problem. Tension grows when people stay that close for so long. Arguments start. Fights can start. Small annoying habits are easy to ignore in ordinary life. Inside a sealed place, over many months, those habits swell. Severe conflict can follow. People hoping to go would need careful screening for compatibility. Friendly relations still could not be promised. In the 1990s, eight carefully picked people were sealed inside an artificial world in Arizona. The lock-in lasted two years. Four were men. Four were women. Biosphere 2 was the experiment's name. It was built to copy life on Mars. By the finish, the volunteers hardly spoke to one another.

6Cost can be answered in a short way: a great deal. The longer answer depends on the mission you imagine. A round trip with a surface stay of weeks, or of months, has been priced as high as 500 billion dollars. The unit is billions, not a smaller count. That price is one reason no mission has launched yet. A real mission will probably be shared. The United States would join several other nations. One privately owned company has another plan. Mars One is based in the Netherlands. It wants SpaceX's Falcon Heavy to lift spacecraft parts. The parts would meet in low orbit around Earth and be joined. Mars One says the mission can be done for 6 billion dollars. That sum is still large. Set beside 500 billion dollars, it looks like a bargain. An artist pictured a settlement built by Mars One. The shape of a trip is coming together. What is the timetable? NASA speaks of a possible round trip near 2033. Three ships would be joined in orbit around Earth. Two would leave first, carrying a habitat and supplies. The third would carry the crew. Weeks or months on the planet would be spent exploring. Soil samples would be gathered. Dennis Tito, an American billionaire, hopes to reach Mars before NASA. His plan is called Inspiration Mars. Two people would fly past in 2018, loop the planet, and return. If Mars still sounds like paradise, Mars One may be the fit. The hoped start is 2024. Several dozen people would go. A lasting colony is the aim. Four people would go first. Four more settlers would follow every two years. The required age is eighteen. After that, a seat might be possible. One limit matters. Every such trip is one way. No Mars One colonist should expect a ride home.

7Would people accept a deal like that? Many would. By 2014, hopeful applicants numbered more than two hundred thousand. Those chosen face eight years of training. If the plan holds, they then embark. Connected domes would be home. Living rooms and work rooms would fill the domes. Hydroponic farming would have space too. Tasks would be varied. Health effects of a life on Mars would be studied. The planet's geology would be studied. Signs of life today would be sought. Signs of ancient life would be sought too. Biosphere 2 offers warnings beyond personal conflict. Crops failed in that Arizona test. Oxygen ran short. Those people could step outside into Arizona's fresh air. Mars would offer no such exit. Danger has not stopped the people pressing Mars One. They want the trip. They want to be picked. A few word meanings help. Hydroponic describes plants grown with no soil, in water that carries what they need. Barren means plants are missing. A colony is a group settled in a new land while still tied to the home they left. Mass is how much matter something holds. On Earth, weight is how it is measured. Compatibility means getting along, or working together, without conflict. An orbit is the path a smaller space object takes around a larger one. To embark means to board a ship, a plane, or some other vehicle. It can also mean to begin something new. Radiation is a strong, dangerous energy. Nuclear reactions release it. A feat is an act that amazes, or a great accomplishment. To simulate is to copy the look of something, or its condition. Gravity is the natural pull of objects toward one another. Objects pulled toward Earth's center are one example. A habitat is a structure for living where people normally could not live. Under the sea is one such place.

99. What Makes a Price Go Up or Down

1During the COVID-19 pandemic, shoppers hunted for paper goods. Toilet paper was one item they wanted. Paper towels were another. Store shelves were often bare. Some scientists say shopping can switch on parts of the brain. Those parts make a person feel truly excited. They can also bring a feeling of happiness. A new movie has just premiered. You badly want a T-shirt that shows a favorite character from it. Then you see the price tag. The shirt costs a great deal, and it is still only a T-shirt. Another part of you feels no price would be too high. The want is that strong. Parents are likely to disagree. Weeks or months later, the shirt may be on sale. You might even look for it online. Buying it on sale is unlikely. A newer movie's merchandise would be the better purchase. The question is worth a pause. Who gets to decide what a T-shirt costs? Whose job is it to set that price?

2Buyers, including you, fill an important role in setting prices. The goods and services involved run from T-shirts to sandwiches. They run from haircuts to airplane tickets. Choosing to buy is an interaction with the seller. A market is the place, physical or virtual, where buyer and seller meet to do business. In a market, money moves from buyers to sellers. Goods and services move the other way. Prices can differ widely, even for things of the same kind. Return to the T-shirt. The character on it is only one factor in the price. The place where the shirt was made matters. The material matters. The stores that sell it matter. The people who appear in its advertisements matter. More factors sit in the price as well. A seller is free to ask any amount, whether the thing sold is a shirt, a good, or a service. Whether a buyer will pay that price is a separate question. Sellers design signs in big letters. They use bright colors. The aim is to catch interest and draw people into a store or onto a website. Economists try to explain how prices work. Economics is their field. It studies buying, selling, and wealth. They look for patterns. Laws of supply and demand help them describe why costs in the market change, and how. Supply is the quantity of a good or a service on hand. Demand means how much of it people want. Those two forces set the price of everything. Products such as lollipops fall under that rule. Computers do too. Services such as dog grooming fall under it. Doctor visits do too. Because supply and demand keep shifting, prices change often. The link also runs backward. A shift in price can make supply fluctuate. It can make demand fluctuate. Was the movie behind that T-shirt a hit at the box office, or a failure? Popularity changes what the related merchandise costs. A hit lets sellers keep asking top price for connected goods. A film that does worse in theaters than expected pushes sellers another way. Price cuts on that merchandise grow more likely. Supply is not fixed. Demand is not fixed. Price is not fixed. The three stay intertwined, each shaping the others from moment to moment.

3Picture lunchtime, and a strong craving for a chicken sandwich. A local restaurant has made chicken sandwiches the special. Two sandwiches cost the price of one. The deal is a welcome one. Here the sandwich price fell, and demand rose. Hunger plus a free extra sandwich leads you to take two instead of one. The lower price created a spike in demand. A special deal can excite buyers so much that they lose track of the true cost. Now look at the same sandwiches from the seller's side. What pushed the restaurant to advertise a two-for-one offer? Maybe too many chicken patties sat in the kitchen. They had to be sold by a certain date, or they would spoil. The supply of patties was a little too large. More patties were on hand than people wanted. That situation is called a surplus. A surplus in the market often sends prices down. Sellers, in general, want the highest price the market will allow. Profit is the gap between the selling price and the cost of making the good or service. Buyers, in general, want to pay as little as possible. Tension between those aims helps balance supply and demand. Price an item too high, and demand will often fall. Imagine arriving to find chicken sandwiches at one hundred dollars each. Another restaurant would probably get your lunch trade. Demand for the sandwich would drop as the price climbed. Price an item too low, and demand is likely to jump. Imagine the same sandwiches at one dollar each. You might buy every sandwich you could eat, and some for friends. The restaurant would likely run out very fast. At a movie theater, people will pay a large sum for snacks such as popcorn.

4Neither the buyer nor the seller benefits over a longer span when the price is far too high or far too low. In the first situation, an overly high sandwich price drives demand down. The restaurant misses the sale. The customer goes home with nothing. In the second situation, the price is too low and the supply runs out. Many customers likely leave disappointed, with no chicken sandwich left to buy. Sales may also fail to pay for what the sandwiches cost to prepare. A table shows how supply and demand move together and affect price. If supply stays the same while demand increases, the price increases. If supply stays the same while demand decreases, the price decreases. A larger supply, with demand unchanged, pushes the price down. A smaller supply, with demand unchanged, pushes the price up. The price of one chicken sandwich at a local restaurant rests on a complex set of calculations. Many factors must be counted. The restaurant pays suppliers for chicken patties. It pays for buns. It pays employees. It pays to keep the restaurant running, including energy bills and rent. It must also judge what other nearby restaurants charge for the same sandwich. It must judge whether customers will actually pay the price being asked. Balancing every factor that touches a price is difficult. Prices fluctuate often as a result. Holiday season offers another view of supply, demand, and price. The next time your area marks a holiday, watch seasonal goods. Holiday-themed candy is one example. Before the holiday, that candy usually costs much more than it does after the holiday has passed. The ideas of supply and demand suggest a reason.

5A graph of chicken sandwiches sets demand against supply. Price runs from low to high. The crossing point is market equilibrium. Buyers and sellers both gain when supply and demand sit in a more even balance. That balance is called market equilibrium. For the imagined chicken sandwiches, equilibrium is a price at which every sandwich sells. The seller never runs out. Customers will buy exactly as many sandwiches as the restaurant has. They want no more and no fewer. Concert tickets offer another scene to ponder. An international pop band plays your city once every summer. Popularity keeps rising. The band stays in the same stadium, so the supply of tickets stays fixed. Each new year is likely to push a ticket's equilibrium price higher. Greater popularity raises demand for a seat at the show. Scarcity can be stated in a short form. Scarcity balances a supply that has limits against a demand that does not. Abundance is the opposite of scarcity. Scarcity shapes daily choices. Money, for most of us, is a scarce item. The supply of it is not unlimited. Everything we want cannot be purchased. A choice has to be made about the goods and services that matter most. We decide which ones we can skip. Toilet paper prices shot upward in 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic was starting. Businesses sold out quickly. Some customers hoarded toilet paper. Other people could not find any to buy. A common household item had suddenly become scarce.

6A fading trend can shake supply and demand for the goods tied to it. Fidget spinners are one example. Preferences differ from person to person. Values differ too. Buying habits shift because of those differences. That is why supply and demand keep changing what goods and services cost. How much is too much for a concert ticket? A fan's answer depends on personal circumstances. It depends on preferences. It depends on enthusiasm for the band. Emotions play a large economic role in the marketplace. Two bands can play the same stadium. Each show can offer the same number of tickets. Ticket prices can still differ sharply. The difference tracks what fans are willing to pay. Perceptions matter as well. A perception is the way a buyer views and judges a good or a service. Buyers often pay more for what they see as valuable or cool. Each buyer runs that calculation differently. Personality is one basis. Budget is another. Sooner or later, most people need someone to cut their hair. What they will pay for it varies widely. Some hunt for the cheapest cut they can find. A salon visit is worth a much higher payment to other people. Sneakers show the same spread. Nike's Air Jordan sneakers take their name from the basketball player Michael Jordan. Since 1985 they have appeared in many editions. Those editions are often very expensive. Plain sneakers usually cost far less than sneakers a famous athlete has endorsed. Some buyers see value in that endorsement. They will pay extra for the celebrity factor. Another kind of buyer hunts for footwear at the lowest price. Values and circumstances make every buyer different.

7A shopper can pick one product, or another product, or nothing at all. As a consumer, you hold power over supply and demand. Daily life puts you, and everyone you know, into economic markets again and again. Pause over the goods and services your family buys on a regular basis. The next time one of those prices rises or falls, notice your own reaction. Did demand, meaning how much you wanted the item, change because the price changed? Why would that happen? Price can also hint at the supply available for the things you buy. What would you conclude? A purchase joins a much larger conversation. A bus ticket is such a purchase. A swim lesson is one. A house is one. An apple is one. Every one of these purchases joins the tug between supply and demand.

100. When the Ocean Sends a Giant Wave

1In this book: a huge wave in the Indian Ocean. Tsunamis in earlier times. What sets a tsunami off. Places that face the greatest danger. Ways people get a warning. How to stay alive. A closing word. Words to know. Topics you can look up. A picture shows the center of the 2004 quake that sent out a tsunami. Another picture shows Banda Aceh, Indonesia, after the Indian Ocean wave of 2004 swept much of that city away. The wave in the Indian Ocean December 26, 2004, brought a powerful quake. It shook the seafloor near Sumatra, in Indonesia. Villages nearby felt the ground move. Those people did not know what would follow. Within minutes, a huge wave would flood their homes. That kind of wave is called a tsunami. A tall wall of moving water wiped out whole towns. Hours later, the water had struck thousands of miles of shoreline. Indonesia was hit. So were India, parts of Africa, Thailand, Bangladesh, Malaysia, the Maldives, Myanmar, and Singapore. Other places were hit as well.

2Day after day, the world was stunned. The reported number of deaths kept climbing. Early reports named 20,000 deaths. New reports named 100,000. The count later stood at 226,000. The true number of deaths may never be known. Mud and wreckage buried many bodies. The sea carried other bodies away. Scientists think fewer people would have died if more of them had understood the danger. They also needed to know how to escape. Pictures show Banda Aceh before the tsunami and after it. One picture shows the wooden raft a survivor used. People who lived through it Stories of loss stood beside stories of amazing survival. A man who lived in Indonesia was carried far out to sea. He pulled himself aboard a raft made of wood. Coconuts kept him fed. Rainwater kept him from dying of thirst. After two weeks, a ship found him. Some people ran ahead of the water. Some were carried inland by the wave itself. Others lived by clinging to trees. Others climbed onto the roofs of strong buildings. The best chance belonged to people who moved uphill the moment the shaking started. Experts say only two places are truly safe when a tsunami hits. One is higher ground. The other is land farther inland.

3Looking back at tsunamis The word tsunami comes from Japanese. It means harbor wave. Japanese fishermen were the first to use it that way. They would sail home and find their towns destroyed. Unusually large ocean waves had done the damage. While those fishermen were out on the water, they had not noticed the waves at all. A tsunami can bring terrible ruin. Large ones are very rare, which is fortunate. In a typical span of 100 years, the world sees about six major tsunamis. Krakatoa, a volcano in Indonesia, blew apart in 1883. The blast set off a tsunami. That wave killed 36,000 people. A picture shows Krakatoa erupting in 1943. Alaska had a landslide in 1958. Rock crashed into Lituya Bay. The splash built a wave 1,720 feet tall. That is 524.26 meters. Chile's coast shook in 1960. The quake set off a tsunami. Parts of South America were devastated. Hawaii was devastated. Japan was devastated too. What starts these waves Most tsunamis begin when the ocean floor quakes. An underwater landslide can start one. A volcanic explosion can start one. A meteor hitting Earth can start one. A quake in the ocean, or near it, does not always make a tsunami. Strength matters. The kind of movement in Earth's crust matters too. On the Richter scale, the quake must reach at least 6.75 before a tsunami can result. The 2004 Indian Ocean wave came from what scientists call a mega-earthquake. Its magnitude was 9.0. How the scale works The Richter scale is how people describe an earthquake's force. A reading of 2.0 is too weak for anyone to feel. A reading of 4.5 can be measured by seismographs everywhere on Earth. Each step up the scale makes the force grow fast. Step from a reading of 5.0 to a reading of 6.0 and the force grows by ten times. A report of 7, then of 8, then of 9, should be read with care. Each whole number is 10 times as strong as the number just below it.

4Ordinary waves and tsunami waves Wind-made waves reach the beach fairly close together. In shallower water, the bottom of a wave rubs the ocean floor. That rubbing slows the bottom. The top of the wave then spills onto land. A tsunami behaves in a similar way. Its bottom drags on the seafloor and slows. Its top spills onto the shore. A tsunami is taller than a surface wave. Its crests sit farther apart. For that reason, a much greater amount of water comes ashore at once. Some people call a tsunami a tidal wave. It can rush in the way a very high tide does. Tides are not the cause. A tsunami is also unlike the ordinary surface waves that wind makes. Those wind waves tend to roll up the beach in a circling motion. A quake happens when pieces of Earth's crust suddenly slip past each other. They slip along a fault. If the seafloor shifts up and down, the water above it shifts too. An enormous bulge of water forms. That bulge is a tsunami. Far from land, the wave is almost impossible to see. Compared with surface waves, it is very wide and very low. A map names pieces of Earth's crust. They are the North American Plate, the Eurasian Plate, the Philippine Plate, and the Arabian Plate. Also shown are the Indian Plate, the Pacific Plate, the Australian Plate, the African Plate, and the Antarctic Plate. A key marks land that stands above sea level. It marks faults. A star marks where the December 2004 tsunami began. The letter N shows north.

5A diagram shows one plate of Earth's crust pushing beneath another plate. Pressure builds where one plate sticks to the other. The land above bulges. An earthquake is that pressure letting go. People can picture it as a pop. The land then jumps. Water above the fault line surges. The water rises into a tsunami. Waves travel outward from the fault line. A map marks where the earthquake began. It labels India, the Indian Ocean, Indonesia, Australia, and Antarctica. Numbers on that map tell how many hours the 2004 tsunami needed to reach land. One question the map asks is how long the wave took to arrive in Australia. A tsunami can race as fast as a jet airplane. Its speed can be 200 to 500 miles in an hour. That equals 321 to 643 kilometers in an hour. As the wave spreads across thousands of miles, it does not lose its strength. Think of ripples moving over a pond. Crossing the Pacific, from one side to the other, can take less than one day.

6Shallow water near shore changes the wave. It grows much taller. It also loses speed. Before it arrives, the sea draws back. Then the sea rushes in past the usual shoreline. Water pours inland. It can run a long way up rivers and streams that meet the ocean. These waves often arrive as a group. People who watched the Indian Ocean tsunami said the opening wave was the smaller one. The wave after it was larger. Some people lived through the first wave. They stopped running. The bigger second wave caught them. A drawing shows a tsunami meeting the shore. The top of the wave moves faster than the bottom. Friction against the ocean floor holds the bottom back. The drawing marks the runup, the shore, the ocean, sea level, and the ocean floor. Where the danger is greatest The highest risk sits on low coasts in places where quakes are common. One famous belt of volcanoes is the Ring of Fire. It circles the whole Pacific Ocean. Volcanoes and frequent earthquakes go together. Both come from movement in Earth's crust. Indonesia is another place where the crust moves often. Nobody can name the exact hour of the next quake. Nobody can name the exact spot either. People can still judge when a region is overdue. A map labels North America, Asia, South America, the Pacific Ocean, Australia, and the Indian Ocean. It traces the Ring of Fire. N marks north.

7A picture shows a warning sign. Signs of this kind line western American shores. They tell people that a tsunami is a danger there. Systems that warn people No practical method can save buildings from a tsunami's ruin. An early warning can still save lives. A quake at sea usually leaves some time before the wave reaches land. Banda Aceh, in Indonesia, was not that lucky. Only a few minutes passed between the shaking and the wave. India was about three or four hours away. Sri Lanka was about that far in time as well. That gap would have been long enough to radio a warning ahead. Governments and scientists are building warning systems for later tsunamis in many parts of the world. A picture shows a buoy in the Pacific Ocean. More buoys like it will be set out. Scientists will use them to watch for tsunamis. The buoys will also help warn places that are at risk. America's Pacific shore already runs a system that warns of these waves. Seismographs along that coast pick up earthquakes. An Alaska quake of 6.8 brings a tsunami warning. In the western United States, the warning level is a quake of 7.5. Buoys fixed in place at sea can sense how fast a tsunami is moving. They can also sense which way it is going. They radio those facts back to shore. Seaside towns hear the news by radio. Loud sirens sound as well. Highway signs mark places where the risk is high. Those signs point out routes for leaving.

8How to stay alive People who live in a risk zone should remember these rules. Learn the safe routes for leaving. Make an emergency plan with your family. If a tsunami warning goes out, follow the order to leave. Do not spend time trying to save belongings. You might have hours. You might have only minutes. It depends on where the quake struck. When the ground shakes, go to higher ground at once. Everyone in the house should know to leave. Do not wait until you see the wave coming. Running from a tsunami that is already there should be the last choice. Go on foot. Cars can jam the roads very fast. A jam wastes minutes you cannot spare. Do not remain in a small building near the coast. Most houses cannot hold against a tsunami's force. Keep away from rivers that meet the coast. A tsunami can travel far inland by following a river channel. Remain in the safe place until officials say it is all clear. Wave number one is not always the tallest. A later wave can still be the one that finishes the danger. A picture shows an elephant clearing wreckage in Banda Aceh. The wreckage was left by the devastating tsunami of December 2004. A last word Quakes and tsunamis remind us how powerful nature is. The reminder can be frightening. People cannot stop these events. People can get ready for them. Knowing the right actions can save lives. So can a warning that arrives early.

9Words to know Buoys: floating objects held in place in water, including the ocean. Some send information from that place back to scientists. Richter scale: a measure from 1 to 10 of how strong an earthquake is. Sirens: machines that make a sharp, loud sound to warn people in an emergency. Devastating: bringing ruin. Tidal: having to do with tides. The pull of the Sun and the Moon raises tides on the ocean twice each day. Earthquake: the shaking of Earth where pieces of the crust meet. Evacuation: moving people out of a dangerous place. Tsunami: a huge sea wave, or a set of them, started by the earth moving under the ocean, as in a strong quake. Fault: a crack in Earth's crust. Movement happens along that crack. Magnitude: how great something is in size or in intensity. Topics in this book Africa. Major tsunamis. Alaska. Meteors. Areas at risk. The Pacific Coast. Buoys. The Pacific Ocean. Chile. The Richter scale. The death toll. The Ring of Fire. Earthquakes. Sri Lanka. Earth's crust. Surface waves. Faults. A survivor. Volcanoes and volcanic eruptions. Hawaii. A wall of water. India. Warnings. The Indian Ocean. Indonesia. Japan. A landslide.

101. Who Should Hold the North Pole?

1Tall ships work in the Arctic’s Beaufort Sea. Towers on those ships drill for oil. An introduction opens this book. Geography comes next. Then the book asks why the North Pole has value. Indigenous peoples of the Arctic have a part. Another part asks who wants the North Pole. A conclusion follows. A glossary explains important words. The words North Pole may bring one picture to mind. You may picture a cold, empty spot in the middle of nowhere. Cold is true. Remote is true. Empty is not. The North Pole and the land and sea around it hold many natural wonders. That wider area is the Arctic region. A hard question follows. Ownership is the hard question. One answer gives the treasures to separate countries. All people might share them. The planet itself might hold them. Several countries want pieces of the Arctic past their own borders. They are competing for those pieces. The grab for Arctic resources will touch the North Pole. The rest of Planet Earth will feel it too. Ice covers the sea around the North Pole. A viewer in outer space can see that ice.

2The North Pole sits in the Arctic Ocean. It is the northernmost place on Earth. Sea ice surrounds it. That ice forms the Arctic ice cap. Seasons change the size of the cap. Temperatures rise, and temperatures fall. Since 1981 the cap has been shrinking overall. Every ten years, the loss comes to 3.2 percent. Scientists have evidence for the cause. They point to climate change. Weather patterns on Earth change and then stay changed. That is what the phrase means. Five countries ring the North Pole. Norway is one of them. Russia is one of them. Canada is one of them. The United States is one of them. Greenland is one of them. Each one controls a band of sea. The band reaches 200 nautical miles out from the coast. That distance is 230 miles, or 370 kilometers. Inside the band, the country or region controls resource rights. Water can be used to make energy. Wind can be used too. Minerals are included. Fish are included. Past that boundary, the waters are international. Minerals lie on the seafloor out in the high seas. The International Seabed Authority writes the rules for taking them. People shorten that name to ISA. The ISA belongs to an agreement among countries. Under that agreement, international waters should help all people. They should not help only separate countries. Patterns in Earth’s climate have not stayed still. A full century holds that shift. Inside the latest twenty years, the hottest ones on record cluster. Warming is not equal in every place. Air around the globe is warmer by about two degrees. A century holds that rise. Scientists are nearly united on one important cause. Carbon dioxide in Earth’s atmosphere is that cause. Human actions make the gas. Factories burn coal for power. Cars use petroleum products. Carbon dioxide and other gases hold the Sun’s heat. The heat cannot escape into space. Scientists tie this warming to human activity for a clear reason. The climate is heating about ten times faster than in older warming periods that happened naturally. Effects differ from place to place. Some places will face droughts. They will also face extremely high temperatures. Rain will increase in other places. Hurricanes will increase there too. Coral reefs out in the sea will die. Coral cannot live in high temperatures. In the Arctic, glaciers are melting. Polar ice caps are melting. Sea levels are rising. Each September, scientists measure sea ice. They catch it at the lowest level of the year. A map can show the 2020 minimum in white. A dashed white line shows the average from 1981 to 2010. The yearly loss of ice is 31,000 square miles. South Carolina covers about the same area.

3The band of 200 nautical miles from a coastline has a name. It is an exclusive economic zone. People shorten that name to EEZ. Exclusive means not shared by others. Economic means tied to buying and selling. A zone is a marked area. A special purpose can set it apart. A set of rules can set it apart too. Some stretches of the Arctic Circle have no owner once those zones end. That is true at least for now. By early 2014, 165 countries had ratified an agreement. The European Union had ratified it too. Ratified means approved. A country that has approved the agreement then gets ten years. In that time it may file a request. The request is allowed if the country believes it deserves areas past its EEZ. If the request is approved, a bigger result follows. Every resource in the larger area belongs to that country. A country might want more territory for that reason. North of the Arctic Circle lies the Arctic region. Natural resources there are abundant. Petroleum is one resource people depend on most. Petroleum includes oil. It also includes natural gas. The supply sits under Earth’s surface. Reaching it is easier now than in the past. Melting of the Arctic ice cap is the reason. About 10 percent of oil used worldwide now comes from the Arctic region. It supplies 25 percent of the world’s natural gas. Experts think still more of both fuels may turn up later. The place would be near the North Pole. The time would be the future. The Environmental Protection Agency has warned about petroleum-based energy. It causes a lot of pollution. That pollution, they say, is what mainly drives climate change. A large share of climate scientists want it cut. They think countries must stop using petroleum-based energy at once. Even so, most energy people use still comes from goods made of petroleum. More than half of our energy comes from them. They are nonrenewable. That means they will run out someday. The day could arrive in forty to fifty years. Many countries are therefore scrambling for new petroleum supplies. Other energy sources could lower that dependence. Wind is one. Solar power is one. Electric power is one.

4Shipping routes are another promise of the Arctic. They sit beyond the natural resources. Warmer months are the only season for most of those paths. By then, sea ice has melted in large amounts. If melting continues, the open season could grow. A large part of the year might allow ships through. One recent voyage shows the change. A ship went from northern Russia to China in February. No ship had done that before. Getting natural resources in the Arctic is a dangerous business. Few other regions of the globe make the job this risky. It costs more too. The climate can defeat ordinary tools. Gear built for this place has to be used. In some cases it must still be invented. The gear has to work in extreme cold. It has to work in wet conditions. Moving materials to such a remote place costs a great deal. Moving people costs a great deal too. Workers in that remote place need higher wages. Accidents raise a further problem. Search-and-rescue stations may be far away. More lives may be lost. Equipment may suffer greater damage. The environment may suffer greater damage too. Spilled oil does not come up easily. A sea otter can end up coated in oil. Ordinary clean-up tools cannot handle an Arctic oil spill. Sea ice makes the job much harder than liquid water does. The U.S. Energy Information Administration supplied these points. Scientists name a further kind of value. Environmental groups name it too. The Arctic matters to humans. It also matters because of its natural environment. A wide variety of life lives there. Tundra vegetation is part of that life. Caribou are part of it. Polar bears are part of it. Whales are part of it. Seals are part of it. Taking more from the Arctic could throw the environment off in many ways. Extinction already threatens polar bears. Polar ice melt is the reason. Many scientists expect most polar bears to die out. The years they name run from 2050 to 2100. Drilling for petroleum worries scientists for another reason. Caribou populations could be hurt. Bird populations could be hurt. Roads make noise and other disruptions. Trucks do too. Power lines do too. Drilling does too. Migratory patterns might change. Mating patterns might change. Autumn tundra in Arctic Canada feeds a grazing caribou. Her calf feeds beside her.

5Indigenous peoples are about 10 percent of the people who live in the Arctic. Forty distinct Indigenous ethnic groups have homes there. The Saami are one group. Say that name SAH-mee. The Inuit are another group. Tribes, nations, and groups in the Arctic are not all the same. A likeness still joins them. Cultures and survival rest on Indigenous knowledge. That knowledge grew over thousands of years. People watched the Arctic’s unique environment. Traditions grew that reflect those surroundings. Inuit people, long ago and today, depend on wildlife. Caribou are part of that wildlife. Seals are part of it. Walruses are part of it. Whales are part of it. Every part of these animals is used. Bones are used. Teeth are used. Fat is used. Skins are used. The resources supply food. They supply clothing. They supply boats. They supply tools. Because daily life depends so deeply on the environment, climate change hurts these peoples in a special way. Melted ice makes hunting harder. The animals that matter to their way of life are harder to reach. Some Indigenous peoples risk hunger. Hunting supplies much of their food. Environmental change also makes water less safe to drink. Four countries have asked for territories larger than the ones they hold now. The four are Norway, Russia, Canada, and Greenland. The EEZ alone is not enough for them. Some claims reach the North Pole itself. Along the Arctic, Russia’s coast stretches about 4,300 miles. That is 7,000 kilometers. No other country on the Arctic Ocean has a longer coast. A small research ship went out from Russia in 2007. It dropped to the sea bottom. That bottom was at the North Pole. Soil samples came up. Water samples came up. They came from an underwater land feature. The samples came from the Lomonosov Ridge. Scientists wanted that ridge counted as part of Russia. They wanted Russia to own it. Any natural resources at that site would then be Russia’s. A wider seabed claim came from Russia in 2021. The added area was 705,000 square kilometers. The same ridge reaches Canada on the other side of the Arctic Ocean. Canada’s Arctic coast is the second longest. Canada says that underwater mountain ridge is part of its seabed. Denmark wants the ridge too. The reason is a historic relationship with Greenland.

6A map of the North Pole neighborhood uses color for depth. Bright blue means shallower water. Dark blue means deep water. The Lomonosov Ridge shows as a bright blue line. The North Pole sits just to the right of that line. The ridge is 1,110 miles long. That is 1,800 kilometers. Canada and the United States do not agree about the Beaufort Sea. That water lies north of western Canada. It also lies north of Alaska. Mineral rights sit inside all these arguments. Control of shipping routes sits there too. Russia wants more territory for military reasons as well. Norway may want that too. Other nations may want it. They worry about a future need to defend Arctic resources. They also want strong sites for military bases. A war between countries of the Eastern Hemisphere and the Western Hemisphere is the case they picture. Arctic routes would cut the travel distance. Military planes could reach targets sooner. Military ships could too. No decision has been made yet. Each country thinks its reasons for a larger territory are good ones. The arguments keep the countries at odds with one another. Another way to plan the changing Arctic might still be found. Earth’s axis has two ends. The South Pole is the far one. Extreme cold is true there too. An international agreement blocks ownership of Antarctica. It also blocks use of Antarctica’s resources. The continent is reserved for scientific research. It is reserved for peaceful purposes only. Military activity is not permitted. Should those same guidelines cover the Arctic region? Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station has a dome over it. The station is in Antarctica. The dome is 165 feet tall. That is 50 meters.

7Look ahead fifty years. Look ahead one hundred years. Should a single country hold the Arctic region, North Pole included? Some people say Indigenous groups deserve a larger place in these debates. Their Indigenous knowledge deserves that place too. Six Arctic Indigenous groups hold a special seat. The Arctic Council names them permanent participants. Nations and other groups are urged to work as partners. Arctic concerns are the shared subject. Solving those problems is the aim. Indigenous groups speak by way of the Arctic Council. Policies that affect the Arctic are part of that voice. Laws are part of it too. Countries that want a wider hold on the Arctic face serious choices. Peaceful cooperation is one path. Competition for control is another. Which path will win? Climate change is a threat. Arctic wildlife matters. Should those facts shape the choices? What choice should those Arctic countries make? A picture shows an Inuit woman cooking outdoors. The ground is tundra. Arctic Indigenous peoples depend on the environment for daily life. Their cultural traditions depend on it too. Petroleum is a natural liquid under the ground. Fuel is made from it. Many other goods are made from it too. Arctic describes the North Pole’s surroundings. The Arctic Ocean belongs to that area. Climate change is a weather shift that lasts, for the whole Earth or for one region. A remote spot is far away or cut off. Resources are useful supplies. People value them. Cooperation is joint work toward one shared aim. A route is a path from a starting point to another point. A dispute is an argument. Territory can be land or water that one state or country controls. A geographic area can carry the same name. Extinction is the end of a species, with no members left alive. International describes a matter that takes in two nations or more. Tundra is cold Arctic ground without trees. The soil stays frozen. Minerals are solid materials from nature. Living things are not their source.

102. Wild and Wacky World of Wigs

1People have cared a lot about hair through recorded history. From ancient Egypt to modern times, wigs have been part of that care. People have worn wigs for fashion and for social standing. Wigs made from human hair last the longest. They are also easier to cut and style than synthetic wigs.

2Wigs come in many styles. A full wig covers the top and sides of the head down to the neck. A toupee covers from the forehead to the crown and from ear to ear. The person's own hair shows at the back. Extensions are pieces of hair or fiber. Pins, clips, or glue hold them on. They make hair look fuller or longer. Double-sided tape can hold a toupee on the scalp. Wigs may be made of wool, goat hair, horsehair, straw, grasses, or nylon. For a long time, human hair looked the most natural. One wig often took hair from six to ten heads. Those wigs cost more.

3Wigs are shown in ancient Egyptian tomb art and sculpture. The oldest known wigs date to 1400 bc in Egypt. Egyptians wore wigs to look like their gods and to cover bald spots. A full head of hair meant strength and health, so they copied the gods' thick braided hair. Wigs were neck, shoulder, or waist length, all thick with curls and braids, and some had extensions set with beeswax. Kings wore human hair wigs with ivory and silver, the rich wore wool or goat hair, and the poor wore straw. Stylists cared for the royal wigs, and in the film Cleopatra each of Elizabeth Taylor's hairstyles needed three wigs. People in Asia rarely wore wigs in daily life, but wigs have been important in Japanese and Chinese theater for many centuries.

4Greek goddess hairstyles, such as Aphrodite's, may have influenced the wigs of Greek women. Wealthy people in the later empires of Greece and Rome also wore false hair. Noblewomen pinned up wigs with many braids and curls, and a more ornate style showed higher status. Wealthy Romans hid bald spots with wigs and favored blond and red hair. Some kept blond and red-haired enslaved people so they had hair for wigs. Some emperors wore wigs as disguises to learn what everyday people thought. Caesar (100 to 44 bc) brushed long hair over his scalp, then tried a potion of mice, horse teeth, and bear grease. Cleopatra, Egypt's last pharaoh, suggested that potion, but it failed, so a laurel wreath hid his baldness and stood for victory.

5From the end of the Roman Empire, wigs lost popularity for several centuries. In the early seventeenth century, King Louis XIII of France brought them back. At twenty-three he began to lose his hair and feared the court would respect him less. He wore wigs that looked like his natural hair, and noblemen copied him. Mainly men wore full wigs then, and some added extensions to make them fuller. Some women who were losing hair wore wigs, and women with full hair added extensions. Fancier court clothes brought fancier hair. Hair was built over a frame or a pillow. It was set with lard, or pig fat, and powdered. Some styles were three feet, or 0.91 meters, tall. Some of those styles held ships. Some styles stayed in place for months. A cartoon from 1778 showed them.

6Lard spoiled over time, and cockroaches, mice, and rats built nests in the hair. Women carried a long stick with a claw to scratch without disturbing the style. By the eighteenth century, people at Western European courts and in some professions wore wigs. Doctors, lawyers, judges, and church members often wore stiff, thick horsehair wigs, which cost less than human hair. United Kingdom judges and lawyers still wear court wigs. An eighteenth-century English court did too. A meeting at Westminster Abbey showed the same custom. Eighteenth-century toupees were curled and powdered but cooler and lighter than hot, heavy full wigs. By the 1850s many Europeans had stopped, seeing wigs as a rich luxury, and old wigs were sold as floor mops and polishing rags. The word bigwig, for an important person, was used in 1703 in English Spy, since the richest wore the biggest wigs, like judge Sir Edward Willes.

7In the twentieth century, better technology let people make wigs from nylon threads. Nylon looked like human hair, cost much less, and came in more colors. Today people wear wigs to look stylish or to change how they look. People who are bald or losing hair wear wigs to feel better about themselves. Clowns and actors may wear wigs as costumes. Styles change with fashion, but wigs have played an important role in history, so who knows the next great style? Some illnesses cause hair loss, and doctors may prescribe wigs that help patients feel positive and respond better to treatment. People donate long hair to groups like Locks of Love, which makes wigs for children who have lost their hair.

103. Wildlife Rescue

1If you see a wild animal in trouble, tell an adult right away. If you cannot find an adult you trust, look in the phone book under Wildlife Rescue or Animal Rescue. A baby bird may hop on the ground when its parents are not in sight. A rabbit may seem unable to hop, or a raccoon may sway as it walks. People with special training know what to do. They may leave a sick raccoon alone, help a rabbit, or care for a baby bird. They can teach you how to help, too. Topsy is a three-month-old female great horned owl who fell from her nest in a windstorm and is healing from neck and back injuries.

2People who help sick, injured, or orphaned wildlife are called wildlife rehabilitators, or rehabbers. Rehabilitate means to bring an animal back to good health. Rehabbers rescue animals, care for them as they heal, and return them to the wild when possible. They train to feed, house, and treat wild animals, and to handle them safely. Caretakers treat a sea turtle hurt on its right flipper. Lisa treats Tripod, a young javelina hit by a car. Farms, houses, and businesses can destroy wild homes and food. Cars, windows, poison, illegal hunting, litter, pollution, and animal attacks cause many injuries.

3Some rehabbers work with many mammals, birds, and reptiles, while others focus on owls, bats, or ocean animals. Many care for city animals such as squirrels, raccoons, and foxes. Some work with bears, mountain lions, and bobcats. A Florida state wildlife worker examines a panther kitten. People often start as unpaid volunteers and learn from trained rehabbers at homes, backyards, and centers. Most rehabbers are not paid and may buy food, medicine, and shelters themselves. They help because they care, and good care supports healthy habitats and protects people. A volunteer holds a baby red-tailed hawk with a broken leg from a fall while a rehabber removes a bandage.

4Do not touch the animal, and call an adult right away. The adult can call a trained rehabber, and you can watch safely and note where the animal hides. A box or laundry basket over a small injured animal can protect it from predators until help arrives. A rescuer gave water to a koala he saved from a fire. Stay away from a ground bat, a wild animal that seems tame, mouth foam, an animal that cannot move, or one that looks very angry. Stay away from a night animal active by day, especially a raccoon, skunk, opossum, fox, or bat. A wire cage may harm birds, wrong holding can injure animals, and human scent may make mammal parents reject a baby. Frightened animals may bite, kick, scratch, peck, or stab, and bats, coyotes, raccoons, foxes, and skunks may carry rabies, so exposed people need treatment right away.

5Many baby animals are taken when they are not in danger. A hopping baby bird may be a fledgling learning to fly, with parents watching nearby. Baby rabbits, seals, and fawns may rest quietly while their mothers eat nearby. Only trained people know if these babies need help, and taking them from their mother can hurt their chance to live. Unless baby animals are wounded, they do not need to be rescued. Taking wild animals home is against the law, and wild care needs much more training than care for dogs and cats. Veterinarians examine a red panda, and wild animals need trained care, a clean place, and the right medicine. Spring is the busiest rescue time, because babies are weak and may be orphaned if a car hits the mother or a hunter or predator kills the parents.

6At a center, the first step is a checkup and first aid. New animals are quarantined in their own cages so others do not get sick. Rehabbers keep notes on health, medicine, and feeding. Broken bones and diseases are treated by veterinarians first. Igor, a black vulture, was fed birdseed instead of meat, so his bones grew fragile and broke during rescue. Babies must stay warm in an incubator or with hot-water bottles, heating pads, or lightbulbs. As young animals grow stronger, an adult may teach them how to act and hunt. A hawk with a broken wing may start in a small dark cage, then practice in a flight cage before release.

7Most wild animals fear people, and too much stress can kill them. Workers keep noise low, cover cages with towels, and avoid staring, because staring can mean an animal is being hunted. A puppet can act as a mother so a young condor does not get used to humans. Baby animals imprint on their mothers, and rehabbers must not let baby birds imprint on people. Birds that think they are human may seek people, and raptors may become too dangerous to release. Meat-eaters need meat, so rehabbers use roadkill, frozen mice called mousecicles, or animals they raise, such as quail, mice, rats, and rabbits. A volunteer feeds a mouse to an adult red-tailed hawk that is almost blind. Store cow's milk can kill many babies, so animals need natural foods or they may starve later in the wild.

8Before release, rehabbers look for a place with food, water, and shelter that is safe from people. The animal must run, climb, or fly well, and it must see, hear, find food, avoid predators, and live with its own kind. This Tasmanian devil will be examined before it is released. First, the animal moves to an outdoor pen with others of its kind to learn the weather and see people less often. Slow release is often used for young animals, especially orphans. A pen is placed in a safe wild spot with the door open, and food is given until the animal can feed itself. Fast release is often used for animals rescued as adults, because they already know how to live in nature. They are taken near where they were found and let go, as when a rehabber lets a bald eagle fly.

9About half the animals at centers are too sick or hurt to be released. Many have lost limbs, beaks, wings, or eyesight. A bird with a wing that will not heal, or with only one eye, cannot fly or hunt well. If an animal can never survive and is in pain, euthanasia, a quick painless death, may end its suffering. This adult female great horned owl is not a quiet flyer because of a wing injury, so prey can hear her and she cannot be released. Natural disasters such as wildfires and hurricanes hurt animals, too. Terri Crisp rescued a Shetland pony in a 1986 California wildfire by coaxing it into a car. She helped sea otters and loons after the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill, rescued animals after Hurricane Andrew in 1992, and started Noah's Wish to train disaster volunteers.

10Many wild animals ran inland before the 2004 Asian tsunami hit land. Pets and farm animals did not do as well. Many people there depended on working farm animals. Large numbers were killed, and others were hurt or left without food. The Humane Society International and others help the animals and the people who care for them. A man carried his daughter and dog to safety after the tsunami in December 2004. Animals that cannot return, such as a bird of prey, may serve as ambassadors so children and adults learn to respect local wildlife and the land. You can help by respecting wildlife and calling a rehabber, and one call may let an animal grow up free and healthy.

11The book index lists topics such as imprinting, release, rabies, food, and training. It also lists the 2004 Asian tsunami, Terri Crisp, the Exxon Valdez oil spill, and Hurricane Andrew. Readers can explore more on the Internet with a search site such as Google. They can search wildlife rehabilitation, veterinarian, or Humane Society International. They can also try words from the book, the glossary, or the index.

104. Wings of Cloth and Air

1On October 13, 2016, five Brazilian pilots took off into the air. They flew with no motors or engines of any kind. Simple canopies made of fabric kept them in the air. After 32 kilometers, or 20 miles, two pilots could not find enough lift. The other three kept soaring across the Brazilian countryside. After nearly twelve hours, they had flown just over 564 kilometers, or 350 miles. Then they came down to the ground. These three pilots set a new world record for long-distance paragliding.

2People have long wished they could fly like birds. Airplanes are heavy and noisy, and sailplanes must be towed into the sky. Paragliders and hang gliders let flyers leave the ground by their own power. They can soar for hours using only the forces of nature. Hang gliders have solid frames and V-shaped wings. A paraglider is lighter, with a soft harness and a flexible, elliptical fabric wing. Cells in the wing trap air, risers join the harness to the lines, and the gear often weighs less than 16 kilograms. Pilots use a helmet, a radio, a vario to find rising air, and a reserve parachute if the wing collapses.

3When winds are strong, a pilot may use a reverse launch for more control of the wing. The pilot runs downhill, air fills the cells, and the wing rises like a kite. It lifts the pilot, who then sits back in the harness. To climb, the pilot finds air rising faster than gravity pulls down. Thermals are hot columns made by the Sun, and ridge lift is wind pushed up by hills, mountains, or dunes. Experienced pilots can climb thousands of meters, fly hundreds of kilometers, and stay up for hours. Handheld brakes change the wing shape, and a weight shift helps the pilot turn. Without rising air, the glider sinks, and the pilot brakes, lands, and runs to a stop.

4In 2013, Gavin McClurg flew 386 kilometers, or 240 miles, from Idaho to Montana. He crossed some of the largest ranges in the American West and set a U.S. distance record. He also sails, kite surfs, and kayaks, and he has flown high in Alaska. He calls paragliding the most intense and pleasurable adventure sport of all. People train with a licensed instructor for ten days to two weeks. Students learn setup, ground kiting, launch, flight, and landing, often after thirty-five supervised flights. Age rules differ by country, and anyone under eighteen needs a parent's permission. In a tandem flight, an instructor takes a passenger, so children and beginners can try the sport.

5Paragliding has risks, but safe habits can greatly reduce the chance of injury. Pilots check their gear and plan where they will launch and land. They must watch for obstacles such as power lines and other structures. Weather matters most, because winds that are too strong or too gusty are dangerous. Storm fronts and rough air can collapse a canopy, so a pilot may need a reserve parachute. If conditions are not right, pilots should choose not to fly. In training over a lake, pilots practice stalls, spins, and collapses, and a rescue boat can pick them up. Acro pilots do the deep spiral, the helicopter, and infinity tumbling, a series of forward somersaults.

6In 2001, Paragliding World Cup pilots filled the sky in Spain. In a race, pilots fly from a start through turn points to a finish as fast as they can. Photos or GPS can prove that each pilot passed each part of the course. Accuracy means landing closest to a bull's-eye, and open distance means the longest flight.
