The X-Alps calls itself the world's toughest adventure race. Every two years, pilots cross the Alps from north to south by paragliding and hiking only. A route may cover five or more countries and more than 1,000 kilometers, or 621 miles. Chrigel Maurer of Switzerland began at age nine and won the X-Alps eight times as of 2023.

7Coastal areas often have steady winds and ridges that pilots can soar. For people who do the sport, nothing beats the feeling of paragliding. More and more people are becoming pilots in countries around the world. Easy access is the key to the sport's growing popularity. It is the easiest, simplest, and most affordable way to reach the air. A person can learn the basics in a few days, and the gear fits in a light pack. Almost anyone can do it with proper training and equipment. With a little help from the weather, a pilot can stay up for hours, and people can finally fly like birds.

105. Yo-Yo Ma and His Cello

1High-school singers joined Yo-Yo Ma on stage in Chicago, Illinois, in 2012. His story begins long before that concert. The year 1955 and the city of Paris, France, mark his birth. Both of his parents had been born in China. Yo-Yo was seven when the family left France for the United States. Those early years set him on a path toward rare skill and wide respect as a musician. His mother was a singer. His father was a violinist. His father was a music professor too. His father had taught at a Chinese university before the family moved. His next teaching post was at a famous school of music in the city of Paris. Once they lived in New York City, his father started a group for young players called the Children's Orchestra Society. The society taught classical music to children. The account ahead follows that early start. It follows his rise as a young star. It follows trouble with his back. It follows three cultures that shaped him. It follows the Silk Road project. It closes with his own view that his success was an accident.

2From his earliest years, both parents pushed him toward music. A violin came into his hands when he was just three. By his own account, the sound he made on it was awful. Talent, he believed, was something he lacked. His older sister is Yeou-Cheng. Speakers say her name YOO-CHANG. Anger led him to break more than one violin, his sister says. The start was rough. He would soon show a large supply of talent. The violin lasted only a few months in his hands. Music did not stay out of his life for long. About a year later, the family went to hear music performed in the city of Paris. There he saw a huge instrument. It was a double bass. Learning that huge instrument became his wish. From end to end, a double bass measures about 6 feet. That height equals 1.8 meters. For a small child, his parents felt, that size was far too big. They agreed to let him play the next-largest stringed instrument instead. That instrument was the cello. Speakers say cello as CHEL-oh. A 1961 photo shows Yo-Yo at age six and Yeou-Cheng at age ten. The photo catches them playing for Denver Symphony members while a practice session paused.

3By the time Yo-Yo started cello, Yeou-Cheng was already strong on the violin. Their parents pushed both children to play hard music. Hard music was required, both inside that children's group and elsewhere. Three suites by Bach were in his memory by the age of five. Bach was a classical composer. Difficult music fills much of what Bach composed. Yeou-Cheng says their father used to tell her something about hard work. A hard job, their father told them, can be split into easier pieces. Those smaller parts were easier. Their mother, Yo-Yo says, pushed them to know every note deeply. Once the notes were that secure, worry about them faded. Feeling inside the music could then take their full attention. In 1962, Leonard Bernstein introduced a young player to an audience. Bernstein was America's most famous conductor. He presented a seven-year-old cellist from a Chinese family. The boy was playing old French music. Bernstein said the boy was playing for his new American compatriots. President John F. Kennedy was there, among the American listeners. A year after that concert, brother and sister performed together on a program called The Tonight Show. Most children that young are just starting a recorder, yet Ma was already well known. Fame already placed him among the leading cello players anywhere. Performance gifts belonged to his sister as well. She left music once it was obvious that her brother outshone everyone else at home. Medicine is her profession now. She also directs the children's music group her father began.

4The 2012 trip to Sweden included Jill Hornor. Emily Ma came too. So did Nicholas Ma. He received a Polar Music Prize there for his musical work. High school ended early for him, at age fifteen. A solo role opened for him with the Harvard Radcliffe Orchestra. That same year he played at a wedding for the first time. He still loves playing weddings. He attended Juilliard. Few schools of music anywhere rank above Juilliard. Soon, however, he dropped out. He switched to Harvard University. There he studied classics. He studied anthropology. He studied German literature. Ma kept studying music. He kept playing cello along with his other studies. He wanted more in his days than cello alone. His first college summer was spent performing at a music festival. He met Jill Hornor there and fell in love. She was a college sophomore. She ran the festival. Later college summers were spent at that same festival. He played music there. He got to know Jill. They later married. They had two children. Back trouble bothered Yo-Yo Ma while he was still young. As soon as he graduated, he had to stop playing the cello. An operation was what the doctors said he must have. His spine bent the wrong way, and the operation was meant to correct that curve. The surgery was risky. A failed operation might have ended his ability to play. Skipping the operation could have meant pain in his back for life. He thought the risk was worth taking. He went ahead with the surgery. The surgery was successful. For six months afterward, a cast covered his body. Walking about was impossible for him then. He was even less able to play the cello.

5Getting well again was extremely hard. As soon as the cast came off, people wanted Ma again at once. Concerts soon took him to countries across the globe. He often booked concerts years in advance. Age twenty-three was when his first album was made. Albums since that first one number more than seventy-five. His Grammy Awards number fifteen. Among classical players still living, few have sold more recordings. Makers finished his usual cello in the year 1733. It is worth 2.5 million dollars. In 1999, Ma left that cello in a taxi by accident. The driver returned it. After that, Ma recorded a message. Every taxi in New York played the message he had recorded. Riders were told to take their belongings when the ride ended. Ma has said that part of him is always charging ahead. He calls himself the curious kid. He says he is always going to the edge. Listeners in many countries count him among the finest players alive. Many events that history remembers have included his playing. He played for the hundredth birthday of the Statue of Liberty. He performed at a memorial when one year had passed since the 9/11 attacks. He took part when the Olympic Games of 2002 opened. He played at President Obama's inauguration. Classical music now treats him as a central person. The wider culture of the United States treats him as a central person too. In 2011, he performed with the Silk Road Ensemble. Dancer Charles Riley, known as Lil Buck, performed with them. Ma's Chinese heritage matters deeply to him. His French childhood matters too. His American adulthood matters as well. His playing carries the mark of all three cultures. Fresh ideas from unfamiliar cultures have filled his whole career. European music in the classical style was his starting point. He then branched into bluegrass. He branched into Argentine tango. He branched into jazz. He also played traditional music from China. He played traditional music from Japan. He played traditional music from Brazil. He says that people who open themselves to new cultures understand music better. They also understand people better. Older albums let him hear how his playing shifted. His music changed as he met new styles and took them in.

6Classical pieces fill most of the albums under his name. Other musical styles appear in his work as well. He made his own recordings of tunes from Cole Porter shows staged on Broadway during the 1930s. He recorded John Williams's themes for Star Wars. He recorded the theme for E.T. He recorded the theme for Jurassic Park. Film music of his own making fills several soundtracks. He has recorded with bluegrass musicians. He has recorded with jazz musicians. Groups of musicians in many countries have recorded with him. When the Winter Olympics of 2002 opened, he played beside the pop artist Sting. Those games were in Salt Lake City, Utah. During 2011 the Silk Road Ensemble joined him for a concert in New York's Central Park. In 1998 he launched the Silk Road Ensemble, because that mix of backgrounds had always mattered to his music. Players in the group come from twenty countries. Composers from those countries take part too. Together they build music from customs found in many lands. Traders once traveled a route known by that silk name. Centuries ago, that route crossed the continent of Asia. It united cultures across the whole continent. The Silk Road project is not only a musical ensemble. It is also a nonprofit group. Linking people across cultures, through music and through art, is the nonprofit's work. He still guides the nonprofit in seasons when he is not on stage with the players. He is its artistic director. He helps plan programs that teach music from around the world. He helps plan programs that perform that music.

7Many successful musicians give credit to hard work. Others give credit to natural talent. Why he became so widely loved as a musician is something Yo-Yo Ma says he cannot explain. He also does not know why other talented performers do not reach the same level. He once said, I'm an accident. Many separate pieces, he says, add up to the success he has had. Those things include his parents. They include his sister. They include various teachers. They include Paris. They include New York. They include his experience of performing at a young age. They include meeting his wife. They include raising his children. Change any single one of those pieces, he feels, and worldwide fame might never have arrived. Missing that huge double bass at age four, he believes, would have sent his life another way. In 2001, he prepared to perform in Germany. He has said that every day he makes an effort. He moves toward what he does not understand. He says this wandering leads to learning that happens by accident. That learning keeps shaping his life. Human societies, their cultures, and where they began are the subject of anthropology. People who perform as one company, whether they act or play music, form an ensemble. Classical can mean European music of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Symphonies and operas are examples of this older music of the West. Heritage is what one generation hands to the next, such as a way of living, a custom, or a trait. An inauguration is the ceremony that places a person into office by oath. Working side by side with others on one project is collaboration. Musicians in a large group who play at the same time form an orchestra. They often perform classical music on stringed instruments. Compatriots are people who live in the same country or are its citizens. A composer is a person who writes music. Short classical pieces gathered into a set are called suites. The pieces have different forms. A shared key is a common choice for those pieces. Players are expected to perform the pieces in one set order. A conductor directs an orchestra, a choir, or another ensemble. A group's shared ideas and its customs are its culture. The word can also point to one society that keeps ideas and customs of its own.

106. Young Players in a Big League

1British Columbia, a province of Canada, gave a totem pole to the Little League Organization. In 1951, a Little League team in British Columbia became one of the earliest outside the United States. The parts of this book come in this order. An introduction opens it. Next comes the start of baseball. Then comes the history of Little League Baseball. The path to the championship follows. The 2006 Little League World Series comes next. A closing section follows. A word list and an index finish the book. Introduction. An announcer describes Josh Lester taking a short lead. Lester is off first base. Japan leads by a score of 1 to 0. The inning is the third. Behind the bleachers, the sun is going down. Players begin to notice a bright glow. The glow comes from lights above the field. The grass has a smell unlike the smell at home. It is as if the field waited a full year for the kids to return. Cody Walker steps up to bat. The pitcher he faces is Go Matsumoto. Two fine pitching jobs have already been seen today. For the United States team, Kyle Carter has pitched at his best. A picture shows Cody Walker swinging the bat.

2Back home in June, the stands held only about 50 people. The month now is August. Almost 5,000 people fill the seats. Still more people watch on national television. Weekend practices helped bring the boys here. Stretching exercises helped too. The 2006 Little League World Series is the event these boys are in. The next pitch is on the way. Each game brings excitement. This game is the one for the championship. These players no longer stand for only their own team. They no longer stand for only their state. They now stand for the whole United States. The ball is gone from the park. No one doubts that it left the field. Cody Walker has just hit a home run. The home run scores two runs. The United States moves ahead, 2 to 1. The moment is huge for this young player. It is huge for his teammates too. That hit turned out to be the play that decided the game. Cody's team comes from Columbus, Georgia. The team went on to win the championship by a score of 2 to 1. Spectators saw players leap with joy. Families leaped too. Gloves sailed through the air. Caps sailed through the air. A scene like this returns every summer. The place is Williamsport, Pennsylvania. Some of the strongest youth teams in the world come to play. The event is the Little League World Series. The series is popular now. How did Little League Baseball arrive at this point? A picture shows teammates from Columbus, Georgia. They celebrate the 2006 Little League World Series championship.

3A picture shows an early professional game of the Washington Senators. The catcher reaches to tag the runner. Baseball Begins. Experts still do not share one date for the birth of baseball. Games with a ball and a stick go far back in many countries. Baseball resembles some older games. Cricket is one of those older games. Rounders is another. Both cricket and rounders come from Britain. Even so, baseball uses rules of its own. It uses equipment of its own. The printed word base-ball first showed up in 1744. That printing shows the game already existed then. During the Civil War, baseball became popular. The war took place in the mid-1800s. Soldiers treated the game as a diversion. They played during free time. A picture shows a crowd at the professional World Series of 1907. The clubs were the Detroit Tigers and the Chicago Cubs. Professional baseball got its start near the end of the Civil War. People organized the first major league in 1871. In 1876 that league became the National League. By the 1890s the game was so loved that it was called the national pastime of the United States. A second major league formed in 1901. The new league was the American League. The first World Series was played in 1903. That series pairs the champion of the American League with the champion of the National League. The Boston Americans defeated the Pittsburg Pirates. The teams needed eight games. That win put the Boston Americans first among baseball teams in the United States.

4History of Little League Baseball. Kids have been eager to play baseball ever since the game began. Before homes had television, many children hurried back from school. They crowded around a radio. They listened to the games of teams they loved. Sometimes a child pretended to be a star. One friend might be named Mickey Mantle for the game. The other child might claim to be Jackie Robinson. Farm families saved a piece of land for a baseball diamond. In cities, kids played stickball in the street. A broomstick served as the bat. A mailbox could be a base. A tree could be a base too. Empty lots were turned into fields. A win felt wonderful. Playing a sport beside friends felt just as important. The games were fun. They were not very well organized. A picture shows kids in a pickup baseball game. A picture shows Carl Stotz. Another picture shows Carl Stotz posing with players. The pose is from before a Little League World Series game in the early 1950s. Then Carl Stotz changed things. As a boy, Carl was left out by older kids. The older kids refused to let Carl play baseball. Grown up, he wanted every young boy to get a chance. The chance he wanted for them was baseball. He hoped a formal league would teach boys strong ideals. Sportsmanship was one ideal. Fair play was another. Teamwork was another. Kids used to knock on doors to ask friends out to play. On a team, they could play games that were scheduled. A coach could help them play better.

5Stotz formed Little League Baseball in 1939. He formed it in Williamsport, Pennsylvania. Only thirty players were in the league. Only three teams were in it. Local businesses sent donations. Stotz managed the Lycoming Dairy team. Two brothers were invited by Stotz to coach the other teams. One of those teams was Lundy Lumber. The other was Jumbo Pretzel. Each team had thirty dollars. That money bought uniforms for every player. Mothers sewed team names onto the uniforms. Gloves had to be shared. The only catcher's mask had to be shared too. Their field was a vacant lot. In 1947, twelve teams entered the first Little League tournament. Years later, that tournament grew into the World Series. The Maynard Midgets were from Williamsport. They beat Lock Haven Little League for the championship. About 2,000 fans showed up. They came even though August was hot. From that day, a great tradition began. A picture shows fans cheering at a tournament game in 1955. Word of the league traveled. Teams formed quickly across the country. Any boy aged 9 to 13 was allowed to play. Race did not bar a boy. Religion did not bar a boy. Color did not bar a boy. Until 1974, girls could not take part. A picture shows a Girls Little League team lined up for a photo. By 1948 the league had ninety-four teams. Little League teams today include about 2.7 million children. Some of those teams are in the United States. Others are in countries around the world.

6A picture shows the team from Chinese Taipei. The photo is from the mid-1980s. The team is preparing to play. The Path to the Championship. More than 100,000 teams now take part. They compete in separate divisions. Age is what places a player in a division. The best-known division is called Little League. Players on those teams are 11 and 12 years old. Each local team belongs to a district. A district gathers teams from one area. In June, each district picks its best players. Those players form an all-star team. An all-star team has no more than 14 players. Someone is chosen as the all-star coach. Someone is chosen as the manager. In July the all-star teams enter many tournaments. The tournaments cut down the number of competitors. A picture shows a batter on the Saudi Arabian team. He swings at a pitch. The swing comes during a win over Whalley Little League. That win was part of the 2006 World Series tournament. By August, the Little League Baseball Division is down to 16 teams. Those 16 have earned the trip to Howard J. Lamade Stadium. The stadium is in Williamsport. They come for the Little League World Series. Teams drop out game by game. At the end, two teams are left. One finalist comes from outside the United States. Little League play reaches 80 countries beyond the United States. The other finalist comes from the United States. Those two teams play a single game. The winner is the Little League World Series champion.

7The 2006 Little League World Series. Teams in the 2006 series traveled a long way to Williamsport. Saudi Arabia was one faraway source of a team. Russia was another. They arrived in late August. Kawaguchi City, Japan, took the International Championship. The team it beat was from Matamoros, Mexico. The final score was 3 to 0. Go Matsumoto was Japan's star. He hit a home run in that championship. He later entered as a relief pitcher. His team faced a bases-loaded jam. Nobody was out. His pitching ended the jam. A picture shows Matsumoto on the mound. In the United States Championship, Columbus, Georgia, won. The team that lost was from Beaverton, Oregon. The score of that game was 7 to 3. Georgia then had to carry the United States banner. Japan would be the opponent in the World Series Championship. Georgia did carry the banner. A picture shows Kyle Carter. He speaks with his catcher on the mound. Other teammates stand there with him. The opponent in the picture is Japan. People called Kyle Carter a pitching phenom. Eleven batters struck out against him. Only three hits came off his pitches. Matsumoto's pitching held the score close. Georgia still came out ahead. The series title went to the United States. It was the second straight year for a United States title. The result was a real feat. Before that final, Kawaguchi City had not lost.

8Successful Little Leaguers. Plenty of Little League World Series players later became pros. Some grew up to play baseball. Some grew up to play hockey. Some grew up to play football. Gary Sheffield has been named a Major League Baseball All-Star nine times. He played in the Little League World Series in 1980. Derek Bell was a teammate of Sheffield in that 1980 series. Bell later reached the Major League World Series. He played then for the Toronto Blue Jays. Chris Drury was in the Little League World Series in 1989. Stephane Matteau was in it in 1982. Pierre Turgeon was in it in 1982 as well. Ray Ferraro was in it in 1976. Later, all four reached the National Hockey League as hockey players. Brian Sipe was once the quarterback of the Cleveland Browns. He played in the Little League Baseball World Series in 1961. A picture shows Gary Sheffield. A picture shows Chris Drury. Wilson Alvarez is shown as a former pitcher in Major League Baseball. Sean Burroughs is shown as a third baseman. He played for the Tampa Bay Devil Rays. Jason Varitek is shown as a catcher for the Boston Red Sox. Conclusion. The Little League World Series is still growing. It is still changing. Tournament games in 2006 drew more than 300,000 people. Television carried those games across the United States. Josh Lester is the second baseman from Columbus, Georgia. He fielded the final out of the championship. Cheers broke out in the crowd. The chant was USA, USA. A picture shows Georgia celebrating the 2006 win for the USA.

9Georgia's players acted in true Little League spirit. They invited the Kawaguchi City players to join them. The two teams took a victory lap around the field together. After decades of growth, the goal of Little League is unchanged. The goal is a game that teaches useful principles. Players can carry those principles as good citizens of the world. An announcer then speaks to the crowd. Ladies, gentlemen, boys, and girls are asked to return next year. Another exciting Little League World Series will be waiting. Readers who want more can look up Little League Baseball. Little League Softball is part of that story too. World Series history can be looked up as well. That history includes records. It includes more famous players from earlier years. Organized means put into groups and guided by leaders. A competitor is a person or a team you play against. A pastime is a hobby or a free-time activity. Divisions are smaller groups inside one larger body. Scheduled means a starting time has been set. Eager means excited and full of interest. Spectators watch an event, yet they do not play in it. Equipment means the tools people use for work or for play. A feat is an action that amazes people, or a fine accomplishment. A tournament is a run of games or competitions. The run decides a final champion. A goal is a result someone hopes to reach. Index. The index names Chris Drury. It names the old printed word base-ball. It names Derek Bell. It names Kyle Carter. It names the championship. It names the Civil War. Under divisions it names the American League and Big League. It names Little League and Major League. It names the National League and Tee Ball. It names Japan. It names Josh Lester. It names Go Matsumoto. It names professional baseball. It names Gary Sheffield. It names stickball. It names Carl Stotz. It names the tournament. It names Cody Walker. It names the World Series.

107. Yusuf, Commander Who Honored the Faith

1A map of the Middle East from 1137 to 1193 shows the world of Salah al-Din. The Caspian Sea lies to the north. The Tigris River and the Euphrates River cross the land. The Mediterranean Sea borders the west. Aleppo, Tikrit, Baalbek, Damascus, Baghdad, Jaffa, Jerusalem, and Cairo are marked. Hattin is marked too. The Syrian Desert and the Arabian Desert cover wide dry ground. The Persian Gulf and the Red Sea meet these lands. Asia, Europe, Egypt, and Africa come together near this region. The book moves through his life in order. It begins with the Muslim world and his early years. It then tells how he rose to power and how he fought the Franks. It describes a fierce opponent and the time after the truce. It ends with the reasons people called him an honorable leader, plus a word list. Jerusalem ranks among the oldest cities on Earth. Salah al-Din lived in the Middle East almost nine hundred years ago. While he was young, this Muslim spent his days studying the faith. He followed its teachings with care. As an adult, he became a famous Muslim military leader. Few commanders of that faith are better known in history. The world of his birth was complex. Three religions hold Jerusalem holy. Those religions are Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. The city holds many buildings that followers treat as sacred. Other sacred sites fill the city as well. Muslims ruled Jerusalem for centuries. Muslims, Christians, and Jews all made the city their home. In 1099, Christians from Western Europe conquered Jerusalem. That conquest came decades before Salah al-Din was born. The conquerors had promised safety to the residents. Instead, they killed thousands. Salah al-Din would later take Jerusalem back for Muslims.

2His birth came in 1137, or possibly in 1138. His Muslim family lived in Tikrit, in Mesopotamia. Tikrit stood many miles from Jerusalem. His father was a wealthy chief. The family left Tikrit while Salah al-Din was still an infant. They traveled west to Aleppo, in northern Syria. Sultan Zengi led that area. The area belonged to a Muslim Turkic empire. When Salah al-Din turned six, his father went to work for Zengi. The family moved again. They lived in Baalbek and in Damascus. At age seven, Salah al-Din began school at a mosque. He learned the Five Pillars of Islam. The pillars are faith, prayer, fasting, alms, and pilgrimage. Alms means money or food for people in need. He studied science and math. He studied poetry and religion. He studied Muslim history and Muslim culture. He hoped to become a scholar. Training for war interested him less. The name Salah al-Din is a nickname given in honor. It names a man who brings honor to the faith. His given name was Yusuf. In the West, people often shorten that name to Saladin. Each pillar shapes daily Muslim life. To show faith, Muslims say that Allah alone is God. They say that Muhammad is his messenger. To pray, Muslims turn toward Mecca. They pray five times a day. The hours are dawn, noon, afternoon, evening, and night. Fasting belongs to the holy month of Ramadan. From first light until dark, Muslims do not eat. They do not drink during those hours either. Almsgiving is a duty. Muslims give a portion of their income to people in need. Pilgrimage means a journey to Mecca when the trip is possible. A Muslim makes that journey once in a lifetime. Muslim society puts great weight on a spiritual life. A bond with Allah, or God, matters deeply. Muslims learn to be fair and generous. They learn to be loving and merciful. They learn to be noble and humble. The year 1146 changed his life. Zengi died. Nur al-Din was Zengi's second son. Part of the father's kingdom passed into the hands of Nur al-Din. Damascus gained a new governor, and that governor was Salah al-Din's father. His uncle Shirkuh became a military general. At age fourteen, Salah al-Din joined the army of Nur al-Din. A few years later, he became the sultan's chief aide. Riches and power both belonged to the sultan. He still lived with honor and simplicity. He ruled in a fair way. He used his wealth to help his people. Nur al-Din became the model for how Salah al-Din would live.

3Salah al-Din went on learning. In his late twenties he traveled to Egypt with his uncle Shirkuh. They went on several military expeditions. The goal was to keep Egypt out of Frankish hands. The Franks were Christians from Western Europe. Egyptian politics were confused at that time. Shirkuh became the ruler of Egypt. He died nine weeks later. In 1169, Salah al-Din became the new ruler. He was thirty-one years old. He also took command of the Syrian troops in Egypt. He made a vow to free Jerusalem from the Franks. He vowed to free the land around the city as well. He improved the economy of Egypt. He built schools. Scholars from Europe and from Asia came to those schools. He ordered workers to build the Citadel of Salah al-Din in Egypt. The work ran from 1176 to 1184. The citadel was meant as protection from Christians of Western Europe. Crusades were wars called by popes. The popes asked Christians of Western Europe to fight in the Middle East. Their aim was to end Muslim control. They wanted the holy city of Jerusalem. They also wanted other lands already taken. In 1095, Pope Urban II gave the order that began the First Crusade. An enormous palace could have been his home. He chose a small and simple house. He gave away most of the palace riches. People gave him loyalty because he was strong. They also stayed loyal because he was gentle and generous. Nur al-Din died in 1174, only a few years later. Salah al-Din believed he was the best person to rule. He led an army into Syria. For nine years he fought the brothers of Nur al-Din. During that fight he ordered respectful treatment of enemies. His men did not loot villages. They did not burn villages. They did not chase an army that was pulling back. They did not treat captives without mercy. He was skilled at politics and at war. His fame grew for being firm, virtuous, and generous. By 1185 a wide region was under his control. That region included Syria, Palestine, and Egypt. It also included northern Mesopotamia. Northern Mesopotamia is the land between the Euphrates and the Tigris.

4In 1187, Salah al-Din opened a war on the Franks. The Franks had taken Jerusalem eighty-eight years earlier, in the First Crusade. He planned to drive the invaders out. He planned to win back the holy city. He planned to help the spread of Islam. At that time the Franks were fighting among themselves. They disagreed about who should rule Jerusalem. Raynald of Châtillon took control of trade routes. His name is said sha-tee-YOHN. He was hostile toward Muslims. Guy of Lusignan became king. His name is said loo-zee-NYON. Before Raynald, Arab traders and Frankish traders crossed one another's lands in peace. Once Raynald was in charge, he broke treaties with Salah al-Din. He attacked Muslim trade caravans. He raided towns along the coast. In early July 1187, the army of Salah al-Din captured the town of Tiberias. The army surrounded the castle. The Crusader force King Guy gathered numbered twenty thousand soldiers. He hoped to take Tiberias back. On the march, Salah al-Din's army forced Guy's troops against two hills. The hills are called the Horns of Hattin. The Franks fought hard. Salah al-Din's army still defeated them badly. King Guy was taken captive. Later, Salah al-Din chose to let Guy live. Raynald was killed. Raynald had broken the truce between Salah al-Din and the Crusaders. Salah al-Din then took the castle at Tiberias. A battle map for 1187 to 1192 shows Tyre, Acre, and Tiberias. It shows Hattin, the Sea of Galilee, and the Dead Sea. It shows Jerusalem, the Syrian Desert, the Arabian Desert, and the Mediterranean Sea. The Franks fled to the fortress at Tyre so they could rebuild their forces. Salah al-Din chose to deal with Tyre later. He turned to the task of retaking Jerusalem. His army attacked the holy city. Two weeks later, on October 2, 1187, the city was his. He had met his goal at last. Jerusalem was back under Muslim control. For the Crusaders, that loss was a crushing blow. The Christian capture of Jerusalem in 1099 had been cruel and vengeful. His capture was not like that. No Christian holy place was destroyed. Many reports said that few people were killed. After the capture, Christians could still visit their shrines in the city.

5Europe was shocked that Muslims now held Jerusalem. European leaders at once called for a Third Crusade. King Richard I of England raised an army to win the holy city back. People called him Richard the Lionheart. Other European kings raised armies too. Richard became the person who led that effort. Salah al-Din tried to capture Tyre, the strongest Frankish fortress still standing. He did not succeed. At about that same time, he set King Guy free. Guy and his supporters went to Acre, which Muslims controlled, and they attacked. By the time Salah al-Din reached Acre, Crusaders from Europe were already there. He could not defeat them. The fight at Acre lasted 638 days. Muslims held the inside of the fortress. Christians surrounded those Muslims. The army of Salah al-Din surrounded the Christians. Leaders of the Third Crusade arrived in the spring of 1191, and their armies came with them. Philip Augustus, from France, was the first leader to arrive. A few weeks after that landing, Richard the Lionheart reached the war. Richard was a brilliant commander. Only one month after he arrived, he forced the Muslims at Acre to surrender. During August 1191, Frankish troops under Richard moved south, with Jaffa as their aim. Archers serving Salah al-Din struck those troops without a pause. Long years of war had weakened the army of Salah al-Din. He could not stop Richard from taking cities on the coast. He moved his own army to Jerusalem instead. He worked to strengthen the city against Frankish troops. The Franks never launched that attack. Richard saw that his army was not large enough to take the holy city and hold it. His choice to turn away marked the end of the Third Crusade. On September 2, 1192, a brother of Salah al-Din spoke with Richard. They discussed the terms of a truce. Salah al-Din let the Franks keep the coast between Tyre and Jaffa. The rest of the land, including Jerusalem, would remain Muslim land. Christians would still be allowed to visit holy places. His honorable conduct won lasting respect from the Christian world. It also won lasting appreciation.

6After the truce was signed, Salah al-Din returned home to Damascus. Only six months later he died, on March 4, 1193. He was fifty-five. Money and luxury had never mattered much to him. He had given everything away, so nothing remained for a proper burial. His son later built a building in Damascus, and Salah al-Din was buried there. After his death, his family kept ruling Egypt and the nearby lands. That rule lasted until 1250. Then a different empire gained power. For centuries after that, Jerusalem stayed mostly under Muslim rule. The building that holds his tomb was raised in 1193. It was restored in 1898. A statue in Damascus today shows Salah al-Din on horseback. Damascus is in South Syria. While he lived, people respected his intelligence. They respected his skill in politics and in war. Muslims honored him for uniting them. They honored him for driving the Crusaders out of Jerusalem. The Crusaders were his enemies, yet they held him in high respect too. Across two continents, people knew him as fierce in battle. They also knew that he showed mercy. He lived during the Middle Ages in Europe. Some people call that same era an Islamic Golden Age. Empires kept changing. They fought one another without mercy. Even so, one of the most respected leaders of that age is remembered for the opposite. Just before death, he spoke to his oldest son. He said his greatness came from winning men's hearts through gentleness and kindness. During his life he showed what an honorable leader can be. He still offers that example today.

7These dates mark the life of Salah al-Din. In 1137 or 1138 he was born in Tikrit, in Mesopotamia. From 1152 to 1169 he served under Nur al-Din, the Syrian ruler. In 1169 he became ruler of Egypt and commander of Egypt's Syrian troops. In 1174 Nur al-Din died, and Salah al-Din began work to unite the Muslim states. In 1185 he succeeded in uniting those states. On July 4, 1187, the Battle of Hattin was fought. On October 2, 1187, he took Jerusalem again after a battle of two weeks. In 1189 the Third Crusade began. On July 12, 1191, the battle at Acre ended. On August 4, 1192, the Battle of Jaffa ended. On September 2, 1192, he and Richard the Lionheart agreed to a truce. On March 4, 1193, Salah al-Din died in Damascus. A shrine is a holy place, or a small space that holds religious objects. It may honor a person or a god. A caravan is a group of people traveling together, often with animals or vehicles. To loot is to steal during a war, a riot, or another destructive event. A sultan rules a Muslim country in a role much like a king or an emperor. A mosque is a place where Muslims worship. A truce is an agreement that both sides will stop fighting. A Muslim is a person who follows Islam. A vengeful person wants to hurt someone back for a wrong. A pilgrimage is a trip to a shrine or another special sacred place. A virtuous person shows goodness and a clear sense of right and wrong. To raid is to strike by surprise for a set purpose. Sacred means holy, or tied to a god, a religion, or a spiritual aim.
